AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS
Richard S. Krause
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Progressive, incurable disease of adults
r Neurodegenerative disease of the motor system at
all levels
r Some patients have associated dementia
r Manifestations:
– Muscle weakness
– Wasting
– Fasciculations
– Babinski sign
– Hyperreflexia
r Variants with predominately upper or lower motor
neuron manifestations also occur
r May begin with bulbar symptoms of dysphagia and
dysarthria
r Also known as “Lou Gehrig Disease” after the
famous baseball player who was affected
r Eventually leads to respiratory compromise
secondary to weakness of diaphragm and other
muscles of respiration
r 80% of cases begin between ages 40 and 70 yr
r Death (usually from respiratory paralysis) typically
occurs within 3–5 yr of the diagnosis
r 50% die within 3 yr
r ∼10% ALS patients live 10 yr or more
r Males > females
ETIOLOGYr Etiology of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is
unknown
r ∼10% of affected patients have another affected
family member
r Cigarette smoking and heavy metal exposure may
be risk factors
r There is a disease cluster in the western Pacific
r Pathologically, there is loss of both upper and lower
motor neuron cells
r Predilection for the motor system and sparing of
other neurons
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Asymmetric limb weakness is the most common
presentation of ALS (80%)
r May begin in either the arms (cervical onset) or the
legs (lumbar onset):
– Later all limbs are affected
r Bulbar ALS:
– Usually presents with dysarthria or dysphagia
– 2nd most common presentation
r Both lower motor neuron (weakness and wasting
with fasciculation) and upper motor neuron signs
(Babinski sign with hyperreflexia) occur
r Respiratory muscles and the vocal cords are affected
late
r Muscle fasciculation is common, but may not be
apparent to the patient
r Extraocular muscles, sphincters, cognition, and
sensation are spared
Historyr Most ED patients with ALS will present with an
established diagnosis
r History should focus on clues regarding acute
medical issues and functional decline
r When ALS is suspected due to a complaint of
“weakness” consider that this occurs with many
illnesses including:
– Pulmonary disease
– Cardiac disease
– Anemia
– Endocrine disorders
– Toxidromes
– Diseases of muscles or joints
– Spinal cord abnormalities
– Depression
r Differentiate true weakness from: Shortness of
breath, chest pain, joint pain, fatigue, poor exercise
tolerance, etc.
r True weakness often leads to complaints of inability
to perform specific tasks:
– Bulbar palsy:
◦Facial weakness
◦Weakness and fasciculation of tongue
◦Dysarthria
– Cervical onset ALS:
◦Difficulty with washing hair, using comb
◦Impaired pincer grip
– Lumbar onset ALS:
◦Frequent trips secondary to foot drop
◦Difficulty walking up stairs
Physical Examr A detailed and thorough neurological exam is the
key to diagnosis but is not typically performed in the
ED
r Upper motor neuron disease causes slow
uncoordinated movements and stiffness
r Lower motor neuron disease causes weakness
accompanied by atrophy and muscle cramps are
common
r Common findings:
– Brisk reflexes
– Fasciculations
– Muscle wasting
r Exam should focus on excluding or confirming other
conditions
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Previously undiagnosed ALS:
– Diagnosis of ALS is clinical and rarely made in the
ED:
◦Recognition of the possibility of this disease is
sufficient and mandates referral for workup
– If ALS is suspected, forced vital capacity (FVC)
should be performed
r Known ALS patient:
– Patients with known disease and progressive
symptoms:
◦Evaluate potentially treatable complications
with lab and imaging studies
– FVC is a sensitive indicator of respiratory muscle
weakness:
◦FVC <50% of predicted is considered a sign of
advanced disease
◦FVC <50% usually requires ventilatory support
◦Start with noninvasive positive pressure
ventilation when possible
◦Compare with the patient’s previous baseline
– CXR may reveal aspiration or pneumonia or
comorbid conditions such as CHF
– Pulse oximetry and blood gas analysis aid in the
diagnosis of respiratory failure
– Electrolytes and other blood chemistry tests may
reveal a treatable cause of increasing weakness
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr In cases of undifferentiated weakness, consider CPK
measurement along with blood chemistry:
– Elevated CPK is associated with myopathy
r Electrolyte abnormalities such as hypokalemia,
hypercalcemia, etc. may cause generalized
weakness but this is typically in association with
other signs and symptoms
r CBC, UA may be indicated to look for source of
infection
Imaging
Cervical spine, other skeletal radiography, or head CT
may be needed in case of falls (common in ALS) or to
rule out other conditions
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Check FVC
r Electromyography (EMG) may help confirm the
diagnosis (not usually an ED test)

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Cervical cord compression:
– Similar symptoms but usually acute onset with
pain and sensory changes
– Spinal MRI or myelography for diagnosis
r Thyrotoxicosis may mimic ALS:
– Usually marked systemic symptoms
r Heavy metal poisoning (lead, mercury, arsenic)
r Syphilis and Lyme disease
r Lymphoma may have an associated lower motor
neuron syndrome, which mimics ALS
r Bulbar ALS:
– Esophageal cancer
– Myasthenia gravis
TREATMENT
r There is no specific therapy for ALS
r The drug riluzole, a glutamate release inhibitor, has
been shown to extend survival in ALS patients for an
average of a few months
r Treatment issues in the ED revolve around
symptomatic therapy and identification and
treatment of complications
PRE-HOSPITAL
Controversies:
r Many patients will have advanced directives:
– Unless immediate intervention is essential,
intubation should be avoided until directives have
been ascertained
– Noninvasive means of ventilatory support may be
tried first
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Respiratory insufficiency or failure:
– Ascertain any advanced directives
– Noninvasive ventilatory support
– Intubation as indicated
r Weaning off the ventilator is very difficult:
– Average survival after institution of ventilation is
19 mo
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Sedation and pain control as indicated:
– Joint pain may respond to NSAIDs
r Insomnia from pressure pain (owing to immobility)
may respond to diphenhydramine or amitriptyline
– Insomnia may also be treated with
benzodiazepines
r Aspiration or drooling may be treated with
amitriptyline, atropine, or hyoscyamine (dries
secretions)
r Muscle cramps may respond to baclofen or
tizanidine
r Constipation is related to immobility and diet:
– Treated with laxatives, stool softeners, and dietary
changes
MEDICATIONr Amitriptyline: 25–100 mg PO QHS
r Atropine: 0.4 mg PO q4–6h
r Baclofen: 10–25 mg PO TID
r Diphenhydramine: 25–50 mg PO nightly at bedtime
r Tizanidine 2–4 mg PO BID

DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Need for respiratory support
r Dehydration
r Unable to be cared for at home owing to
progression of illness
r Complications (e.g., infection) or other diagnosis
that requires admission
Discharge Criteriar Suspected ALS: Refer for outpatient evaluation if
general condition permits and other serious
conditions requiring admission are ruled out
r Complication of known ALS: Discharge if outpatient
treatment available and stable respiratory status
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
If considering diagnosis of ALS, prompt follow-up with
a neurologist should be arranged
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r ALS is a progressive neurodegenerative disease
affecting all components of the motor system
r Many patients with ALS have advanced
directives—inquire prior to any aggressive
intervention
r FVC <50% usually requires ventilatory support.

management of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
(MALS)–revised report of an EFNS task force. Eur J
Neurol. 2012;19:360–375.

DESCRIPTIONr Hard stool passes and “cuts” anoderm

– Anal cancer
– Leukemia
– Syphilis

r Sharp, cutting, throbbing or burning pain with

Careful rectal exam

Lab
Hematocrit if severe bleeding by history
Imaging
CT pelvis:
r To exclude anal rectal abscess/tumor if palpable
mass on rectal exam
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Crohn’s disease
r Chronic ulcerative colitis
r Anorectal carcinoma
r Perirectal abscess
r Thrombosed hemorrhoid
r Sexual abuse
r TB
r Syphilis
r Lymphoma
r Leukemia
r Previous anal surgery

Establish IV access for patients with significant rectal
bleeding.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Administer pain medications for patients with
significant pain.

– Acetaminophen

◦Diazepam

ANAPHYLAXIS
Sean-Xavier Neath
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr An acute, widely distributed form of shock that
occurs within minutes of exposure to antigen in a
sensitized individual
r ∼500–1,000 deaths are attributed annually in the
US to anaphylaxis. There are∼10,000 ER visits per
month for anaphylaxis in the US
r Involves release of bioactive molecules such as
histamine, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins from
inflammatory cells:
– Mediator release results in increased vascular
permeability, vasodilation, smooth-muscle
contractions, and increased epithelial secretion.
– Physiologically, this is manifested in a decrease in
total peripheral resistance, venous return, and
cardiac output, as well as intravascular volume
depletion.
ETIOLOGYr IgE mediated:
– Antibiotics, particularly penicillin family
– Venoms, especially bee and wasp
– Latex
– Vaccines
– Foodstuffs (shellfish, soybeans, peanuts, tree nuts,
wheat, milk, eggs, nitrates/nitrites)
– Monoclonal antibody therapeutics
r Non-IgE mediated:
– Iodine contrast media
– Opiates
– Vancomycin
Pediatric Considerations
In children, foods are an important trigger for
IgE-mediated anaphylaxis:
r Milk, egg, wheat, and soy (MEWS) are the most
common food allergens.
r Peanut allergies are increasingly common and can
be more potent; children can develop anaphylaxis
from residual peanut in a candy bar.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Symptoms begin within seconds to minutes after
contact with an offending antigen.
r Anaphylactic reactions almost always involve the
skin or mucous membranes. >90% of patients have
some combination of urticaria, erythema, pruritus,
or angioedema.
r Some patients may have an initial sensation of
impending doom followed by more clearly definable
symptomatology:
– Respiratory: From sneezing and nasal congestion
to frank bronchospasm and laryngeal edema
– Cardiovascular: Hypotension, dysrhythmias,
myocardial ischemia
– Gastrointestinal: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea
– Ocular: Eye itching and tearing, conjunctival
injection
– Hematologic: Activation of intrinsic coagulation
pathway sometimes leading to disseminated
intravascular coagulation, thrombocytopenia
– Neurologic: Seizures
Historyr Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis.
r A brief history should include previous history of
allergy or anaphylaxis, as well as exposure to
potential new triggers.
Physical Examr Usually will include alterations in a combination of
any 2 or more of the following systems: Cutaneous,
respiratory, gastrointestinal, or cardiovascular
system
r Hypotension or airway compromise is not always
present at onset.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Diagnosis is made based on clinical symptoms.
r It is important not to underestimate the potential
severity of an allergic reaction in its early stages.
r ECG should be done in patients with previous
cardiac history or ischemic symptoms; consider
routinely in the elderly.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
The diagnosis of anaphylaxis is made on clinical
grounds; laboratory tests are usually not useful in
aiding diagnosis in the acute setting. Tryptase levels
remain elevated after an attack and can be useful for
later confirmation of a suspected anaphylactic
episode.
Imaging
Hyperinflation can be seen on CXR.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Pulmonary embolism
r Acute MI
r Airway obstruction
r Asthma
r Tension pneumothorax
r NSAID reaction
r Vasovagal collapse
r Hereditary angioedema
r Serum sickness
r Systemic mastocytosis
r Foreign body aspiration
r Hypoglycemia
r Pheochromocytoma
r Carcinoid syndrome
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr IV access, O2, cardiac and pulse oximetry monitoring
r Early intubation based on the initial progression of
disease and response to treatment:
– Laryngeal edema and spasm can progress rapidly.
– Laryngeal edema can be managed with racemic
epinephrine prior to intubation.
r IM epinephrine can be administered en route even
prior to establishment of an IV .
ALERT
Note that current guidelines advocate the use of IM
over SC epinephrine
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs
r Assure adequate ventilation
r Airway management:
– Orotracheal intubation is the airway technique of
choice.
– If laryngeal edema, spasm, or soft tissue swelling
present; consider using advanced airway adjuncts
when available.
– Consider blind nasotracheal intubation if soft
tissue swelling prohibits an oral approach and
there is absence of stridor.
– Transtracheal jet insufflation or cricothyrotomy
may be necessary to control the airway.
r Epinephrine IM/IV or endotracheal administration:
– Direct injection into the venous plexus at the base
of the tongue is an option.
r Volume resuscitation with crystalloids or colloids

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Reduction below normal in the mass of RBCs
r Measured by 1 or more of the major RBC
components:
– Hemoglobin (Hgb): Concentration of the major
oxygen-carrying component in whole blood
– Hematocrit (Hct): Percent volume of whole blood
occupied by intact RBCs
– RBC count: RBCs contained in a volume of whole
blood
r Adult female: Hgb <12 g/dL or Hct <37%
r Adult male: Hgb <14 g/dL or Hct <42%
r Normal blood count values depend on age:
– Birth: Hgb 16.5, Hct 51
– 1 yr: Hgb 12, Hct 36
– 6 yr: Hgb 12.5, Hct 37
– Adult male: Hgb 14, Hct 42
– Adult female: Hgb 12, Hct 37
r Hgb/Hct depend on oxygen pressure:
– Increased in neonates and people living above
4,000 ft
r Hgb, Hct, and RBC count are concentrations:
– Dependent on RBC mass and plasma volume
– Values decrease if RBC mass decreases or plasma
volume increases.
r Anemia is an indication of an underlying disorder or
deficiency.
ETIOLOGYr Never a normal variant:
– May be the first manifestation of a systemic
disorder
– Always seek a cause.
r Excessive blood loss (most common cause):
– Trauma
– GI bleed
– Menstruation
r Hemolysis (increased RBC destruction, RBC lifespan
<100 days):
– Hypersplenism
– Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
– Mechanical trauma (prosthetic heart valves,
vasculitis, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
[TTP], hemolytic uremic syndrome [HUS], or
disseminated intravascular coagulation [DIC])
– Toxins
– Infections (malaria, babesiosis)
– Membrane abnormalities
– Intracellular RBC abnormalities (G6PD, sickle cell
anemia, or thalassemia)
r Decreased RBC synthesis:
– Classified by measurement of RBC size
– Hypochromic/microcytic:
◦Iron deficiency
◦Thalassemia
◦Sideroblastic
◦Chronic disease
– Normochromic/macrocytic:
◦Hypothyroidism
◦Folate deficiency
◦Vitamin B12 deficiency
◦Liver disease
◦Myelodysplasia
◦Certain leukemias
– Normochromic/normocytic:
◦Aplastic anemia
◦Chronic renal failure
◦Malignancy
◦Adrenal insufficiency
◦Hyperparathyroidism
◦Alcohol abuse
◦Acute blood loss

SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Depends on:
r Rapidity of onset:
– Hypovolemia if acute
– Asymptomatic if mild and chronic

r Severity and type of anemia

r Decreased exercise intolerance
r Shortness of breath
r Dyspnea on exertion
r Chest pain/angina
r Syncope
r Blood in stool/tarry black stools
r Irregular or heavy menses
r Easy bruising or history of excessive bleeding
Physical Examr Cardiovascular:
– Tachycardia, cardiomegaly, or murmurs
– Postural hypotension
r Dermatologic:
– Skin:
◦Cool
◦Pallor
◦Jaundice
◦Purpura
◦Telangiectasia
◦Petechiae
◦Ecchymosis
– Spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia)
r Neurologic:
– Neuropathy
– Altered mental status
r Bone (especially sternal) or joint pain (sickle cell
disease)
r Hepatomegaly, splenomegaly
r Lymphadenopathy
r Findings reflect underlying disease

r Determine if:

– Increased RBC destruction
– Bone marrow suppression
– Iron deficient

– Depends on severity

– RBC indices:
◦Mean corpuscular volume (MCV; normal:
80–100 μm3)
◦Mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH; normal:
27–34 pg/cell)
◦Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration
(MCHC; normal: 33–36%)

◦Thrombocytosis suggests:

ANGIOEDEMA
Sean-Xavier Neath
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Nonpruritic, well-demarcated, nonpitting edema of
the dermis
r Due to the release of inflammatory mediators that
cause dilation and increased permeability of
capillaries and venules:
– Mast cell mediated
– Kinin related from the generation of bradykinin
and complement-derived mediators
r Similar in pathologic basis to urticaria except that
affected tissue lies deeper:
– Urticaria affects superficial tissue and causes
irritation to mast cells and nerves in the epidermis
leading to intense itching.
– Angioedema occurs in deeper layers, which have
fewer mast cells and nerves, therefore causing less
itching.
– Angioedema can affect tissues other than the
skin, for example, the gut.
– Angioedema may be seen in a mixed picture along
with urticaria
r Hereditary and acquired etiologies are due to
deficiencies in the quantity and/or function of
C1-INH rather than classic hypersensitivity reactions
r Hereditary angioedema (HAE):
– An autosomal dominant disorder caused by a
deficiency of C1-INH
– The prevalence of HAE is estimated to range from
1:10,000 to 1:150,000.
– C1-INH has a regulatory role in the contact,
fibrinolytic, and coagulation pathways.
– Deficiency results in unregulated activity of the
vasoactive mediators bradykinin, kallikrein, and
plasmin.
– More than 100 mutations of the C1-INH gene
have been reported.
– Type 1: Decreased expression of C1-INH
– Type 2: Normal plasma levels of C1-INH but the
protein is dysfunctional
– Type 3: Mutation in coagulation factor XII
resulting in increased kinin production:
◦Symptoms increased by estrogen-containing
medications
– Episodes occur in all 3 types when inflammation,
trauma, or other factors lead to depletion of
C1-INH.
r Acquired angioedema:
– Normal quantities and function of C1-INH
– Type 1 is associated with lymphoproliferative
diseases and caused by consumption of the
C1-INH protein by malignant cells.
– Type 2 is autoimmune caused by circulating
antibodies that inactivate C1-INH.
r ACE inhibitor–induced angioedema:
– Accounts for 2030% of all angioedema cases
presenting to ER reported in 0.1–2.2% of patients
taking ACE inhibitors
– Usually occurs during the 1st mo of taking the
medication, however the 1st event may occur
spontaneously after many years.
ETIOLOGYr Kinin-related etiologies:
– HAE
– Acquired angioedema:
◦Lymphoproliferative
◦Autoimmune
– ACE inhibitor induced
r Mast cell–mediated etiologies:
– Food allergies:
◦Additives
◦Nuts
◦Eggs/milk
◦Shellfish
◦Soy/wheat
– Drug allergies:
◦Aspirin
◦NSAID
◦Antihypertensives
◦Narcotics
◦Oral contraceptives
– Insect stings
– Physically induced:
◦Cold/heat
◦Exercise/trauma/vibrations
◦Stress
◦UV light
r Hypereosinophilic syndromes such as Gleich
syndrome
r Thyroid autoimmune disease
r Idiopathic recurrent AE
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr A family history or history of recurrent episodes can
be useful in the diagnosis. Use of culprit foodstuffs
or medications, especially ACEIs should increase
index of suspicion
r Abdominal pain associated with nausea, vomiting,
and diarrhea
r Attacks of HAE are not associated with hives or
itching
r Emotional stress or physical trauma can trigger
attacks.
Physical Examr The lesions of angioedema are large, swollen, and
nonpitting wheals.
r The eyelids and lips are frequently involved.
r Involvement of the pharynx and larynx may cause
airway obstruction.
r Lesions are often asymmetric and do not typically
involve gravitationally dependent areas
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Diagnosis is made of clinical grounds based on the
presentation of large nonpitting, nonpruritic wheals.
r A family history need not be present: 25% of HAE
patients have a new mutation and may not have a
positive family history.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC with differential, ESR, ANA, rheumatoid factor,
C4 and C3 levels.
r Skin biopsy if an urticarial lesion is accessible
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Measurement of C1-INH levels (not routinely available
in EDs):
r Patients affected with HAE type 1 have very low
levels; carriers will have half-normal levels.
r C4 and C2 levels are low during attacks in both
hereditary and acquired forms.

– SVC syndrome
– Right heart failure
– Constrictive pericarditis
– Renal failure
– Nephrotic syndrome
r Allergic contact dermatitis
r Blepharochalasis
r Facial cellulitis
r Facial lymphedema
r Edema secondary to autoimmune disorders:
– Dermatomyositis
– Lupus
– Polymyositis
–S j¨ogren syndrome
r Hypothyroidism

Recurrent angioedema presenting around puberty
should raise suspicion of HAE.

PRE-HOSPITALr Establish IV access
r Early intubation may be necessary due to the rapid
progression of laryngeal swelling.
r Administration of H1 blocker when available
r Epinephrine to be considered for laryngeal edema
especially if itching or other signs of a mast cell
etiology with histamine release is suspected.

are the primary goals of emergency treatment.

but may be difficult because of laryngeal edema,
spasm, or soft-tissue swelling.

gum elastic bougie to assist in securing
endotracheal tube placement.
– Blind nasotracheal intubation if soft tissue
swelling prohibits an oral approach
– Transtracheal jet insufflation or cricothyrotomy
may be necessary to control the airway.
r Epinephrine, antihistamines, and steroids in
obstructive airway swelling, although patient
response can be variable.

hypersensitivity reaction:
– Treat similarly to an allergic reaction with H1 and
H2 blockers along with corticosteroids.
– Epinephrine should be used in refractory cases
where the benefits outweigh the risks.
– For abdominal attacks consider the addition of
parenteral pain relief, antiemetics, and IV fluid
replacement.
r HAE and acquired angioedema:
– C1-INH

alternative to C1-INH.
– The kallikrein inhibitor ecallantide (Kalbitor) was
approved in 2009 for the treatment of acute
attacks of HAE.
– Tranexamic acid (Cyklokapron), an antifibrinolytic
agent, is not as effective for acute attacks and is
used primarily in prevention.

r C1 inhibition has been standard therapy in Europe
for many years; however, the US FDA has only
recently been approving these medications for use
in the US, therefore clinician and pharmacist
recognition of the utility of these drugs may be
limited.
r Therapy with FFP (as a source of nonpurified
C1-HN) is advised with caution as it may
paradoxically worsen some attacks due to its high
concentration of complement components.
r Attenuated androgens, such as the anabolic
steroids and gonadotropin inhibitor danazol, are
used in the long-term prophylactic treatment.
They may not have any effect for 24–48 hr in the
acute setting.
r Angioedema associated with ACE inhibitors
occurs in 0.1–0.2% of cases and requires
immediate withdrawal of the ACE inhibitor. ACE
inhibitor–related angioedema usually occurs
within a week after starting ACE inhibitor therapy,
but may occur much later.

General principles of pharmacologic treatment are
based on suspected underlying cause:

ANKLE FRACTURE/DISLOCATION
Sarah V. Espinoza rLeslie C. Oyama
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Common mechanisms and injury patterns of the ankle:
r Mechanism of injury:
– Inversion injury: Lateral ankle distraction and
medial ankle compression
◦Avulsion fracture of the lateral malleolus
◦Oblique fracture of the medial malleolus
– Eversion injury: Medial ankle distraction and
lateral ankle compression
◦Avulsion fracture of medial malleolus
◦Oblique fracture of the fibula
– External rotation injury:
◦Disruption of the tibiofibular syndesmosis, or a
fibular fracture above the plafond
◦Anterior or posterior tibial fracture with
separation of the distal tibia and fibula
(unstable fracture)
– Inversion and external rotation (Maisonneuve
fracture):
◦Medial malleolus avulsion fracture or deltoid
ligament tear
◦Disruption of the tibiofibular syndesmosis
◦Oblique fracture of the proximal fibula
– Inversion and dorsiflexion (snowboarders’
fracture):
◦Fracture of the lateral process of the talus
r Epidemiology
– Most ankle fractures are malleolar
– Common in young male and 50–70 yr old female
– Associated with cigarette use and high BMI
Pediatric Considerations
r Ankle fractures in children often involve the physis
(growth plate):
– May result in angular deformity from growth plate
injury
– Associated with sports requiring sudden changes
in direction and obese children
– In children <10 yr old, growth plate is weaker
than epiphysis
r Tillaux fracture: Salter–Harris type III injury of the
anterolateral tibial epiphysis external rotation of the
foot
r Triplane fracture: Uncommon fracture of distal tibia
with fracture lines in 3 distinct planes (coronal,
transverse, sagittal)
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr History of trauma
r Local ankle pain, swelling, deformity
r Inability to bear weight
r Soft tissue injury, swelling, ecchymosis, skin tenting,
skin blanching
r Neurovascular compromise:
– Diminished capillary refill
– Diminished posterior tibialis (PT) or dorsalis pedis
(DP) pulses
r Limited range of motion
Historyr Discover the position of the ankle at the time of
injury and area of most significant pain
r Determine if patient was able to bear weight
immediately or if he or she needed assistance to
walk afterward
r Ask if the patient heard audible “pop” or “snap,”
as this may indicate partial or full tendon rupture
Physical Examr Ottawa Ankle Rules (OAR), 100% sensitive:
Decision tool for ordering radiographs in patients
with suspected injury to the ankle and midfoot:
– Malleolar zone (if any finding is present, then
ankle radiographs are indicated):
◦Bony tenderness at the posterior edge or distal
6 cm of either malleoli (points A and B)
◦Inability to bear weight for 4 consecutive steps
both immediately after the injury and in ED
– Midfoot zone (if either finding is present, then
foot radiographs are indicated):
◦Bony tenderness at the base of the 5th
metatarsal (point C)
◦Bony tenderness of the navicular (point D)
◦Inability to bear weight for 4 consecutive steps
both immediately after the injury and in ED
– Considered a reliable tool in children >5y r
r Assess the skin for swelling, ecchymosis, skin
tenting, disruption, or ischemia
r Careful evaluation of distal neurovascular status:
– Capillary refill
– Palpation or Doppler of DP and PT pulses
r Palpate proximal fibula for tenderness, especially
when medial malleolus or deltoid ligament
tenderness is present:
– Peroneal nerve is at risk for injury with a
Maisonneuve fracture:
◦Wraps around the fibular head
◦Test anterior tibialis and extensor hallucis longus
◦Assess sensation in the 1st web space
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Imagingr Radiography:
– Evaluate the mortise view for widening: Distance
between talus to the medial and lateral malleoli
should be uniform
r Unstable ankle fractures or dislocations require
post reduction radiographs in all 3 planes after
splinting
– Anteroposterior (AP), lateral, and mortise (AP with
a2 0◦ lateral angle)
r AP and lateral radiographs of the tibia and fibula are
indicated if a Maisonneuve fracture is suspected
clinically
r Stress testing of the ligaments in a painful ankle is
unnecessary in the ED if the patient will be
re-examined in 3–7 days
r Stress radiographs of the ankle are usually
unnecessary acutely
r CT scan or MRI:
– Assess the degree of injury to the tibial plafond
and associated ligamentous injury
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
N/A
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Ankle sprain
r Achilles tendon injury
r Os trigonum fracture
r 5th metatarsal fracture (Jones fracture)
r Peroneal tendon dislocation or injury
r Talar fractures
r Talar dome fracture/lesion
r Subtalar dislocations
r Calcaneal fractures
r Foot fractures
r Ankle diastasis
r Rattlesnake envenomation
Pediatric Considerations
r Injury to the growth plates may not be apparent on
plain radiographs
r Consider splint immobilization, nonweight-bearing
status, and orthopedic referral if clinical suspicion
warrants, even in the setting of negative radiographs
r CT scan or MRI may be warranted to delineate the
extent of the injury
r Inform parents of the possibility of growth
abnormalities in patients with injury to the physis

TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Immobilize with soft splint to reduce pain, bleeding,
and further injury
r Cautions:
– Traction devices are usually unnecessary:
◦Contraindicated with open injuries
– Protruding bone should not be reduced; the
wound should be covered with a clean dressing
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Nonweight bearing
r Ice
r Compression
r Elevation
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Ankle fracture:
– All ankle fractures or dislocations require
orthopedic referral
– Open ankle fractures:
◦Remove contaminants
◦Apply moist sterile dressing
◦Assess tetanus immunity
◦Antibiotics
◦Emergent orthopedic consultation
– Closed ankle fractures:
◦Dislocations should be reduced promptly to
prevent complications
◦Apply posterior splint to immobilize foot in 90◦
angle with the application of bulky dressings
and covered by a volar posterior and coaptation
(U-shaped stirrup) splint
◦Sugar tong (coaptation) can be added for
mediolateral support
– Stable injury: (one-sided nondisplaced malleolar
fracture without ligamentous injury)
◦Isolated injury to the lateral malleolus without
medial involvement is virtually always stable
◦Apply posterior splint
– Unstable injury: (both sides of the ankle are
injured i.e., bi- or trimalleolar fractures)
◦Urgent orthopedic consultation
◦Posterior splint as in stable injuries
◦May require open reduction and internal fixation
(ORIF) emergently before significant swelling
develops
– Neurovascular injury requires emergent
orthopedic consultation
r Ankle dislocations:
– Closed reduction should be performed as rapidly
as possible to minimize ischemia to the skin and
reduce the risk of avascular necrosis of the talus
– Skin tenting and evidence of neurovascular
compromise are indications for immediate
reduction, even prior to radiographs
– Most ankle dislocations require ORIF
– After reduction, place a posterior splint
MEDICATIONr Closed fractures:
– Primarily analgesics (opioids)
r Dislocations or displaced fractures requiring closed
reduction consider:
– Short-acting benzodiazepine (midazolam
0.05–0.1 mg/kg IV) or barbiturate (methohexital
1–1.5 mg/kg IV) with opioid analgesic
r Open fractures:
– Cefazolin: 2 g loading dose (peds: 50 mg/kg) IV
– Gentamicin: 5–7 mg/kg q24h (peds: 2.5 mg/kg
q8h) IV
– Vancomycin: 1 g loading dose (10 mg/kg in
children) if penicillin allergic
– Tetanus toxoid if indicated
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Unstable ankle fractures require urgent orthopedic
consultation and may require admission
r Open ankle fractures and dislocations should be
admitted for debridement, irrigation, and IV
antibiotics
r Ankle dislocations that are treated with either open
or closed reduction
r Concern for compartment syndrome or
neurovascular injury
Discharge Criteria
Simple nondisplaced stable ankle fractures without
neurovascular compromise may be splinted for
immobilization and discharged
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Splinting
r Elevation of affected lower extremity
r Fitted for crutches and shown how to use them
r Placed on nonweight-bearing status of affected
joint, until seen by orthopedist

r To reduce a dislocated ankle, partial flexion of knee
of affected limb will decrease tension on Achilles
tendon and ankle
r Differentiate between ankle fracture and subtalar
fracture on physical exam: While the latter is rare, it
is also rarely reducible
r Remember to look for other injuries including
lumbar spine, hip, tibia, fibula, especially the
proximal fibular neck, and foot

ANKLE SPRAIN
Taylor Y. Cardall
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Injuries to ligamentous supports of the ankle
r Ankle joint is a hinge joint composed of the tibia,
fibula, and talus.
r Injuries may range from stretching with microscopic
damage (grade I) to partial disruption (grade II) to
complete disruption (grade III).
ETIOLOGYr Forced inversion or eversion of the ankle
r Forceful collisions
r 85–90% of ankle sprains involve lateral ligaments:
– Anterior talofibular (ATFL)
– Posterior talofibular (PTFL)
– Calcaneofibular (CFL)
– Usually the result of an inversion injury
– The ATFL is the most commonly injured.
– If the ankle is injured in a neutral position, the CFL
is often injured.
– The PTFL is rarely injured alone.
r Injury to the deltoid ligament (connecting the medial
malleolus to the talus and navicular bones) is usually
the result of an eversion injury:
– Often associated with avulsion at the medial
malleolus or talar insertion
– Rarely found as an isolated injury
– Suspect associated lateral malleolus fracture or
fracture of the proximal fibula (Maisonneuve
fracture).
r Syndesmosis sprains (injury to the tibiofibular
ligaments or the interosseous ligament of the leg):
– Occur most commonly in collision sports
– Syndesmosis injuries (“high ankle sprains”) have a
higher morbidity and potential for long-term
complications.
Pediatric Considerations
r Children <10 yr with traumatic ankle pain and no
radiologic evidence of fracture most likely have a
Salter–Harris I fracture.
r The ligaments are actually stronger than the open
epiphysis.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
History
History may predict the type of injury found and
should include:
r Time of injury
r Mechanism
r The presence of a “pop” or “crack”
r History of previous trauma
r Relevant medical conditions (e.g., bone or joint
disease)
r Treatments attempted prior to arrival
r Ability to bear weight subsequent to the injury at
scene and ED
Physical Examr Aimed at detecting joint instability and any
associated injuries:
– Note the presence or absence of bony tenderness
at posterior edge of medial and lateral malleoli as
well as at the base of the 5th metatarsal.
r Document neurovascular status distal to the injury.
r Assess range of motion and compare it with the
uninjured side.
r Stress testing in the ED is often limited by pain and
may impair detection of ligament injury.
r The squeeze test helps identify syndesmosis injuries:
– Squeeze tibia and fibula together at the midcalf;
pain felt in the ankle indicates a positive test.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr The Ottawa Ankle Rules, a selective strategy for
obtaining ankle radiographs in adults, suggest that
foot or ankle radiographs are unnecessary except
when any of the following are present:
– Bony tenderness at the posterior edge of the distal
6 cm or tip of either malleolus
– Bony tenderness along the base of the 5th
metatarsal or navicular bone
– Inability to take 4 unassisted steps both
immediately after the injury and in the ED
r The rules have been prospectively validated by the
original authors as well as independently by groups
in the US, the UK, France, and other countries.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Imagingr Ankle injuries should be radiographed if there is
concern for fracture.
r Stress radiographs are rarely useful in the ED and
should not be routinely ordered unless requested by
a consultant.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Ankle fracture (lateral, medial, or posterior
malleolus) or dislocation
r Achilles tendon injury
r Maisonneuve fracture
r Os trigonum fracture
r 5th metatarsal fracture (Jones fracture)
r Transchondral talar dome fracture
r Peroneal tendon dislocation or injury
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Immobilize ankle as necessary.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Prevent further injury; avoid weight bearing if
painful.
r RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation)
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr The goal of treatment is reduction of pain and return
to normal activity without long-term pain or joint
laxity.
r Existing evidence supports early mobilization and
functional treatment:
– Unstable ankles (i.e., grade III) or those with
severe pain may benefit from brief immobilization
followed by early return to functional treatment.

r Grade I or II sprains can be treated with functional
support (elastic bandage, air splint, gel splint, etc.):
– Recent evidence suggests an elastic bandage
dressing coupled with an air stirrup splint is
superior to other forms of immobilization.
r Grade III sprains can be treated by immobilization
(sugar tong with posterior splint or elastic bandage
dressing coupled with air stirrup splint) and early
orthopedic consultation or referral.
r Crutches may be needed initially for comfort, but
encourage weight bearing as tolerated for grades I
and II.
r Once acute pain and swelling have resolved,
strengthening exercises and proprioceptive training
(e.g., balance board, small circle walking) improve
ankle strength and function and prevent reinjury.
r Full sports activities may be resumed only when
running and turning are pain free.
r Ankle taping, air splints, or gel splints reduce the
risk of recurrent injury in high-risk sports such as
basketball, volleyball, soccer, and running.

– Ibuprofen: 800 mg (peds: 5–10 mg/kg) PO TID
r Topical NSAIDs have been shown to control pain and
shorten healing time with acute ankle sprain:

area QID
r Narcotic analgesics may be required for severe pain.

An isolated ankle sprain should not require
admission.

An isolated ankle sprain may be safely discharged

facilitate early follow-up.

instructed to follow up with the primary care

or sports medicine specialist within 7–10 days.

radiographs.

coupled with an air stirrup splint followed by early

ANKYLOSING SPONDYLITIS
Daniel R. Lasoff rBrian K. Snyder
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Chronic inflammatory disease, primarily affects the
axial skeleton with predilection toward the spine
and sacroiliac (SI) joints:
– SI joints 100%
– Cervical spine 75%
– Thoracic spine 70%
– LS spine 50%
– Hip joints 30%
– Shoulder joints 30%
r Spondylitis (inflammation of vertebrae) of
ankylosing spondylitis (AS) begins at the insertions
of the outer fibers of the annulus fibrosus
(enthesitis) of the vertebrae:
– Ossification (syndesmophyte formation) may lead
to complete fusion, ankylosis, of the vertebrae.
– Extensive spinal involvement causes the
radiographic appearance of the brittle “bamboo
spine.”
r Onset 15–35 yr of age
r Male to female ratio is between 2:1 and 3:1.
ALERT
AS patients are at 4 times the risk for fracture and
paralysis compared to the general population. They
are 11 times more likely to have spinal cord injuries.
RISK FACTORS
Genetics
Strong genetic component. HLA-B27 is present in
80–90% of patients with AS.
ETIOLOGY
Disease is likely triggered by environmental factors
such as infection in genetically predisposed
individuals.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Spinal: Low back pain with sacroiliitis is the most
common presentation:
– Inflammatory back pain, improving with
movement and exercise.
– Higher risk for serious injury from milder traumatic
mechanisms.
r Extraspinal inflammatory conditions (which may
precede spinal symptoms):
– Ocular (the most common):
◦Uveitis (25–40% occurrence). Usually acute and
unilateral in onset. Can alternate eyes.
– Cardiac:
◦Slight increased risk of CAD
◦Increased risk for valvular incompetence with
prolonged course of AS.
– Pulmonary:
◦Progressive restrictive lung disease due to
limited expansion and fibrosis
– GI:
◦5–10% of patients with inflammatory bowel
disease.
– GU:
◦Risk for IgA nephropathy or amyloidosis. Also
increased risk for NSAID nephropathy from
anti-inflammatory use.
– Enthesitis (inflammation at tendon or ligament
insertion):
◦Often Achilles tendonitis or plantar fasciitis
Historyr Patients <40 yr of age with insidious onset of low
back pain >3 mo, radiating into gluteal areas from
SI region, and progressing to involve the entire
spinal region:
– Worse with rest and improved with mild activity.
Pain in 2nd half of night waking patient from sleep
– Women may have more cervical and extraspinal
manifestations than men.
r Possible prior history of uveitis, restrictive pulmonary
disease, inflammatory bowel disease, enthesitis, or
migrating or polyarthritis.
Physical Examr Tenderness over SI joints elicited with direct pressure
over both of patient’s ASIS simultaneously.
r Dactylitis or enthesitis.
r Flattening of the normal lumbar lordosis
r Exaggeration of thoracic kyphosis
r Limitation of spinal movement
r Reduction in chest expansion
Pediatric Considerations
r Patients with juvenile ankylosing spondylitis (JAS)
may commonly be misdiagnosed as recurrent sprains
r Onset of JAS is late childhood or adolescence
(between 8 and 12 yr, before age 20); primarily boys.
r JAS has a much greater predilection for extraspinal
joints and entheses of the lower extremities; in
addition to SI tenderness, examine for:
– Asymmetrical pauciarthritis of the joints of the
lower extremities
– Enthesitis of the ankle, knee, or tarsal bones.
Plantar fasciitis and Achilles tendonitis are often
common findings.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Exclude fracture and neurologic injury in any patient
with suspected AS for any new spinal pain (even
without trauma).
r Exclude sepsis or septic joint if clinically indicated.
r Evaluate for sacroiliitis with pelvic rock test
(compression) or Patrick test (downward pressure on
the knee of a flexed and externally rotated leg and
the contralateral ASIS causing sacral distraction).
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC may show mild leukocytosis with slight to
moderate anemia and thrombocytosis.
r BUN, creatinine, and electrolytes may be useful to
assess renal involvement.
r Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C-reactive
protein (CRP) may be elevated, but are of limited
use in the ED.
r HLA-B27 testing can be performed by a specialist. A
negative result does not rule out AS.
Imagingr Pelvic radiograph: Should be done in any adult
patient suspected of undiagnosed ankylosing
spondylitis:
– Sacroiliitis is essential to the diagnosis of AS; this
is seen initially as subchondral bony erosions on
the iliac side of the SI joint, which later manifest
as bony proliferation and sclerosis.
– If plain films are negative for sacroilitis, MRI
should be considered.
r Lumbar, thoracic, and cervical spine radiographs to
exclude fracture for complaint of new pain to these
areas with or without trauma
r CT should be performed to further evaluate possible
fractures on plain radiographs.
r MRI should be performed emergently on any patient
with neurologic deficit.
r Chest radiograph may show patchy inflammatory
infiltrates or apical fibrosis.
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Electrocardiogram indications:
– Symptoms of acute coronary syndrome (slightly
increased risk compared to general population for
CAD)
– Symptomatic arrhythmia:
◦AV block
r Echocardiogram indications:
– New murmur: Increased predilection for aortic
insufficiency with AS
– Evidence of new heart failure.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr JAS:
– Onset before age 20
– More enthesitis and extraspinal joint involvement.
r Reactive arthritis (formerly Reiter syndrome):
– Arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis beginning
about 1 mo after an episode of urethritis or
enteritis.
r Enteropathic arthritis:
– Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis
– Primarily involves knee, elbow, ankle, or wrist, and
usually exacerbated by flares of the bowel disease
r Psoriatic arthritis:
– Psoriasis rash
– Much greater predilection for the hands and feet
with higher incidence of dactylitis.
r Septic arthritis:
– Exclude with arthrocentesis if clinically suspected
in single joint involvement.
r Mechanical low back pain:
– Improved with rest and exacerbated by exercise
without signs of systemic inflammatory process.
r Spinal epidural abscess:
– More constant, unremitting, and typically
associated with fever and history of IVDA or
immunosuppression.
r Neoplastic low back pain:
– Typically in patients older than 40, more constant
and unremitting, and more characteristically at
night.

ANKYLOSING SPONDYLITIS
A
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
ALERT
r High risk of spinal injury from minor trauma.
r Spinal immobilization must avoid creating further
injury:
– Cushion stabilization and scoop board in
position of comfort may be a better approach
than cervical collar and/or backboard.
r Intubation difficulty
– Cervical and TMJ restriction may limit success in
all but fiberoptic techniques.
– Consider alternative airway approaches such as
LMA or bag valve mask with oral airway until
definitive airway can be achieved safely (usually
fiberoptic).
r Ventilation difficulty
– Chest wall restriction from deformity and
pulmonary fibrosis
r CPR may carry a higher likelihood of rib fractures
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Exclude cord compression if clinically suspected
(MRI is the study of choice).
r Exclude spinal fracture for any new spinal pain (CT
may be necessary).
r Exclude infection if clinically suspected with
laboratory analysis and arthrocentesis.
r Control pain and inflammation with NSAIDs
MEDICATIONr Nonselective NSAIDs:
– Ibuprofen: 35 mg/kg/d divided QID, max.
50 mg/kg/d (adult: 300–800 mg PO TID or QID)
– Indomethacin: 1–2 mg/kg/d divided BID or QID,
max. 4 mg/kg/d (adult: 25 mg PO BID or TID)
◦Not well tolerated, especially at higher doses
because of GI and CNS effects
– Naproxen: 10 mg/kg/d divided BID, max.
1,000 mg/d (adult: 250–500 mg PO BID)
r COX 2 inhibitors:
– Celecoxib (adult: 100 mg–200 mg PO BID)
r TNF-α inhibitors:
– Adalimumab (adult: 40mg SubQ q2wk)
– Etanercept (adult: 50mg SubQ qwk)
Pregnancy Considerations
r NSAIDs should be avoided in pregnancy.
– Acetaminophen is 1st line
– Opioids are 2nd line
Geriatric Considerations
NSAID use may increase risk in the elderly for
cardiovascular disease, GI bleeding, renal function,
and hypertension. Although effective in select
patients, close follow-up is prudent.
ALERT
r NSAIDs:
– GI bleeding risks
◦Elderly, history of PUD, concurrent use of
glucocorticoids, anticoagulants, aspirin,
smoking, alcohol.
◦Consider celecoxib or adding an H2 blocker or
PPI if patient is at higher risk for GI bleeding.
Second Line
Consider if NSAIDs or acetaminophen are ineffective
at appropriate doses:
r Opioid analgesics, muscle relaxants, or low-dose
steroids.
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Acute neurologic impairment
r Intractable pain
r Sepsis or septic joint cannot be excluded.
Discharge Criteriar No serious injuries or neurologic deficit
r Pain is manageable to the patient
Issues for Referralr The patient should be encouraged to obtain a
medical alert bracelet.
r Rheumatology:
– Patients with evidence of a new diagnosis of AS
should be considered for early referral to a
specialist in rheumatology for immunomodulative
therapy.
r Physical medicine and rehabilitation:
– Resting splints for inflamed joints
– Orthoses for enthesitis (such as heel cushion
inserts to rest Achilles tendon attachment)
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Routine primary care re-evaluation within 1–2 wk to
assess response to treatment.
r Referral to a rheumatologist for immunomodulating
medications.
r Earlier follow-up in any patient with higher risk for
adverse response to NSAIDs:
– Elderly, hypertensive patients, and patients with
higher GI bleeding risks.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Intubation is likely to be difficult and should avoid
neck repositioning due to risk of C1 subluxation.
– Consider airway adjuncts (such as LMA) until a
definitive airway (usually fiberoptic) can be safely
assured.
r Immobilization must avoid creating additional
injury
– Consider cushion/tape stabilization in position of
comfort rather than standard cervical collar and
backboard
r Minor traumatic injuries in AS can result in spinal
fracture and possible cord injury. Maintain a high
clinical suspicion.
ADDITIONAL READING
r Baraliakos X, van den Berg R, Braun J, et al. Update
of the literature review on treatment with biologics
as a basis for the first update of the ASAS/EULAR
management recommendations of ankylosing
spondylitis. Rheumatology. 2012;51(8):1378–1387.
r Chakravarty SD, Paget SA. Ankylosing spondylitis:
Pathogenesis, diagnosis, and therapy.
Rheumatology. 2012;40:39–43.
r Sieper J, Braun J. Ankylosing Spondylitis: In Clinical
Practice. Britain: Springer, 2010.

ANTICHOLINERGIC POISONING
Patrick M. Whiteley
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Central and peripheral cholinergic blockade
r Depending on the drug involved, antagonism occurs
at muscarinic (most common), nicotinic, or both
receptors.
r Onset of activity: 15–30 min after ingestion
r Duration of effect: 2–24 hr
ETIOLOGYr Many drugs contain anticholinergic properties:
– Mild at therapeutic doses
– Life threatening in overdose
r Anticholinergic substances:
– Antihistamines
– Belladonna alkaloids and synthetic congeners
– Antiparkinsonian drugs
– Cyclic antidepressants
– Antipsychotics (neuroleptics)
– Mydriatics
– Skeletal muscle relaxants (orphenadrine,
cyclobenzaprine)
– Antispasmodics
– Mushrooms—Amanita muscaria, Amanita
pantherina
– Plants—deadly nightshade, mandrake, henbane
– Jimson weed—smoked or ingested
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Onset and duration of symptoms
r Type and extent of ingestion/exposure
Physical Examr Classic toxidrome:
– “Mad as a hatter”—altered mental status
– “Hot as a hare”—hyperthermia
– “Red as a beet”—flushed skin
– “Dry as a bone”—dry skin and mucous
membranes
– “Blind as a bat”—blurred vision secondary to
mydriasis
r General:
– Hyperthermia
– Altered mental status
r Ocular:
– Unreactive mydriasis
– Inability to accommodate
r Cardiovascular:
– Sinus tachycardia
– Dysrhythmias (rare except in massive ingestions)
– Hypotension/HTN
– Cardiogenic pulmonary edema
r Pulmonary:
– Tachypnea
– Respiratory failure
r GI:
– Decreased/absent bowel sounds
– Dysphagia
– Decreased GI motility
– Decreased salivation
r Genitourinary (GU):
– Urinary retention
r Integument:
– Decreased sweating
– Flushed skin
– Dry skin and mucous membranes
r CNS:
– Altered mental status
– Auditory or visual hallucinations
– Coma
– Seizures
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Diagnosis based on clinical presentation and an
accurate history
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Urine toxicologic screen if clinically indicated
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, and glucose
r CBC
r Creatine phosphokinase (CPK) if suspected
rhabdomyolysis
r Urinalysis
r Acetaminophen and salicylate levels:
– Detects occult ingestion (e.g., Tylenol PM)
Imaging
ECG:
r Sinus tachycardia most common
r QRS prolongation
r AV blockade
r Bundle branch block pattern
r Dysrhythmias
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Sympathomimetic intoxication
r Withdrawal syndrome
r Acute psychiatric disorders
r Sepsis
r Thyroid disorder
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Transport all pills/pill bottles involved in overdose for
identification in ED.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Airway, breathing, and circulation (ABCs):
– Airway control essential
– Administer supplemental oxygen.
– IV access
– Cardiac monitor and pulse oximetry
r Naloxone, thiamine, D50 (or Accu-Chek) if altered
mental status
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Supportive care:
– IV rehydration with 0.9% NS
– Standard aggressive cooling measures for
hyperthermia
– Use benzodiazepines for treatment of agitation:
◦Avoid phenothiazines owing to anticholinergic
effects.
– Treat seizures with benzodiazepines and
barbiturates.
– Dysrhythmias:
◦Use standard antidysrhythmics.
◦Avoid class Ia antidysrhythmic owing to the
quinidine-like effect of many anticholinergic
drugs.
◦Sodium bicarbonate boluses may reverse the
quinidine-like effects.
r Decontamination:
– Administer activated charcoal for oral ingestions if
within 1 hr.
– Ocular lavage for eyedrop exposure

ANTICHOLINERGIC POISONING
A
r Physostigmine (Antilirium):
– Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that
crosses the blood–brain barrier
– Short-term reversal of both central and peripheral
anticholinergic effects
– Indicated in the presence of peripheral
anticholinergic signs and the following:
◦Seizures unresponsive to conventional therapy
◦Uncontrollable agitation
– Use with caution if prolonged QRS is present on
ECG owing to risk of dysrhythmias (especially
asystole), seizures, and cholinergic crises:
◦Place on cardiac monitor.
◦Observe for cholinergic symptoms.
– Contraindications:
◦Cyclic antidepressant overdose (potentiates
toxicity)
◦Cardiovascular disease
◦Asthma/bronchospasm
◦Intestinal obstruction
◦Heart block
◦Peripheral vascular disease
◦Bladder obstruction
MEDICATIONr Activated charcoal: 1 g/kg PO
r Dextrose: 50–100 mL D50 (peds: 2 mL/kg of D25
over 1 min) IV; repeat if necessary
r Diazepam: 5–10 mg (peds: 0.2–0.5 mg/kg) IV every
10–15 min
r Dopamine: 2–20 μg/kg/min IV with titration to
effect
r Lorazepam: 2–4 mg (peds: 0.03–0.05 mg/kg) IV
every 10–15 min
r Physostigmine: 0.5–2.0 mg (peds: 0.02 mg/kg) IV
over 5 min; repeat if necessary in 30–60 min
r Phenobarbital: 10–20 mg/kg IV (loading dose);
monitor for respiratory depression
r Thiamine (vitamin B1): 100 mg (peds: 50 mg) IV or
IM
First Line
Lorazepam or Diazepam
Second Line
Physostigmine (use with caution and consult with
medical toxicologist)
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar ICU admission for moderate to severe anticholinergic
symptoms (agitation control, temperature control,
and observation for seizures or dysrhythmias)
r Any patient receiving physostigmine
Discharge Criteria
Mild and improving symptoms of anticholinergic
toxicity after 6–8 hr of ED observation
Issues for Referralr Substance abuse referral for patients with
recreational anticholinergic abuse
r Patients with unintentional (accidental) poisoning
require poison prevention counseling.
r Patients with intentional (e.g., suicide) poisoning
require psychiatric evaluation.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Appropriate psychiatric referral for intentional
ingestions
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Aggressively treat hyperthermia.
r Antipyretic medications are not effective in toxic
hyperthermia.
r Use physostigmine cautiously and consult with
medical toxicologist when available.
ADDITIONAL READING

comparison of physostigmine and benzodiazepines
for the treatment of anticholinergic poisoning. Ann
Emerg Med. 2000;35:374–381.

to physostigmine. J Emerg Med. 1997;15:65–69.

ANTIDEPRESSANT POISONING
Patrick M. Lank
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Antidepressants are the most commonly prescribed
psychiatric medications in US.
r Patients who overdose on antidepressants may be
on various antidepressants, divided into SSRIs,
SNRIs, and atypical. Concomitant usage of atypical
antipsychotics and mood stabilizing medications,
some of which are FDA approved for the treatment
of depressive disorders, is common.
r Antidepressants may be prescribed for multiple
other indications, including chronic pain syndromes,
anxiety, eating disorders, substance abuse, and
sleep disorders.
r Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) are covered in a
separate chapter
ETIOLOGY
Mechanismr SSRIs:
– Increase serotonin at the synapse by preventing
the reuptake of serotonin by the presynaptic
neuron.
– SSRIs include paroxetine, fluoxetine, sertraline,
citalopram, and escitalopram
r SNRIs
– Similar to SSRIs, but also inhibit reuptake of
norepinephrine.
– Developed because said to have fewer side effects
than SSRIs at therapeutic dose, although not true
for toxicity.
– SNRIs include venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, and
duloxetine.
r Atypical antidepressants:
– Have variable effects on serotonin,
norepinephrine, and dopamine.
– Include mirtazapine, trazodone, and bupropion
r Atypical antipsychotics:
– Most antipsychotics have activity at dopamine
receptors, although variable agonism/antagonism
depending on medication and dopamine receptor.
– Additional activity at serotonin, α-adrenergic,
histamine, and muscarinic receptors.
r Psychiatric medications also have variable potassium
and sodium channel blockade, leading to
cardiotoxicity (QT and QRS prolongation,
respectively).
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr SSRIs:
– Traditional SSRIs (fluoxetine, paroxetine,
sertraline):
◦Sedation
◦Serotonin syndrome
◦In single substance overdose, rarely will cause
severe medical effects
– Citalopram/Escitalopram:
◦Somnolence, vomiting, tachycardia
◦QTc prolongation
◦Seizures (more common in citalopram)
◦Exhibit delayed toxicity (up to 12 hr after
ingestion)
r SNRIs:
– Duloxetine:
◦Somnolence, vomiting, tachycardia
◦Seizures rare
– Venlafaxine/Desvenlafaxine:
◦Seizures
◦QTc prolongation
r Atypical antidepressants:
– Bupropion
◦Sedation
◦Seizures
◦QRS & QTc prolongation
– Trazodone:
◦Sedation
◦QTc prolongation
◦Hypotension
◦Priapism
– Mirtazapine:
◦Sedation
◦QTc prolongation
◦Possible neutropenia in chronic dosing
r Atypical antipsychotics:
– Variable dopamine receptor activity
– Developed for fewer extrapyramidal symptoms
(EPS), particularly tardive dyskinesia, than typical
antipsychotics
– Most common symptoms in overdose include
sedation, tachycardia, and miosis
– Clozapine:
◦Agranulocytosis (in up to 1% taking chronically)
◦Sialorrhea
◦Cardiomyopathy
◦Anticholinergic delirium
– Olanzapine:
◦Anticholinergic delirium
◦QTc prolongation
– Quetiapine:
◦Hypotension from significant α1-antagonism
◦QTc prolongation
◦Anticholinergic delirium
– Ziprasidone:
◦Sedation
◦QTc prolongation → increased risk of torsade
– Aripiprazole:
◦No QTc prolongation
◦Hypotension
◦Prolonged CNS dysfunction
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Determine agents ingested, dose, and time of
ingestion:
– Investigate for coingested drugs.
r Rapid bedside glucose if altered mental status
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Specific drug levels rarely available and do not guide
emergent management
r ECG:
– For evaluation of QTc and QRS width
r Urine pregnancy:
– In females of childbearing age
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose
r Urine drug of abuse screening:
– Rarely changes clinical management
r Salicylate and acetaminophen concentrations
– Very common coingestants in suicidal patients
r Serum ethanol:
– To evaluate ethanol intoxication as contributing to
altered mental status
Imagingr CT of brain to evaluate for other causes of
depressed mental status
r CXR if intubated or hypoxic
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr TCA overdose
r Ethanol overdose
r Isoniazid overdose
r Hypoglycemia
r Hypoxemia
r Hyponatremia
r Hypocalcemia
r Withdrawal syndromes
r Serotonin syndrome
r Head trauma
r Opioid intoxication
r Sedative–hypnotic overdose
r Mood stabilizer/antiepileptic overdose
r DKA

TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr In cases of suspected overdose, bring all medication
bottles to hospital with patient.
r ABCs
r 0.9% NS IV fluids as needed for hypotension
r Benzodiazepines as needed for seizures
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs:
– Administer oxygen.
– Place on cardiac monitor and measure pulse
oximetry.
– Establish IV access
– Intubate as needed for airway protection or
respiratory status.
r Rapid bedside glucose measurement
r Naloxone or D50W as indicated for altered mental
status and rapid clinical evaluation
– Flumazenil is not recommended for
mixed-overdose patients, patients with underlying
seizure disorder, or patients chronically on
benzodiazepines.

Cogentin 1 mg IV for EPS
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr GI decontamination:
– Do not attempt decontamination in a patient who
cannot protect their airway.
– Intubation solely for decontamination purposes,
however, is not recommended.
– Activated charcoal may be beneficial in early
presenting overdoses.
r For QRS widening, administer sodium bicarbonate
IV bolus.
– Sodium bicarbonate infusion (i.e., “bicarb drip”) is
NOT appropriate for use with QRS widening, as it
is ineffective and potentially limits ability to
provide sodium bicarbonate boluses.
r Treat hypotension unresponsive to IV fluids with
norepinephrine rather than dopamine owing to α1
receptor antagonism.
r Treat seizures with:
– Initial therapy: Benzodiazepines
– For refractory seizures: Barbiturates
r Treat symptoms of serotonin syndrome (fever, AMS,
tachycardia, rigidity, hyperreflexia) with
benzodiazepines and active cooling

tolerated up to 100g PO

bolus or 0.5 mg/kg rectal)

caution: Likely to develop respiratory depression

8.4%; peds: <50 kg, 4.2%)

r ECG changes

AORTIC DISSECTION, THORACIC
Jeffrey I. Schneider rJonathan S. Olshaker
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Aortic dissection begins when there is an intimal
tear.
r Blood then dissects through the media under aortic
systolic pressure.
r It is thought that hypertension is a major factor in
the dissection process.
r Dissections can start proximally at the root and
dissect distally to involve any or all branches of the
aorta, such as the carotid and subclavian arteries.
r The dissection process can also proceed proximally
to involve the aortic root, the coronary ostia, and
the pericardium.
r Dissection that progresses proximally may lead to
occlusion of the coronary ostia, aortic valve
incompetence, or cardiac tamponade.
r Classification related to portion of aorta involved:
– Stanford classification:
◦Type A: Ascending aorta
◦Type B: Distal to ascending aorta
– DeBakey classification:
◦DeBakey I: Intimal tear in aortic arch or root
◦DeBakey II: Ascending aorta
◦DeBakey III: Distal to takeoff of left subclavian
artery
r Peak age for occurrence:
– Proximal dissection: 50–55 yr
– Distal dissection: 60–70 yr
Pregnancy Considerations
Risk of dissection increases in the presence of
pregnancy:
r In women <40 yr of age, 50% of dissections occur
during pregnancy.
ETIOLOGY
Any process that affects the mechanical properties of
the aortic wall can lead to dissection:
r Hypertension (72% of patients in the Registry of
Acute Aortic Dissection)
r Congenital heart disease (bicuspid aortic valve,
coarctation)
r Aortic wall connective tissue abnormalities (cystic
medial necrosis)
r Connective tissue disease (Marfan disease,
Ehlers–Danlos syndrome)
r Pregnancy
r Infectious/inflammatory conditions that can cause
vasculitis (lupus, syphilis, endocarditis, giant cell
arteritis, rheumatoid arthritis, Takayasu arteritis)
r Previous cardiac surgery including CABG, aortic
valve repair
r Tobacco use
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Chest pain:
– May be absent in as many as 15% of patients
– Substernal if type A dissection
– Intrascapular if descending thoracic dissection
– Lumbar if abdominal aorta involved
– Starts abruptly
– Usually described as sharp
– Most severe at onset
r Back pain:
– Commonly interscapular or lumbar
r Combination of chest, back, and abdominal pain
r Neurologic complaints:
– Visual changes
– Stroke symptoms
r Aortic dissection may present with atypical
symptoms that can result in a delay of diagnosis
– Abdominal pain
– Chest pressure
– Leg pain
– Syncope
– Fever
– Nausea, vomiting
Geriatric Considerations
Elderly are less likely to undergo surgery and have a
higher mortality rate
r Elderly are less likely to describe their pain as abrupt
in onset, have a pulse deficit, or have aortic
insufficiency
Physical Examr HTN:
– 35–40% may be normotensive.
r Pulse deficits:
– Discrepancies in BP between limbs
– Usually in upper extremities
r Neurologic/spinal cord deficits
r Murmur of aortic regurgitation:
– Occurs in up to 31% of patients
– Musical, vibrating quality with variable intensity
– Heard best along right sternal border
r Shock
– If pericardial rupture or myocardial infarction (MI)
from dissection into a coronary artery
r Atypical presentations
– Ischemic lower extremity
– Altered mental status
– Congestive heart failure
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
ECG:
r Useful in ruling in or out ST-elevation MI or ischemia
r Dissection may involve coronary ostia and
cause MI:
– Inferior MI (right coronary artery lesion) is more
common than left coronary artery territory.
r Useful for evaluating the presence of left ventricular
hypertrophy
r A normal ECG in the presence of severe, acute-onset
chest/back pain should heighten one’s suspicion of
an aortic dissection.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Leukocytosis
r Hematuria
r Elevated BUN and creatinine
r Elevated amylase secondary to bowel ischemia
r Elevated cardiac enzymes due to myocardial
ischemia
r D-dimer <500 ng/mL makes the diagnosis of
dissection unlikely
Imagingr CXR:
– Useful in excluding other etiologies such as
pneumothorax and pneumonia
– In dissection, there may be a widened
mediastinum or abnormal aortic contour.
– An enlarged heart secondary to pericardial fluid
(blood) may be present.
– May be completely normal in as many as 12–18%
of cases
r Echo—transthoracic or transesophageal:
– Transthoracic:
◦Not very helpful in the diagnosis of aortic
dissection
◦May be used to evaluate for complications of a
known dissection such as tamponade, valvular
incompetence, or MI (from ostial occlusion)
– Transesophageal:
◦May be performed in the ED
◦Patients may require intubation.
◦Provides information regarding extent of
dissection and complications
r CT:
– Very useful in defining extent of dissection
– May also be used in diagnosing clinical entities
such as pulmonary embolism
– Has a high sensitivity for the diagnosis of aortic
dissection and is the diagnostic modality of choice
in many centers

– Due of overlap of symptomatology with cardiac
ischemia, some patients may have diagnosis made
by cardiac catheterization when an intimal flap is
visualized.

r Unstable angina
r Pneumothorax
r Esophageal rupture
r Pulmonary embolism
r Pericarditis
r Pneumonia
r Musculoskeletal pain
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Monitor
r IV access
r Oxygen
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr 2 large-bore IV lines
r Continuous cardiac monitoring
r Pulse oximetry
r Oxygen
r Type and cross
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr BP reduction to reduce shearing forces on aortic
wall and slow down the dissection process
r Medications: IV β-blockade and nitroprusside
– Medications are used to control HTN and cardiac
contractility and decrease shearing forces.
– Esmolol (IV) or labetalol (IV):
◦Contraindications: Bradycardia, COPD,
hypotension
– Nitroprusside (commonly used in conjunction with
IV β-blocker)
– Caution when using the above together: To
prevent an initial increase in shear forces,
β-blocker therapy should be started prior to the
addition of nitroprusside therapy
r Emergent surgery:
– Treatment of choice for type A dissection
– Treatment for type B dissections in those who
have failed medical therapy
r Medical management:
– Treatment of choice for stable type B dissections

Symptoms of aortic dissection may be similar to
those of cardiac ischemia/infarction and pulmonary
embolus. Treatment with thrombolytics and
anticoagulants may be harmful and potentially fatal
if aortic dissection is present.

min drip
r Labetalol: 10–20 mg IV over 2 min q10–15min.
Then 2–4 mg/min IV drip. Total dose not to exceed
300 mg.
r Nitroprusside: 0.5 μk/kg/min IV and titrate upward
to desired effect. Dose should be based on IBW.

DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar All patients with acute aortic dissection should be
admitted to the intensive care unit.
r Emergency cardiothoracic surgery consultation
should be obtained, especially in cases of type A
dissection.
Discharge Criteria
None
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Close follow-up with cardiology and/or cardiothoracic
surgery is of paramount importance.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Untreated, nearly 75% of patients with ascending
aortic dissection can be expected to die within 2 wk,
with a mortality of 1–3%/hr in the 1st 48 hr.
r Majority of patients present with pain (90%) of
severe intensity (90%) that occurred suddenly
(84%).
r Although some recent literature has suggested a
role for D-dimer testing, there is insufficient evidence
to support its use as the sole screening test for
aortic dissection.
r Should consider the diagnosis in patients with chest
pain in whom conventional therapy (nitrates,
β-blockers) are ineffective, and in those who have
chest pain in addition to another complaint
(extremity weakness, back pain, paresthesias,
abdominal pain).
r Identification of risk factors is critical. These
include:
– HTN
– Male gender
– Cocaine use
– Advanced age
– Pregnancy
– Connective tissue disorders, such as Marfan
syndrome or cystic medial necrosis
– Bicuspid aortic valve
– Turner syndrome
– Family history
– Previous cardiac or valvular surgery

AORTIC RUPTURE, TRAUMATIC (TAI)
Stephen R. Hayden
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Traumatic aortic rupture (also referred to as
traumatic aortic injury or TAI) is the cause of death in
an estimated 20% of lethal motor vehicle collisions.
r An estimated 85% of patients with TAI die before
reaching the hospital.
r Patients surviving to the ED usually have a
contained rupture as aortic blood is tamponaded by
the adventitia.
r Without proper treatment, of the 15% that survive
the initial event, 49% will die within the 1st 24 hr,
and 90% within 4 mo.
r Mean age of patients sustaining aortic rupture is
33 yr, and 70% are male.
r Most tears are transverse, not longitudinal.
r Tears may be partially or completely circumferential.
ETIOLOGYr Most commonly results from motor vehicle collisions
>30 mph
r Unrestrained passengers, driver seat occupants
(injuries from steering column and instruments), and
ejected occupants.
r Other mechanisms: Auto versus pedestrian, airplane
crashes, falls from height >10 ft, crush and blast
injuries, direct blow to chest
r Proposed mechanisms of aortic injury:
– Shear forces arising from unequal rates of
deceleration of the relatively fixed descending
aorta and the more mobile arch
– “Bending” stress at the aortic isthmus may cause
flexion of the aortic arch on the left mainstem
bronchus and pulmonary artery.
– Twisting of the arch forces it superiorly and causes
it to stretch.
– Osseous structures (e.g., medial clavicles,
manubrium, 1st rib) cause pinching of the trapped
aorta as they strike the vertebral column.
– “Waterhammer” fluid wave causes explosive
rupture of aorta just distal to the aortic valve.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
ALERT
Despite the severe nature of the injury, clinical
manifestations are often deceptively subtle or
nonexistent as patients frequently present with
multiple coexisting injuries. 1/3–1/2 of these
patients do not have external signs of chest trauma.
Historyr Substernal chest pain is the most common symptom,
but only present in ∼25% of cases.
r Dyspnea, hoarseness, and stridor (tracheal
compression from expanding hematoma) are less
common.
Physical Examr Neither sensitive nor specific for aortic injury
r Generalized HTN may occur from stimulation of
sympathetic afferent nerves located near aortic
isthmus.
r Harsh precordial or midscapular systolic murmur
(1/3 of patients)
r Ischemic pain in lower extremities, oliguria/anuria,
paraplegia from decreased aortic blood flow distal
to aortic arch
r Swelling of base of neck (extravasation of blood)
r Acute coarctation syndrome (1/3 of patients): Upper
extremity HTN with decreased pressures in low
extremities, caused by periaortic hematoma
compressing aortic lumen
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Plain CXR is the primary screening tool with ∼90%
sensitivity, but low specificity.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC
r Chemistry
r Prothrombin time/partial thromboplastin time
r Type and cross-match (6–8 units PRBC)
Imagingr Plain CXR:
– Findings suggestive of mediastinal hemorrhage,
hematoma, or associated injuries:
◦Widening of the superior mediastinum at the
level of aortic arch (defined as >8c mo na
supine film, >6 cm in an upright PA film, or
>0.25 mediastinum-width to chest-width ratio)
is the most sensitive sign.
◦Obscuration of the aortic knob is also a sensitive
sign.
◦More specific, but less sensitive, signs include
opacification of the aortopulmonary window,
rightward displacement of nasogastric tube,
widened paratracheal stripe, and widened right
paraspinal interface.
– 7–10% false-negative rate with normal
mediastinum on x-ray; consider use of helical chest
CT with high-speed deceleration mechanisms.
– In pediatric patients: The most common findings
are a left apical cap, pulmonary contusion, aortic
obscuration, and mediastinal widening.
r Helical chest CT angiography:
– Preferred confirmatory study in stable patients
– Nearly 100% sensitivity and specificity for
detecting aortic rupture with improved CT
technology
– Has largely eliminated need for aortography
– Advantages over aortography include noninvasive,
provides information on other thoracic structures,
more rapid
r Aortography:
– Still considered by some to be the gold standard
for diagnosis of TAI
– Provides precise anatomic localization of aortic
tears, useful for aorta injured at >1 site (15–20%
of cases)
– Risk of further damage to aorta from catheter
– Need for this modality is declining given advances
in CT imaging quality.

Presence of large thymus may make diagnosis of

mediastinum; obtain upright PA if possible.
r Mediastinal hematoma owing to other causes
r Mediastinal lymphadenopathy or tumor
r Redundant aorta resulting from HTN
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Important information to retrieve at scene of
injury:
r Vehicular speed
r Patient in driver or passenger seat
r Damage to steering column if driver is patient
r Ejection or use of seat belt
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Follow advanced trauma life support protocols.
r Life-threatening intracranial, peritoneal, and
retroperitoneal injuries take precedence.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Immediate trauma surgery consultation
r Immediate cardiothoracic or vascular surgery
consultation (institution dependent)
r Avoid maneuvers that may result in a Valsalva-like
response (e.g., gagging, straining)
r Aggressive pharmacologic treatment of BP and
heart rate, as emerging data suggest delaying
surgical repair may lead to improved outcomes
r Goal of medical therapy is to target heart rate
60 ± 5 bpm, systolic BP 100–120 mm Hg, and
mean arterial BP 70–80 mm Hg to decrease risk of
sudden free rupture and exsanguination:
– β-blockers such as esmolol and labetalol are
1st-line agents
– Calcium-channel blockers in patients with
contraindications to β-blockade (CHF , COPD, 2nd-
or 3rd-degree atrioventricular block)
– Add vasodilator (nitroprusside) if needed to reach
target BP and heart rate goals.
– Antihypertensives are relatively contraindicated in
acute coarctation syndrome.
r For significant hypotension, initiate rapid volume
expansion, including blood.
r Vasopressors for refractory hypotension;
norepinephrine and phenylephrine are preferred
r Central venous and arterial catheters
ALERT
Only administer vasodilator after initiating negative
inotrope (β-blocker or calcium-channel blocker), as
vasodilator alone can cause an increase in shearing
forces on the intact aortic adventitia.
MEDICATIONr Esmolol: 500 μg/kg bolus IV (peds: 100–500 μg/kg
bolus), then 50–150 μg/kg/min IV infusion (peds:
25–100 μg/kg/min IV infusion)
r Labetalol: 20 mg IV , followed by additional doses of
40 mg and 80 mg (peds: 0.2–10 mg/kg per dose,
max. 20 mg per dose) IV q10–15min, to 300 mg IV
total; start infusion at 2 mg/min and titrate up to
10 mg/min (peds: 0.4–3 mg/kg/h infusion)
r Diltiazem: 20 mg (0.25 mg/kg) IV over 2 min; 2nd
bolus 25 mg (0.35 mg/kg) in 15 min if needed;
infusion 5–15 mg/h
r Norepinephrine: Start with 0.5–1 μg/min and titrate
to desired response; 8–30 μg/min is usual dose
(peds: Start 0.05–0.1 μg/kg/min, max.
2 μg/kg/min)
r Phenylephrine: 0.1–0.5 mg IV boluses q10–15min,
initial dose not to exceed 0.5 mg (peds:
5–20 μg/kg/dose q10–15min); 100–180 μg/min or
0.5 μg/kg/min titrated to desired effect (peds:
0.1–0.5 μg/kg/min, titrated to desired effect)
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteria
All patients with aortic injuries must be admitted to
the ICU if not taken directly to the OR.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
All patients with TAI are admitted to the hospital.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Maintain a high degree of suspicion for TAI in
patients with injuries from significant deceleration
mechanisms.
r Clinical signs and symptoms may be subtle or
nonexistent, necessitating some reliance on
radiologic imaging for diagnosis.
r Special attention should be given to assessment of
the mediastinum on CXR in trauma patients.
r Early pharmacologic control of BP and heart rate is
of utmost importance when diagnosis is confirmed.

APHTHOUS ULCERS
Matthew R. Berkman
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Painful ovoid or round ulcerations on the mucous
membranes of the mouth, tongue or genitals:
r Commonly referred to as “canker sores”
ETIOLOGYr Unknown
r Etiology likely multifactorial with some correlation
with:
– Immunologic dysfunction; alteration of
cell-mediated immune system
– Infection
– Food hypersensitivities (i.e., gluten)
– Vitamin deficiency
– Pregnancy
– Menstruation
– Trauma
– Stress
– Ethnicity
– Immunodeficiency
– Medications: β-blockers, anti-inflammatory
r Epidemiology: Usually occurs in children and
young adults (Peak age of onset: Between 10 to
19 yr old)
– Most common inflammatory ulcerative condition
of the oral cavity (20-40% of general population)
– More common in women
– May be familial
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Minor aphthous ulcers:
– 70–90% of all aphthae
– <5 mm in diameter; up to 5 appear at a time
– Painful, shallow ulcers with necrotic centers
– Raised, circumscribed margins and erythematous
halos
– Gray-white pseudomembrane
– Affect nonkeratinized mucosa of anterior oral
cavity
◦Labial and buccal mucosa
◦Floor of mouth
◦Ventral surface of tongue
– Rarely found on dorsum of tongue, hard palate, or
gingiva
– Last for 10–14 days; do not scar
– Fever/constitutional symptoms rarely associated
r Major aphthous ulcers or Sutton disease:
– 10–15% of all aphthae
– Similar in appearance but more painful than minor
form
– >5 mm in diameter; 1–10 ulcers at a time
– Deeper than minor form
– Involve all areas of oropharynx including pharynx,
soft/hard palate, lips
– Last for weeks to months, may scar
– Onset after puberty
– Often associated with underlying disease
– Fever is rarely associated
r Herpetiform aphthous ulcers:
– 7–10% of all aphthae
– Multiple small clusters
– <5 mm in diameter, 10–100 at any time, may
coalesce into plaques
– Herpetiform in nature, but herpes simplex virus
cannot be cultured from lesions.
– Predisposition for women
– Last for 7–30 days; scarring can occur
Historyr Prodrome of burning or pricking sensation of oral
mucosa 1–2 days prior to appearance of ulcers
r Inquire about patient or family history of:
– Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
– Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)
– Beh ¸cet disease
– Reiter disease
– Gluten sensitivity
– Cancer
– HIV
r Inquire about patient sexual history of syphilis or
herpes virus
r Inquire about current medications:
– NSAIDs
– β-blockers
Physical Examr See “Signs and Symptoms.”
r Look for signs of dehydration:
– Vital signs should be within normal limits.
– Evaluate mucus membranes.
r Evaluate for signs of secondary infection.
r Evaluate for signs of systemic causes of ulcers (see
“History”).
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Diagnosis is made by history and clinical
presentation.
r Rule out oral manifestation of systemic disease:
– More likely if persists >3 wk or associated with
constitutional symptoms
r Focus on symptoms of eyes, mouth, genitalia, skin,
GI tract, allergy, diet history and physical exam
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Routine lab testing not indicated:
r Needed only when systemic etiologies causing
ulcers are suspected
r Biopsy should be considered for ulcers lasting more
than 3 wk
r Should be guided by history and physical exam:
– CBC series
– Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) (syphilis)
– Fluorescent treponemal antibody-absorption test
– Antinuclear antibody test
– Tzanck stain: Inclusion giant cells (herpes virus)
– Biopsy: Multinucleated giant cells
(cytomegalovirus)
– Fungal cultures
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
An outpatient biopsy should be considered for any
ulcer >3w k
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Trauma:
– Biting
– Dentures
– Braces
r Drug exposure:
– NSAIDs
– Nicorandil
– β-blockers
