APPENDICITIS
Colleen N. Hickey rJennifer L. Kolodchak
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Most common abdominal emergency
r Acute obstruction of appendiceal lumen results in
distension followed by organ ischemia, bacterial
overgrowth, and eventual perforation of the viscus
r Pain migration:
– Periumbilical pain: Appendiceal distension
stimulates stretch receptors, which relay pain via
visceral afferent pain fibers to 10th thoracic
ganglion.
– RLQ pain: As inflammation extends to surrounding
tissues, pain occurs owing to stimulation of
parietal nerve fibers and localizes to position of
appendix.
Pediatric Considerations
r 28–57% misdiagnosis in patients <12 yr (nearly
100% in patients <2 yr)
r 70–90% perforation rate in children <4y r
r Perforation correlates strongly with delayed
diagnosis.
Geriatric Considerations
r Decreased inflammatory response
r 3 times more likely to have perforation owing to
anatomic changes
r Diagnosis often delayed owing to atypical
presentations
Pregnancy Considerations
r Slightly higher rate in 2nd trimester compared to
1st/3rd/postpartum periods
r Increased perforation rate (25–40%), highest in 3rd
trimester
r RLQ pain remains the most common symptom
r 7–10% fetal loss, up to 24% in perforated
appendicitis
ETIOLOGYr Luminal obstruction of appendix
r Appendiceal lumen becomes distended, inhibiting
lymphatic and venous drainage.
r Bacterial invasion of wall, with edema and blockage
of arterial blood flow
r Perforation and spillage of contents into peritoneal
cavity, causing peritonitis (usually 24–36 hr from
onset)
r May wall off and form abscess
r Gram-negative rods and anaerobic organisms
predominate
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Abdominal pain: Primary symptom:
– Normal location:
◦RLQ pain
◦35% of patients have appendix located within
5 cm of “normal” location.
– Retrocecal appendix (28–68%):
◦Back pain
◦Flank pain
◦Testicular pain
– Pelvic appendix (27–53%):
◦Suprapubic pain
◦Urinary or rectal symptoms
– Long appendix (<0.2%):
◦Inflamed tip may cause pain in RUQ or LLQ.
◦Anorexia
◦Vomiting
r Change in bowel habits: Diarrhea (33%),
constipation (9–33%)
r Classic presentation (<75% adults):
– Initially periumbilical pain
– Followed by anorexia (1st symptom in 95%) and
nausea
– Localizes to RLQ (1–12 hr after onset)
– Finally, vomiting with fever
Pediatric Considerations
r Presentations often nonspecific and difficult to
localize (<50% have classic presentation)
r Anorexia, vomiting, and diarrhea more common
(half-eaten meal hours before complaints of pain
may more accurately indicate duration of symptoms)
r Observe child before exam for subtle indicators of
local inflammation:
– Limping gait
– Hesitation to move or climb
– Flexed right hip
Physical Examr Vital signs:
– Often normal
– Fever: Normal to mild elevation (<1◦F) initially,
increases with perforation
r Abdominal exam:
– Tenderness at McBurney point (1/3 of distance
from right anterior iliac spine to umbilicus)
– Guarding:
◦Voluntary guarding early owing to muscular
resistance to palpation
◦Involuntary guarding (rigidity) later as
inflammation progresses and perforation occurs
– Rebound:
◦Pain with any rapid movement of peritoneum
(e.g., bumping stretcher)
– Specific signs (less useful in pediatrics):
◦Rovsing sign: Pain in RLQ when palpating LLQ
◦Psoas sign: Increased pain on extension of right
hip with patient lying on her or his left side,
owing to inflamed appendix touching iliopsoas
muscle.
◦Obturator sign: Pain with passive internal
rotation and flexion of right hip
r Rectal exam:
– Limited value: May localize tenderness/mass
r Pelvic exam:
– Important to differentiate gynecologic disease
– Vaginal discharge and/or adnexal tenderness or
mass suggests gynecologic disease.
– Cervical motion tenderness when present
suggests PID, but can be seen in up to 25% of
women with appendicitis
r Patient position:
– Supine or decubitus with legs (particularly the
right) drawn up
– Prefer not to move
r Shuffling gait—known as “appy walk”
Pediatric Considerations
Almost all children have generalized abdominal
tenderness with some rigidity.
Pregnancy Considerations
r Enlarging uterus displaces appendix upward and
laterally.
r Hyperemesis gravidarum and other nonsurgical
causes of vomiting should not cause abdominal
tenderness.
Geriatric Considerations
Typical signs of peritonitis may be absent in elderly.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Suggestive history and physical exam sufficient to
establish preoperative diagnosis and warrant
surgical consultation
r Tests listed below may be used to assist in diagnosis
r Atypical cases: Repeat serial exams in conjunction
with some of the tests listed below is effective, with
decreased rates of negative appendectomies and no
increase in rates of perforation
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC:
– WBC >10,000, with left shift (80%)
– Normal WBC does not exclude diagnosis
r C-reactive protein:
– Overall sensitivity 62%, specificity 66%
– May not be elevated early (<12 hr)
– Increased sensitivity with serial measurements
r Urinalysis:
– Generally normal
– Mild pyuria, bacteriuria, or hematuria (25–30%)
– Pyuria present if inflamed appendix lies near
ureter or bladder
r Pregnancy test for females of child-bearing age
Imagingr Unnecessary when diagnosis is clear
r Most helpful in female patients of child-bearing age
where diagnosis is often unclear
r Abdominal radiographs—not recommended
r US: Sensitivity 86–90%; specificity 92–95%:
– Noncompressible appendix 6 mm anteroposterior
(AP) diameter
– Presence of appendicolith
– Periappendiceal fluid/mass
– Limited by obesity, bowel gas, retrocecal
appendix, and operator
– Negative study of limited use

ARSENIC POISONING
Vinodinee L. Dissanayake
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Acute toxicity:
– Caused by intentional ingestion, malicious
poisoning, or medication error
r Minimal lethal ingested dose ∼2 mg/kg
r Chronic toxicity:
– Resulting from occupational exposures, water or
food contamination, or use of folk remedies
containing arsenic
r Ingestion is the primary route of exposure
r Inhalational toxicity is possible from arsine gas
exposure
ETIOLOGYr Most cases seen in the ED result from intentional
ingestion or malicious poisoning
r Sodium arsenate, found in ant killer, is the most
common acute exposure in the US
r Contaminated food and water supplies are the most
common cause worldwide
r Inorganic arsenic trioxide has been recently
approved as a chemotherapeutic agent for acute
myelogenous leukemia (AML)
r Melarsoprol, an organic arsenical, has been used to
treat trypanosomiasis since 1949
r Found in pesticides, certain folk remedies (herbal
balls), industrial wood preservatives
r May be released as arsine gas from combustion of
zinc- and arsenic-containing compounds
Mechanismr Arsenic exists in several forms—gas (arsine, or
lewisite), organic, elemental, and inorganic
r Inorganic forms (pentavalent and trivalent arsenic)
are most frequently involved in toxic exposures:
– Pentavalent arsenic uncouples oxidative
phosphorylation
– Most pentavalent arsenic is converted to the more
toxic trivalent arsenic in the body
– Trivalent arsenic binds sulfhydryl groups and
interferes in hemoglobin production
– Some trivalent arsenic may be methylated into
species of varying toxicity
– The more reactive species are DNA damaging and
genotoxic
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr CNS:
– Altered mental status/encephalopathy
– Neurodevelopmental deficits in children
– Peripheral neuropathy
◦Acute: Sensory neuropathy
◦Subacute: Sensorimotor neuropathy
– Peripheral dysesthesias
– Headache
– Seizures
r Cardiovascular:
– Prolonged QTc interval
– Hypotension (acute) or hypertension (chronic)
– Dysrhythmias, primarily ventricular
– Nonspecific ST segment changes
– Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema
r Pulmonary:
– Inhalational exposure increases lung cancer risk
and respiratory mortality
– Large acute ingestion (8 mg/kg) may lead to
severe respiratory distress
◦Pulmonary edema, hemorrhagic bronchitis, and
bronchopneumonia
r GI:
– Nausea, vomiting after ingestion and possibly
inhalation
◦Protracted and may be refractory to antiemetics
at usual doses
◦Can have hemorrhagic gastroenteritis; corrosive
to GI tract
– Rice water diarrhea
– Abdominal pain
– Garlic odor to breath, vomit, stools
– Causes acute hepatitis; chronically, can cause
portal HTN
– A possible association with diabetes mellitus in
chronic exposure
r Miscellaneous (usually associated with chronic
exposure)
– Acute rhabdomyolysis
– Blackfoot disease in Taiwan: Gangrene from loss
of circulation to extremities
– Dermatitis, such as toxic erythroderma and
hyperkeratotic, hyperpigmented lesions
– Hemolytic anemia (more pronounced with arsine
gas exposure)
– Hypothyroidism (antagonizes thyroid hormone)
– Increased risk of carcinoma (liver/basal
cell/squamous cell of skin/bronchogenic)
– Leukopenia (after several days)
– Mees lines (white bands across the nails owing to
growth arrest caused by arsenic)
– Patchy alopecia
– Raynaud phenomenon and vasospasticity
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Spot urine arsenic level
r CBC
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Spot urine arsenic level >1,000 μg/L may confirm
diagnostic suspicion:
– Peaks 10–50 hr postingestion
r Definitive test is 24 hr urine collection with
speciation into organic and inorganic types of
arsenic.
r Blood levels not routinely helpful owing to short
half-life in serum (∼2 hr)
r CBC to evaluate for anemia, leukopenia, basophilic
stippling
r Electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, and glucose
r Urinalysis to look for evidence of
hemolysis/rhabdomyolysis
r Liver function tests
r Total creatine phosphokinase (CPK) for
rhabdomyolysis
r Hair and nail arsenic levels:
– Do not help in acute setting
– May help determine chronicity of exposure in
select populations
Imagingr Plain abdominal radiographs to look for radiopaque
foreign body
r Cranial CT/other studies as indicated by patient’s
condition
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Acute toxicity:
– Acute appendicitis/colitis/gastroenteritis
– Celiac disease
– Cholera
– Distributive shock
– Encephalopathy
– Toxic ingestions
◦Amanita mushroom poisoning
◦Cyclic antidepressants or other seizure-inducing
toxins
◦Organophosphates
r Chronic toxicity:
– Addison disease
– Guillain–Barr ´ e syndrome or other neuropathy
– Raynaud phenomenon
– Thromboangiitis obliterans, or other vasculitides
– Vitamin deficiency (B3,B 6,o rB 12)
– Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome

A
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
ALERT
r If possible to do so safely, bring containers in
suspected overdose/poisoning.
r Decontaminate skin.
r Support airway/breathing/circulation.
r Cardiac monitoring
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs:
– Cardiac monitor
– Isotonic crystalloids as needed for hypotension
r Naloxone, thiamine, and dextrose (D50W) as
indicated for altered mental status
r Cardiovascular:
– Vasopressors if refractory hypotension is present
– Central venous pressure monitoring to prevent
pulmonary/cerebral edema
– Avoid type IA, IC and III antidysrhythmic agents,
which worsen QTc prolongation
– Continuous cardiac monitoring for QTc
prolongation
r Neurologic:
– Treat seizures with benzodiazepines
– Assist ventilation for respiratory failure from
neuromuscular weakness
r Renal:
– Hemodialysis for renal failure
r Alimentary:
– Dextrose, enteral or parenteral feeding may be
beneficial
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Decontamination:
– Orogastric lavage or aspiration may be helpful
within the 1st hr of ingestion
– Activated charcoal does not bind arsenic
– If opacities are seen on abdominal film, administer
whole bowel irrigation (polyethylene glycol) at
1–2 L/hr until repeat radiographs are clear
– If dermal exposure, decontaminate skin as 1st
step in management
r Ensure that no one else is contaminated and
environment is evaluated
r Ensure that electrolytes such as calcium,
magnesium, and potassium are replaced
r Evaluate need for chelation therapy, based on levels,
acuity of exposure, clinical symptoms:
– Consult with medical toxicologist/poison center
– Agents
◦Dimercaprol (British anti-Lewisite)
◦DMSA (succimer)
r Elimination:
– Hemodialysis not routinely effective
◦Consider for patient with renal failure or other
hemodialysis indications
◦Continue chelation throughout hemodialysis
sessions
MEDICATIONr Dimercaprol (British anti-Lewisite): 3 mg/kg deep IM
q4h for 24 h, then q6h for the next 24 h, then q12h
until able to tolerate PO
– Caution: Contraindicated in patients with peanut
allergies
r Dextrose 50%: 25 g (50 mL) (peds: 0.5 g/kg D25W)
IV for hypoglycemia
r DMSA (succimer): 10 mg/kg PO q8h for 5 d, then
q12h for 14 d
r Sodium bicarbonate: 1 mEq/kg IV bolus, followed by
infusion of 150 mEq in 1 L of D5W at 150 mL/h
– Used to treat rhabdomyolysis
– Ensure that potassium and other electrolytes are
monitored and replaced during infusion
r Naloxone: 0.4–2.0 mg (peds: 0.1 mg/kg) IV , may
repeat up to 10 mg for suspected opioid intoxication
r Thiamine: 100 mg IM or IV (peds: 1 mg/kg)
r Vasopressors after sufficient fluids
– Dopamine 5 μg/kg/min, increase by
5–10 μg/kg/min (q10–30min) Max.:
20 μg/kg/min
– Norepinephrine 0.01–3 μg/kg/min, start at
2 μg/min, titrate to MAP 65–90 mm Hg
r Max.: 20 μg/min
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteria
Symptomatic arsenic exposures should be admitted to
an intensive care setting.
Discharge Criteriar Asymptomatic patients with a spot urinary arsenic
level <50 μg/L may be discharged
r Suspected chronic exposures who do not require
admission should be referred for outpatient
evaluation and 24 hr urine collection
r Ensure that home environment is safe for patient
prior to discharge
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Psychiatric follow-up for intentional overdoses
r Primary care follow-up for cancer screening and
monitoring
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Arsenic poisoning results in a myriad of signs and
symptoms
– Suspect acute arsenic poisoning when patients
present with gastrointestinal distress and
neurologic findings.
– Suspect chronic arsenic poisoning in patients who
present with neurologic deficits, nonspecific
wasting, and hyperkeratotic skin lesions.
r Consult a medical toxicologist/poison center
regarding the need for chelation therapy.
A special thanks goes to Dr. Gerald Maloney Jr, who
contributed to the previous edition.

ARTERIAL GAS EMBOLISM (AGE)
Nicole L. Lunceford r Catherine M. Visintainer r Peter J. Park
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Results when air bubbles enter the pulmonary
venous return from ruptured alveoli, then propagate
through the systemic vasculature:
– Clinical manifestations depend on location of air
bubbles in systemic vasculature system.
r Also known as dysbaric air embolism or cerebral air
embolism
r Caused by overpressurization of lung tissue, causing
pleural tear with air entering the vascular
circulation:
– Trapped air (in lungs with closed glottis) expands
on diver ascent.
– Boyle law: At a constant temperature, pressure (P)
is inversely related to volume (V):
◦PV = K (constant) or P1V1 = P2V2
– As pressure increases/decreases, volume
decreases/increases.
ETIOLOGYr Pulmonary atrioventricular (AV) shunts, or as
paradoxical embolism via a patent foramen ovale
r Breath holding during ascent:
– Symptoms attributable to a shower of bubbles
and multiple blood vessel involvement
r Iatrogenically during placement of central venous
pressure (CVP) lines, cardiothoracic surgery, or
hemodialysis
r Penetrating injuries to heart, with emergent repair
of cardiac wound
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Cerebral:
– Rapid onset:
◦Almost all cases of AGE present within 1st
5 min of surfacing, although most often
symptoms are evident in 1st 2 min
– Dive-related stroke
– 2 main presentations:
◦Apnea and full cardiopulmonary arrest
◦Any combination of neurologic deficits
– Presentation depends on arterial distribution of
gas embolism:
◦Stupor or confusion (24%)
◦Coma without seizure (22%)
◦Coma with seizures (18%)
◦Unilateral motor deficits (14%)
◦Visual disturbances (9%)
◦Vertigo (8%)
◦Unilateral sensory deficits (8%)
◦Bilateral motor deficits (8%)
◦Collapse (4%)
– Spontaneous improvement minutes after initial
deficits may occur:
◦High incidence of relapse
◦Improvement may be transiently related to
postural changes that affect distribution of
bubbles flowing to brain.
r Pulmonary:
– Dyspnea
– Hemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain
– Subcutaneous air
r Cardiac:
– MI owing to air in coronary vessels
– Reduced cardiac output owing to air trapped in
ventricle
– Hamman sign: Crepitus on auscultation of heart
r Renal:
– Renal infarction owing to air embolism
History
Elicit time of symptom onset in relation to dive
surfacing (almost all symptoms occur within the 1st
10 min).
Physical Exam
Careful neurologic exam owing to the wide variety of
neurologic manifestations
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Clinical diagnosis: Recognize risk factors and various
clinical presentations.
r Inquire as to unusual circumstances during ascent:
– Breath holding
– Panic/out-of-air situation
r Thorough neurologic exam must carefully document
the extent of the deficits to the motor, sensory,
cerebellar, and cranial nerves.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Serum creatinine kinase activity:
– Marker of the severity of cerebral AGE
r CBC
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose
r ABG when respiratory symptoms are present
Imagingr CXR:
– For evidence of pneumothorax or mediastinal
emphysema (both rare)
r Chest CT
– For evidence of local lung injury or hemorrhage
r Ventilation Perfusion Scan
– For evidence consistent with pulmonary emboli
r EKG
r Echo:
– Looking for evidence of patent foramen ovale
r CT head:
– For altered mental status
– Do not delay recompression for CT when AGE
almost certain clinically.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Cerebrovascular accident (CVA) from causes
unrelated to gas embolism
r Neurologic deficits owing to decompression sickness

ARTERIAL GAS EMBOLISM (AGE)
A
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Cautions:
– Patients who experience sudden neurologic
recovery can relapse quickly as bubble positions
change.
– Recognize AGE as a potential diagnosis.
r Altered mental status within 10 min of surfacing
from compressed air dive
r Sudden neurologic decompensation following
placement of central line
r Controversies:
– Trendelenburg positioning patients with suspected
AGE is not effective:
◦Hypothesized that elevation of legs could cause
air bubbles to migrate away from cerebral
circulation and that increased hydrostatic
pressure in brain will shrink bubbles
◦Trendelenburg positioning may in fact increase
injury by increasing intracerebral pressure.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
ABCs:
r 100% oxygen by tight-fitting mask
r Intubation for ventilation/protection of airway
required
r IV access with volume augmentation
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Hyperbaric oxygen recompression therapy (see
“Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy”):
– For all AGE
– Arrange transportation to nearest hyperbaric
facility.
– Aircraft capable of cabin pressurization below
1,000 feet barometric pressure best suited for
transfers
– Prophylactic chest tube for simple pneumothorax
to prevent conversion to tension pneumothorax
during recompression
– Fill endotracheal and Foley catheter balloons with
water or saline to avoid shrinkage/damage during
recompression.
r Divers alert network (DAN):
– Based at Duke University Medical Center
– Provides 24 hr emergency hotline for medical
consultation on treatment of dive-related injuries
and for referrals to hyperbaric chambers
(telephone: [919] 684-8111)
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteria
Admit all following initial hyperbaric therapy for
observation and re-exam.
Discharge Criteria
No AGE patients should be discharged from the ED.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Hyperbaric oxygen referral for patients with arterial
gas embolisms
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Symptoms occur during ascent or within 10 min of
reaching the surface.
r Patients who experience sudden neurologic recovery
can relapse quickly as bubble positions change.
r Fill endotracheal and Foley catheter balloons with
water or saline to avoid shrinkage/damage during
recompression.

ARTERIAL OCCLUSION
Richard E. Wolfe
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Immediate and severe compromise of the blood supply
to a limb, threatening its viability, secondary to the
sudden blockage of a peripheral artery
r Arterial embolization
– Thrombus or plaque
– Originates from aneurysms or atherosclerotic
lesions
– Emboli typically lodge where there is an acute
narrowing of the artery
– 75% of emboli involve an axial limb vasculature
◦Femoral 28%
◦Arm 20%
◦Aortoiliac 18%
◦Popliteal 17%
◦Visceral and other 9%
r Thrombosis
r Arterial dissection
r Trauma
– Crush injuries
– Compression
– Arterial contusion and thrombosis
– Arterial transection
r Limb ischemia >6 hr usually results in functional
impairment or limb loss.
– If acute on chronic, collateral circulation may
preserve tissue beyond 6 hr.
ETIOLOGYr Embolus:
– Atrial fibrillation
– Myocardial infarction
– Valvular disease
– Endocarditis
– Atrial myxoma
– Aneurysm
– Atherosclerotic plaques
– Paradoxical embolus
◦Patent foramen ovale
r Thrombosis
– Vascular grafts
– Atherosclerosis
– Thrombosis of an aneurysm
– Entrapment syndrome
– Blood clotting disorders
– Low flow state
– Heparin-induced thrombosis
r Arterial dissection
r Arterial injury:
– Intimal flap
– Dissection
– Pseudoaneurysms
– Iatrogenic
◦Catheterization
◦Arteriography
◦Balloon angioplasty
◦Complication of arterial puncture
– Penetrating trauma
◦Gunshot, stab wounds, shotgun, shrapnel
◦IV drug use
– Blunt trauma
◦Joint displacement
◦Fracture
◦Compartment syndrome
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Sudden onset of a cold, painful leg
r The 6 Ps:
– Pain
◦Gradual, initially increasing in severity then
decreasing with progressive sensory loss
◦Distal progressing proximally
◦Sudden onset with embolization
– Pallor
– Paresthesias
– Paralysis
– Pulseless (late finding)
– Polar (Cold)
r Progressive peripheral nerve dysfunction
– Early loss of proprioception and light touch
– Loss of sensation and weakness follows
r Blue toe syndrome:
– Development of blue or violaceous discoloration in
one or more toes
– The affected digits are often painful.
– The cyanosis initially blanches with pressure or leg
elevation.
r Signs of severe obstruction and poor prognosis
– Absent capillary flow
– Skin marbling
– Loss of distal pulses
– Paralysis
Historyr Time of onset
r History of claudication or cramps
– Reproducible discomfort of a defined group of
muscles that is induced by exercise and relieved
with rest
r Past medical history to identify risk factors for
thrombosis or embolus
Physical Examr Sensory loss
r Muscle weakness
r Skin color changes
r Loss of pulse
r Signs of chronic arterial insufficiency:
– Hair loss
– Atrophic skin
r Ankle-brachial pressure index measurement
– Measure arm systolic pressure with the Doppler
flowmeter for accuracy
– Record pressure in both arms and both tibial
arteries at the ankle.
– Ratio of systolic BP in the lower legs to the
brachial pressure in the arm:
◦Place cuff above malleoli to measure pressure in
lower legs
◦Use Doppler at posterior tibial or dorsalis pedis
artery
– Chronic PVD <0.9
– Acute arterial occlusion <0.5
r Demarcation of the warm part of the extremity to
the cold part to estimate level of the obstruction
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
ALERT
Elevation, cool compress or ice, or warm compress
to the affected extremity is contraindicated.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Electrolytes/anion gap
r BUN
r Creatinine
r CBC
r Creatine phosphokinase

ARTERIAL OCCLUSION
A
Imagingr The utility of imaging in the ED is limited as most of
the decision making is based on the clinical
presentation
r Duplex US
– Provides a “roadmap” of stenosis of the arteries
of the lower extremities
r CT angiography
– With multidetectors, performance is similar to
angiography
– Like angiography it requires IV contrast bolus and
exposure to radiation
r MRI
– Viable alternative to angiography.
– Noninvasive
– Does not required contrast material
r Angiography
Classiﬁcationr Class 1: Viable
– Pain but no paralysis or sensory loss
– Needs attention, not in immediate danger
r Class 2: Threatened but salvageable
– 2A: Some sensory loss, no paralysis: No
immediate threat.
– 2B: Sensory and motor loss: Needs immediate
treatment
r Class 3: Irreversible/nonviable:
– Sensory loss, paralysis, absent capillary flow, skin
marbling, absent arterial Doppler flow
– Will require amputation
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Lumbar spine disorders
r Back pain, mechanical
r Decreased cardiac output owing to advanced
atherosclerotic disease
r Frostbite
r Peripheral neuropathy
r Aneurysm, abdominal
r Ankle injury, soft tissue
r Deep venous thrombosis
r Septic thrombophlebitis
r Superficial thrombophlebitis
r Trauma, peripheral vascular injuries
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Early recognition and rapid transport to an
emergency department
r Place the limb in a dependent position
r Keeping the limb warm
r Oxygen by nasal cannula
r Aspirin
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Prompt consultation with vascular surgeon
r Heparin bolus followed by an infusion
r Class 1: Viable
– Most often due to thrombosis
– Intra-arterial thrombolytic agents versus surgical
revascularization or endovascular repair
depending on viability of limb
r Class 2: Threatened but salvageable
– Immediate surgical revascularization
– Embolectomy if indicated
– Angiography and oral anticoagulation post op
r Class 3: Nonviable
– Prompt amputation
– Clinical assessment, imaging usually not required
r Pain control
MEDICATIONr Heparin: Weight-based protocol anticoagulation
with typical 80 U/kg loading bolus; 18 U/kg/h IV
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar All patients with clinical diagnosis of acute arterial
occlusion or (ABI <0.5) should be admitted after an
emergency consultation with a vascular surgeon.
Discharge Criteriar Patients with chronic occlusive disease, resolved
pain, and stable ABI measurements
r No other acute medical issues (e.g., new atrial
fibrillation)
r Vascular surgical follow-up can be ensured.
r Patients should be instructed to return for any
recurrent or progressive symptoms.
Issues for Referralr PVD patents in which illness is not severe or acute
as to require inpatient treatment may be discharged
with appropriate follow-up with a vascular surgeon.
r Potential effects of various activities and medications
on the course of their illness should be discussed.
r Education on smoking cessation, temperature
extremes, and vasoconstricting medications should
be considered.

ARTHRITIS, DEGENERATIVE
Patrick H. Sweet
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Degenerative arthritis or osteoarthritis (OA) is the
most common progressive joint disease, with
20–30 million cases in the US
r Found almost exclusively in the elderly
ETIOLOGYr Mechanism
r Repetitive stress to synovial joints associated with
age
r May be seen in younger patients secondary to joint
trauma
r Articular cartilage destruction:
– Reactive changes in joint margin bone and
subchondral sclerosis
r Risk factors include age, obesity, trauma, genetics,
sex, and environment.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Chronic progressive joint pain:
– Worse with weight bearing, improved with rest
r Asymmetric joint involvement:
– Involves hand, foot, knee, hip, and spine joints
r Morning joint stiffness usually <30 min
r Joint deformity late in presentation with limited
range of motion
r Heberden nodes at the distal interphalangeal joints
r Bouchard nodes at the proximal interphalangeal
joints
r Absence of systemic symptoms
r Crepitus common
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Thorough joint exam with assessment of range of
motion and functional ability
r Radiographic exam: Typical findings in OA are
decreased joint space, irregular bone at the joint
margin, and osteophytes.
r Synovial fluid analysis in the setting of effusion may
be therapeutic and diagnostic (see below), but is
absolutely necessary if presents with warmth and
erythema so as to rule out a septic joint or gout.
r ESR, CRP , and CBC if infection is in the differential
as arthrocentesis may be indicated if a more
superficial infection cannot be ruled out (e.g., septic
bursitis, cellulitis, etc.).
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Synovial fluid exam typically reveals the following:
r Clear
r Elevated leukocyte cell count, but <4,000/mm3
r <25% polymorphonuclear leukocytes
r Glucose level similar to blood levels (95–100%)
Imagingr Radiographs
r Joint space narrowing
r Osteophyte formation
r Marginal bone erosion
r Subchondral sclerosis
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Gout or pseudogout
r Septic arthritis
r Rheumatoid arthritis
r Charcot joint
r Hemarthrosis
r Overlying bursitis or soft tissue infection
TREATMENT
The general goal of treatment is to provide relief from
symptoms. A patient may have significant radiographic
evidence of disease but have very few symptoms.
Therefore the treatment regimen is tailored to the
patient’s symptomatology.
PRE-HOSPITAL
Immobilization of affected joint may be indicated until
fracture is excluded.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Pain management acutely
r Begin a daily medication that can be managed on
follow-up with primary care physician.
r Instructions for gentle strengthening exercises
r Avoidance of unnecessary joint immobilization
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURES
Intra-articular (IA) arthrocentesis and injection:
r Ultrasound (US) guidance is recommended when
expertise and instrument is available
r Shown to be an effective low-risk intervention for
OA with or without effusion
r Though relatively rare in larger joints, dry tap is a
possible finding due to anatomic features of joint
and periarticular soft tissue (e.g., fat pad).
– US very useful in this case
r Careful attention must be given to aseptic technique
while joint is in proper position to reduce muscle
tension, exposing joint space.
r Vapor coolant or lidocaine 1% or 2% can be used
for local anesthesia.
r Usually 1.5 in or greater 22G or 18G hypodermic
needle should be used with 1 syringe for
arthrocentesis and another for IA corticosteroid
injection.

ARTHRITIS, DEGENERATIVE
A
r If septic joint cannot be ruled out, corticosteroids
should not be administered after arthrocentesis.
Corticosteroid dosing equivalents:
r Small joints—wrist and foot:
– Methylprednisolone
10–20 mg, triamcinolone 10 mg, betamethasone
0.75–1.5 mg
r Medium-sized joints—elbow and ankle:
– Methylprednisolone 40–80 mg, triamcinolone
20 mg, betamethasone 3–6 mg
r Large joints—knee and shoulder:
– Methylprednisolone 80–120 mg, triamcinolone
40 mg; betamethasone 6–9 mg
r Some studies show triamcinolone to be more
efficacious than other corticosteroids; the author
recommends this, if available.
MEDICATION
General guidelines:
r Acetaminophen is drug of choice initially as it has a
safer medication profile compared with NSAIDs and
has been shown to be as efficacious in some
patients.
r If one class fails, consider another class (e.g.,
salicylates vs. COX-2 inhibitors).
r The 2 alternative medications below have been
shown to have a small but positive effect by
meta-analysis of recent studies and can be
considered adjuncts.
r Postprandial administration is recommended for all
these. Patients at increased risk for GI bleeding (e.g.,
history of peptic ulcer disease, etc.) should be placed
on COX-2 inhibitors or alternatively a proton pump
inhibitor can be given with a nonselective COX
inhibitor.
r NSAIDs:
– Celecoxib (reversible COX-2–selective) 400 mg PO
mg PO q24:
◦Note: Contraindicated in sulfonamide allergy
– Ibuprofen (reversible nonselective COX):
400–600 mg PO q6h
– Naprosyn (reversible nonselective COX): 500 mg
PO q12h
– Meloxicam (reversible nonselective COX): 7.5 mg
PO q12h or 7.5–15 mg PO q24h
r Analgesics:
– Acetaminophen: 500 mg (peds: 10–15 mg/kg, do
not exceed 5 doses/24 h) PO q4–6h, do not
exceed 4 g/24 h
– Tramadol: 50 mg PO q4–6h:
◦Note: Use cautiously in elderly, patients with
seizure disorders, concurrently using
antidepressants, or in hepatic or renal
dysfunction.
– Other opioid narcotics rarely used
r Alternative therapies (separate or in combination):
– Glucosamine: 500 mg PO q8h
– Chondroitin: 1200 mg PO q24h
r Lifestyle modification:
– Weight loss for the obese
– Strengthening exercises
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteria
Rarely indicated in the absence of fracture
Discharge Criteriar Ambulatory and capable of activities of daily living
r Improvement in symptoms (i.e., pain)
Sports Medicine Follow-upr Consider referral to sports medicine clinic for
definitive management
ADDITIONAL READING
r Hepper CT, Halvorson JJ, Duncan ST, et al. The
efficacy and duration of intra-articular corticosteroid
injection for knee osteoarthritis: A systematic review
of level I studies. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2009;
17(10):638–646.
r National Center for Complimentary and Alternative
Medicine. The NIH Glucosamine/Chondroitin

ARTHRITIS, JUVENILE IDIOPATHIC
Kathleen A. Kerrigan rKenneth G. Christian
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Previously called JRA
r JIA comprises persistent, unexplained arthritis
lasting >6 wk, occurring <17 yr of age, and
affecting a heterogeneous group of children.
r Prevalence up to 1 in 1,000 children
r Girls > boys for most forms
r Classified into 7 subgroups: Systemic onset,
polyarticular RF+, polyarticular RF-, pauciarticular,
psoriatic, enthesitis, other or unclassified.
r Subtypes are based on number, type, and symmetry
of joints involved; presence of systemic symptoms;
skin involvement; family history; and lab values.
r Up to 20% of JIA patients remain unclassified or are
classified in multiple categories.
r Natural course of the disease depends on the
subtype (pauciarticular with overall best prognosis),
but full resolution occurs in <50% of JIA patients.
r Many will have a fluctuating course and ongoing
disease through adulthood.
ETIOLOGY
Believed to be an autoimmune disease triggered by an
unknown environmental trigger in a genetically
susceptible host
DIAGNOSIS
Subtypesr Systemic onset:
– 10% of cases, girls = boys
– Associated fever and arthritis:
◦Fever: Diurnal (>39◦C) of >2 wk duration,
child looks ill during temperature spike
◦Arthritis: May involve any number of joints and
may appear only weeks to months after onset of
fever
– In addition there must be 1 of the following:
◦Maculopapular, salmon-colored rash on trunk
and axillae
◦Lymphadenopathy
◦Hepatosplenomegaly
◦Serositis
– Most acute, ill appearing of subtypes
– Destructive arthritis >50%
ALERT
r Systemic onset JIA patients are at risk for
macrophage activation syndrome (MAS).
r MAS is a proliferation of macrophages causing a
DIC-like picture with resultant fever, mucosal
bleeding, neurologic changes and multisystem
failure.
r ESR may be normal in active MAS
r MAS mortality is 8–22%.
r Pauciarticular:
– 50% of cases of IJA
– 80% girls, peak incidence 2–4 yr olds
– Insidious onset and child appears healthy
– ≤4 joints involved at 6 mo:
◦Involves larger joints, (89% knee) hip rarely
affected
◦Joints swollen, mildly tender, with decreased
range of motion (ROM), possible leg-length
discrepancy
– Uveitis in about 20%; no other systemic signs
– Subset termed extended pauciarticular
progresses to greater joint involvement after
6 mo and has worse prognosis
r Polyarticular:
– 10–30% of cases, girls > boys, bimodal peaks:
2–5 and 10–14 yr
– >4 joints involved at 6 mo:
◦Arthritis often symmetrical, small or large
joints—commonly knees, wrists, and ankles
◦Decreased ROM of cervical and lumbar spine
and temporomandibular joint (TMJ)
– Systemic involvement rare except for fatigue
and anemia
– Older girls with RF+ often go on to develop
typical adult rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and are
placed in a separate subtype.
r Psoriatic:
– Arthritis; asymmetric large joints of lower
extremities and back
– Psoriatic rash in patient or 2 of the following:
Dactylitis, nail pitting, psoriatic rash in
1st-degree relative
– Enthesitis-related (enthesis means pain at the
insertion of a muscle or tendon)
– Arthritis; asymmetric large joints of lower
extremities
– Boys > girls, age usually >6y r
– Sacroiliac (SI) joint pain
– Limited flexion of lumbar spine
– Uveitis
– Often FH
r Otherwise unclassified:
– Arthritis not fitting into any distinct category
Historyr Findings based on specific subtype
r Classic presentation is insidious arthritis, worse in
AM and with periods of immobility, improved with
ROM.
r New-onset systemic subtype most likely to use ED
because they appear acutely ill, whereas other
subtypes have a more insidious onset.
ALERT
r Child with severe pain and red-hot joint probably
does not have new-onset JIA.
r Rapid onset of polyarticular joint involvement is
atypical for JIA; infectious or reactive cause of
arthritis should be ruled out.
r Beware of occult infection in patients on
immunosuppressants.
Physical Examr Determine if child is systemically ill: Search for fever,
rash, or other nonarthritic involvement.
r Do careful joint evaluation, documenting the
number of joints involved and noting whether they
are red, warm, and swollen or have limited ROM.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Rule out septic joint and malignant bone tumor.
r Rule out other identifiable causes of joint
inflammation.
r Rule out complications from long-term drug therapy.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC, ESR; if ill appearance, add blood cultures
r Other labs if suspicious of specific subtype:
rheumatoid factor (RF), antinuclear antibodies
(ANA), HLA-B27, LFTs:
– Systemic—ESR often elevated, leukocytosis,
thrombocytosis, anemia, minor AST/ALT
elevations, positive RF or ANA rarely seen, MAS
may be associated with elevated LFTs and
abnormal clotting factors but will often have
normal ESR
– Pauciarticular—common to have positive ANA in
young girls; other labs usually normal; if anemic or
elevated ESR, are probably misclassified or
pauciarticular extended subtype
– Polyarticular—may be anemic; if positive RF more
likely to go on to adult RA, ESR may be elevated
– Enthesitis—more likely positive HLA; presence of
positive RF or positive ANA specifically excludes
enthesitis subtype
– Psoriatic arthritis—usually seronegative RF
r Unfortunately, RF and ESR may also be elevated in
acute infection unrelated to JIA.
ALERT
Consider adding Lyme titer if new joint swelling in
endemic area.

effusion
– Late presentation: Osteoporosis, joint destruction,
early growth plate closure
r Ultrasound:
– Evaluate for small effusion, especially if tap
considered.
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Arthrocentesis if concern for septic arthritis:
5,000–8,000 WBC/mm3 with negative Gram stain
and culture typical for JIA
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Trauma
r Infection:
– Septic arthritis, viral infection (especially
parvovirus), Lyme disease, rheumatic fever,
tuberculosis, subacute endocarditis, malaria,
Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection
r Other rheumatic/connective tissue diseases:
– Systemic lupus erythematosus, polyarteritis
nodosa, Henoch–Sch ¨ onlein purpura, sarcoid
– Legg–Calv ´ e–Perthes disease/slipped capital
femoral epiphysis
r Neoplasm:
– Be suspicious of neoplasm in a severely
uncomfortable child with midshaft bone pain.
r Hematologic disease:
– Sickle cell disease, hemophilia
r Drug reactions
TREATMENT
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Toxic-appearing children: IV access, O2
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr ED treatment is directed toward ruling out a septic
joint and other causes of acute arthritis
r If the diagnosis of JIA is already established and the
child presents with an acute flare, a treatment
plan/medication adjustment should be coordinated
with the child’s rheumatologist.
MEDICATIONr Medication in children with JIA is geared toward
eliminating clinical signs of active disease,
maximizing joint function, and preserving growth.
(Chronic inflammation can make affected limb
slightly longer.)
r Efficacy depends on JIA subtype and disease severity.
r Most pauciarticular JIA responds to NSAIDs and
joint injections; polyarticular and systemic JIA
usually require disease-modifying antirheumatic
drug (DMARD) therapy and/or biological agents.
r Antibiotics are indicated only if the joint is infected.
ALERT
As early aggressive therapy may prevent some of
the long-term complications of JIA, it is now
common for children to be placed on DMARDS and
biological agents early in the disease course. These
medications have serious potential side effects,
including:r Immunosuppression
r Decreased vaccine response (live vaccinations are
contraindicated)
r Increased potential for malignancy
r NSAIDs:
– Responsiveness differs within NSAID subtype
– Used alone in mild JIA subtype or with other
medications
– Ibuprofen: 30–45 mg/kg divided TID–QID
– Naproxen: 10–20 mg/kg divided BID; maximum
daily dose 1,000 mg
– Side effects: Gastritis, hepatitis, renal,
headache, dermatitis
– Intra-articular steroids: Triamcinolone
hexacetonide: 1 mL/mg of 20 mg/mL solution
– Often provide long-term (6–18 mo) relief
r DMARDs:
– Include corticosteroids, methotrexate,
sulfasalazine
– Corticosteroids
– Use judiciously because of long-term
complications, but high-dose pulse therapy may
be needed in acute attack.
– Prednisone: 0.5–2 mg/kg PO
– Methylprednisolone: 30 mg/kg daily IV up to 1 g
for 1–5 days for high-dose pulse steroids
– Side effects: Gastritis, adrenal suppression,
osteopenia, Cushing syndrome, infection
– Methotrexate: 5–15 mg/m2 PO/SC or IM per
week
– Considered 1st-line DMARD, as most will
respond
– Side effects: GI, nausea, liver toxicity,
teratogenic
– Sulfasalazine: 30 mg/kg/d divided QID
– Poorly tolerated in up to 30%
– Side effects: GI, rash, anorexia
– Biological agents—engineered to target specific
key cytokines, very expensive
– Tissue necrosis factor binders
r Etanercept: 0.8 mg/kg SC once a week
– Adalimumab: < 30 kg: 20 mg, > 30 kg: 40 mg
given SC administered every other week
– Side effects: Infection, injection-site reactions,
inhibit T-cell activation
– Abatacept: 10 mg/kg infusion q4wk
– Side effects: Infusion reaction, HA, cough,
nausea, infection
r Non-FDA–approved therapies:
r Remicade, rituximab, anakira, leflunomide IL-1
and IL-6 blockers
r Stem cell transplants are used rarely for severe
cases unresponsive to medical treatment:
– Treatment for MAS is nonstandardized but may
include high-dose steroids, cyclosporine,
cyclophosphamide, or intravenous
immunoglobulin
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteria
Unclear diagnosis in ill-appearing child or if concern of
secondary joint infection
Discharge Criteriar No evidence of septic joint, systemic infection, or
organ failure from drug therapy
r Patient appears comfortable.
r Appropriate follow-up has been arranged.
Issues for Referralr Orthopedics if septic joint suspected
r Rheumatologist if meds need adjustment
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Children need long-term consults with a
rheumatologist.
r Children with JIA need frequent eye exams to rule
out uveitis (which is often asymptomatic until
permanent damage has occurred).
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Rule out acute joint infection (always consider Lyme
disease in the appropriate geographic context).
r Consider systemic onset JIA in child with prolonged
diurnal febrile illness that is unresponsive to
antibiotics.
r Consider MAS in systemic onset JIA patients who
appear septic.
r Review patient’s medications to identify potential
side effects or immunosuppression.

ARTHRITIS, MONOARTICULAR
Paul Blackburn
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Localized to 1 joint, not migratory
r 1 etiology does not exclude another
r Infectious (septic) arthritis: Rapidly destructive
process causes significant disability
– Contiguous extension (cellulitis, osteomyelitis),
hematogenous spread, direct inoculation
– Predisposing factors:
◦Local pathology (inflammatory arthritis, trauma,
prosthetic joint)
◦Immunosuppression
◦IV drug use
r Crystalline:
– Gout: Uric acid overproduction or underexcretion,
deposited within and around joints.
– Pseudogout: Calcium pyrophosphate
r Noninflammatory conditions
– Osteoarthritis (DJD), trauma (fractures,
hemarthrosis), autoimmune disorders
– Progressive joint destruction; mechanical
dysfunction
◦Bone reactive changes (spurring)
◦Subchondral bony erosions
ETIOLOGYr Infectious (septic)
– Most common organisms nongonococcal
◦Gram-positives: Streptococcus, Staphylococcus
(80%)
– Some associations:
◦Staphylococcus aureus: (trauma, IV drug use)
◦Neisseria gonorrhea (STD)
◦Salmonella (sickle cell) but most common
causes in sickle cell same (Staphylococcus,
Streptococcus)
◦Less common: Fungal (chronic), spirochete
(Lyme), viral (polyarticular), mycobacteria (TB)
r Crystalline:
– Gout: Uric acid overproduction, underexcretion
within, around joints
– Tophi: Crystal deposits near recurrent flare sites.
Progressive enlargement, may ulcerate “spit out”
(discharge) crystals
– Negatively birefringent crystals
– Pseudogout: Calcium pyrophosphate
– Positively birefringent crystal
– Bariatric surgery: Postoperative gout flares
common, frequent, significant. Prophylactic
treatment effective, recommended
r Inflammatory
– Diligent search for underlying cause, resultant
conditions: arthridites (rheumatoid, psoriatic),
inflammatory bowel disease, Reiter syndrome
r Noninflammatory conditions
– Osteoarthritis or degenerative joint disease (DJD),
overuse, overload (obesity)
– Trauma (fractures, hemarthrosis)
– Hemorrhagic disorders
– Neuropathic disorders (Charcot joint)
Pediatric Considerations
r Infectious (septic) arthritis
– Low incidence, high morbidity, sepsis (8%)
– Most common: S. aureus, hip > knee, 50%
coexisting osteomyelitis
– Present like adults: Joint swollen, painful,
worsened with weight bearing, movement;
constitutionally ill (fever, lassitude)
– Immediate aspiration, empiric treatment,
admission mandatory
r Inflammatory
– A diagnosis only after septic joint excluded; then
considerations same as adults
r Noninflammatory:
r Orthopedic considerations to not overlook:
– Salter–Harris epiphyseal plate fractures
– Congenital hip dysplasia
– Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE)
◦Overweight adolescents
– Legg–Calve–Perthes:
◦Osteonecrosis femoral head
◦Age 4–9
– Bleeding disorders, hemorrhage
DIAGNOSIS
Early accurate diagnosis allows directed therapy,
earlier resumption of function, activities of daily living
(ADL); longer-term morbidity lessened
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Isolated to 1 joint, not migratory
– Acute pain, swelling, redness, warmth
– Decreased range of motion, nonweight bearing
(effusion, pain, osteomyelitis)
r Infectious (septic) arthritis:
– Constitutionally ill, fever, chills
– Larger joints swollen, painful range motion
◦Knee > hip = shoulder > ankle > wrist
– N. gonorrhea: Urethral discharge painful, purulent
(males)
– Lyme disease:
◦Spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi
◦Deer tick (Ixodes dammini)
◦Circular expanding, centrally clearing, eruption
(erythema chronicum migrans)
◦Knees, shoulders most common
r Crystalline:
– Sudden, severe pain, swelling, erythema
– Recurrent, self-limited flares
– Gout: Great toe joint (“podagra”) > ankle >
tarsal joints > knee
– Tophi: Crystal granulomas overlying affected
joints; ulcerate, drain crystals
– Pseudogout: Knee > wrist > ankle = elbow
r Inflammatory:
– Protean manifestations, findings related to
systemic conditions
– Individual, multiple, combination organ system
involvement. Example: Reiter syndrome: Iritis,
urethritis, arthritis
r Noninflammatory conditions
– Osteoarthritis (DJD):
◦Stiffness AM (inactivity), after activity (synovial
gelling), relieved with rest
– Trauma: Acute or distant, gradual swelling
episodes, pain pattern same as DJD
– Neuropathic: Charcot joint (“bag of bones”), little
or no pain—chronic neuropathy
– Hemarthrosis, hemorrhagic disorders
Historyr See “Description,” “Etiology,” “Pediatric
Considerations,” and “Signs and Symptoms.”
r Complete, meticulous history: Joint issues or
involvement (recent, remote), systemic conditions
(direct, local, remote manifestations), immune status
(HIV , medications, disease process), STD (history,
exposure, treatment type and duration), IV drug use.
Physical Exam
See “Description” and “Signs and Symptoms.”
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Meticulous history and physical exam
r Condition—related diagnostic studies
r Arthrocentesis for synovial fluid analysis is the
definitive diagnostic procedure.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Blood testing never the key diagnostic studies of
choice for monoarticular arthritis; provides ancillary,
corroborative, exclusionary information.
r Arthrocentesis for synovial fluid aspiration and
analysis the definitive diagnostic procedure and
studies.
r Synovial fluid culture the definitive synovial study
regarding infection, but results not immediate
(inherent nature of the test)
r Fluid appearance: Clear versus turbid, serous versus
bloody, viscosity (“string sign”), volume removed,
associated pain (levels, trends)
r Synovial fluid white blood cells (WBC),
polymorphonuclear (PMN) predominance suggests
septic etiology
– WBC >50,000/mm3 increases likelihood of septic
arthritis
r Synovial glucose: Most useful compared to
concurrent blood glucose levels
– Synovial glucose less than half blood value
indicates likely septic process

ARTHRITIS, RHEUMATOID
Charles F. Lanzillo rStephen R. Hayden
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Chronic systemic inflammatory disorder that attacks
the joints:
– Nonsuppurative, proliferative synovitis
– Destruction of the articular cartilage
– Ankylosis of the joint
r Involvement of knee is common.
r Baker cysts may be seen in chronic disease.
r Involvement of spine is limited to cervical
region:
– May cause atlantoaxial subluxation
– Rarely results in cord compression
Pediatric Considerations
Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA) is a distinct entity
(see “Arthritis, Juvenile Idiopathic”).
r Genetics:
– Genetic predisposition related to HLA-DR4
– Female-to-male ratio is 3:1.
– Typical age of onset is between 30 and 50.
ETIOLOGYr Etiology is unknown.
r Possible triggers include infection and autoimmune
response.
r Prevalence is about 1% of both US and world
population.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Malaise, fatigue
r Generalized musculoskeletal pain
r After weeks to months, patients develop swollen,
warm, painful joints.
r Often worse in morning
r Joint involvement usually symmetric and
polyarticular
r Starting in small joints of hands and feet:
– Later wrists, elbow, and knees
r Distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of hand generally
not involved:
– Presence of swelling in these joints should suggest
another type of arthritis.
r Synovitis is typically gradual.
r Classic joint findings in long-standing disease:
– Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) swelling with ulnar
deviation
– Swan neck and boutonniere deformities
r Extra-articular complications:
– SC nodules
– Vasculitis
– Pericarditis or myocarditis
– Pulmonary fibrosis
– Pneumonitis
–S j¨ogren syndrome
– Mononeuritis multiplex
r Evidence of mild pericarditis on echocardiogram is
found in up to 1/3 of patients.
r Consider ECG evaluation in these patients
r Patients usually present to ED owing to
exacerbations of the disease or complication in
other organ systems:
– Airway obstruction from cricoarytenoid arthritis or
laryngeal nodules
– Heart block, constrictive pericarditis, pericardial
effusion with possible tamponade or myocarditis
– Pulmonary fibrosis, pleuritis, intrapulmonary
nodules, or pneumonitis

r Rheumatoid factor: Elevated in ∼70% of cases

– Narrowing of joint space

r Gout

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Bacteria can be introduced into a joint by:
– Hematogenous spread (most common)
– Invasive procedures
– Contiguous infection (e.g., osteomyelitis, cellulitis)
– Direct inoculation such as plant thorns or nails
r Acute inflammatory process results in migration of
WBCs into joint.
r Synovial hyperplasia, cartilage damage, and
formation of a purulent effusion
r Irreversible loss of function in up to 50%
r Mortality rate reported as high as 11%
Pediatric Considerations
r Hip infections are most common:
– Often in patients with otitis media, upper
respiratory tract infections or history of femoral
venipuncture
– Complications of septic arthritis (SA) of hip in
children: Avascular necrosis, epiphyseal
separation, pathologic dislocation, and arthritis
r 50% occur in children <3 yr old.
r Infants present with irritability, fever, and loss of
appetite.
r Older children present with fever, and a limp or
refusal to bear weight or use joint.
ETIOLOGYr Risk factors:
– Old age, infancy
– Rheumatoid arthritis and degenerative joint
disease
– Intravenous drug user (IVDU), endocarditis
– Females (gonococcal [GC] infection)
– Immunosuppression (AIDS, diabetes,
chemotherapy, steroid therapy)
– Repeated joint injections, pre-existing joint
diseases, trauma, or prosthesis
– Skin infection, cutaneous ulcers
r No bacterial pathogen is identified in 10–20%.
r Most common organisms:
– Staphylococcus aureus in adults, hip infections
(80%), and patients with rheumatoid arthritis or
diabetes
– Multidrug-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) has been
noted in some studies to be the most common
organism in community-onset adult SA.
– Neisseria gonorrhoeae most common in young,
healthy, sexually active patients (incidence has
decreased over the past decades due to a decrease
in the incidence of mucosal GC infections)
r Other pathogens: Group A β-hemolytic and group
B, C, and G streptococci:
– Gram-negative rods (e.g., Pseudomonas
aeruginosa, Escherichia. coli) in 10% of cases
– Neisseria meningitides (12% of patients with
meningococcal meningitis)
r Common in old age, infancy, immunosuppression,
and IVDU (Pseudomonas)
r Anaerobes: Diabetes, prosthetic joints
r Mycobacterial and fungal causes: Atypical (e.g. in
advanced HIV); more indolent course
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Presents abruptly as a single painful, swollen, warm,
tender joint
r Common findings include:
– Fever
– A separate source of infection (e.g., skin)
– Extremely painful joint motion in all planes
– A joint effusion (less evident in sacroiliac, hip, and
shoulder)
r Any joint can be involved:
– Typically a single joint is involved.
– Most commonly knee, then hip, shoulder, and
ankle
r Commonly seen in IVDUs: Sacroiliac costochondral
and sternoclavicular joints:
– Vertebral involvement such as lumbar facets
possible
r Human and animal bites, plant thorns, local steroid
therapy, and trauma may lead to infection in atypical
locations.
r Polyarticular involvement in 10–20%:
– Mostly with rheumatoid arthritis; delay in
diagnosis from low suspicion and more subtle
presentations (fever in only 50%)
– Patients with sepsis
r GC SA features:
– Develops in 1–3% of untreated gonorrhea and in
42–85% of disseminated GC infection:
r Typically monoarticular but commonly polyarticular
r Migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis (present in
20% of patients with arthritis), and dermatitis:
– Involves small joints (e.g., fingers, wrist, elbow,
ankle)
r Signs of urethral or vaginal GC infection may be
present.
r Painless maculopapular lesions on trunk, arms, legs,
and around affected joint
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Arthrocentesisr Perform joint aspiration in any suspected case.
r Send fluid for protein and glucose, cell count, Gram
stain, and culture.
r Typical SA findings:
– A turbid, purulent, or serosanguineous fluid
– A leukocytosis (50,000–150,000/mm3) with a
polymorphonuclear predominance (>75%)
– Often a decreased glucose and elevated protein
level
r Appearance of crystals does not rule out SA.
r Use special stain or culture media when indicated
(e.g., GC, anaerobes, fungus, mycobacterium)
r Intra-articular lidocaine reduces the sensitivity of
subsequent cultures; immediate emptying of
aspirated sample into a blood culture flask increases
the yield.
r In non-GC SA, Gram stain and culture are positive in
50% and 90% of cases, respectively:
– Drops to nearly 10% and 50% in GC SA,
respectively
r Real-time PCR can detect bacterial pathogen DNA in
many culture-negative aspirates.
r Fluoroscopic, sonographic, or CT guidance can be
used in technically difficult aspirations.
r CT scan and MRI may aid in the diagnosis for joints
such as the sacroiliac joint.
r Arthrocentesis is contraindicated whenever there is
an underlying joint prosthesis or an overlying skin
infection:
– If cellulitis present, use an alternate approach
through normal skin.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Nonspecific serum leukocytosis (more common in
children), left shift, and C-reactive protein (CRP) and
ESR elevation are usually present.
r Procalcitonin can be a helpful aid to rule in rather
than rule out SA
r UA and culture can reveal a urologic source for the
pathogen.
r Blood cultures may be useful: Positive in 50–70% of
non-GC SA.
r Culture any potential focus of infection (pharynx,
urine, cervix, or anus), particularly when suspecting
GC.

◦Obtain spot-urine sodium to evaluate response.
◦Patients with urinary Na >10 mEq/L are more
responsive to diuretics.

◦Avoid hypokalemia since hypokalemia enhances

encephalopathy.

◦Accounts for 10% of patients
◦Ensure compliance with diet and medications.
◦Treated with peritoneovenous
shunt—transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic

◦Liver transplantation

◦Diminish response to diuretics
◦Decrease renal plasma flow and GFR.

r Status asthmaticus refers to disease that does not

– Chronic steroid use

– Inadequate medical management
– Increasing age
– Ethnicity (African Americans)
– Lack of access to medical care

– Mast cells
– Eosinophils
– Macrophages
– T lymphocytes
– Epithelial cells
– Cytokines

– Pollen
– Dust mites
– Molds
– Animal dander
– Other environmental allergens
– Viral upper respiratory infections
– Occupational chemicals
– Tobacco smoke

– Cold air
– Exercise induced
– Emotional factors
– Menstrual associated

◦NSAIDs

– Poor air movement

– Worsening fatigue

– Severe airflow obstruction and fatigue:

– <90% is indicative of severe respiratory distress.
– Patients with impending respiratory compromise
may still maintain saturation above 90% until
sudden collapse.

– Pneumonia
– Chronic steroid use
– Stress of an asthma exacerbation

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Inability to perform coordinated movements
r Caused by a disorder of the cerebellum or its
connections:
– Ipsilateral signs with lateral cerebellar lesions
– Truncal ataxia with midline lesions
ETIOLOGY
Usually cerebellar in origin, but may occur with
sensory, motor, or vestibular dysfunction:
r Trauma
r Mass lesions
r Vascular disorders
r Infections or postinfectious processes
r Toxins/drugs
r Metabolic/endocrine derangements
r Demyelinating diseases
r Congenital malformations
r Hereditary disorders:
– Inborn errors of metabolism
– Progressive degenerative ataxias
r Nutritional deficiencies

SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Gait disturbance:
– Ataxia often presents with unsteady gait
– Initial sense of insecurity while walking
– Problems with special skills (bicycling, skiing,
climbing)
– Sense of imbalance
– Wide base stance and staggering gait
– Test tandem gait to identify subtle ataxia
r Limb ataxia:
– Incoordination
– Intention tremors
– Clumsiness with writing, picking up objects,
buttoning
– Dysmetria: Under- or overshooting on
finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing
– Dysdiadochokinesis: Difficulty with rapid
alternating movements
r Truncal ataxia:
– Head tremors
– Truncal instability
– Titubation: Swaying of the head/trunk while at rest
r Dysarthria and bulbar symptoms:
– Slurred speech
– Staccato, scanning speech
– Choking from incoordination of swallowing
r Visual abnormalities:
– Blurry vision
– Vertigo:
◦Distinguish central from peripheral vertigo
◦Peripheral vertigo is often severe, triggered by
movement, and may be accompanied by ear
pain, hearing loss, or tinnitus
– Nystagmus:
◦Gaze-evoked nystagmus: Repetitive drifts to the
midline followed by fast phase to the eccentric
side
◦Rebound nystagmus
r Abnormalities of muscle tone and strength:
– Isometrataxia: Difficulty sustaining constant force
during hand use:
◦Ask patient to hold slight, steady pinching
pressure against examiner’s finger (examiner
will feel irregular pressure)
– True muscle weakness or hypotonia uncommon in
cerebellar disease
r Sensory ataxia:
– Paresthesias
– Numbness
– Cautious, steppage gait
– Marked worsening of coordination with eyes
closed:
◦A positive Romberg sign is the classic finding in
sensory ataxia
– Loss of position/vibration sense
– Difficulty with fine motor skills

be caused by pain, weakness, lightheadedness,
vertigo, or incoordination
r Onset:
– Hours–days: Acute
– Weeks–months: Subacute
– Months–years: Chronic
r Symmetric or focal symptoms
r Presence of fever, mental status changes, weakness,
sensory loss, or urinary incontinence
r Recent viral illness or immunizations
r History of trauma or toxic ingestion
r Family history of movement disorder

neurological and gait testing
r Assess for signs or symptoms of acute,
life-threatening disorders such as hemorrhage,
stroke, or CNS infection:

– Headache
– Focal neurological deficits
– Elevated intracranial pressure:
◦Bradycardia, HTN, abnormal respiratory pattern
◦Papilledema
◦Bulging fontanelles
– Fever
– Meningismus
– Nystagmus
– Nausea/vomiting
– Examine ears and perform provocative testing for
nystagmus (Dix–Hallpike)
r Note the presence of intoxication or toxidromes in
patients with suspected ingestion
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
A detailed history and physical exam will help
determine which tests are necessary

Labr Blood glucose level
r Serum electrolytes
r Toxicology screen:
– Standard panels may not include the drugs of
interest in the ataxic patient
r Thyroid function testing
r Target additional testing to likely exposures, such as
anticonvulsants

– Head CT can identify mass, hemorrhage, subacute
infarct, or hydrocephalus
– Consider CT with and without IV contrast if mass
suspected
– CT angiography can be performed to evaluate for
vascular disease

– Excellent study to evaluate for acute ischemia,
mass, demyelinating lesions, and vascular
abnormalities
– Superior for imaging the posterior fossa
– MR angiography of head/neck may be indicated if
vascular abnormality is suspected

– Not indicated as part of ataxia workup, but may
be useful in evaluation of nonspecific dizziness
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Lumbar puncture:
– Indicated if infection or Guillain–Barr ´ e suspected
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Acute symmetric ataxia:
– Head trauma
– Drug use/toxic ingestion:
◦Alcohol
◦Lithium
◦Phenytoin
◦Barbiturates
◦Carbamazepine
◦Phenobarbital
◦Valproic acid
◦Benzodiazepines
◦Diphenhydramine
◦Dextromethorphan
– Acute viral cerebellitis
– Meningitis/encephalitis
– Hydrocephalus
– Postinfectious syndrome
– Hypoglycemia
– Hyponatremia
– Severe heat stroke

– Posterior circulation infarction
– Anterior cerebral artery syndrome
– Vertebrobasilar insufficiency (VBI)
– Cerebellar hemorrhage
– Subdural hematoma
– Cerebellar abscess
– Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis
– Complicated migraine
– Atypical seizure

ATRIAL FIBRILLATION
Edward Ullman rTerrance T. Lee
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Dysrhythmia characterized by seemingly
disorganized atrial depolarizations without effective
atrial contraction
r Caused by multiple re-entrant waveforms within the
atria
r Atrial rate ranges from 350–600 beats per minute
(bpm).
r Results in loss of organized atrial contractions and
rapid ventricular rate:
– Decrease in cardiac output
– Prone to embolus formation
r Most common clinical arrhythmia:
– Prevalence increasing with age
– Men are at higher risk
ETIOLOGYr Systemic disease:
– HTN
– Hyperthyroidism
– Chronic pulmonary disease
– Infection
– Pulmonary embolus
– Hypoxia
– Drugs (e.g., sympathomimetics)
– Acute alcohol ingestion (holiday heart syndrome)
– Obesity
– Electrolyte disturbance
– Thyroid disease
r Underlying cardiac disease:
– Cardiomyopathy
– CAD
– Valvular disease, especially mitral
– Pericarditis
– Sick sinus syndrome
– Myocardial contusion
– CHF
– Congenital heart disease
r Idiopathic:
– Absence of any known etiologic factor
– No clinical or echocardiographic evidence of heart
disease
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Palpitations
r Decreased cardiac output:
– Weakness
– Light headedness
– Syncope
– Hypotension
– Angina
– Pulmonary edema
– Altered mental status
– Lower extremity edema
– Hepatojugular reflex
r Embolus formation:
– Acute neurologic injury
– Mesenteric ischemia
Historyr Onset of symptoms
r Duration
r Inciting factors
r Prior episodes of fibrillation
r Prior heart disease
Physical Examr Palpitations
r Irregularly irregular pulse
r Absence of A- waves in the jugular venous pulse
r Pulse deficit with more rapid ventricular rates:
– The auscultated or palpated apical rate is faster
than the rate palpated at the wrist
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr History and physical exam:
– Assess for instability and need for immediate
cardioversion
– Duration of symptoms >48 hr or <48 hr
– Evidence of systemic disease or underlying cardiac
disease
r ECG: Signs of congestive heart failure
– Absent P-waves replaced by fibrillatory (f) waves,
350–600 bpm
– F-waves vary in amplitude, morphology, and
intervals
– R-R intervals are irregularly irregular
– Absence of an isoelectric baseline
– Ventricular rate ranges from 80–150 bpm:
◦If rate >200 associated with wide-irregular
QRS, consider bypass tract
– Slower rate suggests abnormal AV node or
presence of AV nodal blocking medication
– Usually narrow QRS complexes unless:
◦Functional aberration
◦Pre-existing bundle branch
◦Pre-excitation with an accessory pathway
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC
r Electrolytes
r Cardiac enzymes—if ischemia is a concern
r Thyroid function
r Digoxin level—if patient is taking
r Anticoagulation parameters
r Urine drug screen
Imagingr CXR
r ECG
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Atrial flutter with variable AV block
r Multifocal atrial tachycardia
r Sinus rhythm with frequent premature atrial
contractions
r Atrial tachycardia with variable AV block
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr IV access
r Monitor
r Oxygen
r Cardioversion:
– In settings where patient is unstable
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr IV
r Oxygen
r Monitor
r Immediate synchronized electrical cardioversion
starting at 200 J if the patient is unstable
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Hemodynamically unstable and life threatening:
– Myocardial infarction, pulmonary edema, heart
failure that does not respond promptly to
pharmacological measures
– Synchronized electrical cardioversion
◦Biphasic: Start at 100 J, higher success rate
◦Monophasic: Start at 200 J
◦Sx duration <48 hr: Consider IV heparin bolus
prior.
◦Sx duration >48 hr: IV heparin,
transesophageal echo to exclude atrial clot,
cardioversion. Anticoagulate for 4 wk. Do not
delay echo if life-threatening arrhythmia.
◦Consider pretreatment with antiarrhythmic
drugs and use anterior–posterior pad placement
to increase likelihood of success
– Chemical cardioversion:
◦Choice of drug depends on history of CHF , high
BP , LV hypertrophy, and CAD
◦Medications may be proarrhythmic and should
be used with caution
◦As with electrical cardioversion, appropriate
anticoagulation will be necessary depending on
the duration and presence/absence of clot
◦Ibutilide
◦Procainamide
◦Flecainide
◦Propafenone
◦Sotalol
r Hemodynamically stable, mildly symptomatic:
– Treat underlying cause if 1 is identified.
– Identify if symptoms are <48 hr. If so consider
synchronized cardioversion.
– >48 hr: Rhythm control does not offer mortality
benefit over rate control
– Use procainamide to treat stable patients with a
suspected bypass tract
– Rate control:
◦Not necessary if rate <100 bpm or if rhythm
spontaneously converts to sinus
◦AV nodal blockers (calcium channel blockers,
β-blockers, and digoxin) contraindicated if
bypass tract suspected such as WPW
◦Calcium channel blockers: Consider in patient
with pulmonary disease. Use cautiously in
patient with uncompensated CHF and 2nd- or
3rd-degree heart block

ATRIAL FLUTTER
Liesl A. Curtis
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Atrial dysrhythmia
r 200,000 new cases each year
r A macroreentrant circuit in the right atrium is
thought to be the underlying mechanism.
r Most sensitive rhythm to cardioversion
r Seldom occurs in the absence of organic heart
disease
r Less common than supraventricular tachycardia
(SVT) or atrial fibrillation
r Typically paroxysmal, lasting seconds to hours
r Occurs in ∼25–35% of patients with atrial
fibrillation
r Untreated, may promote cardiomyopathy
ETIOLOGYr Alcoholism
r Cardiomyopathies and myocarditis
r CHF
r Electrolyte abnormalities
r Ischemic heart disease
r Pulmonary embolus and other pulm diseases
r Valvular heart diseases
r Post op following cardiac surgery (often in 1st
postoperative week)
r Thyrotoxicosis
Pediatric Considerations
r Occurs in children but is often asymptomatic
r Associated mortality is highest in the neonatal
period.
r Associated with:
– Congenital heart disease
– Infectious etiologies, such as rheumatic fever or
myocarditis
r Be sure to consider potential toxic ingestions in
pediatric patients with new AV block
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Palpitations
r Syncope/presyncope
r Chest pain
r Fatigue
r Dyspnea
r Poor exercise capacity
r Tachycardia—HR>150 bpm:
r Hypotension
r Heart failure
Pediatric Considerations
r Infants do not tolerate atrial flutter well.
r The aortic valve (AV) node is capable of very rapid
conduction.
r Extremely rapid ventricular rates can lead to shock
or CHF .
r Atrial flutter can occur in the fetus and young
infants without associated cardiac defects:
– Often does not recur beyond neonatal period
r Most older children have an underlying cardiac
abnormality
– More likely to recur and difficult to control
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr EKG
r Labs
r CXR
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Electrolytes and mineral panel
r Cardiac enzymes
r Digoxin level
r PT/PTT
Imagingr CXR:
– May identify cardiomyopathy or CHF
r Echo:
– May identify regional wall motion abnormalities or
valvular dysfunction
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr SVT
r Sinus tachycardia
r Atrial fibrillation
r Multifocal atrial tachycardia
r Ventricular tachycardia (VT)
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Oxygen, monitor, IV access
r Unstable patients should be cardioverted in the
field:
– Immediate synchronized cardioversion
– Start with 100 J
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Oxygen, monitor, IV access
r Immediate synchronized cardioversion if
unstable
– Current guidelines recommend starting at
150–200 J min to improve initial success and to
limit cumulative energy doses.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Rate control:
– Rate control should be instituted prior to giving an
antidysrhythmic to avoid risk of a 1:1 AV
conduction ratio and hemodynamic collapse.
– May be difficult to achieve
r Anticoagulation:
– Same guidelines as for atrial fibrillation:
◦INR 2–3 for 3 wk prior to cardioversion if
>48 hr or unknown duration
◦Recommended even if negative transesophageal
echo
◦Risk of thromboembolism ranges from 1.7–7%.
– CHADS2 score: Used for decision regarding
anticoagulation
◦CHF history (1 point)
◦Hypertension history (1 point)
◦Age ≥75 (1 point)
◦DM history (1 point)
◦Stroke symptoms or TIA history (2 points):
■ Score 0: Aspirin is sufficient prophylaxis
■ Score 1: Oral anticoagulants preferred
■ Score 2 or more: Oral anticoagulants strongly
recommended
– Patients at higher thromboembolism risk:
◦Valvular heart disease
◦Fluctuating a fib/flutter rhythms
◦Left ventricular (LV) dysfunction
◦Prior stroke or thromboembolism
◦Longer symptom duration (>48 hr)
r Antiarrhythmic drugs:
– Adenosine:
◦Unlikely to break atrial flutter
◦May aid in the diagnosis of atrial flutter by
unmasking the flutter waves
– Amiodarone:
◦Rate control in patients with pre-excited atrial
arrhythmias (i.e., WPW)
◦Preferable antiarrhythmic agent for patients
with severely impaired heart function
◦Major adverse effects are hypotension and
bradycardia, slower infusions can prevent this.
– Calcium channel blockers:
◦Rate control
◦Verapamil has higher incidence of symptomatic
hypotension than diltiazem.
◦Verapamil should only be used in
narrow-complex arrhythmias
– β-blockers:
◦Rate control
◦Added benefit of cardioprotective effects for
patients with ACS
– Magnesium sulfate:
◦Rate control
◦Low-level evidence
– Digoxin:
◦Rate control
◦3rd-line drug
◦Has inotropic properties so may be useful in
patients with ventricular dysfunction
◦Longer onset to therapeutic effect
– Procainamide:
◦Rhythm control
◦Drug of choice for patients with known
pre-excitation syndromes (i.e., WPW) and
preserved ventricular function
◦Caution if patient has QT prolongation
– Sotalol:
◦Rhythm control
◦Not a 1st-line drug
◦For use in WPW and preserved ventricular
function if duration of arrhythmia is ≤48 hr

ATRIAL FLUTTER
A
– Ibutilide:
◦Rhythm control
◦For acute pharmacologic rhythm conversion in
patients with preserved ventricular function (EF
>30%) if duration of arrhythmia is ≤48 hr
◦Correct potassium and magnesium before use
◦Contraindicated if QTc >440 msec or in
patients with severe structural heart disease
◦Efficacy rate of 38–76%
◦Mean time to conversion is 30 min.
◦Incidence of sustained polymorphic VT
1.2–1.7%
◦Observe for 4–6 hr after administration for QT
prolongation or VT.
r Cardioversion:
– 100–360 J
– Sedation when possible
– Safest and most effective means of restoring sinus
rhythm
r Maintenance of sinus rhythm after cardioversion:
– High recurrence rate: ∼50% at 1 yr; however,
difficult to determine rate because data combines
atrial fibrillation with atrial flutter
– Amiodarone most effective
r Percutaneous catheter ablation:
– Acute success rates exceed 95%.
– 5–10% recurrence in 1–2 yr of follow-up
– Low complication rate
– Candidates include:
◦Recurrent episodes of drug-resistant atrial flutter
◦Patients who are drug intolerant
◦Patients who do not desire long-term drug
therapy
Pediatric Considerations
r Verapamil is not recommended in infants and young
children as it is associated with a low cardiac output
and serious cardiovascular compromise.
r Digoxin is the 1st-line drug therapy for pediatric
atrial flutter.
r Consider cardioversion as 1st-line therapy in
neonates.
MEDICATIONr Amiodarone: 150 mg IV over 10 min, then
continuous infusion at 1 mg/min for 6 hr, then
0.5 mg/min infusion over 18 hr; supplemental
150 mg infusions can be dosed PRN to a max. daily
dose of 2.2 g (peds: 5 mg/kg IV loading dose over
20–60 min, may repeat to max. of 15 mg/kg/d IV)
r Adenosine: 6 mg IV × 1. May give 12 mg IV
q1–2min × 2 if no conversion. Give all doses IV
push
r Atenolol: 5 mg IV over 5 min, may repeat in 10 min
if tolerated, then 50 mg PO q12h
r Digoxin: Loading dose 8–12 Ug/kg lean body
weight, half of which is administered initially over
5 min, and remaining portion at 25% fractions at
4–8 hr intervals (peds: 8–12 μg/kg)
r Diltiazem: 0.25 mg/kg IV over 2 min followed in
15 min by 0.35 mg/kg IV over 2 min, maintenance
infusion of 10–15 mg/h titrated to heart rate
r Dofetilide: CrCl >60 mL/min and QTc 440 msec or
less) initial dose 500 μg ORALLY twice daily;
determine QTc 2–3 h after 1st dose; if QTc increases
by more than 15% OR is >500 msec (550 msec in
patients with ventricular conduction abnormalities),
reduce dose to 250 μg ORALLY twice daily; MAX.
dose 500 μg ORALLY twice daily
r Esmolol: 0.5 mg/kg over 1 min; maintenance
infusion at 0.05 mg/kg/min; can repeat loading dose
and increase in increments of 0.05 mg/kg/min
q4min up to 0.3 mg/kg/min
r Flecainide: A single dose of flecainide 300 mg (body
weight 70 kg or greater), and flecainide 200 mg
(body weight <70 kg) [3]; prior to antiarrhythmic
initiation, a β-blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium
channel antagonist should be administered to
prevent rapid AV conduction if atrial flutter occurs
r Ibutilide: 1 mg IV over 10 min for patients >60 kg;
0.01 mg/kg IV for patients <60 kg infused over
10 min; dose can be repeated once if normal sinus
rhythm not restored within 10 min after infusion
r Magnesium sulfate: 1–2 g diluted in D5W over
5–60 min; slower rate preferable if patient is stable.
r Metoprolol: 5 mg IV push over 5 min at 5 min
intervals to total of 15 mg, then 50 mg PO BID
r Procainamide: 20 mg/min until arrhythmia
suppressed, hypotension, QRS prolongation of
50%, or total of 17 mg/kg; may be given at rate up
to 50 mg/min (peds: 15 mg/kg IV over 30 min, then
20–80 μg/kg/min continuous infusion)
r Propranolol: 0.5–1 mg over 1 min, repeated after
2 min up to a total dose of 0.1 mg/kg (peds:
0.01–0.15 mg/kg/dose slow IV push over 5 min,
max. 1 mg/dose)
r Sotalol: 1–1.5 mg/kg over 5 min (US packaging
recommends infusion over 5 h)
r Verapamil: 2.5–5.0 mg IV bolus over 2 min; may
repeat with 5–10 mg q15–30min to a max. of
20–30 mg.
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar New-onset atrial flutter requiring antidysrhythmics,
rate control
r Symptomatic (i.e., chest pain that warrants a rule
out or cardioversion)
r CHF
Discharge Criteriar New-onset atrial flutter who meet these criteria:
– Rate or rhythm has been controlled
– Underlying cause has been investigated and
addressed
– Anticoagulation has been initiated
– Appropriate follow-up is arranged
r Chronic atrial flutter with good rate control and
appropriate anticoagulation
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Cardiologist: Radiofrequency ablation of atrial flutter
emerging as treatment of choice for patients with
symptomatic atrial flutter without identifiable
reversible cause
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Be aware of WPW:
– Do not use adenosine, β-blockers, calcium
channel blockers, and digoxin (Class III can be
harmful).
◦Can cause increased ventricular response, which
can deteriorate to ventricular fibrillation
r Do not delay cardioversion in an unstable patient for
IV placement.
r Use β-blockers with caution in patients with
pulmonary disease or CHF .
r 4 major treatment issues:
– Rate control
– Prevention of systemic embolization
– Reversion to sinus rhythm
– Maintenance of sinus rhythm
ADDITIONAL READING
r Clausen H, Theophilos T, Jackno K, et al. Paediatric
arrhythmias in the emergency department. Emerg
Med J. 2012;29(9):732–737.
r Fuster V, Ryden LE, Cannom DS, et al. ACC/AHA/ESC
2006 Guidelines for the management of patients
with atrial fibrillation. A report of the American
College of Cardiology/American Heart Association
Task Force on Practice Guidelines and the European
Society of Cardiology Committee for Practice
Guidelines. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2006;48:e149.
r Lee G, Sanders P, Kalman JM. Catheter ablation of
atrial arrhythmias: State of the art. Lancet.
2012;380(9852):1509–1519.

Emergency department management and 1-year
outcomes of patients with atrial flutter. Ann Emerg
Med. 2011;57(6):564–571.

recent-onset atrial fibrillation and flutter in the

38–46.
