CANDIDIASIS, ORAL
Derrick D. Fenchel rDeepi G. Goyal
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Infection of oral mucosa with any species of Candida
r Up to 80% of isolates are Candida albicans (most
common), Candida glabrata, and Candida tropicalis.
r Candida normally present as oral flora in 60% of the
healthy population.
r Variations include:
– Pseudomembranous (thrush)
– Chronic and acute atrophic candidiasis
– Angular cheilitis
– Hyperplastic candidiasis
r More common in neonates, elderly, and
immunosuppressed individuals
r Usually benign course in healthy patients
r In immunocompromised patients, more likely to be
recurrent and a non-albicans species
r May represent an early manifestation of AIDS in
HIV-infected patients
r Typically localized
r Risk factors for systemic infection:
– AIDS
– Diabetes
– Hospitalization
– Immunosuppressive therapy
– Malignancy
– Neutropenia
– Organ transplantation
– Prematurity
ETIOLOGYr Usually overgrowth of C. albicans from alterations in
intraoral environment
r May be medication induced—commonly
antimicrobials, inhaled or systemic steroids,
chemotherapy, immunosuppressive agents
r Immunocompromised patients
r Alterations or impairment of salivary flow:
– Anticholinergic or psychotropic medications
–S j¨ogren disease
– Head or neck radiation
r Presence of dentures or other orthodontics:
– Occurs in up to 50–65% of denture wearers
– Common etiology for chronic atrophic candidiasis
r Interruption of epithelial barrier (cheek biting)
r Endocrinopathies (diabetes, hypothyroidism)
Pediatric Considerations
r Acute pseudomembranous candidiasis (thrush) is
common in infancy likely because of immaturity of
their immune system and lack of mature oral flora
r Initial presentation may be feeding difficulty
secondary to dysphagia
r May have concurrent Candida diaper rash
r Consider maternal treatment if breastfeeding:
– Maternal breast colonization may be cause for
persistent thrush. Query maternal nipple pain,
burning, itching, or cracked skin
Geriatric Considerations
r Candida organisms are normally present as oral
flora from 65–88% of elderly or those in long-term
care facilities
r Dentures can lead to Candida overgrowth
r Angular cheilitis more common in the elderly
secondary to facial wrinkling
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Pseudomembranous candidiasis (thrush):
– Painless white mucosal plaques
– Adherent but removable plaques
– Erythematous base
– May become confluent and curdlike
– Anorexia, dysphagia
r Acute atrophic candidiasis:
– Also referred to as erythematous candidiasis
– Burning sensation in mouth or on tongue
– Erythematous with few, if any white patches
usually on the palate or dorsum of tongue
– Tongue may be bright red in color—similar to
nutritional deficiency
r Chronic atrophic candidiasis:
– Also referred as denture stomatitis
– Irritation around denture-bearing mucosa
r Angular cheilitis:
– Cracking or erythema at the corners of mouth
– Lesion can be asymptomatic, pruritic, or painful
– Superinfection with Staphylococcus or
Streptococcus is common
r Hyperplastic candidiasis:
– Chronic, invasive ulcers
– Typically on lateral borders of tongue or buccal
mucosa
– High incidence of malignant degeneration in
tobacco users
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Minimal workup needed in otherwise healthy infant.
Diagnosis can be made clinically.
r Determine whether there is a cause for a breakdown
of host factors
r If no reason is found, evaluate for possible HIV
infection or diabetes
r Exclude a systemic infection

CARBAMAZEPINE POISONING
James W. Rhee
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Therapeutic uses of carbamazepine:
– Anticonvulsant
– Treatment of chronic pain
– Migraine prophylaxis
– Mood stabilizer
r Mechanism:
– Anticholinergic
– Similarities to phenytoin and tricyclic
antidepressants (TCAs)
– Sodium channel blocker
– Decreases synaptic transmission
ETIOLOGY
Toxicity may occur from:
r Suicide attempt
r Accidental ingestion
r Supratherapeutic dosing
r Drug–drug interaction
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Neurologic manifestations common
r Cardiotoxicity rare, except in massive overdose
r CNS:
– Ataxia
– Dizziness
– Drowsiness
– Nystagmus
– Hallucinations
– Combativeness
– Coma
– Seizures
r Respiratory system:
– Respiratory depression
– Aspiration pneumonia
r Cardiovascular system:
– Hypotension
– Conduction disturbances (mostly in elderly)
– Supraventricular tachycardia
– Sinus tachycardia or bradycardia
– ECG changes:
◦Prolongation of PR, QRS, and QTc intervals
◦T-wave changes
Pediatric Considerations
Higher incidence of neurologic manifestations
Historyr Overdose of carbamazepine or extended-release
versions
r Time of ingestion
r Is the bottle available
r Accidental or intentional ingestion
r Coingestions
Physical Examr May present with seizures or altered mental status
r May be combative or drowsy
r Sinus tachycardia (massive carbamazepine overdose)
r Bradydysrhythmia (often seen in elderly with mild
increase in carbamazepine level)
r Anticholinergic manifestations:
– Decreased bowel sounds
– Mydriasis
– Flushing
– Urinary retention
r Neuromuscular changes:
– Tremor
– Slurred speech
– Myoclonus
– Choreiform and choreoathetoid movements
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Continuous cardiac monitor
r Serum carbamazepine level:
– Therapeutic, 6–12 μg/L
– Levels >25–40 μg/mL associated with serious
toxicity:
◦Coma
◦Seizures
◦Respiratory failure
◦Conduction defects
– Serum levels do not clearly predict clinical toxicity:
◦Active metabolite carbamazepine 10, 11
epoxide not measured
◦Neurologic manifestations depend on CNS (not
serum) level
– Serial levels may be needed owing to erratic
absorption of carbamazepine.
r ECG:
– Conduction delays:
◦Increased QRS interval
◦Increased PR interval
◦QTc prolongation
– Dysrhythmias
r Serum acetaminophen level (to evaluate for
coingestion in a suicide attempt)
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC:
– Leukopenia or leukocytosis
r Electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, glucose:
– Hyperglycemia
– Hypokalemia
– Hyponatremia
r Arterial blood gases (ABGs)
r Urinalysis:
– Glucosuria
– Ketonuria
r Pregnancy test
r ALT, AST, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase:
– May be mildly elevated
– Usually not clinically significant
Imaging
CXR:
r Aspiration pneumonia
r Pulmonary edema
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Drugs that cause decreased mental status:
– Alcohol
– Anticholinergics
– Barbiturates
– Benzodiazepines
– Lithium
– Opiates
– Phenothiazines
r Drugs that cause seizures:
– Alcohol withdrawal
– Anticholinergics
– Camphor
– Isoniazid
– Lithium
– Phenothiazines
– Sympathomimetics:
◦Amphetamine
◦Cocaine
– TCAs
r Drugs that cause abnormal movement:
– Antihistamines
– Butyrophenones
– Caffeine
– Cocaine
– Levodopa
– Meperidine
– Phencyclidine
– Phenothiazines
– Phenytoin
– TCAs

C
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Do not administer ipecac.
r Intubate if significant respiratory depression or
airway compromise.
r Secure IV access.
r Get complete information about all products
potentially ingested.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs
r IV access and fluid resuscitation if hypotensive
r Oxygen
r Cardiac monitor
r Naloxone, thiamine, D50W (or Accu-Chek) if altered
mental status
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr General management:
– Activated charcoal:
◦Administer sorbitol with 1st dose (only) of
activated charcoal.
◦Administer with caution if GI activity is
decreased.
◦Contraindicated if bowel sounds are absent
– Multidose activated charcoal:
◦Decreases mean half-life of carbamazepine
◦Binds unabsorbed drug in GI tract
◦Interrupts enterohepatic circulation
◦Do not give additional sorbitol
– Charcoal hemoperfusion/hemodialysis:
◦Removes small to moderate amount of ingested
dose
◦Patients usually do well with supportive care
without hemoperfusion or dialysis
◦Indicated in cases of clinical deterioration or
lack of improvement with good supportive care
r Respiratory depression:
– Intubation
– Ventilatory support
r Hypotension:
– Bolus with IV isotonic crystalloid solution
– Norepinephrine if unresponsive to IV fluids
r Seizures:
– Diazepam (drug of choice)
– Phenobarbital (if diazepam ineffective)
– Phenytoin not effective in most toxic seizures
r Cardiac conduction delay:
– QRS widening (>100 msec):
◦Sodium bicarbonate (to overcome sodium
channel blockade)
r Psychiatric consultation if suicide attempt
MEDICATION
First Liner Activated charcoal (initial bolus): Slurry 1–2 g/kg up
to 100 g PO
r Multidose activated charcoal: 25 g (peds: 0.25 g/kg)
q2h PO after bolus dose (above); can also use 50 g
q6h PO/NG
Second Liner Dextrose: D50W 1 ampule: 50 mL or 25 g (peds:
D25W 2–4 mL/kg) IV
r Diazepam: 5–10 mg (peds: 0.2–0.5 mg/kg) IV
r Naloxone (Narcan): 2 mg (peds: 0.1 mg/kg) IV/IM
initial dose
r Norepinephrine: 2–4 μg/min (peds:
0.05–0.1 μg/kg/min) IV titrated to effect
r Sodium bicarbonate: 1 or 2 amps IV push (peds:
1–2 mEq/kg)
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Decreased mental status at any time, even if
resolving (tends to recur with fluctuating drug
levels):
– Observe at least 24 hr for late relapse.
r Seizures
r Cardiac dysrhythmias
r Lack of psychiatric clearance after suicidal ingestion
Discharge Criteriar Asymptomatic after 6 hr of observation
r Normal mental status
r Normal or baseline ECG
r GI motility present
r Psychiatric clearance (after suicidal ingestion)
Issues for Referral
Suicidal patients need psychiatric evaluation referral.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Supratherapeutic dosing will need ongoing monitoring
by physician treating underlying disorder.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Carbamazepine levels commonly rebound to higher
levels during treatment. Obtain serial measurements
for severe ingestions.
r Monitor closely for arrhythmias.
r Multidose charcoal may be needed for more serious
ingestions.
r Paradoxical seizures may occur, use benzodiazepines
to treat initially (diazepam is the drug of choice).

CARBON MONOXIDE POISONING
Trevonne M. Thompson
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless,
nonirritating gas.
r Binds to hemoglobin to form carboxyhemoglobin:
– Decreases O2-carrying capacity
r Direct cellular toxin
r Impairs cellular O2 utilization
ETIOLOGYr Endogenous:
– Result of normal metabolism
r Incomplete combustion of carbonaceous fossil
fuel:
– Internal combustion engines
– Natural gas
– Heaters
– Indoor grills
– Fireplaces
– Furnaces
– Accidental fires
– Tobacco smoke
r Methylene chloride:
– Found in some solvents for paint removal and
furniture stripping
– Converted in vivo to CO after exposure
– Peak carboxyhemoglobin levels delayed after
exposure
– Half-life is ∼2 times that of inhaled CO
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr CNS:
– Headache
– Dizziness
– Ataxia
– Confusion
– Syncope
– Seizures
r GI:
– Nausea
– Vomiting
r Cardiovascular:
– Chest pain
– Palpitations
r Respiratory:
– Dyspnea
r Ophthalmologic:
– Decreased visual acuity
Physical Examr CNS:
– Acute encephalopathy
– Seizures
– Coma
r Cardiovascular:
– Tachycardia
– Premature ventricular contractions
– Dysrhythmias
– Myocardial ischemia/infarction
r Respiratory:
– Tachypnea
– Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema
r Ophthalmologic:
– Retinal hemorrhage
r Other:
– Respiratory alkalosis
– Rhabdomyolysis
– Lactic acidosis
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr History:
– Maintain a high index of suspicion
– Symptoms may be mild, nonspecific
– Inquire about the following:
◦Similar symptoms in other household members
◦Malfunctioning furnaces
◦Use of space heaters, open ovens for
supplemental heat
◦Ill pets
r Arterial blood gas:
– Normal PaO2
– Normal calculated O2 saturation
– Low measured O2 saturation
– Metabolic acidosis in severe cases
r Carboxyhemoglobin level:
– Measure as soon as possible
– Level may not reflect clinical severity:
◦Patient may be critically ill despite unimpressive
carboxyhemoglobin level.
◦May be misleadingly low if significant time has
passed since exposure
◦Normal range is 0–3% (up to 10% in smokers).
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Pulse oximetry:
– Falsely elevated SaO2 reading
– Pulse oximeter cannot distinguish oxyhemoglobin
from carboxyhemoglobin.
r Electrolytes:
– Metabolic acidosis and elevated anion gap
associated with increased clinical severity
r Cardiac enzymes:
– When myocardial ischemia/infarction suspected
r Pregnancy test
r ECG:
– CO may precipitate myocardial
ischemia/infarction.
– Dysrhythmias
– Nonspecific ST-segment and T-wave abnormalities
Imagingr Chest radiography:
– Pulmonary edema
r CT scan of the head:
– To evaluate for intracranial causes of altered
mental status when indicated
– Bilateral globus pallidus low-density lesions may
be clue to CO poisoning in unclear cases.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Viral illness/viral syndrome
r Meningitis/encephalitis
r Intracranial hemorrhage
r Gastroenteritis
r Migraine headache
r Tension headache
r Ethanol intoxication
r Sedative–hypnotic overdose
r Cyanide poisoning
r Salicylate overdose
r Toxic alcohol exposure

TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Administer 100% O2
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs
r Establish IV access
r 100% oxygen
r Cardiac monitor
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Oxygen:
– Administer 100% normobaric O2:
◦Via face mask or endotracheal tube
– Continue O2 therapy until carboxyhemoglobin
level <10%.
– Half-life of carboxyhemoglobin:
◦∼300 min in ambient air
◦∼90 min in 100% normobaric O2
◦∼20 min at 3 atm (hyperbaric O2)
r Hyperbaric O2:
– Dose:
◦100% O2 at 3 atm
◦May be repeated
– Benefits:
◦May reduce delayed neurologic sequelae
◦Decreases half-life of carboxyhemoglobin
– Potential adverse effects:
◦Tympanic membrane rupture
◦Pneumothorax
◦Seizure
◦Decompression sickness
◦Pulmonary edema
– Use of hyperbaric O2 remains controversial
– Indications for consulting hyperbaracist:
◦Altered mental status/coma
◦Focal neurologic deficits
◦Seizures
◦Cardiovascular compromise (infarction,
persistent dysrhythmia)
◦Persistent metabolic acidosis
◦Carboxyhemoglobin level >25%
◦Pregnancy with carboxyhemoglobin level>10%
Pregnancy Considerations
r Fetal hemoglobin has higher affinity for CO than
adult hemoglobin.
r Fetal carboxyhemoglobin levels 10–15% higher
than maternal levels
r Delayed clearance of fetal carboxyhemoglobin
compared with maternal

Admission Criteriar Persistent symptoms after 4 hr of treatment with
100% oxygen
r Evidence of myocardial ischemia or cardiac instability
r Seizures
r Persistent metabolic acidosis
r Syncope

r Absence of aforementioned admission criteria
r Psychiatric clearance if suicidal exposure
Issues for Referral
Need for hyperbaric oxygen therapy
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Contact local fire department in cases of CO home
exposures.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Suspect CO poisoning in patients who present with
headaches when home heaters are initiated.
r Suspect CO poisoning when family members living
in the same enclosed space have similar symptoms.
r Administer 100% O2 and transfer to hyperbaric
facility if the above-described criteria is met.

CARDIAC ARREST
Michael W. Donnino r Brandon Giberson r Michael N. Cocchi
BASICS
ALERT
r NOTE: The following information is based on 2010
Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) Guidelines.
Any revisions made by the American Heart
Association since then are not available at time of
publication.
r Major ACLS Changes for the 2010 revision
include:
– Change in the BLS sequence of treatment from
A–B–C (airway, breathing, circulation) to
C–A–B (circulation, airway, breathing) to
emphasize early chest compressions
– Emphasis on postcardiac arrest care, particularly
implementation of targeted temperature
management
– Removal of atropine from PEA/asystole ACLS
algorithms
DESCRIPTIONr Sudden cardiac arrest is characterized by:
– Unresponsiveness
– Pulselessness
– Little to no respiratory effort
r Factors affecting survival:
– Initial rhythm
– Total down time
– Time to successful defibrillation (as indicated)
– Time to basic life-support interventions
ETIOLOGY
Contributing factors to cardiac arrest are outlined by
the American Heart Association as:
r Hypovolemia
r Hypoxia
r Hydrogen ion (acidosis)
r Hypo-/hyperkalemia
r Hypothermia
r Toxins
r Tamponade, cardiac
r Tension pneumothorax
r Thrombosis
r Trauma
Pediatric Considerations
r Sudden cardiac arrest in children is often of a
respiratory rather than cardiac etiology
r Follow current ACLS guidelines for pediatric cardiac
arrest. Major differences between adult and
pediatric cardiac arrest management include:
– Depth of compressions for pediatric populations
should be ∼1/3 to 1/2 the depth of the chest
– For 2 rescuer CPR, a 15:2 compression to
ventilation rate is recommended
– Drug dosage differences: See “Medications”
section
Pregnancy Considerations
Follow current ACLS guidelines for management of the
pregnant cardiac arrest patient:
r Awareness that airway may be difficult
r Compressions should be performed at a higher
location than conventional CPR, slightly above the
center of the sternum
r Follow Adult ACLS guidelines for defibrillation
r Pre- or postcardiac arrest pregnant patients should
be placed in the left lateral recumbent position;
during arrest, perform manual left uterine
displacement
r To ensure a best possible outcome for the fetus, all
efforts must be geared toward maternal survival
r In the event of a failed maternal resuscitation, an
emergent cesarean delivery may be considered
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Unresponsiveness
r Pulselessness
r Shallow, gasping respirations may persist for a few
minutes
r Occasionally preceded by:
– Chest pain
– Dyspnea
– Palpitations
– Seizure activity
r Immediately prior to arrest:
– Shock or hypotension
– Impaired mentation
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Assess circulation, airway, breathing
r Determine shockable vs. nonshockable rhythm and
treat accordingly, per ACLS guidelines
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Indicated only when successful return of spontaneous
circulation (ROSC) is achieved:
r Electrolytes
r BUN/creatinine
r Creatinine kinase with isoenzymes, cardiac troponin
r ABG
r CBC
r Therapeutic drug levels
r Toxicologic testing
r Lactic acid levels
Imagingr EKG:
– Evaluate for STEMI or ACS
r CXR:
– Endotracheal tube position
– Pneumothorax
– Pulmonary etiology of arrest
r Echocardiogram:
– Pericardial effusion
– Wall motion abnormality
– Valvular dysfunction

CARDIAC PACEMAKERS
Susan P. Torrey
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr A device that uses electrical impulses to contract the
heart muscles and provide an adequate pulse
r Methods of cardiac pacing:
– Transcutaneous pacing:
◦2 pads are placed on the chest in the
anterior-lateral or anterior-posterior position.
◦The pacing current is gradually increased until
electrical capture occurs with a pulse.
◦Emergency therapy used only until transvenous
pacing or another therapy can be applied
– Temporary transvenous pacing:
◦A pacemaker wire is placed through central
venous access into the right atrium (RA) or right
ventricle (RV) and connected to an external
generator outside of the body.
◦Used as a bridge until a permanent pacemaker
can be placed or there is no longer a need for a
pacemaker
r Permanent, implanted pacemaker has 3
components:
– A battery-powered energy source:
◦Lithium batteries last 7–10 yr
– Generator:
◦A sophisticated computer with many
programmable parameters
– Leads connected to the RV/RA:
◦Typically sense intrinsic electrical activity of the
heart and pace the myocardium as needed
r Pacemaker magnet:
– Placed over pacemaker generator
– Converts pacer to asynchronous mode
– Useful if pacer spikes not present on ECG
– A depleted battery will result in decrease in
magnet rate by ∼10%.
Pacemaker Terminologyr Fixed mode:
– The pacemaker is set to fire at a set rate
regardless of patient’s underlying rhythm.
– Rarely seen
r Demand mode:
– The pacemaker fires only when necessary.
– It senses the underlying rhythm.
– It will only pace if the intrinsic rhythm is absent or
less than a set rate.
r Sensing:
– Pacemaker’s ability to determine whether the
heart has an intrinsic rhythm
r All pacemakers have a 5-letter code to describe their
function.
r For ED purposes, only the 1st 3 letters of the code
are necessary:
– 1st letter in code indicates chamber being sensed
by pacemaker:
◦A: Atria
◦V: Ventricle
◦D: Dual (both chambers)
– 2nd letter in code indicates chamber that can be
paced:
◦A: Atria
◦V: Ventricle
◦D: Dual (both chambers)
– 3rd letter in code describes pacemaker’s response
to sensed intrinsic complex:
◦T: Trigger (a sensed beat results in a pacing
response as when a sensed atrial beat provokes
a subsequent ventricular beat)
◦I: Inhibit (a sensed beat precludes pacemaker
function)
◦D: Dual (a pacemaker is capable of both
functions)
◦O: No response
– The most common pacemakers are VVI (single
lead) and DDD (two leads).
ETIOLOGYr Pacemaker-associated infection:
– Infection of pacemaker components often
associated with endocarditis
– Staphylococcus epidermidis and Staphylococcus
aureus account for >90% of infections.
– Transesophageal echo is the preferred diagnostic
method.
r Venous thrombosis:
– Very common (overall incidence 30–50%)
– Symptomatic, acute obstruction is rare (<3%).
– Pulmonary embolism is rare.
r Pacemaker failure to discharge impulse
– Component failure is rare.
– Battery depletion is rare with routine checks; it is
not abrupt.
– Lead fracture or disconnection
– Oversensing of muscular activity or external
electrical interference
r Pacemaker failure to capture myocardium:
– Lead dislodgment is common.
– Twiddler’s syndrome:
◦Unintentional manipulation of pacemaker
generator causing lead to be dislodged from
myocardium
– Elevated myocardial threshold:
◦Hyperkalemia
◦Ischemia
– Change in cardiac (QRS) morphology
r Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia:
– Occurs with dual-chamber pacemakers
– A re-entry rhythm using generator and intrinsic
conduction system
– Max. rate typically 140 bpm due to built-in
safeguards
r Runaway pacemaker:
– Rare; triggered by battery depletion or component
failure
– Often rapid rates (>200 bpm) with hemodynamic
compromise
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Pacemaker failure:
– Bradycardia
– Syncope
– Hypotension, progressive to shock and
hemodynamic collapse
– Fatigue and weakness
– Dyspnea on exertion or shortness of breath
secondary to CHF
– Ischemic chest pain
– Altered level of consciousness
r Pacemaker-induced tachycardia:
– Dyspnea
– Ischemic chest pain
– Lightheadedness
– Syncope
r Pacemaker syndrome:
– Symptoms related to asynchronous chamber
contractions (typical with VVI pacer)
– Lightheadedness
– Dyspnea
– Palpitation
– Weakness or exercise intolerance
– Syncope
Historyr Date of placement pacemaker
r Compliance with follow-up (battery checks)
r Type of pacemaker
Physical Exam
General cardiac exam:
r Heart exam for murmurs
r Lung exam for CHF
r Chest wall exam at generator site

CARDIAC PACEMAKERS
C
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr 12-lead EKG to assess whether there is any obvious
evidence of pacemaker failure
r Metabolic workup to determine whether an
acquired medical condition led to an elevated
myocardial threshold
r EKG with pacer magnet:
– Assess magnet rate.
– Particularly useful when the baseline EKG does
not reveal pacer spikes
– The magnet activates asynchronous pacing mode.
– Produces pacer spikes at a preprogrammed rate,
regardless of the intrinsic rhythm
– If the magnet rate equals the preprogrammed rate
set at implantation, the pacer is okay.
– If the magnet rate is >10% slower than at
implantation, the battery is depleted.
– If there are no pacer spikes, there is significant
pacemaker malfunction.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Serum potassium
r ABG
r Serum levels of antidysrhythmic drugs
Imaging
CXR:
r Evaluate integrity of pacer lead(s) and position.
r Fractured lead
r Lead dislodgment:
– Perforation through septum
– Tip of lead moved (e.g., in pulmonary artery)

PRE-HOSPITAL
Record rhythm strips for analysis
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Oxygen administered via 100% nonrebreather
r Intubation as needed
r IV access
r Advanced cardiac life support drugs as per usual
protocol (especially for bradycardia)
r Defibrillation: Avoid placing paddles over generator.
r Transcutaneous pacemaker in hemodynamically
unstable patients with pacemaker failure

– Transcutaneous pacemaker
– Temporary transvenous pacemaker:
◦Obtain central IV access with a Cordis
introducer (right IJ preferred)
◦Perform the procedure under fluoroscopy if
possible.
◦Set the pulse generator to asynchronous mode.
◦Turn the output dial all the way up.
◦Advance the catheter through the central
venous access Cordis until you see a QRS
complex on the monitor.
◦Check the femoral pulse.
◦If you have a pulse and see a QRS complex, the
pacer is “capturing.”
◦Slowly turn the output dial down until you lose
the QRS complex (capture threshold).
◦Turn the output dial up to 2 or 3 times the
capture threshold.
◦Continuous EKG monitoring facilitates correct
placement.

– In extreme situation, may need to disconnect lead
from generator surgically

cardiac decompensation, bradycardia, or syncope.

CARDIAC TESTING
Steve R. Grosse rShamai A. Grossman
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Cardiac testing is indicated for emergency patients
at risk for heart failure (HF) or acute coronary
syndrome (ACS).
r These pathologies may be thought of as a spectrum:
Unstable angina can evolve into MI, which in turn
can cause HF:
– ∼20% of ED malpractice claims are due to missed
diagnosis of ACS.
– ∼2% of patients with ACS are inappropriately
discharged from an ED.
– History, physical exam, and ECG are the critical
elements in working up chest pain and ACS/HF .
– History, physical, and ECG nevertheless miss
1–4% of all heart attacks.
– Additional tools include imaging modalities and
blood tests (e.g., cardiac biomarkers).
ETIOLOGY
ACS is caused by atherosclerotic narrowing of
coronary vessels or by coronary vasospasm.
Pregnancy Considerations
In the pregnant patient with chest pain and ischemic
changes on ECG, also consider spontaneous coronary
artery dissection.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Anginal symptoms usually are produced by bodily
stresses, including exertional and emotional events,
and relieved by rest.
r ACS is less likely when chest pain is sharp, stabbing,
pleuritic, or reproducible with palpation.
r Ischemia is still diagnosed in 13% of pleuritic chest
pain and in 7% of chest pain reproducible with
palpation.
r Nitroglycerin may relieve cardiac ischemia, but can
also relieve pain in GI and aortic pathology.
r A “GI cocktail” of lidocaine and Maalox, or a
proton-pump inhibitor such as omeprazole, may
relieve GI pathology, but can also relieve cardiac
ischemia.
r Anginal symptoms often last <20 min but >5 min
r AMI and UA should be considered if symptoms last
>20 min.
Physical Exam
Often unremarkable
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
EKG:
r Per ACC/AHA guidelines, a 12-lead ECG should be
performed on a patient with chest pain within
10 min of arrival to the ED:
– A single ECG will miss ∼50% AMI.
– Hyperacute T-waves (tall, broad-based, especially
in anterior leads) may be the earliest and only sign
of AMI.
– During an MI, the ECG may evolve. Continuous
ECG monitoring can identify an additional 16% of
acute MIs not seen on initial ECGs. Absent
continuous monitoring, consider a repeat EKG
15–60 min after the initial ECG.
– New ST-segment changes or T-wave inversions are
suspicious for ischemia.
– ST depressions of 1 mm are characteristic of
ischemia; or, could be reciprocal changes, so check
other leads.
– STEMI: ST-elevation of>1–2 mm in ≥2
contiguous leads.
– New left bundle branch block (LBBB) is suggestive
of AMI:
◦Old LBBB makes diagnosing AMI difficult: Apply
Sgarbossa criteria: AMI is likely if LBBB and
>1 mm ST-elevation concordant with QRS, or ST
depression >1 mm in leads V1, V2, or V3.
◦Current ACCF/AHA guidelines advise that LBBB
“not known to be old” in isolation is not
diagnostic of AMI, and should be further
evaluated with serum biomarkers and
immediate cardiac consultation for
consideration of echocardiography and invasive
angiography.
r Additional-lead EKGs: Standard 12 leads often
miss infarcts in the posterior, right, and high lateral
walls.
– Right-sided EKG:
◦Move lead V4 to the right side of chest,
midclavicular line, 5th intercostal space, and
repeat EKG, to capture infarct in right ventricle.
◦A right-sided EKG is often performed in the
setting of a STEMI in inferior leads (II, III, aVF) to
diagnose a right ventricular (RV) infarct.
– Posterior EKG:
◦Leads V7, V8, V9 are placed posterior thorax
along 5th intercostal space: V7 at posterior
axillary line, V8 at inferior angle of scapula, V9
paraspinal.
◦Performed in setting of inferior or lateral wall
MI; or if ST depression in V1–V3. May identify a
lateral or left circumflex infarct.
r EKG may be helpful in diagnosing other etiologies of
chest pain:
– Pericarditis is suggested by diffuse ST-elevations
followed by T-wave inversions and P-R depression.
– Pulmonary embolism is suggested by unexplained
tachycardia, signs of right heart strain (RVH,
RBBB, “p” pulmonale), new-onset atrial
fibrillation, or rarely with S1, Q3, T3 pattern.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Cardiac biomarkers:
– Indicated if the history is suspicious for ACS.
– Should not be elevated in stable angina and may
be normal in unstable angina.
r Troponin T and I: Starts to rise 2–3 hr after onset of
chest pain of ACS and peaks in 8–12 hr. Remains
elevated 7–14 days:
– A single troponin has low sensitivity for ACS
(1 study of low-risk chest pain in patients with
negative initial troponin: 2.3% rate of AMI and
1% rate of death at 30 days).
– Timing of biomarker testing is critical: ACEP
endorses with “moderate clinical certainty” that a
single negative troponin can rule out AMI if drawn
8–12 hr after onset of symptoms. However,
uncertainty in time of symptom onset, unreliable
history, and possibility of preinfarction angina
complicates utilizing single troponin.
– Newer, more sensitive assays may in the future
eliminate the need for a 2nd troponin.
– Minor troponin elevations may occur with renal
failure, structural heart disease, CHF (acute or
chronic), cardiac pacing, pulmonary embolism,
sepsis, stroke.
– Lack of standardization between assays
(particularly with troponin I) means values from 1
lab cannot always be simply compared to values
from another.
r CK/CK-Mb: Less sensitive than troponin, rises more
slowly. Little gained by using both CK-Mb and
troponin assays. Obtain CK-Mb if
– Renal failure is present (Tn less accurate)
– Recent prior infarct
r Myoglobin: Rises faster than standard troponin
assays and thus able to detect AMI sooner, but max.
sensitivity is 70%.
r B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP):
– Release and synthesis activated by diastolic
ventricular stretch.
– Useful for detecting HF .
– A cutoff of >100 pg/mL diagnosed HF with a
sensitivity of 90% and specificity of 76%.
– Unclear significance of elevated BNP in setting of
ACS.
Imagingr CXR:
– Usually normal
– May show cardiomegaly
– May show pulmonary edema
– May identify other etiologies of chest pain, such
as pneumonia or widened mediastinum of aortic
dissection.
r Rest echocardiography:
– May identify ACS or AMI based on wall motion
abnormalities; also can detect pump failure and
valvular abnormalities.
– Rest echo has a sensitivity of 70% and specificity
of 87% for ACS.
– Rest echo has a sensitivity of 93% and specificity
of 66% for AMI.

CARDIAC TESTING
C
r Technetium99m sestamibi:
– Radioactive IV dye taken up by myocardium, and
detected by single photon emission CT (SPECT)
imaging. (Also known as myocardial perfusion
imaging.)
– Can be imaged at rest to detect low- or no-flow
areas of myocardium; can also be imaged after
exercise or pharmacologic stress.
– Per 2009 AHA/ACC guidelines, reserve for
intermediate- to high-risk patients.
– Has a sensitivity of 81% and specificity of 73% for
ACS.
– Has a sensitivity of 92% and specificity of 67% for
AMI.
r CT coronary angiography (CTCA):
– Imaging to evaluate degree of coronary artery
stenosis and calcium deposits
– Negative predictive value between 97% and
100%, accuracy comparable to stress testing
– Recent NEJM article suggests CTCA decreases ED
length of stay but leads to further downstream
testing, radiation exposure, and no decrease in
cost of care.
r Exercise stress testing (ETT):
– May help establish diagnosis of angina, provide
prognostic information.
– 1-mm depression of the ST-segment in
3 consecutive beats and 2 consecutive leads is
characteristic of cardiac ischemia.
– Early positive (within 3 min) stress tests are
worrisome for unstable angina.
– 6 min of exercise using a standard Bruce protocol
suggests an excellent prognosis.
– Exercise stress testing with EKG alone has a
sensitivity of 68% and specificity of 77%.
– Exercise stress testing with echo has a sensitivity
of 85% and specificity of 77%.
– Exercise stress testing with technetium99m
sestamibi has a sensitivity of 87% and specificity
of 64%.
r Cardiac catheterization:
– Considered the gold standard for evaluating
coronary arteries.
– A history of a recent negative catheterization does
not fully exclude AMI, i.e., in cases of vasospasm
or cocaine use.
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
EKG, cardiac enzymes, echo, stress testing
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
See ACS chapters.
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Cardiac monitoring
r Out-of-hospital EKG:
– Alone has a sensitivity of 76% and specificity of
88% for ACS.
– Alone has a sensitivity of 68% and specificity of
97% for AMI.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Cardiac monitoring
r Oxygen saturation
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr See “Acute Coronary Syndrome: Stable Angina”;
“Acute Coronary Syndrome: Unstable Angina”; and
“Acute Coronary Syndrome: MI” for more detail.
r Guidelines for cardiac testing
r History suggestive of ACS:
– Obtain ECG and 1st troponin (or other cardiac
biomarkers).
r ECG or 1st troponin abnormal:
– Admit; consider cardiology consult.
r Ongoing chest pain or pressure:
– Obtain sestamibi or echo.
– Consider serial EKGs
r Sestamibi, serial EKG or echo abnormal:
– Admit or cardiology consult.
r Second troponin (or other cardiac biomarkers)
abnormal:
– Admit; consider cardiology consult.
r Ancillary testing:
– For low- to moderate-risk patients: standard
exercise testing (ETT).
◦If low-risk patient with good follow-up,
ACC/AHA guidelines allow for outpatient stress
testing within 72 hr.
◦Per 2007 AHA/ACC guidelines CTCA
“reasonable alternative” to stress testing.
– For abnormal or uninterpretable EKG: Stress echo
or sestamibi.
– For patient unable to exert self: Pharmacologic
ETT (i.e., dobutamine stress or dipyridamole
sestamibi).
– Ancillary testing abnormal:
◦Cardiology consult or admit.
MEDICATION
Patient should not be started on new antianginal
medication before stress testing in the ED.
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar History suggestive of cardiac etiology for chest pain
and ED observation for serial testing unavailable
r Abnormal or changed EKG and ED observation
unavailable
r Positive cardiac biomarkers
r Positive rest imaging
r If the diagnosis is unclear, admission to the hospital
or an ED observation unit may be useful for serial
cardiac biomarkers, EKGs, and further ancillary
testing.
r Early positive stress test:
– If the patient has a positive stress test, the decision
for admission should be made in consultation with
the primary care physician or cardiologist.
Discharge Criteria
Patients who meet the following criteria are safe to
discharge:
r History not suggestive of cardiac etiology for chest
pain
r Normal ECG
r Normal cardiac testing
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Abnormal stress test will require close follow-up
with cardiology or PCP .
r Undifferentiated CP should have ED stress testing
unless clear follow-up is available.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Normal EKG or enzymes do not rule out CAD.
r Repeat EKG or additional leads improve sensitivity in
detecting AMI.
r Most ED patients with undifferentiated chest pain
will need some form of additional testing.

Jarrod Mosier rSamuel M. Keim
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Cardiac transplant recipients are a unique
population with increased risk for cardiac ischemia,
heart failure, as well as general risks as an
immunocompromised host.
r 1,900–2,300 cardiac transplants per yr in US
r 1-yr survival 85–90%; 5-yr survival ∼75%
r Typical immunosuppressive therapy to control

after cardiac transplantation

r The proportion of elderly patients on the transplant
list, and receiving transplants are increasing.
r Due to changes in immune system with age, elderly
transplant recipients are at increased risk of
life-threatening infections, and acute rejection.

r Pregnancy after cardiac transplant is becoming more
common. Between 1988 and 2010, 63 women
received either heart or heart–lung transplants. They
have reported 108 pregnancies, all progressing to
live births.
r Most common complications include hypertension,
pre-eclampsia, and rejection.
r Physiologic changes that occur with pregnancy do
not relate to increased rate of heart failure in

regarding rejection and infection given their

◦Most common in 1st 6 wk

◦Fibrosis and graft vascular disease

– Limits long-term survival, leading cause of

– Form of chronic rejection

cyclosporine), tacrolimus:

◦Neurotoxicity
◦Hyperlipidemia, diabetogenic
– Azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil:

– Sirolimus:

◦Wound healing
– Steroids

– Lymphomas
– Kaposi’s sarcoma

CARDIOGENIC SHOCK
Nadeem Alduaij
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Persistent hypotension and tissue hypoperfusion due
to cardiac dysfunction in the presence of adequate
intravascular volume and left ventricular (LV) filling
pressure
r Most common cause of death in hospitalized
patients with acute MI (AMI)
r Underlying mechanisms in AMI:
– Pump failure:
◦≥40% LV infarct
◦Infarct in pre-existing LV dysfunction
◦Reinfarction
– Mechanical complications:
◦Acute mitral regurgitation
◦Ventricular septal defect
◦LV rupture
◦Pericardial tamponade
– Right ventricular (RV) infarction
r 5–8% of patients with STEMI develop cardiogenic
shock
r Role for a systemic inflammatory response syndrome
via excess nitric oxide in the pathophysiology of
cardiogenic shock
r Role of initial treatment with β-blockers, ACEI, and
high-dose diuretics in cardiogenic shock
development
ETIOLOGYr AMI
r Sepsis
r Myocarditis
r Myocardial contusion
r Valvular disease
r Cardiomyopathy
r Left atrial myxoma
r Drug toxicity:
– β-blocker
– Calcium channel blocker
– Adriamycin
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr ABCs and vital signs:
– Patent airway (early)
– Labored breathing and tachypnea (early);
respiratory failure (late)
– Diffuse crackles or wheezing
– Hypoxia
– Hypotension:
◦Systolic BP <90 mm Hg
◦Decline by at least 30 mm Hg below baseline
level
– Tachycardia
– Weak pulses
r General:
– Cyanosis
– Pallor
– Diaphoresis
– Dulled sensorium
– Decrease in body temperature
– Urine flow of <20 mL/hr
r Neck:
– Jugular venous distention
r Cardiac:
– Ischemic chest pain
– Systolic apical blowing murmur
– Gallop rhythm:
◦S3 reflects severe myocardial dysfunction.
◦S4 is present in 80% patients in sinus rhythm
with AMI.
– Systolic click:
◦Suggests rupture of the chordae tendineae
r Abdominal:
– Epigastric pain
– Nausea and vomiting
r Neurologic:
– Obtundation
Historyr Obtain history from patient, family, or EMS for clues
to possible etiology
r Medications history
Physical Examr Perform rapid survey and stabilize ABCs
r Distended neck veins and cool extremities
distinguish cardiogenic shock from distributive and
hypovolemic shock
r Careful heart and lung exam
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Ancillary studies further define the type and degree of
cardiac injury and determine the indications for
emergent catheterization or surgical intervention.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
ECG:
r Normal ECG does not rule out AMI.
r Findings of AMI (ST-elevations in 2 or more
contiguous leads)
r May occur in non–ST-elevation acute coronary
syndrome
r Dysrhythmias
r LV hypertrophy
Labr B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP):
– Diagnostic and prognostic value
r Creatine kinase (CK), CK-MB, troponin
r Electrolytes and renal function:
– Acute renal failure is a strong predictor of
mortality.
r CBC:
– Identify anemia or elevated WBC.
r Drug levels (e.g., digoxin)
Imagingr CXR:
– Pulmonary congestion
– Pleural effusion
– Cardiomegaly
– Pneumonia
– Pneumothorax
– Pericardial effusion
r Emergent echocardiography:
– Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) with color
Doppler
– LV contractility looking for hypokinesis, akinesis,
or dyskinesis
– Acute mitral regurgitation or septal defects
– RV dilatation, tricuspid insufficiency, high
pulmonary artery and RV pressures suggest
pulmonary embolism
– RV hypokinesis or akinesis, RV dilatation, normal
pulmonary pressures suggest RV infarction
– Pericardial effusion, right atrium or RV diastolic
collapse suggest cardiac tamponade

CARDIOMYOPATHY, HYPERTROPHIC
L. Kristian Arnold
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM):
– Genetic disorder affecting the sarcomere:
◦Various mutations
◦Many phenotypic variations
– Hypertrophied (regionally or globally), nondilated
left or, rarely, right ventricle in the absence of
another cause of degree of hypertrophy observed,
such as hypertension or aortic stenosis
– 2 general types:
◦Nonobstructive (HCM)—75% of patients.
Estimated around 1% annual mortality
◦Obstructive (HOCM)—25% of patients. More
severe—estimated 2% annual mortality
– Manifests at all ages, from neonate to elderly:
◦Most manifest in childhood and
adolescence—pubertal growth spurt
◦Usually more severe when diagnosed at younger
age
◦Small percent progress to reduced LV function
– Clinical presentation in mid and late life not
uncommon
◦May initially be misdiagnosed as asthma, COPD,
deconditioning or sleep apnea
– Lethal arrhythmias more common in younger
patients
◦Most common cause of atraumatic death in
young (<35 yo) athletes
– Supraventricular arrhythmias common with
incidence increasing with age
◦Atrial fibrillation both common and poorly
tolerated
r Prevalence ∼1 in 500 adults general population:
– Based on echocardiographic diagnosis
r Structural pathology:
– Irregular, marked ventricular wall thickening with
disarray of myofibrils in the thickened regions and
fibrin deposition:
◦Affects higher-pressure LV more than right and,
in obstructive form, if obstruction removed,
hypertrophy decreases
◦Some phenotypes have progressive wall
thinning with age—usually associated with
thicker wall early
– Thickening usually asymmetric involving the
septum to a greater extent than the free
ventricular wall
– Atrial dilatation secondary to diastolic filling
stiffness
– Impaired microvascular dilation associated with
intimal thickening and perivascular collagen
deposition
r Outpatient long-term management
– Avoidance of volume depletion and elevated
cardiac demand—depending on degree and
location of hypertrophy
– Pharmacologic
◦β-Blockers or verapamil to slow and control
rate, thus prolonging diastole
– Implantable cardiac defibrillator
◦In patients with history of syncope, cardiac
arrest, family member with sudden death,
asymptomatic nonsustained ventricular
tachycardia (VT), abnormal BP response to
exercise, massive hypertrophy
– Alcohol ablation of hypertrophic
outflow-obstructing septal tissue
– Surgical septal myectomy—improving statistics
with more centers performing
RISK FACTORS
Geneticsr 1st cardiac disorder for which genetic basis
identified (1989)
r Autosomal-dominant inheritance:
– >10 associated genes found:
◦Most encode proteins for sarcomere
◦>700 distinct mutations recognized
– High penetrance
– Variable phenotypic expression
– Some genotypes significantly more lethal:
◦Routine screening impractical at present
◦Increasing complexity with more understanding
of interplay between primary sarcomere
abnormalities and other genetic and nongenetic
factors
◦Some mutations affect cell wall pumps—thus,
association with dysrhythmias.
ETIOLOGY
See “Genetics.”
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Obstructive symptoms correlate with exertion or
suddenly assuming upright position—activities that
decrease venous return or ventricular filling.
– Severity depends on the location and degree of
ventricular wall thickening.
r Shortness of breath
r Dyspnea on exertion
r Exertional or postprandial angina
r Presyncope
r Syncope
r CHF
r Cardiovascular collapse
r Dysrhythmias:
– Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation:
◦Often leads to significant, rapid clinical
deterioration when present with CHF
◦Elevated CVA risk from clots
– Supraventricular tachycardia
– Nonsustained VT
– Bradydysrhythmia rare
– VT or ventricular fibrillation may lead to sudden
death.
r Prior therapy for known HCM might include surgery
or alcohol injection to reduce septal bulk:
– Potential for conduction blocks
– Potential septal rupture
r Known cases with higher risk of arrhythmia may
have implanted defibrillators.
r Family history of sudden death without apparent
cause or known HCM
Pediatric Considerations
Due to potential increasing severity in adolescence,
any young child with syncope without clear cause, or in
association with exercise, should have more extensive,
focused history for familial sudden death (standard is
3 generations) and possible referral for evaluation.
Physical Examr No or subtle physical findings
r Most findings in patients with outflow tract
obstruction, variably:
– Loud, left-sided S4
– Double apical cardiac impulse at the mid to upper
sternum
– Murmur:
◦Crescendo–decrescendo midsystolic murmur at
the left sternal edge
◦Radiation to aortic and mitral areas, not to neck
or axilla
◦Increasing in intensity with Valsalva maneuver
or standing up
◦Quieter with recumbency, squatting, or
handgrips
◦Frequent associated mitral regurgitation
– With more severe obstruction, a more apparent
murmur with radiation to the left sternal border
– Radiation to the axilla if there is associated mitral
insufficiency
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
ECG findings:
r Abnormal in >90% pts with HCM
r T-wave inversion>1m m2o r+ leads V2-V6, II and
aVF , or I and aVL or deep TWI in V4-V6 in
non-African-Caribbean descent athletes >16 yo
r ST-segment depression>0.5 mm in 2 or more leads
requires further investigation
r Q-waves >3 mm in depth or >40 ms duration in at
least 2 leads other than III & aVR
r P-wave >120 ms leads I or II with negative portion
≥1m ma n d≥40 ms in lead V1
r Nonspecific IVCD >140 ms
Labr Clinical lab testing is of no assistance.
r Genetic testing may help in outpatient workup, but
not in ED.
Imagingr CXR:
– Normal in the vast majority
– Bulge along left heart border representing
hypertrophy of free wall of LV
– Right or left atrial enlargement
– Pulmonary vascular redistribution
r Transthoracic cardiac echo/Doppler:
– LV wall>15 mm, with normal or small LV cavity
(13–14 mm with other features; e.g., family
history in adults), in children ≥2 times standard
deviation above mean for age, sex, size
– Systolic outflow obstructions
– Diastolic filling abnormalities
r Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR)
– Supplements ECHO
– Allows more structural detail for evidence of
fibrosis
r Stress thallium and PET evaluate ischemia.
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
No ED-based procedures are of diagnostic utility.

C
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Vagal and other causes of syncope and presyncope
r Heatstroke
r Aortic stenosis
r Pulmonic stenosis
r Ventricular septal defect
r Mitral regurgitation
r Mitral valve prolapse
r Arteriosclerotic coronary vascular disease
r Differentiate in patients presenting with CHF or
angina:
– More ominous in the setting of HCM
TREATMENT
ALERT
Consider HCM in patients who decompensate
during standard treatments for CHF , ischemia, or
supra-VT, and in young athletes who collapse during
or just after exertion—rule out heat stroke. HCM
patients may decompensate with IV fluids due to
diastolic stiffness.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs
r IV catheterization
r Supplemental oxygen
r Cardiac monitor
r Pulse oximetry
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Depends on type of presentation: Dysrhythmia,
cardiac failure, chest pain or ischemia
r Underlying principle to understand sensitivity to any
situation that may impair cardiac filling.
r Patient may need to remain supine.
r Standard CHF or anginal vasodilator therapy may
lead to cardiovascular collapse; if this occurs, treat
with fluid bolus.
r Attention to any hypovolemia as small degree may
significantly impair cardiac output.
r Control rate and improve diastolic filling (underlying
principle in treating HCM-associated CHF and
angina):
– β-Blockers:
◦Mainstay of therapy
◦Decrease dysrhythmias and lower elevation of
pressure gradient across the LV outflow tract
– Calcium channel blockers:
◦Verapamil reduces obstruction by decreasing
contractility and improving diastolic relaxation
and filling.
◦Nifedipine relatively contraindicated due to
vasodilatation
r Dysrhythmia management:
– β-Blockers and calcium channel blockers 1st line
for supraventricular dysrhythmias
– Amiodarone:
◦Drug of choice for ventricular dysrhythmias
◦Used when β-blockers and calcium channel
blockers fail
– Electrical cardioversion:
◦Use early in HCM with new atrial fibrillation and
CHF
MEDICATION
All medications must be assessed for effect in face of
possible outflow track restriction
r Amiodarone: 150 mg over 10 min, then 360 mg
over 6 hr, then 540 mg over next 18 hr (peds:
5 mg/kg IV rapid IV/IO bolus, off-label use per
manufacturer, but class IIb for VT with a pulse and
class indeterminate for VF and pulseless VT, per
American Heart Association. Do not use in infants.)
r Propranolol: 1–3 mg (peds: 0.01–0.1 mg/kg slow IV
push over 10 min; not to exceed 1 mg/dose) slow IV
bolus
r Verapamil: 2.5 mg (peds: >1 yr: 0.1–0.2 mg/kg/
dose over 2 min; repeat q10–30min as needed; not
to exceed 5 mg/dose [1st dose] or 10 mg/dose [2nd
dose]) IV bolus over 1–2 min, may repeat as 5 mg in
15–30 min
r Phenylephrine: 0.1–0.2 mg (peds: 1–20 μg/kg) IV
slow bolus for severe hypotension (shock) not
responding to fluid bolus. Repeat in 10–15 min as
needed or start IV drip to titrate to BP; or other pure
vasoconstrictor (i.e., no inotropic effect).
Maintenance dose: 0.05 μg/kg/min (peds:
0.1–0.5 μg/kg/min) IV
First Line
N/A
Second Line
Diltiazem: 0.25 mg/kg (peds: Contraindicated <12 yr
old) IV over 2 min; may repeat in 15 min at
0.35 mg/kg
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Unexplained syncope, especially in younger adults.
r ICU admission:
– Syncopal episodes
– CHF
– Angina
– Hemodynamically significant tachydysrhythmia
Discharge Criteria
When increased myocardial wall thickness is an
incidental finding during the ED evaluation for another
presentation with:
r No history of familial sudden death (proposed
guidance—3 generations to rule out in face of
suspicion) or personal history of syncope
r Need urgent follow-up with a cardiologist
r Counsel against any activities that may decrease
diastolic filling pending follow-up:
– Counsel against physical exertion until evaluated
by cardiologist
Issues for Referral
See “Discharge Criteria.”
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
See “Discharge Criteria.”
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Increasing awareness of genetic and phenotypic
variants with implications in definition of “normal
variant”:
– Some authors advocate cardiac ECHO screening
for any youth participation in sports.
– Some authors advocate AICD at diagnosis.
r If HCM is considered in a patient with syncope, it
must be ruled out because it is much more likely to
be fatal with repeat episodes.

CARDIOMYOPATHY, PERIPARTUM
David W. Callaway
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Dilated cardiomyopathy occurring during the last
month of pregnancy up to 5 mo following the
delivery
r Diagnostic criteria (all required):
– Onset of myocardial failure during last month of
pregnancy or 1st 5 mo after delivery
– Absence of a specific cause
– Absence of prior cardiac disease
r Diagnosis requires strict criteria of
echocardiographic dysfunction
r Incidence: 3–5/10,000 live births
r ∼50% of cases resolve spontaneously
r Mortality: 18–56%
r Risk factors:
– Older women (>30 yr)
– Multiparous women
– Multiple gestations
– Prolonged tocolytic therapy (>4 wk)
– Obesity
– Preeclampsia
– African American
r Systemic and pulmonary embolism more frequent
than with other forms of cardiomyopathy
r Factors indicating a poor prognosis:
– Lower left ejection fraction at 6 mo postpartum
– Onset >2 wk postpartum
– Age >30 yr
– African American descent
– Multiparity
ETIOLOGY
Various causes are suggested but remain unproved:
r Viral infection leading to myocarditis in presence of
immunosuppression during pregnancy (most likely)
r Immunologic response to an unknown maternal or
fetal antigen
r Maladaptive response to the hemodynamic stresses
of pregnancy
r Stress-activated cytokines
r Prolonged tocolysis
r Selenium deficiency
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Dyspnea
r Dizziness
r Chest pain
r Orthopnea
r Cough
r Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
r Anorexia
r Fatigue
r Arrhythmias
Historyr Onset and duration of symptoms
r Unexplained persistent cough
r Excessive weight gain:
– >2–4 lb/wk
r Prior cardiac disease
r Prior pregnancies and complications
Physical Examr Palpitations
r Jugular venous distention
r Gallop rhythm
r Mitral regurgitation murmur
r Loud P2
r Pulmonary rales
r Peripheral edema (especially rapid onset)
r Hepatomegaly
r Hepatojugular reflux
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr CXR views:
– Pulmonary venous congestion
– Cardiomegaly (can be difficult to differentiate with
pregnancy)
– Pleural effusions
r EKG:
– Nonspecific
– Left ventricular hypertrophy
– Left atrial enlargement
– T-wave flattening or inversion
– Arrhythmias
– Ventricular ectopy (40%)
– Atrial fibrillation (20%)
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Electrolytes:
– Generally normal
r BUN, creatinine
r CBC:
– Mild postpartum anemia may contribute to
fatigue and dyspnea.
r Creatine kinase with muscle and brain fraction
r β-Natriuretic peptide (BNP):
– Useful for distinguishing between heart failure
due to diastolic and/or systolic dysfunction and a
pulmonary cause of dyspnea
– BNP >100 pg/mL diagnosed heart failure with a
sensitivity of 90%, a specificity of 76%, and a
predictive accuracy of 83%. BNP of ≤50 pg/mL
has a high negative predictive value.
Imagingr CXR:
– Cardiomegaly
– Effusions (usually right sided)
– 3 phases of pulmonary findings:
◦Stage I: Pulmonary redistribution to upper lung
fields (cephalization)
◦Stage II: Interstitial edema with Kerley B lines
◦Stage III: Alveolar edema
◦Bilateral confluent perihilar infiltrates leading to
classic butterfly pattern
◦May be asymmetric and mistaken for pneumonia
r Echo:
– Demonstrates global dilation, cardiac wall
thinning, and decreased ejection fraction
– Criteria for the diagnosis were established by
Hibbard et al.:
◦Ejection fraction <45% or M-mode fractional
shortening of <30%
◦End-diastolic dimension >2.72 cm/m2
– Exclude valvular pathology and cardiac
tamponade.
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Endomyocardial biopsy:
r Indicated to assess for myocarditis and steroid
therapy
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Other causes of dilated cardiomyopathy:
– Ischemia
– Infarction
– Valvular rupture or disease
– Chronic HTN
– Familial
– Toxins:
◦Ethanol, anthracyclines, cocaine, drug allergy
– Metabolic:
◦Thiamine
◦Selenium
◦Hypothyroidism
◦Thyrotoxicosis
◦Hypophosphatemia
– Infectious:
◦Viral
◦Parasitic or rickettsial
◦Bacterial
◦Fungal
– Systemic disorders:
◦Sarcoidosis
◦Scleroderma
◦Systemic lupus erythematosus
– Eosinophilic myocarditis
– Neuromuscular dystrophies
– Mitochondrial cardiomyopathies

CARDIOMYOPATHY, PERIPARTUM
C
r Other causes of shortness of breath or edema:
– Pulmonary embolism
– Pneumonia
– Asthma
– Cardiac ischemia
– Anemia
– Hyperthyroidism
– Constrictive pericarditis
– Pericardial tamponade
– Nephrotic syndrome
– Cirrhosis
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Differentiate pulmonary edema from acute reactive
airway disease.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
ABCs:
r Prompt evaluation of respiratory and hemodynamic
status
r Control airway as needed
r Supplemental oxygen
r Continuous positive airway pressure, as needed
r Preload and afterload reduction
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Antepartum therapy:
– Nitrates
– Hydralazine
– IV furosemide
– Amlodipine: A dihydropyridine calcium channel
blocker that has been shown to improve survival
in nonischemic cardiomyopathy patients
– Digoxin to control rate due to atrial fibrillation
– Carvedilol (antepartum and not in acute
decompensated phase)
– LMWH if EF <35%
– Fetal monitoring
r Invasive cardiac monitoring if unstable
r Postpartum therapy:
– Consider adding ACE inhibitors (enalapril) or
ARBs.
– Anticoagulation therapy often recommended:
◦30% of cases complicated by systemic or
pulmonary embolism
◦During pregnancy, use SC or IV heparin rather
than warfarin, which causes birth defects.
r For severe symptoms or lack of response to standard
therapy:
– Dobutamine
– Dopamine
– Nitroprusside
– Assist devices
◦Intra-aortic balloon pump
◦LV assist device
◦Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation
– Immunosuppressive therapy:
◦Advocated for patients who fail to improve
within 2 wk of standard medical therapy
◦Prednisone with cyclosporine or azathioprine
◦Immunoglobulin therapy remains controversial
MEDICATIONr Amlodipine: 2.5–10 mg/d PO
r Bumetanide: 0.5–2 mg IV
r Digoxin: 0.5 mg IV , then 0.25 mg IV q4h for
2 doses; 0.125–0.375 mg/d PO
r Milrinone: 50 μg/kg over 10 min
r Dobutamine: 2–10 μg/kg/min IV
r Dopamine: 2–20 μg/kg/min IV
r Enalapril: 0.625–1.25 mg IV; 2.5–20 mg/d PO
r Furosemide: 20–100 mg IV
r Metoprolol: 12.5 mg PO BID
r Morphine sulfate: 2–4 mg IV q5min
r Nitroglycerin: 0.4 mg sublingual; 1–2 in of
nitroglycerin paste; 5–20 μg/min IV , max. of
100–200 μg/min IV . USE NON-PVC tubing
r Nitroprusside: 0.5–10 μg/kg/min IV
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Patients with pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock,
or evidence of ischemia should be admitted to the
ICU.
r All symptomatic patients with new onset of
peripartum cardiomyopathy should be admitted.
Discharge Criteriar Mild left ventricular dysfunction
r Established history of peripartum cardiomyopathy:
– Mild fluid overload attributable to excessive salt
intake
– Complete resolution of symptoms following ED
treatment
– No evidence of cardiac ischemia
r Close follow-up arranged
Issues for Referral
Close follow-up with a cardiologist
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Drink 6–8 glasses of liquid each day.
r Limit salt intake.
r Avoid alcohol because it may worsen
cardiomyopathy.
r Support socks may help decrease the swelling in
legs and prevent clot formation.
r Daily weights:
– Weight gain can be a sign of extra fluid in the
body.
– Call doctor if gain of >2l bi nad a y .
r Return for shortness of breath, feeling faint,
palpitations.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Remember high rates of thromboembolism in
pregnancy and peripartum cardiomyopathy.
r Utilize multidisciplinary approach with cardiology
and obstetrics consultations.

CARPAL FRACTURES
Mary R. Mulcare rWallace A. Carter
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Most commonly injured region of upper extremity
– Most commonly fractured carpals are the scaphoid
(68%) and triquetrum (18%)
r Carpal bone fractures commonly occur with other
wrist injuries:
– Capitate fractures along with scaphoid
(scaphocapitate syndrome) sometimes occur with
perilunate dislocations
– Hamate fractures associated with injuries to 4th
and 5th CMC and metacarpals concurrent with
distal radius fractures
ETIOLOGYr Fall on outstretched hand (FOOSH) with a
hyperextended or hyperflexed wrist
r Direct blow
r Axial loading
r Chronic use injury
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr FOOSH or direct blow
– Hyperflexion → dorsal avulsion fracture
– Hyperextension → volar avulsion fracture
r Hook of hamate fractures:
– Associated with a forceful swing of a racquet or
club
Physical Examr Pain, swelling, decreased range of motion
r Individual palpation of each carpal bone is possible
with correct positioning of wrist
r Scaphoid fractures:
– Snuffbox tenderness is sensitive but not very
specific
– Specificity improved with pronation and ulnar
deviation of wrist
– Scaphoid compression test (axial loading thumb
causes pain) is also not very specific
– Tenderness of tubercle on palmar aspect at distal
wrist crease with wrist in extension
– More specific than snuffbox tenderness
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr A complete physical exam of the entire upper
extremity and shoulder girdle:
– Evaluate for associated injuries
r Neurovascular exam is essential
r Hamate fractures may be associated with ulnar
nerve or artery injuries
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Imagingr Anterior–posterior, lateral, oblique views of the
hand and wrist
r Special views (e.g., scaphoid views) may be obtained
for most of the carpals if physical exam is suspicious
r CT scan has superior sensitivity for fractures
r MRI can diagnose ligamentous injuries
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Metacarpal base fractures
r Distal radius or ulna fractures
r Lunate or perilunate dislocations
Pediatric Considerations
Be wary of epiphyseal injuries of the distal radius:
Children rarely get simple sprains or fractures of the
wrist.
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Prevent contamination of any lacerations overlying
the area
r Patients with swelling or significant pain at the wrist
or hand:
– Elevate extremity and apply ice
– Remove jewelry, watches
– Immobilize extremity with padded board splints to
reduce further injury
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
As in any trauma, assess for other more serious
injuries.

CARPAL FRACTURES
C
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Isolated carpal bone fractures can be initially
managed with splinting
– Goal to obtain and maintain normal alignment
r Thumb spica:
– Scaphoid and trapezium fractures
– Wrist held in slight extension
r Sugar tong splint:
– Capitate and lunate fractures
– Extends from MCP joint on dorsal side of hand,
wrapping around the elbow, ending at midpalmar
crease
– Wrist neutral
r Volar splint:
– Triquetrum, pisiform, trapezoid, hamate fractures
– Extends from midpalmar crease to below the
elbow
– Wrist in slight extension
– Splint suspected fractures (especially scaphoid)
based on physical exam despite negative
radiographs
r Open carpal fractures:
– Requires extensive, high-pressure irrigation
– Parenteral antibiotics against Staphylococcus
aureus, with gram-negative coverage in Grade III
(involving significant soft tissue damage) open
fractures
– Monitor neurovascular status
– Tetanus prophylaxis
– Immediate orthopedic consultation
MEDICATIONr Mild oral analgesics, oral narcotics, NSAIDs for
patient comfort
r Proper splinting will relieve most of the pain for
these injuries
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Open fractures are admitted for early operative
irrigation and d ´ ebridement
r Patients with injuries requiring surgical management
(open reduction, unstable displaced fractures)
sometimes are admitted for early intervention
Discharge Criteria
Closed, nondisplaced carpal fractures treated with
adequate splinting may be discharged to have
orthopedic follow-up in 7–10 days.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Confirmed fractures are referred to orthopedics for
definitive casting and further management
r Missed fractures or improper splinting can lead to
long-term complications and disability:
– Untreated scaphoid, capitate, and lunate fractures
lead to high rates of nonunion and avascular
necrosis
– Splinting is crucial for long-term function and
mobility
– Immobilize any injury with significant pain and
refer for repeat radiographs in 7–10 days or more
advanced imaging (CT or MRI)
PEARLS AND PITFALLS

radiographs and may lead to long-term disability if
not treated appropriately

radiographs or consider CT scanning in ED or
outpatient setting
r Most (90%) scaphoid fractures are isolated injuries:
– All other carpal fractures are more often
associated with other wrist or hand injuries
r Adequate treatment involves splinting in position of
function and referral for definitive casting and
management

CARPAL TUNNEL SYNDROME
Matthew T. Spencer rLinda L. Spillane
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Carpal tunnel syndrome is caused by compression of
the median nerve as it passes through the carpal
tunnel.
r The carpal tunnel is the area bound by the carpal
bones and the transverse carpal ligament.
r The median nerve, flexor digitorum profundus, flexor
digitorum superficialis (FDS), and flexor pollicis
longus are located in the carpal tunnel.
r Carpal tunnel syndrome can be classified as acute or
chronic.
ETIOLOGYr Acute:
– Trauma
– Infection
– Snake bite
– Hemorrhage
– High-pressure injection injury
r Chronic:
– Occupational/overuse syndromes—high impact,
repetitive motion
– Pregnancy, birth control pills
– Granulomatous disease: Tuberculosis, sarcoidosis
– Mass lesions with median nerve compression
– Osteophytes
– Amyloid
– Multiple myeloma
– Rheumatoid arthritis
– Endocrine disorders: Hypothyroidism, diabetes
mellitus, acromegaly
– Chronic hemodialysis
– Idiopathic
Pediatric Considerations
Idiopathic causes are rare in children; most cases have
a correctable cause including:
r Trauma
r Mucolipidosis
r Hamartoma of the median nerve
r Anomalous FDS
r Hemophilia with hematoma
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Acute or chronic onset
r Numbness/paresthesia in a median nerve
distribution:
– Thumb, index, middle, and radial aspect of ring
finger
r Pain:
– Location: Wrist or hand, sometimes radiating to
elbow, forearm, or shoulder
– Often worse at night—relieved by “shaking out”
the hand
– Exacerbated by repetitive wrist movement and by
activities in which the wrist is flexed (e.g., driving)
Physical Examr Weakness of the abductor pollicis brevis and
opponens muscles:
– Innervated by the recurrent branch of the median
nerve
– Patient may complain of dropping things or
having decreased fine motor control.
r Loss of 2-point discrimination:
– Late finding, highly specific
r Atrophy of thenar muscles:
– Late finding, highly specific
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr History of characteristic nocturnal pain and
paresthesia in the median nerve distribution.
r Muscle weakness and thenar wasting are later
findings.
r Provocative testing:
– Overall poor sensitivity and specificity
– Phalen test:
◦Wrist flexion for 60 sec produces numbness or
tingling in the median nerve distribution.
– Tinel sign:
◦Gentle tapping over the median nerve at wrist
produces tingling in the fingers in the median
nerve distribution.
– Carpal compression test:
◦Direct pressure applied over the proximal carpal
ligament for 30 sec produces tingling in the
fingers in the median nerve distribution.
– Tourniquet test:
◦BP cuff inflated to just above the patient’s
systolic BP for 2 min produces paresthesia in the
median nerve distribution.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Not indicated in most cases
r Thyroid function studies; rheumatoid factor and
immune panel if indicated by history and physical
exam
Imagingr Wrist radiograph if trauma or degenerative arthritis
suspected
r CT in select cases (not routine):
– May show encroachment of carpal tunnel
r MRI displays the soft tissues well but not
recommended for routine diagnosis:
– Findings: Palmar bowing of transcarpal ligament,
flattened median nerve, median nerve or synovial
swelling, fluid in carpal tunnel, signal abnormality
of median nerve
r Ultrasound can be diagnostic:
– Sensitivity of 44–95%; specificity of 57–100%
– Findings: Median nerve swelling at proximal
canal, median nerve flattening at distal canal,
bowing of transcarpal ligament
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography are
criterion standard tests.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Cervical nerve root compression:
– Origin of median nerve is at the 6th and 7th
cervical roots.
– Symptoms are aggravated by erect posture and
neck movement.

CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME
Daniel F. Morris
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Compression of lumbar and sacral nerve fibers in
cauda equina region:
r Nerve fibers below conus medullaris
r Fibers end at L1–L2 interspace.
RISK FACTORSr Neoplasm
r IV drug use
r Immunocompromised state
r Trauma
ETIOLOGYr Herniated disc most common:
– L4–L5 discs > L5–S1 > L3–L4
– Most common in 4th and 5th decades of life
r Mass effect from:
– Myeloma, lymphoma, sarcoma, meningioma,
neurofibroma, hematoma
– Spine metastases (breast, lung, prostate, thyroid,
renal)
– Epidural abscess (especially in IV drug users)
r Blunt trauma
r Penetrating trauma
r Spinal anesthesia
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Low back pain
r Sciatica/radicular pain (unilateral or bilateral)
r Lower-extremity numbness or weakness
r Difficulty ambulating owing to weakness or pain
r Bladder or rectal dysfunction:
– Retention or incontinence
Physical Examr Lumbosacral (LS) tenderness
r Lower-extremity sensory or motor deficits:
– May be asymmetric
r Decreased foot dorsiflexion strength
r Decreased quadriceps strength
r Decreased deep tendon reflexes
r Saddle hypalgesia or anesthesia
r Decreased anal sphincter tone
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Neurologic exam most essential:
– Straight-leg raise
– Las ` egue sign:
◦With patient supine, flex hip and dorsiflex foot.
◦Pain or spasm in posterior thigh indicates nerve
irritation.
– Perineal sensation
– Rectal tone
– Anal wink: Reflex contraction of external anal
sphincter with gentle stroking of skin lateral to
anus
r Postvoid residual volume:
– Estimate by bladder catheterization or using US.
– >50–100 mL is considered abnormal.
– Residual increases with age.
– Diagnosis unlikely if normal
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Based on differential diagnoses
r CBC, urinalysis, ESR, and C-reactive protein (CRP)
Imagingr Radiographs of LS spine
r MRI of spine is definitive study.
r CT myelogram if MRI unavailable
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Osteoarthritis, LS strain, sciatica
r Vertebral fracture (pathologic and nonpathologic)
r Osteomyelitis
r Spinal epidural abscess
r Conus medullaris or higher cord compression
r Ankylosing spondylitis, spinal stenosis
r Abdominal aortic aneurysm dissection
r Vascular claudication
r Hip pathology
r Acute transverse myelitis

PRE-HOSPITALr Manage airway and traumatic injuries as indicated.
r If evidence of trauma, patient should be transported
with full spine immobilization.
ALERT

immobilization given possibility of unstable lesion.

lesion suspected

consultation with neurosurgery.

decompression:

to within 24 hr.

decompression.

surgical decompression.

Patients with established cauda equina syndrome with
prior complete evaluation and no new neurologic
deficits may be discharged with close follow-up with
their neurosurgeon.

irreversible neurologic dysfunction:

CAUSTIC INGESTION
Paul Kolecki
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Alkalis:
– Dissociate in the presence of H2O to produce
hydroxy (OH− ) ions, which leads to liquefaction
necrosis
– Postingestion—mainly damages the esophagus:
◦Gastric damage can occur (see “Acids”).
– Esophageal damage (in the order of increasing
damage) consists of:
◦Superficial hyperemia
◦Mucosal edema
◦Superficial blisters
◦Exudative ulcerations
◦Full-thickness necrosis
◦Perforation
◦Fibrosis with resulting esophageal strictures
–D o not directly produce systemic complications.
r Acids:
– Dissociate in the presence of H2O to produce
hydrogen (H+) ions, which leads to a coagulation
necrosis with eschar formation
– Postingestion—damages the stomach because of
rapid transit time through esophagus:
◦Esophageal damage can occur (see “Alkalis”).
– Gastric damage (in the order of increasing
damage) consists of:
◦Edema
◦Inflammation
◦Immediate or delayed hemorrhage
◦Full-thickness necrosis
◦Perforation
◦Fibrosis with resulting gastric outlet obstruction
– Well-absorbed and can cause hemolysis of RBCs
and a systemic metabolic acidosis
ETIOLOGYr Direct chemical injuries
r Injuries occur secondary to acid and alkali exposures.
r Many caustic agents (acids and alkalis) are found in
common household and industrial products.
r Caustic substances:
– Ammonia hydroxide
r Glass cleaners:
– Formaldehyde:
◦Embalming agent
– Hydrochloric acid:
◦Toilet bowel cleaners
– Hydrofluoric acid:
◦Glass etching industry
◦Microchip industry
◦Rust removers
– Iodine:
◦Antiseptics
– Phenol:
◦Antiseptics
– Sodium hydroxide:
◦Drain cleaners
◦Drain openers
◦Oven cleaners
– Sodium borates, carbonates, phosphates, and
silicates:
◦Detergents
◦Dishwasher preparations
◦Sodium hypochlorite
◦Bleaches
– Sulfuric acid:
◦Car batteries
◦Button batteries
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Oropharyngeal:
– Pain
– Erythema
– Burns
– Erosions
– Ulcers
– Drooling
– Hoarseness
– Stridor
– Aphonia
– Absence of visible lesions in the oropharynx does
not exclude visceral injuries.
r Pulmonary:
– Tachypnea
– Cough
– Pneumonitis if aspirated
r GI:
– Pain
– Emesis or hematemesis
– Melena, dysphagia
– Odynophagia
– Esophageal or gastric perforation
– Peritonitis owing to perforation
r Cardiovascular:
– Tachycardia
– Hypotension
– Orthostatic changes
r Hematologic:
– Acid ingestion can cause RBC hemolysis.
r Dermatologic:
– Pain
– Erythema
– 1st-, 2nd-, or 3rd-degree burns
r Ocular:
– Pain
– Erythema
– Injection
– Corneal burns
– Full-thickness corneal damage
r Metabolic:
– Metabolic acidosis
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr History of or signs and symptoms of an exposure
r Absence of oropharyngeal lesions does not exclude
visceral injury.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose
r Arterial blood gas
r Blood cultures:
– If mediastinitis or peritonitis suspected
r Type and cross-match
Imaging
Chest and abdominal radiographs for:
r Esophageal or gastric perforation
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Esophageal and gastric endoscopy:
– For symptomatic patients to determine the extent
of injury
– Perform within the 1st 12–24 hr after ingestion.
– Not recommended in the presence of respiratory
distress without proper airway management
– Not recommended in the presence of severe
pharyngeal damage
r Radiographic oral contrast imaging not
recommended acutely:
– May be used in follow-up for assessment for
strictures
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Chemical injuries from corrosives, acids, alkalis,
desiccants, vesicants, and oxidizing and reducing
agents
r Foreign body ingestion
r Upper airway infection or angioedema

C
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr For oral burns or symptoms: Rinse mouth liberally
with water or milk.
r Water or milk can be given to following patients:
– Able to drink
– Not complaining of significant abdominal pain
– Do not have airway compromise or vomiting
r Copious irrigation for ocular or dermal exposure

respiratory compromise

– Dermal or ocular exposure:

or 0.9% NS until physiologic pH attained
◦Alkalis typically require more irrigation than
acids.
– Ipecac, activated charcoal, gastroesophageal
lavage (large-bore or an NG tube), and a
neutralizing acid or base are all contraindicated

ingestions

worsen esophageal damage.
– If respiratory distress, intubate before dilution.

perforation suspected

peritonitis suspected

recommendations.

symptomatic relief
r Gastroenterology and surgical consultation

damage is controversial:
– May prevent the formation of esophageal stricture
– May promote bacterial invasion, immune
suppression, and tissue softening
– The decision to initiate corticosteroids requires
input from entire team caring for patient.
– Initiate broad-spectrum antibiotics if
corticosteroids are given.
r Laparoscopy or laparotomy for perforation and
full-thickness necrosis

on severity and location):
– IM injection of 5% calcium gluconate (0.5 mL/cm2
of skin with 30G needle)
– Intra-arterial infusion of 10 mL of 10% calcium
gluconate in 40 mL D5W over 4 hr

visible lesion; no drooling; no respiratory
compromise; no deep throat, chest, or abdominal
pain; and able to swallow without difficulty

exposure:
– Alkalis require more irrigation than acids.

CAVERNOUS SINUS THROMBOSIS
Joanna W. Davidson
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Thrombosis of a branch of the major intracerebral
venous drainage system
r Most commonly infectious
r Spreads from facial, odontogenic, or sinus infection
r Less frequently occurs with hypercoagulable state
Anatomy
3 primary sites of thrombosis:
r Cavernous sinus—Most common:
– Drainage from superficial venous system
r Superolateral to the sphenoid sinus and surrounds
the sella:
– Cranial nerves (CN) III, IV , V1, and V2 traverse the
lateral wall of the sinus.
– CN VI and the internal carotid artery occupy the
medial portion of the sinus.
r Can also involve transverse sinus and superficial
sagittal sinus
PATHOPHYSIOLOGYr Hematogenous spread of facial, otic, or neck
infection into venous drainage system
r Contiguous spread directly from infected sinus
cavities (sphenoid, ethmoid > frontal)
r Bacterial overgrowth leads to inflammation and
coagulation, resulting in thrombosis.
r Venous engorgement of cavernous sinus can affect
adjacent structures:
– Ophthalmoplegia from inflammation of CN III, IV ,
or VI
– Pupillary fixation from CN III
– Sensory deficits or paresthesia of forehead or
cheek from CN V1 and V2
ETIOLOGYr Septic:
– Staphylococcus aureus accounts for 70%
– Streptococcus pneumoniae, gram-negative bacilli,
and anaerobes also seen
– Fungi less common; include Aspergillus and
Rhizopus species
r Aseptic:
– Less common
– Granulomatous conditions (TB)
– Inflammatory disorders
– From mass effect (tumors at base of skull,
aneurysms)
r Hypercoagulable states
Pediatric Considerations
r Children may present with nonspecific symptoms
such as decreased energy, vomiting, fever.
r Have high level of suspicion for any child with recent
otitis or pharyngitis with worsening symptoms,
declining mental status, or signs of increased
intracranial pressure (ICP):
– HTN, bradycardia, lethargy, vomiting, gait
instability
r More common in the neonatal period, when
diagnosis can be extremely difficult to make
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Symptoms:
– Headache occurs in 90% of patients.
– Fever
– Ocular or retrobulbar pain
– Facial swelling
– Visual disturbance
– Facial dysesthesia
– Lethargy or altered mental status
r Signs:
– Periorbital edema is earliest sign
– Chemosis with retinal vein engorgement
– Ptosis, proptosis
– Ophthalmoplegia
– CN palsies:
◦Lateral gaze palsy (CN VI)
◦Hypo/hyperesthesia of V1 and V2 (CN V)
– Meningismus
– Altered level of consciousness or coma
– Seizures
– Sepsis with cardiovascular instability or collapse
History
High-risk historical factors include:
r A history of trauma
r Previous ear/nose/throat (ENT) or neurosurgical
instrumentation
r History of central face furuncle that was manipulated
r Diabetes or immunocompromised state (HIV , steroid
use, cancer) may increase risk
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Clinical diagnosis: Venous engorgement, ocular
symptoms, unilateral symptoms that become
bilateral, rapidly progressive
r Labs nonspecific
r Imaging findings can be subtle
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Neither sensitive nor specific
r CBC:
– Leukocytosis
– Bandemia
r PT/PTT/INR
r ESR and D-dimer usually elevated
r Lumbar puncture/CSF: Parameningeal inflammation
or frank mengingitis
Imagingr CT scan:
– Can be normal early in disease course
– Noncontrast can show increased density
– Contrast can show filling defect
◦May identify original source of infection (e.g.,
sinusitis)
◦Dilated superior ophthalmic vein
◦Associated intracranial hemorrhage
