CELLULITIS
John Mahoney rDolores Gonthier
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Acute, spreading erythematous superficial infection
of skin and SC tissues:
– Variety of pathogens
– Extension into deeper tissues can result in
necrotizing soft tissue infection
r Progressive spread of erythema, warmth, pain, and
tenderness
r Predisposing factors:
– Lymphedema
– Tinea pedis
– Open wounds
– Pre-existing skin lesion (furuncle)
– Prior trauma or surgery
– Retained foreign body
– Vascular or immune compromise
– Injection drug use
ETIOLOGYr Simple cellulitis:
– Group A streptococci
– Staphylococcus aureus—including resistant
strains such as community-associated
methicillin-resistant S. aureus (CA-MRSA;
see below):
◦CA-MRSA risk factors include: Prior MRSA
infection, household contact of CA-MRSA
patient, daycare contact of MRSA patients,
children, soldiers, incarcerated persons, athletes
in contact sports, IV drug users, men who have
sex with men
◦Different antibiotic susceptibility than
nosocomial MRSA
◦CA-MRSA now sufficiently prevalent to warrant
empiric treatment
◦Suspect CA-MRSA in unresponsive infections
r Nosocomial MRSA:
– Risk factors: Recent hospital or long-term care
admission, surgery, injection drug use, vascular
catheter, dialysis, recent antibiotic use,
unresponsive infection
– Resistant to most antibiotics (see “Treatment”)
r Extremity cellulitis after lymphatic disruption:
– Nongroup A β-hemolytic streptococci (groups C,
B, G)
r Cellulitis in diabetics:
– Can be polymicrobial with S. aureus, streptococci,
gram-negative bacteria, and anaerobes, especially
when associated with skin ulcers
r Periorbital cellulitis:
– S. aureus
– Streptococcal species
r Buccal cellulitis:
– Haemophilus influenzae type B
– Anaerobic oral flora, associated with intraoral
laceration or dental abscess
r Less common causes:
– Clostridia
– Anthrax
– Pasteurella multocida—common after cat and
dog bites
– Eikenella corrodens—human bites
– Pseudomonas aeruginosa:
◦Hot-tub folliculitis—self-limited
◦Foot puncture wound
◦Ecthyma gangrenosum in neutropenic patients
– Erysipelothrix species—raw fish, poultry, meat, or
hide handlers
– Aeromonas hydrophila—freshwater swimming
– Vibrio species—seawater or raw seafood
Pediatric Considerations
r Facial cellulitis in children:
– Streptococcus pneumoniae
– H. influenzae type B, although incidence declining
since introduction of HIB vaccine
r Perianal cellulitis:
– Group A streptococci
– Associated or antecedent pharyngitis or impetigo
r Neonates:
– Group B streptococci
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Common to all syndromes:
– Pain, tenderness, warmth
– Erythema
– Edema or induration
– Fever/chills
– Tender regional lymphadenopathy
– Lymphangitis
– Accompanying SC abscess possible
– Suspect deep abscess especially if treatment
failure on initial antibiotic
– Superficial vesicles
r Buccal cellulitis:
– Odontogenic cases more serious:
◦Toothache, sore throat, or facial swelling
◦Progressive extension into soft tissues of neck
with fever, erythema, neck swelling, and
dysphagia
Pediatric Considerations
r Facial cellulitis in children:
– Erythema and swelling of the cheek and eyelid
– Rapidly progressive
– Usually unilateral
– Upper respiratory tract symptoms
– Risk for cavernous sinus thrombosis and
permanent optic nerve injury
r Perianal cellulitis:
– Erythema and pruritus extending from the anus
several centimeters onto adjacent skin
– Pain on defecation
– Blood-streaked stools
History
Patients often incorrectly attribute CA-MRSA infection
with spontaneous abscess to a spider bite
Physical Exam
In simple cellulitis, physical findings can suggest
the etiology and help narrow empiric antibiotic
coverage:
r Staph etiology: Focal abscess or pustule with:
Fluctuance, yellow or white center, central point or
“head,” or draining pus, indolent progression
r Strep etiology: Sharply demarcated borders,
lymphangitis, pre-existing lymphedema,
concomitant nausea from toxin
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Cellulitis is a clinical diagnosis.
r Physical exam to reveal infection source
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr WBC generally unnecessary
r Gram stain and culture to focus antimicrobial
selection and reveal resistant pathogens (MRSA):
– Aspirate point of maximal inflammation or punch
biopsy if there is no wound to culture
– Perform in treatment failures and consider in
admitted patients
r Blood culture:
– Usually negative in uncomplicated cellulitis
– May identify organism in patients with:
◦Lymphedema
◦Buccal or periorbital cellulitis
◦Saltwater or freshwater source
◦Fever or chills
Imagingr Plain radiographs may reveal abscess formation, SC
gas, or foreign bodies:
– Extension to bone (osteomyelitis) not visualized
early on plain radiographs
r Extremity vascular imaging (Doppler US) can help
rule out deep venous thrombosis (DVT).
r US useful for diagnosing abscess if physical exam is
equivocal or if there is a broad area of cellulitis
– In cellulitis may see characteristic “cobblestone”
appearance and thickening of SC layer, both due
to edema
r CT or MRI can help rule out necrotizing fasciitis
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Necrotizing fasciitis
r Lymphangitis or lymphadenitis
r Thrombophlebitis or DVT:
– Differentiation from cellulitis:
◦Absence of initial traumatic or infectious focus
◦No regional lymphadenopathy
◦Presence of risk factors for DVT
r Insect bite
r Allergic reaction
r Acute gout or pseudogout
r Ruptured Baker cyst
r Herpetic whitlow
r Neoplasm
r Phytophotodermatitis
r Erythema chronicum migrans lesion of Lyme disease
r Differential diagnosis of facial cellulitis:
– Allergic angioedema
– Conjunctivitis
– Contusion
Pediatric Considerations
Differential diagnosis of perianal cellulitis:
r Candida intertrigo
r Psoriasis
r Pinworm infection
r Child abuse
r Behavioral problem
r Inflammatory bowel disease

CENTRAL RETINAL ARTERY OCCLUSION
Yasuharu Okuda rBraden Hexom
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Obstruction of the central retinal artery associated
with sudden painless loss of vision
r Usually occurs in persons 50–70 yr of age
r Ophthalmic artery is 1st branch of carotid.
r Risk factors include HTN, atherosclerotic disease,
sickle cell disease, vasculitis, valvular heart disease,
lupus, trauma, and coronary artery disease.
r Incidence of 1–10/100,000
r Often described as a “stroke of the eye”
ETIOLOGYr Embolic:
– Occlusion by intravascular material from a
proximal source:
◦Atherosclerotic disease (majority)
◦Carotid artery stenosis
◦Valvular heart disease (cardiogenic emboli)
◦Atrial myxoma
◦Dissection of the ophthalmic artery
◦Carotid artery dissection
r Thrombotic:
– Obstruction of flow from the rupture of a
pre-existing intravascular atherosclerotic plaque
– Hypercoagulable states (sickle cell)
r Inflammatory:
– Due to temporal arteritis, lupus, vasculitis
r Arterial spasm:
– Associated with migraine headaches
r Decreased perfusion:
– Low-flow conditions such as in severe
hypotension or high-pressure situations seen in
acute angle-closure glaucoma or retrobulbar
hemorrhage
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Sudden, painless, monocular loss of vision
r Prior episodes of sudden visual loss:
– May last a few seconds to minutes (amaurosis
fugax)
– Caused by transient embolic phenomena or
decreased ocular blood flow
Physical Examr Significantly decreased visual acuity
r Afferent pupillary defect usually present
r Retinal appearance:
– Emboli visualized within vascular tree of the retina
– Appears as glinting white or yellow flecks
(Hollenhorst plaques) within the vessels
– Ischemic edema visible within 15–20 min of
occlusion
– “Cherry-red spot” remains over the fovea (only
area where there is very thin retina allowing the
vascular choroids to show through).
– Affected arteries empty or showing dark red
stationary or barely pulsatile segmented rouleaux
(“box-carring”)
– Within 1–2 hr opacification of the usually
transparent infarcting retinal nerve layer occurs.
r Partial field deficits:
– Occur only if branch of central retinal artery
involved
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Visual acuity and visual field testing
r Fundoscopic exam
r Intraocular pressure measurements
r Emergent ophthalmologic consultation
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Directed toward evaluating underlying etiology of
occlusion:
r CBC with differential and platelet count
r PT/PTT
r Electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, glucose
r Electronic spin resonance for giant cell arteritis (in
patients >55 yr old)
r ANA, RF , CRP , ESR
r Rapid plasma reagin (RPR)
r Hemoglobin electrophoresis
r Serum protein electrophoresis
Imaging
Directed toward evaluating underlying etiology of
occlusion:
r Carotid artery ultrasound/Doppler
r Possibly echocardiography
r Fluorescein angiography or electroretinography to
confirm the diagnosis
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Acute angle-closure glaucoma
r Central retinal vein occlusion
r Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis)
r Optic neuritis
r Retinal detachment

CENTRAL RETINAL ARTERY OCCLUSION
C
TREATMENT
ALERT
Initiate treatment immediately because irreversible
visual loss occurs at 90 min:r Only immediate treatment may help to salvage or
restore sight to the affected eye.
r Goals of therapy include dislodging or dissolving
the embolus, arterial dilation to improve forward
flow, and reduction of intraocular pressure to
improve the perfusion gradient.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Immediate global massage in an attempt to
dislodge the embolus:
– Lay patient flat and apply digital global massage
bolus.
– On closed eyelid, apply constant pressure for
15 sec and remove for 15 sec. Repeat for 5 cycles.
r Initiate high-flow oxygen via 100% nonrebreather:
– Consider transfer to a facility capable of providing
hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) if <24 hr from symptom
onset
– May use inhaled carbogen (a mixture of carbon
dioxide and oxygen gas) if available
r Administer IV acetazolamide to decrease intraocular
pressure.
r Apply topical timolol maleate to reduce intraocular
pressure.
r Administer aspirin and IV heparin for prevention of
clot propagation.
r Obtain emergent ophthalmology consultation for:
– Anterior chamber paracentesis to help reduce
intraocular pressure
– Possible intra-arterial fibrinolysis for clot lysis
r Administer high-dose systemic steroids in suspected
cases of inflammatory arteritis.
MEDICATION
First Liner Acetazolamide: 500 mg IV or PO
r Carbogen: Inhalation of 95% oxygen and 5%
carbon dioxide mixture
r Heparin: 80 U/kg IV bolus then 18 U/kg/h
continuous infusions (rate adjusted based on PTT
level)
r Timolol maleate 0.5% solution: 1 drop topically to
affected eye
Second Liner Methylprednisolone: 250 mg IV in suspected cases
of inflammatory arteritis
r Aspirin: 325 mg PO
r Mannitol
r Sublingual nitroglycerin
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteria
Required for workup of proximal cause in acute cases
(source of embolism, thrombosis, or inflammatory)
Discharge Criteria
Chronic retinal artery occlusion with no evidence of
active disease can be worked up as an outpatient.
Issues for Referral
All suspected cases warrant emergent ophthalmology
consultation.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Most cases will require carotid ultrasound to exclude
atherosclerotic disease.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Amaurosis fugax (transient, possibly resolved retinal
artery occlusion) is a sentinel event and may lead to
complete occlusion or stroke. Do not ignore these
symptoms and urgent workup is required.
r Retinal artery occlusion is a medical emergency
requiring immediate treatment to prevent loss of the
eye.
r It is important to document a full eye exam including
visual acuity and evaluation of the optic fundus.

vision loss

– Usually worse than 20/200

r Dilated tortuous veins

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Abnormal, localized dilation or outpouching of
cerebral artery wall:
– Occurs in 5–10% of population
r Rupture of saccular aneurysms account for 5–15%
of strokes
r Of those that rupture:
– 40% occur at anterior communicating artery
(ACA)
– 30% at internal carotid (IC)
– 20% in middle cerebral artery (MCA)
– 5–10% in vertebrobasilar artery (VBA) system
ETIOLOGYr Asymptomatic in 3.2% of population
r “Congenital,” saccular, or berry aneurysms most
common (90%):
– Develop at weak points in arterial wall and
bifurcations of major cerebral arteries
– Incidence increases with age
– Multiple in 20–30%
– Increased incidence:
◦Polycystic kidney disease
◦Cerebral arteriovenous malformation
◦Type III collagen deficiency
◦Fibromuscular dysplasia
◦Ehlers–Danlos syndrome
◦Marfan syndrome
◦Pseudoxanthoma elasticum
◦Neurofibromatosis
◦Moyamoya syndrome
◦Coarctation of the aorta
◦Tuberous sclerosis
◦Sickle cell disease
◦Osler–Weber–Rendu syndrome
◦α1-Antitrypsin deficiency
◦Systemic lupus erythematosus
◦Glucocorticoid remediable hyperaldosteronism
r Arteriosclerotic, fusiform, or dolichoectatic (7%):
– More common in peripheral arteries
r Inflammatory (mycotic):
– 10% of patients with bacterial endocarditis
r Traumatic, associated with severe closed head injury
r Neoplastic, embolized tumor fragments
r Familial correlation: 1st-degree relative with history
of aneurysm essentially doubles lifetime risk
Pediatric Considerations
r Although rare in children, more likely to be giant
(>25 mm)
r Occur in the posterior circulation
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Commonly asymptomatic before rupture
r Sentinel headaches occur in 30–60% of patients
before rupture:
– Can be unilateral
r Seizures, syncope, or altered level of consciousness
Historyr Onset of headache
r Family history
r Altered mental status
r Focal neurologic deficits
r Rupture results in subarachnoid hemorrhage:
– Headache: Severe (“worst headache ever”) with
sudden onset (“thunderclap”)
◦Different from prior headaches
◦Classically without focal deficits
– Nuchal rigidity (most common sign) secondary to
blood in CSF
Physical Exam
Compression of adjacent structures may cause
neurologic symptoms:
r ACA aneurysms:
– Optic tract: Altitudinal field cut or homonymous
hemianopsia
– Optic chiasm: Bitemporal hemianopsia
– Optic nerve: Unilateral amblyopia
r Aneurysms at IC–posterior communicating artery
junction:
– Oculomotor nerve: Fixed and dilated pupil, ptosis,
diplopia, and temporal deviation of eye with
inability to turn eye upward, inward, or downward
r Aneurysms in cerebral cortex may produce focal
deficits including:
– Hemiparesis
– Hemisensory loss
– Visual disturbances
– Aphasia
– Seizures
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Complete neurologic examination
r Emergent noncontrast head CT scan will diagnose
90–95% of subarachnoid hemorrhages
r Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis if CT scan is
negative
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Coagulation studies
r Baseline CBC with platelets and differential
r Electrolytes
r Renal and liver function tests
r Arterial blood gas
Imagingr CXR for pulmonary edema
r 4-vessel cerebral angiography remains gold standard
r MRA
r Helical CT scanning may be useful in detecting
aneurysms >3m m
r Transcranial Doppler US may be useful in detecting
vasospasm.
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Lumbar puncture if suspect aneurysmal leak or rupture
with normal head CT
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Neoplasm
r Arteriovenous malformation
r Optic neuritis
r Migraine
r Meningitis
r Encephalitis
r Hypertensive encephalopathy
r Hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia
r Temporal arteritis
r Acute glaucoma
r Subdural hematoma
r Epidural hematoma
r Intracerebral hemorrhage
r Thromboembolic stroke
r Air embolism
r Sinusitis
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Cautions:
– Neurologic examination in the field can be
extremely helpful
– Assess:
◦Level of consciousness
◦Glasgow coma scale score
◦Gross motor deficits
◦Speech abnormalities
◦Gait disturbance
◦Facial asymmetry
◦Other focal deficits
r Patients with subarachnoid hemorrhage may need
emergent intubation for rapidly deteriorating level of
consciousness
r Patients must be transported to a hospital with
emergent CT scanning and intensive care unit
(ICU)-level treatment

treatment of ruptured or leaking aneurysms are to
prevent re-rupture, cerebral vasospasm, and
hydrocephalus (see “Subarachnoid Hemorrhage”).

controversial, but trend is toward early surgery to
decrease incidence of rebleeding and cerebral
vasospasm

and should be repaired early

CEREBRAL VASCULAR ACCIDENT
Veronique Au rRebecca Smith-Coggins
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Interruption of blood flow to a specific brain region:
r Neurologic findings are determined by specific area
affected
r Onset may be sudden and complete, or stuttering
and intermittent
r Responsible for 1 in 18 deaths in US
r 610,000 new strokes every year in US
RISK FACTORSr Diabetes
r Smoking
r HTN
r Coronary artery disease, dysrhythmias
r Peripheral vascular disease
r Oral contraceptive use
r Polycythemia vera
r Sickle cell anemia
r Deficiencies of antithrombin III, protein C or S
ETIOLOGYr May be ischemic (thrombotic, embolic, or secondary
to dissection/hypoperfusion) or hemorrhagic
r Thrombotic stroke is caused by occlusion of blood
vessels:
– Clot formation at an ulcerated atherosclerotic
plaque is most common
– Sludging (sickle cell anemia, polycythemia vera,
protein C deficiency)
r Embolic stroke is caused by acute blockage of a
cerebral artery by a piece of foreign material from
outside the brain, including:
– Cardiac mural thrombi associated with mitral
stenosis, atrial fibrillation, cardiomyopathy, CHF ,
or MI
– Prosthetic or abnormal native valves
– Atherosclerotic plaques in the aortic arch or
carotid arteries
– Atrial myxoma
– Ventricular aneurysms with thrombi
r Arterial dissection:
– Carotid artery dissection
– Arteritis (giant cell, Takayasu)
– Fibromuscular dysplasia
r Global ischemic or hypotensive stroke is caused by
an overall decrease in systemic BP: Sepsis,
hemorrhage, shock
r Hemorrhagic stroke:
– Intracranial hemorrhage
– Subarachnoid hemorrhage
Pediatric Considerations
r Usually attributable to an underlying disease
process, such as sickle cell anemia, leukemia,
infection, or a blood dyscrasia
r Younger children often present with seizures and/or
altered mental status
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Time of onset (or time last seen at baseline)
r Trauma/surgery
r Medications
r Altered mentation/confusion
r Headache
r Vertigo/dizzy
r Focal neurologic deficits
Physical Examr General:
– Cheyne–Stokes breathing, apnea
– HTN
– Cardiac dysrhythmias, murmurs
r Anterior cerebral artery:
– Contralateral hemiplegia (lower/upper)
– Hemisensory loss
– Apraxia
– Confusion
– Impaired judgment
r Middle cerebral artery:
– Contralateral hemiplegia (upper/lower)
– Hemisensory deficits
– Homonymous hemianopsia
– Dysphasia
– Dysarthria
– Agnosia
r Posterior cerebral artery:
– Cortical blindness in half the visual field
– Visual agnosia
– Altered mental status
– Impaired memory
– 3rd-nerve palsy
– Hemiballismus
r Vertebrobasilar system:
– Impaired vision, visual field defects, nystagmus,
diplopia
– Vertigo, dizziness
– Crossed deficits: Ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits
with contralateral motor and sensory deficits
r Basilar system:
– Quadriplegia
– Locked-in syndrome
– Coma
r Watershed area (boundary zone between anterior,
middle, and posterior circulation):
– Cortical blindness
– Weakness of proximal upper and lower
extremities with sparing of face, hands, and feet
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Detailed neurologic exam; consider calculating
National Institutes of Health stroke scale (NIHSS).
r Emergent noncontrast head CT scan to distinguish
ischemic from hemorrhagic events:
– May be normal in 1st 24–48 hr
– GOALS:
◦CT completed within 25 min of arrival
◦CT read by a radiologist within 45 min
◦Thrombolytics administered within 1 hr of
presentation
r If CT is normal and subarachnoid hemorrhage is
suspected, emergent lumbar puncture is indicated
r EKG to evaluate for dysrhythmias or presence of MI
r Oxygen saturation measurement
r Rapid glucose determination
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Baseline CBC, electrolytes, renal function tests, liver
function test, prothrombin time, partial
thromboplastin time
r Urinalysis:
– Hematuria can be seen in subacute bacterial
endocarditis with embolic stroke.
r Sedimentation rate:
– Elevated in subacute bacterial endocarditis,
vasculitis, hyperviscosity syndromes
r Consider additional tests: Cardiac enzymes, urine
pregnancy test, drug screen, alcohol level, ABG, and
blood cultures.
Imagingr Noncontrast head CT
r MRI can detect ischemia <2 hr after onset
r CXR
r Carotid US
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr EKG to evaluate for arrhythmia
r Lumbar puncture if subarachnoid hemorrhage is
suspected and head CT nondiagnostic
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Intracranial bleeding
r Hypoglycemia
r Seizure disorder; Todd paralysis
r Panic attacks, depression, conversion reaction
r Transient global amnesia
r Meningoencephalitis
r Peripheral neuropathy
r Intracranial abscess
r Migraine
r Air embolism
r Transient ischemic attack
r Encephalopathy
r Neoplasm
r Giant cell/Takayasu arteritis
r Multiple sclerosis
r Compressive myelopathy
r Vestibulitis
r Medication effect/toxidrome
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Patients may have difficulty moving or
communicating after cerebral vascular accident
r Neurologic exam in field is helpful:
– Should include assessment of consciousness level,
Glasgow coma scale score, gross motor deficits,
speech abnormalities, gait disturbance, facial
asymmetry, and other focal deficits
r Check fingerstick glucose
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Manage airway:
– Supplemental oxygen 2–4 L
– Rapid-sequence intubation may be required for
airway protection or controlled ventilation to
decrease intracranial pressure
r For altered mental status, give naloxone and
thiamine and check blood glucose

ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Treat elevated BP with labetalol, nicardipine,
nitroprusside, or hydralazine:
– Systolic BP >220 mm Hg or diastolic BP
>120 mm Hg on repeated measurements
– If indicated for other concurrent problems (MI,
aortic dissection, CHF , hypertensive
encephalopathy)
– Initial goal is systolic BP <180 mm Hg, diastolic
<110 mm Hg
r Control seizures with benzodiazepines, then
fosphenytoin/phenytoin
r Maintain euvolemia and normothermia.
r Thrombolytics:
– Ischemic stroke only; administer within 4.5 hr of
symptom onset
– Contraindications:
◦Any history of intracranial hemorrhage
◦Recent stroke or head trauma <3m oa g o
◦Major surgery <14 days ago
◦Systolic BP >185 mm Hg; diastolic BP
>110 mm Hg
◦Bleeding diathesis
◦Noncompressible arterial puncture <7 days ago
◦MI <3m oa g o
◦Anticoagulation: INR >1.7, PT >15 sec, or
prolonged PTT; use of heparin within 48 hr
◦Platelets <100,000
◦Intracranial neoplasm
◦Seizure at stroke onset
◦Minor or rapidly improving symptoms
◦Pregnancy
◦Internal bleed (GI/GU) <3w ka g o
◦Blood glucose <50
◦Age <18 yr
– Avoid anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs for
24 hr
r Treat increased intracranial pressure and cerebral
edema:
– Elevate head of bed 30◦
– Controlled ventilation to keep partial pressure of
carbon dioxide 35–40 mm Hg
– Mannitol
r Urgent neurosurgical decompression may be
required with brainstem compression in cases of
vertebrobasilar stroke or hemorrhage.
r In patients with completed or minor strokes, aspirin
may prevent recurrence.
r For focal embolic/thrombotic strokes:
– Recannulation
– US-enhanced thrombolysis
– Intra-arterial thrombolysis or clot retrieval

For patients presenting between 3 and 4.5 hr of
onset, there are additional exclusion criteria:r Age >80 yr
r Oral anticoagulant use (regardless of INR)
r NIH-SS >25 or >1/3 MCA territory involved
r History of previous stroke and diabetes

DESCRIPTIONr Acute bacterial infection of a cervical lymph node
– Often arising after a prior bacterial infection of the
head or neck area
r Primarily a pediatric disease:
– Becoming more common in adults owing to
immunocompromised disease states (HIV , cancer,
transplant patients)
r Any cervical node can become infected:
– >80% of childhood cervical lymphadenitis
involves the submandibular or deep cervical nodes
– Jugulodigastric node located just below the angle
of the mandible is common site
– Cervical nodes act as the final common pathway
for lymphatic drainage of all areas of the head and
neck
– Initial lymphadenopathy results after bacterial
invasion of regional areas of the head and neck
– Local lymph nodes swell secondary to hyperplasia
of sinusoidal cells and infiltration of lymphocytes
– If the infection is not contained, the bacteria enter
the lymph system and proliferate (lymphadenitis)
– Pus forms when neutrophils are incited, and an
abscess develops when host defenses are unable
to clear infection
– Clinically manifests as warm, tender, swollen,
erythematous node

Streptococcal infection
– 20% Staphylococcal infection
– 10% related to viral infection or other bacteria
r Infections secondary to community-acquired MRSA
(CA-MRSA) have increased in frequency
r Children have one of the highest rate of CA-MRSA
colonization and invasive disease
r Mycobacteria TB:
– Scrofula or tuberculous lymphadenitis
– Rarely seen
– Usually a chronic lymphadenitis in the posterior
cervical nodes
– Purified protein derivative (PPD) is usually strongly
reactive
– Treatment is nonsurgical
r Atypical mycobacteria (nontuberculous)
Mycobacterium avium complex:
– More commonly seen
– Usually a chronic lymphadenitis in the
submandibular or anterior cervical nodes
– PPD test results are unreliable
– Treatment is primarily surgical
r Bartonella henselae (catscratch disease):
– Subacute lymphadenitis
– Fever and mild systemic symptoms occur in only
∼3% of patients
– Has indolent course but usually spontaneously
resolves after 4–6 wk
r Anaerobes:
– Consider when associated with infections of the
teeth or gingiva
r Rare organisms:
– Gram-negative bacilli
– Yersinia pestis
– Group B streptococcus
– Francisella tularensis
– Alpha-streptococcus
– Anthrax

r One of the most common causes of a neck mass in a
child
r Overall, group A Streptococcus and Staphylococcus
aureus most common causes
r In neonates, group B Streptococcus and S. aureus
most common
r Group B Streptococcal cellulitis–adenitis syndrome:
– Infants are usually 3–7 wk of age, male, febrile,
with submandibular or facial cellulitis, and an
ipsilateral otitis media
– 94% incidence of concurrent bacteremia
r S. aureus associated with more indolent course and
higher frequency of suppuration
r Viral infections generally result in bilateral
lymphadenopathy
Geriatric Considerations
r Consider malignancy over infection in this
population, especially in the absence of fever,
leukocytosis, etc.
r Fixed, nontender, hard node most likely not cervical
adenitis
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Enlarged, tender cervical lymph node
r Usually unilateral and solitary
r Warmth and erythema of overlying skin
r Early in course, node is firm but may become
fluctuant later
r With or without fever
r Malaise
r Irritability in infants and children
r Usually a concurrent head and neck infection:
– Pharyngitis, tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess
– Otitis media, otitis externa
– Dental infection
– Impetigo, scalp infection

r Associated symptoms: Fever, weight loss, rash
r Exposures/travel history
r Comorbidities/birth history for infants
Physical Exam
Complete evaluation of head and neck with attention
to airway and patient’s clinical appearance
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Cervical adenitis is a clinical diagnosis
r Identify primary source of infection in head and neck
area (e.g., otitis media, tonsillitis)
r If no primary inflammatory source of infection in
head and neck:
– Address possible TB exposure with PPD
– Look for signs of systemic disease and viral illness
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Unnecessary if a treatable primary source of
infection confirmed
r Blood cultures for toxic-appearing patients
r Sepsis workup in neonates
r If cause unclear, the following lab tests may help to
discern a nonbacterial cause (see “Differential
Diagnosis”):
– Leukocyte count with differential
– Monospot
– Throat cultures
– Antibody titers (Epstein–Barr virus, CMV ,
toxoplasmosis)
Imagingr CXR study, lateral neck, or Panorex:
– Helpful if source of infection unclear or to rule out
a deep space infection
– Chest radiograph study to screen for TB
r CT or MRI of neck:
– Helpful to exclude deep space infections or
delineating embryonic developmental masses
r US:
– Can differentiate cystic from solid structures, but
other findings nonspecific
– Can identify deep-cavity abscess if not palpable
on exam
r Excisional biopsy

– All fluctuant nodes should be aspirated
– Send for Gram stain and acid-fast stains, aerobic
and anaerobic cultures, mycobacteria, and fungi
– If any suspicion of tuberculous lymphadenitis, the
node should not be aspirated owing to risk for
sinus development and chronic drainage
r Intradermal skin testing:
– Mycobacteria, catscratch disease

bacterial infection) can be a sign of many systemic
diseases; usually these nodes are multiple and
bilateral
r Viral infections are a common cause:
– Respiratory viruses (adenoviruses, rhinoviruses,
enteroviruses)
– Epstein–Barr virus, herpes simplex virus,
varicella-zoster virus, CMV
– Mumps, rubella, rubeola

BASICS
ALERT
r The sole indication for ED physician to perform
emergency perimortem cesarean section is a
gravid female (>24 wk gestation) in
cardiopulmonary arrest who has not responded to
initial resuscitative measures, regardless of cause
r The most important predictor of fetal survival is
length of time between maternal cardiac arrest
and cesarean delivery:
– Cesarean section should begin within 4 min of
maternal arrest
– Goal is delivering fetus within 1 min
r Obtain immediate consultations from obstetrics,
pediatrics (and surgery, if trauma related):
– Do not defer or delay performing procedure
until arrival of consultants
r Do not perform emergent cesarean section if
patient is <24 wk gestation
ETIOLOGYr Trauma (penetrating or blunt):
– Major cause of maternal mortality
r Pulmonary embolus:
– Thromboembolism is most common cause of
nontraumatic maternal mortality
r Cerebral vascular accident
r Amniotic fluid embolism
r DIC
r Placenta previa
r Eclampsia
r Miscellaneous medical disorders:
– Asthma
– CHF
–M I
– Drug overdose
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
History
Gravid female (>24 wk gestation determined by
uterine fundal height) who is in cardiopulmonary
arrest
Physical Exam
Patient is determined to be>24 wk gestation if uterus
is at least 4 finger breadths above umbilicus
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Physical exam for apnea and pulselessness in
obviously gravid female:
– Quickly evaluate for reversible causes of
cardiopulmonary arrest:
◦Hypoxia
◦Hypovolemia
◦Hydrogen ion (acidosis)
◦Hypokalemia/hyperkalemia
◦Hypoglycemia
◦Hypothermia
◦Trauma
◦Thromboembolism
◦Toxins/poisons
◦Tension pneumothorax
◦Tamponade (pericardial)
– Supine hypotension syndrome (compression of
inferior vena cava by enlarged uterus)
r Assess gestational age by uterine fundal height
– Distance from pubis to fundus in centimeters is
roughly equivalent to gestational age in weeks,
i.e., 24 cm = 24 wk
r US is beneficial if immediately available to assess
fetus.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Imagingr None necessary to establish cardiopulmonary arrest
r Do not use valuable time attempting to determine
fetal heart tones
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
Cardiopulmonary arrest is final common pathway:
r Evaluate for underlying cause
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Cautions:
r Minimal scene time, “scoop and run”
r Place the patient in the left lateral decubitus
position to avoid compression of inferior vena cava
(supine hypotension syndrome)
r Trauma patient requiring spinal immobilization:
– Uterus can be manually displaced to left
– Backboard can be wedged to keep right hip
elevated 45◦
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Standard resuscitation measures:
– Emergency intubation
◦Use a smaller endotracheal tube (0.5–1 mm less
in internal diameter compared to that used for
nonpregnant women)
– High-flow oxygen
– Cardiac and BP monitoring
– 2 large-bore peripheral IV lines:
◦Fluid resuscitation
◦O-negative blood if indicated
r Fetal survival correlates with maternal survival and
adequacy of initial maternal resuscitation
r If patient is at <24 wk gestation, use advanced
cardiac life support (ACLS) and advanced trauma
life support protocols directed at maternal
resuscitation
–D o not perform emergent cesarean section
r If patient is >24 wk gestation, use 4-min rule:
– Perform ACLS or advanced trauma life support for
4 min
– If no response, proceed to immediate emergency
cesarean section
– Goal is to deliver fetus within 1 min
– If it is obvious there is no chance for maternal
survival, begin perimortem cesarean section
immediately

ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Call for immediate obstetric, surgical, and pediatric
consultations:
–D o not delay performing procedure while waiting
for consultants
r Ensure a Foley catheter has been inserted to
decompress bladder, but do not delay procedure
r Perform cesarean section:
– Use linea nigra as landmark for vertical midline
incision
– Incise abdominal wall from pubic hairline to 5 cm
above umbilicus.
– This incision should pass through fascial and
peritoneal layers
– Retract urinary bladder inferiorly against pubic
symphysis
– Make small vertical incision in lower uterine
segment, just cephalad to urinary bladder
– Extend incision cephalad with scissors:
◦Insert your free hand into uterus
◦Lift uterine wall away from fetus to avoid fetal
injury
– Deliver fetus
– Clamp umbilical cord in 2 places and cut between
the 2 clamps
– Manually deliver placenta
– Perform neonatal resuscitation, as indicated
– Immediately reassess maternal vital signs because
occasionally spontaneous circulation may return
– Continue maternal resuscitation as appropriate
– Suture uterus with running lock stitch using no. 0
polyglactin suture
– Suture fascia and peritoneum with running stitch
using no. 0 polyglactin suture
– Close the skin with staples or suture
– Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics
r If maternal return of circulation is obtained, consider
starting therapeutic hypothermia protocol

CHEMICAL WEAPONS POISONING
Patrick M. Whiteley
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Chemical agents that affect CNS, pulmonary,
cardiovascular, dermal, ocular, or GI systems when
exposed to victims
ETIOLOGYr Blood agents: Cyanide:
– Inhibition of cellular respiration by binding to
ferric ion in cytochrome oxidase a-a3 and
uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation
r Blister agents: Sulfur mustard, nitrogen mustard,
lewisite, phosgene oxime:
– Alkylation and cross-linking of purine bases of
DNA and amino acids resulting in change in
structure of nucleic acid, proteins, and cellular
membranes
r Lacrimators and riot control agents:
1-chloroacetophenone (CN; Mace),
o-chlorobenzylidene malononitrile (CS), oleoresin
capsaicin-pepper spray (OC), chloropicrin, adamsite
(DM):
– Mucous membrane irritators
r Pulmonary irritants (choking agents):
– High water solubility: Ammonia:
◦Mucous membrane irritation of eyes and upper
airway
– Intermediate water solubility: Chlorine:
◦Forms hydrochloric acid, hydrochlorous acids,
which form free radicals causing upper airway
and pulmonary irritation
– Low water solubility: Phosgene:
◦Mild irritant effects initially, then delayed
pulmonary edema as late as 24 hr
◦Direct pulmonary damage after hydrolysis in
lungs to hydrochloric acid
r Nerve agents:
– Anticholinesterase inhibitors—causes cholinergic
overstimulation at muscarinic, nicotinic, and CNS
sites
r Incapacitating agents: 3-quinuclidinyl benzilate (BZ):
– Anticholinergic (antimuscarinic)
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
History
Multiple victims, house fire, known exposure (agent
determines history findings)
Physical Examr Blood agents (cyanide and cyanogens):
– Vital signs:
◦Tachypnea and hyperpnea (early); respiratory
depression (late)
◦Hypertension and tachycardia (early);
hypotension and bradycardia (late)
◦Death within seconds to minutes
– CNS:
◦Headache
◦Mental status changes
◦Seizures
– Pulmonary:
◦Dyspnea
◦Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema
◦Cyanosis uncommon
– GI:
◦Odor of bitter almonds (sometimes)
◦Burning in mouth and throat
◦Nausea, vomiting
r Blister agents (mustards, lewisite):
– General:
◦Mortality, 2–4%
– Dermatologic:
◦Skin erythema, edema, pruritus can appear
2–24 hr after exposure.
◦Necrosis and vesiculation appear 2–18 hr after

– Irrigate skin and eyes with copious amounts of

– Chemical-resistant suit

– Benzodiazepines for seizures
– Hydroxocobalamin (1st line)
– Cyanide antidote kit (2nd line), may be repeated.
r Blister agents:
– Supportive care
– Standard burn management
– Atropine to relieve eye pain
– Monitor fluids, electrolytes, complete blood
chemistry.

– Supportive care for sepsis, anemia, hemorrhage
– Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) for

– Eye irrigation
– CXR and careful monitoring for respiratory

– Phosgenes require monitoring for delayed

r Nerve agents:
– Supportive care:
◦100% oxygen
◦Frequent airway suctioning
– Atropine 2 mg IV q5min until reversal of
bronchorrhea, bronchoconstriction, and
hypoxemia:
◦Antagonizes muscarinic effects and some CNS
but no effect on skeletal muscle weakness or
respiratory failure
◦Pupillary response and heart rate are not useful
measures of adequate atropinization.
◦Stop atropine after patient regains
consciousness and spontaneous ventilation

as it takes to reverse respiratory compromise.

phosphorylation (unless aging has occurred)

CHEST PAIN
Josh W. Joseph rEdward Ullman
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr One of the most frequent chief complaints in the ED
r Often the presenting symptom of a high-risk
etiology:
– Acute coronary syndrome
– Pulmonary embolism
– Aortic dissection
r Assume life threatening until proven otherwise.
r Categorization may suggest the underlying etiology,
but the presentation of chest pain can be extremely
variable and vague.
r Thoracic pain:
– May involve the myocardium, pericardium, the
ascending aorta, pulmonary artery, mediastinum,
and esophagus
– Pain is deep, visceral, and poorly localized.
– Characteristics vary from severe and crushing to
mild, burning, or indigestion.
r Epigastric pain:
– May involve the descending aorta, diaphragmatic
muscles, gallbladder, pancreas, duodenum, and
stomach
– Pain is generally referred to the xiphoid region and
in the back.
r Pleuritic pain:
– Inflammation or trauma to the ribs, cartilage,
muscles, nerves, pleural or pericardial surface
– Pain increased by breathing, laughing, coughing,
sneezing
– Tenderness to palpation may be present.
– Diaphragmatic pleurisy:
◦Sharp shooting pains in the epigastrium, lower
retrosternal area, or shoulder intensified by
thoracic movement
r Chest wall pain:
– Inflammation of skin and SC structures of the
chest wall
– Pain is reproduced by:
◦Palpation
◦Horizontal flexion of the arms
◦Extension of the neck
◦Vertical pressure on the head
ETIOLOGYr Thoracic:
– Acute coronary syndrome
– Pericarditis
– Myocarditis
– Stress-induced cardiomyopathy
– Cardiac syndrome X
– Stimulant use
– Thoracic aortic dissection
– Esophagitis
– Esophageal spasm
– GERD
– Esophageal hyperalgesia
– Abnormal motility patterns and achalasia
– Esophageal rupture and mediastinitis
r Epigastric:
– Dissection of the descending aorta
– Peptic ulcer disease
– Pancreatitis
– Cholecystitis
– Splenic rupture
– Hepatic injury
– Subdiaphragmatic abscess
r Pleuritic pain:
– Pulmonary embolism
– Pneumothorax
– Pneumonia
– Costochondritis
r Diaphragmatic pleurisy:
– Splenic rupture
– Hepatic injury
– Subdiaphragmatic abscess
r Esophageal rupture
r Intercostal myositis
r Intercostal neuralgia
r Pectoralis minor strain
r Pericarditis
r Pleuritis
r Pneumonitis
r Rib fractures
r Acute chest syndrome of sickle cell
r Chest wall twinge syndrome:
– Brief episodes of sharp anterior chest pain lasting
30 sec–3 min, aggravated by deep breathing and
relieved by shallow respirations
r Chest wall pain:
– Chest wall hematoma
– Chest wall laceration
– Herpes zoster
– Thrombophlebitis of the thoracoepigastric vein
– Xiphisternal arthritis
– Adiposis dolorosa
– Breast abscess, fibroadenosis, carcinoma
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Coronary artery disease:
– Pressure
– Squeezing pain
– Radiation to arm, jaw
– Shortness of breath
– Diaphoresis
– Nausea
– Vomiting
– Weakness
– Fatigue especially in women or elderly
– Signs of CHF
– Anxiety
r Aortic dissection:
– Sudden onset of pain with maximal intensity early
– Tearing pain
– Radiation to back and/or flank
– HTN
– Diastolic murmur of aortic insufficiency
– Difference in upper-extremity pulses
– Syncope
– Nausea
– Vomiting
– Associated neurologic changes (i.e., visual
changes)
r Pulmonary embolism:
– Pleuritic pain
– Shortness of breath
– Anxiety
– Diaphoresis
– Tachypnea
– Tachycardia
– Low-grade fever
– Syncope
– Localized rales
– Wheezing
r Acute pericarditis:
– Substernal pain
– Varies with respiration
– Increased with recumbency
– Relieved by leaning forward
– Anxiety
– Anorexia
– Fever
– Pericardial friction rub
r Pneumothorax:
– Pleuritic pain
– Shortness of breath
– Anxiety
– Tachypnea
– Decreased unilateral breath sounds
– Can be spontaneous (young), or associated with
very minor trauma (elderly)
Historyr The history is the most important tool to distinguish
between the various etiologies.
r Have the patient define the key features:
– Duration
– Location:
◦Retrosternal
◦Subxiphoid
◦Diffuse
– Frequency:
◦Constant
◦Intermittent
◦Sudden vs. delayed onset
– Precipitating factors:
◦Exertion
◦Stress
◦Food
◦Respiration
◦Movement
– Timing:
◦Context of onset of pain (i.e., at rest, exertional)
◦Duration of pain
– Quality:
◦Burning
◦Squeezing
◦Dull
◦Sharp
◦Tearing
◦Heavy

CHEST TRAUMA, BLUNT
Lisa G. Lowe Hiller
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Significant source of morbidity and mortality in US
r ∼12 thoracic trauma victims per million population
per day
r ∼33% of these injuries require hospital admission.
r Directly responsible for 20–25% of all deaths
attributed to trauma
r Contributing cause of death in 25% of patients who
die from other traumatic injuries
ETIOLOGYr Common mechanisms of injury include:
– Motor vehicle collisions (70–80%)
– Motorcycle collisions
– Pedestrians struck by a motor vehicle
– Falls from great heights
– Assaults
– Blast injuries
– Sports-related injuries
r Injuries can result from direct blunt force to the
chest or from forces related to rapid deceleration.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Obvious contusion, wound, or other defect of the
chest wall
r Paradoxical chest wall movement suggests flail chest
segment.
r Usually occurs in combination with other injuries
r Hypotension
r Some patients with severe intrathoracic injuries,
such as traumatic aortic disruption, may have no
visible external signs of trauma.
Historyr Time of injury
r Mechanism of injury
r Estimates of motor vehicle accident (MVA) velocity
and deceleration
r Loss of consciousness
r Chest pain
r Pain with deep inspiration or cough
r Dyspnea
Physical Examr Unilaterally absent breath sounds
r Crepitus or subcutaneous air in the chest wall
r Decreased or absent breath sounds
r Tenderness to palpation on the chest wall
r Jugular venous distention
r Tracheal deviation away from midline
r Hyper-resonance to percussion on involved side
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Check airway, breathing, and circulation (ABCs) to
determine the patient’s stability
r Focused exam of the chest:
– Respiratory effort and rate
– Chest wall excursion
– Crepitus
– Subcutaneous air
– Breath sounds and heart sounds
– Presence of jugular venous distention
r Obtain a supine CXR immediately:
– Avoid an upright CXR because of potential for
other injuries (especially spinal injuries)
r ECG and monitor to detect myocardial ischemia or
dysrhythmias
r Consider use of US for detecting small
pneumothoraces, especially given the poor
sensitivity of supine CXR in detecting such injuries.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Baseline hemoglobin
r Pulse oximetry
r ABG
r Serum lactate
r Type and cross-match
r Coagulation profile
r Cardiac enzymes when indicated
r Periodic chemistry panel for patients receiving
significant fluid resuscitation
Imagingr CXR is the initial radiologic study of choice:
– If CXR reveals widened mediastinum and patient
hemodynamically stable, repeat film in upright
position.
r Chest CT is more specific for pneumothoraces and
pulmonary contusions/occult injuries.
r Thoracic US can be efficiently used for detecting
pneumothoraces and pericardial injuries. The
sensitivity, specificity, and overall accuracy in the ED
setting for such injuries is >90%.
r Chest CT with contrast, or aortic angiogram, is
useful in identifying aortic and large-vessel injuries.
r Esophagoscopy for direct endoscopic visualization if
esophageal injury suspected
r Contrast esophagogram (with water and then
barium) for possible esophageal injuries if
esophagoscopy negative, but patient at risk for
esophageal injury (e.g., pneumomediastinum)
– Combination of these 2 tests in sequence (each
80–90% sensitive individually) reaches close to
100% sensitivity
r ECG if sternal tenderness is present or abnormalities
on cardiac monitor
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr If patient’s condition is unstable, emergency
thoracotomy may be necessary to repair a traumatic
aortic disruption.
r If there are signs of cardiac tamponade, and patient
is stable, perform an echocardiogram urgently:
– Pericardial effusions, wall motion defects, aortic
injuries, valvular or other intracardiac pathology
may also be identified.
r If there are signs of cardiac tamponade and the
patient is unstable, consider emergent
pericardiocentesis, followed by immediate transport
to the OR for a pericardial window.
r Bronchoscopy often indicated for possible upper
airway injuries (e.g., a large persistent air leak after
chest tube)
Pregnancy Considerations
r In pregnant patients, remember to use the least
amount of radiation available and to shield the
uterus during imaging when possible.
r Take note of the differences in anatomy of the
thoracic cavity in pregnant patients, as well as
differences in lab values, intravascular volume, and
cardiovascular physiology.
r See “Pregnancy,” “Trauma in,” for details.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Simple pneumothorax
r Tension pneumothorax
r Open pneumothorax
r Hemothorax
r Rib fractures
r Flail chest
r Sternoclavicular fractures/dislocations
r Pulmonary contusion
r Myocardial contusion
r Myocardial rupture
r Cardiac (pericardial) tamponade
r Traumatic aortic disruption
r Esophageal injury
r Large vascular injury (subclavian artery, pulmonary
artery)
r Tracheobronchial injury
r Diaphragmatic injury
Pediatric Considerations
The rib cage is highly elastic in children and can
withstand significant forces without overt signs of
external trauma and can underestimate even major
intrathoracic injuries.
Geriatric Considerations
Elderly patients have been shown to have greater
respiratory complications, including ARDS and
pneumonia, than younger patients in the setting of
blunt chest trauma. This is especially true in those
>85 yr of age.

C
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr All patients with any signs of life in the field should
be transported to a trauma center.
r Full spinal precautions should be employed.
r Needle decompression is indicated for tension
pneumothorax:
– Unilaterally absent breath sounds
– Hypotension
– Jugular venous distention
– Hyper-resonance to percussion
r If large, open pneumothorax exists, tape an
occlusive dressing on 3 sides only to prevent causing
a tension pneumothorax.
r Do not delay transport to hospital for IV access.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs management; intubate patient early if signs of
respiratory insufficiency, shock, or altered mental
status exist.
r Resuscitation attempts should be initiated only in
patients who arrive in the ED with vital signs.
r Any patient who presents in blunt traumatic arrest is
not likely to survive a thoracotomy in the ED, and it
is therefore generally not indicated in this group.
r If the patient’s condition is unstable and clinically
shows signs of a tension pneumothorax, perform
needle thoracostomy and place a chest tube
immediately afterward.
r Do not wait to obtain a CXR.
r Place chest tube on the affected side or bilaterally if
injury site is unclear.
r Deliver oxygen by nonrebreather face mask for
stable patients.
r Obtain vascular access, preferably 2 large-bore IV
lines (>18G).
r Maintain spinal immobilization.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Tube thoracostomy if pneumothorax or hemothorax
is identified:
– 36F chest tube in an adult
– In children, use the largest tube that the
intercostal space will accommodate.
r Provide resuscitation with isotonic fluids and blood
products as necessary:
– Aggressive fluid resuscitation may be harmful if
severe pulmonary contusions exist (consider
permissive hypotension).
r Workup for associated intra-abdominal injuries (e.g.,
with abdominal US, abdominal CT scan, less
commonly diagnostic peritoneal lavage):
– Patients with chest trauma frequently have
concomitant intra-abdominal injuries.

laparotomy.

a repeat radiograph at that time reveals no

r Blunt chest trauma is responsible for up to 1/4 of all
trauma-related deaths.

can provide definitive care as soon as possible.
r Open thoracotomy in the ED has not been shown to
improve survival in patients found to be in

r The extent of injury is not always clinically obvious

tube thoracostomy decompression of the

to reports from EMS personnel should be

– Never remove objects impaled in the chest
because exsanguination may follow.

– If large open pneumothorax exists, occlusive

CHOLANGITIS
Robert G. Buckley
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Partial or complete obstruction of the common bile
duct owing to gallstones, tumor, cyst, or stricture
r Increased intraluminal pressure in biliary tree
r Bacterial multiplication results in bacteremia and
sepsis.
r Purulent infection of biliary tree, which may involve
the liver and gallbladder
r Mirizzi syndrome is defined as common bile duct
obstruction owing to extrinsic compression from
gallbladder or cystic duct edema or stones.
ETIOLOGYr Bacterial sources of infection include:
– Ascending duodenal source
– Gallbladder infection
– Portal venous seeding
– Hematogenous spread with hepatic secretion
– Lymphatic spread
r Bacterial organisms include:
– Anaerobes (Bacteroides and Clostridium species)
– Intestinal coliform (Escherichia coli)
– Enterococcus
r AIDS sclerosing cholangitis characterized by:
– Papillary stenosis
– Sclerosing cholangitis
– Extrahepatic biliary obstruction
– Cytomegalovirus (CMV), Cryptosporidium, and
microsporidia isolated, but causal role not
established
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Charcot triad:
– Classic presentation of fever and chills; right upper
quadrant (RUQ) pain and jaundice found in only
50–70%
r Addition of shock and altered mental status denotes
a more advanced form of biliary sepsis known as
Reynolds pentad.
r Abdominal pain present in >70%—localizing to
RUQ.
r AIDS sclerosing cholangitis presents with similar
symptoms but with more chronic indolent course
and near-normal serum bilirubin levels.
Physical Examr Fever found in >90%
r Peritoneal findings found in 30%
r Clinically apparent jaundice may be absent in up to
40%.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr ECG in patients at risk for coronary artery disease
r CBC
r LFT
r Amylase, lipase
r Urinalysis
r Blood cultures
r Gallbladder US or hepatoiminodiacetic acid (HIDA)
scan
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC:
– Leukocytosis with left shift unless
immunocompromised or severe sepsis
r LFTs consistent with cholestasis:
– Elevated direct bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase
r Minimal elevation of transaminases (<200 IU/mL)
r Changes may lag symptom onset by 24–48 hr.
r Amylase and lipase normal or mildly elevated
r Urinalysis positive for bilirubin
Imagingr US detects the level of ductal obstruction and the
presence of gallstone etiology.
r Radionuclide scanning (HIDA):
– Indicates obstruction when tracer not found in
duodenum within 1 hr
– More sensitive than US in detecting obstruction in
the 1st 24–48 hr before ductal dilation occurs
r CT scan and CRX:
– Useful to rule out intestinal obstruction,
perforation, or pneumonia
– 20% gallstones radiopaque
r Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography
(MRCP) is highly accurate for biliary obstruction but
unnecessary if endoscopic retrograde
cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) will be
performed.
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Emergency invasive biliary imaging and drainage by
ERCP (or surgical/percutaneous if not available), if no
response to medical treatment in 12–24 hr

r Hepatitis or hepatic abscess
r Acute pancreatitis
r Right pyelonephritis
r Right lower lobe pneumonia or pulmonary embolism
r Perforated duodenal ulcer
r Appendicitis
r Sepsis with nonspecific elevation of LFTs
r Fitz-Hugh and Curtis syndrome

CHOLECYSTITIS
Robert G. Buckley
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Cholecystitis is defined as inflammation of the
gallbladder.
ETIOLOGYr Acute calculous cholecystitis:
– Owing to bile stasis secondary to prolonged
obstruction by a gallstone (see “Cholelithiasis”) in
the gallbladder neck, cystic duct, or common bile
duct
– Leads to increased intraluminal pressure and
mucosal damage
– Release of inflammatory mediators results in
distention, edema, and increased vascularity.
– Coliforms and anaerobes lead to
infection—primary causal role is controversial.
r Acalculous cholecystitis:
– 10% of cases
– Underlying critical illness leads to biliary stasis and
mucosal ischemia.
– Subsequent mucosal inflammation and infection
Pediatric Considerations
r Acute calculous cholecystitis extremely rare in
childhood (see “Cholelithiasis”)
r Acalculous cholecystitis more common than
calculous form in children:
– Associated with systemic bacterial infections,
scarlet fever, Kawasaki disease, and parasitic
infections
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Acute calculous cholecystitis:
– Dull, aching, epigastric, or right upper quadrant
(RUQ) pain
– Radiation to tip of right scapula, acromion, or
thoracic spine
– Duration >6 hr more suggestive of cholecystitis
than uncomplicated biliary colic
– As inflammation progresses, parietal peritoneal
irritation leads to sharp, localized pain.
– Nausea, vomiting, fever, and chills often reported,
but absent in most cases
– Jaundice in 20%
– History of prior attacks of biliary colic or known
gallstones favors diagnosis.
r Acalculous cholecystitis:
– Occurs in critically ill patients (burns, sepsis,
trauma, or postoperative)
– Localized pain and tenderness frequently absent
– Often presents with symptoms of generalized
sepsis of unknown source
Physical Examr Localized parietal peritoneal signs:
– Percussion tenderness
– Rebound
– Found as the disease progresses
r Murphy sign:
– Inspiratory arrest with gentle palpation of RUQ
owing to increased pain
– Found in most cases
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr ECG in patients at risk for coronary artery disease
r CBC
r LFT
r Amylase, lipase
r Urinalysis
r Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
r Gallbladder US or HIDA scan
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC:
– WBC >12,000 cells/mm3 supports diagnosis, but
may be normal in more than half of cases
r LFTs:
– Transaminases, bilirubin, amylase, and lipase may
be minimally elevated, but are generally normal.
– Disproportionate elevation of direct bilirubin and
alkaline phosphatase compared with
transaminases suspicious for common duct
obstruction or cholangitis
Imagingr US:
– Generally the 1st-line imaging procedure
– Positive findings include gallbladder wall
thickening (>5 mm) or pericolic fluid—sensitivity,
90%; specificity, 80%.
– Optimal if patient NPO >8h r
r Radionuclide scanning (HIDA):
– Most useful when clinical suspicion remains high
despite equivocal findings on US or when
acalculous cholecystitis suspected
– Positive when tracer seen in small bowel but
inflamed gallbladder fails to visualize
– Sensitivity, >95%; specificity, 90%
– False-positive results increase in nonfasting state.
– Addition of IV morphine induces Sphincter of Oddi
contraction which improves gallbladder filling and
reduces false-positive scan results.
r CT scanning:
– Exclude intestinal perforation or obstruction
– Air in the gallbladder wall consistent with
emphysematous cholecystitis
– Gallstones radiopaque in up to 20%
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Biliary colic
r Hepatitis or hepatic abscess
r Cholangitis
r AIDS sclerosing cholangitis
r Pancreatitis
r Intestinal perforation
r Peptic ulcer disease
r Gastritis
r Duodenal perforation
r Right lower lobe pneumonia, pleurisy, or pulmonary
infarction
r MI
r Abdominal aortic aneurysm
r Appendicitis
r Fitz-Hugh and Curtis syndrome
r Pyelonephritis
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Establish IV access for patients with vomiting or severe
pain.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr IV , oxygen, cardiac monitoring until myocardial
ischemic cause excluded
r Initiate IV fluid therapy for dehydration,
hemodynamic compromise, or sepsis.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Broad-spectrum antibiotics for coliforms, anaerobes,
and enterococcus:
– Ampicillin/sulbactam
– Piperacillin/tazobactam
– Add aminoglycoside if sepsis or cholangitis
suspected (see “Cholangitis”).
r Alternative antibiotics for penicillin allergic:
– Adults: Levofloxacin (Levaquin) and metronidazole
– Peds: Clindamycin with aminoglycoside
r NPO
r IV fluid replacement and maintenance
r Antiemetics (ondansetron) if vomiting
r Nasogastric (NG) suctioning if refractory vomiting or
ileus

CHOLELITHIASIS

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Symptoms arise when gallstones pass through the
cystic or common bile ducts leading to impedance of
normal bile flow and gallbladder spasm.
r Biliary dyskinesia produces symptoms identical to
biliary colic in the absence of stones.
r Choledocholithiasis (common bile duct stones), may
lead to prolonged pain, elevated LFTs and bilirubin,
and to more complications like cholangitis or
pancreatitis.
ETIOLOGYr Cholesterol stones:
– Most common type of gallstone
– Form when solubility exceeded
r Pigment stones:
– 20%
– Composed of calcium bilirubinate
– Associated with clinical conditions such as
hemolytic anemias that lead to increased
concentration of unconjugated bilirubin
r Incidence increases with age and favors females to
males 2:1. Other risk factors include Hispanic
ethnicity, obesity, pregnancy, rapid weight loss, and
drugs that induce biliary stasis (e.g., ceftriaxone and
oral contraceptives).
r Gallstones are exceedingly rare in childhood and are
most commonly associated with sickle cell disease,
hereditary spherocytosis, or other hemolytic anemias
that result in pigment stone formation.
r Biliary sludge:
– Nonstone, crystalline, granular matrix
– Associated with rapid weight loss, pregnancy,
ceftriaxone or octreotide therapy, and organ
transplantation
– May develop symptoms identical to cholelithiasis
and its complications
r “Porcelain gallbladder” from mucosal precipitation
of calcium salts owing to recurrent obstruction of
cystic duct.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Dull, aching epigastric or right upper quadrant
(RUQ) pain:
– Arising over 2–3 min, continuous (rather than
colicky), and lasting from 30 min–6 hr before
dissipating
– May radiate to the tip of right scapula, acromion,
or thoracic spine
– Often correlated with ingestion of large, fatty meal
r Anorexia
r Nausea and vomiting
r Afebrile:
– Fever and chills suggest cholecystitis or cholangitis
Physical Examr Tenderness to deep palpation but without rebound
r Murphy sign (inspiratory arrest during deep
palpation of the RUQ) may be present during the
episode of colic, but should resolve when symptoms
pass.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Obtain ECG on those whose pain may be owing to
myocardial ischemia.
r CBC
r LFTs
r Amylase, lipase
r Urinalysis
r Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC:
– WBC count usually normal, but may elevate after
vomiting
– Leukocytosis suggestive of cholecystitis or
cholangitis
r LFTs:
– Usually normal
– Elevation suggests common duct obstruction,
cholangitis, cholecystitis, or hepatitis.
r Amylase/lipase
– Normal or minimally elevated with passage of
gallstone
– Elevation in context of severe persistent epigastric
pain suggests pancreatitis.
r Urinalysis:
– Exclude nephrolithiasis or pyelonephritis.
– Bilirubinuria suggests common duct obstruction or
hepatitis.
Imagingr US:
– Detects gallstones with sensitivity and specificity
>90%
– Dilation of common bile duct >10 mm indicates
obstruction, but no dilation may be present with
acute obstruction.
– Gallbladder wall thickening >5 mm or pericolic
fluid 90% sensitive and 80% specific for
cholecystitis
– Accuracy enhanced in fasting patient (>6 hr) with
noncontracted gallbladder
r Radionuclide scanning (HIDA):
– Cannot detect gallstones
– Passage of tracer into small intestine without
visualization of gallbladder highly diagnostic of
cystic duct obstruction and cholecystitis:
◦Sensitivity and specificity roughly 95%
– Failure of tracer to pass into duodenum suggests
common bile duct obstruction. Accuracy enhanced
by morphine injection during scan causing
sphincter of Oddi spasm and improving
gallbladder filling.
r CT scanning:
– Less sensitive than US to detect gallstones:
◦Only 20% radiopaque.
– Most useful to exclude other causes of upper
abdominal pain such as aortic aneurysm,
perihepatic abscess, or pancreatic pseudocyst
– Detects rare complications such as air in
gallbladder wall in emphysematous cholecystitis,
air-filled gallbladder in biliary-enteric fistula or a
“Porcelain gallbladder.”
r Plain radiographs:
– Most useful for diagnosis of intestinal obstruction
or rare abnormalities such as air in gallbladder
wall in emphysematous cholecystitis, air-filled
gallbladder in biliary-enteric fistula or a “Porcelain
gallbladder.”

CLAVICLE FRACTURE
Sean Patrick Nordt
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Clavicular fractures account for 5% of all fractures in
all age groups.
r 80% of clavicular fractures involve the middle 3rd.
r 15% occur in the distal 3rd.
r 5% occur in the medial 3rd.
Classification
r Group I: Middle-3rd fractures
r Group II: Distal-3rd fractures:
– Type I: Coracoclavicular ligaments are intact
(nondisplaced).
– Type II: Severing of the coracoclavicular ligaments
(conoid)
– Type III: Articular surface involvement of the
acromioclavicular joint
r Group III: Medial (proximal)-3rd fractures
ETIOLOGY
Mechanism:
r Direct trauma to the clavicle
r Fall on the lateral shoulder
r Fall on the outstretched hand
Pediatric Considerations
r Most common of all pediatric fractures
r May occur in newborns secondary to birth trauma
Geriatric Considerations
Geriatric patients who sustain a clavicular fracture
may have difficulty performing activities of daily living.
The patient’s social and living situations should be
assessed to determine a safe discharge plan that may
require additional assistance at home.
Pregnancy Considerations
Clavicular fractures are the result of direct trauma.
Patients who are pregnant should be appropriately
worked up for other injuries but also should receive
fetal monitoring to ensure the health of the fetus. Even
minor injuries can result in trauma or harm to the fetus.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Local pain, tenderness, and swelling over the
fracture site
r Crepitus is often present owing to the clavicle’s SC
position
r Arm held in adduction against the chest wall with
resistance to motion
r Shoulder displaced anteriorly and inferiorly
Physical Examr Palpate the clavicle for tenderness, crepitus, and
swelling.
r Examine the humerus and shoulder joint for other
fractures, dislocations, or subluxations.
r Determine whether the fracture is open or closed.
r Evaluate for associated injuries (often serious and
life threatening) that must be excluded:
– Skeletal injuries:
◦1st rib fracture with underlying aortic injury
◦Sternoclavicular joint
separation/fracture-dislocation
◦Acromioclavicular joint
separation/fracture-dislocation
◦Cervical spine injuries
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Imagingr AP radiographs of both clavicles are mandatory and
must include:
– Upper 3rd of the humerus
– Shoulder girdle (rule out other fractures)
– Upper lung fields (rule out pneumothorax)
r Oblique and apical lordotic views:
– May be helpful, especially for medial and distal
clavicle fractures that are not easily visualized on
the AP view
– Stress views (weight bearing) for distal clavicle
fractures are no longer routinely recommended.
r Angiography:
– Should be performed if there is any evidence or
suspicion of vascular injuries (most commonly
subclavian vessels)
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Distal fractures: Consider acromioclavicular
separation.
r Medial fractures: Consider sternoclavicular
separation.
r Shoulder fracture–dislocation
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Ice packs to affected area
r Pain management using either narcotics or NSAIDs
r Immobilize affected side in a sling.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Airway management and resuscitate as indicated
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Open fracture: Uncommon occurrence, but usually
requires open d ´ ebridement and internal fixation
(obtain immediate orthopedic referral)
r Closed fracture: If severely displaced, attempt closed
reduction and immobilize depending on type of
fracture:
– Middle 3rd:
◦If nondisplaced, a sling or shoulder immobilizer
is enough to provide support.
◦Controversy exists as to whether closed
reduction is necessary because the alignment is
rarely maintained regardless of splinting
technique.
◦To perform a closed reduction, 1% lidocaine
should be injected into the fracture hematoma.
The shoulders are pulled upward, outward, and
backward, and the fracture is then manipulated
into place.
◦Sedation may be given to alleviate pain or
anxiety.
◦A figure-of-eight splint or shoulder immobilizer
is then applied.
◦Ice should be applied for the 1st 24 hr.
◦Analgesia (narcotics or NSAIDs) for pain
– Distal 3rd type I:
◦Ice for the 1st 24 hr.
◦Immobilization with a sling or shoulder
immobilizer
◦Orthopedic referral
◦Analgesia (narcotics or NSAIDs) for pain
◦Early range of motion

COAGULOPATHY REVERSAL (NONWARFARIN AGENTS)
Susanne M. Hardy rJohn P. Lemos
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Patient on anticoagulant medications with minor,
major, or clinically significant bleeding needing close
monitoring +/− anticoagulant reversal
r Anticoagulant medication
– Indirect inhibitors of thrombin
◦Unfractionated heparin (UFH)
◦Low–molecular-weight heparin (LMWH)
■ Enoxaparin
■ Dalteparin
■ Tinzaparin
– Anti-platelet agents
◦Aspirin
◦Clopidogrel hydrogen sulfate (Plavix)
– Factor Xa inhibitors (FXa inhibitors)
◦Fondaparinux (Arixtra)
◦Rivaroxaban (Xarelto)
– Direct thrombin inhibitors (DTIs)
◦Argatroban
◦Bivalirudin (Angiomax)
◦Dabigatran (Pradaxa)
◦Hirudin derivatives
■ Desirudin
■ Lepiruden (Refludan)
Pediatric Considerations
r Heparin and LMWH are the most commonly utilized
anticoagulants beyond warfarin
r Routine use of DTIs is being studied
Geriatric Considerations
Excretion primarily renal with FXa inhibitors,
Dabigatran, and Hirudin derivatives necessitating
caution with impaired renal function
EPIDEMIOLOGY
Incidence and Prevalence Estimatesr Indirect inhibitors of thrombin
– Up to 1/3 patients develop bleeding complication
– 2–6% of bleeding is major
r Anti-platelet agents
– >300 over-the-counter medications contain
aspirin
– Conflicting studies regarding increased hematoma
expansion and mortality
r FXa Inhibitors
– Unknown
r DTIs
– Unknown
ETIOLOGYr Indirect inhibitors of thrombin
– Combines with antithrombin III to inactivate
activated FXa and also inhibits thrombin
– LMWH has a reduced ability to inactivate thrombin
– Half-life is dose dependent (30–150 min), can be
up to 8 hr with LMWH
r Anti-platelet agents
– Inactivates cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) preventing
formation of thromboxane A2, which inactivates
platelets
– Single dose suppresses for 1 wk
– New platelet production recovers 10%/day
– Patients may manifest normal hemostasis with as
few as 20% platelets with normal COX1 activity
– Aspirin half-life 15–30 min
– Clopidogrel half-life 8 hr
r FXa inhibitors
– Binds to antithrombin III, catalyzing FXa inhibition
– No direct inhibitory effect on thrombin
– Half-life 12–21 hr in normal renal function
r DTIs
– Competitively targets active site of thrombin +/−
exosite (substrate binding site)
– Half-life long with dabigatran (14–17 hr) and
short with others (20–45 min)
DIAGNOSIS
r Patient on anticoagulants with active bleeding
r Indications for reversal
– Serious or life-threatening bleeding
◦Trauma
◦GI bleeding
◦Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH)
– Procedural
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Type of anticoagulant
r Last anticoagulant use
r Length of anticoagulant
r Recent injury or trauma
r Bleeding location
r Symptoms (fatigue, lightheadedness, headache,
abdominal pain)
Physical Examr VS +/− orthostatics
r Search for hemorrhage locations/signs of trauma
r Comprehensive neurologic exam
r Rectal with stool guaiac test
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr CBC
r PT/INR
r PTT
r Stool guaiac test
r +/− Fibrinogen/DIC panel
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATIONr Indirect inhibitors of thrombin
– PTT
– Anti-FXa
◦High is >0.8 U/mL
r Anti-platelet agents
– Bleeding time
r FXa inhibitors
– Anti-FXa
– PT, PTT minimally helpful
– Fondaparinux level (institution specific)
r DTIs
– PTT minimally helpful
– Dabigatran level aka dilute thrombin time
(institution specific)
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy
r Inherited coagulation disorders
r Platelet dysfunction:
– TTP/HUS
– HIT
– ITP
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Pressure to hemorrhage (if possible)
r 2 large-bore IVs
r IV fluids
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Same as pre-hospital
r Hold anticoagulants
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Indirect inhibitors of thrombin
– Level bleeding
◦Minor: Observe PTT, anti-FXa
◦Major: Protamine (Class II for UFH and Class III
for LMWH)
– Protamine
◦1 mg IV neutralizes 100 U UFH administered in
prior 3–4 hr
■ If <30 min since UFH, use 1 mg/100 U UFH
■ If 30–120 min, use 0.5 mg/100 U UFH
■ If >120 min, use 0.25 mg/100 U UFH
◦Give slowly IV over 1–3 min not to exceed
50 mg in any 10-min period
◦Short half-life, may need to re-dose
◦Protamine reversal effectiveness is compound
specific for LMWH (does not reverse enoxaparin
completely)

■ Factor 4 is now available widely in the US

◦If ingestion within 1–2 hr of rivaroxaban
r DTIs
– Level bleeding
◦Minor: Observe bleeding (DTIs have short
half-life except dabigatran, which is 14–17 hr),

◦Major: PCC or rFVIIa (no strong evidence for

COCAINE POISONING
Steven E. Aks
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Sympathomimetic
r Inhibits neurotransmitter reuptake at the nerve
terminal
r Metabolism:
– Hepatic degradation
– Nonenzymatic hydrolysis
– Cholinesterase metabolism
ETIOLOGYr IV , nasal, oral administration of cocaine
r Oral ingestion:
– Body stuffers:
◦Ingest hastily wrapped packets in attempt to
evade police.
– Body packers:
◦Ingest cocaine packets to smuggle the drug
using couriers’ oral, rectal, and vaginal cavities.
◦Cocaine is wrapped carefully in packets
containing large amounts of drug.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Sympathomimetic toxidrome
r Cardiovascular:
– HTN
– Tachycardia
– Chest pain (angina)
r Respiratory:
– Tachypnea
– Pleuritic chest pain:
◦Pneumomediastinum
◦Pneumothorax
◦Bronchitis
◦Pulmonary infarction
– Cough
r CNS:
– Agitation
– Tremulousness
– Coma
– Seizures
– Stroke
r Miscellaneous:
– Hyperthermia (poor prognosis)
– Limb ischemia (inadvertent intra-arterial injection)
– Corneal ulcerations (heavy crack smokers):
◦Owing to local chemical and thermal irritation
that disrupts corneal epithelium
– Rhabdomyolysis
History
For body packers and stuffers:
r Time since ingestion
r Route of ingestion (oral, rectal, vaginal)
r Number of packets ingested
r Material and method of packing
Physical Exam
Sympathomimetic toxidrome:
r HTN
r Tachycardia
r Tachypnea
r Hyperthermia
r Diaphoresis
r Mydriasis
r Neuromuscular hyperactivity
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Recognition of the sympathomimetic toxidrome
caused by cocaine:
– Distinguish from anticholinergic toxidrome.
r Toxidrome recognition:
– Sympathomimetic:
◦Heart rate (tachycardia)
◦BP (increased)
◦Moist skin
◦Bowel sounds present
◦Temperature (increased)
◦No urinary retention
– Anticholinergic:
◦Heart rate (tachycardia)
◦BP (increased)
◦Dry skin
◦Bowel sounds diminished
◦Temperature (increased)
◦Urinary retention present
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose
r Urinalysis dip for myoglobin
r Cardiac enzymes (troponin, creatine phosphokinase
[CPK]) for:
– Anginal chest pain
– Abnormal results on ECG
r CPK for evidence of myoglobinuria
r Toxicology screen
Imagingr ECG:
– For anginal chest pain
– Consider possibility of myocardial infarction with
cocaine-related chest pain.
r CXR:
– For chest pain or shortness of breath
– Check for pneumomediastinum, pneumothorax,
aortic rupture.
r Abdominal radiograph:
– For body packers/stuffers
– Usually produces negative result for stuffers
because drug is loosely packed in cellophane
– Positive for packers because drug is densely
packed and usually radiopaque
r CT of the abdomen with contrast:
– When unreliable history of body packers/stuffers
and nothing visualized on abdominal frontal
radiograph
r CT brain scan:
– For altered mental status or severe headache
– Detects cerebral ischemia or hemorrhage
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
Other agents with sympathomimetic effects
r Theophylline
r Caffeine
r Amphetamines
r Albuterol
r Tricyclic antidepressants
r Antihistamines
r Phencyclidine (PCP)
r Thyrotoxicosis
r Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
r Hallucinogens
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Establish IV access
r Cardiac monitor:
– Chest pain may be ischemic.
– Benzodiazepine therapy to control agitation
r When drug is used as a “speedball” (combination of
heroin and cocaine), administer naloxone in
increments to reverse coma.

COLON TRAUMA
Stephen R. Hayden
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Trauma that perforates the colon inflames the cavity
in which it lies.
r Peritoneal inflammation from hollow viscus
perforation often requires hours to develop.
r Mesenteric tears from blunt trauma cause
hemorrhage and bowel ischemia.
r Delayed perforation from ischemic or necrotic bowel
may occur.
r Peritonitis and sepsis may develop from the
extravasated intraluminal flora.
r Ascending and descending colon segments are
retroperitoneal.
r The left colon has a higher bacterial load than the
right.
r Morbidity and mortality increase if the diagnosis of
colon injury is delayed.
ETIOLOGYr Penetrating abdominal trauma:
– The colon is the 2nd most commonly injured
organ in penetrating trauma.
– Gunshot wounds have the highest incidence.
– Transverse colon is most commonly injured.
– Often presents with peritonitis
r Blunt abdominal trauma:
– Colon rarely injured in blunt trauma
– Burst injury occurs from compression of a closed
loop of bowel.
– Intestine may be squeezed between a blunt object
(lap belt) and vertebral column or bony pelvis.
– Sudden deceleration may produce
bowel–mesenteric disruption and consequent
devascularization.
– With deceleration, the sigmoid and transverse
colon are most vulnerable.
r Transanal injury:
– Iatrogenic endoscopic or barium enema injury
– Foreign bodies used during sexual activities may
reach and injure the colon.
– Compressed air under high pressure such as at
automobile repair facilities can perforate the colon
even if the compressor nozzle is not fully inserted
anally.
– Swallowed sharp foreign bodies (toothpick) may
penetrate the colon, particularly the cecum,
appendix, and sigmoid:
◦Most foreign bodies pass without complications.
Pediatric Considerations
Unlike adults, children have an equal frequency of
blunt and penetrating colon injuries.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Colon trauma is generally associated with other
intra-abdominal and extra-abdominal injuries,
commonly to the small intestine.
r Injuries of significant severity may have minimal
early findings.
r It is uncommon to determine specific organ injury on
physical exam.
r Assess on exam:
– Abdomen for peritoneal signs
– Ecchymosis or hematoma on lower abdomen from
lap-belt compression
– Ecchymosis on epigastric region from
steering-wheel compression
– Grey Turner sign (flank hematomas) resulting from
retroperitoneal bleeding.
– Foreign bodies or blood on digital rectal exam (be
careful if sharp object suspected)
– Note: Abdominal wall ecchymosis or hematoma is
not always present despite existing injury.
– Note: Bowel sounds are not helpful.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Serial abdominal exam because inflammation takes
time to develop
r Abdominal CT with contrast is the best diagnostic
study in stable patients.
r US and diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) are
helpful in the potentially unstable patient.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATIONr No individual test or combination of currently
available diagnostic modalities is adequate to
exclude blunt colonic injury.
r Signs of peritoneal irritation owing to intestinal
injury typically develop hours after the event.
Labr Electrolytes
r Calcium, magnesium
Imagingr CT is more useful for detecting penetrating vs. blunt
colon injury.
r CT with triple contrast allows intraperitoneal and
retroperitoneal visualization.
r Oral contrast is not essential in blunt abdominal
trauma CT evaluation.
r Although CT may miss colon injuries, abnormal
findings are typical.
r CT is only moderately sensitive at identifying hollow
viscus injury.
r Hollow viscus injury–associated CT findings include
extraluminal gas or contrast, mesenteric fat
streaking, and free fluid without solid organ injury.
r Water-soluble enema with fluoroscopy is useful if
other test results are inconclusive.
r Plain abdominal radiographs can show indirect signs
such as intraperitoneal and retroperitoneal free air.
r FAST US exam does not evaluate for enteric injury
and retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
r See “Abdominal Trauma, Blunt”; “Abdominal
Trauma, Imaging.”
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr DPL or ultrasound in addition to CT will increase
sensitivity.
r In blunt trauma, DPL will often not detect
retroperitoneal injuries and enteric injury as
intra-abdominal bleeding is limited.
r Fecal or vegetable material on DPL analysis indicates
hollow viscus injury.
r Lavage white cell response may be negative
secondary to delayed peritoneal inflammation.
r In hollow viscus injury, lavage WBC count: RBC ratio
is higher than that seen with solid organ injuries.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Other intra-abdominal injuries
r A fractured pelvis may present similarly to
intraperitoneal injuries in children.
