ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Maintain adequate oxygenation and ventilation.
r Monitor O2 saturation and respiratory rate.
r In conscious and alert patients, O2 administration
via face mask is first-line therapy.
r If patient cannot maintain a PaO2 >80 mm Hg on
high-flow oxygen, consider continuous positive
airway pressure via mask or nasal bilevel positive
airway pressure.
r Consider early endotracheal intubation and
mechanical ventilation if the above fails:
– Physiologic internal fixation of the flail segment
r External fixation or stabilization of the flail segment
is not indicated.
r Adequate pain control is critical to maintaining
adequate pulmonary function:
– Avoid splinting, atelectasis, and pneumonia.
r Search for associated injuries and treat exacerbation
of underlying lung disease.
r Intercostal nerve blocks with 0.5% bupivacaine are
safe and effective when performed properly:
– Provides 6–12 hr of pain relief
– Perform intercostal nerve block posteriorly 2–3
fingerbreadths from the vertebral midline.
– Inject 0.5–1 mL just under the inferior surface of
the rib where the neurovascular bundle is located.
– Aspirate 1st to be certain that the intercostal
vessels have not been punctured.
r Prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated.
ALERT
Avoid overhydration:
r In the setting of pulmonary contusion, the need
for IV crystalloid resuscitation must be weighed
against the risk of increasing interstitial
pulmonary edema.
MEDICATIONr Multiple acetaminophen/opioid analgesic
combinations are available; see the alert below.
r Acetaminophen: 300 mg/codeine 30 mg (peds:
0.5–1 mg/kg codeine) PO q4–6h
r Acetaminophen: 500 mg/hydrocodone 5 mg PO
q4–6h
r Acetaminophen: 750 mg/hydrocodone 7.5 mg PO
q4–6h
r Acetaminophen: 325 mg/hydrocodone 10 mg PO
q4–6h
r Acetaminophen: 325 mg/oxycodone 5 mg PO q6h
r Bupivacaine: 0.5% 0.5–1 mL per injection for
intercostal nerve blocks
r Hydromorphone: 2–8 mg (peds: 0.03–0.08 mg/kg)
PO q4–6h
r Hydromorphone: 1–4 mg (peds: 0.015 mg/kg)
IV/IM/SC q4–6h
r Morphine sulfate: 0.05–0.1 mg/kg IV/IM/SC q2–6h
r Patient-controlled analgesia using fentanyl,
hydromorphone, or morphine sulfate is effective.
ALERT
r Consider thoracic epidural analgesia for patients
with intractable pain, oversedation, or
hypoventilation secondary to opioid analgesics.
r NSAIDs discouraged due to the risk of GI bleeding.
r The dose of acetaminophen/opioid analgesic
combinations is limited by the hepatic toxicity of
acetaminophen.
r The max. acetaminophen dose is 1 g per dose and
4 g/d (peds: 15 mg/kg per dose, do not exceed
5 doses/24 hr)

pain control.

Patients found to have flail chest, with or without
pulmonary contusion, should not be discharged.

r Early pain control is key.
r Beware of concomitant injuries such as pulmonary
contusion and pneumothorax.
r Elderly patients have significantly poorer outcomes.

FOOT FRACTURE
Stephen R. Hayden
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Injury to tarsal bones or metatarsals including
calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuboid, cuneiform, and
metatarsals
ETIOLOGYr Most common foot injuries are of the metatarsals
and phalanges.
r The calcaneus is the most commonly fractured of the
tarsal bones.
r Calcaneus fractures: Compression injury from
sudden high-velocity impact to heel:
– 75% are intra-articular; 50% have associated
injuries:
◦10% spine fractures
◦25% with associated lower extremity trauma
◦9% bilateral, 5% open
r Metatarsal fractures: Divided into stress fractures,
twisting injuries, or direct trauma:
– 1st metatarsal: Direct applied force
– 2nd and 3rd metatarsals are most often involved
in stress fractures and twisting injuries.
– 5th metatarsal: Avulsion fracture (dancer’s
fracture) of proximal apophysis is the most
common injury.
– Jones fracture: Transverse fracture of the
metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction of 5th
metatarsal; results from twisting while foot
inverted.
r Talus: Caused by dorsiflexion with axial load,
common snowboarder’s injury
r Navicular: Results from axial compression or stress
fractures
r Cuboid and cuneiform fractures are rare and occur
in conjunction with other injuries, often with
tarsal–metatarsal injuries.
r Tarsal–metatarsal injuries (Lisfranc injuries) are
high-energy injuries:
– Axial load on plantar-flexed foot, or hindfoot fixed
with forced foot eversion
– Unstable forefoot on hindfoot
– 20% go undiagnosed on initial visit.
– 3 types: Convergent, divergent, and incongruent
Pediatric Considerations
r Metatarsal fractures account for 90% of foot
fractures in children, usually from direct trauma:
– Lesser metatarsal fractures (2–4) most common
followed by base of 5th then base of 1st
metatarsal.
– Physeal injury may occur with proximal 1st
metatarsal fractures.
r Other common injuries include phalangeal fractures
(17%) and navicular fractures (5%).
r Fractures of talus or calcaneus occur with distal tibia
or fibula fractures (8%).
r Calcaneus fractures are less likely intra-articular.
Less common to have associated spine fractures.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr History of preceding trauma most common
r Stress fractures may present with increasing pain in
the setting of repetitive activities.
Physical Examr Ecchymosis, pain, swelling, or deformity of foot
r Pain with weight bearing
r Joint instability
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Physical exam of extremity is necessary to assess
neurovascular status, skin integrity, gross swelling,
deformity, or loss of function.
r Exam of spine is also essential in suspected
calcaneus fractures, as there is a 10% incidence of
coexistent injury.
r Anteroposterior/lateral and oblique views are
necessary for all foot fractures.
r Complications:
– Compartment syndrome most commonly presents
as severe pain in a swollen foot:
◦Pressures >35 mm Hg require opening of all
major foot compartments.
◦May have hypesthesia of plantar foot
◦Weak toe flexion
◦Late findings include claw toe deformity.
– Nonunion and avascular necrosis are common
complications with talar neck fractures owing to
distal blood supply.
– Calcaneus fractures may be accompanied by sural
nerve injury; test sensation along lateral aspect of
foot.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Imaging
Special views may be needed for some fractures:
r Lisfranc fractures may require stress views with
weight bearing. They may require MRI to evaluate
ligamentous stability. May require CT for evaluation
of small fractures if clinically suspicious
r Fleck sign: Pathognomonic—avulsion of ligament
from 2 MT base or medial cuneiform
r Talar fractures may require a 45◦ internal oblique
view. May require CT.
r Midfoot fractures may require an external oblique
foot view.
r Calcaneus fractures require an axial view and may
require CT:
– Bohler’s angle <20◦ suggests a compression
fracture of calcaneus.
– Lumbosacral spine films are necessary in all
patients with calcaneus fractures.
r Stress fractures may require 2 wk to appear on plain
films; bone scan or CT may be used to elucidate
suspected fractures.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Anterior effects of calcaneus and talar dome
fractures can be misdiagnosed as ankle sprains.
r Foot contusions
r Freiberg disease: Osteochondrosis of 2nd metatarsal
head may be mistaken for stress fracture.

FOREARM FRACTURE, SHAFT/DISTAL
Stephen R. Hayden
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Forearm shaft fractures (single or paired) are often
displaced by contraction of arm muscles; sometimes
associated with concurrent dislocations:
– Galeazzi fracture:
◦Distal radius fracture with distal radioulnar
dislocation
– Monteggia fracture:
◦Proximal ulnar fracture with dislocation of radial
head
r Distal fractures include extension, flexion, and
intra-articular classifications:
– Colles fracture:
◦Hyperextension fracture of distal radius
◦Distal fragment displaced dorsally
◦Radial deviation
◦Often involves ulnar styloid and distal radioulnar
joint
– Smith fracture:
◦Hyperflexion fracture of distal radius
◦Distal fragment displaced volarly
– Barton fracture:
◦Intra-articular fracture of dorsal rim of distal
radius
◦Often associated with dislocation of carpal
bones
– Hutchinson fracture:
◦Intra-articular fracture of radial styloid
Pediatric Considerations
r Shaft fractures:
– Torus fracture:
◦Compression (buckling) of cortex on 1 or both
sides
– Greenstick fracture:
◦Distraction of 1 side of cortex with opposite side
intact
– Plastic deformity:
◦Bowing of radius or ulna without apparent
disruption of cortex
◦Multiple microfractures
r Distal fractures:
– Salter–Harris type fractures (see Salter–Harris
classification)
ETIOLOGYr Direct blow to forearm
r Longitudinal compression load:
– Fall on outstretched hand (FOOSH)
– Horizontal force
r Excessive pronation, supination, hyperextension, or
hyperflexion
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Deformity
r Pain, edema, erythema
Historyr Associated events and concurrent injuries
r Past history of bone disease or old fractures
r History of repetitive stress of forearm movement
r Occupation
r Hand dominance
Physical Examr Physical exam with special attention to skin
integrity, deformity, and neurovascular status
r Forearm pain, crepitus, tenderness to palpation,
deformity, shortening of forearm
r Forearm edema, ecchymosis, elbow or wrist joint
effusions
r Abnormal mobility or loss of function at
elbow/wrist/hand
r Neurologic abnormalities
r Vascular compromise
ALERT
Impending compartment syndrome
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Suspected forearm fractures require anteroposterior
(AP) and lateral radiographs, including joint above and
joint below injury: Hand, wrist, and elbow.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Preoperative labs as warranted
Imaging
Some intra-articular fractures may require CT imaging.
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Compartment pressures should be measured for
suspected compartment syndrome.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Upper extremity muscle, ligamentous injury
r Elbow or wrist dislocations, including pediatric
nursemaid’s elbow
r Forearm contusions, hematomas
r Cellulitis, abscesses, soft tissue masses
r Forearm osteogenic tumors
r Osteomyelitis
r Upper extremity vascular or neurologic injuries
r Elbow or wrist arthritis, joint effusions
r Pediatric growth plates, nutrient vessels may be
mistaken for fractures
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr All suspected forearm fractures should be elevated,
splinted, and immobilized, including elbow and
wrist joints.
r All open fractures should be wrapped with sterile
dressing before immobilization:
– Do not reduce open fractures back under skin in
the field.
– In patients with isolated extremity trauma,
analgesia may be administered.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Shaft fractures, nondisplaced:
– Long-arm splint
– Orthopedic referral
r Shaft fractures, displaced:
– Orthopedic consultation
– Often require open reduction, internal fixation
r Distal fractures, nondisplaced:
– Forearm sugar-tong or AP splint
– Orthopedic referral

F
r Distal fractures: Colles/Smith:
– Simple, noncomminuted, extra-articular Colles
and Smith fractures may be reduced in ED:
◦Splint (long-arm sugar-tong splint)
◦Sling
◦Referred to orthopedics
– Complicated Colles and Smith fractures require
orthopedic consultation.
r Distal fractures: Barton/Hutchinson:
– Uncomplicated Barton and Hutchinson fractures
◦Splint (AP or sugar-tong splint)
◦Place in sling
◦Referred to orthopedics
– Complicated fractures require orthopedic
consultation.
r Open fractures:
– Cover with sterile dressings.
– IM/IV antibiotics
– Tetanus immunization (if indicated)
– Splint
– Immediate orthopedic consultation
r Forearm fractures associated with compartment
syndrome or neurovascular compromise require
immediate orthopedic consultation.
Pediatric Considerations
r Torus and Greenstick fractures with <10◦ of
angulation may be treated with long-arm splint,
sling, and orthopedic referral.
r Plastic deformities require orthopedic consultation:
– Some minimally displaced plastic deformities may
be placed in long-arm splint and sling.
r Salter–Harris type fractures require orthopedic
consultation.
MEDICATIONr Acetaminophen: 325–1,000 mg PO q4h (peds:
10–15 mg/kg q4h PO)
r Antibiotics:
– Open fractures require IM/IV antibiotics.
– Cefazolin: 1–2 g IM/IV or equivalent
1st-generation cephalosporin; if contaminated,
add an aminoglycoside
r Codeine: 15–60 mg PO/IM q4h (peds: >2y r ,
0.5–1 mg/kg q4h PO/IM)
r Hydrocodone: 5–10 mg PO q4h
r Ibuprofen: 200–800 mg q4–8h (peds: >6m o ,
5–10 mg/kg per dose q6h)
r Morphine sulfate: 2–10 mg IV/IM; titrate to pain
(peds: 0.1 mg/kg per dose IV/IM)
r Tetanus: 0.5 mL IM every 10 yr

DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Open fractures
r Fractures with compartment syndrome or
neurovascular compromise
r Fractures needing immediate operative management
or general anesthesia for reduction
r Suspected nonaccidental trauma
Discharge Criteriar Appropriate reduction and immobilization
r Arranged orthopedic follow-up
r Adequate pain control measures
r Cast/splint care discharge instructions provided and
understood by patient
r Documentation of intact neurovascular function
after ED treatment
Issues for Referral
All fractures (or suspected fractures) discharged from
ED should be referred to orthopedic surgeon for close
follow-up.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
All patients should be referred to an orthopedic
surgeon or hand surgeon.

FOREIGN BODY, EAR
Kathleen Nasci rCharles V. Pollack, Jr.
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Foreign bodies (FBs) lodged in the external auditory
canal
r The external auditory canal:
– Cartilaginous and bony passage lined with
periosteum and skin
– The periosteum is extremely sensitive, making
removal a painful procedure:
◦In small children general anesthesia may be
required to remove the object
◦FBs usually impact at the junction of the inner
end of the cartilaginous portion of the canal or
at the isthmus
◦Innervated by the facial, glossopharyngeal,
vagus nerves
r Inanimate foreign objects are often associated with
delayed presentations:
– Children often delay reporting because of fear of
punishment
– Often the FB is an incidental finding in children
during an ear exam
r Physical findings may change due to length of time
the object is in the canal
r Children with cerumen impaction or those with pica
are predisposed
r The location is often the right ear, due to the
predominance of right handedness
r Children and psychiatric patients may insert
anything sufficiently small to enter the external
auditory canal.
r Ear FBs are most common in children <8y r
r Complications:
– Canal laceration:
◦Usually caused by repeated attempts to remove
a nongraspable object
– Perforation of tympanic membrane:
◦More likely to result from removal procedure
than the FB
– Otitis externa
– Malocclusion from erosion into the
temporomandibular joint
– Parapharyngeal abscess
– Mastoiditis
– Meningitis
– Brain abscess
– Insects may injure the tympanic membrane or
canal by stinging, biting, or scratching
– Button batteries can cause significant destruction
due to the strong electrical currents and pressure
necrosis
– Typically, the most damage is caused by negative
side of the battery
– Damage to the facial nerve and ossicles have been
reported
r Symptoms usually resolve within a few days after FB
removal
ETIOLOGYr Children:
– Stones
– Small beads
– Paper
– Toys
– Seeds and popcorn kernels
– Beans and other food and organic materials
– Button batteries:
◦Higher risk for necrosis than other FBs
r Competent adults:
– Cotton-swab tips
– Earplugs
– Insects:
◦Cockroach most common in US
– Hidden illicit drugs
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Decreased hearing
r Excessive crying in infants
r Unilateral ear pain
r Fullness
r Loud noises
r Buzzing sound (with live insects)
r Nausea
r Dizziness
r Ipsilateral tearing
r Purulent discharge from the external ear
r Itching
r Bleeding
Historyr Travel or camping history or poor living conditions
suggests insects in the external ear canal
r Inquire about previous attempts to remove the FB
and any trauma associated with these attempts
Physical Exam
Otoscopic exam should be performed before and after
removal of the FB:
r Identify type of FB to determine removal procedure:
– Button battery
– Live insect
– Vegetable
– Inanimate object
– Size
– Risk of swelling when exposed to water
r Perform a bilateral exam; especially important in
children and psychiatric patients, and prevent
overlooking a quiescent FB in the contralateral ear
r Attempt to visualize tympanic membrane to assess
for rupture
r Assess for otitis externa
r Assess for retained fragments after the removal
r Always exam the nonaffected ear and nostrils for
additional FBs
r Significant pain, vertigo, or ataxia, nsytagmus,
hearing loss, otorrhea, or facial nerve paralysis are
concerning signs and an otolaryngologist
consultation should be considered
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Careful otoscopic exam:
r Minimize pain
r Gain the patient’s trust
r Identify the FB before attempting removal
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
None indicated
Imaging
CT scan if infectious or erosive sequelae are suspected
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Otomicroscope:
r May be used when standard ED techniques fail or
the equipment is available to emergency medical
staff
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Cerumen impaction
r Granuloma
r Hematoma
r Injury
r Otitis externa
r Perforated tympanic membrane
r Residual otitis externa after self-extraction of the FB
r Tumor
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Cautions:
– Severe ear pain, sensation of movement, and
loud, buzzing sound:
◦Typical signs of a live insect in external auditory
canal
◦Instill warm lidocaine or mineral oil into affected
ear to kill insect
r Controversies:
– Attempts at removal in the field are not indicated:
◦Lack of appropriate equipment
◦Prior failed attempts may make future attempts
more difficult
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
For a patient in distress because of a live insect:
r Drown or immobilize insect before any removal
attempts
r Instill warm solution into the external auditory
canal:
– 2% lidocaine solution
– Ether
– Alcohol
– Mineral oil
r Cold fluids should not be used so as to avoid a
caloric response
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Prepare the equipment and the patient:
– Strong light source
– Otoscope or operating microscope
– Achieve proper head immobilization
– Retract the pinna of the ear in a posterosuperior
direction to straighten the canal
r Analgesia:
– Lidocaine instillation for topical anesthesia:
◦Liquid 1–2% solution is preferred to viscous
lidocaine.
◦Lidocaine injection of the 4 quadrants of the
canal using a tuberculin syringe through the
otoscope
◦1–2% lidocaine, with or without epinephrine
r Procedural sedation:
– Indicated for children and uncooperative adults
– Use before attempts, as unsuccessful efforts may
produce bleeding, edema, or injury to the
tympanic membrane
– Ketamine for children
– Benzodiazepines for older patients
– Consider fentanyl if analgesia is indicated during
removal

FOREIGN BODY, EAR
F
r Options for removal:
– Water irrigation:
◦Perform careful visualization
◦Place an Angiocath catheter adjacent to, or
preferably distal to, the FB
◦Inject warm water or sterile saline through
catheter via a syringe
◦Backwash the FB out
◦Never attempt removal by irrigation when the
FB is a button battery
– Use of instruments to dislodge the FB:
◦Alligator forceps removal
◦Cupped forceps: Numbers 3, 5, and 7 suction
tips, preferably with Frazier suction cups
◦Cerumen loops
◦Right-angle blunt hooks
– Suction catheters:
◦Best used for small objects
– Fogarty catheter:
◦Carefully pass beyond the FB and inflate and
withdraw; this approach puts the tympanic
membrane at particular risk of inadvertent injury
– Cyanoacrylate glue on the tip of a blunt probe:
◦Place on the FB for 10 sec, and then pull
◦May contaminate the ear with glue, and this
technique has been associated with tympanic
membrane rupture
– Acetone:
◦Used to dissolve Styrofoam FBs or loosen
superglue
– Otomicroscopy:
◦Usually performed in the OR although reports of
use in the ED have been positive
r Vegetable matter:
– Avoid irrigation of FBs that will swell when
exposed to water
– Attempt removal with instrument
– Forceps usually work with graspable objects
– Be certain to delineate clearly between FB and
inflamed external auditory canal tissue
r Nonvegetable inanimate FB removal:
– If easily grasped, attempt removal with forceps
– If not accessible, attempt removal with irrigation
r Polished or smooth object extraction:
– Visualize
– Direct suction
– Blunt right-angled probe: Pass beyond the FB;
rotate 90◦; remove it with the FB
– Fogarty catheter
– Cyanoacrylate glue
r Insect removal:
– Kill insect by rapidly instilling alcohol, 2%
lidocaine (Xylocaine), or mineral oil into the ear
– Once killed, remove with forceps or by irrigation
– Re-examine to ensure that all insect parts are
removed
r Sharp objects:
– Remove with operating microscope
– Consider otolaryngologic referral if there is
evidence of trauma or if patient is uncooperative
MEDICATION
First Liner Fentanyl: 1 μg/kg IV
r Ketamine: 1–2 mg/kg IV or 4 mg/kg IM
r Midazolam: 1 mg IV slowly q2–3min up to 5 mg
(peds: 6 mo–5 yr, 0.05–0.1 mg/kg, titrate to max. of
0.6 mg/kg; 6–12 yr, 0.025–0.05 mg/kg, titrate to
max. of 0.4 mg/kg)
Second Liner Cortisporin otic: 4 gtt in ear QID
r Amoxicillin: 500 mg PO (peds: 80–90 mg/kg/24 h)
PO TID for 7–10 days.
r Augmentin: 875 mg (peds: 90 mg/kg/24 h) PO BID
for 7–10 days.
r Fill ear canal 5× per day with a combination of
antibiotic and steroid otic solution for 5–7 days if
there is suspected infection or abrasion
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteria
Hospital admission if the FB is a button battery that
cannot be removed
Discharge Criteriar FB removed
r Inability to remove a FB that will not cause rapid
tissue necrosis
r Oral antibiotics (amoxicillin or Augmentin) should be
initiated in cases with tympanic membrane
perforation
Issues for Referral
Follow-up with ENT specialist as an outpatient:
r Inability to remove a FB
r Immunocompromised patients with signs of otitis
externa
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Patient should be instructed not to place any objects
in ear
r A short course of analgesics after traumatic FB
removal
r Otitis externa:
– Topical antimicrobial such as Cortisporin
suspension
r Immunocompromised patients may require oral
antibiotics
r Perforated tympanic membrane:
– Prophylaxis with antibiotics
– Follow-up with ENT specialist
r Avoid submersion in water until follow-up if trauma
or infection present
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Use procedural sedation with uncooperative
patients or when a difficult removal is anticipated
r Irrigation in patients with button batteries in the ear
should never be performed as the electrical current
or battery contents can cause liquefaction tissue
necrosis.
ADDITIONAL READING
r Brown L, Denmark TK, Wittlake WA, et al.
Procedural sedation use in the ED: Management of
pediatric ear and nose foreign bodies. Am J Emerg
Med. 2004;22:310–314.
r Cederberg CA, Kerschner JE. Otomicroscope in the
emergency department management of pediatric
ear foreign bodies. Int J Pediatr Otorhinolaryngol.
2009;73:589–591.
r Dance D, Riley M, Ludemann P. Removal of ear
canal foreign bodies in children: What can go wrong
and when to refer. BCMJ. 2009;51:20–24.
r Davies PH, Benger JR. Foreign bodies in the nose
and ear: A review of techniques for removal in the
emergency department. J Accid Emerg Med.
2000;17:91–94.
r Erkalp K, Kalekolu Erkalp N, Ozdemir H. Acute
otalgia during sleep (live insect in the ear): A case
report. Agri. 2009;21:36–38.
r Heim SW, Maughan KL. Foreign bodies in the ear,
nose, and throat. Am Fam Physician. 2007;76:
1185–1189.
r Kumar S, Kumar M, Lesser T, et al. Foreign bodies in
the ear: A simple technique for removal analysed in
vitro. Emerg Med J. 2005;22:266–268.

FOREIGN BODY, ESOPHAGEAL
Joanna W. Davidson
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Esophageal foreign bodies (FBs) typically lodge at
3 sites of physiologic constriction:
– Cricopharyngeal muscle—63%, most common
(C6)
– Gastroesophageal junction—20% (T11)
– Aortic arch—10% (T4)
r 90% of ingested FBs pass spontaneously.
r 10–20% are removed endoscopically, and 1% or
less require surgery.
ETIOLOGYr Most common adult and adolescent FBs are food
boluses and bones
r Increased risk:
– Edentulous adults
– Intoxicated patients
– Patients with underlying esophageal disease:
Schatzki B-rings or peptic strictures are most
common
Pediatric Considerations
r 80% of FB ingestions occur in pediatric age group,
peak ages 6 mo–6 yr, particularly younger than 2 yr.
r Coins are most common:
– Most common: 80% of esophageal FBs
r 2 additional areas of constriction: Thoracic inlet (T1)
and tracheal bifurcation (T6)
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Acute ingestion:
– Dysphagia
– Odynophagia
– Drooling
– Retching/self-induced vomiting
– Choking
– Gagging
– Blood-stained saliva
r Chronically retained FB:
– Respiratory symptoms predominate
(paraesophageal tissue swelling compromises
adjacent trachea):
◦Cough
◦Stridor
◦Hoarseness
– Chest pain
– Site of FB sensation usually corresponds to
esophageal level of FB
– Esophageal perforation
– 15–35% if ingest sharp object:
◦Redness
◦Swelling
◦Crepitus in the neck
◦Peritonitis
– <20% asymptomatic
Pediatric Considerations
Signs/symptoms:
r Refusal to eat
r Stridor
r Upper respiratory tract infection
r Neck/throat pain
Historyr Adults:
– Usually provide unequivocal history
◦80% present within 1st 24 hr
◦5% will present with airway obstruction (cafe
coronary)
r Children:
– 50% asymptomatic
– History can be unclear if unwitnessed ingestion is
not witnessed
– Drooling, refusal to eat, unexplained gagging,
cough, wheeze, choking
– More likely than adults to have respiratory
symptoms
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr History about object ingested: Type, when, and how
r Physical exam focused by degree of distress
exhibited:
– Esophagus:
◦Obstruction—saliva pooling, aspiration
◦Perforation—crepitus, pain, pleurisy
◦Hemorrhage
– Oropharynx:
◦Red, irritated throat
◦Palatal abrasions
– Lung:
◦Stridor and wheezing
– Abdomen:
◦Peritonitis or bowel obstruction
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Imagingr Biplane chest radiograph including all of neck for FB
localization:
– Food boluses usually do not need radiographs.
– Esophageal FBs often align themselves in coronal
plane.
– Esophageal perforation is noted by air in
retropharyngeal space, in soft tissues of neck, or
by pneumomediastinum.
r Ingested, impacted bones visible on plain film
<50%
r CT scan replacing esophageal contrast studies for
nonradiopaque FBs:
– Radiolucent objects include small pieces of glass,
bone fragments, aluminum, plastic, pieces of
wood
– Visualizes perforation or infection
r Endoscopy is a method of choice for localizing and
managing most esophageal FBs
– Ability to inspect surrounding esophageal mucosa
for pathology
– Diagnostic and therapeutic
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Globus hystericus phenomenon (“lump in throat”)
r Esophageal mucosal irritation
r Esophagitis
r Croup
r Epiglottitis
r Upper respiratory tract infection
r Retropharyngeal abscess
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Cautions:
r Airway maintenance and prevention of aspiration
paramount
r Oxygen for patients in distress
r Place patient in whatever position gives most
comfort.
r Ipecac and cathartics contraindicated
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Airway, breathing, and circulation management 1st
priority
r Prevent aspiration
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Direct laryngoscopy or fiberoptic scope may allow
removal of very proximal objects
r Urgent endoscopy recommended:
– Ingestion of sharp or elongated objects
◦>6 cm long
◦>2.5 cm
◦Irregular/sharp edges (toothpicks, soda can tabs)
◦Ingestion of multiple FBs; especially magnets
– Evidence of perforation
– Coin at level of cricopharyngeus muscle in a child
– Airway compromise
– Presence of FB for >24 hr
– Food bolus with complete obstruction
r Observation can be considered
r Asymptomatic patients with coins or smooth objects
(not button batteries) in distal esophagus:
– Observe up to 24 hr after ingestion to see whether
it will pass into stomach.
– Objects that reach stomach and are shorter than
5c ma n d<2 cm in diameter usually pass through
GI tract without difficulty, but daily radiographs
are still recommended.
◦Danger of perforation increases after 24 hr.
r Removal options:
– IV glucagon:
◦Decreases lower esophageal sphincter tone
without interfering with esophageal
contractions
◦Falling out of favor for endoscopy
◦Less effective if underlying Schatzki ring or
stricture
◦Permits distal food boluses to pass into the
stomach
◦For impactions <24 hr duration
– Fluoroscopically guided Foley catheter extraction:
◦Successful and safe in experienced hands
◦Foley catheter (10F–16F) placed nasally, passed
into esophagus, tip and balloon pushed beyond
FB under fluoroscopic control
◦Foley balloon inflated with contrast and catheter
slowly withdrawn
◦Contraindicated in chronic ingestions,
uncooperative patients, sharp–pointed objects
◦Foley catheters or dilator (bougienage) may also
be used to push distal FB into stomach

FOREIGN BODY, ESOPHAGEAL
F
– Endoscopy:
◦Preferred method to remove acute or chronic FBs
◦98% effective
◦Always used with impactions of long duration
(>2–4 days) because of associated esophageal
irritation/edema
◦General endotracheal anesthesia needed in
difficult cases: Infants, psychiatric patients,
difficult FB
◦Risk of complications increases after 24 hr, ideal
to be done within 6–12 hr
– Surgical intervention:
◦Reserved for patients in whom FB cannot be
removed by other methods
◦∼1–2% of all patients
◦Toothpicks and bones common objects
r Specific ingestions
– Impacted food bolus obstructing esophagus:
◦Emergent removal indicated
◦Proteolytic enzymes (papain) not recommended
because of esophageal perforation,
hypernatremia, and aspiration complications
r Button batteries:
– Extract emergently
– Batteries frequently leak: Potassium hydroxide and
mercuric oxide are the most toxic constituents.
– Alkali produced from external flow of current can
cause liquefaction necrosis.
– Full-thickness mucosal burns can occur within
4–6 hr (combination of chemical, electrical,
pressure injuries).
– Battery in stomach will usually pass without
difficulty; batteries remaining in stomach for
>3–4 days should be removed.
– Once past duodenal sweep, 85% are passed
within 72 hr.
r Narcotic/amphetamine packets:
– Body packing seen in regions of high drug traffic
– Packets usually seen on radiographs
– Rupture or leakage of contents can be fatal.
r Magnets/“Bucky Balls”:
– Opposing magnets attract bringing sections of
stomach/bowel together creating obstruction
– Early GI consult for removal vs. laparotomy
MEDICATION
Glucagon: 1–2 mg IV push after test dose to
determine hypersensitivity
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Seriously ill patients and those with complications
such as esophageal perforation, migration of FB
through esophageal wall, significant bleeding
r Airway compromise
r Symptomatic patients in whom attempts to remove
FB are unsuccessful
Discharge Criteriar Asymptomatic patients in whom FB has been
removed or passed distal to esophagus
r Asymptomatic patients with distal esophageal
smooth FBs need re-exam within 12–24 hr to
ascertain whether spontaneous passage into
stomach has occurred.
Issues for Referral
GI consult for sharp or pointed esophageal FBs, those
obstructed in upper or mid esophagus and battery
button FBs.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
GI referral for patients with suspected underlying
etiology for esophageal obstruction
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Perform radiographs to locate radiopaque FBs.
r Maintain a high suspicion for esophageal
perforation.

2003;3:150–156.

FOREIGN BODY, NASAL
Bradley E. Efune rDavid A. Pearson
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Object impacted in the nasal cavity
r Most common site of foreign body insertion in
children
r Type of foreign body limited only by nostril size
r Population at risk:
– Children between 2–6 yr most common
– Mental retardation
– Psychiatric illness
r Causes of worsening impaction and difficulties with
removal:
– Organic material may expand if moistened
– Mucosal swelling over time
r Complications:
– Sinusitis is the most common complication
– Foreign bodies may migrate into the sinuses
– Septal perforation
– Bronchial aspiration
– High risk of complications with button batteries:
◦Ischemic mucosa
◦Turbinate or septal damage
◦Saddle-nose deformity
ETIOLOGYr Food
r Beans
r Seeds
r Beads
r Rocks
r Paper
r Pieces of toys
r Sponge pieces
r Vegetable matter
r Insects and live worms
r Button batteries:
– High risk of complications compared with other
foreign bodies (tissue necrosis, septal perforation,
saddle nose); require rapid removal
r Magnets:
– Used to mimic nasal piercing
– Often imbedded in nasal tissue, leading to difficult
removal
– May cause intestinal perforation if swallowed,
especially newer high-powered neodymium
magnets
r Glass fragments
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Most nasal foreign bodies are asymptomatic.
r Unilateral nasal obstruction
r Nasal pain
r Difficulties with nasal breathing
r Nasal discharge:
– Acute or chronic
– Unilateral
– Foul smelling
– Halitosis
r Sinus discomfort
r Persistent epistaxis
r Local inflammation
r Septal perforation
r Ingestion or aspiration of foreign body
Historyr Child witnessed putting object into nose
r Foreign body noticed by parent or caretaker
r Many children are reluctant to admit to placing a
foreign body for fear of adult disapproval
r Delayed presentation:
– When placement of the object is unwitnessed, the
child may present weeks after with nasal
discharge and bleeding
– Often misdiagnosed at this stage as sinusitis
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Visualization of the foreign body in the nostril: Always
check both nostrils
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Imagingr Fiberoptic visualization if foreign body cannot be
visualized on rhinoscopy

r Rectal pain
r Perirectal abscess (with imbedded bones/toothpick)

rectal exam.
– Low-lying FBs are usually located in rectal ampulla

– Grade II—Laceration 50% circumference
– Grade III—Laceration >50% circumference
– Grade IV—Full-thickness laceration with
extension into perineum
– Grade V—Devascularized segment

rectal exam

– For bleeding or peritonitis
r Urinalysis:
– For urethral/bladder injuries

(KUB) radiograph prior to rectal exam to rule out
objects harmful to examiner.
– Define and locate FB.
– Assess for complications of retained FB including

– May be used serially to follow descent of FB
r CT scan of abdomen/pelvis:
– To exclude perforation or abscess formation

– Patients insist there is FB when radiograph, rectal
exams, and proctoscopy results are normal.
r Perirectal abscess
r Hemorrhoid

PRE-HOSPITAL

r Patient has usually tried to remove FB and failed.
r Further attempts at extraction will not work and
could cause perforation.

– 0.9% NS IV fluid 500 mL bolus

gram-negative aerobes):

ampicillin–sulbactam, imipenem, meropenem,
ertapenem, or

aminoglycoside/3rd-generation
cephalosporin/fluoroquinolone/aztreonam

of other trauma

FOURNIER GANGRENE
Gary M. Vilke
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Inadequate hygiene leads to scrotal skin maceration
and excoriation:
– Portal of entry for bacteria in tissue
r Once skin barrier is broken, polymicrobial flora
spread along fascial planes of perineum.
r Colles fascia fuses with urogenital diaphragm,
slowing propagation posteriorly and laterally.
r Anteriorly, Buck and Scarpa fascia are continuous,
allowing rapid extension to anterior abdominal wall
and laterally along fascia lata.
r Testes and urethra are usually spared.
r 3 anatomic origins account for most cases:
– Lower urinary tract (40%): Urethral strictures,
indwelling catheters
– Penile or scrotal (30%): Condom catheters,
hydradenitis, balanitis
– Anorectal (30%): Fistulas, perirectal infections,
hemorrhoids
r Rarely, intra-abdominal sources such as perforating
appendicitis, diverticulitis, or pancreatitis have
produced Fournier gangrene by dependent
contiguous spread.
ETIOLOGYr Infection by polymicrobial flora (mixed aerobic and
anaerobic organisms)
r Mixed bacteria exert synergistic tissue-destructive
effect.
r End arterial thrombosis in subcutaneous tissues
produces anaerobic environment.
r Bacterial toxins and tissue necrosis factors may
contribute to clinical presentation.
r Risk factors:
– Trauma
– Diabetes
– Alcoholism
– Other immunocompromised states
– Morbid obesity
– Abdominal surgery
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Rapidly progressive necrotizing infection of
perineum involving subcutaneous and fascial tissues
and often muscle layers:
– Usually seen in diabetics or immunocompromised
patients
r Sources of infection may be flora from genitourinary,
rectal, or penile/scrotal regions.
Pediatric Considerations
r Though unusual in children, >50 cases have been
described.
r Most often are complications of burns, circumcision,
balanitis, severe diaper rashes, or insect bites
r Organisms are more frequently Staphylococcus or
Streptococcus.
r Pediatric patients have more local disease and are
less toxic.
Historyr Duration of symptoms:
– Fevers or chills
– Pain is out of proportion to exam in early phases,
but eventually dead tissue becomes insensate.
– Nausea and vomiting
– Urinary infection symptoms
r Rapidity with which symptoms are progressing
r Identify if diabetic or immunocompromised
r Lethargy and inappropriate indifference to the
illness are common.
Physical Examr Patients are often toxic in appearance with nausea,
vomiting, fever, chills, and pain.
r Careful exam of the genitalia and perirectal region
r Assess for skin findings:
– Bronze or violaceous discoloration of skin
– Thin brown watery discharge
– Ulceration, bullous vesicles
– Crepitance, SC air
– Frank necrosis and eschar formation
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Fournier gangrene is a clinical diagnosis.
r History and physical exam with special attention to
perineum
r Evaluate for signs of sepsis.
r Early surgical consultation for emergent
d´ebridement is essential.
r Other workup directed toward relevant comorbid
factors such as diabetes or immunocompromised
status
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Other than Gram stain of tissue and associated
drainage, there are no specific lab tests that are
diagnostic of Fournier gangrene.
r Urinalysis should be performed.
r Leukocytosis, anemia, electrolyte imbalances,
acidosis, and renal failure are common.
r Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) may
be present; PT, PTT, fibrin-split products, and
fibrinogen levels help identify.
r If patient is suspected of or known to have diabetes,
glucose, electrolytes, and serum ketones to evaluate
for diabetes and diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
r Culture of blood, urine, and tissue (when available)
Imagingr Plain films of the pelvis may reveal subcutaneous
emphysema and ileus.
r CT scanning helps if intra-abdominal or ischiorectal
source is suspected.
r US may be useful in differentiating from other
causes of acute scrotum.
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Retrograde urethrography, anoscopy,
proctosigmoidoscopy, and barium enemas may be
helpful to localize anatomic sources of infection.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Epididymitis/orchitis
r Insect and human bites
r Perirectal infections
r Scrotal abscess/inguinal abscess
r Scrotal cellulitis
r Testicular torsion
r Tinea cruris

FRACTURES, PEDIATRIC
Adam Z. Barkin
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr 20% of pediatric patients with acute traumatic
injuries will have a fracture
r Boys have fractures more commonly than girls
r Anatomy:
– Diaphysis: Physis to physis; bone shaft
– Epiphysis: Cartilaginous center at or near end of
bone that is site of bone growth
– Epiphyseal (growth) plate: Radiolucent line
between epiphysis and metaphysis; cartilaginous
– Metaphysis: Region of rapidly growing trabecular
bone underlying base of cartilaginous growth
plate; between diaphysis and epiphysis
– Most long bones are ossified by the end of puberty
r Bones are highly resilient, elastic, and springy
r Allow for fractures not seen in adults:
– Greenstick fracture:
◦Incomplete fracture through cortex on opposite
side of impact
– Torus (buckle) fracture:
◦Usually at junction of metaphysis and diaphysis
◦Compression of bone of 1 cortex
– Plastic deformity:
◦Bowing without disruption of cortex
– Fractures involving the physis
r Cartilaginous growth plates are potential areas of
injury.
r Ligaments more resistant to injury than growth
plates
r Salter–Harris classification:
– Risk of growth disturbance increases from type I
to type V .
– Type I:
◦Separation of epiphysis from metaphysis without
displacement or injury to the growth plate
◦Tenderness and pain at point of growth plate
◦Radiograph typically normal
◦Growth disturbance is rare.
– Type II:
◦Metaphyseal fracture extending to physis
◦Most common
◦Growth disturbance is rare.
– Type III:
◦Intra-articular fracture extending through the
epiphysis into the physis
◦Most common site is distal tibial epiphysis.
◦Growth disturbance possible
– Type IV:
◦Epiphyseal, physeal, and metaphyseal fracture
◦Lateral condyle of humerus is the most common
site.
◦Growth disturbance highly likely
– Type V:
◦Crush injury to epiphyseal plate, producing
growth arrest
◦Usually occurs in joints that move in only 1
plane such as knee
r Fractures often accompany dislocations.
r Nonaccidental trauma (NAT) if history inconsistent
with findings
ETIOLOGYr Mechanism is useful in defining the potential and
type of injury
r Obesity and rapid growth spurts are risk factors.
r NAT:
– Any fracture in a child younger than 1 yr of age in
whom history is not consistent with injury
– Metaphyseal “corner” fractures are
pathognomonic.
– Posterior rib fractures
– Spiral femur fracture
– Fractures at different stages of healing
– Skull fractures crossing suture lines, especially in
children younger than 1 yr
– Unusual behavior in child or parent
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Decreased limb movement, unwilling to use
r Swelling
r Tenderness
r Deformity
r Ecchymosis
r Crepitus
r Limp
r Abnormal neurovascular status of extremity
r Compartment syndrome:
– Severe pain, especially in forearm, calf, foot
– Pain with passive stretching of fingers or toes
– Sensory deficit in the distal extremity
– Cool extremity
– Pulseless extremity
r Open fracture may be obvious or subtle (collection
of blood with fat globules under skin)
Historyr Mechanism of injury:
– Velocity of car, bike, etc.
– Height of fall
r Neurologic compromise
r Events surrounding injury
r Other injuries
Physical Examr Thorough secondary survey looking for deformities,
bruising, other injuries
r Assess neurovascular status:
– Motor/sensation
– Distal pulses
– Capillary refill
r Range of motion of all joints involved
r Exclude concurrent injuries
r Ensure that history is consistent with injury
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Prompt immobilization
r Imaging as below
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Required only if concomitant injuries, surgery
anticipated, or multiple/major bone involvement
r CBC, ESR if infection suspected
Imagingr Anteroposterior (AP), lateral, and oblique
radiographs as necessary, including the joint above
and below the fracture
r Comparison views may be useful if growth plates
are involved.
r Follow-up radiographs at 7–10 days may be required
to exclude avascular necrosis or Salter I fractures.
r Bone scan/CT/MRI may be useful to exclude
fractures if plain radiographs are unhelpful or to
evaluate for infection.
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Arthrocentesis if infection is suspected
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Sprain or strain
r Contusion
r Infection
r Tumor
r Neurologic deficits
r Subtle dislocations such as radial head subluxation
(nursemaid’s elbow)
r NAT
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Immobilization
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Resuscitation for concurrent injuries
r Immobilization
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Management of life-threatening concurrent injuries
r Pain control
r Dislocations require immediate assessment and
attention to neurovascular compromise:
– Mechanism helps in understanding the direction
of the force required to reduce.
r Alignment is essential, particularly when fracture
involves a joint surface.
r Appropriate reporting of NAT
Salter–Harris Fracturesr Type I and type II fractures require immobilization
and orthopedic follow-up.
r Type II distal femur fractures, type III, and type IV
require urgent orthopedic consultation for anatomic
reduction.
r Type V fractures require immobilization and
consultation.
r Anatomic reduction does not eliminate possibility of
growth disturbance.
Clavicle Fracturer Figure-of-8 splint or sling for comfort
r Distal 3rd clavicle fractures should be referred with
initial sling and swathe or shoulder immobilizer.

FROSTBITE
Joseph M. Weber
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Tissue damage caused by cold temperature exposure
r Mechanism:
– Tissue damage results from:
◦Direct cell damage: Intracellular ice crystal
formation
◦Indirect cell damage: Extracellular ice crystal
formation leads to intracellular dehydration and
enzymatic disruption.
◦Reperfusion injury: Occurs upon rewarming.
Fluid rich in inflammatory mediators
(prostaglandin and thromboxane) extravasates
through damaged endothelium promoting
vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation.
◦Clear blisters form from extracellular exudation
of fluid.
◦Hemorrhagic blisters occur when deeper
subdermal vessels are disrupted, indicating
more severe tissue injury.
◦The end result is arterial thrombosis, ischemia,
and ultimately, necrosis.
– Devitalized tissue demarcates as the injury evolves
over weeks to months, hence the phrase
“frostbite in January, amputate in July.”
ETIOLOGYr Cold exposure: Duration of exposure, wind chill,
humidity, and wet skin and clothing all increase the
likelihood of frostbite.
r Predisposing factors:
– Extremes of age
– Altered mental status (intoxication or psychiatric
illness)
– Poor circulatory status
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Extremities (fingers, toes) and head (ears, nose)
most commonly affected.
r After rewarming frostbite can be classified; however,
initial classification often fails to provide an accurate
prognosis and does not alter initial management.
r Superficial frostbite:
– Only skin structures involved. Usually no tissue
loss.
– 1st degree: Erythema and edema with stinging,
burning, and throbbing. No blisters or necrosis.
– 2nd degree: Significant edema, clear blister
formation. Numbness common.
r Deep frostbite:
– Tissue loss inevitable.
– 3rd degree: Involves subcutaneous tissue.
Hemorrhagic blister formation due to subdermal
venous plexus injury:
◦Initially insensate, injuries develop severe
pain/burning on rewarming.
– 4th degree: Involves muscle, tendon, and bone.
Initially mottled, deep red, or cyanotic.
– Unfavorable prognostic indicators include:
Hemorrhagic blisters, persistent cyanosis, mottling,
anesthesia, and reduced mobility after rewarming.
– Devitalized tissue demarcates as the injury evolves
over weeks to months forming skin necrosis and
dry black eschar.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Diagnosis is based on the clinical presentation.
Wound description should include skin color and
temperature, blister formation and color, and soft
tissue consistency.
r A neurologic and vascular exam should include
pulses (by Doppler if necessary), cap refill, and
2-point discrimination.
r Look for underlying factors contributing to cold
exposure and comorbid conditions requiring
emergency management:
– Hypothermia
– Trauma
– Hypoglycemia
– Cardiac or neurologic problems
– Intoxication/overdose
– Compartment syndrome
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr None indicated in mild cases
r For deep frostbite:
– CBC
– Electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, glucose
– Urinalysis/CK for evidence for myoglobinuria
r Cultures and Gram stains from open areas when
infection suspected
Imaging
Technetium-99 scintigraphy or MRA:
r May be helpful in early identification of salvageable
vs. unsalvageable tissue
r Permits earlier decision about amputation
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Method to create a warm water bath in the ED:
r Whirlpool hydrotherapy ideal, however, most EDs do
not have
r Mix hot and cold tap water from a standard hospital
sink in a large basin
r Use a thermometer to keep temperature between
40◦C and 42◦C.
r The water will cool quickly: Intermittently add warm
water or replace the water to keep the temperature
in the proper range.
r Warmer temperatures can cause thermal injury
while cooler temperatures delay thawing and
decrease tissue survival.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Frostnip:
– Superficial, reversible ice crystal formation without
tissue destruction
– Transient numbness and paresthesia resolve after
dry rewarming.
r Trench (immersion) foot:
– Exposure to wet cold for prolonged periods
– Neurovascular damage without ice crystal
formation
– Pallor, mottling, paresthesias, pulselessness,
paralysis, and numbness
– May be difficult to distinguish from post-thaw
phase of frostbite
– Hyperemia with dry rewarming may last up to 6
wk.
r Chilblains:
– Chronic repeated exposure to dry cold
– Localized erythema, cyanosis, plaques, and
vesicles
– Recurrent episodes common in patients with
underlying vasculitis
– Symptomatic treatment, dry rewarming
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Protect and immobilize frostbitten area during
transport
r Remove restrictive or wet garments
r Avoid dry rewarming of the frostbitten limb if there
is a likelihood of refreezing injury during transport.
r If evacuation will be delayed and suitable facilities
are available, field rewarming in warm (40◦C–42◦C)
water can be attempted.
r Rubbing, manipulating the limb, or applying snow
while it is still frozen is contraindicated.
ALERT
r Hypothermia:
r Common in frostbite victims
r In the severely hypothermic patient, avoid rough
handling to minimize risk of cardiac dysrhythmias.

INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs management
r Identify and correct hypothermia.
r IV fluid volume expansion with 0.9% NS for severe
frostbite
r Protect frostbitten areas from excessive handling
during resuscitation.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr If the injury is <24 hr old and has not yet been
rewarmed:
– Initiate rapid rewarming of the frostbitten
extremity in a 40–42◦C water bath for 15–30 min.
– Stop treatment when the limb is warm, red, and
pliable.
– Monitor water temperature closely to prevent
thermal injury.
r Analgesia: IV morphine
r NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) to combat the effects of
prostaglandins on skin necrosis.
r Aloe vera topical cream:
– Recommended for all intact blisters
– Combats the arachidonic acid cascade
– Avoid preparations containing alcohol, scent,
salicylates, all of which interfere with aloe
effectiveness.
r Blister d ´ ebridement or aspiration:
– Indicated for clear blebs:
◦Removes thromboxane and prostaglandins
– Contraindicated for hemorrhagic blebs:
◦Exposes deeper structures to dehydration and
infection
r Tetanus prophylaxis
r Antibacterial prophylaxis:
– Consider during the hyperemic recovery phase (at
least 2–3 days) in severely frostbitten areas
– Against Streptococci, Staphylococci, and
Pseudomonas species (cephalosporin,
penicillinase-resistant penicillin, quinolone)
– Topical antibacterial agents interfere with the use
of aloe vera cream and should be considered a
2nd-line approach.
r Elevation and splinting of frostbitten area
r Change dressing 2–4 times daily.
r Avoid vasoconstrictive agents (including tobacco).
r Adjunctive treatments include:
– Thrombolytic therapy (<24 hr of cold exposure):
◦Both intra-arterial and systemic tPA may
improve tissue salvage rates.
◦Consult with plastic/burn surgeon before
treatment.
– Vasodilator therapy:
◦Pentoxifylline—limited data
◦Iloprost—limited data and availability

GALLSTONE ILEUS
Joanna W. Davidson
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Mechanical intestinal obstruction secondary to
impaction of a gallstone within bowel lumen
r Stone is usually >2.5 cm
r 1–3% of all intestinal obstructions
r Most cases occur in patients >65
r Female > male (5:1)
r Mortality 15–18%
ETIOLOGYr Chronic gallbladder inflammation causes adhesions
between gallbladder and adjacent bowel wall
r Cholecystocolonic fistula develops, permitting stone
passage into intestine:
– Duodenum is the most common site of fistula
formation, followed by colon
– Gastric fistulas are possible but rare
r Site of impaction
– Terminal ileum most common (54–65%)
◦Narrowest part of small intestine at level of
ileocecal valve
– Jejunum (27%)
– Duodenum (1–3%)
◦Gastric outlet obstruction caused by duodenal
impaction referred to as Bouveret syndrome
– Large bowel obstruction is rare
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr “Tumbling” abdominal discomfort:
– Episodic abdominal pain as stone lodges and
dislodges throughout the intestines.
– Complete impaction leads to severe, often acute
abdominal pain.
r Nausea
r Vomiting:
– Can be bilious or feculent
r Obstipation
r Abdominal distention and tympany
r Abdominal tenderness:
– Peritoneal findings develop late in the course of
disease
r Abnormal bowel sounds
Historyr Only 50–60% of patients have a history of biliary
colic or gallstone disease.
r Gallstone ileus has been associated with
cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and obesity.
Physical Examr Abdominal exam for:
– Abdominal distension/tenderness
r Jaundice may occur
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Evaluate for intestinal obstruction.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, glucose since
decreased oral intake and vomiting leads to
electrolyte abnormality
r Liver function panel and bilirubin may be elevated
r Amylase:
– Elevated in late obstructions
r CBC/hematocrit:
– Hemoconcentration secondary to dehydration
r Elevated WBC nonspecific
Imagingr Flat and upright abdominal radiographs:
– Multiple air–fluid levels and distended bowel
consistent with bowel obstruction
– Rigler triad: 2 of 3 pathognomonic (present in
30–50%):
◦Air in the biliary tree (pneumobilia)
◦Partial or complete bowel obstruction
◦Ectopic stone visualized within the intestinal
tract
r CXR:
– Evaluate for pneumoperitoneum
r Abdominal CT scan:
– Test of choice
– Can directly visualize and localize stone within
intestinal lumen
r Abdominal US:
– Can identify pneumobilia and gallstones, but
lower yield in locating obstructing stone

GANGRENE
Stephen R. Hayden
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Gas gangrene or clostridial myonecrosis
r An acute, rapidly progressive, gas-forming
necrotizing infection of muscle and subcutaneous
tissue
r Can be seen in post-traumatic or postoperative
situations
r Progressive invasion and destruction of healthy
muscle tissue
ETIOLOGYr Clostridial organisms:
– Facultative anaerobic, spore-forming,
gram-positive bacillus
– Produces a number of toxins; the most prevalent
and lethal is α-toxin.
r Clostridium perfringens is the most common
bacterium; found in 80–90% of wounds.
r Other clostridial bacteria include Clostridium novyi,
Clostridium septicum, Clostridium histolyticum,
Clostridium bifermentans, and Clostridium fallax.
r 2 distinct mechanisms for introduction of clostridial
organisms:
– Traumatic and postoperative
– Nontraumatic associated with diabetes mellitus,
peripheral vascular disease, alcoholism, IV drug
abuse, and malignancies
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Sudden severe pain of extremity or involved area
r Low-grade fever
r Tachycardia out of proportion to fever
r Bronzing of the skin over involved area; later can
turn purple or red
r Crepitus
r Formation of blebs and bullae
r Thin, serosanguinous exudate and sweet odor
r Rapid local extension
r Obtunded sensorium
r Systemic toxicity
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr History and physical exam with special attention to
clinical evidence of crepitus in soft tissue
r Soft tissue x-rays of involved area to detect gas
dissecting along fascial planes:
– The absence of gas does not exclude significant
disease.
r Stat Gram stain of wound exudate for gram-positive
bacillus with paucity of leukocytes
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC with differential, electrolytes, BUN, and
creatinine
r Coagulation studies
r Evaluate for hemolysis
r Stat Gram stain of wound exudates
r Anaerobic cultures of wound or tissue biopsy
Imagingr Radiographs may reveal soft tissue gas.
r CT if area involves abdomen or flank.
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
All patients with gas gangrene must undergo surgical
d´ebridement.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Cellulitis
r Necrotizing fasciitis
r Nonclostridial myositis and myonecrosis
r Other causes of gas in tissues, as from dissection
from respiratory or GI tracts

GASTRIC OUTLET OBSTRUCTION
Jenny J. Lu
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Any process impeding the passage of gastric
contents into the duodenum
r Causes not limited to gastric pathology and may be
duodenal or extraluminal in origin
r Benign and malignant causes, including:
– Neoplasms (most common cause in adults),
intrinsic or extrinsic neoplasms (pancreatic, gastric
lymphoma, duodenal, gallbladder). Extrinsic
masses may cause compression at pylorus or
proximal duodenum
– Peptic ulcer disease (PUD), no longer most
common cause in adults, with treatment of
Helicobacter pylori and use of H2 blockers
– Pyloric stenosis (most common pediatric cause):
Incidence 2–5/1,000
– Postoperative complications, especially from
gastric surgeries (e.g., edema, scarring, stricture,
or hyperplasia of pylorus or duodenum)
– Mechanical causes: Gastric volvulus, polyps,
bezoars, duplication cysts
– Edema, scarring, strictures/webs, or hyperplasia of
pylorus or duodenum from various causes (e.g.,
caustic injury, chronic pancreatitis)
ETIOLOGYr Regardless of exact cause, gastric outlet obstruction
characteristically leads to nausea and nonbilious
vomiting
r Persistent vomiting may lead to dehydration,
electrolyte and acid–base derangements
– Chronic symptoms may lead to weight loss,
malnutrition, failure to thrive
– Hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis is
classic finding
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Symptoms may be intermittent until obstruction
becomes complete
r Nausea and vomiting, usually nonbilious
r Abdominal pain, variable in character and often
vague
r Early satiety and epigastric fullness
r Epigastric discomfort relieved with emesis
r Weight loss, failure to thrive
Physical Examr Vital signs:
– May be normal
– Tachycardia, hypotension if volume depletion is
significant
r Abdominal exam:
– Variable amount of epigastric/abdominal
distention
– Tympanitic to auscultation
– Succession splash >4 hr after eating
– Digital rectal exam: Evaluate for occult blood
r Signs of dehydration in eyes, oral pharynx, mucous
membranes, skin turgor
r Signs of malnutrition in chronic or late obstruction
r Weight loss when chronic and with malignancy
Geriatric Considerations
r Abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting: GI symptoms
may be more vague/subtle in elderly patients
r If appropriate, consider other causes of symptoms
(cardiac causes, neurologic causes)
Pediatric Considerations
r Idiopathic hypertrophic pyloric stenosis:
– Most common cause in pediatric population
– “Typical” patient is male (Caucasian and US-born
Asians more common)
– Usually 2–8 wk old but may be diagnosed as early
as 1st wk and up to 3 mo of age
– Initially intermittent, nonprojectile, postprandial
vomiting, which progresses to projectile,
nonbilious vomiting
– A midepigastric peristaltic wave occurring prior to
vomiting may be visible on exam
– Epigastric “olive” mass may be palpable in
80–90% of patients
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Careful history and physical exam
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC:
– Anemia if malignancy or GI blood loss
– High hematocrit indicating hemoconcentration
r Electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, glucose:
– Hypokalemia
– Hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis
– Hypoglycemia
– Prerenal azotemia
r Urinalysis
r Amylase/lipase
r Liver profile, if malignancy suspected
r H. pylori, if PUD suspected
Imagingr Plain abdominal radiographs (obstructive series):
– Often nondiagnostic
– Dilated stomach or absence of air in bowel distally
may be suggestive
r Abdominal US in pediatric patients:
– No ionizing radiation
– Elongated hypertrophic pyloric sphincter
r Abdominal CTs are often very helpful for detecting
neoplastic, intraluminal, and extraluminal causes of
obstruction.
– Likely to be most commonly used modality in
adults
– Radiation load is especially undesirable in
pediatric population; ultrasound and fluoroscopic
UGI series are preferred initial approaches
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Upper GI series:
– To demonstrate site and character of obstruction
– “String sign,” “double track sign,” “beak sign,”
“shoulder sign” are characteristic findings in
pyloric stenosis
r Upper endoscopy:
– To visualize gastric interior, gastric outlet, proximal
duodenum
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Proximal bowel obstruction
r Exacerbation of PUD
r Gastroenteritis
r Cholelithiasis
r Cholecystitis
r Acute pancreatitis
r Diabetic gastroparesis
r Psychogenic vomiting

GASTRITIS
Yanina Purim-Shem-Tov
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Inflammatory response of gastric mucosa to
injury—“gastritis”
r 3 lines of defense of gastric mucosa:
– Mucous layer that forms protective pH gradient
– Surface epithelial cells that can repair small defects
– Postepithelial barrier that neutralizes any acid that
has traversed 1st 2 layers
r No definite link between histologic gastritis and
dyspeptic symptoms
r Epithelial cell damage with no associated
inflammation—“gastropathy”
ETIOLOGYr Common causes of gastritis: Infections,
autoimmune, drugs (i.e., cocaine), hypersensitivity,
stress
r Common causes of gastropathy: Endogenous or
exogenous irritants, such as bile reflux, alcohol, or
aspirin and NSAIDs, ischemia, stress, chronic
congestion
r Acute gastritis:
– Stress (sepsis, burns, trauma):
◦Decrease in splanchnic blood flow leading to
decreased mucus production, bicarbonate
secretion, and prostaglandin synthesis
◦Results in mucosal erosions and hemorrhage
– Alcohol:
◦Induces production of leukotrienes that cause
microvascular stasis, engorgement, and
increased vascular permeability
◦Leads to hemorrhage
– NSAIDs, including aspirin:
◦Interfere with prostaglandin synthesis, leading
to similar cascade as induced by alcohol
◦Results in mucosal erosions
– Steroids
r Chronic gastritis:
– Produced by Helicobacter pylori
– Mechanism of H. pylori unclear:
◦Gram-negative spiral bacteria found in gastric
mucous layer
◦Contains enzyme urease that allows it to change
pH level (alkaline) of its microenvironment
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Dyspepsia
r Bloating
r Nausea/vomiting
r Anorexia
r Epigastric tenderness
r Heartburn
Historyr Dyspepsia
r Epigastric pain or discomfort (episodic and chronic)
r Bloating, indigestion, eructation, flatulence, and
heartburn
r Anorexia, nausea/vomiting
r Hematemesis, melena
Physical Examr Careful physical exam including stool Hemoccult
testing and vital signs with orthostatics
r Dehydration, tachycardia (with vomiting)
r Pallor (hemorrhagic gastritis)
r Abdominal exam
r Nonspecific
r Epigastric tenderness
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr ABCs
r Hematocrit determination
r Evaluation for dehydration/shock
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Normal lab values in uncomplicated gastritis
r CBC:
– Anemia with acute hemorrhagic gastritis
– Leukocytosis: Infection
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose
r Amylase/lipase for pancreatitis in differential
r Urinalysis:
– Assess dehydration/ketosis (starvation)
– Bilirubin present with hepatitis
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr ECG:
– For elderly patients
– Myocardial ischemia in differential
r Endoscopy:
– Outpatient unless significant hemorrhage
– Allows for visualization of bleeding sites,
histologic confirmation of mucosal inflammation,
and detection of H. pylori
r Noninvasive H. pylori testing:
– 13C and 14C urea breath tests
– Stool antigen test
– Serology to detect antibodies to H. pylori
– Serum pepsinogen isoenzymes
◦The ratio of pepsinogen isozymes I and II in
serum correlates with presence of metaplastic
atrophic gastritis (principally autoimmune
metaplastic atrophic gastritis and pernicious
anemia)
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Peptic ulcer disease (PUD)
r Nonulcer dyspepsia (symptoms without ulcer on
endoscopy)
r Gastroesophageal reflux
r Biliary colic
r Cholecystitis
r Pancreatitis
r Hepatitis
r Abdominal aortic aneurysm
r Aortic dissection
r Myocardial infarction
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr ABCs
r IV fluid resuscitation
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs with acute erosive or hemorrhagic gastritis
that presents with hemodynamic instability
r IV fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer solution or
0.9% normal saline (NS) via 2 large-bore catheters
r NGT for gastric decompression and lavage when
history of hematemesis or unstable vital signs
r Foley catheterization to assess volume replacement

GASTROENTERITIS
Isam F. Nasr
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Inflammation of stomach and intestines associated
with diarrhea and vomiting; often the result of
infectious or toxin exposure.
ETIOLOGY
Infectiousr Viruses:
– 50–70% of all cases with Norovirus cases on the
rise in travelers returning from Mexico and India.
r Invasive bacteria:
– Campylobacter: Contaminated food or water,
wilderness water, birds, and animals:
◦Most common cause
◦Gross or occult blood is found in 60–90%.
– Salmonella: Contaminated water, eggs, poultry, or
dairy products:
◦Typhoid fever (Salmonella typhi) characterized
by unremitting fever, abdominal pain, rose
spots, splenomegaly, and bradycardia
◦Immunocompromised susceptible
– Shigella: Fecal–oral route
– Vibrio parahaemolyticus: Raw and undercooked
seafood
– Yersinia: Contaminated food (pork), water, and
milk:
◦May present as mesenteric adenitis or mimic
appendicitis
– Specific food-borne disease (food poisoning):
◦Staphylococcus aureus:
■ Most common toxin-related disease
■ Symptoms within 1–6 hr after ingesting food
◦Bacillus cereus:
■ Classic source is fried rice left on steam tables.
■ Symptoms within 1–36 hr
– Cholera: Profuse watery stools with mucous
(rice-water stools)
– Ciguatera:
◦Fish intoxication
◦Onset 5 min–30 hr (average 6 hr) after ingestion
◦Paresthesias, hypotension, peripheral muscle
weakness
◦Amitriptyline may be therapeutic.
– Scombroid:
◦Caused by blood fish: Tuna, albacore, mackerel,
and mahi-mahi

GASTROESOPHAGEAL REFLUX DISEASE
Yanina Purim-Shem-Tov
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Spectrum of pathology in which gastric reflux causes
symptoms and damage to esophageal mucosa
r Reflux esophagitis vs. nonerosive reflux disease
r 40% of general population experience symptoms
monthly
ETIOLOGYr Incompetent reflux barrier allowing increase in
frequency and duration of gastric contents into
esophagus
r Lower esophageal sphincter (LES):
– Main antireflux barrier
– Crural diaphragm attachment (diaphragmatic
sphincter)
– Contributes to pressure barrier at
gastroesophageal junction
– Esophageal acid clearance via peristalsis and
esophageal mucosal resistance are additional
barriers.
– Most healthy individuals have brief episodes of
reflux without symptoms.
r Transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations
(TLESRs):
– Occur with higher frequency in gastroesophageal
reflux disease (GERD) patients
– Exposed esophageal mucosa becomes acidified
and with time necroses
r Decreased LES tone:
– Smoking
– Foods: Alcohol, chocolate, onion, coffee, tea
– Drugs: Calcium channel blockers, morphine,
meperidine, barbiturates, theophylline, nitrates
r Delayed gastric emptying, increased body mass, and
gastric distention contribute to reflux
r Hiatal hernias associated with GERD:
– Significance varies in any given individual
– Most persons with hiatal hernias do not have
clinically evident reflux disease
r Acid secretion is same in those with or without
GERD
r Associated medical conditions: Pregnancy, chronic
hiccups, cerebral palsy, Down syndrome,
autoimmune diseases, diabetes mellitus (DM),
hypothyroidism
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Esophageal manifestations
– Heartburn (or pyrosis)
– Regurgitation
– Dysphagia
r Extraesophageal manifestations
– Bronchospasm
– Laryngitis
– Chronic cough
Historyr Typical signs and symptoms:
– Heartburn (pyrosis):
◦Retrosternal burning pain
◦Radiates from epigastrium through chest to
neck and throat
– Dysphagia:
◦Dysphagia suggests esophageal spasm or
stricture.
– Odynophagia:
◦Odynophagia suggests ulcerative esophagitis.
– Regurgitation
– Water brash
– Belching
– Esophageal strictures, bleeding
– Barrett esophagus (esophageal carcinoma)
– Early satiety, nausea, anorexia, weight loss
– Symptoms worse with recumbence or bending
over
– Symptoms usually relieved with antacids, although
temporarily
r Atypical signs and symptoms:
– Noncardiac chest pain
– Asthma
– Persistent cough, hiccups
– Hoarseness
– Pharyngeal/laryngeal ulcers and carcinoma
– Frequent throat clearing
– Recurrent pneumonitis
– Nocturnal choking
– Upper GI tract bleeding
Physical Examr Nonspecific, may have some epigastric tenderness.
r Symptoms worsen with placing patient flat on the
bed or Trendelenburg position
Pediatric Considerations
r Regurgitation is common in infants:
– Incidence decreases from twice daily in 50% of
those age 2 mo to 1% of 1-yr-olds.
r Signs:
– Frequent vomiting, irritability, cough, crying, and
malaise
– Arching the body (hyperextension) at feeding and
refusals of feedings
r Failure to thrive
r Formula intolerance
r Sepsis
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Differentiate GERD from more emergent conditions
such as ischemic heart pain, esophageal perforation,
or aortic pathology.
r Obtain typical history
r Perform thorough physical exam: Vital signs, head,
ears, eyes, nose, throat (HEENT), chest and
abdominal exams
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
No gold standard
Labr CBC:
– Chronic anemia from esophagitis
r Stool testing for occult bleeding
Imagingr No routine Imaging
r Chest radiograph:
– Evidence of esophageal perforation, hiatal hernia,
aortic disease
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Diagnostic trial of antacid:
– Those with persistent symptoms should be
referred for endoscopy
– 90% of GERD patients respond to proton pump
inhibitor (PPI) therapy
r Barium esophagram for prominent dysphagia
r Esophageal pH monitoring:
– Correlate symptoms to acid reflux
r Esophageal manometry (poor sensitivity):
– Evaluate LES resting pressure and esophageal
peristaltic contractions
r Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD)—detects
reflux esophagitis and complications (Barrett
esophagus, hiatal hernia, stricture, ulcers,
malignancy)
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Ischemic heart disease
r Asthma
r Peptic ulcer disease
r Gastritis
r Hepatitis/pancreatitis
r Esophageal perforation
r Esophageal foreign body
r Esophageal infection
r Cholecystitis/cholelithiasis
r Mesenteric ischemia

– Increases LES pressure

– ADX10059

injection

ulceration, severe bleeding

therapy in selected cases
– Currently newer incisionless procedure called
transoral incisionless fundoplication available

GASTROINTESTINAL BLEEDING
Czarina E. S ´anchez rLeon D. S´anchez
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Bleeding from GI tract:
– Upper GI tract: Proximal to ligament of Treitz
– Lower GI tract: Distal to ligament of Treitz to anus
r Mortality rate:
– 10% overall; from <5% in children up to 25% for
adults of age >70
– Upper GI bleed (UGIB) 6–8%; variceal 30–50%
– Lower GI bleed (LGIB) 2–4%
ETIOLOGY
Upper GI Bleed (UGIB):r Ulcerative disease of upper GI tract:
– Peptic ulcer disease (40%):
◦Helicobacter pylori infection
◦Drug-induced (NSAIDs, aspirin, glucocorticoids,
K+ supplements, Fe supplements)
– Gastric or esophageal erosions (25%):
◦Reflux esophagitis
◦Infectious esophagitis (Candida, HSV , CMV)
◦Pill-induced esophagitis
◦Esophageal foreign body
– Gastritis and stress ulcerations:
◦Toxic agents (NSAIDs, alcohol, bile)
◦Mucosal hypoxia (trauma, burns, sepsis)
◦Cushing ulcers from severe CNS damage
◦Chemotherapy
r Portal HTN:
– Esophageal or gastric varices (10%)
– Portal hypertensive gastropathy
r Arteriovenous malformations:
– Aortoenteric fistula (s/p aortoiliac surgery)
– Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
(Osler—Weber–Rendu syndrome)
– Dieulafoy vascular malformations
– Gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE or
watermelon stomach)
– Idiopathic angiomas
r Mallory–Weiss tear (5%)
r Gastric and esophageal tumors
r Pancreatic hemorrhage
r Hemobilia
r Strongyloides stercoralis infection
Lower GI Bleed (LGIB):r Diverticulosis (33%)
r Cancer or polyps (19%)
r Colitis (18%):
– Ischemic, inflammatory, infectious, or radiation
r Vascular:
– Angiodysplasia (8%)
– Radiation telangiectasia
– Aortocolonic fistula
r Inflammatory bowel disease:
– Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis
r Postpolypectomy
r Anorectal (4%):
– Hemorrhoids (internal and external)
– Anal fissures
– Anorectal varices
– Rectal ulcer
– Foreign body
Pediatric Considerations
Meckel diverticulum and intussusception are the most
common causes of LGIB in children.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Both UGIB and LGIB may present with
signs/symptoms of hypovolemia
r UGIB classic presentation:
– Hematemesis or coffee ground emesis
– Melena: Black tarry stool
r LGIB classic presentation:
– Hematochezia: Bright red or maroon stool
ALERT
Hematochezia classically signals an LGIB, but can
also be seen with brisk UGIB.
Historyr Hematemesis and melena most common
r Coffee ground emesis
r Black stools
r Bright red blood per rectum
r Abdominal pain
r Weakness or lightheadedness
r Dyspnea
r Confusion or agitation
Physical Examr Tachycardia
r Hypotension
r Pale conjunctiva
r Dry mucous membranes
r Bloody, melanotic, or heme-positive stools
r Shock
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr CBC, coagulation studies, electrolytes
r Perform ENT exam. Distinguish between hemoptysis
and hematemesis:
– Pulmonary source:
◦Bright red and frothy in appearance
◦Sputum mixed with blood is likely pulmonary
◦pH >7
– GI source:
◦Dark red/brown blood, ± gastric contents
◦Associated with nausea/vomiting
◦pH <7
r Consider nasogastric lavage:
– Might help determine if bleeding is ongoing and
facilitate endoscopy
– Controversialstudies have failed to demonstrate
outcome benefit. False-negatives, if bleeding
beyond pylorus.
r Rectal exam:
– Inspect for hemorrhoids and anal fissures
– Examine stool color
– False-positive Hemoccult result:
◦Raw red meat
◦Iron supplements
◦Fruits: Cantaloupe, grapefruit, figs
◦Vegetables: Raw broccoli, cauliflower, radish
◦Methylene blue, chlorophyll
◦Iodide, bromide
– False-negative Hemoccult result:
◦Bile
◦Mg-containing antacids
◦Ascorbic acid
– Agents causing black stools, but negative
Hemoccult:
◦Iron
◦Charcoal
◦Bismuth (i.e., Pepto-Bismol)
◦Food dyes
◦Beets

Bloody stool in newborns may be caused by the infant
swallowing maternal blood.

Labr CBC:
– Anemia (low mean corpuscular volume seen with
chronic blood loss)
– Thrombocytopenia
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose
r Coagulation profile
r Lactate
r LFTs, if upper GI bleeding suspected
r Type and screen/cross for active bleeding or
unstable vital signs
r BUN/Cr ratio >36 has a high sensitivity but low
specificity for UGIB

Hematocrit can remain normal for a period after
acute blood loss; a drop may not be immediately
seen.

r Angiography/arterial embolization:
– Effective for identifying large, active bleeding
r Radionucleotide (tagged red blood cell) scan:
– Effective for identifying slow, active bleeding
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Anoscopy:
– For suspected internal hemorrhoids or fissures
r Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD):
– Diagnostic and possibly therapeutic
r Colonoscopy:
– Diagnostic only
– Best after adequate bowel prep
r Bowel resection:
– Reserved for refractory bleeding

r Oropharyngeal bleeding
r Hemoptysis
r Hematuria
r Vaginal bleeding
r Visceral trauma

PRE-HOSPITALr Stabilize airway
– Intubate for massive UGIB, if patient unable to
protect airway

crystalloid to keep SBP >90 mm Hg

bleeding, or unable to protect airway

repeat once, if necessary
– Transfuse RBCs if significant anemia or unstable
after crystalloid boluses
◦Cross-matched or type-specific blood, if
available
◦Otherwise, O negative for premenopausal
women, O positive for others
◦Provide fresh frozen plasma (FFP) along with
RBC transfusion in ratio of 1:2–4. For patients
requiring massive transfusion, consider adding
FFP and platelets in 1:1:1 ratio with RBCs

INR >1.5) and platelets (if platelets <50,000/uL)

◦Hemoglobin <10 g/dL when at increased risk of
ischemia (e.g., CAD and CVA)
◦Evidence of end-organ ischemia
◦Ongoing chest pain/ischemic EKG changes

precipitate further bleeding

counterbalanced by increased mortality due
to ischemia
◦Administer with IV nitroglycerin to reduce
tissue ischemia
– High risk for active bleeding with 2 out of 3 risk
factors:
◦Bright blood from NGT
◦Hemoglobin <8 g/dL
◦WBC >12,000/uL
– Emergent endoscopy
– Therapeutic options:
◦Cauterization of bleeding ulcers/vessels
◦Endoscopic sclerotherapy
– Balloon tamponade with Blakemore tube is a
last resort for varices
– In cirrhotics with UGIB prophylactic antibiotic
use reduce bacterial infections and all cause
mortality
r LGIB treatment
– Consider angiography for massive, active
bleeding with directed vasopressin infusion
– Consider bowel resection for massive bleeding
refractory to medical management
MEDICATIONr Pantoprazole: 80 mg (peds: Dosing not approved) IV
bolus followed by an infusion of 8 mg/h for 72 hr
r Octreotide: 50 μg (peds: 1–2 μg/kg) bolus, then
50 μg/h (peds: 1–2 μg/kg/h) IV
r Somatostatin: 250 μg (peds: Not established) IV
bolus and 250–500 μg/h for 2–5 days (not
available in US)
r Vasopressin: 0.4–1 IU/min (peds: 0.002–0.005 IU/
kg/min) IV
r Nitroglycerin: 10–50 μg/min (peds: Not
established) IV
r Vitamin K: 10 mg (peds: 1–5 mg) PO/SC/IV q24h
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Active bleeding
r Age >65 or comorbid conditions
r Coagulopathy
r Decreased hematocrit
r Unstable vital signs at any time
Discharge Criteriar Resolution of UGIB with negative nasogastric lavage
and EGD
r Minor or resolved LGIB
r Stable hematocrit >30 or hemoglobin >10 g/dL
r Otherwise healthy patient
Issues for Referral
Consider referral to gastroenterologist for outpatient
colonoscopy and/or EGD
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Patients discharged from the ED should have close
follow-up within 24–36 hr
r Give strict discharge instructions to return if further
bleeding or other concerning symptoms
(lightheadedness, dyspnea, chest pain, etc.) occur
r Patients with UGIB should be discharged on a PPI,
and advised to avoid caffeine, alcohol, tobacco,
NSAIDs, and aspirin
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r 10–15% of UGIB present with hematochezia
r Consider GIB in patients presenting with signs of
hypovolemia or hypovolemic shock
r Common pitfall: Failure to adequately resuscitate
with crystalloid and blood products
Geriatric Considerations
PUD is the predominant cause of GIB in elderly and
has a higher associated mortality.

gastrointestinal hemorrhage: A prospective cohort
