GERIATRIC TRAUMA
Charles W. O’Connell rPeter Witucki
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Geriatric specific considerations and approach to the
elderly trauma patient
r Should be used in conjunction with the accepted
standard treatment of traumatic injuries (see
trauma, multiple)
r Advanced age is a known risk factor for adverse
outcomes following trauma
r Generally age >65, age not well defined, difficult to
target due to discrepancies between physiologic and
chronologic age in individuals
EPIDEMIOLOGY
Incidence and Prevalence Estimates
ETIOLOGY
Most common mechanisms:
r Falls—most common cause of injury in patients of
age >65, often occurs on an even, flat surface
r Motor vehicle crashes—2nd leading cause, most
common fatal etiology
r Pedestrian—motor vehicle collisions, diminished
cognitive skills, poor vision/hearing, impaired gait
contribute to increased incidence
r Burns—higher fatality rate than young adults with
same extent of burn
r Violence—less common mechanism than in younger
ages, have heightened suspicion for elderly abuse,
an under recognized issue
r Elderly more susceptible to serious injury from
low-energy mechanisms
DIAGNOSIS
r Triage to major trauma center is determined by local
protocols
r Injured patients with potential need for surgical,
neurosurgical, or orthopedic intervention should be
transferred to major trauma center
r Threshold for scene triage or transfer to trauma
center should be lower for elderly
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr The same pattern of assessment using primary
survey (ABCDE) and secondary survey should be
used with geriatric patients as with younger patients
(see trauma, multiple)
r Normal vital signs can lead to false sense of security
– Hypoperfusion often masked by inadequate
physiologic response, underlying medical
pathology, and medication effects
Primary survey (ABCDE)
r Airway, cervical spine—establish and maintain a
patent airway with C-spine immobilization
– Anatomic variation in elderly can lead to more
difficult airways (dentures, cervical arthritis, TMJ
arthritis)
– Failure to recognize indications for early
intubation is a common mistake
r Breathing—maintain adequate and effective
breathing and ventilation
– Weakened respiratory muscles and degenerative
changes in chest wall result in diminished effective
ventilation
– Blunted response to hypoxia, hypercarbia, and
acidosis delays onset of clinical distress
– Lower threshold to intubate elderly patients
r Circulation—ensure adequate perfusion
– Vigilant hemodynamic monitoring, heart rate, and
BP do not always correlate well with cardiac
output
– Geriatric patients often have impaired
chronotropic response to hypovolemia
– Cardiovascular response may be blunted by rate
controlling meds (β-blockers, Calcium channel
blockers)
– Baseline hypertension, common in elderly, may
obscure relative hypotension
– Bleeding made worse by antiplatelet and
anticoagulation medicines
r Disability—rapid neurologic evaluation to assess for
intracranial and spinal cord injury
– Brain atrophy may delay onset of clinical
symptoms from compressive effects
– Grave error to assume alterations in mental status
due solely to underlying dementia or senility
r Exposure—patient should be undressed completely
r Secondary survey
– After the primary survey has been completed
– Stabilization at each level
– Complete physical exam from head to toe
Historyr The geriatric trauma patient should be viewed as
both a trauma and a medical patient
r Elderly patients can have significant comorbidities,
past medical history, medications, and allergies are
essential
r Comorbid medical conditions may have precipitated
the traumatic event
r Consider hypoglycemia, syncope, cardiac
dysrhythmia, CVA, UTI, etc.
r Details of the mechanism, initial presentation, and
treatment rendered should be elicited from EMS
personnel
r Concurrent medical conditions impede
compensation, confound interpretation of severity
and response, and complicate resuscitation.
Physical Exam
Should follow primary and secondary surveys
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATIONr Primary and secondary survey
r Cervical spine and chest imaging are mandatory for
victims of major traumas
r Pelvic radiographs should be performed with clinical
suspicion of pelvic trauma or with hemodynamic
instability
r CBC, ABG, blood type
r Electrolytes, renal function, serum glucose
r Urine dip for blood, UA if dip shows positive result
r Coagulation profile
r Base deficit, lactate
r Ethanol screen
Imagingr Liberal use of head CT is recommended for elderly
with closed head trauma
r Nexus criteria has been validated in ages >65;
however, cervical spine imaging needed in majority
of geriatric traumas. CT scan emerging as study of
choice for high suspicion, high-risk mechanism or
age related changes likely to limit plain films
r Significant blunt and penetrating chest trauma
requires objective evaluations of the heart and great
vessels with echocardiography, CT scan,
angiography, or direct visualization.
r Blunt abdominal trauma requires objective
evaluation, modality depends on patient’s condition
r Hemodynamically stable patients should have an
abdominal CT with IV contrast
r Ensure adequate hydration and assess baseline
renal function prior to contrast load when clinical
status permits.
r Unstable patients should have FAST exam or
diagnostic peritoneal lavage
r CT with contrast is a valuable diagnostic tool for
abdominal trauma, but predispose to risk of contrast
related renal impairment
r Extremity injury:
– Radiographs
– Suspected vascular damage requires angiography
or duplex ultrasound
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Emphasis should be placed on airway maintenance,
control of external bleeding and shock,
immobilization, and immediate transfer to
appropriate facility
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Airway—take into account anatomical variations
when establishing an airway
r Breathing
– Continuous pulse oximetry and capnometry
helpful
– Administer supplemental oxygen to maintain
oxygen saturation >95%
– Serial ABGs may provide early insight to
respiratory function and reserve
– Timely intubation in patients with ventilatory
compromise and more severe injuries
– Intubation indications: Respiratory rate >40
breaths/min, PaO2 is <60 mm Hg or PaCO2
>50 mm Hg
– Adequate analgesia of chest wall pain is essential
for optimizing ventilation

GERIATRIC TRAUMA
G
r Circulation—severity of hemodynamic instability
often underappreciated by clinicians
– Serial crystalloid fluid boluses of 250–500 mL
– Early invasive monitoring has been advocated,
better assess need for volume loading and
inotropic support
– Geriatric patients can decompensate from overly
aggressive volume replacement
– Strong consideration for early and liberal use of
red blood cell transfusion
– Target hemoglobin level is controversial, but many
authors recommend 10 g/dL
– Recognize the harmful effects and complications
of red blood cell transfusions
– Blood viscosity, infection, and impairment of
immune response
– Serial base deficit and lactate levels provide good
initial measures of shock and can guide
resuscitation decisions
– Creatinine clearance reduced in elderly
– Kidneys more susceptible to injury from
hypovolemia, medications, and nephrotoxins
r Disability:
– Head Injury: Age is an independent risk factor for
morbidity and mortality
– Age-related atrophy and mental decline may
confound the evaluation of mental status
– Anticoagulated patients with blunt head injury at
increased risk for intracranial bleeds and delayed
bleeding.
– Strongly consider repeat imaging to detect
delayed bleeds in anticoagulated patients
– When indicated, initiate treatment for intracranial
hypertension, maintain spinal immobilization, and
obtain definitive airway
r Exposure: Completely undress patient, but prevent
hypothermia
– Age-related changes and medications make
elderly more susceptible to hypothermia
– Hypothermia not attributable to shock or exposure
should raise concern for sepsis, endocrinopathy, or
drug ingestion
r Common injury patterns:
r Head injury
– Less prone to epidural hematomas
– Higher incidence of subdural hematomas
r Cervical spine injuries
– Propensity to sustain cervical spine injuries from
seemingly minor trauma (fall from standing or
seated height)
– C1–C2 and odontoid fractures are particularly
more common among elderly
– Underlying cervical spine pathology, such as
arthritis may predispose to spinal cord injuries
– With hyperextension injuries, increased risk of
developing a central cord syndrome
r Vertebral injuries
– More susceptible to fractures, especially anterior
wedge compression fractures
r Chest trauma
– Rib fracture is most common; in geriatric patients
these is an increased risk of pneumonia and
mortality with each additional rib fracture
– Hemopneumothrorax, pulmonary contusion, flail
chest, and cardiac contusion can quickly lead to
decompensation
r Abdominal trauma
– Similar pattern of injury as younger adults
– Paramount to recognize signs of hemodynamic
stability early
– Nonoperative treatment of hemodynamically
stable blunt hepatic and splenic injuries has
emerged as the trend
– Should have high index of suspicion for internal
injuries with associated pelvic and lower rib cage
injuries
r Orthopedic injuries—more predisposed due to
osteopenia and osteoporotic changes
– Uniquely susceptible to pelvic and hip fractures
– Goal of orthopedic injuries is to undertake the
least invasive, most definitive procedure that will
permit early return to function
r Anticoagulation—consider fresh frozen plasma,
cryoprecipitate, and concentrated factor for
significant bleeds depending on indications
– Beware of fluid overload and thrombotic
complications
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Early monitoring of pulmonary and cardiovascular
systems must be instituted
r Prompt stabilization, early recognition of the need
for operative intervention, and appropriate and
expedient surgical consultation are paramount
r Definitive treatment is often surgical
r Elderly patients benefit from preferential transfer to
trauma centers and aggressive, yet thoughtful care
r No reliable age-based criteria upon which to base
decisions to triage away from care
r Good outcomes can be achieved with appropriately
aggressive trauma care
r Equally important to limit intensive treatment to
injuries which are survivable and allow potentially
acceptable quality of life
r Seek existence of advance directives, living will, or
similar legal document
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Most major trauma patients should be admitted for
observation, monitoring, and further evaluation
r Lower threshold for admitting geriatric patients to
ward, monitored settings, or ICU
r Elderly patients with polytrauma, significant chest
wall injuries, abnormal vital signs, evidence of
hypoperfusion should be admitted to the ICU
Discharge Criteria
Patients with minor trauma and negative
workup/imaging may be observed in the ED for several
hours and then discharged
Issues for Referral
Follow-up should be determined by the types of
injuries sustained and specialty care required.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Follow-up and referral should be determined by the
types of injuries sustained and specialty care required
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Minor mechanisms of injury can produce serious
injury and complication because of the effect of
limited physiologic reserve, medication effects, and
unrecognized hypoperfusion
r Frequent use of medications, especiallyβ-blockers
and anticoagulants complicate assessment and
management
r Mistaken impression that “normal” BP and heart
rate imply normovolemia.
r Geriatric trauma patients must be treated as both
trauma and medical patients.
ADDITIONAL READING

Comprehensive Emergency Medicine Approach.
Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press; 2011.

Normal presenting vital signs are unreliable in
geriatric blunt trauma victims. J Trauma. 2010;69:
813–820.

outcomes are improved by a geriatric trauma
consultation service. J Trauma. 2006;61(5):
1040–1046.

Trauma. Advanced Trauma Life Support for Doctors.
8th ed. Chicago, IL: American College of Surgeons;
2008.

GHB POISONING
Amy V. Kontrick rMark B. Mycyk
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Naturally occurring analog of γ-aminobutyric acid
(GABA)
r Used medically for narcolepsy
r Nonmedical uses:
– Bodybuilding agent
– Euphoric agent
– Date-rape/predatory agent
r γ-Hydroxybutyrate (GHB) precursors
(γ-butyrolactone [GBL], 1,4 butanediol [1,4-BD],
GHV [γ-hydroxyvalerate], and GVL) have same
effects as GHB.
r Onset of activity: 15–30 min after ingestion
r Duration of effect: 2–6 hr
ETIOLOGY
Deliberate or accidental ingestion of GHB
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr CNS:
– CNS depression
– Ataxia/dizziness
– Impaired judgment
– Aggressive behavior
– Clonic movements of the extremities
– Coma
– Seizures
r Pulmonary:
– Respiratory depression
– Apnea
– Laryngospasm (rare)
r GI:
– Nausea
– Vomiting
r Cardiovascular:
– Bradycardia
– Atrioventricular block
– Hypotension
r Other:
– Nystagmus
– Hypothermia
r Withdrawal symptoms:
– HTN
– Tachycardia
– Hyperthermia
– Agitation
– Diaphoresis
– Tremors
– Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramping
– Hallucinations, delusions, and psychosis
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Diagnosis based on clinical presentation and an
accurate history
r Exclude coingestants if signs and symptoms
inconsistent with GHB intoxication
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Confirmatory GHB screen is typically a send-out lab
and does not change ED management.
r Urine toxicology screen to exclude coingestants
r Serum alcohol level
r Urinalysis and creatine kinase (CK) if suspected
rhabdomyolysis from prolonged immobilization or
agitation
Imagingr ECG:
– Sinus bradycardia
– Atrioventricular block
r CXR:
– Aspiration pneumonia
r Head CT if suspected occult head trauma
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Alcohol intoxication
r Barbiturate overdose
r Benzodiazepine overdose
r Neuroleptic overdose
r Opiate overdose
r Withdrawal:
– Alcohol withdrawal
– Sedative–hypnotic withdrawal
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Transport all pills/bottles and drug paraphernalia
involved in overdose for identification in ED.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs:
– Airway control essential
– Administer supplemental oxygen
– Intubate if indicated
r Administer thiamine, dextrose (or Accu-Chek), and
naloxone for depressed mental status.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Supportive care
r Bradycardia:
– Atropine
– Temporary pacing
r Hypotension:
– 0.9% NS IV fluid bolus
– Trendelenburg
– Dopamine titrated to pressure
r Seizures:
– Treat initially with benzodiazepine.
– Treat refractory seizures with phenobarbital.
r Withdrawal:
– Treat aggressively with benzodiazepine.
– Treat with phenobarbital or propofol if large doses
of benzodiazepines unsuccessful.
MEDICATIONr Dextrose: 50–100 mL D50 (peds: 2 mL/kg of D25
over 1 min) IV; repeat if necessary
r Diazepam: 5–10 mg (peds: 0.2–0.5 mg/kg) IV
q10–15min
r Dopamine: 2–20 μg/kg/min with titration to effect
r Lorazepam: 2–4 mg (peds: 0.03–0.05 mg/kg) IV
q10–15min
r Naloxone: 0.4–2 mg (peds: 0.1 mg/kg; neonatal:
10–30 μg/kg) IV or IM
r Phenobarbital: 10–20 mg/kg IV (loading dose)
monitor for respiratory depression with IV
administration
r Propofol: 0.5–1 mg/kg IV (loading dose), then
5–50 μg/kg/min (maintenance dose)
r Thiamine (vitamin B1): 100 mg (peds: 50 mg) IV or
IM

GIANT CELL ARTERITIS (GCA) (TEMPORAL ARTERITIS)
Donald J. Lefkowits
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Chronic vasculitis of large- and medium-sized vessels
that occurs among individuals over 50 yr of age
r Often referred to as temporal arteritis (TA)
r Median age of onset is 72
r Most commonly causes inflammation of arteries
originating from the arch of the aorta
r Although usually clinically silent, involvement of the
thoracic aorta occurs in a significant minority of
patients, and aortic aneurysm or dissection may
result
r Thoracic aortic aneurysm is a late manifestation with
an incidence 17 times those without TA
r Abdominal aortic aneurysm is about twice as
common in those with giant cell arteritis (GCA)
r Pathologic specimens feature patchy mononuclear
granulomatous inflammation resulting in a markedly
thickened intima and occlusion of the vessel lumen
r Occlusive arteritis may involve thrombosis of the
ophthalmic artery resulting in anterior ischemic optic
neuropathy (AION) and acute visual loss:
– Visual symptoms are an ophthalmic emergency
r Inflammation of arteries supplying the muscles of
mastication results in jaw claudication and tongue
discomfort
r Age is the greatest risk factor:
– Rare in patients <50 yr old
– >90% are >60 yr old
– Prevalence in individuals >50 yr is estimated at
1:500
r Increased prevalence in Northern latitude
r 2 to 4 times more common in women
r Rare in African American patients, common in
Whites
r There is a strong association with polymyalgia
rheumatica (PMR) ∼50%
Genetics
Genetic predisposition is linked to HLA-DR4—60%
prevalence
ETIOLOGYr Unknown
r Genetic, enviromental and autoimmune factors have
been identified
DIAGNOSIS
r Presence of any 3 or more of the following in
patients with vasculitis:
– ESR >50
– Age greater than 50 yr
– New onset of localized headache
– Tenderness or decreased pulsation of temporal
artery
– New visual symptoms
– Biopsy revealing necrotizing arteritis
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr May present with acute, subacute, or chronic
symptoms:
– Headache is the single most frequent symptom
(70%)
– Often localized, boring, or lancinating in quality
– Often described as unilateral over a temple
r Tongue or jaw claudication upon mastication is the
common symptom (50%)
r Constitutional symptoms:
– Fatigue
– Malaise
– Anorexia
– Weight loss
– Weakness
– Arthralgias
– Low-grade fever
r Visual findings:
– Findings are usually in 1 eye
– May develop weeks to months after the onset of
other symptoms
– May fluctuate, but visual impairment does not
usually improve over time, even with treatment
– Amaurosis Fugax
– Blindness
– Diplopia
– Ptosis
– Extraocular muscle weakness
– Scotomata
– Blurred vision
r Scalp tenderness, especially over the temporal artery
r Pulsations over temporal artery:
– Increased pulsations early in disease
– Decreased pulsations late in the disease
r Erythema, warmth, swelling, or nodules over scalp
arteries
r Bruits or decreased pulses over large arteries
r Sore throat, cough, dysphagia
r Rare findings:
– Respiratory symptoms
– Ischemic chest pain
– Congestive heart failure
r Neurologic problems:
– Occur in up to one-third of patients:
◦Neuropathies
◦Transient ischemic attacks
◦Cerebral vascular accidents
r Occult manifestations include:
– Glossitis
– Lingual infarction
– Tongue infarction
– Raynaud phenomenon
r Up to 30% may not present with the classic features
of headache, scalp tenderness, visual changes, or
jaw claudication
r Frequently associated with PMR (up to 50%):
– Stiffness
– Aching pain in the proximal muscles
– Worse in the morning and decreasing with
exercise
r Often associated with synovitis, especially in the
knees
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Focused physical exam with emphasis on:
– Temporal artery and scalp abnormalities
– Complete neurologic exam
– Ophthalmic exam including visual acuity and
visual field testing
r Fundoscopy:
– Often normal initially
– Iritis and fine vitreous opacities may be early
findings
– Optic nerve edema
– Swollen, pale disc with blurred margins
– Pallor
– Hemorrhage
– Scattered cotton-wool spots
– Vessel engorgement and exudates are seen later
r Any pulse differences in the extremities or bruits
over large arteries should be noted
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Elevated ESR, often >100 mm/hr
– ESR <40 is rare
r C-reactive protein above 2.45 mg/dL
r Complete blood count (CBC):
– A mild normochromic anemia is typical
– Thrombocytosis (often mild)
– White cell count can be normal or slightly elevated
and differential is usually normal
r Liver function tests and prothrombin time may be
elevated; creatine phosphokinase, tests of renal
function, and urinalysis are generally normal
r Elevation in interleukin-6 (IL-6) is seen during flares
Imagingr Doppler ultrasound:
– Decreased blood flow in temporal, facial, and
ophthalmic arteries
– Presence of a halo is highly suggestive of active
TA.
r MRI:
– Indicated for exam of large arteries
r Angiogram:
– Smooth, tapered occlusions or stenosis
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Temporal artery biopsy:
– Multiple sections should be done in as soon as
feasible after initiation of steroid therapy
– Gold standard for diagnosis
– Contralateral biopsy is recommended if 1st is
negative and index of suspicion high
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Vasculitides:
– Polyarteritis nodosa
– Hypersensitivity vasculitis
– Systemic lupus erythematosus
– Takayasu arteritis
– Wegener granulomatosis
r Thrombosis of retinal, ophthalmic, or temporal
arteries
r Lyme disease
r Nonarteritic anterior ischemia optic neuropathy
(NAAION)

GIANT CELL ARTERITIS (GCA) (TEMPORAL ARTERITIS)
G
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Acute symptoms may be confused with stroke
r Initiate appropriate monitoring and oxygen
r Patients may be hypotensive from 1 of the rare
sequelae (aortic dissection, abdominal aortic
aneurysm, or myocardial infarction)
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Although rare, patients may present with vascular
catastrophe such as aortic dissection or myocardial
infarction and need appropriate aggressive early
management
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Steroids:
– Strong clinical indications should be present if
started before temporal artery biopsy
– Scheduling of TA biopsy should not delay steroid
therapy when clinical suspicion is high as
pathologic vessel changes resolve slowly and will
remain for weeks
– Early, aggressive treatment can significantly
reduce the incidence of blindness
– Steroids effectively control systemic and local
symptoms within days to weeks
– Treatment with prednisone may continue for
years—usual disease length is 3–4 yr
r Symptomatic pain management with NSAIDs,
salicylates, and/or narcotics as indicated
MEDICATIONr Prednisone: 60–100 mg PO per day for at least 2 wk
before considering tapering
r For acute onset visual symptoms, consider 1,000 mg
methylprednisolone IV pulse therapy for the 1st
1–3 days
r Low-dose aspirin therapy to reduce thrombotic risks
r Pain management with NSAIDs or narcotics
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Patients with impending vascular complications or
acute focal neurologic findings
r Patients with associated acute visual loss
Discharge Criteriar Less symptomatic patients without evidence of
end-organ involvement
r Follow-up arranged within 1–2 days
Issues for Referralr Rheumatology
r Ophthalmology if associated with visual symptoms
r Neurology with acute focal neurologic findings
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Rheumatology for steroid management and search
for associated connective tissue disorders
r Ophthalmology and neurology for visual disturbance
and/or focal neurologic findings.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Permanent visual loss is the most feared
complication of GCA
r Do not delay initiation of steroid therapy to await
biopsy if strong clinical suspicion for GCA exists or if
visual changes are reported
r Jaw claudication and amaurosis fugax, while often
dramatic, are symptoms patients often neglect to
report. Query directly and specifically about them if
TA/GCA is being considered
r 25–50% of patients who present with acute loss of
vision in 1 eye who go untreated will develop
bilateral blindness
ADDITIONAL READING
r Firestein SG, Budd RC, Gabriel SE, et al., eds.
Kelley’s Textbook of Rheumatology. 9th ed.
Philadelphia, PA: Saunders Elsevier; 2013.
r Mackie SL, Pease CT. Diagnosis and management of
giant cell arteritis and polymyalgia rheumatic:
Challenges, controversies, and practical tips.
Postgrad Med J. 2013;89:284–292.

329–335.

GIARDIASIS
Benjamin Mattingly rJoseph B. Schneider
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Noninvasive diarrhea
r Found worldwide:
– 2–15% prevalence in developed nations
– 20–40% prevalence in developing nations
r 5% of all travelers’ diarrhea
r Most common intestinal parasite in US:
– Highest incidence in early summer months
through fall
– Highest incidence in children aged 1–9 yr and
adults aged 30–39 yr
– In 2010, 19,888 cases reported in US (mostly
from Northern States)
r Fecal–oral transmission:
– Humans are major reservoir
– Zoonotic reservoir in both domestic and wild
mammals
– Reservoir in contaminated surface water
r Populations at risk:
– Travelers to endemic areas (developing countries,
wilderness areas of US)
– Children in day care centers and their close
contacts
– Institutionalized persons
– Practitioners of anal sexual activity
ETIOLOGYr Giardia lamblia:
– A protozoan flagellate
r Also called Giardia intestinalis or Giardia duodenalis
r Ingested Giardia attach to intestinal villi
r Alters the intestinal brush-border enzymes,
impairing digestion of lactose, and other saccharides
r No toxin produced
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Onset 1–2 wk postexposure
r Infection may be asymptomatic (most common).
r Diarrhea of acute onset (90% of symptomatic
patients):
– Foul-smelling stools
– Steatorrhea
– Nonbloody
– Self-limiting within 2–4 wk
– More severe in immunocompromised patients and
patients with underlying bowel disease
r Flatulence and bloating (70–75%)
r Abdominal cramping (70%)
r Nausea (70%)
r Vomiting (30%)
r Malaise (86%)
r Anorexia (66%)
r Weight loss (60–70%)
r Fever is rare (15%)
r 30–50% of acute cases progress to chronic
giardiasis (>4 wk):
– Fat malabsorption
– Severe macrocytic anemia secondary to folate
deficiency
– Secondary lactase deficiency (in 20–40% of
patients)
r Infection is more severe and harder to eradicate in
immunosuppressed patients.
Pediatric Considerations
r Acute infection:
– Severe dehydration
r Chronic infection:
– Failure to thrive
– Growth retardation and cognitive impairment
owing to nutrient malabsorption
Physical Examr Abdominal exam is benign.
r Extraintestinal manifestations (10% of patients):
– Polyarthritis
– Urticaria
– Aphthous ulcers
– Maculopapular rash
– Biliary tract disease
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr History:
– Possible sources of exposure
– Membership in high-risk group
r Physical exam:
– If gross or occult blood on digital rectal exam,
unlikely to be Giardia
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Stool sample for microscopy (ova and parasites):
– 50–70% sensitive if 1 sample
– 85–90% sensitive if 3 samples taken at 2-day
intervals (ideal)
– 100% specific
– Ability to detect other parasites as well
r Stool ELISA or immunofluorescent antibody (IFA)
assay for Giardia antigen:
– 95% sensitive, 95–100% specific
– Unlike microscopy, cannot rule out other parasites
r Stool polymerase chain reaction (PCR):
– 100% sensitive and 100% specific
r Fecal leukocytes and stool culture unnecessary
unless enteroinvasive organisms suspected (fever,
bloody stool)
r Serology for anti-Giardia antibodies not helpful in
the ED setting
r Electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, glucose:
– If prolonged diarrhea or evidence of dehydration
r CBC:
– Macrocytic anemia in chronic giardiasis
– Nondiagnostic in acute giardiasis
Imaging
Abdominal CT or ultrasound may show bowel wall
thickening and flattened duodenal folds (nonspecific
findings)
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Duodenal sampling:
– Entero-Test (patient swallows a weighted string,
which is later retrieved and examined for Giardia
using microscopy)
r Endoscopy:
– Duodenal aspiration
– Endoscopic duodenal biopsy
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Viral gastroenteritis:
– Norwalk virus
– Rotavirus
– Hepatitis A
r Bacterial infections:
– Staphylococcus
– Escherichia coli
– Shigella
– Salmonella
– Yersinia
– Campylobacter
– Clostridium difficile
– Vibrio cholerae
r Other protozoa:
– Cryptosporidium
– Microsporidia
– Cyclospora
– Isospora
– Entamoeba
r Inflammatory bowel disease
r Irritable bowel syndrome
r Lactase deficiency
r Tropical sprue
r Drugs and toxins:
– Antibiotics
– Calcium channel blockers
– Magnesium antacids
– Caffeine
– Alcohol
– Sorbitol
– Laxative abuse
– Quinidine
– Colchicine
– Mercury poisoning
r Endocrine:
– Addison disease
– Thyroid disorders
r Malignancy:
– Colorectal carcinoma
– Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid

GIARDIASIS
G
TREATMENT
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs: Airway, breathing, circulation
r IV 0.9% NS if signs of significant dehydration
Pediatric Considerations
r For severe dehydration (>10%):
– IV bolus with 0.9% NS at 20 mL/kg
– Cardiac monitor
– Blood glucose determination
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Oral fluids for mild dehydration
r Correct any serum electrolyte imbalances.
r Stool sample for microscopy
r If stool sample is positive for Giardia: Treat as listed
below under medication
r If stool sample negative for Giardia:
– Refer to gastroenterologist for further specialized
testing.
– Consider empiric course of metronidazole if high
suspicion for Giardia.
MEDICATION
First Liner Metronidazole or tinidazole are the treatment of
choice:
– 90% cure rate for each
r Metronidazole: 250–500 mg (peds: 15 mg/kg/24h)
PO q8h for 5–10 days
r Tinidazole: 2 g (peds [>3 yr]: 50 mg/kg) PO once
Second Line
Albendazole (78–90% efficacy), quinacrine (90%
efficacy), or nitazoxanide (75% efficacy) if 1st-line
therapy fails
r Albendazole: 400 mg (peds: 10–15 mg/kg/24h) PO
daily for 5–7 days
r Furazolidone: 100 mg (peds: 6–8 mg/kg/24h) PO
q6h for 7–10 days (not available in US)
r Nitazoxanide: 500 mg (peds: 100 mg for ages
2–3 yr, 200 mg for ages 4–11 yr) PO BID for 3 days
r Paromomycin: 500 mg (peds: 25–30 mg/kg/24h) PO
q8h for 5–10 days
r Quinacrine: 100 mg (peds: 6 mg/kg/24h) PO q8h for
5–7 days (limited availability)
Pediatric Considerationsr Metronidazole is 1st-line therapy (80–95% efficacy)
r Alternatives:
– Furazolidone (80–85% efficacy)
– Nitazoxanide (60–80% efficacy)
– Paromomycin (55–90% efficacy)
Pregnancy Considerations
r Metronidazole contraindicated in 1st trimester
r Albendazole, quinacrine, and tinidazole are
contraindicated throughout pregnancy
r Use nitazoxanide instead
r If mild symptoms only, consider deferring treatment
until late pregnancy or postpartum
Immunocompromised Considerationsr Immunocompromised patients at risk for disease
that is refractory to standard drug regimens:
– Try drug of a different class/mechanism or
metronidazole + quinacrine for at least 2 wk
ALERT
r Use furazolidone in older children only:
– Causes hemolytic anemia in infants
– Causes hemolytic anemia in persons with G6PD
deficiency
r Avoid quinacrine in G6PD deficiency (causes
hemolytic anemia)
r Avoid paromomycin in renal failure
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Hypotension or tachycardia unresponsive to IV fluids
r Severe electrolyte imbalance
r Children with >10% dehydration
r Signs of sepsis/toxicity (rare in isolated giardiasis)
r Patients unable to maintain adequate oral
hydration:
– Extremes of age, cognitive impairment, significant
comorbid illness
Discharge Criteriar Able to maintain adequate oral hydration
r Dehydration responsive to IV fluids
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Gastroenterology referral for diagnostic endoscopy if
symptoms persist for >4 wk despite drug therapy
r Acquired lactose intolerance may develop and last
for weeks to months
r Association with postinfectious fatigue syndrome
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
Diagnosis is the greatest challenge in this disease:
r Include giardiasis in the differential diagnosis of all
patients with diarrhea:
– Giardia occasionally reported in domestic water
supply
– Patients may not present with the classic history
and risk factors to have giardiasis
– 1 stool sample is frequently insufficient for
diagnosis

Treatment of intestinal protozoan infections in
children. Arch Dis Child. 2009;94:478–482.

treatment of giardiasis in children: Single-dose
tinidazole compared with 3 days of nitazoxanide.
Ann Trop Med Parasitol. 2008;102:199–207.
r Escobedo AA, Cimerman S. Giardiasis: A
pharmacotherapy review. Expert Opin
Pharmacother. 2007;8:1885–1902.

Cryptosporidium and Giardia. Gastroenterol Clin
North Am. 2006;35:291–314.

J Fam Pract. 2008;57(4):270–272.

GLAUCOMA
Yasuharu Okuda rLisa Jacobson
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Disease characterized by elevation of intraocular
pressure, optic neuropathy, and progressive loss of
vision.
ETIOLOGYr Primary glaucoma:
– Open-angle glaucoma:
◦Normal anterior chamber angle
◦Insidious onset with persistent rise in intraocular
pressure
◦Most common type accounting for 90% of
glaucomas in US
◦Leading cause of blindness in African Americans
◦Risk factors include African American, age
>40 yr, family history, myopia, diabetes, and
HTN
– Acute angle-closure glaucoma:
◦Narrowing or closing of anterior chamber angle
precluding natural flow of aqueous humor from
posterior to anterior chamber of eye and
through its filtering portion of trabecular
meshwork
◦Usually abrupt onset with sudden increase in
intraocular pressure
◦Risk factors include Asians and Eskimos,
hyperopia, family history, increased age, and
female gender
r Secondary glaucoma occurs from other diseases,
including diseases of eye, trauma, and drugs:
– Can be either open or closed angle
– Drugs: Steroids, sertraline, bronchodilators,
topiramate
– Diseases: Neurofibromatosis, uveitis,
neovascularization, and intraocular tumors
– Trauma
– Rapid correction of hyperglycemia
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Classic descriptions:
r Open angle:
– Painless and gradual loss of vision
r Closed angle:
– Painful loss of vision with fixed midsized pupil
Historyr Primary open-angle glaucoma:
– Gradual reduction in peripheral vision or night
blindness
– Typically bilateral
– Painless
r Primary angle-closure glaucoma:
– Severe deep eye pain and ipsilateral headache
often associated with nausea and vomiting
– Decrease in visual acuity often described as visual
clouding with halos surrounding light sources
– Associated abdominal pain, which may misdirect
diagnosis
– Concurrent exposure to dimly lit environment such
as movie theater
– Use of precipitating medications:
◦Mydriatic agents: Scopolamine, atropine
◦Sympathomimetics: Pseudoephedrine, albuterol
◦Antihistamines: Benadryl, Antivert
◦Antipsychotics: Haldol
◦Phenothiazines: Compazine, Phenergan
◦Tricyclic antidepressants: Elavil
◦Sulfonamides: Topiramate
Physical Examr Primary open-angle glaucoma:
– Decreased visual acuity
r Primary angle-closure glaucoma:
– Decreased visual acuity
– Pupil is mid-dilated and nonreactive.
– Corneal edema with hazy appearance
– Conjunctival injection, ciliary flush
– Firm globe to palpation
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Detailed ocular exam
r Visual acuity:
– Hand movements typically all that is seen
r Tonometry:
– Normal pressures are 10–21 mm Hg.
– Primary open-angle glaucoma:
◦Degree of elevation can vary, but 25–30% of
patients may have normal intraocular pressures.
– Primary angle-closure glaucoma:
◦Any elevation is abnormal, but usually seen in
ranges >40 mm Hg.
r Slit-lamp exam:
– Evaluation of anterior chamber angle
– Used to eliminate other possibilities in differential
including corneal abrasion and foreign body
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Directed toward workup of differential
Imaging
Directed toward workup of differential
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Gonioscopy:
r This is direct measurement of the angle of closure
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Cavernous sinus thrombosis
r Acute iritis and uveitis
r Retinal artery or vein occlusion
r Temporal arteritis
r Retinal detachment
r Conjunctivitis
r Corneal abrasion
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr No specific interventions need occur prior to arrival
at the hospital in regard to the eye:
– Pain control may be necessary
– In traumatic etiologies, stabilize other injuries
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Initiate steps to lower intraocular pressure in acute
closed-angle glaucoma:
– Address other effects of trauma if this was the
etiology
– Discontinue inciting medication when involved
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Primary open-angle glaucoma:
– Recognition and prompt ophthalmologic referral
– Patients maintained on topical β-blockers or
prostaglandin analogs to decrease IOP
r Primary angle-closure glaucoma (ophthalmologic
emergency):
– Intraocular pressure reduction:
◦Topical β-blocker, timolol maleate, to decrease
aqueous humor production
◦Topical α2-agonist, apraclonidine, to decrease
aqueous humor production
◦Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, acetazolamide, for
reduction of formation of aqueous humor
◦Hyperosmotic agent, mannitol, to draw aqueous
humor from vitreous cavity into blood (indicated
for severe attacks).
– Movement of iris away from trabecular meshwork:
◦Topical parasympathomimetic, pilocarpine
hydrochloride, to constrict pupil once intraocular
pressure is <40 mm Hg
– Reduction of inflammation:
◦Topical corticosteroid, prednisolone acetate
– Emergent ophthalmology consultation for possible
definitive surgical treatment, laser iridectomy, if
no improvement with medical management
– Adequate narcotic analgesia and antiemetics as
needed
MEDICATIONr Acetazolamide: 500 mg IV or PO
r Mannitol 20%: 1–2 g/kg IV over 30–60 min
r Pilocarpine hydrochloride 1–2% solution: 1 drop
q15–30min until pupillary constriction occurs, then
1 drop q2–3h
r Prednisolone acetate 1% solution: 1 drop
q15–30min for total of 4 doses

GLOBE RUPTURE
Alexander T. Limkakeng, Jr. rMegan G. Kemnitz
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr A full-thickness corneal or scleral injury owing to
trauma
r Blunt trauma/globe rupture:
– Causes an abrupt rise in intraocular pressure
diffusely
– Subsequent rupture of the eye either opposite the
point of impact or at the weakest points:
◦Extraocular muscle insertion
◦Corneoscleral junction
◦Limbus, where the sclera is thinnest
r Penetrating injury/globe laceration:
– Occurs with sharp objects or projectiles injuring
the sclera or anterior eye directly
– Most commonly anterior—the bony orbit protects
the globe laterally and posteriorly
– Posterior injury can occur with fracture of the bony
orbit or with penetrating injuries of the eyelid or
eyebrow.
r Prognosis worse with:
– Larger lacerations
– Injury posterior to the rectus insertion
– Blunt injury
– Intraocular foreign body, especially if made of
organic material
– Vitreous extrusion
– Lens damage
– Hyphema
– Retinal detachment
– Poor visual acuity at presentation
– Afferent pupillary defect
– Increased time to OR
ETIOLOGYr Falls, impact injuries
r Sport-related injuries (e.g., elbow, ball impacts,
arrows, game controllers, etc.)
r Indirect concussive injuries (explosions)
r Sharp instrument/stabbing injuries, accidental or
intentional
r Projectile injuries (industrial, firearms, BB pellets,
blast explosion shrapnel—glass, etc.)
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Pain
r Localized ecchymosis and swelling
r Scleral or corneal laceration
r Extrusion of intraocular contents
r Markedly decreased visual acuity
r Limited extraocular motion
r Hyphema
r Severe subconjunctival hemorrhage and edema,
especially if circumferential bloody chemosis
r Abnormally deep or shallow anterior chamber
r Low intraocular pressure:
– Note: Do not perform tonometry if there is
suspected rupture.
r Irregular pupil (points toward lesion)
r Subluxed lens
r Commotio retinae—gray-white discoloration of the
retina
Historyr Mechanism of injury:
– Assess for possibility of retained intraocular
foreign body
r History of previous eye surgery
r Preinjury visual acuity
r Assess tetanus status
r Ascertain time of last PO intake
Physical Examr Penlight or slit-lamp exam observing for signs of
globe rupture
r If the diagnosis of ruptured globe is made, defer
further ocular exam until the time of surgical repair:
– Prevents placing any undue pressure on the eye
and risking extrusion of the intraocular contents
r If no evidence of globe rupture on initial survey,
proceed with thorough ophthalmologic exam:
– Visual acuity
– Slit-lamp exam
– Cornea
– Anterior chamber
– Iris
– Sclera
– Fundus
– Retina
r Seidel test: Observe if fluorescein moves away as
contents (which appear yellow-green) leak out at
site of rupture:
r Measure intraocular pressure
– Perform only if globe rupture is definitely not
present.
r Ultrasound (only if rupture not suspected)
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Perform thorough ocular exam as outlined above:
r Once diagnosis of globe rupture is suspected or
made, defer further exam until time of repair.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Preoperative labs:
r CBC
r Electrolytes
r Coagulation studies
Imagingr Orbital radiograph (anteroposterior/lateral) for
metallic intraocular foreign body
r CT scan of the orbits (axial and coronal views)
r MRI scan of the orbits after retained metallic foreign
body is ruled out
r B-scan US of the eye
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Slit-lamp
r Fluorescein
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Intraocular foreign body
r Hyphema
r Severe subconjunctival hemorrhage and chemosis
r Partial corneal laceration
r Partial scleral laceration

G
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Place a shield (not patch) over eye with no pressure
on the globe.
r Use a Styrofoam cup if no shield available.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Keep manipulation of the eye to a minimum if
ruptured globe is suspected.
r Try to prevent any activity that will cause an increase
in intraocular pressure such as straining, coughing,
or vomiting.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Prepare for definitive surgical management:
– Emergent ophthalmologic consultation
– Thorough physical exam to identify concurrent
injuries
– Preoperative labs and ECG as indicated
– No food or drink (NPO)
r Minimize intraocular pressure to reduce further
injury
– Administer antiemetic for nausea/vomiting
– Elevate the head of the bed
– Protective eye shield (NO pressure on the globe
itself)
r Update tetanus status.
r Administer prophylactic antibiotics IV:
– Skin organisms (staph, strep) most common
– Consider injury-specific contaminants in cases of
animal bites, organic foreign body, etc.
– Vancomycin + ceftazidime OR vancomycin +
ciprofloxacin if allergic to penicillin
r Succinylcholine is relatively contraindicated:
– However, with a defasciculating dose of a
nondepolarizing agent and sufficient anesthesia, it
may be used.
Pediatric Considerations
r Consider nonaccidental trauma
r Because of risk of extrusion of intraocular contents,
straining/crying should be avoided. Try to keep them
happy!
MEDICATIONr Ceftazidime: 1–2 g (peds: 30–50 mg/kg) IV q8h
r Ciprofloxacin: 400 mg (peds: 10 mg/kg) IV q12h
r Clindamycin: 450 mg (peds: 8–12 mg/kg) IV q8h
r Ondansetron (Zofran): 4 mg IV
r Prochlorperazine (Compazine): 5–10 mg IV/IM
r Tobramycin: 2 mg/kg (peds: 2 mg/kg) IV q8h
r Vancomycin: 15 mg/kg IV q8–12h (peds: 10 mg/kg
IV q6h)
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar All patients with globe rupture/penetrating eye
injuries
r Early enucleation for severe injury
Discharge Criteria
Globe penetration excluded
Issues for Referralr Emergent ophthalmologic consultation in the ED
may be needed to definitively rule out globe rupture
owing to difficulty with exam and the desire to
minimize manipulation of the eye.
r Speed is of the essence since the risk of infection
increases with prolonged time to operative repair.
r If appropriate, patient should be counseled on use
of protective eyewear to prevent recurrence.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Postoperative ophthalmology follow-up
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Do not manipulate the eye if you suspect or confirm
a ruptured globe:
– Place eye shield over affected eye.
r Administer antiemetic for patients with nausea and
vomiting to prevent elevation of intraocular pressure
and extrusion of globe contents.

r Empiric antibiotics tailored to clinical scenario

GLOMERULONEPHRITIS
Melissa H. White rCarolyn Maher Overman
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Syndrome characterized by:
– Hematuria
– Proteinuria
– Red blood cell casts
– Hypertension
– Renal insufficiency
r Common pathway of multiple diseases resulting in
intraglomerular inflammation and cellular
proliferation
r Contributing factors:
– Genetics
– Infectious
– Rheumatologic
– Leading to antibody deposition:
◦Antibody attaches to glomerular antigen (native
or implanted).
◦Circulating antigen–antibody complex deposited
– Causing an influx and activation of inflammatory
mediators:
◦Leukocytes, complement, cytokines
◦Cell-mediated immune mechanisms
r Results in glomerular dysfunction
r Persistent inflammation that can lead to scarring
and permanent damage.
ETIOLOGYr Postinfectious:
– Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN):
◦Occurs 7–21 days after Streptococcal
pharyngitis or skin infection
◦Highest prevalence in ages 2–14 and the elderly
◦Male predominance
◦Ranges from asymptomatic hematuria to
oliguric renal failure
– Can follow other bacterial, fungal, viral, or
parasitic infections
r IgA nephropathy (Berger disease):
– Most common in men in the 3rd and 4th decades
of life
– Possibly related to increased production of IgA
after infection usually a URI
– Henoch–Sch ¨ onlein purpura (HSP) has IgA
nephropathy but affects a younger age and has
systemic symptoms
r Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN):
– Can destroy renal function in days
– Crescentic deposits in glomeruli destroy function.
– Pauci-immune (small vessel vasculitides):
◦Often antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody
(ANCA)-positive
◦Can involve other areas (i.e., lungs, skin)
◦Wegener granulomatosis
◦Microscopic polyangiitis
◦Churg–Strauss syndrome
– Immune complex deposits:
◦Postinfectious
◦Endocarditis associated
◦Systemic disease (i.e., systemic lupus
erythematosus [SLE], HSP)
– Anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM)
deposits:
◦Older patients of age >60
◦Goodpasture disease with pulmonary
involvement
r Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN):
– Complement deposits in basement membrane
– Hepatitis C
– Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
– Occult infection
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Cardinal signs:
– Hematuria
– Proteinuria
r Edema:
– Owing to renal salt and water retention
– Periorbital
– Ascites
– Pleural effusion
r HTN
r Oliguria
r Azotemia
r CHF
r Renal failure
r Nonspecific manifestations:
– Fatigue
– Weight loss
– Abdominal pain
– Nausea/vomiting
r Autoimmune disorders:
– Arthralgias
– Arthritis
– Rash
– Fever
r Goodpasture syndrome:
– Hemoptysis
r Wegner granulomatosis:
– Purulent rhinorrhea/sinus pain
– Arthritis/arthralgias
– Hemoptysis
r HSP:
– Abdominal pain
– Purpura
– Arthritis
Geriatric Considerations
r Pauci-immune RPGN is common in this population
(hematuria, proteinuria, and elevated CR).
r Urgent diagnosis and biopsy are indicated as this
may progress to ESRD.
r Consult nephrology to discuss steroids,
cyclophosphamide, and plasma exchange.
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Urinalysis for:
r Hematuria, proteinuria, and RBC casts
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Electrolytes, BUN, Creatinine, GFR:
– Renal function
– Hyperkalemia
r Albumin, total protein:
– Varying degrees of hypoalbuminemia depending
on clinical process
r CBC:
– Anemia secondary to chronic renal disease,
neoplasm, Goodpasture, and Wegener
– With or without elevated WBC in infections
r PT, PTT:
– Coagulation factors consumed in certain types of
GN
r Labs to be considered for consultants:
– Cultures—throat, skin, blood
– 24-hr urine collection—protein, urine electrolytes
– Streptozyme or antistreptolysin O titer
– Complement levels (C1, C3, C4, CH50)—reduced
in PSGN, MPGN, SLE
– ANA, rheumatoid factor—connective tissue
diseases
– ESR and CRP inflammatory markers
– Anti-GBM—Goodpasture
– c-ANCA—Wegener; p-ANCA-pauci-immune
– Anti-DNA antibodies (SLE)
– Hepatitis B and C serologies
– HIV
Imagingr Renal ultrasound (if GFR is decreased):
– Kidney size predictor of potential reversibility of
disease, alternative diagnosis (i.e., neoplasm,
stone)
r Chest radiograph (CXR): Heart size, pulmonary
edema, or hemorrhage
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Renal biopsy: Discern primary glomerulopathies vs.
other causes
r Cystoscopy: If concern for bladder neoplasm
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Hematologic:
– Sickle cell disease
– Coagulopathy
r Renal:
– Infectious
– Malformation
– Neoplasm
– Ischemic
– Trauma
– Vasculitis
r Postrenal:
– Mechanical (i.e., stones, reflux, obstruction,
catheterization)
– Inflammatory (i.e., cystitis, prostatitis, epididymitis,
endometriosis, periurethritis)
– Neoplasm
r Factitious:
– Food
– Drugs
– Pigmenturia (i.e., myoglobin, porphyria,
hemoglobin)
– Vaginal bleeding

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr 2nd most frequently reported STD in US:
– Estimated 820,000 new cases per year
– <50% reported
– Highest rates in 15–24-yr-old males and females,
African Americans
– Increasing incidence in men who have sex with
men (MSM):
◦Higher in HIV-positive individuals
– Humans only known host
r Concurrent infection with Chlamydia trachomatis is
common
r Affects the urethra, rectum, cervical canal, pharynx,
upper female genital tract, and conjunctiva
r Urethritis most common presentation in men
r Often asymptomatic in women
ETIOLOGY
Neisseria gonorrhoeae:
r Gram-negative aerobic diplococci
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Cervicitis:
– Defined as:
◦Mucopurulent endocervical discharge; OR
◦Easily induced endocervical bleeding
– Most common site of infection
– Up to 80% asymptomatic
– Most symptoms nonspecific:
◦Vaginal discharge
◦Menorrhagia
◦Pelvic pain
◦Dyspareunia
◦Frequency and dysuria
r Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID):
– Up to 20% of untreated cases
– Lower abdominal pain—most common presenting
symptom
– Other common signs and symptoms:
◦Dyspareunia, abnormal bleeding, abnormal
cervical or vaginal discharge
– Symptoms often occur at onset of menses.
– Fever (50%)
– 2/3 have mild, vague symptoms; may go
unrecognized
– Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome: (perihepatitis):
◦10% occurrence rate
◦Right upper quadrant pain/tenderness
r Bartholin abscess
r Urethritis:
– Incubation period 2–5 days
– Symptoms:
◦Penile discharge
◦Dysuria
r Prostatitis—can occur in untreated urethritis
r Epididymitis:
– Acute, unilateral testicular pain and swelling
r Proctitis:
– Often asymptomatic
– Only site of infection in 40% of MSM
– Rectal infection occurs in 35–50% of women with
endocervical infection
– 3-fold increase in HIV infection risk
– Symptoms:
◦Perianal pruritus, mucopurulent discharge, mild
rectal bleeding, severe rectal pain, tenesmus,
and constipation
r Pharyngitis:
– Sore throat, exudative tonsillitis
r Disseminated gonococcal infections (DGI):
– Gonococcal bacteremia
– Arthritis: Dermatitis syndrome:
◦0.5–3% of untreated mucosal infections
◦Triad of tenosynovitis, dermatitis, and
polyarthralgia
◦Fever, chills, malaise
– Dermatitis:
◦Tender necrotic pustules on an erythematous
base, few lesions, begin distally
– Acute monoarticular or oligoarticular arthritis:
◦Knee most common
◦Warm, erythematous joint with effusion and
pain with range of motion
– Female > male, 3:1:
◦Risk factors: Recent menstruation or recent
pregnancy
– Rare manifestations:
◦Hepatitis
◦Myocarditis
◦Endocarditis
◦Meningitis

– Cervical edema, congestion, friability
r PID:
– Uterine tenderness, adnexal or cervical motion
tenderness
r Urethritis:
– Yellow-white thick discharge, urethral meatal
erythema

– Gram stain 95% sensitive
r Cervical culture in female gonorrhea
r Also test for chlamydia and syphilis

Labr Cultures (gold standard):
– Thayer-Martin medium
◦Mainstay for blood and synovial fluid
r Gram stain:
– Intracellular gram-negative diplococci:
◦Approaches 100% sensitive in symptomatic men
r Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs):
– DNA or RNA sequences using polymerase chain
reaction (PCR)
– Many also test for chlamydia
– Useful in urethral, cervical, and urine specimens
r Pharyngeal/rectal cultures for local symptoms in
high-risk individuals

– Synovial fluid analysis:
◦Neutrophilic leukocytosis, >50,000 cells/mm3
◦Positive cultures when >80,000 cells/mm3
– 2 or more sets of blood cultures
– Synovial, skin, urethral or cervical, and rectal
cultures:
◦Thayer-Martin media

– CBC
– Urinalysis
– Pregnancy test
– Consider pelvic ultrasound for tubo-ovarian
abscess
r Rapid plasma reagin (RPR): For associated syphilis

– Chlamydia
– Trichomonas
– UTI
– Syphilis

– Bacterial arthritis:
◦Meningococcus (rash)
– Hepatitis B
– Connective tissue disease:
◦Reiter syndrome
◦Rheumatoid arthritis
◦Psoriatic arthritis
– Acute rheumatic fever:
◦Poststreptococcal arthritis
– Infective endocarditis
– Others:
◦HIV
◦Secondary syphilis
◦Viral infection
◦Lyme disease (rash)
◦Gout (arthritis)

GOUT/PSEUDOGOUT
Delaram Ghadishah
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Uric acid deposition into tissues, affecting mainly
middle-aged men and postmenopausal women:
– Most common crystalline diseases
– 4 phases:
◦Asymptomatic hyperuricemia (serum urate
>7 mg/dL)
◦Acute gout
◦Intercritical gout: Quiet intervening periods
◦Tophaceous gout (up to 45% of cases)
– Risk factors:
◦Age >40
◦Male/female ratio 2:1–6:1 <65 yr old; 1:1
≥65 yr old
◦Hypertension
◦Use of loop or thiazide diuretics
◦High intake of alcohol, meat, seafood, and
fructose-sweetened beverages
◦Obesity
– Urologic deposition of uric acid calculi may cause
renal dysfunction.
– Associated with avascular necrosis and deforming
arthritis
– Most frequent in previously damaged joints,
tissues:
◦Synovium
◦Subchondral bone
◦Bursae (olecranon, infrapatellar, prepatellar)
◦Achilles tendon
◦Extensor surface of the forearms, toes, fingers,
ear
◦Rarely CNS or cardiac (valves)
r Pseudogout: A disorder caused by calcium
pyrophosphate crystal deposition:
– Most common cause of acute monoarthritis
>60 yr of age
– Risk factors:
◦Hypercalcemia (e.g., hyperparathyroidism,
familial)
◦Hemochromatosis; hemosiderosis
◦Hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism
◦Hypophosphatemia, hypomagnesemia
◦Amyloidosis
◦Gout
ETIOLOGYr Deposition of monosodium urate crystals in tissues
from supersaturated extracellular fluid owing to:
– Underexcretion (most commonly) or excessive
production of uric acid
– Any rapid change in uric acid levels
◦Initiation or cessation of diuretics
◦Alcohol, salicylates, niacin
◦Cyclosporine
◦Lead acetate poisoning
◦Uricosurics or allopurinol
r Pseudogout occurs secondary to excess synovial
accumulation of calcium pyrophosphate crystals
r Precipitants for both gout and pseudogout include
minor trauma and acute illnesses:
– Surgery, ischemic heart disease
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Gout and pseudogout both present as acute
monoarticular or polyarticular arthritis:
– Increased warmth, erythema, and joint swelling
are present.
– Early attacks subside spontaneously within
3–21 days, even without treatment.
– Later attacks may last longer, cluster, be more
severe, and be polyarticular.
r Gout:
– Symptoms present maximally within 12–24 hr.
– Tophi and joint desquamation may be present.
– Women predominantly present after menopause
and have polyarticular predominance (up to 70%).
– Less dramatic presentations in immunosuppressed
and elderly
– Most common: 1st metatarsophalangeal joint
(75%) > ankle; tarsal area; knee > hand; wrist
r Pseudogout:
– Typically involves larger joints than with gout

GRANULOCYTOPENIA
Richard E. Wolfe r William D. Timbers r Elicia Sinor Kennedy
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr A significant decrease in the number of granulocytes
in the peripheral blood.
r 3 classes of granulocytes:
– Neutrophils or polymorphonuclear (PMN) cells
and bands
– Eosinophils
– Basophils
r As PMN cells predominate, the term neutropenia is
often used interchangeably with granulocytopenia,
as almost all granulocytopenic patients are
neutropenic.
r Granulocytes are a key component of the innate
immune system.
r The clinical risks resulting from granulocytopenia are
best defined by the level of the absolute neutrophil
count (ANC):
– ANC = WBC × percentage (PMN + bands)
– Modern automated instruments often calculate
and report ANC.
r Neutropenia: ANC <1,500 cells/mm3:
– Mild: Between 1,000 and 1,500
– Moderate: Between 500 and 1,000
– Severe: <500
– Agranulocytosis: <100
– Patients with a count <1,000 that has recently or
rapidly fallen are at greater risk for infection than
those with a count <500 but rising.
– Patients with myelodysplastic syndromes should
be considered granulocytopenic with higher
counts because of defective neutrophils.
r 4 basic mechanisms cause granulocytopenia:
– Decreased production
– Ineffective granulopoiesis
– Shift of circulating PMN cells to vascular
endothelium
– Enhanced peripheral destruction.
r Mortality of fever and neutropenia is as high as
50% if untreated:
– Mortality correlates with the duration and severity
of the neutropenia and the time elapsed until the
1st dose of antibiotics.
r 21% of patients with cancer and neutropenic fever
develop serious complications.
Pediatric Considerations
r Newborn infants have a physiologically elevated
ANC in the 1st few days of life and may be
granulocytopenic with levels >1,500/μL.
r Children >3 mo without underlying
immunodeficiency or a central venous catheter
unexpectedly found to have isolated moderate
neutropenia are not at high risk of serious bacterial
infection.
ETIOLOGYr Most common in patients undergoing
myelosuppressive drug therapy or radiation
treatment for neoplasms. Most common 5–10 days
after chemo.
r Adverse reaction to drugs is the 2nd most common
cause:
– Excludes cytotoxic drugs and requires at least
4 wk of administration prior to the onset of
granulocytopenia
– Discontinuation usually results with correction
within 30 days.
– Drugs with the highest risk:
◦Antipsychotic: Clozapine
◦Antibiotic: Sulfasalazine
◦Antithyroid: Thioamides
– Antiplatelet agents
– Antiepileptic drugs
– NSAIDs
r Drugs that suppress the bone marrow:
– Methotrexate
– Cyclophosphamide
– Colchicine
– Azathioprine
– Ganciclovir
r Chemicals
r Bacterial infections:
– Typhoid
– Shigella enteritis
– Brucellosis
– Tularemia
– Tuberculosis
r Parasitic infections:
– Kala azar
– Malaria
r Rickettsial infections:
– Rickettsialpox
– Ehrlichiosis
– Rocky Mountain spotted fever
r Viral infections
r Postinfectious neutropenia:
– Most severe and protracted following HIV ,
hepatitis B, and Epstein–Barr viral infections
r Immune-related:
– Primary immune neutropenia:
◦Due to antineutrophil antibodies
– Crohn’s disease
– Systemic lupus erythematosus
– Rheumatoid arthritis
– Goodpasture disease
– Wegener granulomatosis
– Thymoma
– Compliment activation
r Bone marrow infiltration
r Transfusion reaction
r Alcoholism
r Vitamin deficiency (B12/folate/copper)
r Chronic idiopathic neutropenia
r Pure white cell aplasia
Pediatric Considerations
r Congenital neutropenia:
– Neutropenia with abnormal immunoglobulins
– Reticular dysgenesis
– Severe congenital neutropenia or Kostmann
syndrome
– Cyclic neutropenia
r Chronic benign neutropenia
r Neonatal isoimmune neutropenia
r Shwachman–Diamond syndrome
r Cartilage–hair hypoplasia
r Dyskeratosis congenita
r Barth syndrome
r Ch ´ ediak–Higashi syndrome
r Myelokathexis
r Lazy leukocyte syndrome
r Cohen syndrome
r Hermansky–Pudlak syndrome type 2
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Signs of bacterial or fungal infection:
– Fever
– Localized erythema or fluctuance
r Signs of pancytopenia:
– Fatigue
– Pallor
– Petechiae
– Epistaxis and other spontaneous bleeding
Historyr Medical list should be reviewed for causative drugs.
r Family history of granulocytopenia in neonates and
children
r Records of past ANC levels to assess for chronicity
r Question the patient carefully about fever, chills,
dizziness, and vomiting as indicators of an
underlying serious infection.
r Ask about localizing signs of infection such as
cough; shortness of breath; chest pain; dysuria;
urinary retention, urgency, or frequency; abdominal
pain; and rectal pain.
Physical Exam
Focus on finding signs of infection:
r Oral exam: Thrush, ulcers, periodontal disease,
mucositis
r Lungs: Rales, rhonchi
r Abdominal: Splenomegaly
r Skin: Rashes, ulcers, abscesses
r Perirectal: Although the rectal exam is relatively
contraindicated until antibiotics are started, check
for abscesses and mucosal lesions.
r Evaluate indwelling catheter sites

GUILLAIN–BARR´E SYNDROME
Erin F. Drasler rJeffrey Druck
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Group of peripheral nerve disorders characterized by
autoimmune demyelination and axonal
degeneration of peripheral nerves leading to acute
ascending paralysis
r Humoral and cellular immune mediated
r Leading cause of acute flaccid paralysis worldwide
(since polio vaccination)
r Triggered by antecedent bacterial/viral infection
r Increasing incidence with advancing age, male
gender
– Average 1.1 per 100,000 per yr
r Weakness reaches nadir at 2–4 wk
r Spontaneous resolution occurs over weeks to
months
– 80% full recovery at 1 yr
– 20% unable to walk at 6 mo
– 5% die of complications (PE, infection, cardiac)
r Acute inflammatory demyelinating
polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP):
– Most common form of Guillain–Barr ´ e syndrome
(90% of all GBS cases)
– Demyelination sometimes accompanied by axonal
loss
r Other forms of GBS:
– Acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN):
◦Pure motor axonal involvement
◦67% seropositive for Campylobacter jejuni
◦Recovery often rapid
◦Often pediatric patients
– Acute motor sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN):
◦Degeneration of myelinated motor and sensory
nerves without significant inflammation or
demyelination
◦Similar to AMAN, but also involves sensory
nerves
– Acute panautonomic neuropathy:
◦Very rare
◦Involves sympathetic and parasympathetic
nerves
◦Postural hypotension, dysrhythmias,
tachycardia, hypertension
◦Blurry vision, dry eyes, anhidrosis
◦Recovery gradual, often incomplete
– Miller Fisher syndrome:
◦Rare
◦Rapidly evolving ataxia, areflexia, and
ophthalmoplegia without weakness
◦Demyelination and inflammation of cranial
nerves II and VI, spinal ganglia, and peripheral
nerves
◦Resolves in 1–3 mo
ETIOLOGYr Postinfectious:
– 2/3 with antecedent illness, usually respiratory or
GI
– Different autoantibodies associated with different
subtypes
– 1–3 wk between prodromal illness and neurologic
symptoms
– C. jejuni most common antecedent bacterial
infection
– Cytomegalovirus most common antecedent viral
infection
– Epstein–Barr virus, VZV , HIV , mycoplasma also
associated
r Relationship to vaccines is questionable
– Slight increased risk ascribed to 1976 swine flu
vaccine, no other vaccines have same risk

SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Rapidly evolving, symmetric, ascending paralysis
r Absent or mild sensory symptoms (e.g., paresthesias
of fingertips or toes)
r Pain, commonly of pelvis, shoulder girdles, posterior
thighs
r Cranial nerve involvement may affect swallowing,
facial muscles, eye movements
r Preceding bacterial or viral infection
r Progression of symptoms over 8 wk not consistent
with GBS, but chronic inflammatory demyelinating

than arms
r Loss of deep tendon reflexes
r Look for cranial nerve involvement
r Respiratory insufficiency (25% patients)
r Normal sensory exam
r Other subtypes:
– Autonomic dysfunction:
◦Hypertension
◦Orthostatic hypotension
◦Ileus
◦Dysrhythmias
◦Urinary retention
– Miller Fisher variant:
◦Ataxia
◦Areflexia
◦Ophthalmoplegia

– Fever

– Upper motor neuron signs
– Asymmetric neurologic deficits
– Sharply demarcated sensory level

HALLUCINATIONS
Michael Ganetsky
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Hallucinations are a symptom or feature and not a
diagnosis. They may be auditory, visual, tactile,
gustatory, or olfactory. Hallucinations and similar
phenomena are often defined as follows:
r Hallucination:
– Sensory perception that has the compelling sense
of reality of a true perception without external
stimulation of the relevant sensory organ and is
experienced as a sensation through that organ
– Patients may or may not have insight that they are
having the hallucination
r Illusion:
– Misperception or misinterpretation of a real
external stimulus
r Flashback:
– Recurrence of a memory, feeling, or perceptual
experience from the past that may have the
compelling sense of reality
r Pseudohallucination:
– Hallucination that is not experienced by a sensory
organ (i.e., voices inside head or “inner voice” as
opposed to hearing voices)
EPIDEMIOLOGY
Incidence and Prevalence Estimatesr Lifetime incidence of auditory hallucinations is
4–8% in general population (although some
estimates are higher due to vague definitions or
inclusion of pseudohallucinations)
r More than 50% of elderly patients with dementia
have paranoia or hallucinations
ETIOLOGY
There are numerous causes of hallucinations. The
following are common: (An exhaustive list is beyond
the scope of this chapter)
r Psychiatric
– Schizophrenia
– Bipolar disorder, mania
– Major depression
r Acute intoxications
– Ethanol
– Cannabis
◦Marijuana alternatives (i.e., K2, Spice)
– Sympathomimetics
◦Amphetamine
◦Methamphetamine
◦Cocaine
◦Synthetic cathinones (i.e., MDPV , “bath salts”)
– NMDA antagonists
◦Ketamine
◦PCP
◦Dextromethorphan
– Serotonergic
◦MDMA (Ecstasy)
◦LSD
◦Peyote cactus (mescaline)
◦Mushrooms (psilocybin)
◦2C series (i.e., 2CB, 2CT-7)
◦5-MeO series (i.e., 5-MeO-DMT)
– Kappa opioid receptor agonist
◦Salvia divinorum (cause synesthesias – i.e.,
hearing colors or smelling sounds)
– Opiates
– Inhalants
◦Toluene
◦Nitrous oxide
r Medications
– Anticholinergic agents
– Steroids
– Methylphenidate
r Withdrawal
– Ethanol
– Benzodiazepines
– Barbiturates
– GHB
r Substance-induced disorders
– Methamphetamine-associated psychosis
◦Prolonged duration of psychosis, auditory
hallucinations and recurrence without relapse of
using drug
– Cannabis-induced psychosis
r Infectious
– Meningitis
– Encephalitis
– In patients with dementia, any infection (i.e., UTI,
pneumonia) can trigger hallucinations
r Metabolic
– Hypoglycemia
– Electrolyte imbalances
– Thyroid disease
– Adrenal disease
– Wilson’s disease
– Thiamine deficiency
r Neurologic
– Seizures
◦Partial simple or complex seizures can result in
visual, auditory, olfactory, and gustatory
hallucinations
– Migraines
– CNS hemorrhage or tumor
–C V A
– Tourette syndrome
– Neurodegenerative disorders
◦Parkinsons
◦Dementia (Lewy body, Alzheimer)
◦HIV
r Ocular
– Glaucoma
– Macular degeneration
– Charles Bonnet syndrome
r Others
– Food, sensory, sleep deprivation
– Fatigue, extreme stress
– Heat-related illness
– Religious and ritual activities
– Falling asleep and awakening from sleep
Pediatric Considerations
Hallucinations are relatively common in children and
adolescents and are often developmentally normal.
Most children with hallucinations do not have
psychosis. Hallucinations can occur as part of a
delirium, such as from fever. As with the adult patient,
carefully conduct a search for a medical or neurologic
etiology.
Geriatric Considerations
In the elderly patient, hallucinations are most often
from an organic cause. They can commonly
accompany dementia, depression, medication
reactions and substance abuse, and are often
associated with agitation. Atypical antipsychotic
agents are effective treatment for hallucinations with
agitation in the elderly.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Obtaining accurate and thorough history often
difficult
– Collateral history should be obtained from
bystanders, EMS, police, family, physicians
r Assess for changes in behavior from baseline
r Explore for delusions or persecutory beliefs
r Previous episodes of hallucinations
r Change in medications
r Substance abuse history
r Alteration in cognition that rapidly develops and
waxes and wanes throughout course of the day
suggests delirium
r Headache may suggest CNS lesion or migraine
Physical Examr Acute psychosis
– Disorganized thought
– Responding to internal stimuli
r Mania
– Excessive talking or pressured speech
r Delirium
– Altered level of consciousness
– Not oriented
– Abnormal vital signs
r CNS lesion
– Cranial nerve deficit
– Aphasia
– Any focal neurologic finding
– Gait abnormality
– External signs of trauma
r Systemic or infectious illness
– Asterixis
– Fever
– Nuchal rigidity
– Myoclonus
– Jaundice
– Ascites
r Signs of intoxication or withdrawal
– Sympathomimetic intoxication,
ethanol/benzodiazepine withdrawal
◦Agitation, excited delirium
◦Mydriasis
◦Tachycardia, hypertension
◦Hyperthermia
◦Diaphoresis
– Opiate
◦Miosis
◦Bradypnea
◦Needle marks
– Serotonergic
◦Tachycardia, hypertension
◦Hyperreflexia
◦Clonus
◦Tremor
– NMDA antagonism
◦Nystagmus

HALLUCINATIONS
H
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATIONr Common tests:
– CBC, serum chemistries
– Ethanol, acetaminophen, salicylate serum
concentrations
– Urinalysis
r More focused studies depending on comorbid
conditions or clinical concerns:
– Urine drug of abuse screen
◦Interpretation can be difficult as this is a test of
use and not intoxication. In addition, it is not
designed to detect newer drugs of abuse,
although some may cross-react with this assay.
– EKG
– Thyroid function
– Liver function tests
– RPR, folate, B12, thiamine
– Specific drug concentrations
Imagingr Brain imaging (CT, MRI)
r Chest x-ray
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr If suspicion exists for medical cause, should consider
procedures such as:
– Lumbar puncture
– EEG
r If hallucinations are from acute psychiatric illness or
decompensation of chronic psychiatric illness
– Obtain emergent psychiatric consultation
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Patients with a clear psychiatric history with
characteristic symptoms need minimal testing (CBC,
chemistries). However, patients with undifferentiated
hallucinations, especially those in high-risk groups,
require extensive testing.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
The primary goal of ED evaluation is to differentiate
psychiatric from nonpsychiatric cause of hallucination.
(See Psychosis, Medical vs. Psychiatric)
r More likely to be from psychiatric illness:
– Auditory and command hallucination
– Hallucinations and illusions incorporated into
delusional system
– Age of onset 13–40 yr old
– Flat affect
– Normal orientation
– Disorganized attention
r The following groups are considered to be at higher
risk for nonpsychiatric illness:
– Elderly
– History of substance abuse
– No pre-existing psychiatric history
– Presence of pre-existing medical disorders
– Lower socioeconomic level
r Visual hallucinations more common:
– Delirium
– Dementia
– Migraines
– Dopamine agonist therapy (i.e., carbidopa)
– Posterior cerebral infarcts
– Narcolepsy
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Observe details of patient’s environment not available
to hospital care team
r Disorganized living environment
r Drug paraphernalia
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Address ABC’s and any abnormal vital signs
(i.e., supplemental oxygen for hypoxia)
r Check FSBG
r Consider thiamine 100 mg IV/PO
r Treat acute agitation (see Agitation)
– De-escalation techniques
– Physical restraints
– Chemical sedation
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr If underlying medical cause identified
– Treat medical etiology
– These patients typically do not require
antipsychotic medications
r In patients with acute psychosis or decompensation
of chronic psychotic illness
– Use antipsychotics and benzodiazepines (see
Psychosis, Acute)
r In patients with hallucinations due to intoxication
with excited delirium
– General supportive care
– Benzodiazepines
r If dementia with hallucinations
– Treat underlying medical etiology, if any
– Atypical antipsychotics have benefits and harm
(CVA, extrapyramidal symptoms)
ALERT
When treating hallucinations with an excited
delirium due to acute intoxication (except for
ethanol), use benzodiazepines.
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteria
Disposition determined by medical condition or
psychiatric evaluation. Hallucinations from some
intoxications such as methamphetamine or cannabis
may persist even after drug is metabolized.
Admission Criteriar Medical condition requiring admission
r Acute psychiatric illness or decompensation of
chronic psychiatric illness requiring psychiatric
hospitalization
Discharge Criteriar Symptoms have resolved and reversible medical
cause (i.e., intoxication, UTI)
r Decompensation of chronic psychiatric condition has
been addressed, home environment appropriate and
mental health follow-up available.
Issues for Referral
Alcohol/drug treatment as appropriate
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
As appropriate for medical or chronic psychiatric
condition(s)
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Do not assume that auditory hallucinations are
always from psychiatric illness whereas visual,
tactile, olfactory, and gustatory hallucinations are
nonpsychiatric – always perform thorough
evaluation.
r Even though 10% of cases of schizophrenia occur in
patients older than 45, do not assume
hallucinations are from psychiatric cause in older
age group without extensive workup.
r Do not treat hallucinations with excited delirium
from an acute intoxication (except due to ethanol)
with antipsychotic agents.
ADDITIONAL READING
r El-Mallakh RS, Walker KL. Hallucinations,
psuedohallucinations, and parahallucinations.
Psychiatry. 2010;73(1):34–42.
r Piechniczek-Buczek J. Psychiatric emergencies in the
elderly population. Emerg Med Clin North Am.
2009;24(2):467–490.
r Sood TR, Mcstay CM. Evaluation of the psychiatric
patient. Emerg Med Clin North Am. 2009;27(4):
669–683.
r Sosland MD, Edelsohn GA. Hallucinations in
children and adolescents. Curr Psychiatry Rep.
2005;7(3):180–188.

hallucinations
r 368.16 Psychophysical visual disturbances
r 780.1 Hallucinations

disorder w hallucin

HALLUCINOGEN POISONING
Joanne C. Witsil
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Predominantly alters perception, cognition, and
mood
r All hallucinogens potentiate neurotransmitter
release or bind directly to receptors:
– Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; 5-HT): Many
hallucinogens are agonists or antagonists at 5-HT
receptor subtypes.
– Norepinephrine, N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA),
dopamine
ETIOLOGYr Most exposures are intentional
r Common hallucinogens:
– Indoleamine:
◦Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) (duration
6–12 hr)
◦Morning glory (Ipomoea spp.)
– Tryptamines:
◦Psilocybin (Psilocybe mushrooms); frequently
adulterated with LSD
◦N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT); 5-MeO-DMT
(“foxy-methoxy”), and other tryptamine
congeners
– Phenylethylamines (hallucinogenic
amphetamines):
◦Methylenedioxyamphetamine (MDA)
◦Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDEA)
◦Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA;
“ecstasy”; duration 8–12 hr)
◦Paramethoxyamphetamine
◦Dimethoxyamphetamine
◦Mescaline (peyote cactus); frequently
adulterated with LSD (duration 6–12 hr)
– Arylcycloalkylamines:
◦Phencyclidine (PCP), (duration is variable
11–96 hr in 1 report)
◦Ketamine, (duration depends on route of
administration 30–120 min)
– Anticholinergic:
◦Deadly nightshade (Atropa belladonna)
◦Jimsonweed (Datura stramonium)
– Other:
◦Piperazines: Benzyl piperazine (BZP) and
trifluoromethyl phenylpiperazine (TFMPP)
◦Dextromethorphan (DXM), (duration
3–6 hr)
◦Marijuana
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Considerable individual variation; effects may last
4–12 hr and ≤96 hr depending on agent/dose
r Symptoms characterized by sympathetic arousal
r Usually oriented and able to give history of exposure
even while having delusions
r Initial symptoms:
– Nausea, flushing, chills, tremor
r Neurologic symptoms:
– Restlessness and dizziness early after ingestion
– Desire to laugh (especially with Psilocybe
mushrooms)
– Anxiety, despair, helplessness, dread
– Intensified perceptions, visual
distortions/intensification
– Tactile distortions (especially with mescaline)
– Synesthesia (blending of sensory modalities, e.g.,
seeing sounds)
– Religious or mystical experiences
– Sleep disruption
r Neurologic signs:
– Unusual/bizarre behavior
– Speech disruption
– Mydriasis
– Piloerection
– Hyperreflexia
– Coma with massive exposure
– Convulsions:
◦Hallucinogenic amphetamines
◦Children who become hyperpyrexic after
Psilocybe mushroom ingestion
r Pulmonary:
– Mild tachypnea
– Respiratory arrest (with massive exposure)
r Cardiovascular:
– Tachycardia
– HTN (with hallucinogenic amphetamines)
– Dysrhythmia (with hallucinogenic amphetamines)
– Intracerebral hemorrhage (with hallucinogenic
amphetamines)
r GI:
– Nausea/vomiting (especially with mescaline)
r Metabolic:
– Hyperpyrexia:
◦Especially with MDMA use at “rave” clubs
◦Hepatic failure, renal failure, and disseminated
intravascular coagulopathy may follow.
◦May be lethal
– Hyponatremia: Has been reported with MDMA use
r Hematopoietic:
– Coagulopathies and hemorrhage at high doses
owing to disruption of platelet serotonin function
History
Identity of agent or agents used including:
r Method of usage
r Quantity
r Time of exposure
r Knowledge of place of exposure
Physical Examr Obtain accurate vital signs including temperature.
r Perform detailed neurologic and psychiatric exam
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Core temperature measurement and other vital signs
r ECG monitoring
r Determination of risk of rhabdomyolysis:
– Creatine kinase level
– Urine dip or myoglobin level
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose levels,
coagulation screen, arterial, or venous blood gas
r Urine toxicology screen:
– Rarely indicated
– Distinguishing between hallucinogens is of little
value
– Most hallucinogenic substances are not tested for
on routine drug screens
– Amphetamine screen is frequently negative for
hallucinogenic amphetamines (e.g., MDMA)
Imagingr Consider chest x-ray if looking for aortic dissection,
pulmonary aspiration, or trauma-related injury
r Consider CT of head if looking for intracranial bleeds
or lesions
r Consider abdominal x-ray if there is suspicion of
ingested packets
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Hypoglycemia
r Meningitis, encephalitis
r Sepsis
r Intracranial bleeds or lesions
r Withdrawal (ethanol, sedative–hypnotic, baclofen)
r Serotonin syndrome (especially with concomitant
serotonergic agents involved)
r Psychiatric illnesses:
– LSD associated with prolonged psychoses
resembling schizoaffective disorders
– Chronic amphetamine/cocaine abuse
– Steroids
r Infectious/febrile seizures in hyperpyretic child
Pediatric Considerations
Assess parent–child relationships for possibility of
neglect or abuse.
