HYDATIDIFORM MOLE
Emi M. Latham
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Noninvasive localized tumors arising from
trophoblastic tissue
r Can be associated with malignancy
r Twinning with normal pregnancy possible:
– Higher risk for persistent maternal disease and
metastasis
– Possible to have normal infant
r Complete mole:
– Estimated in 1/1,500 pregnancies
– Fetal tissue not present
– Diffuse chorionic villi swelling
– Diffuse trophoblastic hyperplasia
– Malignancy associated in 15–20%, usually lung
– Genetics:
◦Karyotype: 46,XX (90%); 46,XY (10%)
◦Paternal DNA expressed
◦Enucleate egg fertilized by 2 sperms or by a
haploid sperm that duplicates
r Partial mole:
– Estimated in 1/750 pregnancies
– Fetal or embryonic tissue often present
– Focal chorionic villi swelling
– Focal trophoblastic hyperplasia
– Malignancy associated in 4–12%
– Genetics:
◦Karyotype: 90% are triploid 69XXX, 69XXY ,
rarely 69XYY
◦Maternal and paternal DNA
◦Haploid ovum duplicates and is fertilized by
normal sperm, or haploid ovum fertilized by
2 sperms
ETIOLOGYr Largely unknown
r Extremes of maternal age best estimated risk factor:
– >35 yr old carries 5–10-fold risk
– <20 yr old
r Previous molar pregnancy carries 1–2% risk in
future pregnancies
r Frequency multiple times greater in Asian and Latin
American countries:
– 1 per 1,000–1,500 live births in US and Western
Europe
– Reported up to 1 per 12–500 live births in other
countries
r Deficiency in animal fat and vitamin A
r Smoking (>15 cigs/day)
r Maternal blood type AB, A, or B
r History of infertility, nulliparity
r Finding in 1 of 600 therapeutic abortions
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Usually exaggerated subjective symptoms of
pregnancy
r Complete mole:
– Vaginal bleeding, most common (97%):
◦Late 1st trimester
◦Usually painless and like “prune juice”
– May also have vaginal tissue passage:
◦Often described as grapelike vesicles
◦Usually occurs in 2nd trimester <20 wk
– Hyperemesis from high levels β-hCG
– Preeclampsia (27%):
◦Visual changes
◦HTN
◦Proteinuria
◦Hyperreflexia
◦Possibly convulsions
– Hyperthyroidism (7%):
◦Marked tachycardia, tremor
◦Due to high levels of β-hCG or thyroid
stimulating substance (thyrotropin)
– Acute respiratory distress (2%):
◦Tachypnea, diffuse rales, tachycardia, mental
status changes
◦Possible embolism of trophoblastic tissue
◦May also be due to cardiopulmonary changes
from preeclampsia, hyperthyroidism, or
iatrogenic fluid replacement
r Partial mole:
– Usually does not exhibit dramatic clinical features
of complete mole
– Frequently presents with symptoms similar to
patients with threatened or spontaneous abortion:
◦Vaginal bleeding
◦May have fetal heart tones
– Often presents at more advanced gestational age
History
Similar to that of pregnancy:
r Missed menstrual periods
r Positive pregnancy test
r Nausea, vomiting, vaginal bleeding
Physical Examr Uterine size/date discrepancy occurs in 50–66% of
cases
– Complete mole usually larger than dates would
indicate
– Partial mole can be smaller than dating suggests
r Ovarian masses:
– Present in complete moles, rarely in partial moles
– Usually from ovarian enlargement
– Multiple bilateral theca lutein cysts due to high
levels of β-hCG, usually found by US
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr hCG
– Complete mole β-hCG >100,000 mIU/mL, but
can be normal
– Partial mole: Usually lower than that seen with
normal pregnancy
– β-hCG >40,000 mIU/mL carries poor prognosis
r US:
– Complete mole:
◦Characteristic “snowstorm” vesicular pattern
◦Absence of fetal tissue and swelling of chorionic
villi with anechoic spaces
◦No amniotic fluid
◦Theca lutein cysts
– Bilateral, multiloculated
– Large at 6–12 cm
– Partial mole:
◦“Swiss-cheese” appearance
◦Cystic changes in placenta with scalloping of
villa and in shape of gestational sac
◦Fetus may be present
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr β-hCG
r Blood type, Rh, and cross-match
r CBC to assess for anemia and thrombocytopenia
r Coagulation profile to assess for disseminated
intravascular coagulation
r Electrolytes with BUN and creatinine
r LFTs
r TSH and thyroxin (free T4) if hyperthyroidism
suspected
r Urinalysis to evaluate for protein if preeclampsia
suspected
Imagingr US:
– May be performed at bedside
r CXR:
– Assess for pulmonary edema in acute respiratory
distress
– Check for metastatic disease
– For baseline study
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Pathology/histology:
r All conception products should be sent for formal
evaluation
r Products may be the only way to diagnose a partial
molar pregnancy
r Complete mole:
– Edematous chorionic villi
– Hyperplasia of trophoblasts
r Partial mole:
– Fetal tissue and vessels
– Amnion
– Edematous chorionic villi

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Threatened abortion
r Missed abortion
r Incomplete abortion
r Ectopic pregnancy
r Hyperthyroidism
r Hyperemesis gravidarum
r Hypertension
r Preeclampsia
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Ensure patent airway, provide oxygen
r IV access
r Treat convulsions appropriately with benzodiazepine
r Save passed tissue for histologic evaluation
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr IV access
r Cardiac monitoring
r Type and cross-match for blood, especially if patient
requires uterine extraction
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Acute respiratory distress:
– Intubation and mechanical ventilation
– CXR
r Hyperthyroidism:
– β-adrenergic blockers:
◦Administer before molar evacuation
◦Stress of anesthesia or surgery may precipitate
thyroid storm
r Preeclampsia/eclampsia:
– Convulsions
◦Administer benzodiazepine (diazepam)
◦Administer magnesium sulfate
– Hypertension:
◦Administer hydralazine or labetalol
r Coagulopathy:
– Transfuse with blood products as needed
– Human anti-D immunoglobulin (RhoGAM):
◦Although fetal blood not present in complete
mole, may be delay in distinguishing partial vs.
complete
r Suction curettage:
– Done by obstetrician, possibly in ED
– Curative in 80% of cases
– Method of choice in women wishing to preserve
fertility
– Oxytocin infusion to induce myometrial tone, may
require other uterotonic formulations
r Chemoprophylaxis:
– Very controversial
– Prescribed by obstetrician only for patients with
follow-up
– Usually used in high-risk complete mole or if
hormonal monitoring is unavailable
r Hysterectomy:
– Patients in older age group
– Patients not interested in keeping fertility
– High-risk disease
– Does not prevent possible metastasis
MEDICATIONr Diazepam: 0.2–0.4 mg/kg IV , or 0.3–0.5 mg PR, up
to 5–10 mg, for max. 30 mg
r Hydralazine: 5–10 mg IV q20min, up to 60 mg.
r Labetalol: 20 mg IV with doubled dosing q10m for
max. 300 mg
r Magnesium sulfate: 4–6 g IV over 15–20 min then
maintain 1–2 g/h
r Oxytocin: Postpartum bleeding, 10 U IM
r Propranolol: 1 mg IV increments q2m
r RhoGAM: 300 μg within 72 hr
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Enlargement of uterus beyond 16 wk of gestation
size:
– The larger the uterus, the greater the risk for
uterine perforation during suction curettage,
hemorrhage, and pulmonary complications due to
embolism
r Clinical evidence of preeclampsia hyperthyroidism,
respiratory distress
r Hysterectomy
r Partial molar pregnancy
r Hemodynamic instability
Discharge Criteriar Uncomplicated dilation and curettage of low-risk
and small-size mole in reliable patient
r Stress importance of follow-up
r Pelvic rest for 4–6 wk after uterine evacuation
r Recommend no pregnancies for 12 mo
r Future pregnancies should have early sonographic
evaluation due to increased risk in future
pregnancies
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Close follow-up and monitoring by OB-GYN
r Serial hCG levels:
– Obtained weekly for at least 4 wk, then monthly
intervals
– Levels should consistently drop and never increase
– If increase is noted, evaluation for metastatic
disease should ensue
r Use contraception
r US:
– Early in all future pregnancies
– Increased risk for future molar pregnancies
(1–1.5% with 2nd, 20% after 2 moles)
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Missed diagnosis in conjunction with:
– Normal pregnancy
– Preeclampsia, especially <24 wk gestation
– Hyperemesis with normal pregnancy
r The importance of follow-up must be stressed:
– If hCG is not followed, may lead to undiagnosed
metastatic disease
– 20% can develop malignancy

HYDROCARBON POISONING
James W. Rhee
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Main complication from hydrocarbon exposure is
aspiration:
– Hydrocarbon aspiration primarily affects central
nervous and respiratory systems.
r Physical properties determine type and extent of
toxicity:
– Viscosity (resistance to flow):
◦Higher aspiration risk from products with lower
viscosity
– Volatility (ability of a substance to vaporize):
◦Hypoxia from aromatic hydrocarbons displacing
alveolar air
– Surface tension (ability to adhere to itself at
liquid’s surface):
◦Low surface tension allows easy spread from
oropharynx to trachea, promoting aspiration
(e.g., mineral oil, seal oil).
r Volatile-substance abuse:
– Common solvents abused:
◦Typewriter correction fluid
◦Adhesive
◦Gasoline
◦Cigarette-lighter fluid
– Sniffing: Product inhaled directly from container
– Huffing: Product inhaled through a soaked rag
held to face
– Bagging: Product poured into bag and multiple
inhalations taken from bag
r Major classes of hydrocarbons:
– Aliphatics:
◦Include kerosene, mineral oil, seal oil, gasoline,
solvents, and paint thinners
◦Pulmonary toxicity via aspiration
◦Asphyxiation from gaseous methane and
butane by displacement of alveolar oxygen
– Halogenated hydrocarbons:
◦Include carbon tetrachloride and trichloroethane
◦Found in industrial settings as solvents
◦Well absorbed by lungs and gut
◦High toxicity
◦Liver and renal failure associated with ingestion
– Cyclics or aromatic compounds include toluene
and xylene:
◦Highly volatile and well absorbed from gut
◦Death from benzene reported with 15 mL
ingestion
– Terpenes or wood distillates include turpentine
and pine oil:
◦Significant GI tract absorption
◦Significant CNS depression
ETIOLOGYr Accidental exposures typical in young children
r Inhalation abuse of volatile hydrocarbons
r Suicide attempts in adolescents and adults
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Often asymptomatic at presentation
r Odor of hydrocarbons on breath
r Early: Euphoria:
– Disinhibition
r Late: Dysphoria:
– Ataxia
– Confusion
– Hallucination
r Sudden sniffing death:
– Cardiac arrest in volatile-substance abusers
secondary to hypersensitization of myocardium
leading to malignant dysrhythmias on adrenergic
stimulation
r Pulmonary:
– Mild to severe respiratory distress
– Cyanosis
– Aspiration (primary complication)
r CNS:
– Intoxication
– Euphoria
– Slurred speech
– Lethargy
– Coma
r GI tract:
– Local mucosal irritation
– Gastritis
– Diarrhea
r Cardiac:
– Tachycardia
– Dysrhythmias (volatile-substance abuse)
r Dermal:
– Local erythema
– Maculopapular or vesicular eruptions
– Defatting dermatitis from chronic skin exposure
– Huffer face rash in chronic abusers
Historyr Route, type, quantity, and time of exposure:
– Determine intentionality and coingestions
r Symptoms:
– Vomiting, respiratory distress, mental status
change or pain
r Bystander actions or pre-hospital interventions
Physical Examr Evaluate for airway compromise in patients with
decreased level of consciousness and vomiting
r Respiratory symptoms generally occur within 30 min
but are frequently delayed several hours
r Monitor for hypoxia, hypotension, and cardiac
dysrhythmias
r Cyanosis and hypoxia suggest respiratory failure but
may result from methemoglobinemia
r Temperature may be elevated at presentation
following aspiration and indicates pneumonitis:
– Fever after 48 hr suggests bacterial superinfection
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Obtain information on the following:
r Product: Exact name on label, manufacturer, and
ingredients
r Nature of ingestion or exposure: Accidental or
intentional
r Estimated amount ingested
r In industrial settings, Material Safety Data Sheets
(MSDSs)
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
ECG for intoxicated volatile-substance abusers
Labr Pulse oximetry:
– If abnormal, follow with arterial blood gases.
r Electrolytes; BUN, creatinine, and glucose levels;
and liver function tests:
– For halogenated and aromatic hydrocarbon
exposure
– Metabolic acidosis
– Hypokalemia
r Carboxyhemoglobin levels for methylene chloride
exposure:
– Methylene chloride metabolized to carbon
monoxide in vivo
Imaging
CXR:
r Abnormalities visible 20 min–24 hr after exposure
(usually by 6 hr)
r Increased bronchovascular marking and bibasilar
and perihilar infiltrates (typical)
r Lobar consolidation (uncommon)
r Pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, and pleural
effusion (rare)
r Pneumatoceles resolve over weeks
r Repeat chest radiograph if worsening respiratory
symptoms
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Caustic, pesticide, or toxic alcohol ingestions
r Accidental vs. intentional:
– Psychiatric evaluation for all intentional ingestions
r Child neglect:
– Poor supervision or unsafe home environment
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Decontaminate clothes, skin, and hair of any
hydrocarbon exposure
r Do not induce emesis.
r Ipecac contraindicated owing to increased risk of
aspiration
r Keep volatile-substance abusers calm and avoid
interventions that cause anxiety or distress.
r Management of accidental hydrocarbon exposures
at home controversial:
– <1% require physician intervention.
– For asymptomatic or quickly asymptomatic after
ingestion with reliable observer available
– Applies only when exact product and its
components are known and there is no indication
for gastric decontamination or possibility for
delayed organ toxicity

HYDROCARBON POISONING
H
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs
r IV access and fluid resuscitation if hypotensive or
ongoing fluid losses
r Oxygen
r Cardiac monitor
r Naloxone, thiamine, D50W (or Accu-Chek) if altered
mental status
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Supportive care
r Treat respiratory symptoms:
– Oxygen
– Nebulized
– β2-agonist for bronchospasm (albuterol)
– Endotracheal intubation and mechanical
ventilation for respiratory failure
– Steroids not indicated for bronchospasm
– Avoid using epinephrine in volatile-substance
abusers as it may precipitate dysrhythmias
ALERT
r Gastric evacuation not indicated for vast majority
of hydrocarbon ingestions:
– Increases risk of aspiration which can cause
significant chemical pneumonitis
– Aspiration risk higher than risk of systemic
absorption for aliphatic hydrocarbon mixtures,
which account for most ingestions
– Contraindicated if spontaneous emesis has
occurred
– Small-bore nasogastric tube aspiration of
stomach contents may be indicated for some
hydrocarbon (CHAMP) ingestions that have
systemic toxicity:
◦CHAMP: Camphor, halogenated
hydrocarbons, aromatic hydrocarbons, metals
(e.g., lead, mercury), pesticides
◦Only for very recent ingestions (60 min)
◦Benefit of doing this procedure needs to be
weighed heavily against risk of aspiration and
subsequent pneumonitis.
◦Cuffed-tube endotracheal intubation for
airway protection during lavage if no gag
reflex or altered mental status
r Activated charcoal does not bind to hydrocarbons
well, and is not indicated except for significant
life-threatening coingestants
r Cathartics not indicated:
– Diarrhea common with hydrocarbon
MEDICATIONr Albuterol 2.5–5 mg NEB (peds: 0.15–0.3 mg/kg) for
bronchospasm
r Dextrose: D50W 1 ampule of 50 mL or 25 g (peds:
D25W 2–4 mL/kg) IV
r Naloxone (Narcan): 2 mg (peds: 0.1 mg/kg) IV or IM
initial dose
r Thiamine (vitamin B1): 100 mg (peds: 50 mg) IV or
IM
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Symptomatic patients
r Patients with potential delayed organ toxicity
(carbon tetrachloride or other toxic additives)
Discharge Criteriar Observe for 6 hr then discharge:
– Asymptomatic patients with normal chest
radiograph and pulse oximetry findings
– Asymptomatic patients with abnormal CXR and
normal oxygenation and respiratory rate may be
discharged if reliable follow-up is ensured.
– Symptomatic patients on presentation who quickly
become asymptomatic
r Observe volatile-substance abusers until mental
status clears.
Issues for Referral
Psychiatry consultation as needed
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Follow up in 24 hr for patients who remain
asymptomatic after a minimum of 6 hr observation
r Asymptomatic patients with an abnormal CXR
should have a repeat study in 24 hr
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Main complication from hydrocarbon exposure is
aspiration:
– Aspiration risk is inversely related to viscosity and
surface tension and directly related to volatility
r Provide external decontamination
r Gastric decontamination is rarely indicated
r Avoid induced emesis and cathartics
r Observe patients a minimum of 6 hr post ingestion
for evidence of toxicity
r Admit symptomatic patients to hospital
r Admit when there is potential for delayed organ
toxicity
– CHAMP

HYDROCELE
Jessica L. Osterman
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Most common cause of painless scrotal swelling.
r Classified as congenital or acquired (secondary):
– Congenital result from a patent process vaginalis
and communication between tunica vaginalis and
peritoneal cavity:
◦Normally occurs spontaneously and most are
closed by 2 yr of age
– Acquired occur secondary to interscrotal infection,
neoplasm, inguinal or scrotal surgery, or regional
or systemic disease.
r Communicating hydrocele:
– Patent processus vaginalis
– Scrotum fills and empties with peritoneal fluid
depending on body position and intraperitoneal
pressures.
r Noncommunicating hydrocele is due to production
of serous fluid by a disease process or impaired
absorption within the scrotum itself
ETIOLOGYr Imbalance between production and resorption of
fluid within the space between tunica vaginalis and
tunica albuginea.
r Disease processes causing adult noncommunicating
hydrocele include:
– Epididymitis
– Hypoalbuminemia
–T B
– Trauma
– Mumps
– Spermatic vein ligation
– In developing world, hydrocele is primarily caused
by infections such as Wuchereria bancrofti or Loa
Loa (filariasis is the cause of most hydroceles
worldwide)
– Rarely malignancy (1st-degree testicular neoplasm
or lymphoma)
r Rare etiology is the abdominoscrotal hydrocele that
may cause hydroureter or unilateral limb edema
owing to compression:
– US reveals single sac extending from scrotum into
abdominal cavity via the deep inguinal ring.
Pediatric Considerations
r Congenital in 6% of newborn boys
r Usually diagnosed in newborn nursery
r Caused by patent processus vaginalis, a structure
that remains patent in 85% of newborns
r May vary in size owing to position or crying:
– Patients may present with history of scrotal mass
that has resolved.
r Most close by the age of 2 yr
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Painless scrotal swelling with a sensation of pulling,
dragging, or heaviness.
History
History and exam with special attention to identifying
torsion of testicle.
Physical Examr Mass may be soft and doughy or firm depending on
the amount of fluid present.
r Initial evaluation includes transillumination of
affected side (looking for a homogeneous area
without internal shadows):
– This is rapidly being replaced as diagnostic test of
choice by bedside US.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Bedside US:
– Allows visualization of hydrocele as well as of
testicle
– Especially in cases of massive fluid collection,
bedside US should be the diagnostic test of choice.
– May help to identify an underlying mass
r Because of possibility in adults that a hydrocele may
be owing to a primary neoplasm, the testicle must
be palpated in its entirety.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
No specific lab testing is indicated unless underlying
cause demands it (UA, AFP , hCG).
Imaging
US is diagnostic and allows visualization of testicular
anatomy:
r Appears as large anechoic fluid-filled space
surrounding the anterolateral testicle
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Epididymitis
r Indirect inguinal hernia
r Orchitis
r Testicular neoplasm
r Testicular torsion
r Varicocele
TREATMENT
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Stabilization should focus on underlying cause (e.g.,
trauma).
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURES
Appropriate exam of testicle to exclude primary
neoplasm and referral.
MEDICATION
Treat underlying cause.

HYDROCEPHALUS
Richard S. Krause
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Increased volume of CSF in cranial cavity
r Cerebral atrophy also leads to increased CSF in the
cranial vault but CSF pressure is not increased
r Obstructive hydrocephalus is the most common
form:
– Obstruction is within ventricular system or in
subarachnoid space
r Acute obstructive hydrocephalus may cause rapid
rise in intracranial pressure (ICP), rapidly leading to
death or permanent cerebral damage
r Nonobstructive hydrocephalus causes subacute
symptoms and is a potentially treatable form of
dementia
r Also described as “communicating” and
“noncommunicating”:
– Communicating hydrocephalus: Flow of CSF is
blocked after it exits the ventricles (ventricles still
“communicate”)
– Noncommunicating hydrocephalus: Flow of CSF
blocked along 1 or more of the passages
connecting the ventricles (ventricles do not
“communicate”)
ETIOLOGYr Obstructive hydrocephalus:
– Obstruction of:
◦Aqueduct of Sylvius (most common, both lateral
ventricles and 3rd ventricle dilated, 4th ventricle
is spared)
– Aqueductal stenosis can be congenital or acquired
(tumor, subarachnoid hemorrhage, post
meningitis, idiopathic)
◦Foramen of Monro (lateral ventricles dilated,
usually both but may be unilateral)
◦Foramina of Luschka and Magendie (4th
ventricle blocked followed by 3rd and lateral
ventricles)
◦Subarachnoid space around brainstem
(postinfectious or postsubarachnoid
hemorrhage [post-SAH] entire system dilated)
– Acute presentations usually secondary to CSF
shunt blockage, SAH, or severe head trauma
r Nonobstructive hydrocephalus:
– Normal pressure hydrocephalus:
◦Increased intracranial volume of CSF without
intracranial hypertension
◦Increased ventricular size on CT (without
volume loss as in atrophy)
◦Sometimes called “chronic hydrocephalus”
◦Usually occurs due to inadequate CNS
absorption
r Pediatric hydrocephalus:
– Congenital hydrocephalus owing to neonatal
hemorrhage, congenital malformations, or
acquired post meningitis secondary to
subarachnoid scarring around brainstem
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Obstructive hydrocephalus:
– Headache
– Nausea and vomiting
– Decreased level of consciousness
– Urinary incontinence
– Ocular palsies
– Papilledema, decreased vision
– Pupillary dilation
– Cushing response:
◦Raised systolic pressure and bradycardia
secondary to increased ICP
– Pediatric patients:
◦Full fontanelle, irritability, and lethargy
– BP often elevated
– May present like nonobstructive hydrocephalus if
obstruction develops slowly
r Nonobstructive hydrocephalus:
– Progressive dementia, somnolence
– Gait disturbance
– Urinary incontinence
– Impaired upward gaze
– Generalized weakness and lethargy
– Dementia is often insidious with subacute onset of
progressive intellectual deterioration
– No headache or papilledema
Pediatric Considerations
r Pediatric patients increase CSF volume slowly:
– Craniomegaly
– Retardation
– Prominent scalp veins
– Impaired upward gaze (setting sun sign)
Historyr Onset of symptoms
r History of CSF shunt
r Nausea/vomiting
r Headache
r Weakness
r Confusion
r Visual changes
r Incontinence of urine
Physical Examr Thorough neurologic exam:
– Motor
– Sensation
– Deep tendon reflexes
– Gait
– Cranial nerve exam
– Papilledema may be seen
r Confusion
r Decreased level of consciousness
r Palpate CSF shunt if present
– Malfunction indicated by failure to compress
(distal shunt malfunction) or failure to refill
(proximal shunt obstruction)
r Full anterior fontanelle in children:
– Other findings as noted in Signs and Symptoms
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
CT scan of the head w/o contrast will allow
assessment of ventricular size and symmetry:
r Aid in diagnosis of cerebral edema, mass lesions,
and hemorrhage
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Lumbar puncture (LP) is typically performed after head
CT (for nonobstructive causes):
r Opening pressure on LP will reflect increased ICP in
nonobstructive hydrocephalus.
r CSF should be sent for routine tests if infection is
suspected.
– Gram stain, culture, protein, glucose, and cell
count
Imaging
MRI of brain reveals ventricular size and symmetry and
may allow for better visualization of masses than CT
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
LP may be indicated
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Acute cerebral infarction or hemorrhage
r Intracranial infection
r Mass effect from fast-growing tumor or hematoma
r Dementia or delirium of other cause
r Toxic or metabolic encephalopathies
Pediatric Considerations
r Suspect hydrocephalus in an infant whose head
circumference is increasing excessively, has
progressive lethargy, persistent vomiting, impaired
upward gaze, etc.
r Congenital anomalies:
– Dandy–Walker malformation
– Arnold–Chiari malformation
– Meningomyelocele
– Choroid plexus papilloma
– Hypoplasia/dysfunction of arachnoid villi
r Infections:
– Rubella
– Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
– Toxoplasmosis
– Syphilis
– Bacterial meningitis
– Reye syndrome
r Tumors, especially posterior fossa tumors:
– Medulloblastoma
– Astrocytoma
– Ependymoma
r Hemorrhage:
– Intraventricular
– Subarachnoid

HYDROCEPHALUS
H
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Cautions:
r Elevated ICP/hydrocephalus cannot be definitively
diagnosed in the field
r When it is suspected, supplemental O2 and airway
management (if needed) are indicated
r Patients should be transported with head elevated
at ∼30◦
– HOB should not be elevated if patient is
hypotensive for concern about decreased cerebral
perfusion
– Initial treatment for hypotension is usually volume
expansion with normal saline
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Signs of impending herniation:
– Rapid-sequence intubation (RSI)
◦Thiopental or etomidate for induction
◦Paralytic choice is controversial
◦Depolarizing agents (succinylcholine) may
transiently increase ICP , this effect may not be
clinically significant
◦Nondepolarizing agents (rocuronium,
vecuronium) may be preferable
– Controlled ventilation to maintain PaCO2 at ∼35
mm Hg
– Maintain systolic BP >100 mm Hg (adult) with
fluids or pressors.
– Mannitol
r If a CSF shunt is present and there are signs of
impending herniation:
– Forced pumping of shunt chamber:
◦Flush device with 1 mL saline to remove distal
obstruction
◦Slow drainage of CSF from reservoir to achieve
pressure <20 cm H2O
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Hydrocephalus does not generally require ED
treatment unless:
– Signs of impending herniation
– Acute shunt malfunction
r Definitive treatment involves either placement (or
revision) of shunting device or treatment of
underlying cause (e.g., tumor)
r Neurologic symptoms (gait disturbance) or severe
headache associated with normal pressure

r Patients who are agitated or intubated should be

HYPERBARIC OXYGEN THERAPY
Trevonne M. Thompson
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Administration of 100% oxygen at>1 atm (typically
2–3 atm)
r Mechanisms of action:
– Increases oxygen availability at the cellular level:
◦Breathing 100% oxygen at 3 atm supplies
enough dissolved oxygen to support life without
hemoglobin.
– Compresses formed gas bubbles (in cases of air
embolism or decompression sickness)
r 2 types of hyperbaric oxygen chambers:
– Monoplace:
◦Accommodates 1 supine patient
◦Technician outside the chamber for monitoring
◦Compressed with 100% oxygen
– Multiplace:
◦Holds multiple patients
◦Holds attendants who “dive” with the patients
◦Airlocks available for medication/equipment
transfer outside of the chamber
◦Compressed with air—patients breath oxygen
by face mask, endotracheal tube, or face hood.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Indications for hyperbaric oxygen therapy:
r Arterial gas embolism
r Decompression sickness
r Carbon monoxide toxicity
r Soft tissue infections:
– Clostridial myonecrosis
– Necrotizing fasciitis
– Refractory osteomyelitis
– Chronic nonhealing wounds
r Wound care:
– Radiation-induced tissue injury
– Crush injuries
– Thermal burns
– Compromised skin grafts and flaps
ALERT
The ED physician should focus on arterial
embolism, decompression sickness, and carbon
monoxide toxicity as uses for hyperbaric oxygen.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Determine need for hyperbaric oxygen therapy as
described above.
r Perform a comprehensive physical exam to screen
for contraindications to therapy and to establish a
pretreatment baseline exam.
r Contraindications to therapy:
– Untreated pneumothorax is the absolute
contraindication:
◦May convert to a tension pneumothorax
– Cardiovascular instability:
◦Unstable patient cannot be treated in a
monoplace chamber.
◦Such a patient may be treated in multiplace
chamber if benefit outweighs risk.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Arterial blood gas:
r To evaluate for hypoxia in appropriate cases
Imaging
Chest radiography:
r To evaluate for occult pneumothorax

HYPERCALCEMIA
Matthew A. Wheatley rRyan A. Stroder
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Severity depends on serum calcium level and rate of
increase
r 0.1–1% of patients on routine screening
r Most cases mild (<12 mg/dL) and asymptomatic
r Hypercalcemic crisis, usually >14 mg/dL, causes
serious signs and symptoms
r Calcium in bloodstream in 3 forms:
– Ionized: 45%
– Bound to protein (primarily albumin): 40%
– Bound to other anions: 15%
r Ionized calcium—only physiologically active form
ETIOLOGYr Primary hyperparathyroidism
r Malignancy
r Miscellaneous
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Neurologic:
– Headache
– Fatigue, lethargy
– Weakness
– Difficulty concentrating
– Confusion
– Depression, paranoia
r Renal:
– Polyuria, polydipsia
– Complaints related to oliguric renal failure
– Chronic, complaints related to:
◦Renal calculi
◦Nephrocalcinosis
◦Interstitial nephritis
r GI:
– Anorexia
– Nausea, vomiting
– Abdominal pain
– Constipation
– Chronic, complaints related to:
◦Peptic ulcer disease
◦Pancreatitis
r Dermatologic:
– Pruritus
– Mnemonic: “Stones, Bones, Groans, Thrones and
Psychiatric Overtones,” “bones” refers to bone
pain and “thrones” refers to polyuria.
Pediatric Considerations
r Failure to thrive
r Slow development
r Mental retardation may ensue
Physical Examr Neurologic:
– Irritability
– Lethargy
– Stupor
– Coma
– Hyporeflexia
r Cardiovascular:
– Hypotension, if severely volume depleted, or HTN
– Sinus bradycardia
– Cardiac arrest with severe hypercalcemia (rare)
r Renal:
– Signs of dehydration
r Dermatologic:
– Band keratopathy
– Ectopic calcification
Pediatric Considerations
r Characteristic facies: Pug nose, fat nasal bridge,
“cupid’s bow” upper lip
r Hypotonia
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Ionized and total serum calcium levels, albumin
levels:
– Normal total calcium level is <10.5 mg/dL
– Must correct for calcium that is protein bound,
primarily to albumin
– Corrected total calcium (mg/dL) = measured total
calcium (mg/dL) + 0.8 × [4.0 – albumin
concentration (g/dL)]
r Electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, glucose
– Possible oliguric renal failure
r ECG:
– Shortening of QT interval
– Prolongation of PR interval
– QRS widening
– Accentuated side effects of digoxin
– Sinus bradycardia, bundle branch block, AV block,
cardiac arrest with severe hypercalcemia (rare)
– Can cause Osborn J-wave at the end of QRS
complex that is usually associated with
hypothermia
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Phosphate
r Protein
r Urinalysis
r Parathyroid hormone (PTH) level:
– If elevated or high normal, likely primary
hyperparathyroidism.
–I f <20 pg/mL, consider testing PTH-related
peptide and vitamin D metabolites.
r Vitamin D metabolites, if suspected
– 25-hydroxy vitamin D (calcidiol):
◦If elevated, consider exogenous source (i.e.,
meds, vitamins, supplements).
– 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D (calcitriol):
◦If elevated, consider lymphoma or sarcoid
r Digoxin level, if taking
r Thyroid function tests
Imagingr CT head for altered mental status
r Chest x-ray and workup for occult malignancy, if no
other cause for hypercalcemia
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Parathyroidectomy:
r For primary hyperparathyroidism resulting in
symptomatic or severe hypercalcemia
r Some patients require urgent parathyroidectomy.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Primary hyperparathyroidism:
– Most common cause among outpatients
– Parathyroid adenoma 80%; hyperplasia 15%;
carcinoma 5%
– Usually mild, <11.2 mg/dL
– Patients can be asymptomatic or have chronically
elevated calcium
– Increased bone resorption, relative decrease in
calcium excretion, increased intestinal calcium
absorption
r Malignancy:
– Most common cause in hospitalized patients
– Usually a rapid rise in serum calcium
– Patients are more often symptomatic
– Higher serum calcium concentrations
– Most common paraneoplastic complication of
cancer
– Common tumors causing hypercalcemia: Breast,
lung, colon, stomach, cervix, uterus, ovary, kidney,
bladder, head and neck, multiple myeloma, and
lymphoma
– Most commonly from production of PTH-related
protein with similar actions
– May result from production of other
bone-resorbing substances by tumor
– May result from local effects of osteolytic skeletal
metastasis
r Miscellaneous:
– Hypercalcemia associated with granulomatous
diseases
– Excessive calcium supplements
– Thiazide diuretics causing increased renal
reabsorption
– Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia
– Acute vitamin A intoxication
– Exogenous vitamin D intake
– Milk-alkali syndrome from excessive ingestion of
calcium and nonabsorbable antacids, such as milk
or calcium carbonate
– Long-term lithium therapy
– Renal transplantation
– Hyperthyroidism
– Acute tubular necrosis

HYPERCALCEMIA
H
Pediatric Considerations
Differential diagnosis: Differences from adults:
r Primary hyperparathyroidism:
– Less common than in adults
r Infantile hypercalcemia:
– Uncertain cause
– Possibly hypersensitivity and in utero excessive
exposure to vitamin D
r Immobilization hypercalcemia:
– Typically adolescent who is growing rapidly
– Prolonged immobilization, especially in traction,
leads to hypercalciuria and then hypercalcemia
– Presumably from increased bone resorption with
decreased or arrested bone mineralization
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Routine stabilization techniques
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs, IV access, oxygen, cardiac monitor
r 0.9% NS 1 L bolus (20 mL/kg) for hypotension or
severe dehydration
r Naloxone, thiamine, D50W (or stat serum glucose
measurement) for altered mental status
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr General:
– Immediate therapy for severe hypercalcemia
(corrected total >14 mg/dL) regardless of
symptoms, or for symptomatic hypercalcemia
– Asymptomatic, mild hypercalcemia does not
require emergency treatment
r Restoration of IV volume:
– Isotonic saline:
◦200–300 mL/hr adjusted to maintain urine
output 100–150 mL/hr
– Often need 2–5 L/day
– Bedside vigilance necessary to prevent fluid
overload
– Correct other electrolyte abnormalities
– Cardiovascular status of patient may necessitate
central venous pressure monitoring to adjust fluid
administration rates
r Renal elimination:
– After volume expansion and if needed to avoid
overload, administer loop diuretics (furosemide)
– Avoid thiazide diuretics
– May need peritoneal or hemodialysis against a
low calcium dialysate in renal failure
r Inhibition of osteoclastic activity:
– Reduce mobilization of calcium from bone
– Administer drug therapy when corrected calcium
level >14 mg/dL or signs or symptoms
– First-line drug therapy:
◦Bisphosphonates: Pamidronate (more potent
and possibly less toxic), etidronate
◦Calcitonin: Rapid onset but modest decrease in
levels
– Other potential drug therapy:
◦Plicamycin: Efficacious but numerous side effects
◦Hydrocortisone: Especially useful with
malignancies, granulomatous disorders, or
vitamin D intoxication
– Encourage ambulation in appropriate patients
r Treat underlying disorder:
– Parathyroidectomy for primary
hyperparathyroidism resulting in symptomatic or
severe hypercalcemia
– Discontinue medication if cause of hypercalcemia
MEDICATION
First Liner Calcitonin: 4 IU/kg IM/SC q12h
r Etidronate: 7.5 mg/kg over 4 hr daily for 3–7 days IV
r Furosemide: 10–40 mg q6–8h (peds: 1–2 mg/kg) IV
r Pamidronate: Single 2–24 hr infusion of 60–90 mg
IV (peds: Consult pediatrician)
Second Liner Gallium nitrate: Continuous infusion of 200
mg/m2/d for 5 days IV
r Hydrocortisone: 200–400 mg/d IV for 3–5 days
(peds: Consult pediatrician)
r Plicamycin: 25 μg/kg/d over 4–6 hr IV for 3–8 doses
Pediatric Considerations
r In infants, loop diuretics are rarely necessary and
possibly harmful as they may decrease glomerular
filtration rate and worsen hypercalcemia
r Bisphosphonates have not been extensively studied
in pediatrics but do appear to be safe
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Corrected total calcium level >13 mg/dL
r Signs or symptoms attributed to hypercalcemia,
especially EKG changes
r Monitored bed or ICU for corrected level >14 or
serious signs and symptoms
Discharge Criteria
Corrected calcium level <13 mg/dL and no signs or
symptoms of hypercalcemia
Issues for Referralr Rapid follow-up arranged to determine cause and
long-term therapy
r Consultation with endocrinologist should be
considered
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Fluid hydration
r Watch for mental status changes
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Make decisions based on symptoms or corrected Ca
levels
r All patients with serum Ca >14 mg/dL require
treatment regardless of symptoms
r Pay careful attention to EKG changes
r Careful monitoring is required for patients receiving
IV volume repletion:
– They often require a large volume of fluid but care
must be taken to avoid volume overload
ADDITIONAL READING
r Ariyan CE, Sosa JA. Assessment and management of
patients with abnormal calcium. Crit Care Med.
2004;32(suppl 4):S146–S154.
r Inzucchi SE. Management of hypercalcemia.
Diagnostic workup, therapeutic options for
hyperparathyroidism and other common causes.
Postgrad Med. 2004;115:27–36.
r Lietman SA, Germain-Lee EL, Levine MA.
Hypercalcemia in children and adolescents. Curr
Opin Pediatr. 2010;22(4):508–515.
r Marx JA, Hockberger RS, Walls RM, eds. Rosen’s
Emergency Medicine. Philadelphia, PA: Elsevier;
2009.

HYPEREMESIS GRAVIDARUM
David Della-Giustina
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Hyperemesis gravidarum is the most severe form
along the continuum of nausea and vomiting of
pregnancy
r Also known as pernicious vomiting of pregnancy
r Characterized by unexplained intractable vomiting
and dehydration
r Occurs in 0.3–2% of pregnancies
r Diagnosis of exclusion
ETIOLOGYr Exact cause unknown
r Possible causes include the following:
– Elevated gestational hormone levels of human
chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and/or estradiol
– Thyrotoxicosis
– Upper GI motility dysfunction
– Hepatic abnormalities
– Autonomic nervous system dysfunction
– Psychological factors
– Helicobacter pylori infection
– Genetic predisposition
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Nausea and vomiting during pregnancy affects
between 50% and 90%
r Onset of symptoms by the 4th–10th wk of
pregnancy with resolution by the 20th:
– Symptoms after the 20th wk should raise one’s
suspicion of another process
r Peak onset is at 8–12 wks
r Hyperemesis gravidarum is a clinical diagnosis
defined by the following:
– Persistent and severe nausea and vomiting
– Dehydration
– Weight loss of >5% of total body weight
– Lab findings: Increased urine specific gravity,
ketonuria, electrolyte disturbances, ketonemia
Historyr Onset of vomiting
r Gestational history:
– Similar symptoms in prior pregnancies
r Last menstrual period
r Oral intake
r Urine output
r Bloody or bilious vomiting
r Abdominal pain
r Vaginal bleeding
r Risk factors include the following:
– History of motion sickness
– Younger age
– Migraine headaches
– Symptoms earlier in the day
– Low prepregnancy body mass index
– More common in nulliparous women
– 15% recurrence rate if manifested in previous
pregnancy
Physical Examr Observe for signs of dehydration
r Abdominal tenderness
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr History and physical exam with special attention to
state of hydration and abdominal exam for other
diagnoses associated with vomiting (appendicitis,
cholecystitis, etc.)
r Obtain an uncontaminated urinalysis
r If patient has unremitting vomiting for >24 hr,
obtain a CBC, electrolytes, renal function, liver
enzymes, bilirubin, and lipase
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Urinalysis:
– Increased specific gravity and ketonuria
– Presence of glucose mandates checking serum
glucose to rule out diabetes
– Presence of bilirubin mandates a search to rule
out hepatobiliary cause for the vomiting
r CBC:
– May have an elevated hematocrit owing to
dehydration
– WBC is usually normal
r Electrolytes:
– Elevated BUN indicating volume depletion;
elevated creatinine if renal failure present
– Hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypochloremia, and
metabolic alkalosis from loss of HCl in emesis
r Liver function tests:
– Mild increases in bilirubin may occur, but should
be <4 mg/dL.
– AST and ALT may also be mildly elevated, but not
>100 IU/L
r Amylase/lipase:
– In 1 study, amylase was elevated in 24% of
patients with hyperemesis gravidarum; however,
the amylase was salivary in origin; use lipase
rather than amylase to evaluate for pancreatitis
r TSH
r Serum hCG levels are not indicated if known
intrauterine pregnancy
Imagingr US when 1st trimester US has not been performed
to evaluate for:
– Molar pregnancy
– Multiple gestations
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Pyelonephritis; most commonly missed
r Gastroenteritis; gastroparesis; intestinal obstruction;
Mallory–Weiss tear
r Hepatobiliary disease; hepatitis, cholecystitis, fatty
liver of pregnancy, achalasia
r Pancreatitis
r Appendicitis
r Diabetic ketoacidosis
r Hyperthyroidism; hyperparathyroidism
r Uremia; persistent nausea and vomiting are seen
with severe renal dysfunction.
r Pseudotumor cerebri
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr IV , monitor if signs of significant volume depletion
r IV hydration
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
IV hydration using a crystalloid solution (LR or NS)
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr IV hydration using LR or NS
r Dextrose may be added to help break cycle of ketosis
r Treat until patient is no longer symptomatic from
hypovolemia
r Antiemetics administered IV are given to break the
vomiting cycle
r Most commonly used medications:
– Metoclopramide:
◦FDA category B
– Promethazine and prochlorperazine:
◦Both FDA category C
◦Recent FDA warning regarding complications of
IV promethazine administration
– Ondansetron:
◦FDA category B with recent warning about the
risk of prolonged QT syndrome and the
recommendation for ECG monitoring of the
patient with electrolyte abnormalities such as
hypokalemia or hypomagesemia
– These have been used extensively in pregnancy,
and there is little or no evidence associated with
increased risk of congenital anomalies
– Antiemetics are preferable to the risk of prolonged
ketosis and hypovolemia

H

– Metoclopramide (category B): 10 mg PO q6–8h
PRN
– Prochlorperazine (category C): 5–10 mg PO q6h
or 25 mg PR q12h PRN
– Promethazine (category C): 12.5–25 mg PO or PR
q4–6h PRN
– Pyridoxine (vitamin B6; category A): 25 mg PO TID
(OTC)

bid/tid

usually with pyridoxine (vitamin B6)

× 3 days and then taper. Should be prescribed in

DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Inability to tolerate oral intake after treatment
r Inability to control the emesis despite treatment
r Severe electrolyte or metabolic disturbances
r At highest risk <8 wk gestation

able to tolerate oral intake and have adequate
follow-up
r Correction of dehydration and associated symptoms
r Decreased ketonuria
r Reassure patient that their symptoms are common
and usually self-limited
r Patients should be counseled that frequent, small
meals may be helpful:
– Meals should contain simple carbohydrates and
be low in fats
– Avoid irritant or spicy foods
r Home IV therapy can be arranged if indicated

thiamine/day to help prevent Wernicke
encephalopathy; a supplement of 50 mg/day PO is
recommended
r Risk for 1st trimester fetal loss is less in women with
hyperemesis

r Other diagnoses should be explored in patients
presenting after 9 wk gestation with nausea and
vomiting as initial symptoms
r The use of PICC lines has been shown to carry
significantly increased risk of maternal morbidity
when compared to patients managed with either
NG tube or medications alone
r Be aware of the risk for central pontine myelinosis in
hyponatremia patients when replacing sodium
r Wernicke encephalopathy is the most devastating
maternal complication:
– Patients may not have the classic triad of ataxia,
nystagmus, and dementia. Be concerned for any
evidence of apathy or confusion
– Be sure to give patients thiamine 100 mg IV for
any patient who presents with apathy or confusion

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Potassium distribution:
– Extracellular space: 2%
– Intracellular space: 98%
r Potassium excretion:
– Renal: 90%
– GI: 10%
r Renal (80–90%) and extrarenal mechanisms
maintain normal plasma concentration between 3.5
and 5 mmol/L.
r Renal excretion of potassium affected by:
– Dietary intake
– Distal renal tubular function
– Acid–base balance
– Mineralocorticoids
r Regulation between intracellular and extracellular
potassium balance is affected by:
– Acid–base balance
– Insulin
– Mineralocorticoids
– Catecholamines
– Osmolarity
– Drugs

– Most common cause: Renal failure (acute or
chronic)
– Distal tubular diseases:
◦Acute interstitial nephritis
◦Renal transplant rejection
◦Sickle cell nephropathy
◦Renal tubular acidosis (diabetes)
– Mineralocorticoid deficiency:
◦Addison disease
◦Hypoaldosteronism
– Drugs:
◦ACE inhibitors/angiotensin receptor blockers
◦β-blockers
◦Potassium-sparing diuretics
◦NSAIDs
◦Cyclosporine
◦High-dose trimethoprim
◦Lithium toxicity

– Metabolic acidosis:
◦Serum K+ rises 0.2–1.7 mmol/L for each 0.1 U
fall in arterial pH.
– Hyperosmolar states
– Insulin deficiency
– Cell necrosis
– Rhabdomyolysis
– Hemolysis
– Chemotherapy

◦Digitalis toxicity
◦Depolarizing muscle relaxants (e.g.,
succinylcholine)
◦β-blockers
◦α-agonists
– Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis

– Cellular breakdown:
◦Trauma
◦Tumor lysis
– Salt substitutes
– Oral potassium
– Potassium penicillin G
– Rapid transfusions of banked blood

– Traumatic venipuncture with hemolysis
– Postvenipuncture release of potassium can occur

◦Extreme leukocytosis (WBC >100,000/mm3)

which can progress to paralysis.
r Dyspnea owing to respiratory muscle weakness.
r Cardiac dysrhythmias may be the initial
manifestation, so patients could also present with
chest pain, palpitations, or syncope.

– Hyponatremia with mineralocorticoid deficiency
– Mild metabolic acidosis with type IV renal tubular
acidosis
r Arterial blood gases:
– Assess acid–base status
r Creatinine kinase:
– Rhabdomyolysis can lead to renal insufficiency
and result in hyperkalemia
r Ca2+
r For hyperkalemia in face of normal renal
function, calculate transtubular potassium gradient
(TTKG):
– TTKG = urine K × Posm/plasma K × Uosm
– Posm, plasma osmolality; Uosm, urine osmolality
– TTKG >8 suggests extrarenal cause; TTKG <6
indicates renal excretory defect.

hyperkalemia:

interval
– >6.5–8: PR prolongation; loss of P-waves;
widening of QRS complexes
– >8: Intraventricular blocks; bundle branch blocks;

r Serum potassium cannot be reliably predicted by
ECG:

renal failure) will tolerate higher potassium levels
than others.
– Potassium effects (as seen on ECG) are more
important than potassium level
– While unusual, the ECG can be normal in the
setting of severe hyperkalemia

ALERT
Most common cause of hyperkalemia reported by
lab is pseudohyperkalemia owing to hemolysis of
red blood cells.

dysrhythmias/cardiac arrest involves different drugs
from usual advanced cardiac life support (ACLS)
measures (see Treatment, below):

metered-dose inhaler or intravenously
– Sodium bicarbonate can be effective in the setting
of a metabolic acidosis.

prehospital systems and should be considered in
the unstable patient when hyperkalemia is
suspected.

in at-risk populations (renal failure)

HYPEROSMOLAR SYNDROME
Matthew T. Robinson
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Results from a relative insulin deficiency in the
undiagnosed or untreated diabetic
r Sustained hyperglycemia creates an osmotic diuresis
and dehydration:
– Extracellular space maintained by the osmotic
gradient at the expense of the intracellular space
– Eventually profound intracellular dehydration
occurs.
r Total body deficits of H2O, Na+,C l− ,K − ,P O4− ,
Ca2+, and Mg2+
r In contrast to diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), severe
ketoacidosis does not occur:
– Circulating insulin levels are higher.
– The elevation of insulin counter-regulatory
hormones is less marked.
– The hyperosmolar state itself inhibits lipolysis (the
release of free fatty acids) and subsequent
generation of keto acids
Geriatric Considerations
r Most commonly seen in elderly type II diabetics who
experience a stressful illness that precipitates
worsening hyperglycemia and reduced renal function
r In the elderly, 30–40% of cases are associated with
the initial presentation of diabetes.
Pediatric Considerations
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic states (HHS) rare in
pediatric patients
ETIOLOGYr Hyperosmolar state precipitated by factors that:
– Impair peripheral insulin action
– Increase endogenous or exogenous glucose
– Decrease patient’s ability to replace fluid loss
r Infection is the most common precipitating factor in
32–60% of cases.
r Other precipitating causes include:
– Inadequate diabetes therapy
– Medication omission
– Diet indiscretion
– Infections
– Pneumonia
– UTI
– Sepsis
– Medications/drugs
– Diuretics
– β-blockers
– Calcium channel blockers
– Phenytoin
– Cimetidine
– Amphetamines
– Ethanol
– Myocardial infarction
– Stroke
– Renal failure
– Heat stroke
– Pancreatitis
– Intestinal obstruction
– Endocrine disorders
– Burns
– Heat stroke
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Progression of signs and symptoms typically occur
over days to weeks.
r Polyuria/polydipsia/weight loss
r Dizziness/weakness/fatigue
r Blurred vision
r Leg cramps
Physical Examr Dehydration
r Tachycardia
r Sunken eyes
r Hypotension
r Orthostasis
r Dry mucous membranes
r Decreased skin turgor
r Collapsed neck veins
r Coma/lethargy/drowsiness
r Urinary output maintained until late
r Seizures/focal neurologic deficits
r Concurrent precipitating medical illness
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Diagnostic criteria:
r Serum glucose ≥600 mg/dL (usually >1,000 mg/dL)
r Minimal ketosis
r pH ≥ 7.30, HCO3 ≥15 mEq/L
r Effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg:
– = 2 × Na+ + glucose/18
– BUN not included because it is freely permeable
between fluid compartments
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Broad testing indicated to evaluate hyperosmolar
syndrome and for precipitating causes
r Electrolytes:
–K + may be elevated even in the presence of total
body deficit owing to shift from intracellular space
to extracellular space.
– Mild anion gap metabolic acidosis owing to lactic
acid, β-hydroxybutyric acid, or renal insufficiency
– Increased sodium—correct for hyperglycemia:
Corrected [Na+] = [Na+] + 1.6 × [(glucose in
mg/dL) – 100]/100
r BUN, creatinine:
– Azotemia with elevated BUN/creatinine ratio
owing to prerenal and intrarenal causes
r Venous blood gas (VBG) or arterial blood gas (ABG)
to rapidly determine pH:
– ABG necessary to evaluate mixed acid–base
disorders
r Serum ketones,β-hydroxybutyrate, and lactate level
if pH < 7.3 or significantly elevated anion gap to
evaluate mixed acid–base disorder
r Serum osmolarity
r CBC:
– Leukocytosis due to infection, stress, or
hemoconcentration
– Increased hemoglobin and hematocrit due to
hemoconcentration
r Lipase and amylase:
– Pancreatitis common
– Elevated amylase and lipase with no evidence of
pancreatitis common
– May be due to increased salivary secretion,
hemoconcentration, or decreased renal clearance
r Urinalysis:
– Check for ketones/glucose.
– Assess for UTI.
r Magnesium, calcium, phosphate
r Blood cultures in sepsis
r Creatine kinase for rhabdomyolysis:
– Incidence as high as 17%
r Urine pregnancy test in females of childbearing years
r Cardiac enzymes and troponin for myocardial
infarction

r Head CT: When indicated for AMS or with focal
neurologic deficit
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
ECG:
r Evaluate for electrolyte abnormalities causing
conduction impairment
r Evaluate for signs of ischemia as triggering event

Differentiate from DKA:
r If acidosis or significant anion gap present, must
determine cause (i.e., ketosis, DKA, lactic acidosis,
[hypoperfusion, sepsis, or postictal], or other causes
of metabolic acidosis)
r Mixed disorder of HHS and DKA present in up to
33% of patients

IV fluid resuscitation and initial stabilization

ABCs:

HYPEROSMOLAR SYNDROME
H
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr General strategy:
– Frequent reassessment of volume and mental
status
– Electrolyte assessment difficult:
◦Serum levels of Na+,K +,P O4− do not
accurately reflect the total body solute deficits
or the intracellular environment.
◦Repeat electrolyte and glucose levels hourly.
– Search for a precipitating illness.
r Fluids:
– Begin resuscitation with 0.9% NS 1–2 L over
1–2 hr to restore intravascular volume and
achieve hemodynamic stability.
– Use 0.45% saline after initial resuscitation
– Calculate total body water (TBW) deficit using
corrected serum sodium:
◦TBW deficit = 0.6 × weight (kg) ×
(1 – 140/corrected Na+)
– Average fluid deficit is 9 L.
– Replace 50% of the fluid deficit over the next
12 hr.
– Change fluid to D5 1/2 NS when serum glucose is
<250 mg/dL.
r Potassium:
– Anticipate hypokalemia:
◦Total body deficit of ∼5–10 mEq/kg body
weight (replace over 3 days)
– Begin potassium repletion after urine output is
established. Do not start in anuric patients or if
initial K+ level is >5 mEq/L.
◦If the initial K+ is normal (4–5 mEq/L), give
20–30 mEq KCl in the 1st L of fluids, then give
20 mEq/hr.
◦If the initial K+ is low (3–4 mEq/L), give 40 mEq
in 1st L
◦If serum K+ is <3 mEq/L hold insulin and give
10–20 mEq/h until K+ >3.3, then add 40 mEq
to each lister
◦Follow repeat serum K+ levels q1–2h and
adjust treatment accordingly.
r Insulin:
– No role in the early resuscitation
– Earlier use of insulin may cause rapid correction of
hyperglycemia with collapse of the intravascular
space, hypotension, and shock or hypokalemia
and dysrhythmias.
– Some patients will not require insulin.
– Use insulin as sole therapy in patients with fluid
overload (i.e., acute renal failure [ARF]).
– Begin only after achieving hemodynamic stability
and evaluating for hypokalemia:
◦Do not use unless serum K+ >3.3 mEq/L
– SC or IM insulin not recommended due to erratic
absorption
– Titrate drip to optimally decrease serum glucose
by 50–90 mg/dL/hr. More rapid correction places
the patient at risk for developing cerebral edema.
– Decrease drip rate by 1/2 when serum glucose
<250 mg/dL.
– Adjust insulin drip to maintain serum glucose
between 150–200 mg/dL, and continue until
serum bicarbonate is >18 mg/dL and pH > 7.3
r Phosphate:
– Routine replacement not recommended
– If serum levels <1 mg/dL, give 20–30 mmol
potassium phosphate over 24 hr
– Monitor serum calcium levels closely
r Magnesium:
– 0.35 mEq/kg magnesium in fluids for 1st 3–4 hr
(2.5–3 g MgSO4 in 70 kg patient)
– Caution in ARF
r Anticoagulation:
– Arterial thrombosis may complicate hyperosmolar
state:
◦Consider SC heparin as prophylaxis.
– Remain vigilant to detect thrombotic
complications (e.g., MI, pulmonary embolus,
mesenteric ischemia).
MEDICATIONr Insulin: Begin with 0.05–0.1 U/kg/h; modify after
assessing clinical response.
r MgSO4 (magnesium sulfate): 50% (5 g/10 mL;
dilute to at least 20% before IV use)
r Naloxone: 2 mg (peds: 0.1 mg/kg) IV push (IVP)
r Potassium phosphate IV: Phosphorous serum level
<0.5 mg/dL: 0.5 mmol/kg IV infused over 4–6 hr;
phosphorous serum level 0.5–1 mg/dL:
0.25 mmol/kg IV infused over 4–6 hr
r Potassium phosphate PO: Phosphorus 250 mg per
tablet and potassium 1.1 mEq per tablet
r Thiamine: 100 mg (peds: 10–25 mg) IVP
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar All but the mildest cases should be admitted to
ICU:
– Frequent serial labs for the 1st 24 hr
– Rapid shifts in fluids and electrolytes and the
potential for deterioration in mental status and
arrhythmias mandate close monitoring.
r Mild cases may be managed in an observation unit
over 12–24 hr.
Discharge Criteriar Patients meeting the diagnostic criteria for
hyperosmolar syndrome should not be discharged.
r Mild hyperglycemia patients with mild volume
deficits and normal serum osmolarity can be
discharged after hydration and correction of
hyperglycemia.
Issues for Referral
Patient should follow-up with endocrinology and with
their primary physician within 1 wk postdischarge for
long-term blood glucose monitoring and insulin
therapy.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Failure to look for precipitating event or cause
r Too rapid correction of glucose—may lead to
hypotension
r Continuing isotonic fluids after volume
resuscitation—may lead to hypernatremia
r Continuing hypotonic fluids without frequent
electrolytes—may lead to cellular edema, cerebral
edema
r Failure to prevent hypokalemia: Respiratory
depression, dysrhythmias
r Avoid phenytoin in the event of seizure activity:
– Inhibits the endogenous release of insulin

Am. 2004;88:1063–1084.

hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state. Endocrinol
Metab Clin North Am. 2006;35(4):725–751.

management of hyperglycemic emergencies in
diabetes mellitus. Diabetes Res Clin Pract. 2011;
94:340–351.

HYPERPARATHYROIDISM
Rami A. Ahmed rBrad D. Gable
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Parathyroid hormone (PTH) excess with symptoms
owing to PTH actions:
– Decreases urinary Ca2+ loss
– Increases urinary PO42− loss
– Stimulates vitamin D conversion from 25(OH)-D to
1,25(OH)-D in kidney
– Liberates Ca2+ and PO42− from bone
– Hypercalcemia is the primary metabolic finding
r Hypercalciuria from hypercalcemia (despite
decreased urinary loss) produces increased
magnesium loss in urine
r Magnesium (negative feedback to prevent
hypercalcemia causes hypomagnesaemia):
– Cofactor in the production of PTH
– Essential for action of PTH in target tissues
r Genetics:
– Associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia
type 1:
◦Hyperparathyroidism
◦Pancreatic islet disease
◦Pituitary disease
– Associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia
type 2:
◦Hyperparathyroidism (type 2A, rare in 2B)
◦Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid (type 2A and
2B, less virulent in type 2A)
◦Pheochromocytoma (type 2A and 2B)
◦Mucosal neuroma (type 2B)
ETIOLOGYr Excess secretion of PTH owing to:
– Primary hyperparathyroidism (adenoma 85%,
hyperplasia 14%, carcinoma <1%)
– Secondary hyperparathyroidism (response to
vitamin D deficiency or chronic renal failure with
hyperphosphatemia):
◦Calcium is low or normal, but PTH levels are
elevated
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Stones, bones, abdominal groans, and psychiatric
moans
ALERT
r Hypercalcemic crisis:
– Anorexia, nausea, vomiting
– Mental obtundation
History
Depends on the severity and rapidity of hypercalcemia
Pediatric Considerations
r Neonate:
– Hypotonia, weakness, and listlessness
– Following delivery to hypoparathyroid mothers
r Hypercalcemic infants:
– Broad forehead
– Epicanthal folds
– Underdeveloped nasal bridge
– Prominent upper lip
Physical Examr Dehydration
r Cardiac:
– Hypertension (even in the face of dehydration)
– Cardiac conduction abnormalities (not
proportional to degree of hypercalcemia)
– Bradydysrhythmia
– Bundle branch blocks
– Complete heart block
– Asystole
– Short QT interval (shortened ST segment)
– Potentiation of digitalis effects (Hypercalcemia
+digoxin = digitalis toxicity)
r Neurologic:
– Headaches
– Decreased reflexes
– Proximal muscle weakness
– Dementia
– Lethargy
– Coma
r Psychiatric:
– Personality changes
– Depression
– Inability to concentrate
– Anxiety
– Psychosis
r GI:
– Anorexia, nausea, vomiting
– Constipation
– Peptic ulcer disease
– Pancreatitis
r General:
– Fatigue
– Weight loss
– Polyuria and polydipsia
r Musculoskeletal:
– Gout/pseudogout
– Bone pain, bone cysts (osteitis cystica)
– Arthralgias
– Chondrocalcinosis
r Renal:
– Kidney stones
– Nephrocalcinosis
– Decreased renal concentrating ability
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Calcium level
r Albumin:
– Elevated albumin—falsely elevated calcium level
– Low albumin—falsely lowered calcium level
r Evaluate for symptoms of hypercalcemia, especially
impending parathyroid storm (hypercalcemic
crisis—anorexia, nausea, vomiting, obtundation
progressing to coma).
r Review history for medication ingestion (see
Differential Diagnosis below)
r No further ED workup if:
– Asymptomatic
– Normal ECG
– Calcium level <14 mg/dL when corrected for
albumin
r If symptomatic with Ca2+ <14 mg/dL or any
patient with Ca2+ ≥14 mg/dL, check:
– Ionized calcium
– Chest radiograph (for CHF/malignancy)
– Phosphorus
– Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine
– Sedimentation rate
– Alkaline phosphatase
– Magnesium
– Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
– CBC
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Calcium correction for albumin:
– Corrected Ca2+ (mg/dL) = measured Ca2+
(mg/dL) + 0.8 [4 – albumin (g/dL)]
– Acidosis:
◦Decreases affinity to albumin—increases
ionized (metabolically active) Ca2+
◦Decrease of 0.1 pH unit increases the ionized
Ca2+ by 3–8%
r Phosphorus:
– Low in primary hyperparathyroidism
– Usually high in secondary hyperparathyroidism
– Normal or high in malignancy-related
hypercalcemia
r Chloride/PO42− ratio:
– >33—hyperparathyroidism
– <30—malignancy
r Alkaline phosphatase:
– Increased in 50% of patients with
hyperparathyroidism
– Normal with vitamin D excess
r Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR):
– Normal in hyperparathyroidism
– Elevated in malignancy or granulomatous diseases
r Anemia:
– Present with malignancy or granulomatous
disease
– Absent in hyperparathyroidism
r Magnesium:
– Low or low normal
r PTH:
– Elevated in primary and secondary
hyperparathyroidism
r PTH-related peptide:
– Secreted by squamous cell carcinomas of lung,
head, neck; renal carcinomas, bladder carcinomas,
adenocarcinomas, and lymphomas
Imagingr Chest radiograph:
– To assess CHF risk during IV hydration
– Granulomatous disease or malignancy if cause of
hypercalcemia is uncertain
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Definitive treatment is parathyroidectomy to treat and
establish cause of hyperparathyroidism

HYPERPARATHYROIDISM
H
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr PTH related:
– Primary or secondary hyperparathyroidism
– Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia
r Malignancy related:
– PTH-related peptide or Ca2+ release from
osteolytic tumor
r Vitamin D related:
– Excess vitamin D intake or vitamin D production
by granulomas
r Immobilization:
– Associated with Paget disease
r Drug induced:
– Thiazide diuretics
– Lithium
– Aluminum-containing antacids
– Tamoxifen
– Estrogens
– Androgens
– Vitamin A
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
May present as a primarily psychiatric disorder
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Cardiac monitor if:
– Symptomatic hypercalcemia
–C a2+ level >14 mg/dL
r Hydrate with IV 0.9% NS.
r Correct acidosis
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Treat hypercalcemia:
– Vigorous hydration with 0.9% NS at minimum of
250 mL/hr unless CHF:
◦Lowers calcium 1.5–2 mg/dL in 24 hr
◦Achieve urine output 100 mL/hr
– Administer furosemide or other loop diuretic
(calciuric) after adequate volume replacement or
in the presence of CHF:
◦Common error: Administration of furosemide
before adequate hydration
◦If urinary sodium losses exceed replacement
sodium, then renal conservation measures
impede calcium excretion
– Avoid thiazide diuretics (impede calcium excretion)
– Consider glucocorticoid administration (decreases
gut absorption and increases renal excretion of
Ca2+); most effective with vitamin D intoxication
or granulomatous diseases
– Start bisphosphonates (pamidronate or
etidronate) in conjunction with primary physician
(inhibits calcium mobilization from bone)
r Treat cardiac dysrhythmias in standard fashion:
– Correct acidosis
r Determine the cause of the hypercalcemia.
r Stop all medications that may contribute to
hypercalcemia
r Exercise extreme caution in the use of digoxin.
r Anticipate CHF and electrolyte imbalance with
frequent reassessment of patient and monitoring of
serum electrolytes and magnesium levels
r Calcitonin if unable to use hydration
r Emergent dialysis with renal failure
MEDICATION
First Liner NS hydration: Initial 250–300 mL/h depending on
patient’s propensity to CHF
r Furosemide: 40 mg IV q2–4h after assurance of
adequate hydration
r Prednisone: 40–60 mg PO OR Hydrocortisone:
100 mg (peds: 1–2 mg/kg) IV
Second Liner IN CONSULTATION WITH ENDOCRINOLOGIST
r Calcitonin salmon 4 U/kg SC if saline hydration
contraindicated
– Test dose: Intradermal 0.1 mL of 10 U/mL solution
recommended
– Initial dose: 4 U/kg SC q12h
r Pamidronate:
– If albumin-corrected Ca2+ level 12–13.5 mg/dL:
60 mg IV infused over 2 hr
– If albumin-corrected Ca2+ level > 13.5 mg/dL:
90 mg IV over 4 hr
– Dosage should be reduced in renal impairment
and infusion time may be extended to reduce
nephrotoxic potential but no formal
recommendations exist (pregnancy category
D – maternal benefit may outweigh fetal risk)
r Zoledronic acid: 4 mg IV over 15–30 min (first-line
agent due to efficacy and convenience, but less
preferred due to lack of less expensive available
generic)
r Cinacalcet (Sensipar): 30 mg PO daily or BID
(calcimimetic for secondary hyperparathyroidism or
parathyroid carcinoma)
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Corrected calcium >14 mg/dL
r Symptomatic hypercalcemia
r Evidence of abnormal cardiac rhythm or conduction
Discharge Criteriar Not meeting admission criteria
r Able to maintain adequate hydration
Issues for Referral
If diagnosis is suspected, referral to check PTH levels
and response to therapy
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr If hyperparathyroidism is suspected arrange
follow-up and send a PTH level
r Patient needs to be instructed to maintain hydration
and stop medications associated with hypercalcemia
(see the list in Differential Diagnosis)
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r The hypercalcemia of hyperparathyroidism is rarely
symptomatic and Ca2+ level rarely >14. (Higher
levels are most frequently attributable to neoplastic
disease)
r The importance of diagnosis is to prevent long-term
complications
r Calcium level should be measured as ionized Ca2+,
or corrected for albumin level
r Administration of loop diuretics prior to adequate
saline hydration will worsen hypercalcemia; some
experts suggest that loop diuretics may be no longer
warranted for this indication
ADDITIONAL READING
r Andreoli TE, Carpenter CCJ, Cecil RL. Andreoli and
Carpenter’s Cecil Essentials of Medicine. 7th ed.
Philadelphia, PA: Saunders-Elsevier; 2007.
r Goldman L, Bennett JC, eds. Cecil’s Textbook of
Medicine. 23rd ed. Philadelphia, PA: Saunders-
Elsevier; 2008.
r Jamal SA, Miller PD. Secondary and tertiary
hyperparathyroidism. J Clin Densitom. 2013;16(1):
64–68.
r Khan AA. Medical management of primary
hyperparathyroidism. J Densitom. 2013;16(1):
60–63.
r Marcocci C, Cetani F. Primary hyperparathyroidism.
N Engl J Med. 2011;365:2389–2397.

HYPERTENSIVE EMERGENCIES
David F. M. Brown rEva Tovar Hirashima
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Hypertensive crisis:
– Severely elevated BP defined by a SBP
>179 mm Hg or a DBP >109 mm Hg
r Hypertensive urgency:
– Severely elevated BP without end-organ damage
r Hypertensive emergency:
– Severely elevated BP associated with acute
end-organ damage
r Loss of autoregulation of blood flow in hypertensive
emergency:
– Arterioles vasoconstrict to counter pressure
– High pressures overwhelm arterioles and
endothelial damage occurs
– Endothelial injury leads to increase permeability,
activation of the coagulation cascade and
platelets, and deposition of fibrin
r Activation of the renin–angiotensin system and the
sympathetic nervous system:
– Leads to further vasoconstriction and production
of proinflammatory cytokines
r End-organ ischemia:
– Renewed release of vasoconstrictors
– Worsened by pressure natriuresis
– Triggers a vicious cycle
r Organs affected:
– Brain (encephalopathy, CVA, ICH)
– Retina (hemorrhage, papilledema)
– Heart (MI, aortic dissection, acute HF)
– Kidneys (acute renal failure)
– Placenta (preeclampsia/eclampsia)
ETIOLOGYr Essential HTN
r Renal:
– Vascular disease
– Parenchymal disease
r Coarctation of the aorta
r CNS disorders:
– Head trauma
– CVA/ICH
– Brain tumor
– Spinal cord injury
r Endocrine:
– Pheochromocytoma
– Cushing syndrome
– Primary hyperaldosteronism
– Renin-secreting tumor
r Drugs:
– Cocaine, phencyclidine, amphetamines
– Erythropoietin, tacrolimus, cyclosporine,
corticosteroids, oral contraceptives
– MAOI interactions
– Antihypertensive medication withdrawal
– Lead intoxication
r Autonomic hyperreactivity:
– Guillain–Barr ´ e syndrome
– Acute intermittent porphyria
r Postop pain and/or anesthesia complications
r Pregnancy related:
– Preeclampsia/eclampsia
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Inquire about:
– Use of any prescribed and OTC medication
– Duration and control of pre-existing HTN
◦Prior end-organ damage
– Details of antihypertensive therapy
– Comorbid conditions (obesity, CAD, DM)
– Recreational drug use
r Assess for end-organ compromise in decreasing
order of frequency:
– Dyspnea
– Chest pain
– Headache
– Altered mental status/confusion
– Focal neurologic symptoms
Physical Examr BP measured in both arms
– Use proper cuff size
r Assess for end-organ compromise:
– Neurologic:
◦Level of consciousness
◦Visual fields
◦Focal motor/sensory deficits
– Ophthalmologic:
◦Funduscopic exam (retinal hemorrhages,
papilledema)
– Cardiovascular:
◦Elevated JVP
◦Lung crackles
◦Aortic insufficiency murmur
◦S3
◦Asymmetrical pulses
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr 12-lead EKG:
– Ischemic changes, LV hypertrophy
r Assess kidney function
– Acute renal failure may be asymptomatic
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC
– Anemia and thrombocytopenia are present in
thrombotic microangiopathy
r Standard hospital protocols for chest pain
r BUN, creatinine
r Electrolytes
– Hypokalemia present in primary mineralocorticoid
excess
r Urinalysis:
– Proteinuria, hematuria, and casts
r Urine toxicology screen:
– If recreational drugs are suspected
r HCG
Imagingr Chest x-ray:
– If cardiopulmonary symptoms are present
r Head CT:
– If headache, confusion, neurologic findings
r CTA chest and abdomen:
– If concern for aortic dissection
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Arterial line
r Lumbar puncture:
– Exclude subarachnoid hemorrhage
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Acute coronary syndrome (ACS)
r Acute heart failure (AHF)
r Aortic dissection
r Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH)
r CVA (ischemic or hemorrhagic)
r Preeclampsia/eclampsia
r Withdrawal syndromes:
– β-blockers
– Clonidine (central α2-agonist)
r States of catecholamine excess:
– Pheochromocytoma
– Cocaine/sympathomimetic drug intoxication
– Tyramine ingestion when on MAOIs
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr ABCs
r Consider gentle BP reduction.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABC, cardiac monitoring, pulse oximetry
r Oxygen administration
r IV access
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Hypertensive urgency:
– No need to treat, but close follow-up
– Use oral agents only
– Give any missed home dose
– Goal: Lower the BP gradually over 24–48 hr
r Hypertensive emergency:
– Treat end-organ damage, not absolute BP
– Reduce MAP by ≤20–25% in the 1st hr
– Goal: Systolic ∼160 mm Hg, diastolic ∼100 mm
Hg in 2–6 hr
– Once BP stable with IV therapy, transition to oral
therapy within 6–12 hr
– More gradual reduction recommended in:
◦Acute ongoing injury to CNS
– More rapid reduction recommended in:
◦Aortic dissection
r Hypertensive encephalopathy:
– Goal: MAP lowered by max. 20% or to DBP
100–110 mm Hg within 1st hr then gradual
reduction in BP to normal over 48–72 hr
– Drug of choice: Nicardipine, clevidipine, or
labetalol
r Ischemic stroke:
– CPP = MAP – ICP
– Decreased CPP from hypotension (low MAP) or
cerebral edema (high ICP) may extend infarct
– Treat only SBP>220 mm Hg or DBP>120 mm Hg
– Lytic candidates should have BP lowered to
<185/110 mm Hg
– Goal: MAP lowered by no more than 15–20%,
DBP not <100–110 mm Hg in first 24 hr
– Goal post tPA: BP <180/105 mm Hg
– Drug of choice: Nicardipine, clevidipine, or
labetalol

HYPERTENSIVE EMERGENCIES
H
r Hemorrhagic CVA or SAH:
– Treat if SBP >180 mm Hg/DBP >100 mm Hg
– Goal: MAP lowered by 20–25% within the 1st hr
or SBP 140–160 mm Hg
– Drug of choice: Nicardipine, clevidipine, or
labetalol
– Avoid dilating cerebral vessels with nitroglycerin
or nitroprusside
r ACS:
– Goal: MAP to 60–100 mm Hg
– Drug of choice: Labetalol or esmolol in
combination with nitroglycerin
– Avoid: Hydralazine (reflex tachycardia) and
nitroprusside (“coronary steal”)
r AHF:
– Goal: MAP to 60–100 mm Hg
– Drug of choice nitroprusside or NTG with ACEI
and/or loop diuretic
r Acute renal failure/microangiopathic anemia:
– Goal: MAP lowered by 20–25% within 1st hr
– Drug of choice: Nicardipine, clevidipine, or
fenoldopam. For scleroderma renal crises ACEI are
drugs of choice.
r Aortic dissection:
– Reduce shear force (dP/dT) by reducing both BP
and HR
– β-blockade must precede any drug that may
cause reflex tachycardia
– Goal: SBP 100–120 mm Hg and HR <65 bpm
within 1st 20 min
– Drug of choice: Esmolol in combination with
dihydropyridine CCB or nitroprusside
– Consult vascular surgery if type A
r Sympathomimetics (pheochromocytoma, cocaine,
amphetamines):
– Goal: MAP lowered by 20–25% within 1st hr
– Avoid pure β-blockade (α is left unopposed)
– Drug of choice: Phentolamine or calcium channel
blocker with benzodiazepine. Use clonidine in
cases of clonidine withdrawal
Pregnancy Considerations
r Preeclampsia:
– Definition: SBP >140 or DBP >90 mm Hg with
proteinuria (>300 mg/24 hr or a urine
protein/creatinine >0.3 or dipstick 1+)
– Occurs >20 wk gestation – 4 wk postpartum
– Headache, vision changes, peripheral edema, RUQ
pain
– Complications: Eclampsia, HELLP
– Goal: SBP 130–150 mm Hg and DBP 80–100 mm
Hg
– Drug of choice: Labetalol, nicardipine,
hydralazine, magnesium
– Consult Obstetrics
r Esmolol:
– β1-blockade
– Onset 60s, duration 10–20 min
– Avoid in AHF , COPD, heart block
r Labetalol:
– Combined α- and β-blocker
– Onset 2–5 min, duration 2–6 hr
– No reflex tachycardia due to β-blockade
– Avoid in: COPD, AHF , bradycardia
r Clevidipine:
– 3rd generation dihydropyridine CCB
– Onset 2–4 min, duration 5–15 min
– Elimination independent of liver/renal function
– Avoid in allergies to soy or egg products, defective
lipid metabolism, AFib
r Nicardipine:
– 2nd generation dihydropyridine CCB
– Onset 5–15 min, duration 4–6 hr
– Avoid in: AHF , coronary ischemia
r Nitroglycerin:
– Venous > arteriolar dilation
– Onset 2–5 min, duration 10–20 min
– Perfuses coronaries, decreasing ischemia
– Causes reflex tachycardia, tachyphylaxis,
methemoglobinemia
r Nitroprusside:
– Short-acting arterial and venous dilator
– Onset 3 s, duration 1–2 min
– Complications:
◦Reflex tachycardia, “coronary steal”, increase
ICP
◦Cyanide toxicity after prolonged use
– Avoid in pregnancy, renal failure (relative)
r Hydralazine:
– Arteriolar dilator
– Onset 5–15 min, duration 3–10 hr
– Hypotensive effect may be less predictable
– Safe in pregnancy
r Enalaprilat:
– ACE inhibitor
– Onset 0.5–4 hr, duration 6 hr
– Avoid in: Pregnancy, AMI
r Fenoldopam:
– Selective postsynaptic dopaminergic receptor
agonist (DA1)
– Onset 5–15 min, duration 1–4 hr
– No reflex tachycardia
– Maintains renal perfusion
– Avoid in: Glaucoma
r Phentolamine:
– α1-blocker, peripheral vasodilator
– Onset 1–2 min, duration 10–30 min
MEDICATIONr Clevidipine: 1–16 mg/h IV infusion
r Enalaprilat: 1.25–5 mg q6h IV bolus
r Esmolol: 80 mg IV bolus, then 150 μg/kg/min
infusion
r Fenoldopam: 0.1–0.6 μg/kg/min IV infusion
r Hydralazine: 10–20 mg IV bolus
r Labetalol: 20–80 mg IV bolus q10min (total
300 mg); 0.5–2 mg/min IV infusion
r Nicardipine: 2–15 mg/h IV infusion
r Nitroglycerin: 5–100 μg/min IV infusion; USE
NON-PVC tubing
r Nitroprusside: 0.25–10 μg/kg/min IV infusion
r Phentolamine: 5–15 mg q5–15min IV bolus
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar All patients with end-organ damage
r ICU for cardiac and BP monitoring
Discharge Criteriar Absence of end-organ damage
r Likely to be compliant with primary care
r Known history of HTN
r Reversible precipitating cause (e.g., medication
noncompliance)
r Able to resume previous medication regimen
r Return with chest pain or headache
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Initiation of a suitable medication regimen under care
of a primary care provider
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Avoid IV agents for hypertensive urgency
r BP goal in hypertensive emergency is a reduction of
the MAP by 20–25% within the 1st hr except in
ischemic CVA and aortic dissection
r Avoid excessive or precipitous decrease in BP
because it may exacerbate end-organ damage
r Avoid reflex tachycardia in aortic dissection
r Avoid unopposed α in catecholamine excess

in the emergency department. Cardiol Clin. 2012;
30(4):533–543.

2009;11(5):307–314.
