HYPERTHERMIA
Michelle J. Sergel rEmily Singer
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Range of progressively more severe illnesses due to
increasingly overwhelming heat stress
r Begins with dehydration and electrolyte
abnormalities and progresses to thermoregulatory
dysfunction and multisystem organ failure
r Body temperature is maintained within a narrow
range by balancing heat production with heat
dissipation
r Oxidative phosphorylation becomes uncoupled and
essential enzymes cease to function above 42◦C
(108◦F)
Heat Stroker Core body temp >105◦F (40.5◦C)
r Failure of thermoregulatory function leads to severe
CNS dysfunction and multisystem organ failure
r Classic heat stroke (nonexertional)
– Occurs in patients with compromised
thermoregulation or an inability to remove
themselves from a hot environment (e.g.,
extremes of age, debilitated)
– Develops over days to weeks, usually during heat
waves
– Severe dehydration, skin warm and dry
r Exertional heat stroke
– Younger, athletic patients with combined
environmental and exertional heat stress (e.g.,
military recruits)
– Develops over hours
– Internal heat production overwhelms dissipating
mechanisms, often despite persistent sweating
Heat Exhaustionr Core temp moderately elevated but usually <104◦F
(40◦C)
r Fluid and/or salt depletion occurs secondary to heat
stress
r Thermoregulatory function is maintained and CNS
function is preserved
r Variable nonspecific symptoms including malaise,
headache, fatigue, and nausea
r If left untreated, progresses to heat stroke
ETIOLOGYr Pre-existing conditions that hinder the body’s
ability to dissipate heat predispose for heat-related
illness
– Age extremes
– Dehydration (incl. gastroenteritis, inadequate fluid
intake)
– Cardiovascular disease (incl. CHF , CAD)
– Obesity
– Diabetes mellitus, hyperthyroidism,
pheochromocytoma
– Febrile illness
– Skin diseases that hinder sweating (incl. psoriasis,
eczema, cystic fibrosis, scleroderma)
r Pharmacologic contributors
– Sympathomimetics
– LSD, PCP , cocaine
– MAO inhibitors, antipsychotics, anxiolytics
– Anticholinergics
– Antihistamines
– β-blockers
– Diuretics
– Laxatives
– Drug or alcohol withdrawal
r Environmental factors
– Excessive heat/humidity
– Prolonged exertion
– Lack of mobility
– Lack of air conditioning
– Lack of acclimatization
– Occlusive, nonporous clothing
Pediatric Considerations
Children are at increased risk of heat illness due to
increased body surface area to mass ratio and lower
sweat production
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Heat Stroker Classic triad: Hyperthermia, CNS dysfunction, hot
skin (often with anhidrosis)
r Core temp: >105◦F (40.5◦C)
r CNS:
– Severe confusion/delirium
– Lethargy or coma
– Seizure
– Ataxia
r CV:
– Tachycardia
– Wide pulse pressure
– Low peripheral vascular resistance
– Hypotension
– Conduction disturbances
r Pulmonary:
– Tachypnea
– Rales due to noncardiac pulmonary edema
– Respiratory alkalosis (may be substantial enough
to cause tetany)
– Hypoxemia (due to aspiration, pneumonitis,
pulmonary edema, and high metabolic demand)
r GI:
– Nausea/vomiting
– Diarrhea
r Skin:
– Cutaneous vasodilation → Hot skin
– Usually dry, though sweating may be present if
not dehydrated
r Acute oliguric renal failure due to dehydration +/−
rhabdomyolysis
r Hepatic failure with elevation of transaminases in
the tens of thousands
r Coagulopathy, including DIC (poor prognostic sign)
→ purpura, melena, hematochezia, hematuria, CNS
hemorrhage
Heat Exhaustionr Core temp moderately elevated, usually <104◦F
(40◦C) and never >40.5◦C
r CNS:
– Frontal headache
– Fatigue/malaise
– Impaired judgment
– Vertigo
– Agitation
– No severe CNS dysfunction
r CV:
– Mild tachycardia
– Dehydration
r Pulmonary: Tachypnea
r GI: Nausea, vomiting
r Skin: Perspiration present, often profuse
Heat Crampsr Cramps in heavily worked muscles after exercise
r Occurs after profuse sweating and rehydration with
hypotonic fluid (i.e., water)
r Results in hyponatremia and hypochloremia without
rhabdomyolysis or renal damage
r Treat with oral salt solutions if minor or NS IV if
severe
Heat Edemar Swelling of feet/ankles from environmental heat in
nonacclimatized people
r Due to vasodilatation and orthostatic pooling and
increased aldosterone
r Resolves after acclimatization. Treatment with
elevation or compression stockings.
Heat Syncoper Unexplained syncope during heat exposure with
prolonged standing, especially in elderly
r Cutaneous vessels dilate in an effort to dissipate
heat → decreased central blood volume→ syncope
r Self-limited illness. Resolves when the patient lays
flat.
Prickly Heatr Pruritic maculopapular/vesicular rash over clothed
areas after profuse sweating in tight clothing
r Due to blockage of pores and secondary
staphylococcus infection
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Accurate core temperature
r History of heat exposure
r Heat exhaustion is a diagnosis of exclusion
r Core temperature >105◦F (40.5◦C) and CNS
dysfunction required to make diagnosis of heat
stroke

DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
For Heat Stroke and Heat Exhaustion
r CBC
– Leukocytosis, hemoconcentration
r Electrolytes, BUN, Cr, glucose
– Hypernatremia with severe dehydration
– Hyponatremia can occur if drinking copious free
water
– Acute renal failure
r UA
– Myoglobin present in rhabdomyolysis
r Blood and urine cultures to rule out septic etiology
r Toxicology screen
r Serum creatinine kinase to rule out rhabdomyolysis
r ABG
– Acidosis is common with exertional heat stroke,
and lactate is usually elevated
For Heat Stroker PT/PTT/DIC panel – coagulopathy implies poor
prognosis
r Liver function tests
r Troponin I – poor prognosis if elevated
r Consider lumbar puncture to distinguish from
meningitis/encephalitis
Imagingr EKG in elderly or patients at cardiac risk
r CT head for altered mental status
r CXR for ARDS, aspiration pneumonia, and to rule
out septic etiology
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Febrile illness/sepsis
r Thyroid storm
r Pheochromocytoma
r Cocaine/PCP
r Anticholinergics
r MAO inhibitors
r Meningitis/encephalitis
r Cerebral falciparum malaria
r Delirium tremens
r Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
r Malignant hyperthermia
r Serotonin syndrome
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Initiate cooling measures for severe heat illness
– Remove from heat stress
– Disrobe patient
– Cover body with wet sheet
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs
r Continuous core temperature monitoring with a
rectal or esophageal probe
r Rapid cooling if temperature >104◦F (40◦C)
r Start with IV 0.9% NS 500 cc fluid bolus if
hypotensive
r If altered mental status, administer glucose (or
Accu-Chek), thiamine, naloxone
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURES
Cooling Measuresr Initiate for body temperature >104◦F (40◦C)
r Evaporative cooling
– Extremely effective (0.05–0.3◦C/min)
– Spray disrobed patient with fine mist of warm
water (prevents shivering)
– Airflow with fans blowing over patient
r Conductive cooling
– Ice packs to groin/axilla. Combine with
evaporative cooling treatment above
– Iced or cold water immersion—effective but
impractical
r Iced peritoneal lavage, cardiopulmonary bypass, or
HD with cold dialysate for refractory cases – not well
studied
r Stop cooling therapy at 102◦F (39◦C) to avoid
overshooting and hypothermia
r Antipyretic agents are not helpful because
underlying mechanism does not involve a change in
the hypothalamus set point
r Avoid alcohol sponge baths. Toxicity can occur due
to dilated cutaneous vessels.
Supportive Measuresr Rehydration for heat stroke/heat exhaustion
– Initial rehydration with 0.5–1.0 L 0.9% NS
– Aggressive fluid resuscitation until BP >90/60 or
central venous pressure (CVP) >12 mL H2O
– Avoid overhydration, which can contribute to
pulmonary edema and ARDS
– Peds: Start with 20 cc/kg bolus
– Place Foley catheter to monitor urine output for
heat stroke victims and CVP monitor if feasible.
Maintain UOP >2 mL/kg/hr if rhabdomyolysis is
present
– Rehydrate to hemodynamic stability with NS then
slowly administer free water if needed for
correction of hypernatremia
r Benzodiazepines for seizure, agitation, or to stop
shivering
r Tachyarrhythmias can develop, which usually resolve
with cooling. Avoid electricity or α-adrenergics until
after the myocardium is cooled
r Heat cramps: Analgesics and oral or IV hydration
with electrolyte-containing fluid
r Heat edema: Lower extremity elevation +
compression stockings
r Prickly heat: Chlorhexidine cream/lotion +/−
salicylic acid 1% TID
MEDICATIONr Diazepam: 5–10 mg (peds: 0.2–0.4 mg/kg) IVP
r Lorazepam: 1–2 mg (peds 0.05–0.1 mg/kg) IVP
r Naloxone (Narcan): 2 mg (peds: 0.1 mg/kg) IVP
FOLLOW-UP
Admission Criteriar Heat stroke – admit to the ICU
r Heat exhaustion – admit to general or monitored
floor if:
– Severe electrolyte abnormalities
– Renal failure or evidence of rhabdomyolysis
– Elderly
Discharge Criteria
All patients except those with heat stroke or severe
heat exhaustion may be discharged
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Cannot make diagnosis of heat stroke without temp
>40.5◦C and severe CNS dysfunction.
r Management of heat stroke requires management
of ABCs and rapid cooling.
r Continuous core monitoring with a rectal or
esophageal probe is standard of care.
r Evaporative cooling is the cooling method of choice.

Care. 2010;14(3):R99.

hospitalization. Eur Psychiatry. 2007;22(6):
335–338.

Rosen’s Emergency Medicine: Concepts and Clinical
Practice. 7th ed., Vol 2. Philadelphia, PA: Mosby
Elsevier; 2010:1882–1892.

exertional heat illness. Br J Sports Med. 2005;39(8):
503–507.

HYPERTHYROIDISM
Rita K. Cydulka rChristopher S. Campbell
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Excessive thyroid hormone production results in a
continuum of disease caused by both the direct
physiologic effect of thyroid hormones as well as
increased catecholamine sensitivity:
– Subclinical or mild hyperthyroidism
– Thyrotoxicosis
– Thyroid storm or thyrotoxic crisis with
life-threatening manifestations:
◦1–2% of patients with hyperthyroidism
r Regulation of thyroid hormone:
– Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) from
hypothalamus acts on the anterior pituitary
– Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) released by
anterior pituitary gland and results in increased T3
and T4 from the thyroid gland:
◦Most of circulating hormone is T4, which is
peripherally converted to T3
◦T3 is much more biologically active than T4
although it has a shorter half-life
r Genetics:
– Interplay between genetics and environment
– Graves disease is associated with HLA-B8 and
HLA-DR3
– Autosomal dominant inheritance seen in some
families with nontoxic goiter
ETIOLOGYr Primary hyperthyroidism:
– Toxic diffuse goiter (Graves disease)
– Toxic multinodular (Plummer disease) or
uninodular goiter
– Excessive iodine intake (Jod-Basedow disease)
r Thyroiditis:
– Postpartum thyroiditis
– Radiation thyroiditis
– Subacute thyroiditis (de Quervain)
– Chronic thyroiditis (Hashimoto/lymphocytic)
r Metastatic thyroid cancer
r Ectopic thyroid tissue (struma ovarii)
r Pituitary adenoma
r Drug induced:
– Amiodarone
– Lithium
– α-interferon
– Interleukin-2
– Iodine (radiographic contrast agents)
– Excessive thyroid hormone (factitious
thyrotoxicosis)
– Aspirin overdose
DIAGNOSIS
ALERT
Thyroid storm is a life-threatening condition, which
may be precipitated by:r Infection
r Trauma
r Diabetic ketoacidosis
r Organophosphate intoxication
r Cytotoxic chemotherapy
r Myocardial infarction
r Cerebrovascular accident
r Surgery
r Abrupt withdrawal of antithyroid medication or
acute ingestion of thyroid medication
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Signs and symptoms reflect end-organ
responsiveness to thyroid hormone:
– Signs:
◦Fever
◦Tachycardia, wide pulse pressure
◦Diaphoresis/sweating
◦Congestive heart failure (CHF)
◦Shock
◦Tremor
◦Disorientation/psychosis
◦Goiter/thyromegaly
◦Thyrotoxic stare/exophthalmos/lid lag
◦Hyperreflexia
◦Pretibial myxedema
– Symptoms:
◦Weight loss despite increased appetite
◦Dysphagia or dyspnea secondary to obstruction
by a goiter
◦Rash/pruritus/hyperhidrosis
◦Palpitations/chest pain
◦Diarrhea and vomiting
◦Myalgias and weakness
◦Nervousness/anxiety
◦Menstrual irregularities
◦Heat intolerance
◦Insomnia and fatigue
r Thyroid storm involves exaggerated signs and
symptoms of thyrotoxicosis:
– Extreme tachycardia/dysrhythmias
– CHF
– Shock
– Disorientation and mental status changes
including coma and seizure
– Thromboembolic events
Geriatric Considerations
Apathetic hyperthyroidism:
r Owing to multinodular goiter, often have history of
nontoxic goiter
r Subtle clinical findings that often reflect
single-organ system dysfunction:
– CHF
– Refractory atrial fibrillation (AFib)
– Weight loss
– Depression, emotional lability, flat affect
– Tremor
– Hyperactivity
History
Gradual onset of aforementioned signs and
symptoms
Physical Examr Vital signs:
– Fever
– Tachycardia
– Elevation of systolic blood pressure
– Widened pulse pressure
– Tachypnea/hypoxia
r Alopecia
r Exophthalmos or lid lag
r Thyromegaly or goiter, thyroid bruit
r Fine, thin, diaphoretic skin
r Irregularly irregular heartbeat
r Lung rales (CHF)
r Right upper quadrant tenderness/jaundice
r Muscular atrophy/weakness
r Tremor
r Mental status changes/coma
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Find underlying cause/precipitating factors.
r Plasma TSH is the initial ED test of choice:
– Normal level usually rules out hyperthyroidism:
◦TSH may be low with normal T4. Get T3 level to
rule out T3 thyrotoxicosis
– If TSH levels unavailable, clinical suspicion should
prompt initiation of therapy
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Thyroid function tests for:
– Symptoms of hyperthyroidism
– Elderly patient with new-onset CHF
– New AFib/supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)
r TSH (usually decreased)
r Free T4 (usually elevated):
– If free T4 is unavailable, total T4 and resin T3
uptake
– 5% will have T3 thyrotoxicosis, if low TSH with
normal T4, send T3 to rule out
r Lab studies are often not helpful/nonspecific, get as
needed to look for underlying precipitants:
– CBC to rule out anemia
– Chemistry panel:
◦BUN, creatinine may be elevated secondary to
dehydration
◦Hypokalemia, hyperglycemia
r Liver function tests (increased transaminases)
r ABG for hypoxemia and acidosis
r Cardiac markers
Imaging
CXR (in CHF or sepsis)
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
EKG:
r Most commonly sinus tachycardia
r Rule out MI as precipitant of thyroid storm
r New-onset AFib

HYPERTHYROIDISM
H
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Pheochromocytoma
r Sepsis
r Sympathomimetic ingestion
r Psychosis
r Heat stroke
r Delirium tremens
r Malignant hyperthermia
r Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
r Hypothalamic stroke
r Hypothyroidism (may mimic apathetic
hyperthyroidism)
r Factitious thyrotoxicosis
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Stabilization and supportive care
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Airway, breathing, and circulation management
r Cardiac monitor
r Supplemental oxygen
r IV fluids
r Initiate cooling measures:
– Acetaminophen for fever:
◦Avoid aspirin (displaces thyroid hormone from
thyroglobulin, elevates free T4)
– Cooling blanket
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Identify and treat the precipitating event
r For thyroid storm, initiate treatment sequence
outlined below based on clinical suspicion
r Inhibit hormone synthesis using thioamides:
– Propylthiouracil (PTU):
◦Drug of choice
◦Decreases hormone synthesis and reduces
peripheral conversion of T4
– Methimazole (MMI)
r Block hormone release using iodine only after
hormone synthesis is inhibited as above:
– Oral Lugol solution (saturated potassium iodide
solution), or
– Iopanoic acid (Telepaque)
– Give iodine at least 1 hr after thioamides to
prevent increased hormone production
– Consider lithium in patient allergic to iodine
r Block peripheral effects of thyroid hormone:
– β-blockade:
◦Propranolol is first line as it also inhibits T4
conversion to T3
◦Esmolol, β-1 selective so may be used in patient
with active CHF , asthma, etc.
– Reserpine, guanethidine
– Albumin solution
– Cholestyramine to reduce enteric reabsorption of
thyroid hormone
r Dexamethasone/hydrocortisone:
– Prevents peripheral T4 to T3 conversion
r Treatment of thyrotoxicosis, secondary thyroiditis:
– β-blockade
– Anti-inflammatory medications
r General thyrotoxicosis support:
– Acetaminophen for hyperpyrexia
– Treat CHF with usual methods
– Manage dehydration with 10% dextrose solution
(D 10) to restore depleted hepatic glycogen
r Identify and treat associated and underlying
conditions (infection, ketoacidosis, pulmonary
thromboembolism, stroke, etc.)
MEDICATIONr Cholestyramine: 4 g PO QID
r Dexamethasone: 2 mg IV q6h (peds: 0.15 mg/kg
q6h)
r Esmolol: 500 μg/kg IV over 1 min followed by
50 μg/kg/min IV; titrate to effect
r Guanethidine: 30–40 mg PO q6h for 1–3 days
r Hydrocortisone: 100 mg IV initially, followed by
100 mg IV q8h for first 24–36 hr
r Iopanoic acid: 1 g IV q8h for first 24 hr, then
500 mg IV BID
r Lithium carbonate: 300 mg PO QID (peds:
15–60 mg/kg/d div. TID–QID)
r Lugol solution: 5 drops (250 mg) PO q6h
r MMI: 60–80 mg/d PO (peds: 0.4 mg/kg) (peds:
0.2 mg/kg/d) in 3 div. doses
r Propranolol: 0.5–1 mg IV + subsequent 2–3 mg
doses over 10–15 min q several hours, or 60–80 mg
PO q4h
r PTU: 100–150 mg PO q8h initially then
200–250 mg PO q4h (peds: 5–7 mg/kg/d in 3 div.
doses)
r Reserpine: 1–5 mg IM, then 0.07–0.3 mg/kg in the
1st 24 hr
First Liner PTU
r Propranolol
r Iodine therapy (Lugol), 1 hr after PTU
Second Liner MMI
r Esmolol
r Lithium (only with iodine allergy)
r Guanethidine (for patients with bronchospasm),
reserpine
Pregnancy Considerations
r Physiologic changes associated with pregnancy may
resemble many symptoms of hyperthyroidism
r Poorly controlled hyperthyroidism during pregnancy
may result in:
– Hyperemesis gravidarum
– Premature labor
– Preeclampsia
– Low birth weight
– Spontaneous abortion
– Stillbirth
r Thyroid storm often precipitated by stressors
including infection, labor, birth
r Treatment:
– Initial stabilization as in the nonpregnant patient
(ABCs, supportive measures)
– PTU considered safer than MMI. Both cross the
placenta. PTU should be ≤ 200 mg/day
– Propranolol may be safely used
– Radioactive iodine absolutely contraindicated
when pregnant or nursing
– Thyroidectomy is the only other option if unable to
tolerate PTU while pregnant
r Postpartum thyroiditis:
– 5–10% of patients within 6 mo of delivery
– May require antithyroid medications
– 50% affected become euthyroid within 1 yr
– Transient hypothyroidism may follow
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Thyroid storm
r Requiring IV medications to control heart rate
r Significantly symptomatic or unstable patients
Discharge Criteria
Minimal symptoms that respond well to PO therapy
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Should have PCP follow-up within a few weeks
depending on symptoms
r May benefit from endocrinology referral
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Thyroid storm can be fatal. Diagnosis requires a high
level of suspicion and treatment often needs to be
started presumptively
r Radioactive iodine is never a treatment option in the
pregnant patient with hyperthyroidism
r Never give iodine before blocking hormone
synthesis with PTU or MMI in thyroid storm

emergencies. Med Clin North Am. 2012;96(2):
385–403.

HYPERVENTILATION SYNDROME
Robert F. McCormack
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Hyperventilation syndrome describes a constellation
of symptoms:
– Most commonly: Dyspnea, chest pain,
lightheadedness, and paresthesias
r Produced by a nonphysiologic increase in minute
ventilation:
– Minute ventilation may be increased by increasing
respiratory rate or tidal volume (sighs).
r Pathologic or physiologic causes of hyperventilation
must be excluded before the diagnosis of
hyperventilation syndrome can be assigned.
r Prevalence:
– 10–15% in the general population
– More common in women (may be related to
progesterone)
ETIOLOGYr Etiology of symptoms is unclear:
– Usually a response to psychological stressors
r Controversy exists regarding underlying disorders
that may contribute to hyperventilation:
– Hypocapnia
– Hypophosphatemia
– Hypocalcemia
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Past episodes
– Duration
– Triggers
– Past treatment
– Typical time point of onset during the day
r Cardiac:
– Chest pain
– Dyspnea
– “Air hunger”
– Palpitations
r Neurologic:
– Dizziness
– Lightheadedness
– Syncope
– Paresthesias
– Headache
– Carpopedal spasm
– Tetany
r Psychiatric:
– Intense fear, anxiety
– Giddiness
– Feeling of unreality
r General:
– Fatigue
– Weakness
– Malaise
Physical Examr Clinical signs are rare and varied:
– Tachypnea most common
– However, tachypnea may not be present. Patient
may increase tidal volume rather than respiratory
rate.
r Carpopedal spasm:
– May be dramatic
r Chvostek sign may be present
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Diagnosis of exclusion:
– Primary pathologic or physiologic causes of
hyperventilation must be investigated and
excluded.
r Clinical diagnosis based on the history and physical
exam
r Vital signs including pulse oximetry
r Hyperventilation syndrome will not result in hypoxia.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Consider an ABG in any hypoxic patient.
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, and glucose levels for
suspected acidosis/diabetic ketoacidosis
r EKG if chest pain present
Imaging
CXR of any patient with hypoxia or focal findings on
lung exam
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Hyperventilation provocation test after resolution of
symptoms:
– Forced overbreathing for 3 min may be attempted
to reproduce the symptoms.
– Diagnostic accuracy is controversial.
– Reproducibility of the symptoms may help the
patient understand the role of overbreathing and
help manage future attacks.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Pathologic
r Hypoxia:
– Asthma
– CHF
– Pulmonary embolus
– Pneumonia
r Severe pain
r CNS lesions
r Acidosis (DKA)
r Pulmonary HTN
r Pulmonary embolus
r Hypoglycemia
r Mild asthma
r Drugs:
– Aspirin intoxication
– Withdrawal syndrome (e.g., alcohol,
benzodiazepines)
r Physiologic
r Pregnancy
r Pyrexia
r Altitude

HYPERVISCOSITY SYNDROME
Matthew B. Mostofi
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Hyperviscosity syndrome (HVS) is the clinical
consequence of increased blood viscosity.
r The classic clinical symptoms are the triad of mucosal
bleeding, visual disturbances, and neurologic signs.
r Viscosity is the resistance a material has to change
in form.
r The higher the blood viscosity, the more the internal
resistance to blood flows.
r Increased cardiac output is required to provide
adequate perfusion of hyperviscous blood.
r Oxygen delivery is impaired as transit through the
microcirculatory system slows. This impaired
microcirculatory oxygenation gives rise to the clinical
symptoms of this syndrome.
ETIOLOGYr Hyperviscosity occurs when there is elevation of
either the cellular or acellular components of
circulating blood.
r Acellular (protein) hyperviscosity:
– The most common cause (85–90%) of
hyperviscosity is increased concentration of
γ globulins:
◦Monoclonal gammopathies: From malignant
diseases like Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia
and multiple myeloma
◦Polyclonal gammopathies: Usually rheumatic
diseases (very rare)
r Cellular (blood cell) hyperviscosity:
– Much less common (10–15%)
– Increased numbers of RBC, as in polycythemia vera
– Increased concentration (>100,000) of WBC, as
in acute and chronic leukemia
– Thrombocytosis
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Classic triad:
– Mucosal bleeding
– Visual disturbances
– Neurologic
r Hematologic:
– Bleeding is the most common manifestation.
Mechanism thought to be platelet dysfunction.
– Epistaxis
– Gingival, rectal, uterine bleeding
– Prolonged postprocedural bleeding
– Blood dyscrasias
– Pruritus owing to red cell breakdown products
– Splenic enlargement
r Ocular:
– Change in visual acuity:
◦Blurring
◦Diplopia
◦Visual loss
– Characteristic “link-sausage effect” on
funduscopy
– Alternating bulges and constrictions within the
retinal veins
– Retinal hemorrhage, detachment
– Exudate, microaneurysm formation
– Papilledema
r Renal:
– Nephritic or nephrotic syndrome
– Hematuria
– Sterile pyuria
r Neurologic:
– Headache
– Ataxia
– Mental status changes/coma
– Dizziness/vertigo
– Nystagmus
– Tinnitus, hearing loss
– Paresthesia, peripheral neuropathy
– Seizure
– Intracranial hemorrhage
r Cardiovascular:
– Angina or myocardial infarction
– Dysrhythmias
– CHF
r Dermatologic:
– Raynaud phenomenon
– Livedo reticularis
– Palpable purpura
– Eruptive spider nevus–like lesions
– Digital infarcts
– Peripheral gangrene
History
HVS should be considered in the following patient:
r Any patient presenting with the classic symptom
triad of bleeding, visual disturbance, and neurologic
dysfunction.
r Any patient with an established
immunoglobulin-producing hematologic disease
that presents with signs or symptoms of
microvascular end-organ damage or cardiac
decompensation.
r Any patient with an established hypercellular
hematologic disease who presents with signs or
symptoms of microvascular end-organ damage or
cardiac decompensation.
Physical Exam
There are no specific physical exam findings unique to
HVS. However, patient will exhibit findings based on
the affected end organs. Mucosal bleeding, petechial
rash or bruising, focal neurologic findings, signs of
decompensated heart failure, and funduscopic
abnormalities have all been reported.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Evaluate end-organ ischemia and bleeding.
r Measure serum or whole blood viscosity.
r Suspect diagnosis if the lab evaluation is hampered
by serum stasis and increased viscosity causing
analyzer blockage
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC with WBC differential:
– Anemia or erythrocytosis can be seen in HVS.
– Anemia usually normocytic and normochromic
– Rouleaux of erythrocytes on the peripheral smear
is an important diagnostic clue
– WBC for leukemia
r Electrolyte, BUN, creatinine, and glucose levels:
– Renal dysfunction is commonly noted in HVS.
– Hypercalcemia and pseudohyponatremia in
multiple myeloma
r Urinalysis:
– Proteinuria
– Hematuria
– Sterile pyuria
r Coagulation profile
r Serum and urine protein electrophoresis
r Measurement of serum viscosity (not routinely
available in ED setting):
– Ostwald viscosimeter
– Normal range for the serum viscosity relative to
water is 1.4–1.8.
– Minimal viscosity at which symptoms develop is 4
centipoise (cp).
r Elevated leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, lactate
dehydrogenase, and serum vitamin B12 levels

H
Imaging
One should consider CT of head in patients with signs
or symptoms of central neurologic dysfunction to
exclude intracranial hemorrhage.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Bleeding and clotting disorders:
– Platelet disorders (qualitative and quantitative)
– Hereditary factor deficiencies
– Acquired disorders (vitamin K deficiency, liver
disease)
– Disseminated intravascular coagulation
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
IV fluid resuscitation with hemorrhage
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Rehydrate with 0.9% NS IV fluid.
r Bleeding or end-organ ischemia may not be
controlled by any treatment except plasmapheresis.
r In patients with anemia and a leukemic picture,
avoid blood transfusion until plasmapheresis is
performed to avoid exacerbation of HVS.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Hydration, supportive care, and early hematologist
consultation are initial ED management.
r Phlebotomy or emergent plasma exchange: This
temporizing measure can be performed in a patient
with HVS and severe neurologic findings like coma
or seizures:
– Easily performed in the ED and is useful in acute
severe cases if plasmapheresis not readily
available
– Simply draw off (100–200 mL) of whole blood
and replace volume with isotonic saline.
– Should be performed in consultation with
hematologist when possible.
– Treatment of choice in patients with polycythemia
vera.
r Plasmapheresis/leukapheresis:
– In stable patients: 40 mL/kg of body weight
– In critical patients: 60 mL/kg of body weight
– Side effects include hypocalcemia with use of a
citrate-containing anticoagulant and dysrhythmia
(rare).
◦Many patients require more than 1
plasmapheresis.
◦Definitive treatment for HVS. Should be
performed in consultation with
plasmapheresis/hematology team.
◦Leukapheresis is reserved as the initial
treatment in patients with hyperleukocytosis
(usually WBC >100,000)
r ED physician can help in urgent situations by
establishing or facilitating the establishment of
large-bore central dialysis catheter, caution should
be taken to avoid bleeding complications of this
procedure
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Patients with hyperviscosity and significant
symptoms or any evidence of end-organ ischemia or
hemorrhage should be admitted for treatment of the
underlying hematologic disorder.
r ICU admission for the following:
– Hemorrhage
– Altered mental status
– Acute MI
Discharge Criteria
Discharge after definitive treatment of the underlying
disorder.
Issues for Referral
All patients with HVS should be referred to
hematologist.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Avoid diuretics in patients with HVS because they
can increase blood viscosity.
r The classic triad of symptoms of HVS includes visual
disturbances, bleeding, and neurologic
manifestations.

viscosity: A brief clinical review. Clin Hemorheol

HYPHEMA
Jamil D. Bayram rSami H. Uwaydat
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Blood in anterior chamber (AC) of the eye (between
iris and cornea).
r Hyphema: Grossly visible layering of blood.
r Microhyphema: Suspended RBCs visible by slit-lamp
only.
r Genetics:
– Genetic predisposition is related to hereditary
blood dyscrasias (see below).
ETIOLOGYr Blunt trauma: Most common (70–80%).
r Anteroposterior compression of the globe with
simultaneous equatorial globe expansion causing
rupture of iris stromal/ciliary body vessels
r Penetrating trauma: Direct injury to stromal vessels
or sudden ocular decompression.
r Spontaneous: Less common, lower incidence of
complications:
– Tumors:
◦Melanoma
◦Retinoblastoma
◦Xanthogranuloma
◦Metastatic tumors
– Blood dyscrasias:
◦Hemophilia
◦Leukemia
◦Thrombocytopenia
◦Von Willebrand disease
– Blood thinners: Aspirin, Coumadin, heparin
– Neovascularization of iris: In proliferative diabetic
retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion, carotid
stenosis.
– Postsurgical: Cataract extraction, trabeculectomy,
pars plana vitrectomy.
ALERT
In children with no history of trauma, suspect child
abuse.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Photophobia
r Blurring of vision
r Decreased visual acuity
r Ocular pain
r Nausea/vomiting
Historyr Previous visual acuity
r Prior eye surgery
r Prior glaucoma treatment.
r Past medical history (blood disorders including sickle
cell disease).
r Mechanism of trauma.
r Exact time of injury and of visual loss.
r History of excessive tearing after injury.
ALERT
History of excessive tearing may indicate open globe
injury.
Physical Examr General physical exam with emphasis on associated
bodily injuries.
r Periorbital ecchymosis
r Eyelid lacerations
r Enophthalmos (depression of the globe within the
orbit)
r Limited ocular movement with diplopia (may
indicate orbital floor fracture)
r Proptosis (may indicate retro-orbital hemorrhage)
r Ocular exam:
– Visual acuity
– Rule out open globe (positive Seidel sign, corneal
laceration, diffuse subconjunctival hemorrhage,
decreased ocular motility, prolapse of intraocular
structures)
– Pupillary reaction to light (check for afferent
pupillary defect prior to using dilating drops)
– Tonometry for intraocular pressure (IOP)
measurement
ALERT
Exclude open globe injury before measuring IOPr Slit-lamp exam; look for layer of blood in AC:
– 4 grades of hyphema depending on percentage
of AC occlusion by blood:
◦Grade I: <1/3
◦Grade II: 1/3–1/2
◦Grade III: >1/2
◦Grade IV: Total (called 8-ball hyphema; blood
is dark and filling 100% of AC)
– High-grade hyphemas are:
◦More likely to rebleed (25% of grade I
compared with 67% of grade III)
◦More likely to develop glaucoma and corneal
staining
◦Less likely to recover visual acuity
– Dilated fundus exam (avoid pressure on globe)
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Lab tests should be individualized depending on the
case.
r Platelet count, PT/PTT, bleeding time if bleeding
disorder is suspected, or if the patient is on
anticoagulants.
r BUN, creatinine, and pregnancy test if aminocaproic
acid is to be used (see below)
r Factor VIII assay if family history of hemophilia
r Sickle cell screen especially in African Americans and
Mediterranean descent
Imagingr CT orbits (1 mm cuts) if open globe injury, intraocular
foreign body, or orbital wall fracture is suspected
r US biomicroscopy (B scan) if total hyphema and
intraocular structures cannot be visualized.
ALERT
Do not perform B scan if open globe injury is
suspected (pressure applied during this procedure
may cause extrusion of intraocular contents).
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Exam: Visual acuity, status of globe, IOP , associated
ocular/bodily injuries
r Labs: Platelet count, PT/PTT, and sickle cell screen if
indicated
r Imaging: B scan or CT orbits if indicated
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Uveitis
r Endophthalmitis
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Place eye shield in case of corneal perforation or
suspected open globe injury.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Keep head upright to allow blood in AC to settle
down.
r Limit activity; avoid bending, straining, or exertion.
r Place metal or plastic shield over involved eye until
integrity of globe is confirmed.
r Do not patch affected eye (if eye is patched, patient
cannot notice sudden loss of vision).
r Note that metal and plastic shields have holes that
let patient see through whereas patch completely
blocks patient’s vision.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Mild analgesics (avoid NSAIDs because of
antiplatelet effect)
r Antiemetics (associated N/V may worsen hyphema
by increasing IOP)
r Cycloplegics decrease pain from iritis:
– Atropine 1% or cyclopentolate 1% eye drops:
BID–TID until hyphema resolves.
r Topical steroids may decrease inflammation from
iritis:
– Prednisolone acetate: 1% eye drops (or
equivalent) 4–8 times per day until hyphema
resolves (usually 7–10 days).

r Aminocaproic acid (antifibrinolytic):
– Use in consultation with ophthalmologist:
◦Not commonly used because of frequent
systemic side effects.
– Stabilizes fibrin clot in AC and decreases incidence
of rebleed, but has no effect on final visual
outcome.
– 50 mg/kg PO q4h for total of 5 days (do not
exceed 30 g/day). Dose should be adjusted in
renal failure.
– May cause postural hypotension, nausea,
vomiting, diarrhea.
– New topical form is not yet FDA approved.
– Do not use in pregnant women or in patients
prone to thrombosis. It can also cause acute renal
failure in patients with hemophilia.
r Oral prednisone:
– Indications:
◦Hemophilia
◦Uncooperative children
◦Total hyphema
◦History of thrombotic disease
– Dose: 0.6–0.75 mg/kg/24 hr in div. doses, up to
60 mg/day for 5 days
r For increased IOP:
– For non–sickle cell patients, treat if IOP
>30 mm Hg.
– For sickle cell patients, treat if IOP >24 mm Hg.
– Treat until IOP is controlled as indicated above.
– Always start with 1 medication. Add another if
unsuccessful in controlling pressure:
◦β-blockers—drug of choice: Timolol or
Levobunolol 0.5% BID
◦α-agonist: Brimonidine 0.2% or apraclonidine
0.5% TID
◦Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (CAI):
Dorzolamide 2% or brinzolamide 1% TID
◦Oral CAI: Acetazolamide 500 mg PO q12h
(peds: 8–30 mg/kg/24 hr q6–8h) or
methazolamide 50 mg q8h.
◦Mannitol (1–2 mg/kg IV over 45 min q24h)
when all other eye drops fail to lower IOP to
acceptable level.
◦Avoid CAI and Mannitol in sickle cell patients,
as they may cause acidosis and induce sickling.
– Allow 25–30 min for each eye drop to work. If
after using all the drops and mannitol, IOP is still
high, then surgical evacuation of blood clot is
warranted (AC tap or washout).
r Drugs to avoid:
– Pilocarpine: Constricts pupil and prevents
visualization of lens and retina
– Prostaglandin eye drops (e.g., Latanoprost):
Increase inflammatory response
ALERT
Criteria for immediate consultation with
ophthalmologist from the ED (If possible,
consultation should be arranged within 24 hr.):r Visual acuity worse than 20/200 at presentation.
r Sickle cell disease/trait with high IOP
r Large hyphema (filling >1/3 of AC).
r Medically uncontrolled IOP .
r Suspected open globe injury

First Liner Atropine: 1% TID
r Prednisolone acetate: 1% QID
Second Liner Timolol 0.5% or levobunolol 0.5% BID
r Brimonidine 0.2% or apraclonidine 0.5% TID
r Dorzolamide 2% or brinzolamide 1% TID
r Acetazolamide: 500 mg PO q12h.

DISPOSITIONr Discharge patient on atropine, prednisolone, and
any appropriate IOP-lowering medications.
r Continue aminocaproic acid if decision was made to
start it in ED.
r Antiemetics if needed.
r Stool softeners to minimize straining during bowel
movements.
Admission Criteriar Hyphema size is not a criterion for discharge or
admission; IOP control is the most important factor.
r Medically uncontrolled IOP requiring surgical
intervention
r Ruptured globe
r Noncompliant patients
r Associated ocular or orbital injuries
r Children <7 yr of age:
– Age group is usually at risk of amblyopia (also
called lazy eye, which is irreversible visual loss
secondary to visual deprivation in early childhood).
r Patients at risk of complications (sickle cell disease,
hemophilia).

Absence of any admission criteria with IOP <30 mm
Hg for non–sickle patients and <24 mm Hg for
patients with sickle cell disease/trait.

Arrange for follow-up with ophthalmologist:
r Daily slit-lamp exam for 3 days after initial trauma to
monitor for rebleeding, corneal staining, and
increased IOP .

r Rule out ruptured globe prior to checking IOP and

HYPOCALCEMIA
Michelle J. Sergel rDamali N. Nakitende
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Hypocalcemia is defined as a total plasma calcium
level <8.7 mg/dL:
– Ionized calcium may be normal and, therefore,
have no clinical manifestations.
r Normal total serum calcium concentrations are
8.7–10.5 mg/dL.
ETIOLOGYr Incidence in the general population is 0.6%.
r Mechanism:
– From either increased loss of calcium from the
circulation or decreased entry into the circulation
– Intravascular calcium circulates in 3 forms:
◦Bound to proteins (mainly albumin): 45–50%
◦Bound to complexing ions (citrate, phosphate,
carbonate): 5–10%
◦Ionized (free) calcium (physiologically active
form): 45–50%
– Serum levels of calcium are primarily controlled by
3 hormones:
◦Parathyroid hormone (PTH)
◦Decrease in calcium levels leads to an increase
in PTH secretion (increasing bone resorption,
renal absorption, intestinal absorption, urinary
phosphate excretion).
– Vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D):
◦Decrease in calcium level activates vitamin D
(increasing bone resorption and intestinal
absorption).
– Calcitonin:
◦Causes a direct inhibition of bone resorption
with increased calcium levels
r Hypoalbuminemia—the most common cause:
– Each 1 g/dL decrease in serum albumin decreases
protein-bound serum calcium by 0.8 mg/dL.
– Ionized (free) calcium levels do not change.
Pediatric Considerations
r Children have higher values of normal calcium
(9.2–11 mg/dL).
r Neonatal hypocalcemia: Total serum calcium
concentrations <7.5 mg/dL or serum-ionized
calcium levels <4 mg/dL
r Symptoms of hypocalcemia in infancy:
– Hyperactivity, jitteriness
– Tachypnea
– Apneic spells with cyanosis
– Vomiting
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Occur when ionized calcium <3.2 mg/dL
r Dependent upon absolute calcium concentration
and rate at which it falls
r Neuromuscular:
– Paresthesias
– Hyperreflexia
– Muscle spasm
– Tetany:
◦Neuromuscular irritability
◦Uncommon unless ionized calcium <4.3 mg/dL
– Latent tetany
– Chvostek sign (finger taps of parotid gland over
the facial nerve causes facial muscle spasm)
– Trousseau signs (an inflated blood pressure cuff
over the arm causes carpopedal spasm)
– Laryngeal stridor
– Seizures
– Choreoathetosis
r Cardiovascular:
– Dysrhythmias:
◦Torsades de pointes
◦Heart block
– Hypotension
– Impaired contractility (heart failure)
– ECG changes:
◦Bradycardia
◦QT and ST prolongation
◦T-wave abnormalities
r Psychiatric:
– Irritability/anxiety
– Psychosis
– Depression
– Confusion
– Delusions
– Chorea
– Parkinsonisms
r Ocular:
– Papilledema
– Cataracts
– May occur in patients with acute onset
hypocalcemia
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Serum-ionized calcium level confirms the diagnosis
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Arterial blood gas:
– Change from normal pH of 0.1 U equals a
reciprocal change in ionized calcium of
∼1.7 mg/dL.
r Serum albumin
r Electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, glucose
r Magnesium
r Phosphate:
– Increase in phosphate associated with
hypoparathyroidism
– Decrease in phosphate associated with vitamin D
deficiency
r PTH:
– Very high levels of PTH associated with
pseudohypoparathyroidism
– High levels of PTH associated with vitamin D
deficiency
– Low levels of PTH associated with
hypoparathyroidism
r Serum calcidiol or calcitriol
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
ECG:
r Prolonged QT interval
r Heart block
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Impaired PTH action or secretion:
– Parathyroid or thyroid surgery or radical neck
surgery and/or irradiation for head and neck
cancer
– Autoimmune disease (typically presents in
childhood)
– Congenital hypoparathyroidism
– Neonatal secondary to maternal
hyperparathyroidism
– Pseudohypoparathyroidism (resistance to PTH)
– Infiltrative (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, metastases,
iron overload)
– HIV infection
r Impaired vitamin D synthesis or action:
– Nutritional malabsorption or poor intake
– Renal disease
– Pronounced hypophosphatemia
r Sepsis or severe burns:
– Impaired secretion of PTH and calcitriol
– End-organ resistance to the action of PTH
r Calcium complex formation or sequestration:
– Hyperphosphatemia
– Ethylene glycol, ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid
(EDTA), citrate (from transfusion)
– Pancreatitis, rhabdomyolysis
– Alkalosis (i.e., hyperventilation)
r Hypomagnesemia:
– Causes end-organ PTH resistance
– Decreased PTH secretion

– Treat symptomatic hypocalcemia as a medical
emergency with parenteral calcium administration.
– Calcium IV bolus:

dextrose
◦Infuse over 20 min

◦Calcium salts are irritating to veins.

◦Individual responses vary.

◦Initiate with calcium supplementation—alone

◦600 IU for ages 19–50 yr
◦600 IU for ages 51–70 yr
◦800 IU for ages 71 and older

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Deficiency in counterregulatory hormones
(glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol, growth hormone)
or excessive insulin response
r Serum glucose < 70 mg/dL

r Prior hypoglycemia episodes
r Hypoglycemia unawareness
r Decreased counterregulation

– Malnutrition
– Coronary artery disease
– Liver disease

decrease gluconeogenic ability (e.g., hereditary
fructose intolerance)
r Congenital hyperinsulinism
r Neonatal diabetes mellitus (often a mutation
effecting an ATP-dependent potassium channel)

– Overdose of oral hypoglycemic agent or insulin
– Oral antihyperglycemics (i.e., α-glucosidase
inhibitors, biguanides, and thiazolidinediones) do
not cause hypoglycemia alone, but may enhance
the risk when used with insulin or sulfonylureas.
– Sepsis
– Insulinoma
– Autoimmune hypoglycemia
– Alimentary hyperinsulinism
– Renal failure (partially responsible for insulin
metabolism)
– Liver cirrhosis (responsible for significant insulin
metabolism)

– Alcohol (inhibitory effect on glycogen storage and
gluconeogenesis)
– Drugs
– Salicylates
– β-blockers (including eye drops)
– SSRIs
– Some antibiotics (e.g., sulfonylureas, pentamidine)
– Adrenal insufficiency
– Malnutrition
– Dehydration

r Extremes of age
r Congestive heart failure
r Counterregulatory hormone deficiency
r Hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism
Pregnancy Considerations
r 3rd-trimester pregnant patients risk relative
substrate deficiency–induced hypoglycemia.
r The fetus is less likely to become hypoglycemic
during mother’s hypoglycemic episode secondary to
active glucose transport across placenta:

profound and prolonged neonatal hypoglycemia.

of life is persistent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia of
infancy (PHHI) in mothers with diabetes.

– Tachycardia/palpitations
– Hunger
– Paresthesias
– Chest pain
– Ischemic ECG changes

– Any focal or general neurologic change
– Dizziness
– Confusion
– Mood changes
– Hyperactive or psychotic behavior
– Slurred speech
– Cranial nerve palsies
– Seizures
– Hemiplegia
– Decerebrate posturing

– Asymptomatic
– Limp
– Bradycardia
– Irritable
– Tremulous
– Seizures
– Poor feeding

hypoglycemic agents—are more concerning.
r Possible insulin or oral hypoglycemic overdose.

r Sepsis
r Metabolic derangements
r Endocrine derangements
r Environmental stressors
r Psychosis, depression, or anxiety

r Growth hormone deficiency
r Inborn errors of metabolism
r Ketotic hypoglycemia
r Reye syndrome
r Salicylate ingestion

HYPOGLYCEMIC AGENT POISONING
Timothy J. Meehan
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Oral or parenteral agents that may cause
hypoglycemia or other metabolic imbalances
r Hypoglycemic poisoning may be intentional or
unintentional (accidental)
ETIOLOGYr Insulin:
– Enhances glucose uptake into cells
– Limits glucose availability to the brain (most
sensitive to hypoglycemia)
– Influences potassium redistribution (hypokalemia)
r Sulfonylurea and Meglitinide agents:
– Enhance insulin release from pancreatic β cells,
reduce hepatic glucose production, and increase
peripheral insulin sensitivity
– Hypoglycemic effect enhanced by:
◦Polypharmacy (drug interactions)
◦Alcohol use and hepatic dysfunction (poor
nutritional stores)
◦Renal insufficiency (decreased clearance)
r GLP1 modulators:
– Exenatide is an analog of glucagon-like peptide 1
(GLP1)
– Gliptins (sitagliptin and saxagliptin) inhibit DDP4
which normally inactivates GLP1
– Net effects: Enhanced insulin secretion, delayed
gastric emptying, and increased satiety
– Unclear effects on glucose metabolism in
overdose (data are lacking at this time)
r Biguanide agents (metformin):
– Antihyperglycemic agents:
◦Decrease elevated serum glucose concentrations
◦Generally do not cause hypoglycemia in
isolation.
– In the presence of insulin, biguanides do the
following:
◦Increase glucose uptake into cells
◦Limit glucose availability to the brain (most
sensitive to hypoglycemia)
◦Influence potassium redistribution
(hypokalemia)
◦Decrease GI glucose absorption
◦Decrease hepatic gluconeogenesis
◦Metabolize glucose to lactate in intestinal cells,
which may accumulate and lead to profound
lactic acidosis
r Thiazolidinediones:
– In the presence of insulin, thiazolidinediones
increase glucose uptake and use and decrease
gluconeogenesis
r α-glucosidase inhibitors:
– Lower systemic glucose by decreasing GI
absorption of carbohydrates
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Insulin or sulfonylureas:
– Overdose causes hypoglycemia
– Symptoms most often occur when glucose
<40–60 mg/dL (may occur at higher levels in
diabetics)
– Symptoms blunted by β-antagonists
– Facial flushing, diaphoresis, pallor, piloerection
– Hunger, nausea, abdominal cramping
– Labored respirations, apnea
– Headache, blurred vision
– Paresthesias, weakness, incoordination, tremor
– Anxiety, irritability, bizarre behavior, confusion,
stupor, coma, seizures
– Palpitations, tachycardia, bradycardia (late)
– Hypertension
– Hypothermia
r Biguanides:
– Toxicity primarily owing to lactic acid accumulation
– Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain
– Agitation, confusion, lethargy, coma
– Kussmaul respirations
– Hypotension, tachycardia
Pediatric Considerations
r Neonatal hypoglycemia may occur after maternal
use of sulfonylureas during labor
r Ingestion of 1 sulfonylurea tablet may cause
hypoglycemia in a child:
– Death has been reported after ingestion of a
single tablet
r Onset of symptomatic hypoglycemia may be delayed
up to 8 hr
Historyr Diagnosis of diabetes in patient
r Access to diabetic medications:
– If occurring in a medical setting (hospital, nursing
home), consider:
◦Dosing error
◦Malicious intent
Physical Examr Vital signs:
– Tachycardia (may be blunted if on β-blockers)
r Neurologic:
– Confusion, obtundation, coma
– Ataxia, other cerebellar signs
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Diagnosis based on clinical presentation and an
accurate history
r Monitor serum glucose concentration
r Monitor vital signs and neurologic status
r Obtain serum electrolytes and lactate for biguanide
ingestion
r Obtain liver function tests for thiazolidinedione
ingestion
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Serum glucose before and after treatment
r Electrolytes:
– Check for hypokalemia
– Anion gap acidosis
r BUN, creatinine:
– May reveal renal insufficiency, causing drug
accumulation
r CBC
r Ethanol level
r Lactate level (especially if biguanide medications
involved)
r Liver function tests
r Arterial blood gas
r Assays for immunoreactive insulin and C-peptide
levels:
– Confirms administration of exogenous insulin if
insulin level is high and C-peptide is low in the
setting of hypoglycemia
– Do not correlate with severity of clinical symptoms
Imagingr ECG: Sinus tachycardia, premature ventricular
contractions (PVCs), atrial dysrhythmias
r EEG: Diffuse slowing without focal abnormalities
r CT scan: Cerebral edema if prolonged hypoglycemia
r Chest radiograph: Aspiration pneumonia or
pulmonary edema
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Addison disease
r Panhypopituitarism
r Sepsis
r Insulinoma
r Neuroendocrine tumors
r Cirrhosis
r Chronic ethanol abuse
r Ethanol ingestion
r Salicylate ingestion
r β-antagonist ingestion
r Ackee fruit poisoning

HYPOKALEMIA
David N. Zull
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Defined as a serum potassium level <3.5 mEq/L:
– Mild: 3–3.5 mEq/L
– Moderate: 2.5–3 mEq/L
– Severe: <2.5 mEq/L
r Frequency:
– Up to 20% of inpatients have documented
hypokalemia (5% have levels <3 mEq/L).
– Up to 14% of outpatients are mildly hypokalemic
(most are related to diuretics or GI loss).
– 5% of geriatric patients have K <3 mEq/L.
r Potassium is the major intracellular cation:
– Gradient is maintained by Na–K ATPase activity
(enhanced by insulin and β-agonists) and
mineralocorticoids.
r Total body potassium is ∼55 mEq/kg of body
weight (98% ICF , 2% ECF).
r Electrophysiologic effects of hypokalemia:
– Increase in the normal intracellular to extracellular
potassium gradient:
◦Alters the depolarization threshold for muscles
and nerves
◦Inhibits the termination of action potentials
– Alterations in intracellular potassium directly
affect cellular function.
ETIOLOGY
Renal Lossesr Diuretics (thiazides, loop diuretics, carbonic
anhydrase inhibitors), usually associated with loss of
other cations (Mg2+,C a2+,P 3+,N a+)
r Renal tubular damage:
– Primary renal tubular disorders (RTA type I and II)
– Interstitial nephritis, analgesic nephropathy, drug
toxicity (amphotericin, gentamicin, toluene,
cisplatin), myeloma kidney
– Overdose toxicity: Acetaminophen, NSAIDs,
hydroxychloroquine
r Hyperaldosteronism:

– Ileus

HYPOKALEMIA
H
TREATMENT
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Establish IV access/volume resuscitation
r ABCs
r Cardiac monitoring
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Total body deficit is 200–300 mEq per 1 mEq/L
decrement in serum potassium level.
r Rate of replacement and route dependent on
presence of symptoms, severity of hypokalemia, and
comorbidities.
r Complete replacement over several days
r Oral potassium preferable to IV therapy whenever
possible
r Identify and prevent ongoing K losses:
– Hold diuretics or laxatives
– Treat vomiting or diarrhea
– Minimize nasogastric suction losses by
administering H2 blockers or PPIs
– Avoid glucose-containing fluids
MEDICATIONr Oral potassium chloride:
– Preferred replacement in almost all cases
– Liquid (or powder dissolved in water or juice) is
more bioavailable, but nausea may occur:
◦10–40 mEq per dose
◦Rapid rise in K, but will drop after 4 hr from
transcellular shift
– Tablets (wax matrix and microencapsulated):
◦More palatable, more sustained effect
◦Slowly absorbed
◦Potential for small bowel ulceration.
– Dosage for hypokalemia:
◦Mild to moderate: 10–20 mEq q6–12h
◦Moderate to severe: 40–60 mEq q8–12h
◦Continue until K remains 3–3.5 mEq/L
r Oral potassium gluconate or citrate:
– Use in acidotic patients (e.g., RTA)
– Ineffective if accompanying metabolic alkalosis
– Less effective than KCl
– Can be used as prophylaxis of calcium oxalate
renal stones or may dissolve uric acid stones
r IV potassium:
– Recommended if neuromuscular symptoms,
cardiac arrhythmias, ongoing GI losses, or severe
hypokalemia
– Potassium chloride is the preferred replacement:
◦Potassium phosphate is used only if
accompanying severe hypophosphatemia.
– Administration:
◦A potassium rider at 10 mEq/h piggybacked into
maintenance 0.9 NS is safest and best tolerated
(peds: 0.1–0.2 mEq/kg/h)
◦15–20 mEq/h are feasible by peripheral vein but
not recommended due to risk of phlebitis and
pain
◦If K is added to maintenance fluids, the
concentration should not be >40 mEq/L and
dextrose solutions should be avoided
◦If sustained life-threatening dysrhythmias,
20–40 mEq/h by central line or 2 peripheral
lines can be considered.
◦If cardiac arrest occurs in a patient with known
severe hypokalemia, 20 mEq could be given IV
over 2–3 min
◦Monitor serum potassium after every 40 mEq IV
– Hypokalemic periodic paralysis and other
situations in which there is significant transcellular
K shifts (adrenergic excess):
◦Small amounts of K are effective (20 mEq IV).
◦More zealous administration may lead to
rebound hyperkalemia.
r Electrolyte corrections:
– Magnesium:
◦Consider if hypokalemia is resistant to K
replacement.
◦Magnesium sulfate 2 g slow IV infusion
– Chloride:
◦Hypokalemia with alkalosis is resistant to
replacement unless volume depletion and
hypochloremia is corrected by saline
administration.
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Need of IV potassium repletion
r Cardiac dysrhythmias
r Profound muscle weakness
r Ongoing K losses
r Serum potassium <2.5 mEq/L
r Associated with significant hypotension or severe
HTN
r Significant comorbidities or geriatric
Discharge Criteriar Asymptomatic
r Able to replete deficiency with oral potassium
r Early follow-up available and reliable patient
r Repeat electrolyte determination in 2–3 days with
the primary care doctor.
r Nephrology referral or consult if suspicion of renal
wasting.
r Continue K replacement for 2–3 days if acute,
self-limited loss, but ongoing therapy if the cause is
not corrected (e.g., diuretic therapy, chronic
diarrhea).
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r If hypokalemia is accompanied by acidosis, correct
hypokalemia 1st before treating the acidosis so as
to avoid life-threatening hypokalemia from
transcellular shifts.
r Minimize glucose administration when treating
hypokalemia, since glucose will stimulate insulin
release, which will lead to K movement into cells.
r Large doses of oral potassium can be given safely in
patients with normal renal function, limited only by
GI tolerance.
r Check for hypomagnesemia if hypokalemia is severe
or resistant to replacement therapy.
r Relatively small amounts of IV potassium are
required to reverse hypokalemia in periodic paralysis
and states of adrenergic excess since transcellular
shifts are transient.

DESCRIPTIONr Sodium <136 mEq/L

◦Hypothyroid
◦Stress

– Opiates
– Oxytocin

– NSAIDs

– Ecstasy
– Fluoxetine
– Fluphenazine
– Haloperidol
– Sertraline
– Thiothixene

HYPOPARATHYROIDISM

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Hypoparathyroidism occurs secondary to a
deficiency in parathyroid hormone (PTH)
r Pseudohypoparathyroidism occurs secondary to
end-organ unresponsiveness to PTH
r PTH:
– Decreases urinary Ca2+ loss
– Increases urinary PO4 loss
– Stimulates vitamin D conversion from 25(OH)-D to
1,25(OH)2-D in kidney
– Liberates Ca2+ and PO4 from bone
r Hypocalcemia is the major metabolic derangement
r Calcitonin:
– Promotes deposition of Ca2+ and PO4 into bone
(produced primarily in C cells in thyroid)
r Magnesium:
– Cofactor in production of PTH
– Essential for action of PTH in target tissues
r Hypoparathyroidism:
– Primary failure of the parathyroid gland (may have
associated Addison disease)
r Pseudohypoparathyroidism:
– Tissue unresponsiveness with elevated PTH levels
– Associated with hypothyroidism and
hypogonadism
r Genetics:
– Congenital absence
– DiGeorge syndrome:
◦Hypoparathyroidism
◦Thymic dysplasia
◦Severe immunodeficiency
– Wilson disease:
◦Destruction of gland owing to copper deposition
– Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type I
◦Hypoparathyroidism
◦Adrenal insufficiency
◦Mucocutaneous candidiasis
– Albright syndrome (hereditary osteodystrophy):
◦Short stature
◦Obesity
◦Round face
◦Short neck
◦Short 4th and 5th metacarpals and metatarsals
(type I pseudohypoparathyroidism)
ETIOLOGYr Failure of parathyroid gland:
– Autoimmune destruction
– Surgical interruption of blood supply or gland
removal
– Radiation damage
– Hypomagnesemia (PTH cofactor)
r End-organ unresponsiveness to PTH
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
ALERT
The most common symptomatic presentation is
postoperatively after parathyroidectomy.
Pediatric Considerations
Neonates/infants:
r Transient hypoparathyroidism in 1st yr of life
r Below normal intelligence proportional to duration
of hypocalcemia
r Dental hypoplasia
Historyr Most common presentation is in the postoperative
period after parathyroidectomy or thyroidectomy
r Prolonged severe hypomagnesemia, in the alcoholic
or high-dose diuretic patient, is the next most
common presentation and can be slow in onset;
usually less symptomatic
Physical Examr Related to severity, rapidity of onset, and duration of
hypocalcemia
r General:
– Weakness
– Malaise
r Neuromuscular:
– Paresthesias (especially circumoral and
extremities)
– Carpal pedal spasm
– Latent spasm elicited by:
◦Chvostek sign (twitching of circumoral muscles
after tapping facial nerve in front of the tragus)
◦Trousseau sign (spasm after inflating BP cuff
20 mm above patient’s systolic BP for 3 min)
– Laryngospasm/bronchospasm
– Blepharospasm
– Muscle cramps
– Tetany
– Seizures (presenting symptom of 1/3 with
hypoparathyroidism)
– Increased intracranial pressure (ICP) with
papilledema
– Parkinson syndrome and other extrapyramidal
disorders
– Myelopathy
r Cardiovascular:
– Prolonged QT interval (owing to ST-segment
prolongation)
– Heart block
– CHF
– Ventricular fibrillation (VFib)
– Vasoconstriction
r Psychiatric:
– Impaired memory
– Confusion
– Hallucinations
– Dementia
r Dermatologic:
– Brittle hair and nails
– Psoriasis
r Hyperpigmentation:
– Lenticular cataracts

check albumin level:
– If still low after correcting for hypoalbuminemia,
check ionized Ca2+
r If hypocalcemic symptoms with normal total Ca2+,
check pH for alkalosis:
– If not alkalotic, check ionized Ca2+ (active form)
– Metabolic or respiratory alkalosis increases the
binding to albumin reducing the ionized Ca2+
r If hypocalcemic symptoms with low ionized Ca2+,
check a PTH level:
– Low in primary hypoparathyroidism and in vitamin
D deficiency
– Elevated in pseudohypoparathyroidism and
hypocalcemia from renal failure

Labr Calcium: Correct for albumin using formula:
– Corrected Ca2+ (mg/dL) = measured Ca2+
(mg/dL) + 0.8[4.0 – albumin (g/dL)]
r Ionized Ca2+ if symptomatic with low total calcium
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose
r Magnesium
r Arterial blood gas (ABG) if symptomatic with normal
total Ca2+
– Elevation of 0.1 pH unit decreases the ionized
Ca2+ by 3–8%.
r Phosphorus:
– Elevated except when hypocalcemia caused by
vitamin D deficiency
– Metastatic calcification can cause hypocalcemia
by tissue deposition when the calcium/phosphorus
product is >60.
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
ECG:
r Prolonged QT interval:
– Owing to ST-segment prolongation from
hypocalcemia
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Must differentiate from a variety of causes of
hypocalcemia
r Lab artifact:
– Low total calcium that is normal when corrected
for albumin level with no symptoms of
hypocalcemia

Ca2+/mL):

elemental Ca2+/kg/24 hr)

◦Intoxication

◦Convection
◦Evaporation
◦Respiration

◦Increased thyroxine
◦Increased epinephrine

– Burn
– Exfoliative dermatitis
– Severe psoriasis
r Drug induced:
– Ethanol
– Phenothiazines
– Sedative–hypnotics
r Environmental:
– Immersion
– Nonimmersion
r Iatrogenic:
– Aggressive fluid replacement
– Heat stroke treatment
r Metabolic:
– Hypoadrenalism
– Hypopituitarism
– Hypothyroidism
r Neurologic:
– Acute spinal cord transection
– Head trauma
– Stroke
– Tumor

◦Ataxia
◦Cold diuresis

– Decreased respiratory rate:

– Diminished gag reflex

– Hypotension

r Serum lactate

r Sepsis
r Primary CNS disorder

r Drug induced

HYPOTHERMIA
H
r Administer Narcan, D50W (or Accu-Chek), and
thiamine to a patient with altered mental status.
r Stress-dose steroids (Solu-Cortef 100 mg IV) for
known adrenal insufficiency or treatment failure.
r Obtain accurate core temperatures using rectal
thermometer.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Cardiac arrest resuscitation:
– Most dysrhythmias correct with rewarming alone.
– Ventricular fibrillation induction occurs with rough
handling, chest compressions, hypoxia, and
acid–base changes.
– CPR is less effective owing to decreased chest wall
elasticity.
– Defibrillation is rarely successful at temperatures
<28–30◦C
◦Defibrillate 1–3 times and then again post
rewarming.
◦Once >30◦C, if ventricular fibrillation persists
consider amiodarone.
◦Direct current results in myocardial damage.
r Dysrhythmia management:
– Atrial fibrillation:
◦Commonly <32◦C
◦Usually converts spontaneously
– Malignant ventricular dysrhythmias:
◦Amiodarone drug of choice though limited proof
of effectiveness.
r Rewarming techniques:
– Faster rewarming rates (1–2◦C/hr) generally have
better prognosis than slower rewarming rates
(<0.5◦C/hr).
– Active rewarming is necessary at core temperature
of <32◦C:
◦Internal thermogenesis insufficient to increase
body temperature
◦Shivering extinguished
r Passive external rewarming:
– Ideal technique for most healthy patients with
mild hypothermia
– Must have intact thermoregulatory mechanisms,
normal endocrine function, and adequate energy
stores
– Cover the patient with dry insulating material.
– Endogenous thermogenesis must generate an
acceptable rate of rewarming:
◦Must increase 0.5–2◦C/hr
– Disadvantage: Core rises very slowly.
r Active external rewarming:
– Delivers heat directly to the skin
– Safe in previously healthy, young, acutely
hypothermic victims
– Requires intact circulation to remove peripherally
rewarmed blood to core
– Associated with core temperature afterdrop
– Rewarming shock: Venous pooling in warmed
extremities secondary to vasodilatation
– Cover trunk preferentially.
– Bair Hugger device provides forced warm air:
Prevents shock or afterdrop.
r Active core rewarming techniques:
– Airway rewarming (complete humidification at
40–45◦C):
◦Administer to all patients.
– Heated IV (40–42◦C) D5.9 NS:
◦Administer to all patients.
◦High flow rates must be maintained.
◦Use blood warmer or calibrated microwave.
– Heated gastric irrigation via NG or orogastric
tubes:
◦Not recommended
◦Low amount of surface area
◦Aspiration risk if airway not secured
– Pleural irrigation (0.9 NS at 30–42◦C):
◦Use in severe hypothermia without cardiac
activity.
◦1–2 chest tubes; midaxillary and midclavicular
bilaterally
◦Contraindicated in patients with cardiac rhythm
because the chest tube may induce ventricular
fibrillation
– Heated peritoneal lavage (0.9 NS at 40–45◦C):
◦Use in unstable hypothermic patients or stable
patients with severe hypothermia whose
rewarming rates are <1◦C/hr.
◦1–2 catheters
◦Advantageous in patients with overdose or
rhabdomyolysis
r Extracorporeal rewarming:
– Most effective rewarming method
– Hemodialysis:
◦Initiate for patients with drug overdoses or
severe electrolyte disturbances.
– Continuous arteriovenous rewarming:
◦BP must be >60 mm Hg.
◦Blood circulated through warmer from
percutaneously inserted femoral arterial and
contralateral venous catheters
– Extracorporeal venovenous rewarming:
◦Blood is removed via central venous catheter,
heated to 40◦C, and returned via 2nd central or
large peripheral venous catheter.
– Cardiopulmonary bypass:
◦Treatment of choice in severe hypothermia with
cardiac arrest
r Additional therapy:
– Methylprednisolone or hydrocortisone for
suspicion of adrenocortical insufficiency or steroid
dependence
– Empiric treatment with levothyroxine only for
myxedematous patients
MEDICATIONr Amiodarone: 300 mg IV push (IVP) for ventricular
fibrillation followed by 1 mg/min infusion
r Dextrose: D50W 1 amp—50 mL or 25 g (peds:
D25W 2–4 mL/kg) IV
r Hydrocortisone: 250 mg IVP
r Levothyroxine: 50–500 μg IV over several minutes
r Methylprednisolone: 30 mg/kg IVP
r Naloxone (Narcan): 2 mg (peds: 0.1 mg/kg) IV or IM
initial dose
r Thiamine (vitamin B1): 100 mg (peds: 50 mg) IV or
IM
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Moderate to severe hypothermia (<32◦C)
r Young, healthy patients with no comorbid illness
who have mild accidental hypothermia (>32◦C)
that responds well to warming:
– Admit to an observation area.
– Discharge if asymptomatic after 8–12 hr and they
remain asymptomatic.
Discharge Criteriar Young, healthy patients with no comorbid illness
r Very mild accidental hypothermia (>35◦C) that
responds well to warming
r Safe, warm environment to go to after discharge
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Social work follow-up for homeless patients with cold
exposure and hypothermia
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Defibrillation is rarely successful at temperatures
<28–30◦C:
– Defibrillate 1–3 times and then again post
rewarming.
r Atrial fibrillation usually converts spontaneously.
r Faster rewarming rates (1–2◦C/hr) generally have
better prognosis than slower rewarming rates
(<0.5◦C/hr).
r Afterdrop is the continued decline in core temp after
removed from cold
– Ongoing conduction of heat from core warming
periphery prior to the core

volume during resuscitation.

HYPOTHYROIDISM
Rita K. Cydulka rTammy L. Weiner
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Decreased level of effective circulating thyroid
hormone leads to decreased metabolic rate and
decreased sensitivity to catecholamines.
r More common in woman and the elderly
r Myxedema coma is a rare, extreme form of
hypothyroidism characterized by altered mental
status and defective thermoregulation triggered by a
precipitating event in a patient with hypothyroidism.
ETIOLOGYr Primary:
– Idiopathic
– Congenital
– Autoimmune:
◦Thyroiditis
◦Hashimoto disease
– Iatrogenic:
◦Postsurgical
◦External radiation
◦Radioiodine therapy
◦Drugs (iodides, lithium, amiodarone, sunitinib,
bexarotene, interferons, narcotics, sedatives)
– Neoplasm: Primary (carcinoma) or secondary
(infiltration)
– Infection: Viral (rarely aerobic or anaerobic
bacteria)
– Iodine deficiency (most common cause worldwide)
r Central (very rare):
– Pituitary or hypothalamic disorder induced by
drugs or severe illness
– May have other associated hormone deficiencies
r Myxedema coma:
– Critical decompensation of a patient with
hypothyroidism due to a stress, often during
winter months. Stressors include:
◦Infection
◦Hypothermia
◦Intoxication
◦Drugs
◦Cerebrovascular accident
◦Heart failure
◦Trauma
Pregnancy Considerations
r Hypothyroid women require increased exogenous
thyroid hormone replacement during pregnancy
above baseline
r Postpartum thyroiditis occurs in up to 10% of
women:
– Usually 3–6 mo postpartum
– Typically resolves without treatment
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Exhaustion
r Cold intolerance
r Headaches
r Diminished hearing
r Myalgias and muscle weakness
r Menorrhagia
r Infertility
r Carpal tunnel syndrome
r Constipation
r Weight gain
r Depression, hallucinations, or paranoia
r Cognitive impairment
Physical Examr Periorbital edema
r Sparse, coarse hair and brittle nails
r Absent lateral 1/3 of eyebrows (Queen Anne sign)
r Husky or hoarse voice
r Goiter
r Prolonged relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes
(DTRs)
r Yellow, dry, pale, cool, coarse skin
r Myxedema (dry, waxy swelling of skin)
r Nonpitting edema of hands and feet
r Myxedema coma:
– Altered mental status
– Hypotension
– Hypothermia
– Respiratory failure
– Bradycardia
Pediatric Considerations
r Undiagnosed hypothyroidism in infants has largely
been eliminated via universal screening at birth
r Hypothyroidism in childhood is usually due to
Hashimoto disease.
r Children may manifest with retardation of mental
developmental, linear growth, and sexual
maturation
Geriatric Considerations
Typical symptoms of hypothyroidism may be confused
with changes associated with aging.
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Lab confirmation of the diagnosis of hypothyroidism/
myxedema coma may not be available in the ED, and
therapy should be initiated based on clinical suspicion.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Search for the underlying cause of myxedema coma.
Labr Thyroid function studies:
– Low total and free thyroxine (T4)
– Low total and free triiodothyronine (T3)
– Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH):
◦Increased in primary hypothyroidism but normal
or decreased in central pathology
r Anemia
r Hyponatremia
r Hypoglycemia
r Hypoxemia
r Hypercapnia
r Respiratory acidosis
r Elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), creatine
kinase (CK), cholesterol, creatinine
Imaging
CXR:
r Enlarged cardiac silhouette due to pericardial
effusion
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
ECG:
r Sinus bradycardia, low voltage, PR interval
prolongation, bundle branch blocks, QT interval
prolongation and nonspecific ST–T-wave changes
r May see Osborn wave if profoundly hypothermic
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Chronic nephritis
r Chronic renal disease
r Heart failure
r Depression
r Hypoalbuminemia
r Pernicious anemia
r Nephrotic syndrome
r Sepsis
ALERT
r Euthyroid sick syndrome:
– Illness, surgery, fasting may produce abnormal
thyroid function test results
– Thyroid function tests performed during acute
nonthyroid illness may be abnormal and should
be interpreted with caution

IDIOPATHIC THROMBOCYTOPENIC PURPURA
Matthew T. Keadey rRichard D. McCormick
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is
thrombocytopenia without apparent cause or
abnormalities in other cell lines.
r Incidence is ∼2–5/100,000/yr—may be an
underestimate owing to undetected, subclinical
cases.
r Acute ITP:
– 1/2 of cases involve children.
– 80% of children recover within 8 wk with or
without therapy.
– Adult recovery is delayed and requires specific
therapy to achieve remission.
r Chronic ITP:
– Occurs mostly in adults
– Young women are most susceptible in adult onset
ITP
– Characterized by variable response to
corticosteroids and other immune suppressants
– 60–70% respond to splenectomy
r Chronic refractory ITP:
– Platelet counts may often wax and wane.
– Often do not respond to therapy
– No clear optimal course of treatment
r Genetics:
– ITP appears to run in families, as do variations in
response to corticosteroids for treatment.
ETIOLOGYr Autoantibodies produced by B cells and plasma cells
cause immune-mediated destruction of circulating
platelets
r Macrophages in spleen and liver mediate
destruction of platelets via IgG autoantibodies
r IgM and IgA rarely have been seen
r Some patients do not possess autoantibodies,
suggesting a role for T cell-mediated cytotoxicity.
r C3 and C4 complements have also been shown to
play a role in patients that lack autoantibodies
r Poor platelet production may also play a role
especially in chronic or refractory cases of ITP
r Eradication of Helicobacter pylori can sometimes be
associated with platelet recovery (unclear
mechanism).
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Bleeding is the most common complaint:
– Common:
◦Mucous membrane: Gingiva, epistaxis,
conjunctival, menorrhagia
– Rare (more common in coagulopathies):
◦GI bleeding, hemarthrosis, hematuria, and
hematomas
r 84% of pediatric cases are 2–3 wk following a viral
illness:
– Small percentage found following vaccinations
r Most adult cases have an insidious onset:
– Up to 28% of patients are asymptomatic and

r Increased mean platelet volume

r All adults >60 yr to evaluate for malignancy

r Children with persistent thrombocytopenia >6m o

– Neoplastic infiltration
– Sickle cell disease

– TTP/HUS
– Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
– HELLP syndrome
– Cardiac valvular disease

– Decreased platelet production:
◦Chemotherapy
◦Thiazide diuretics
◦Ethanol
◦Estrogen

◦Aspirin
◦Heparin
◦Chlorpropamide
◦Chloroquine
◦Gold salts
◦Sulfonamides
◦Insecticides

IDIOPATHIC THROMBOCYTOPENIC PURPURA
I
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Stabilize ABCs
r Significant oral or laryngeal bleeding may affect
airway.
r CNS event may affect ability to control airway
r Establish IV access for cases of significant bleeding
r Control any bleeding with direct pressure
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs
r Stabilize life-threatening bleeding:
– ICH:
◦Airway control
◦Neurosurgery consultation: Craniotomy not
typically possible until platelet counts >75 K
– Hemorrhagic shock:
◦2 large-bore IVs
◦Direct pressure for hemostasis
◦Resuscitation with blood transfusions and
isotonic crystalloid
◦Medications and platelets for acute
life-threatening episodes of bleeding:
■ IV high-dose dexamethasone or
methylprednisolone
■ IVIG infusion
■ Platelet transfusions: 2–3 times the normal
amount
– Platelets typically infused after steroids and/or
IVIG
– Mucous membrane bleeding:
◦Topical agents
◦Other:
■ IV Aminocaproic acid may be considered
■ In rare cases, plasmapheresis has been
proven helpful
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Initial treatment options for ITP are based on:
– Degree of thrombocytopenia
– Severity of illness
– Duration of symptoms
– Age
– Risk factors for bleeding (hypertension, peptic
ulcer disease, vigorous lifestyle)
– Hematologist preference
r Efficacy of treatment is demonstrated in terms of
platelet recovery time and not morbidity or mortality.
r Specific treatment options:
– Observation is recommended for children without
bleeding complications or profound
thrombocytopenia (<20–30 K)
– Profound thrombocytopenia (<20 K):
◦High-dose corticosteroids: 75% response
◦IVIG: 80% response, but costly, so reserved in
time critical emergencies
◦Anti-D IG: 70% response (used only in Rh+
patients)
– Splenectomy:
◦2nd-line therapy if inadequate response to a
course of glucocorticoid therapy
◦Two-thirds of adult patients respond,
three-fourths of pediatric patients respond.
◦No specific indications for emergent
splenectomy
Pregnancy Considerations
r Differential diagnosis of thrombocytopenia during
pregnancy:
– Gestational thrombocytopenia (75%):
◦Usually of no clinical significance
◦Does not cause neonatal thrombocytopenia
◦Remits 1–2 wk after delivery
◦Platelets typically >50 K
r HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes,
and low platelets)
r ITP (15%):
– Platelets typically <50 K
– Maternal platelet count does not correlate to
neonatal thrombocytopenia.
– Treatment with steroids or IVIG does not alter
incidence of neonatal thrombocytopenia.
– Degree of thrombocytopenia should not alter
decision of vaginal birth vs. C-section.
– Measure neonatal CBC and check brain
ultrasound for ICH.
– Treat neonatal thrombocytopenia with IVIG and
steroids
MEDICATION
First Liner Glucocorticoids (high dose over 2–3 wk):
– Dexamethasone: 40 mg PO daily
– Prednisone: 1–2 mg/kg/24 hr PO/day
– Methylprednisolone: 1 g IV q8h (30 mg/kg/24 hr
pediatric dose)
r IVIG: 1–2 g/kg IV × 1 dose and possibly repeated in
24 hr:
– Used only for critical bleeding or when the need to
acutely raise platelets is required such as
emergency surgery
r Anti-D immunoglobulin: 50 μg/kg/24 hr IV:
– Used only presplenectomy and in Rh+ patients
Second Liner Chronic long-term suppression and steroid bolus
therapy
r Immunosuppressive agents:
– Azathioprine
– Cyclosporin
– Mycophenolate
– Chemotherapeutic agents:
– Vinca alkaloids
– Cyclophosphamide
– Combinational chemotherapy
r Other:
– Rituximab: Monoclonal antibody directed against
B cell antigens
– Danazol: Antiandrogen
r Experimental:
– Other monoclonal antibodies directed at B cells
– Stem cell transplants
– Thrombopoietin and thrombopoietin-like agonists
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Life-threatening bleeding regardless of platelet
count
r Any bleeding with platelet count <20 K
r Asymptomatic patient with platelet count <20 K
with issues of noncompliance or poor follow-up
Discharge Criteriar Asymptomatic patients
r Patients with minor bleeding and platelets >30 K
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Hematology referral is indicated in all cases (either
outpatient or inpatient consultation)
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Before low platelet counts are evaluated,
pseudothrombocytopenia should be excluded.
r Spontaneous bleeding usually does not occur until
platelet counts are <10 K.
