MITRAL VALVE PROLAPSE
Liudvikas Jagminas
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Bulging of 1 or both of the mitral valve leaflets into
the left atrium during systole
r Occurs when the leaflet edges of the mitral valve do
not coapt
r Commonly due to abnormal stretching of 1 of the
mitral valve leaflets during systole:
– Myxomatous proliferation of the spongiosa layer
within the valve causing focal interruption of the
fibrosa layer
– Excessive stretching of the chordae tendineae,
leading to traction on papillary muscles
r Theoretical explanations for associated chest pain:
– Focal ischemia from coronary microembolism due
to platelet aggregates and fibrin deposits in the
angles between the leaflets
– Coronary artery spasm
r Mitral regurgitation (MR) may occur in some
patients.
r Age of onset is 10–16 yr
r Female > male (3:1)
r Typically benign in young women, whereas men
>50 yr tend to have serious sequelae and more
often develop severe regurgitation requiring surgical
intervention
r Can be identified by ECG in 2–4% of the general
population and in 7% of autopsies
r A variety of neuroendocrine and autonomic
disturbances occur in some patients
r Genetics:
– Strong hereditary component
– Sometimes transmitted as an autosomal dominant
trait with varying penetrance
ETIOLOGYr Marfan syndrome
r Relapsing polychondritis
r Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (i.e., types I, II, IV)
r Osteogenesis imperfecta
r Pseudoxanthoma elasticum
r Stickler syndrome
r Systemic lupus erythematosus
r Polyarteritis nodosa
r Polycystic kidney disease
r von Willebrand syndrome
r Duchenne muscular dystrophy
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Separated into 3 categories:
r Symptoms related to autonomic dysfunction
r Symptoms related to the progression of MR
r Symptoms that occur as a result of an associated
complication (i.e., stroke, endocarditis, or
arrhythmia)
Historyr Palpitations in up to 40% of cases:
– Usually ventricular premature beats or paroxysmal
supraventricular tachycardia
– Up to 40% have symptoms of dysautonomia
r Chest pain occurs in 10%:
– Sharp, localized, of variable duration, and
nonexertional
– Rarely may respond to nitroglycerin
r Panic attacks
r Anxiety
r Fatigue
r Depression in up to 70%
r Nervousness
r Migraine headaches
r Irritable bowel
r Syncope/presyncope:
– Occurs in 0.9% of patients
r Orthostasis
r Dyspnea and fatigue relatively uncommon
Physical Examr Mid to late systolic click at the cardiac apex:
– Standing or Valsalva moves click closer to S1.
– S1 may be accentuated when prolapse occurs
early in systole.
– Squatting moves click closer to S2.
r Late systolic murmur
r Skeletal abnormalities are observed in 2/3 of
patients:
– Asthenic body habitus: Height-to-weight ratio >
normal
– Arm span > height (dolichostenomelia)
– Scoliosis or kyphosis
– Pectus excavatum
– Arachnodactyly
– Joint hypermobility
r Hypomastia
r Cathedral palate
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr History and auscultation of a midsystolic click are
often sufficient to make the diagnosis.
r Echocardiography confirms the diagnosis when
clinical information is insufficient.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Not required to establish the diagnosis
Imagingr EKG:
– Usually normal
– Occasionally ST-T wave depression and inversion
in leads III and aVF
– Prolonged QT interval or prominent Q waves
– Premature atrial and ventricular contractions
r CXR:
– Typically normal
– If MR is present, may show both left atrial and
ventricular enlargement
– Calcification of the mitral annulus in patients with
Marfan syndrome
r Echocardiography:
– Classic MVP: The parasternal long-axis view
shows >2 mm superior displacement of the mitral
leaflets into the left atrium during systole, with a
leaflet thickness of at least 5 mm.
– Nonclassic MVP: Displacement is >2 mm, with a
maximal leaflet thickness of <5 mm.
– Other ECG findings that should be considered as
criteria are leaflet thickening, redundancy, annular
dilatation, and chordal elongation.
– Minor criteria:
◦Isolated mild to moderate superior systolic
displacement of the posterior mitral leaflet
◦Moderate superior systolic displacement of both
mitral leaflets
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Cardiac studies may be indicated in patients with
chest pain when the etiology is uncertain.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr MI/ischemia
r Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with obstruction
r Idiopathic hypertrophic subaortic stenosis
r Tachyarrhythmias
r Atrial fibrillation/flutter
r Ventricular septal defect
r Papillary muscle dysfunction
r Hypokalemia
r Hypomagnesemia
r Valvular heart disease
r Pheochromocytoma
r Anemia
r Thyrotoxicosis
r Pregnancy
r Toxicity from cocaine, amphetamines, or other
sympathomimetics
r Ventricular tachycardia
r WPW syndrome
r Rheumatic endocarditis
r Anxiety/panic disorder
r Stress
r Menopause
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr ABCs
r IV access
r Supplemental oxygen
r Cardiac monitoring
r Pulse oximetry
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Cardiac monitoring
r Supplemental oxygen
r IV catheter placement

MITRAL VALVE PROLAPSE
M
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Medications generally are not necessary. β-blockers
may be helpful if palpitations are severe.
r Antiplatelet agents (aspirin, aspirin with
extended-release dipyridamole, or clopidogrel) are
indicated for patients with transient ischemic attack
or stroke symptoms.
r Orthostatic hypotension and presyncope symptoms
may be treated with sodium chloride tablets;
however, if this treatment is not successful,
fludrocortisone may be used.
r Magnesium supplementation may improve
symptoms of the classic MVP syndrome.
r Significant MR in the setting of HTN (systolic blood
pressure >140 mm Hg) may be improved with the
use of ACE inhibitors.
r β-Blockers:
– Patients with tachycardia or severely symptomatic
chest pain
r Digoxin is an alternative for supraventricular
tachycardia and prevention of chest pain and
fatigue.
r Antibiotic prophylaxis:
– When performing surgical procedures (e.g.,
contaminated wound repair, abscess incision and
drainage)
– Indicated in the following settings:
◦Presence of a murmur
◦Evidence of nontrivial MR on Echocardiogram
◦Men >45 yr with valve thickening
– Prophylaxis is not recommended for patients who
have an isolated click without a murmur or for
patients without evidence of MR on an
echocardiogram or previous history of
endocarditis.
MEDICATION
First Liner Amoxicillin: 2 g PO 1 hr before the procedure (peds:
50 mg/kg PO 1 hr before procedure)
r Ampicillin: 2 g IV/IM 30 min before the procedure
(peds: 50 mg/kg IV/IM 30 min before the procedure)
r Clindamycin: 600 mg PO 1 hr before procedure
(peds: 20 mg/kg PO 1 hr before procedure; not to
exceed 600 mg)
r Propranolol: 1–3 mg IV at 1 mg/min, 80–640 mg/d
PO (peds: 1–4 mg/kg/d PO div. BID/QID
r Isoproterenol: 0.02–0.06 mg IV × 1, 0.01–0.02 mg
IV or 2–20 mg/min infusion
r Atenolol: 0.3–2 mg/kg/d PO, max. 2 mg/kg/d
Second Liner Digoxin: 0.5–1 mg IV/IM div. 50% initially then
25% × 2 q6–12h or 0.125–0.5 mg/d PO
r Fludrocortisone: 0.05–0.10 mg/d PO
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Severe MR
r Severe chest pain with ischemic symptoms
r Syncope or near syncope
r Life-threatening dysrhythmias
r Cerebral ischemic events, including transient
ischemic attack
Discharge Criteriar Asymptomatic
r No lab abnormalities
r No significant MR or dysrhythmias
Issues for Referralr Cardiology consultation is warranted in cases of
ventricular dysrhythmia or risk of sudden death, as
well as when symptoms of severe MR are present.
r Cardiothoracic surgery follow-up is recommended
for consideration of valve replacement or repair
– Symptomatic patients
– Atrial fibrillation
– Ejection fraction <50–60%
– Left ventricular end-diastolic dimension
>45–50 mm
– Pulmonary systolic pressure >50–60 mm Hg
r Valve repair rather than replacement is preferred to
avoid the need for anticoagulation.
r Pilots with mitral valve prolapse may develop MR
under positive G force and be at risk for dysrhythmia
or syncope.
Pediatric Considerations
Dysrhythmias, sudden death, and bacterial
endocarditis have been reported.
Geriatric Considerations
r Often present in an atypical manner:
– More likely to have holosystolic murmurs and a
greater degree of MR.
r Heart failure may be presenting symptom complex
associated with ruptured chordae tendineae.
Pregnancy Considerations
MVP does not predispose women to any increased risk
during pregnancy.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Repeat evaluations are necessary every 3–5 yr to
identify any progression of disease.
r Infective endocarditis prophylaxis is indicated in
patients with MVP and MR while undergoing at-risk
procedures.
r Coronary artery anomalies should be excluded in
patients with chest pain before they participate in
sports.
r Patients with MVP and a murmur should avoid
high-intensity competitive sports in the following
settings:
– Syncope associated with dysrhythmia
– A family history of sudden death associated with
MVP
– Significant supraventricular or ventricular
dysrhythmias
– Moderate to severe MR
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r The diagnosis of MVP should not be an excuse to
terminate further diagnostic evaluation of patients
with symptoms of chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea,
or syncope.
r MVP is the 3rd most common cause of sudden
death in athletes.
ADDITIONAL READING

MOLLUSCUM CONTAGIOSUM
Evan Small rDeepi G. Goyal
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Molluscum contagiosum (MC) is a generally benign
human disease characterized by multiple small,
painless, pearly lesions.
r MC appears on epithelial surface and spreads
through close contact or autoinoculation.
r Confined to the skin and mucous membranes
r 5–20% of patients with HIV have coinfection with
MC.
r Found worldwide with an incidence of 2–8%, with
higher distribution in tropical areas
ETIOLOGYr MC is caused by a double-stranded DNA poxvirus of
the Molluscipox genus
r Transmission in children is by direct skin-to-skin
contact, fomites, or pool or bath water.
r Transmission in adults is most often by sexual
contact; autoinoculation is common at any age.
r There are rare reports of transmission to infants
during childbirth.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Incubation period: 14–50 days
r Patients are usually asymptomatic, with occasional
pruritus or tenderness.
r 10–25% of patients may have eczematous reaction
surrounding the lesions.
r Untreated lesions in immunocompetent hosts
usually resolve within several months but can last up
t o5y r .
Physical Examr Lesions are smooth-surfaced, firm, spherical papules
2–6 mm in diameter.
r May be flesh colored, white, translucent, or light
yellow
r Lesions have a waxy, curd-like core composed of
collagen–lipid-rich material containing large
numbers of maturing virions
r Distinctive central umbilication in 25%
r Atypical presentations include nonumbilicated,
persistent, disseminated, or giant lesions, usually in
the setting of immunosuppression.
r Distribution:
– Children:
◦Face
◦Trunk
◦Extremities
– Healthy adults:
◦Genitals
◦Lower abdomen
◦Occasionally perioral
– Rarely on palms and soles
r MC is commonly seen with HIV infection, causing
atypical involvement of face, neck, and trunk,
lesions to 1.5 cm, and a progressive course. Lesions
may also appear with initiation of highly active
antiretroviral therapy (HAART) as a manifestation of
the immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.
r Occasional intraocular or periocular involvement
presenting as trachoma or chronic follicular
conjunctivitis
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr History and careful skin exam
r Skin biopsy for confirmation
r Lesions in adult men necessitate evaluation for an
immunocompromised state.
r MC in children is rarely associated with
immunodeficiency, and usually no further evaluation
is needed.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Test for immunocompromised state if no clear
etiology:
– CBC with differential
– HIV if indicated
r If anogenital lesions:
– Consider syphilis, hepatitis C, HIV
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Skin biopsy for confirmation
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Basal cell carcinoma
r Histiocytoma
r Keratoacanthoma
r Intradermal nevus
r Darier disease
r Nevoxanthoendothelioma
r Syringoma
r Epithelial nevi
r Sebaceous adenoma
r Atopic dermatitis
r Dermatitis herpetiformis
r Mycosis fungoides
r Jessner lymphocytic infiltration
r Cryptococcus neoformans
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Maintain universal precautions.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Not applicable in routine cases.

MOLLUSCUM CONTAGIOSUM
M
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Aimed at destruction or removal of virus-infected
epithelial cells and is indicated to prevent
autoinoculation and transmission:
– Intervention is not always indicated: Lesions are
self-limited in immunocompetent hosts.
– Untreated immunocompromised patients are at
greater risk for secondary inflammation and
bacterial infections
r If treatment is necessary, consider referral to
dermatology.
r If dermatology referral is not an option, physical
treatment modalities generally most effective:
– Curettage after local anesthesia with EMLA
(eutectic mixture, lidocaine, prilocaine) or ethyl
chloride
– Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen
– Podophyllin, trichloroacetic acid, cantharidin,
tretinoin, and cidofovir applied topically are
variably effective.
– Repeatedly applying adhesive tape to the lesions
as a means of removing the superficial epidermis
r Griseofulvin and methisazone orally for extensive
disease have given mixed results.
r HAART has been effective in reducing incidence in
HIV-infected patients.
r Topical imiquimod has shown effectiveness in
several small studies.
r Examine sexual partners for MC and other sexually
transmitted diseases:
– Patients should avoid contact sports, swimming
pools, shared baths and towels, scratching, and
shaving until lesions have resolved.
r Re-examine treated patients for recurrence every
2–4 wk; 2–4 treatments are often needed to clear
lesions completely.
r Discourage picking and scratching lesions, a
common habit, as it may lead to scarring or pigment
alteration.
MEDICATIONr Cantharidin 0.9% solution with equal parts of
acetone and flexible collodion: Apply topically 1–3
treatments every 7 days or until resolution.
r Imiquimod 5%: Apply topically daily for 3–5
consecutive days for 16 wk.
r Podophyllin (podofilox 0.5%): Apply topically q12h
for 3 days, withhold for 4 days; repeat 1-wk cycle up
to 4 times until resolved.
r Tretinoin 0.1%: Apply topically q12h for 10 days or
until resolution of lesions.
r Trichloroacetic acid (50–80%): Apply and cover with
bandage 5–6 days.
r Oral cimetidine (40 mg/kg/d) in 2 div. doses for 2 mo
has been used to treat extensive infections; however,
further study is needed to determine efficacy.
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteria
Widespread disease with extensive superinfection in
an immunocompromised host
Discharge Criteria
Patients without extensive superinfection may be
safely treated as outpatients.
Issues for Referral
Consider referral to dermatology if treatment or
confirmatory testing is necessary.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Re-examine treated patient for recurrence every
2–4 wk.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Active nonintervention is an option in
immunocompetent hosts.
r Search for an immunocompromised state if no clear
etiology.
r Physical destruction of lesions is often most effective
treatment vs. medication.
ADDITIONAL READING

molluscum in adolescents. Adolesc Med. 2001;
12(2):vi, 229–242.

for physician intervention and new treatment
options. Cutis. 2004;73(3):202–206.

anogenital molluscum contagiosum. Am Fam
Physician. 2009;80:864–865.

(review). Dermatol Online J. 2003;9(2):2.

in children. Br Med J. 2004;329:403.

contagiosum in an HIV-positive patient in rural
South Africa. BMJ Case Rep. 2012;2012.
doi:10.1136/bcr-2012-007539.

cutaneous molluscum contagiosum (review).

MONOAMINE OXIDASE INHIBITOR POISONING
James W. Rhee
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Primarily for depression
r Selegiline, a selective monoamine oxidase B
inhibitor, is sometimes used to treat Parkinson
disease, and also comes in a transdermal
preparation.
r Monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) pharmacologic
actions:
– Disruption of equilibrium between endogenous
monoamine synthesis and degradation, resulting
in:
◦Increased neural norepinephrine levels
◦Downregulation of several receptor types
– Inhibition of irreversible (noncompetitive) enzyme
– Inhibition of other B6-containing enzymes
r MAO: Principal inactivator of neural bioactive
amines:
–M A OA :
◦Present in the gut and liver
◦Protects against dietary bioactive amines
–M A OB :
◦Present in neuron terminals and platelets
◦Sympathomimetic amines: Types of bioactive
amines
ETIOLOGYr MAOI overdose:
– Toxicopharmacology poorly understood
– MAO inhibitors: Amphetamine-like in structure:
◦Early: Indirect sympathomimetic effect
◦Late: Sympatholytic response (hypotension)
r MAOI hypertensive crisis syndrome:
– Results from impaired norepinephrine degradation
and large norepinephrine release precipitated by
an indirect- or mixed-acting sympathomimetic
agent
– Common precipitants: Tyramine, cocaine,
amphetamines
r Serotonin syndrome (SS):
– Commonly results from exposure to combinations
of agents that affect serotonin metabolism or
action
– Increases serotonin synthesis: Tryptophan
– Increase serotonin release:
◦Indirect- and mixed-acting sympathomimetic
agents and dopamine receptor agonists
– Decrease serotonin reuptake:
◦Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors
◦Tricyclic antidepressants
◦Newer antidepressants: Trazodone, nefazodone,
venlafaxine
◦Phenylpiperidine opioids: Meperidine,
dextromethorphan, tramadol, methadone,
propoxyphene
– Direct serotonin receptor agonists:
◦Buspirone, sumatriptan, lysergic acid
diethylamide
– Decrease serotonin breakdown:
◦MAOIs
– Increases nonspecific serotonin activity:
◦Lithium
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr MAOI overdose:
– Delayed onset (6–12 hr)
– Initial hypertension with headache
– Hyperadrenergic activity:
◦Tachycardia
◦Hypertension
◦Mydriasis
◦Agitation
– Neuromuscular excitation:
◦Nystagmus
◦Hyperreflexia
◦Tremor
◦Myoclonus
◦Rigidity
◦Seizures
– Hyperthermia
– Associated complications:
◦Rhabdomyolysis
◦Renal failure
◦Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
◦Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
r MAOI hypertensive crisis syndrome (MAOI
interaction with drug or food):
– Hypertension
– Tachycardia or bradycardia
– Hyperthermia
– Headache, usually occipital
– Altered mental status
– Intracranial hemorrhage
– Seizures
r SS:
– Increased neuromuscular activity
– Increased deep tendon reflexes:
◦Lower extremity may be greater than upper
– Tremor
– Myoclonus
– Rigidity (when severe)
– Autonomic nervous system hyperactivity:
◦Hyperthermia
– CNS:
◦Agitation
◦Hallucinations
◦Delirium
◦Coma
– Diarrhea
– SS vs. neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS):
◦Both present along a spectrum of severity (mild
to severe)
◦Onset: Hours (SS) vs. days (NMS)
◦Gastrointestinal symptoms: May be present (SS)
vs. absent (NMS)
◦Only drug/medication history may differentiate
in many cases
Historyr Time of ingestion
r Bottle available
r Intentional or accidental
r Coingestions
Physical Examr Neuromuscular hyperactivity:
– Myoclonus
– Rigidity
– Tremors
– Hyperreflexia
r Autonomic hyperactivity:
– Tachycardia or bradycardia
– Fever
– Diaphoresis
r Altered mental status:
– Agitation, confusion, or excitement
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr History of ingested substances
r Rectal temperature monitoring as indicated
r Blood pressure/cardiac monitoring
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Urinalysis:
– Blood
– Myoglobin
r Electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, glucose:
– Hypoglycemia may contribute to altered mental
status.
– Acidosis may accompany severe toxicity.
– Rhabdomyolysis may cause renal failure.
– Hyperkalemia—life-threatening consequence of
acute renal failure
r Coagulation profile to monitor for potential DIC:
– INR, prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin
time, platelets
r Creatinine kinase:
– Markedly elevated in rhabdomyolysis
r Urine toxicology screen:
– May be positive for amphetamines, given the
structural similarities between some MAOIs and
amphetamines
r Aspirin and acetaminophen levels if suicide attempt
a possibility
r Arterial blood gas
Imagingr Chest radiograph:
– ARDS
r Head CT if significant headache or altered mental
status or focal neurologic signs:
– Subarachnoid hemorrhage, intracerebral bleed
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Lumbar puncture for:
r Suspected meningitis (headache, altered mental
status, hyperpyrexia)
r Suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage and CT normal

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Hyperthermia:
– Infection
– Hyperthyroidism
– Heat stroke
– Anatomic thalamic dysfunction
– NMS
– Malignant hyperthermia
– Malignant catatonia
– Ethanol or drug withdrawal
– Anticholinergic toxicity
– Sympathomimetic overdose
– Cocaine-associated delirium/rhabdomyolysis
– Salicylate toxicity
– Theophylline toxicity
– Nicotine toxicity
r Hypertension:
– Hypoglycemia
– Carcinoid syndrome
– Pheochromocytoma
– Accelerated renovascular hypertension
– Ethanol or drug withdrawal
– Sympathomimetic toxicity
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Patient may be uncooperative or violent.
r Secure IV access.
r Protect from self-induced trauma.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Airway, breathing, and circulation (ABCs)
r IV access and fluid resuscitation if hypotensive
r Oxygen
r Cardiac monitor
r Naloxone, thiamine, D50W (or Accu-Chek) if altered
mental status
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Gastrointestinal decontamination:
– In potential life-threatening ingestions gastric
lavage may be carefully considered if within 1h r
of ingestion
– Administer activated charcoal
r Hyperthermia:
– Benzodiazepines if agitated
– Active cooling if temperature >40◦C:
◦Tepid water mist
◦Evaporate with fan
– Paralysis:
◦Indicated if muscle rigidity and hyperactivity
contributing to persistent hyperthermia
◦Nondepolarizing agent (e.g., vecuronium)
◦Avoid succinylcholine
◦Intubation; mechanical ventilation
– Administer acetaminophen.
– Apply cooling blankets.
r Severe, malignant hypertension:
– Nitroprusside (for MAOI overdose)
– Calcium-channel blocker or phentolamine (for
MAOI + food interaction)
– Use short-acting IV agent that can be rapidly
“turned off.”
r Hypotension:
– Initially bolus with isotonic crystalloid solution
– If no response, administer norepinephrine.
– Dopamine may be ineffective
r Dysrhythmias (premorbid sign in MAOI overdose):
– Treatment based on dysrhythmia
r Seizures:
– Benzodiazepines
– Barbiturates if benzodiazepines unsuccessful
– Pyridoxine for refractory seizures
r Rigidity:
– Benzodiazepines
– Paralysis with vecuronium, endotracheal
intubation, and mechanical ventilation
r ARDS:
– Oxygen
– Intubation and positive end-expiratory pressure as
indicated
r DIC:
– Fresh-frozen plasma
– Platelets
– Whole-blood transfusions
r Rhabdomyolysis:
– IV isotonic crystalloid solution
– Maintain hydration to ensure adequate urine
output
r Specific treatment for SS:
– Mainstay: Supportive care, discontinuation of
offending agents
– Nonselective serotonin antagonist:
◦Cyproheptadine
ALERT
Phentolamine contraindicated in MAOI overdose
(results in unopposed β-agonist)
MEDICATIONr Activated charcoal: 1–2 g/kg PO
r Cyproheptadine: 4–8 mg PO/nasogastric tube
q1–4h until therapeutic response; max. daily dose:
0.5 mg/kg (peds: 0.25 mg/kg/d; max. 12 mg/d;
safety not established age <2 yr)
r Dextrose: D50W 1–2 amp (50–100 mL or 25–50 g)
(peds: D25W 2–4 mL/kg) IV push (IVP)
r Diazepam: 5–10 mg (peds: 0.1 mg/kg slowly)
increments IVP
r Lorazepam: 1–2 mg increments IVP
r Nitroprusside: 0.3–10 μ/kg/min IV
r Norepinephrine: 2-4 μ/kg/min (peds: 0.05–0.1
μ/kg/min) IV
r Phentolamine: 5 mg (peds: 0.05–0.2 mg/kg/dose)
increments IVP
r Sodium bicarbonate: Bolus 1–2 mEq/kg IVP; adult
infusion: 3 amp (50 mEq per amp) sodium
bicarbonate in 1,000 mL D5W at 2–3 mL/kg/h IV
r Vecuronium: 0.1 mg/kg IVP
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
ALERT
MAOI toxicity can occur in delayed fashion
necessitating an extended observation period
Admission Criteriar All MAOI overdose patients require admission to a
monitored unit for 24 hr.
r ICU admission for seriously ill patients
Discharge Criteriar Resolved mild hypertensive syndrome or resolved
mild serotonin syndrome may be discharged after
several hours of ED observation.
Issues for Referral
Intentional overdoses should receive a psychiatry
consult for suicide attempt.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Following significant MAOI toxicity, medications need
to be reassessed to prevent future crises.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Delayed onset of 6–12 hr prior to symptoms
r Linezolid and methylene blue are MAOIs.
r Phentolamine is contraindicated in MAOI overdose
secondary to unopposed β-agonist.

New Engl J Med. 2005;352:1112–1120.

inhibitor poisoning resulting from Internet
misinformation on illicit substances. J Toxicol Clin
Toxicol. 2004;42:191–195.

analgesics and serotonin toxicity. Br J Anaesth.
2005;95:434–441.

tryptophan in patients receiving a monoamine
oxidase inhibitor. Neurology. 1960;10:1076–1078.

MONONUCLEOSIS
Steven C. Rogers rAlberto Cohen-Abbo
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Results in most cases from infection with the
Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) (a herpesvirus):
– Non-EBV causes of infectious mononucleosis (IM):
◦Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
◦Adenovirus
◦Hepatitis A
◦Herpesvirus 6
◦HIV
◦Rubella
◦Toxoplasma gondii
◦Group A β-hemolytic streptococci
r >90% of adults on serologic testing demonstrate
prior infection with EBV:
– Most do not recollect specific IM symptoms
r Mode of transmission is close or intimate contact
particularly with saliva from “shedders” who may or
may not be symptomatic:
– Nickname “kissing disease”
– Viral shedding in saliva can persist intermittently
for life
– May occur after transfusions/transplants
r Incubation period: 4–6 wk
r Immunologic response:
– T-cells response:
◦T-cell response is responsible for an elevated
absolute lymphocyte count and the associated
clinical symptoms and complications
◦Subtype of the T-cell lineage, cytotoxic CD8 cells
(Downey cells), contain eccentrically placed and
lobulated nuclei with vacuolated cytoplasm: The
“atypical lymphocytes” seen on differential
– B-cell response:
◦EBV infects and replicates in B-cells
◦B-cells are then transformed into plasmacytoid
cells that secrete immunoglobulins
◦IgM antibody secreted: The heterophile antibody
which is reactive against red cell antigens
r Mortality from IM is rare, but may occur due to the
following complications:
– Airway edema
– Neurologic complications
– Secondary bacterial infection
– Splenic rupture
– Hepatic failure
– Myocarditis
r EBV infection has also been strongly linked to
African Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal
carcinoma
Pediatric Considerations
r In children <4 yr, infection with EBV is often
asymptomatic
r In children who do become symptomatic, there is
propensity toward atypical presentations:
– Neutropenia, pneumonia, and varied rashes
– Mesenteric lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly
can cause the illness to present with abdominal
pain and be confused with appendicitis.
– Infants and toddlers can present with only
irritability and failure to thrive so must be
considered when no other source can be identified
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Typically an insidious onset over several days to
weeks but may be abrupt onset
r Prodromal fatigue, malaise, arthralgias, and
myalgias with a biphasic or “waxing and waning”
course
r Prominent or “worst ever” sore throat and fever.
Airway edema may be reported as difficulty
breathing or respiratory distress.
r Swollen lymph nodes
r Headache
r Significant abdominal pain is uncommon but when
present should raise concern about marked splenic
enlargement or splenic rupture.
r Varied rashes can be seen in 18–34% of children
and adolescents (not associated with antibiotics)
r Administration of ampicillin or amoxicillin in patients
with IM is associated with development of a rash
Physical Examr Malaise and/or fatigue (90–100%)
r Pharyngitis (65–85%) and tonsillar enlargement
r Fever (80–95%)
r Eyelid edema (15–35%)
r Symmetric tender lymphadenopathy (100%)
r Hepatomegaly (15–25%)
r Splenomegaly (50–60%)
r Nonspecific rashes
r Morbilliform rash can be seen if the patient has
been given ampicillin or amoxicillin:
– Typically develops 5–9 days after the onset of
antibiotic therapy (should not be interpreted as a
penicillin allergy)
r Petechia can occur on the skin or at the junction
between the hard and the soft palate.
r Complications found on exam:
– Airway compromise due to edema (1–5%)
– Severe abdominal tenderness may be due to
splenic rupture (may also cause referred pain to
left shoulder)
– Jaundice (∼5%) due to hepatitis or hepatic failure
◦Hepatitis is the most common complication
– Neurologic findings consistent with:
◦Encephalitis or cerebellitis
◦Aseptic meningitis
◦Guillain–Barr ´ e syndrome
◦Optic neuritis
◦Bell palsy
r Anemia (palor): May be due to hemolytic anemia,
thrombocytopenia, agranulocytosis, hemophagocytic
lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)
r Orchitis
r Neck tenderness and/or limited range of motion due
to pain: Secondary bacterial soft tissue infection
such as retropharyngeal or peritonsillar abscesses
r Signs of shock: May be due to dehydration or a
secondary anaerobic sepsis
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr WBC with differential:
– Typically a modest elevation in total WBC
between 10,000 and 20,000, which peaks during
week 2 of the illness but occasionally can be
30,000–50,000
r Lymphocyte count—findings suggestive of IM:
– >50% lymphocytes on differential
– Absolute lymphocyte count >4,500
– Elevated lymphocyte count with >10% atypical
lymphocytes (up to 90% of patients)
r Liver function tests:
– Elevated with transaminases up to 3 times normal
found in 80–85% of patients in the 1st 2 wk
– Significant elevations in bilirubin to the point of
causing clinical jaundice in ∼5% of cases
r Monospot test detects presence of heterophile
antibodies:
– Moderately sensitive (85%) and highly specific
(practically 100%)
– Rarely false positives can occur with CMV ,
leukemia, lymphoma, rubella, hepatitis, HIV , or
lupus
– Most patients develop heterophile antibodies after
∼1 wk of illness
– Small percentage of patients (<10%) never
develop heterophile antibodies
– Heterophile antibodies peak at 2–5 wk and may
persist for several months
– Positive test relates to a titer >1:40
– Results likely to be negative in children <4y ro l d
r Testing does exist for EBV-specific antibodies but is
expensive, time consuming, and rarely needed
– Useful in patients with atypical/severe cases or
when monospot testing is negative and
confirmation of IM is desired
– Acute infection is indicated by antibodies (IgG,
IgM) against viral capsid antigens (VCAs) without
antibodies against the Epstein–Barr nuclear
antigen (EBNA) which are only present during the
latency period 3–4 wk after onset of illness
– Past infection indicated by negative IgM and
positive EBNA
Imaging
Sonography or CT scan of abdomen for significant
abdominal pain to identify splenic rupture and to
ensure no signs of appendicitis
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
Divided into infectious and noninfectious causes:
r Infectious:
– Adenovirus
–C M V
– Streptococcal pharyngitis
– HIV
– Rubella
– Hepatitis A, B, C
– Diphtheria in nonimmunized populations
– Mumps
– Toxoplasmosis
r Noninfectious:
– Leukemia
– Lymphoma
– Medication-induced syndrome—phenytoin, sulfa
drugs

TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
ALERT

MRSA, COMMUNITY ACQUIRED
Benjamin S. Heavrin
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)
has historically been a pathogen endemic within
healthcare settings, usually affecting the elderly and
chronically ill. This strain of S. aureus has been
termed “healthcare-associated MRSA” (HA-MRSA).
r Throughout the past decade, MRSA has become an
increasingly common pathogen among younger,
healthier populations who do not have a
healthcare-related exposure history. This type of
MRSA pathogen has been termed
“community-acquired MRSA” (CA-MRSA).
r CA-MRSA is the most common cause of skin and
soft tissue infections seen in the ED
r While CA-MRSA may cause skin and soft tissue
infection, it may also lead to severe multisystem
disease, including sepsis and necrotizing pneumonia
Geriatric Considerations
HA-MRSA (see below) is a different genotypic form of
MRSA that frequently causes morbidity among the
elderly, especially those living within extended-care
facilities or those with healthcare-related exposures.
ETIOLOGYr S. aureus is a gram-positive cocci frequently
colonizing the skin
r MRSA refers to a specific strain of S. aureus that has
resistance against the antimicrobial properties of
numerous antibiotics, including methicillin
r Prisoners, athletes, soldiers, children in daycare, IV
drug users, and those with prior treatment for MRSA
or exposure to MRSA are at highest risk for
colonization and subsequent infection.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Skin and soft tissue infections:
– Increasing redness
– Pain
– Warmth
– Swelling
– Fever
– Chills
– Malaise
r Sepsis/pneumonia:
– Weakness
– Dyspnea
– Fever
– Rigors
– Productive cough
– Chest pain
r Inquire about prior diagnosis of MRSA infections,
MRSA exposures, and family members or close
contacts with a history of MRSA, as such a patient is
at risk for CA-MRSA infection.
Physical Examr Skin and soft tissue infections:
– Abscess: Tender, raised boil with underlying
induration and fluctuance
– Cellulitis: Warm erythema possibly with
lymphangitic streaking
r Sepsis:
– Vital sign abnormalities including tachycardia and
hypotension, respiratory failure, mental status
changes, petechiae, systemic signs of toxicity
r Pneumonia:
– Tachypnea, crackles, retractions, hypoxia
– Alveolar opacities on chest radiographs
Pediatric Considerations
MRSA is the leading cause of skin and soft tissue
infections among children presenting to the
emergency department.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Abscess:
– I&D with packing and prompt follow-up is
warranted for abscess
– Microbiology often performed for antibiotic
sensitivity given the changing antimicrobial
resistance patterns
r Sepsis:
– Source identification, including blood culture/urine
culture, CXR, is indicated as resuscitation begins
r Pneumonia:
– Chest radiographs and continuous vital sign
monitoring is indicated
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Skin and soft tissue infections:
– Bacterial culture is often warranted to monitor for
CA-MRSA resistance patterns
r Sepsis and pneumonia:
– Blood, urine, and body fluid cultures. CBC, CMP to
assess for organ dysfunction
Imagingr Bedside US:
– Abscess: Anechoic fluid collection
– Cellulitis: “Cobblestoning” within the soft tissue
r CXR:
– Indicated for patients with presumed sepsis,
systemic illness, or pneumonia
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Cultures of skin and soft tissue infections are
frequently obtained to monitor microbiology and
antimicrobial resistance patterns should a patient fail
a course of therapy.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Other skin and soft tissue infections:
– Pathogens beyond MRSA which cause abscesses
and cellulites should be considered (i.e.,
streptococcus)
r Necrotizing fasciitis
r Contact dermatitis
r Deep vein thrombosis
r Spider/insect bite
r Drug reaction
ALERT
Empiric antimicrobial treatment of skin and soft
tissue infections should cover for common skin
pathogens beyond MRSA (i.e., streptococcus)
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Contact precautions for all providers if MRSA is
suspected
r IV access and fluid resuscitation if sepsis is suspected
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Begin resuscitation and administer early empiric
antibiotics if pneumonia, fasciitis, or sepsis is
suspected:
r Include early coverage with antibiotics effective
against MRSA
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Skin and soft tissue infections:
– Abscess:
◦I&D with packing
◦Antibiotics may not be necessary if there is no
evidence for deep tissue infection or cellulitis
– Cellulitis:
◦Cellulitis caused by CA-MRSA in a healthy,
well-appearing patient may be treated with oral
antibiotics in the outpatient setting
◦Ill appearing patients, patients with underlying
medical conditions, and patients failing
outpatient therapy require IV antibiotics with
coverage against CA-MRSA
r Sepsis and pneumonia:
– Early administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics
that cover against MRSA should be given
promptly if the patient is at risk for CA-MRSA
MEDICATION
ALERT
Review antimicrobial resistance patterns of
CA-MRSA within your community prior to choosing
a specific antibiotic regimen, as many antibiotics
listed below may not be 100% effective against
CA-MRSA.
First Liner Bactrim:
– Adults: Bactrim DS 160/800 PO BID
– Children: 10 mg/kg PO BID
r Clindamycin:
– Adults: 150–450 mg PO QID
– Children: 5 mg/kg PO/IV TID–QID
r Doxycycline:
– Adults: 100 mg PO BID
– Children: 2.2 mg/kg PO BID
r Vancomycin:
– Adults: 1 g IV q8–12h
– Children: 15 mg/kg IV q8–12h

MULTIPLE MYELOMA
Nicole M. Franks
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Normal cells transform into myeloma cells at the
hematopoietic stem cell level.
r Pathologic derangements:
– Tumor cells within marrow lead to bone
destruction and cytopenia.
– Immunodeficiency develops secondary to
suppression of normal immune functions.
– Myeloma proteins lead to hyperviscosity and
amyloidosis.
– Multifactorial renal failure
r Plasma cell secretions activate osteoclasts, leading
to:
– Bone lysis, pathologic fractures, and neurologic
impairment
– Hypercalcemia (exacerbated by impaired renal
function)
r Anemia due to marrow infiltration and renal
insufficiency
r Immunocompromised due to:
– Decrease in the number of normal
immunoglobulins
– Qualitative and quantitative defects in T- and
B-cell subsets
– Granulocytopenia
– Decreased cell-mediated immunity
r Hyperviscosity secondary to protein accumulation:
– Leads to high-output congestive heart failure
r Myeloma light chains accumulate in the renal
epithelial cells and destroy the entire nephron.
r Clinical signs such as anemia, renal insufficiency, or
lytic bone lesions
r Complications:
– Pathologic fractures
– Hypercalcemia
– Renal failure
– Recurrent infection
– Anemia
– Spinal cord compression (10% of all multiple
myeloma [MM] patients)
ETIOLOGYr Incidence: 4/100,000 population:
– 1% of all cancers
– 15% of all hematopoietic malignancies
– 10,000 deaths/yr
r Mean age at diagnosis is 70 yr
r Slightly higher incidence in men and African
Americans (reason unknown)
Pediatric Considerations
r Rarely seen in children.
r <2% in patients <40 yr of age
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Bone pain predominates (with secondary disuse or
neurologic sequelae):
– Ribs/sternum
– Spine
– Clavicle
– Skull
– Shoulder
– Hip
r Constitutional symptoms:
– Anemia
– Weakness
– Fatigue
– Recurrent infection
– Weight loss
r Asymptomatic (20%):
– MM found on follow-up of routine blood screening
r Multiple bouts of sepsis secondary to the
encapsulated organisms (Streptococcus
pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and
Staphylococcus).
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr CBC, ESR, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, urinalysis
r Plain radiographs related to bone pain:
– Skeletal survey: Lateral skull, AP/lateral spine, AP
of pelvis, humerus, and femur
r CT or MRI for persistent bone pain with negative
plain radiographs
r Confirmation of diagnosis:
– Serum and urine protein electrophoresis
– Serum and urine protein immunofixation
(diagnostic when electrophoresis is normal or
nonspecific)
– Vitamin D levels
– Bone marrow biopsy
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC:
– Normochromic, normocytic anemia
– Thrombocytopenia
– Leukocytosis
r “Rouleaux” formation on peripheral blood smear
(stacks of red blood cells)
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose:
– Renal insufficiency
r Serum calcium:
– Hypercalcemia due to bone resorption
r Urinalysis:
– Dipstick selects for albumin and not light-chain
proteinuria.
– False-negative screening urinalysis for Bence
Jones protein is common.
r Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
r Urinary and serum electrophoresis show a
monoclonal protein spike:
r Quantitative screening for light chain is diagnostic.
Imagingr Plain radiographs demonstrate:
– Lytic bone lesions
– Pathologic fractures
r CT:
– More sensitive for small lesions
– Can differentiate malignant from benign vertebral
compression fractures in non-MRI candidates
r MRI:
– Preferred to detect spinal compression or
soft-tissue plasmacytomas
r PET with MR or CT: May have future role in
surveying response to treatment
r Technetium pyrophosphate bone scan:
– Lights up bone deposition
– False-negative scan with MM due to an
uncoupling of bone absorption and deposition
that results in a negative bone scan even when
lytic lesions are present
r Bone marrow biopsy: Increase in plasma cells
r Cytogenetic screening may offer prognostic
significance.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined
significance
r Amyloidosis
r Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
r Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
r Waldenstr ¨ om macroglobulinemia
r Bone marrow plasmacytosis includes collagen
vascular disease, cirrhosis, immune complex disease,
viral illness, and papular mucinosis.
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Immobilize appropriately patients with MM who
present with back pain or neurologic symptoms:
r Presume to have a pathologic spinal fracture
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Recognition and treatment of:
r Hypercalcemia
r Renal failure
r Sepsis
r Spinal cord compression
r Anemia

Richard S. Krause
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Pathophysiology: Recurrent episodes of CNS
demyelination:
– Signs and symptoms depend on location of lesions
and timing of demyelination
r Multiple sclerosis (MS) occurs in distinct patterns:
– Relapsing recurring MS: 2 or more episodes
lasting ≥24 hr separated by ≥1m o
– Primary progressive MS: Slow or stepwise
progression over at least 6 mo
– Secondary progressive MS: Initial exacerbations
and remissions followed by slow progression over
at least 6 mo
– Stable MS: No progression (without treatment)
over at least 18 mo
ETIOLOGYr MS is a chronic demyelinating disease of CNS:
– Etiology is not well understood
r Presumed to be T cell–mediated autoimmune
disease
r There is evidence for a viral trigger
r Plaques in white matter:
– Characterized by infiltrate of T cells and
macrophages
r Persons of northern European origin most often
affected (in US)
r Increased prevalence is seen moving away from
equator
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Initial attacks usually (∼85%) represent single
lesions, are abrupt in onset, and are seen in
characteristic patterns (in order of decreasing
frequency):
– Optic neuritis:
◦Eye pain exacerbated by movement progressing
to visual loss
– Paresthesias (or changed sensory level) in 1 limb
– Limb (usually leg) weakness
– Diplopia:
◦Intranuclear ophthalmoplegia from lesion of
medial longitudinal fasciculus
◦Results in unilateral or bilateral paralysis of
adduction of eye on horizontal gaze
– Trigeminal neuralgia
– Urinary retention
– Vertigo
– Transverse myelitis:
◦Acute onset of motor and sensory findings at
specific spinal cord level
◦Often associated with bladder or bowel
incontinence
◦Can be early manifestation of MS
◦Unusual initial manifestations include psychosis,
aphasia, etc.
◦Initial symptoms may be minor and only be
recognized as due to MS in retrospect
r Symptoms typically develop abruptly (minutes to
hours) and last 6–8 wk
r Most common in young women of Northern
European descent:
– Increased risk in 1st-degree relatives
– Peak age: 30 yr
– Female-to-male ratio: 2:1
r Pain is an uncommon symptom in MS:
– Exceptions: Trigeminal neuralgia, early optic
neuritis
Physical Exam
Physical exam: Focused on “hard” neurologic signs:
r Focal neurologic deficits
r Afferent pupillary defect
r Internuclear ophthalmoplegia
r Sensory level or sphincter disturbance (transverse
myelitis)
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr MS is suspected based on history and physical exam
r Definitive diagnosis is not typically made in ED:
– Requires observation over time and confirmatory
testing
ALERT
Infection, especially with fever, is a common cause
of MS exacerbation
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
CSF analysis:
r CSF gel electrophoresis reveals “oligoclonal bands”
not present in serum
– Oligoclonal bands are found in ≥95% of patients
with clinically definite MS
Imaging
MRI most useful imaging test:
r Lesions appear as areas of high signal, in cerebral
white matter or spinal cord on T2-weighted images
r Abnormal in almost all patients who have clinically
diagnosed MS
r McDonald diagnostic criteria for MS include specific
MRI findings
r May also see plaques on CT (less sensitive)
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Sensory-evoked potential testing:
r Not an ED test

MUMPS
Austen-Kum Chai
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Vaccine preventable infectious diseases characterized
by swelling of salivary glands, in particular the parotid
glands.
ETIOLOGYr Rubulavirus, single stranded RNA virus, in the
Paramyxovirus family
r Humans only known reservoir
Pediatric Considerations
r Mumps vaccine with measles and rubella ±
varicella (MMR or MMRV) should be administered to
children on or after 12 mo of age. 2nd dose is
usually administered at the age of 4–6 yr, before
start of school.
r Catch-up vaccination should include 2 doses
separated by at least 4 wk between vaccinations.
r Systemic symptoms and serious complications are
less common in children when compared to adults
with the infection.
Pregnancy Considerations
Infection during 1st trimester of pregnancy is
associated with increased spontaneous abortion.
Although mumps virus may cross the placenta, there is
no evidence that mumps virus causes congenital
malformation.
Geriatric Considerations
Adults born before 1957 are considered to have been
exposed to mumps and are considered immune.
However, during outbreaks, healthcare workers born
before 1957 and without lab evidence of immunity to
mumps should receive 2 doses of the MMR vaccine.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Incubation period from exposure to onset of
symptoms (14–18 days):
– Viral transmission is via respiratory droplets,
saliva, contact with contaminated fomites
– Replication in nasopharynx and regional lymph
nodes
– Viremia to glands as salivary, pancreas, testes,
ovaries and also to meninges
r Contagious 1–7 days prior to onset of symptoms
and 6 days afterward
r Often history of none or incomplete immunization
r Active illness (1–10 days):
– Nonspecific prodromal symptoms such as
low-grade fever, headache, malaise, myalgia,
anorexia, otalgia, jaw pain up to 48 hr prior to
presentation of parotitis
– Up to 20% of infections are asymptomatic but still
contagious
– Up to 50% of cases have nonspecific symptoms of
upper respiratory tract infection along with fever,
malaise, anorexia, and headache without
apparent salivary gland swelling.
– Parotitis (30–40% of patients):
◦Most common manifestation of mumps. Present
in 95% of symptomatic cases of mumps
◦Painful and tender unilateral or bilateral (90%
of the time) enlargement of parotid gland
◦May begin as earache or pain at angle of jaw
◦Other salivary gland may be affected.
◦Stensen’s duct is often edematous and
erythematous and exudes a clear fluid.
◦Skin overlying swollen gland is
nonerythematous.
◦Symptoms decrease after 1 wk and resolve by
10th day.
◦Considered contagious until swelling resolves
– Orchitis (20–50% of postpubertal males):
◦Most common complication in postpubertal
males
◦May occur alone, before, during, but most
commonly, after parotitis
◦Unilateral or bilateral (up to 30%)
◦Abrupt, painful, tender swelling with nausea,
vomiting, and fever
◦Pain and swelling resolve in 1 wk
◦Testicular atrophy in up to 50% of patients
◦Sterility rare
– Oophoritis (5% of postpubertal females):
◦May mimic appendicitis if right-sided
◦Fertility not impaired
– Pancreatitis (2–5%):
◦May occur without any other manifestations of
mumps
◦Fever, nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain
◦May see transient hyperglycemia
◦May be complicated by pseudocyst formation
and shock
– CNS involvement:
◦Aseptic meningitis (10–15% of patients)
◦Usually resolves without sequelae in 3–10 days
◦Encephalitis (very rare)
◦Sensorineuronal deafness (80% unilateral) with
permanent hearing impairment
◦Cerebellar ataxia
◦Transverse myelitis
– Other:
◦Myocarditis (rarely with symptomatic
involvement)
◦Glomerulonephritis
◦Polyarthralgia and arthritis
◦Thrombocytopenic purpura
◦Ocular complaints
◦Thyroiditis
◦Mastitis
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Diagnosis is based on clinical findings of parotitis and
associated signs, symptoms, and complications.

MUNCHAUSEN SYNDROME
Sophie Galson rRichard E. Wolfe
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr A neurotic disorder in which the patient fakes signs
or symptoms without tangible personal benefit other
than to experience the sick role.
r Most dramatic form of chronic factitious disorder
with a predominance of physical findings.
r The nature of the disorder resists rigorous study but
possible risk factors include:
– Males
– Less severe factitious disorders are more common
in women
– Unmarried
– Age in the forties
– Personality disorder
– A history of sadistic and rejecting parents
– A history of chronic childhood illness
ETIOLOGYr Factitious disorder:
– 3 DSM-IV diagnostic criteria:
◦Intentional production of physical or
psychological signs
◦Motivation to assume the sick role
◦Absence of external incentives
◦Predominance of symptoms rather than physical
findings
r Classic Munchausen syndrome:
– Most severe and chronic form of factitious
disorders
– Predominantly physical findings
r Clinical clusters:
– Self-induced infection
– Simulated specific illnesses with no actual disorder
– Chronic wounds
– Self-medication
Pediatric Considerations
r Munchausen by proxy:
– The patient’s illness is caused by the caregiver, not
the patient
– The motivation for the caregiver’s behavior is to
assume the sick role by proxy
– The caregiver inflicts injury or induces illness in
their charge, usually a child
– Commonly parents (mostly mothers)
r May simulate injury and disease in a number of
ways:
– Inflicts injury
– Induces Illness
– Fabricates symptoms
– Exaggerates symptoms of the child’s illness
causing overaggressive medical interventions
r The perpetrator usually refuses to acknowledge the
deception
r Cessation of the symptoms when the patient and
caregiver are separated
Geriatric Considerations
Caregivers of elderly patients may also be perpetrators
in Munchausen by proxy
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Inappropriate or bizarre use of the ED
r Frequent visits
r Numerous hospital admissions
r Peregrination: Travel from hospital to hospital
r Pseudologia fantastica:
– Intricate and colorful stories associated with the
presentation
r Alteration of biographical information:
– Use of aliases
– Change date of birth by 1 digit
r Escalating demands for diagnostic testing and
therapeutic interventions
r Hostility toward the health care providers when
questioned
r Evasiveness regarding details of the presenting
complaint
r The patient provides excessive medical
documentation
r Masochistic acceptance of painful procedures
r The patient appears more comfortable than is likely
considering the disease
r The patient demonstrates unusually strong medical
knowledge
r Frequent homelessness and significant wandering
between cities and states
r An absence of close interpersonal relationships
r Self-medication
r Abdominal complaints with history of repeated
negative laparotomies (laparotomaphilia migrans)
r Witnessed intentional acts to fake illness:
– Inappropriate ingestion of medication to
reproduce physical findings
– Injection of contaminants (feces, bacteria, sputum,
corrosives)
– Self-induced wounds
– Swallowing blood to simulate a GI hemorrhage
– Self-phlebotomy
– Instrument tampering
Physical Examr Fever:
– Factious from manipulation of thermometer
– Induced from injection of contaminants
r Self-induced wounds
r Chronic wounds
r Multiple scars
r Foreign bodies in wounds, ear canals, urethra
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Diligent detective work is needed:
– Retrieval of records from other hospitals
– Call on family members to discuss past history for
inconsistencies and excessive use
– Call personal physician for background and to
coordinate information
– Search patient’s room and belongings to establish
the method of deception
r Conclusive proof of faking disease is needed to
make the diagnosis
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Direct observation of the patient when obtaining
tests to prevent faking results
r Commonly faked lab results:
– Hemoccult positive stool
– Hematuria (intentionally dripping blood into urine
sample)
– Hypoglycemia (self-administration of insulin)
r Abnormal results from self-medication:
– Low hematocrit (ingestion of warfarin or
self-phlebotomy)
– Elevated INR (ingestion of warfarin)
– Thyroid function tests (ingestion of thyroxine)
– Low serum glucose (injection of insulin or
ingestion of sulfonylurea)
r Evidence of intent to fake illness:
– Testing stool for phenolphthalein may detect
laxative abuse
– Serum C-peptide with high insulin levels:
◦Low C-peptide: Exogenous administration of
insulin
◦Elevated C-peptide: Endogenous hypoglycemia
or sulfonylurea ingestion
Imaging
Do not rely on imaging brought by the patient
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Avoid unless clear objective findings indicate the
necessity of a procedure

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr True illness:
– Primary illness unrelated to a psychiatric disorder
r Secondary to a comorbid condition associated with
factitious disorders:
– Secondary to self-destructive acts in patients with
dementia, psychotic disorders, or mental
retardation
– Secondary to diagnostic and therapeutic
procedures
r Malingering:
– Clear-cut secondary gain
r Conversion disorder:
– Deficits of the voluntary motor or sensory
neurologic system that are not consciously
produced
r Somatization disorder (hysteria, Briquet syndrome):
– Symptoms that involve multiple organs, that varies
over time, and are not consciously produced
r Other neurotic disorders:
– Anxiety
– Depression
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Treatment should be limited to stabilization of life or
limb threats caused by acts of self-harm
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Identify objective physical illness and treat as
appropriate
r Document history and findings suggestive of
factitious illness
r List of all the aliases, addresses, and date of births
that the patient is known to use
r Summarize the patient’s known modus operandi
(the factitious histories and behaviors that he or she
has presented with)
r Ensure that the information will be communicated
or available to all doctors who are likely to come
into contact with the patient
r Confrontation of the patient in the ED is
controversial and should only occur when
unambiguous evidence is gathered
r Report Munchausen syndrome by proxy to child
protective services
MEDICATION
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Injuries and disease caused by self-harm
r Munchausen by proxy:
– When the diagnosis is suspected but there is not
enough evidence to have child protective services
take custody
r Observation to collect evidence of faking disease:
– May also allow setting to rule out rare organic
etiologies
r To establish a long-term plan to prevent future
self-harm and iatrogenic adverse events
r Psychiatric admission may be of benefit, but it is
rarely accepted by the patient
Discharge Criteriar Medical stability
r Not an active threat to harm self
r Appropriate referral for medical and psychiatric
follow-up arranged
Issues for Referralr May offer psychiatric referral as a method of dealing
with stress caused by illness
r Psychiatric providers located directly in medical
settings (e.g., primary care physician office) may be
more accepted. Overall, this is a chronic illness with
poor prognosis
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Maintain contact between the patient and an
identified provider for that patient.

MUSHROOM POISONING
Michael E. Nelson rTimothy B. Erickson
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Amanitin/phalloidin:
– Species:
◦Amanita phalloides (“death cap”)
◦Amanita virosa/Amanita verna (“destroying
angel”)
◦Galerina marginata, Galerina venenata
– Mechanism:
◦Cyclopeptide toxins inhibit RNA polymerase 2,
which kills GI epithelium, hepatocytes,
nephrocytes
r Gyromitrin:
– Species:
◦Gyromitra esculenta (“false morels”)
◦Other Gyromitra spp.
– Mechanism:
◦Inhibits pyridoxal phosphate
◦Damage to RBCs, hepatocytes, neurons
r Muscarine:
– Species:
◦Inocybe (several species)
◦Clitocybe (several species)
– Mechanism:
◦Parasympathomimetic
r Coprine:
– Species:
◦Coprinus atramentarius (“inky caps”)
– Mechanism:
◦Blocks acetaldehyde dehydrogenase
◦Causes disulfiram-like reaction if mixed with
alcohol
r Ibotenic acid/muscimol:
– Species:
◦Amanita pantherina (“the panther”)
◦Amanita muscaria (“fly agaric”)
– Mechanism:
◦GABA agonists
r Psilocin/psilocybin:
– Species:
◦Psilocybe and Panaeolus spp. as well as others
– Mechanism:
◦Similar structure to lysergic acid diethylamide,
effect serotonin receptor
r Gastric irritants:
– Many various mushrooms, including those
normally considered edible
r Orellanine:
– Species:
◦Cortinarius (several species)
– Mechanism:
◦Direct renal toxicity
r Tricholoma equestre (“man on horse”):
– Rhabdomyolysis-inducing mushrooms
– Unidentified myotoxin
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Amanitin/phalloidin:
– Nausea
– Vomiting
– Abdominal cramps
– Bloody diarrhea
– Clinical course:
◦Onset of symptoms delayed 6–36 hr with
development of GI symptoms
◦Transient latent phase may last 2 days (no
pain/symptoms)
◦Can progress to hepatic or renal failure and
death in 2–6 days
◦Most lethal mushroom toxins
r Gyromitrin:
– 1st 5–10 hr:
◦Abdominal cramps
◦Nausea/vomiting
◦Watery diarrhea
– Later symptoms:
◦Weakness
◦Cyanosis
◦Confusion
◦Seizures
◦Coma
r Muscarine:
– Cholinergic symptoms include:
◦Miosis
◦Salivation
◦Lacrimation
◦Sweating
◦Diarrhea
◦Flushed skin
◦Nausea
◦Bradycardia
◦Bronchoconstriction
– Onset usually within 1 hr (may be delayed)
r Coprine:
– Disulfiram-like reaction within minutes to hours
when combined with alcohol:
◦Flushing
◦Sweating
◦Nausea/vomiting
◦Palpitations
r Ibotenic acid/muscimol:
– Relatively rapid onset of 30–120 min
– GABA agonist effects include:
◦Hallucinations
◦Dysarthria
◦Ataxia
◦Somnolence/coma
– Glutamatergic effects (mainly pediatrics):
◦Seizures
◦Muscle cramps/myoclonic movements
r Psilocin/psilocybin:
– Rapid onset, usually resolves in 6–12 hr
– Visual hallucinations
– Alteration of perception
– Mydriasis
– Tachycardia
– Fever and seizures in children
r Gastric irritants:
– Group of toxins that cause nausea, vomiting,
intestinal cramps, and watery diarrhea
– Onset 30 min to 3 hr, usually resolved in 6–12 hr
r Orellanine/Amanita smithiana:
– Nausea/vomiting
– Headache
– Sweating
– Chills
– Low-back pain
– Polydipsia
– Clinical course:
◦May progress to oliguria and acute renal failure
◦Markedly delayed onset of symptoms
(2–14 days)
r T. equestre:
– Acute rhabdomyolysis:
◦Myalgias/arthralgias
◦Hematuria/dark urine
◦Decreased urine output
– Dehydration
Historyr Time of ingestion
r Time of symptom onset
r Quantity ingested
r Preparation: Raw or cooked
r Picked in the wild or store-bought
r Coingestants, other mushrooms
r Alcohol/drug use history
r Symptoms of family members, friends
Physical Examr Vital signs
r Changes in mental status
r Pupillary response
r Cardiopulmonary exam
r Abdominal exam
r Neurologic exam
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Mushroom description:
– Pileus (cap); margin shape
– Stipe (stem)
– Lamellae (gills)
– Veil
– Annulus (ring)
– Volva
r Store mushroom in brown paper bag for future
identification:
– <3% of cases result in an exact mushroom
identification.
– Digital photography and electronic image transfer
to poison control center or regional mycologist

MUSHROOM POISONING
M
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC
r Prothrombin time (PT), partial thromboplastin time
(PTT)
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose
r Urinalysis
r LFTs, creatine phosphokinase (CPK)
r Imaging
r Spore print: Mycologist needed for specific
genus/species interpretation
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Very broad differential
r Gastroenteritis
r Hepatitis/acetaminophen hepatotoxicity
r Acute renal failure (many causes)
r Rhabdomyolysis (many causes)
r Cholinergic syndrome (e.g., organophosphates)
r Anticholinergic syndrome
r Seizures (many causes)
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Bring any unconsumed mushrooms or mushroom
pieces to hospital to aid in diagnosis:
r Refrigerate specimens if possible, place in brown
paper bag.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs
r Establish IV 0.9% NS saline
r Monitor
r Naloxone, D50W (or Accu-Chek), and thiamine for
altered mental status
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURES
General Measuresr Decontamination:
– Activated charcoal (50–100 g)
– Gastric decontamination if early after ingestion
and patient:
◦Has not yet vomited.
◦Has normal mental and respiratory status
◦Is not undergoing hallucinations
r Fluid rehydration and electrolyte replacement as
necessary
r Call local poison control center at 800-222-1222
and request mycologist—digital picture may be
electronically sent for identification.
r Obtain specimens (vomitus if needed) for
identification.
Mushroom-speciﬁc Therapyr Amanitin/phalloidin:
– Administer activated charcoal PO q2–4h.
– Hypoglycemia and elevated PT:
◦Signs of liver failure
◦Administer fresh-frozen plasma and vitamin K
for coagulation disorders with active bleeding.
– Administer calcium in presence of hypocalcemia.
– Liver transplant for severe hepatic necrosis
– Consider N-acetylcysteine, high-dose penicillin G,
or silibinin if available (thioctic acid controversial)
r Gyromitrin:
– Treat seizure with benzodiazepines.
◦Administer pyridoxine (vitamin B6) in severely
symptomatic patients.
– Treat liver dysfunctions as outlined for
amanitin/phalloidin group.
– Dialysis for renal failure
r Muscarine:
– Administer atropine in severe cases.
r Coprine:
– Self-limited toxicity—supportive care
– Avoid syrup of ipecac (contains alcohol)
– β-Blockers for cardiac dysrhythmias
r Ibotenic acid/muscimol:
– Usually self-limited toxicity
– Provide supportive care
– Monitor for hypotension
– Treat moderate symptoms with benzodiazepines,
if severe anticholinergic symptoms; consider
physostigmine.
r Psilocin/psilocybin:
– Self-limited toxicity
– Dark, quiet room and reassurance
– Benzodiazepines for agitation
– External cooling measures if needed in children
r GI Irritants:
– When poisoning from above groups not
suspected, administer fluids and antiemetics.
– Provide supportive care
r Orellanine and A. smithiana:
– Closely monitor BUN, creatinine, electrolytes, and
urine output.
– Forced diuresis with Lasix contraindicated
– Diuresis with alkalinization of urine with NaHCO3
if signs of rhabdomyolysis
– Hemodialysis/renal transplantation may be
needed.
r T. equestre (“man on horse”):
– Fluid hydration
– Check and follow CPK.
– Monitor urine output.
MEDICATIONr Activated charcoal slurry: 1–2 g/kg up to 100 g PO
r Atropine: 0.5 mg (peds: 0.02 mg/kg) IV; repeat
0.5–1 mg IV (peds: 0.04 mg/kg) q10min if
secretions recur, to max. 1 mg/kg in children and
2 mg/kg in adults
r Dextrose: D50W 1 amp: 50 mL or 25 g (peds: D25W
2–4 mL/kg) IV
r Diazepam (benzodiazepine): 5–10 mg (peds:
0.2–0.5 mg/kg) IV
r Lorazepam (benzodiazepine): 2–6 mg (peds:
0.03–0.05 mg/kg) IV
r Naloxone (Narcan): 2 mg (peds: 0.1 mg/kg) IV or IM
initial dose
r Physostigmine: 0.5–2 mg IM or IV in adults
r Propranolol: 1 mg (peds: 0.01–0.1 mg/kg) IV
r Pyridoxine: 25 mg/kg IV over 30 min
r Thiamine (vitamin B1): 100 mg (peds: 50 mg) IV or
IM
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar All symptomatic patients:
– Protracted vomiting, dehydration, liver or renal
toxicity, or seizures
r Transfer to tertiary medical center for early signs of
renal or hepatic failure.
r Symptomatic infants and young children found with
mushrooms:
– Assume ingestion.
r ICU admission for known ingestion of an
amanitin-containing mushroom:
– Early liver service consultation
Discharge Criteria
Asymptomatic during 6–8 hr with 24 hr of close home
observation and close follow-up (if reliable caregivers)
Issues for Referral
Potential liver or renal transplantation
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Drug detoxification programs if chronic recreational
use

r There are old mushroom pickers, and bold

MYASTHENIA GRAVIS
Douglas W. Lowery-North
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Antibody-mediated condition that results in
painless, fatigable muscle weakness
r Ocular or generalized:
– Ocular (eyelids and extraocular) muscle weakness:
◦Most common initial symptom (60%)
◦∼80% of myasthenia gravis (MG) patients who
present with ocular weakness initially will
progress to general weakness within 2 yr.
– Generalized:
◦Usually affects proximal limbs, axial muscle
groups such as neck, face, bulbar muscles
r Acute or subacute, with relapses and remissions
r Associated with thymoma in 15% and thymic
hyperplasia in 65%
r Myasthenic crisis:
– Respiratory failure or inability to protect airway
due to weakness
– Triggers:
◦Infection
◦Surgery
◦Trauma
◦Pregnancy
◦Medication changes (e.g., rapid tapering of
steroids)
– Difficult to distinguish from cholinergic crisis
resulting from excessive doses of
acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitors:
◦Cholinergic crisis may also include muscarinic
effects such as sweating, lacrimation, salivation,
and GI hyperactivity in addition to weakness.
EPIDEMIOLOGYr Pediatric MG is rare and distinct:
– Congenital MG: Genetic defect
– Juvenile MG: Autoimmune disorder
– Transient neonatal MG: Postdelivery complication
from placental transfer of maternal antibodies
r Adult MG has bimodal distribution:
– 1st peak in 2nd and 3rd decades affecting mostly
women
– 2nd peak in 6th and 7th decades affecting men
ETIOLOGYr Antibody-mediated attack on nicotinic acetylcholine
receptors
r Up to 20% of patients may be acetylcholine
receptor antibody (AChR Ab) negative
r Penicillamine can cause MG as well as other
autoimmune conditions
r Many medications may worsen myasthenic
weakness:
– Aminoglycosides, macrolides, quinolones,
antimalarials
– Local anesthetics
– Antidysrhythmics (propafenone, quinidine,
procainamide)
– β-Blockers, calcium-channel blockers
– Anticonvulsants (phenytoin, carbamazepine)
– Antipsychotics (phenothiazine, atypicals)
– Neuromuscular blocking agents
– Iodine-containing radiocontrast
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Fluctuating focal weakness
Historyr Symptoms worsen with repeated activity:
– Improve with rest
r Ocular weakness:
– Diplopia
– Ptosis while driving or reading
r Bulbar and facial muscle weakness:
– Trouble chewing, speaking, swallowing
– Inability to keep jaw closed after chewing
– Slurred, nasal speech
r Limb weakness:
– Difficulty climbing stairs, rising from chair,
reaching up with arms
Physical Examr Ocular findings:
– Ptosis, diplopia
– Inability to keep eyelid shut against resistance
– No pupillary changes
r Bulbar and facial findings:
– Ask patient to count to 100; look for changes in
speech.
– Decreased facial expression
– Head droop
r Limb findings:
– Repetitive testing of proximal muscles or small
muscles of hand results in weakness.
– Reflex and sensory exam are normal.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Assess for respiratory compromise
r Search for secondary triggers (e.g., infectious source)
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC
r Electrolytes
r LFTs
r Thyroid function tests
r Anti-AChR Ab:
– Positive in 90% with generalized disease
– Positive in 50% with ocular disease
r Other tests for initial diagnosis:
– Antistriated muscle antibody
– Antinuclear antibody
– Rheumatoid factor
– ESR
Imagingr Head CT or MRI to rule out compressive lesions
causing cranial nerve findings
r Chest CT with contrast to look for associated
thymoma
r CXR as needed to evaluate for infectious source
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Edrophonium (Tensilon) test:
– Short-acting AChE inhibitor
– A positive test produces rapid, short-lived
(2–5 min) improvement in strength
– Sensitivity 95% in generalized MG and 86% in
ocular MG
– False positives possible with Lambert–Eaton,
Guillain–Barr ´ e, MS, botulism, and others
– Keep patient on cardiac monitor during test.
– Atropine at bedside for possible bradycardia
– Suction at bedside for possible increased
secretions
r Ice test:
– Place ice on eyelid for 2 min.
– Improvement in ptosis suggests MG.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
r Botulism
r Electrolyte abnormalities
r Graves disease
r Guillain–Barr ´ e syndrome
r Hyperthyroidism
r Inflammatory muscle disorders
r Intracranial mass lesions
r Lambert–Eaton syndrome
r Multiple sclerosis
r Periodic paralysis
r Tick paralysis
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Attention to airway management
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Myasthenic crisis:
r Most important is early intubation and mechanical
ventilation.
r Signs of impending failure:
– Vital capacity <20 mL/kg
– Negative inspiratory pressure >–30 cm H2O
– Negative expiratory pressure <40 cm H2O
r Considerations regarding paralytics:
– Decreased sensitivity to depolarizing agents may
necessitate higher dose; consider doubling the
usual dose of succinylcholine.
– Nondepolarizing agents can cause extended
paralysis; consider halving the usual dose.
– Others recommend midazolam, etomidate, or
thiopental instead.

MYOCARDIAL CONTUSION
Sean Patrick Nordt
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Also known as blunt cardiac injury
r Pathologically characterized by discrete and
well-demarcated area of hemorrhage
r Usually subendocardial
r May extend in pyramidal transmural fashion
r Most commonly involves anterior wall of right
ventricle or atrium due to anatomic location
ETIOLOGYr Blunt trauma to chest:
– High-speed deceleration accidents
– May occur in accidents with speeds as low as
20–35 mph
r Auto–pedestrian injuries
r Falls
r Prolonged closed-chest cardiac massage
r Heart may be compressed between sternum and
vertebrae.
r Heart strikes sternum during deceleration.
r Heart is damaged by abdominal viscera upwardly
displaced by force on abdomen.
r Concussive forces (e.g., explosion)
r Associated conditions:
– Life-threatening dysrhythmias
– Cardiogenic shock/CHF
– Hemopericardium with tamponade
– Valvular/myocardial rupture
– Intraventricular thrombi
– Thromboembolic phenomena
– Coronary artery occlusion from intimal tearing or
adjacent hemorrhage and edema may rarely occur.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Clinical picture is varied and nonspecific:
– Chest pain
– Cardiogenic shock
– Subtle EKG changes without clinical symptoms
r Most common sign is tachycardia out of proportion
to degree of trauma or blood loss.
r Friction rub may occur rarely.
r Retrosternal chest pain unrelieved by nitroglycerin:
– Often delayed up to 24 hr
– May respond to oxygen
r Evidence of significant thoracic trauma:
– Contusions, abrasions
– Palpable crepitus
– Sternal fracture alone with normal EKG and
negative serial troponin I does not predict BCI
– Visible flail segments
r Other injuries may mask signs and symptoms of
myocardial contusion.
Historyr Mechanism of injury (e.g., MVA, fall, explosion,
missile to chest wall)
r Any syncope or loss of consciousness suggests
possible dysrhythmia.
r Crush injury
Geriatric Considerations
Obtain and consider pre-existing cardiac disease and
concurrent medications in elderly patients following
blunt cardiac injury.
Pediatric Considerations
Due to increased compliance of pediatric chest wall,
significant cardiac compression and contusion may be
present with minimal or no external signs of trauma.
Physical Exam
Complete physical exam as in any trauma patient:
r Evaluate for jugular venous distention (JVD)
r Decreased or muffled heart sounds
r Extra heart sounds
r Crepitus
r Pulsus paradoxus
r Evidence of chest wall trauma
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr No single diagnostic study (other than autopsy
findings!) confirms presence of myocardial
contusion.
r EKG:
– Best initial screening tool
– Most common rhythm is sinus tachycardia (70%).
– Normal EKG does not rule out myocardial damage.
– EKG changes may be subtle or include nonspecific
findings such as ST changes, right bundle branch
block, and premature atrial and ventricular
contractions.
– At least 1 repeat EKG is recommended because
changes may occur over time.
– Serious dysrhythmias may result in hemodynamic
instability:
◦Atrial fibrillation/atrial flutter
◦Ventricular tachycardia/ventricular fibrillation
(commotio cordis)
r Troponin I is now the recommended screening lab
test over CK-MB to be interpreted with EKG.
r Echocardiography should be performed on all
patients with any EKG changes, elevated troponin I
or troponin T.
r Transesophageal ECG (TEE) more sensitive than
transthoracic ECG (TTE) but technically more difficult
and time-consuming.
r Multidetector CT angiography or MRI may be of
benefit.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Troponin I is the preferred lab test.
r Troponin T less sensitive than troponin I.
– Levels should be sent on all patients where BCI
suspected.
– Should be repeated at 6–8 hr after injury.
– Any elevation requires admission.
r Cardiac troponins are more specific than CK-MB for
cardiac injury.
r CK-MB no longer routinely recommended.
Imagingr Radiographs, CT, MRI detect associated injuries:
– Pulmonary contusion
– Rib or sternal fractures
– Acute pulmonary edema
– No specific findings in cardiac contusion
r Focused assessment with sonography for trauma
(FAST) should be performed on all patients to assess
pericardium and possible concurrent
intra-abdominal injuries.
r ECG:
– Generally regarded as best imaging study for
detecting cardiac contusion
– Detects wall-motion abnormalities and effusions
– Allows direct visualization of cardiac chambers
and valves
– May not visualize small (possibly clinically
insignificant) contusions
– TEE preferable to TTE if patient stable enough for
procedure.
– TTE may be performed although may also visualize
great vessels.
r Radionuclide ventriculography:
– Has been largely abandoned owing to wide
availability of ECG
r Thallium201 scintigraphy (single photon emission CT
[SPECT]):
– Sensitive and specific to left ventricular injury
– Unable to evaluate right ventricle, which is most
commonly injured
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Pericardiocentesis:
– For treatment of cardiac tamponade, preferably
under US guidance
r Thoracotomy:
– Consider in patient with acute cardiac arrest or
decompensation in ED or after unsuccessful
pericardiocentesis
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Cardiac rupture
r Tamponade
r Valvular damage
r Other traumatic chest wall injury
r Angina or MI
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Pre-hospital personnel should convey accurate
information to emergency department personnel:
r Mechanism of injury
r Motor vehicle status
r Steering wheel and dashboard damage
r Use of restraint devices
r Vehicle speed
r Patient position
r Time to extrication
r Any loss of consciousness

INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Manage airway and resuscitate as indicated:
r Oxygen:
– IV access
– Cardiac monitoring
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Dysrhythmias may be treated with same
pharmacologic agents used for nontraumatic
dysrhythmias:
– Supraventricular tachycardia:
◦Adenosine or calcium channel blocker if patient
not hypovolemic
– Bradycardia:
◦Atropine
◦Pacing
– Ventricular dysrhythmias:
◦Electrical conversion
◦Amiodarone
◦Lidocaine
◦Procainamide
– Cardiac arrest:
◦Epinephrine
◦Atropine
◦Other interventions as appropriate
– Rapid atrial fibrillation or flutter:
◦Diltiazem, or digoxin if patient not hypotensive
r Prophylactic treatment of dysrhythmias is not
indicated.
r Cardiogenic shock caused by myocardial contusion:
– Judicious fluid administration
– Inotropic support (dopamine or dobutamine)
– Intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation may be
necessary.
MEDICATIONr Medications used in cardiac contusion are
supportive for dysrhythmias or hemodynamic
compromise secondary to injury.
r There is no primary therapy for cardiac contusion.
r Adenosine: 6 mg rapid IVP (peds: 0.05–0.1 mg/kg
rapid IVP), may repeat 12 mg q1–2min twice if no
response
r Amiodarone: Load 150 mg IV over 10 min (peds:
5 mg/kg), then 1 mg/min for 6 hr, then 0.5 mg/min
(peds: 5 μg/kg/min)
r Atropine: 0.5–1 mg (peds: 0.02 mg/kg/ dose, min.
0.1 mg) IV or endotracheal tube (ET)
r Digoxin: Load 0.5 mg (peds: 0.02 mg/kg) IV , then
0.25 mg (peds: 0.01 mg/kg) IV q6h for 2 more
doses
r Diltiazem: 0.25 mg/kg IV for both adults and peds
over 2 min, may rebolus 0.35 mg/kg (adult and
peds) 15 min later
r Dobutamine: 2–15 μg/kg/min (adults and peds)
r Dopamine: 2–20 μg/kg/min (adults and peds)
r Epinephrine: 1 mg (peds: 0.01 mg/kg) IV or ET for
cardiac arrest (1:10,000 solution)
r Lidocaine: Load 1 mg/kg IV , then 0.5 mg/kg
q8–10min to max. 3 mg/kg (adults and peds);
infusion 1–4 mg/min (peds: 20–50 μg/kg/min) IV
r Procainamide: start at 3 to 6 mg/kg/dose over 5
minutes not to exceed 100 mg to a titrated
maximum of 15 mg/kg/loading dose
r Verapamil: 0.1–0.3 mg/kg up to 5–10 mg IV over
2 min (not approved in children)
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITIONr Adverse outcomes, particularly dysrhythmias, are
uncommon but generally occur within 1st 24 hr.
r No single test or combination of tests will accurately
predict which patients can be discharged safely from
ED:
– All patients in whom diagnosis is seriously being
entertained should be admitted to a monitored
setting.
Admission Criteriar EKG abnormalities
r Cardiac enzyme abnormalities
r Hemodynamic instability
r Other studies suggesting cardiac contusion
r Admit to monitored unit for close observation.
Discharge Criteria
Asymptomatic patients with no EKG abnormalities or
dysrhythmia and with normal cardiac enzymes after
6–8 hr period may be discharged.
Issues for Referral
Immediate surgical consultation:
r Suspected myocardial wall rupture
r Suspected valve or papillary muscle rupture
r Suspected septal rupture
r Coronary artery thrombosis
r Pericardial effusion
r Cardiac tamponade
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Discharged patients:
r Should have follow-up within 24 hr of injury
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Obtain EKG in patients following chest wall trauma.
r Perform FAST exam on all patients to assess
pericardium.
r External signs of chest wall trauma should increase
concern of blunt cardiac injury.
r Pediatric patients may have little or no external
signs of chest wall trauma.
r Do not administer thrombolytics to patients with ST
elevation MI following trauma.
r Negative troponin I and normal EKG make
significant blunt cardiac injury unlikely.

– Appropriate in heart transplant recipients

r Acute and chronic pulmonary embolus
r Aortic dissection
r Adrenal insufficiency

r Supplemental oxygen

r Pulse oximetry
