Michele Zell-Kanter
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX), thereby blocking the
conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandin.
r Typically morbidity is low when an NSAID is ingested
r Most literature on nonselective NSAID toxicity
involves ibuprofen exposure likely due to its OTC
availability.
r Fatalities have been reported with large ingestions.
r Greater potential for toxicity with underlying CHF or
renal failure:
– NSAIDs cause sodium and water retention and
decrease renal blood flow.
– Little overdose experience with the COX-2
inhibitors (celecoxib); treatment should be the
same as for the traditional NSAIDs.
– Patients may ingest rofecoxib and valdecoxib from
stored supplies even though both are no longer
available in US
ETIOLOGYr Nonsteroidal medications are available by
prescription and over-the-counter.
r NSAIDs include:
– Diclofenac
– Diflunisal
– Etodolac
– Fenoprofen
– Ibuprofen
– Indomethacin
– Ketoprofen
– Ketorolac
– Meclofenamate
– Meloxicam
– Nabumetone
– Naproxen
– Oxaprozin
– Piroxicam
– Sulindac
– Tolmetin
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr GI:
– Nausea
– Vomiting
– Epigastric pain
r CNS:
– Drowsiness
– Dizziness
– Lethargy
– Aseptic meningitis
– Seizures
r Cardiovascular:
– Hypotension
– Tachycardia
r Pulmonary:
– Eosinophilic pneumonia
– Apnea
– Hyperventilation
r Renal:
– Acute renal failure, hyperkalemia
– Acute tubular necrosis
– Acute interstitial nephritis
r Liver:
– Hepatocellular injury
– Cholestatic jaundice
r Metabolic:
– Mild, short-lived metabolic acidosis
r Hypersensitivity:
– Aseptic meningitis
– Asthma exacerbation
– Angioedema, urticaria
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Generally, NSAID ingestion results in mild toxicity.
r Exact identification of drug helpful:
– Subtle toxicologic differences among the NSAIDs
– Aseptic meningitis more common with ibuprofen
exposure
– Liver toxicity more common with diclofenac and
sulindac exposure

Labr Electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, glucose:
– Baseline renal function
– Check for metabolic acidosis.
r CBC
r Arterial blood gas for large overdoses
r PT/PTT:
– False-positive bilirubin/ketone dipstick with
etodolac ingestion
r Acetaminophen and salicylate level—patients often
confuse salicylate, acetaminophen, and NSAID
products thinking they are all the same.
r NSAID difficult to detect on toxicology screens and
is not beneficial in management
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
Agents causing metabolic acidosis, altered mental
status, and GI irritation:
r Salicylates
r Isoniazid
r Ethylene glycol
r Methanol
r Isopropanol

NURSEMAID’S ELBOW
Neha P. Raukar rDaniel L. Savitt
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
The most common elbow injury in children<5 yr old.
ETIOLOGYr Sudden traction of the distal radius leads to a portion
of the annular ligament slipping over the radial head
and becoming trapped between the radius and the
capitellum. Traction can occur by swinging the child,
wrestling, and lifting the child by the arms.
r By the time the child is 5 yr, the annular ligament is
thick and strong and resists tearing and/or
displacement.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Child refuses to use arm.
r Elbow is slightly flexed, with forearm held close to
the trunk.
r Pain with flexion of the elbow
r Pain with forearm supination or pronation
r Absence of point tenderness
r Minimal to no swelling
Historyr Child not using affected arm
r 50% report the classic history of pulling the arm.
r Can also be due to a fall, minor trauma to the
elbow, or twisting of the forearm
r In children <6 mo, can be due to the child rolling
onto the arm.
Physical Examr Affected arm is held close to the body.
r Arm is usually pronated.
r Elbow is either fully extended or slightly flexed.
r Child will not use the elbow.
r Can be mildly tender over anterolateral radial head,
but the rest of the elbow is nontender.
r Painless passive range of motion
r Painful with supination
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Clinical diagnosis:
r Classic history, passive position of arm, and physical
exam are sufficient for diagnosis.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Imaging
Radiographs:
r Not routinely indicated
r Obtain to exclude or diagnose other injuries if any of
the following are present:
– Point tenderness
– Soft tissue swelling
– Deformity
– Ecchymosis of the elbow
– Failed reduction
– Child continues to favor extremity after reduction
maneuver.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Humerus, radius, or ulna fracture
r Elbow dislocation
r Joint infection
r Osteomyelitis
r Tumor
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Cautions:
r Place ice on the injured elbow to reduce pain and
swelling.
r Immobilize in a sling or splint to facilitate transport
and prevent further injury.
r Assess distal neurovascular status.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Assess distal motor, sensory, and vascular function.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr 2 common reduction techniques:
– Supination/flexion:
◦More commonly used
– Hyperpronation/extension:
◦Nurses and caretakers perceive this method to
be less painful
◦More successful
r Supination/flexion technique:
– Grasp child’s hand in handshake position and
apply mild axial traction.
– Stabilize injured elbow with the other hand with
the thumb over the radial head exerting moderate
pressure.
– In 1 smooth, swift motion, fully supinate the
forearm and flex the elbow.
r Hyperpronation/extension technique:
– Grasp child’s hand in handshake position and
apply mild axial traction.
– Stabilize injured elbow with the other hand with
the thumb over the radial head exerting moderate
pressure.
– Hyperpronate the arm and extend if arm is not
already extended.

OCULOMOTOR NERVE PALSY
Adam Z. Barkin
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Typical presentation of a 3rd cranial nerve (CN)
palsy:
– Eyelid drooping
– Blurred or double vision
– Light sensitivity
– May also have other neurologic signs/symptoms:
◦Hemiplegia
◦Ataxia
◦Tremor
r CN III controls elevation, adduction and depression
of the eye. This nerve also raises the lid and mediates
pupillary constriction and lens accommodation:
– Medial rectus:
◦Moves eye medially toward nose (adduction)
– Superior rectus:
◦Moves eye upward
◦Rotates top of eye toward nose
◦Slight adduction
– Inferior rectus:
◦Moves eye inferiorly
◦Rotates top of eye away from nose
◦Slight adduction
– Inferior oblique:
◦Rotates top of eye away from nose
◦Slight elevation and abduction
– Levator palpebrae superioris:
◦Raises eyelid
r CN IV innervates the superior oblique:
– Moves eye down when looking medially
– Rotates eye internally
r CN VI innervates the lateral rectus:
– Moves eye laterally (abduction)
– Lesions categorized as:
– Complete vs. incomplete
– Pupil involving vs. pupil sparing
r Complete: Total loss of CN III function (“down and
out”):
– Compressive lesions:
◦Aneurysms
◦Tumors
◦Brainstem herniation with compression
◦Increased intracranial pressure
r Incomplete: Partial loss of CN III function:
– Vascular infarction of vasa vasorum
r Pupil involving:
– 95–97% of compressive lesions (aneurysm,
tumor, etc.) involve the pupil
– Parasympathetic fibers sit peripherally in CN III
r Pupil sparing:
– Ischemic injury to nerve
– Diabetics, uncontrolled hypertension
ETIOLOGYr Intracranial or orbital tumor
r Aneurysm (particularly posterior communicating
artery)
r Trauma
r Intracranial hemorrhage
r Diabetes mellitus
r Migraine headache
r Infection, meningitis
r Arteriovenous malformation or fistula
r Cavernous sinus thrombosis
r Neuropathy (e.g., myasthenia gravis, Guillain–Barr ´ e)
r Collagen vascular diseases (e.g., sarcoidosis)
r Idiopathic
Pediatric Considerations
Trauma is the most common cause of acquired
oculomotor nerve palsies
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
A careful history and physical exam are vital to narrow
down the differential diagnosis
History
History is of utmost importance in determining cause:
r Headache
r Pupillary dilation
r Eye pain
r Diplopia
r Blurry vision
r History of long-standing diabetes mellitus
r Head trauma, either recent or distant
r Unintentional weight loss
r Signs and symptoms of infection
r Sudden onset of severe headache, meningeal signs,
photophobia
r Proptosis
r Lid swelling
Physical Examr Ophthalmologic exam:
– Extraocular movements
– Fundoscopic exam for papilledema
– Ipsilateral and contralateral pupillary reaction
– Ptosis
– Diplopia
– Chemosis or conjunctival injection
– Tenderness
– Visual acuity
– Exophthalmos
r Pupil sparing lesion:
– Ptosis
– Globe is “down and out”
– No elevation, depression, or adduction
– Normal pupil exam
– CN IV , V , VI intact
– Usually no other neurologic signs/symptoms
– Most commonly caused by ischemia in adults
– Also consider giant cell arteritis and trauma
r Pupil-involving lesion:
– Anisocria is present with a dilated pupil on
affected side
– Need to rule out compressive aneurysm
r Incomplete, 3rd CN palsy:
– May have involvement of 1 or more extraocular
muscle and may or may not involve pupil
r Look for associated symptoms:
– Extremity weakness
– Changes in speech
– Dysfunction of other CNs
– Gait or coordination
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
CT/MRI of brain, orbit, sinuses
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
When indicated based on history and physical exam:
r CBC with differential
r ESR
r Antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor to
evaluate for vasculitis
r Lumbar puncture
Imagingr MRI/MRA of brain and cerebral vessels particularly
when pupil is involved
r CT angiogram
r Cerebral arteriogram: Has associated risk of
neurologic morbidity and mortality
r Doppler imaging for arteriovenous malformations,
dural sinus thrombosis
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Intraocular pressure to exclude glaucoma
r Slit-lamp exam:
– Observe structural abnormalities of iris or anterior
chamber

– Meningitis:
◦Rapid administration of IV antibiotics

inflammatory response and edema
– Vasculitis and collagen vascular diseases: Decrease

palsy

– Strychnine
– Dextromethorphan
– Quinine
– Scopolamine

– CNS depression
– Coma
– Seizures
r GI:
– Nausea
– Vomiting
– Constipation
r Cardiovascular:
– Hypotension
– Bradycardia
– Palpitations
r Pulmonary:
– Respiratory depression
– Bronchospasm
– Pulmonary edema
– Apnea
r Other:

– Hypothermia
r Withdrawal:

– Tachycardia
– Tachypnea
– Abdominal cramps
– Diarrhea
– Piloerection
– Yawning

significant exposure:

r Barbiturate overdose
r Benzodiazepine overdose
r γ-hydroxybutyrate (GHB) overdose
r Neuroleptic overdose
r Occult head injury

methadone.

– Administer phenobarbital for persistent seizures.

DESCRIPTION
Unusual infections that occur when host suffers a
decrease in resistance against normally nonpathogenic
organisms

– Cryptococcosis

– Human herpesvirus-8 (Kaposi sarcoma)
– JC virus (progressive multifocal
leukoencephalopathy)
– Hepatitis B virus
– Penicilliosis marneffei
– Bacterial species

– Hematologic malignancies
– Lymphoma
– High-dose glucocorticoid therapy
– Autoimmune disorders
– Viral infections
– Cytotoxic drugs/chemotherapy
– Radiation therapy
– Associated with:
◦Legionella
◦Nocardia
◦Salmonella
◦Mycobacteria

– Cytotoxic drugs
– Aplastic anemia

◦Dapsone
– Neoplastic invasion of bone marrow
– Arsenic
– Penicillin
– Chloramphenicol

r Tachypnea
r Fever
r Chills
r Night sweats

– Congestion
– Rales

– Dysuria
– Increased frequency
– Urinary retention
r GI source of infection:

– Vomiting
– Diarrhea
– Bleeding
– Jaundice

– Focal neurologic deficits
– Headache
– Seizure

r Use of cytotoxic drugs
r Use of high-dose glucocorticoid therapy

r Signs of infection in the immunocompromised

OPTIC NEURITIS
Douglas W. Lowery-North
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Optic nerve dysfunction due to an inflammatory
process, commonly associated with myelin
destruction
r Highly associated with multiple sclerosis (MS);
presenting feature in 15–20% of MS patients
r Grouped by site of inflammation:
– Papillitis: Inflammation of the optic disk
– Retrobulbar neuritis: Inflammation of the optic
nerve proximal to the globe
r 5 yr risk for clinically definite MS following optic
neuritis:
– Normal MRI—16%
– >3 lesions on MRI—51%
r Recurrence is seen in 35% of patients.
RISK FACTORS
Genetics
High prevalence of A23, B7, and DR2 HLA alleles in
patients with optic neuritis:
r Especially those that progress to clinically definite
MS
ETIOLOGYr Idiopathic:
– Most common
– Single isolated events
r MS:
– 20–50% of patients with optic neuritis
r Viral infections:
– Chicken pox
– Measles
– Mononucleosis
– HSV and HZV
– Encephalitis
r Postviral optic neuritis:
– Usually occurs 4–6 wk after a nonspecific viral
illness
r Granulomatous inflammation:
–T B
– Syphilis
– Sarcoidosis
– Cryptococcal infection
r SLE
r HIV:
– Cytomegalovirus
– Toxoplasmosis
– Histoplasmosis
– Cryptococcus
r Lyme disease
r Contiguous inflammation of meninges, orbit,
sinuses, and intraocular inflammation
r Drug induced:
– Amiodarone
– Ethambutol
– Tamoxifen
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Vision loss and pain most common symptoms
r Visual loss occurring over days (rarely over hours),
peaks in 1–2 wk:
– Adults usually unilateral (70%)
– Bilateral visual loss more common in children
r Retrobulbar pain: Increased with movement of the
affected eye
r Light, color vision, and depth perception loss more
pronounced than visual acuity loss
r Afferent pupillary defect almost always occurs in
unilateral cases if other eye is healthy.
r Visual field defects:
– Usually characterized by central scotoma
– Deficits resolve by 1 yr in 56% of patients, and
73% resolve by 10 yr
r Funduscopic exam usually reveals either swollen
(papillitis) or normal disk
r Uhthoff sign:
– Visual deficit occurring with exercise or increased
body temperature
– Unusual sign seen occasionally
Historyr Age (typically women 18–45 yr)
r Pain on eye movement
r Speed of onset of symptoms
r Associated symptoms
r Previous episodes
r Family history of optic neuritis, MS
Physical Examr Check BP .
r Complete ophthalmologic and neurologic exam,
especially assessment of:
– Pupillary function
– Afferent pupillary defect
– Visual field defect
– Color vision (Ishihara color plates)
– Evaluation of the vitreous body for cells
– Dilated retinal exam (swollen optic disk)
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC
r ESR
r Rapid plasma reagin, fluorescent treponemal
antibody-absorption (FTA-ABS)
r Lyme titer
r Antinuclear antibody
r Purified protein derivative
r HIV
Imagingr CXR for TB, sarcoid
r CT scan or MRI of brain and orbits:
– Inflammation of the retrobulbar optic nerve during
the acute phase may appear as enlargement, thus
falsely raising the issue of an optic nerve mass.
– Optic nerve inflammation is seen in 95% of
gadolinium-enhanced MRIs.
– Visual field testing (preferably automated testing,
such as Octopus or Humphrey)
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Acute papilledema
r Ischemic optic neuropathy
r Severe systemic hypertension
r Intracranial tumor compressing the afferent visual
pathway
r Orbital mass compressing the optic nerve
r Toxic or metabolic neuropathy:
– Heavy metal poisoning
– Anemia
– Malnutrition
– Ethanol/Methanol
– Chloroquine
– Ethambutol
– Isoniazid
r Leber hereditary optic atrophy
Pediatric Considerations
In children, infectious and postinfectious causes
should be considered.
Geriatric Considerations
In patients >50 yr, ischemic optic neuropathies (e.g.,
diabetes and giant cell arteritis) are more common,
and appropriate workup should be obtained.

ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Early ophthalmologic and neurologic consultations
r IV steroid pulse followed by oral steroids:
– Recommended for those with ≥2 demyelinating
lesions on MRI without a prior history of MS or
optic neuritis, or severe vision loss
– Decreases recurrence and progression to MS over
2 yr and shortens duration of visual impairment,
but does not affect visual outcome at 1 yr nor rate
of progression at 5 yr
– Treatment should be individualized for those with
1 lesion on MRI.
– Oral steroids used alone increases recurrence and
should be avoided.

followed by oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/d) for 11 days
with subsequent 4 day taper

out

Issues for Referral
Referral for interferon β-1a treatment as outpatient
for high-risk patients (those with ≥2 demyelinating
lesions on MRI):
r Reduces progression to MS

Needs Ophthalmology referral

r Rule out space-occupying lesions before making the
diagnosis of optic neuritis.

diplopia should raise concern for pituitary apoplexy.

should consult with appropriate specialists to

ORGANOPHOSPHATE POISONING
Vinodinee L. Dissanayake
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Organophosphates (pesticides and nerve agents)
irreversibly bind and deactivate cholinesterases,
including acetylcholinesterase
r Acetylcholine accumulates at neural synapses,
causing central and peripheral cholinergic overdrive
r Predominant effects (muscarinic, nicotinic, CNS)
may vary and can overlap.
r Mortality is secondary to respiratory failure:
– Weakness of respiratory muscles
– Bronchorrhea and bronchoconstriction
– Central depression of respiratory drive
Pediatric Considerations
r Symptoms are difficult to differentiate in toddlers
r Common symptoms: Miosis, salivation, and muscle
weakness
r Seizure activity in 25% of pediatric cases:
– Only 3% in adults
ETIOLOGYr Exposure to insecticides (organophosphorus
compounds)
r Exposure to chemical nerve agents (sarin, soman,
tabun, VX)
r Extremely well absorbed from lung, GI tract, skin,
mucosa, eyes

SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Classic presentation: Cholinergic toxidrome:
– DUMBELS:
◦Diarrhea/diaphoresis
◦Urination
◦Miosis/muscle fasciculations
◦Bradycardia, bronchorrhea, bronchospasm
◦Emesis
◦Lacrimation
◦Salivation
– May have garlic odor
r Chronic intermittent exposure, nonspecific
symptoms:
– Weakness
– Fatigue
– Malaise
– Anorexia
r Mild exposure:
– CNS:
◦Headache
◦Dizziness
◦Tremors of tongue and eyelids
◦Weakness
– GI:
◦Anorexia
r Moderate exposure:
– CNS:
◦Muscle fasciculation then flaccid paralysis
◦Respiratory muscle weakness

TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Decontamination is initial priority:
– Decontaminate, airway, breathing, circulation
(DABC)
– Remove all clothes and store as toxic waste
(double bagged)
r Protection of health care workers of utmost
importance:
– Impenetrable gloves (neoprene, nitrile), gowns,
eye protection
r Decontaminate skin with soap and water:
– Shower or gentle scrubbing ideal if done before
entrance into the ED
r Maintain airway and oxygenate.
r IV access and place on cardiac monitor
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Decontaminate ABCs:
– Decontamination and protection of staff
– Maintain airway and oxygenate.
– For unstable airway, intubate, and ventilate.
– IV access with D5W 0.9% NS
r Altered mental status: Administer thiamine, glucose,
and naloxone (Narcan)
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Atropine:
– Blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptor sites.
– No effect on nicotinic receptors
– Onset of action is 1–4 min, peaks at 8 min.
– Goal of therapy/end point:
◦Drying secretions of tracheobronchial tree
– Administer test dose 1–2 mg IV/IM:
◦No clinical response: Double dose q5min until
muscarinic findings subside
– Dose: 1–4 mg IV q5min (peds: 0.05–0.2 mg/kg)
– Common pitfalls in therapy:
◦Not giving enough atropine
◦Using pupillary findings (mydriasis) as end point
of treatment
◦Mistaking dilated pupils or tachycardia as
contraindications to atropine
r Pralidoxime (2-PAM):
– Regenerates cholinesterase by reversing the
phosphorylation of the enzyme.
– Synergistic with atropine—muscarinic
signs/symptoms will start to resolve in 10–40 min.
– Side effects: Neuromuscular blockade with rapid
infusion, respiratory arrest, HTN, nausea/vomiting,
dizziness, blurred vision.
– End point is resolution of muscle weakness and
fasciculations.
– Effective before enzyme aging occurs (permanent
inactivation of cholinesterase)
– Onset of aging varies among products
– No restriction to its use even if 24–48 hr have
passed
r Supportive care:
– Dermal decontamination: Remove clothes and
flush skin with water
– Gastric lavage (early presentation of severe
ingestion):
◦Gastric emptying with continuous suction via a
nasogastric tube.
◦Handle contents with care—avoid direct
contact to prevent personal exposure.
– Respiratory difficulty:
◦Frequent oropharyngeal suction
◦Treat bronchospasm with atropine, not
bronchodilators.
◦Tachycardia may result from hypoxia (pulmonary
secretions and bronchospasm).
◦Atropine will dry secretions and paradoxically
lower the heart rate.
◦Intubate and ventilate if necessary.
◦Avoid succinylcholine; may have prolonged
duration as it is metabolized by cholinesterase.
MEDICATIONr Atropine: 1–2 mg (peds: 0.05–0.2 mg/kg) IV q5min
(see the previous section for details)
r Dextrose: D50W, 1 amp (25 g) of 50% dextrose
(peds: 2–4 mL/kg D25W) IV push
r Naloxone (Narcan): 2 mg (peds: 0.1 mg/kg) IV/IM
r Pralidoxime: 1–2 g (peds: 25–50 mg/kg) dissolved
in 0.9% NS over 30 min IV; repeat in 1 hr if
necessary, then q6h as needed:
– Some propose continuous infusion (500 mg/h) for
serum concentration of 4 mg/L.
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar ICU admission for any exposure confirmed with
atropine response.
r Any symptomatic patient should be admitted for
monitoring.
r Avoid opioids, phenothiazines, and antihistamines;
these may potentiate toxicity of organophosphates.
Discharge Criteriar Asymptomatic for 6–12 hr after exposure
r Ensure close reliable follow-up and specific
instructions when to return for evaluation.
Issues for Referral
Contact toxicologist or poison center for patients with
significant exposures requiring repeat atropine
administration.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Psychiatry referral for intentional ingestions.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Treatment failure often secondary to inadequate
atropine dosing
r Recognize nicotinic manifestations (tachycardia,
seizures).
ADDITIONAL READING

Goldfrank LR, ed. Goldfrank’s Toxicologic
Emergencies. New York, NY: McGraw-Hill; 2010.

therapeutic approaches to nerve agent poisoning.
Toxicol Lett. 2011;206:5–13.

experiences in Japan: Acute toxicity and long-term
effects. J Neurol Sci. 2006;249:76–85.

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Most frequent cause of knee pain in children aged
10–15 yr
r Pain and edema of the tibial tuberosity:
– Tenderness at insertion site for patellar tendon

r Extra-articular disease:

– Caused by repetitive stress and is common in

the apophysis
r Pain occurs during activities that stress the patellar
tendon insertion onto tibial tubercle.

r Pain exacerbated by running, jumping
r Pain relieved by rest

– Age: 10–15 yr of age, associated with growth
spurt in puberty
– More common in boys
– Sports: Activities with running, jumping, swift
changes in direction (i.e., soccer, basketball, figure
skating)
r Knee pain is worse with activity and improves with
rest.
r Usually unilateral, with 20% occurring bilateral

tuberosity
r Pain reproduced by extending the knee against
resistance
r Tenderness over tibial tuberosity at patellar tendon

unaffected side

r Patellar or quadriceps tendonitis
r Prepatellar or infrapatellar bursitis
r Osteochondritis dissecans
r Osteomyelitis
r Patellofemoral pain syndrome
r Septic joint

r Fat pad impingement (Hoffa disease)

r Apply ice to affected knee.

– Avoid cutting and jumping sports, such as
basketball, soccer, volleyball, etc.
r Ice affected area.
r Analgesic medications
r Stretch the quadriceps and hamstrings.
r Apply protective padding to knee during activities.
r Infrapatellar tendon strap may be worn for 6–8 wk.
r Avoid corticosteroid injections.
r Reassurance; it is a benign, self-limited condition.

OSTEOGENESIS IMPERFECTA
Daniel Davis rChad M. Valderrama
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Inherited abnormality of procollagen amino acid
sequence
r Bone hypomineralization and incomplete
ossification result in brittle bones.
r Abnormal collagen affects all connective tissue to
varying degrees.
r Time course is variable:
– Most cases involve fractures during childhood
followed by quiescence during adolescence and
early adulthood.
ETIOLOGYr Procollagen defects result in abnormalities of bone
and connective tissue matrix.
r Defects in different sites on procollagen protein
chain result in more severe forms.
r Defects are inherited, either autosomal recessive
(generally milder) or autosomal dominant (more
severe).
r Lethal cases involve sporadic or new mutations.
r Ehlers–Danlos syndrome involves mutations of the
same procollagen protein in different locations.
Pediatric Considerations
r Most cases involve pathologic fractures during
childhood.
r Multiple fractures often initiate evaluation for abuse,
but the possibility of pathologic fractures also
should be considered.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Multiple heritable defects that lead to brittle bones:
– Often associated with other connective tissue
abnormalities
r A suspected fracture with a relatively minor
mechanism or a history of multiple fractures in a
child suggests the diagnosis.
r Careful social history with consideration for the
possibility of nonaccidental trauma
r Bones:
– Multiple recurrent fractures (especially in long
bones) are the hallmark of this disease.
– Fractures may be present at birth or may recur in
the elderly.
– Shortened or bowed limbs, pectus excavatum,
curving of long bones, vertebral compression
fractures, scoliosis, kyphosis, and abnormal skull
shape
– All bones are affected to some extent (see
Imaging/Special Tests).
r Eyes:
– Blue sclerae are another hallmark of this disease.
– No visual changes are reported.
r Ears:
– Hearing loss usually begins in adolescence;
>90% of patients have some deficit by age 30 yr.
– Hearing loss is generally sensorineural, although
some middle ear abnormalities have been
demonstrated.
– Academic difficulties should raise suspicion of
possible hearing deficits.
r Other:
– Discolored, fragile, and abnormal shape of teeth
– Shares several features with Ehlers–Danlos
syndrome:
◦Loose joints
◦Valve problems
◦Vascular abnormalities
r Thyroid abnormalities may be seen.
r Extreme cases may result in perinatal death.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Diagnosis is usually made as combination of clinical
and radiographic findings.
r History of repeated fractures or fractures with
unimpressive mechanism
r Thorough search for other tender areas and
evaluation of eyes, teeth, and joints is important for
diagnosis.
r Careful exam of neurovascular status distal to
fracture
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Evaluate for metabolic derangements such as
hyperparathyroidism, vitamin C or D deficiencies,
and calcium/phosphate abnormalities.
r DNA studies may be indicated for familial analysis,
prenatal testing, and genetic counseling.
r Tissue biopsy is controversial but may help
differentiate from tumors.

OSTEOMYELITIS
Stephen R. Hayden
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Osteomyelitis (OM): Infection of bone with ongoing
inflammatory destruction
r Usually bacterial, but fungal OM does occur
r Could be acute or chronic
ETIOLOGYr Hematogenous OM:
– Primarily in children, elderly, IV drug abuse (IVDA)
patients
– Seeding of bacteria to bone from remote site of
infection via bloodstream
– Children have acute OM and adults subacute or
chronic.
– Hematogenous OM of long bones rarely occurs in
adults.
– Most children with acute hematogenous OM have
no preceding illness.
– 1/3 have history of trauma to affected area.
– Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause
of OM in all ages.
– Neonates: S. aureus, Enterobacteriaceae, group A
and B streptococci, and Escherichia coli
– Children: S. aureus, group A streptococci,
Haemophilus influenzae, Enterobacteriaceae
– Salmonella: Common in sickle cell disease
– Adults: S. aureus, Enterobacteriaceae,
Pseudomonas, gram-negative rods,
Staphylococcus epidermidis, gram-positive
anaerobes, especially Peptostreptococcus
– Illicit drug users: Candida, Pseudomonas, Serratia
marcescens
– Prolonged neutropenia: Candida, Aspergillus,
Rhizopus, Blastomyces, coccidioidomycosis
r Hematogenous vertebral OM:
– Uncommon
– Most prevalent in adults >45 yr
– Involves the disk and vertebra above and below
– Often in the setting of long-term urinary catheter
placement, IVDA, cancer, hemodialysis, or diabetes
– IVDA: OM of pubic symphysis, sternoclavicular,
and sacroiliac (SI) joints
– Lumbar vertebrae most common, followed by
thoracic, then cervical
– Posterior extension leads to epidural/subdural
abscess or meningitis.
– Anterior extension may lead to paravertebral,
retropharyngeal, mediastinal, subphrenic,
retroperitoneal, or psoas abscess.
r Direct or contiguous OM:
– Organism(s) directly seeded in bone due to
trauma, especially following open fractures:
◦Spread from adjacent site of infection or from
surgery
– More common in adults and adolescents
– S. aureus, Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas
– Normal vascularity:
◦S. aureus and S. epidermidis, gram-negative
bacilli, and anaerobic organisms
– Vascular insufficiency/diabetes:
◦Small bones of feet are common sites.
◦Infection resulting from minor trauma, infected
nail beds, cellulitis, or skin ulceration
◦Polymicrobial, including anaerobes
– Puncture wound through tennis shoe: S. aureus,
Pseudomonas
– Clavicular OM can occur as complication of
subclavian vein catheterization.
r Chronic OM:
– OM that persists or recurs
– Distinguishing characteristic is necrotic bone
(sequestrum) that must be d ´ ebrided.
– S. epidermidis, S. aureus, Pseudomonas
aeruginosa, S. marcescens, and E. coli
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Vary with duration of disease
Historyr Mainly nonspecific symptoms
r Pain: Localized, deep, dull, and throbbing; occurs
with and without movement
r Fever and chills; may be absent in chronic OM
r Malaise, nausea, vomiting
r Reluctance to use extremity
r Nonhealing ulcers despite proper therapy
r Consider OM as a cause of fracture nonunion
r Predisposing factors: DM, vasculopathy, IVDA,
invasive procedures, trauma
Physical Examr Tenderness to palpation, warmth, erythema, edema,
decreased range of motion
r Drainage of sinus tract
r Deep ulcers and palpable bone (+ “probe to bone”
test has very high positive predictive value)
r If ulcer size >2c m2 and >3 mm in depth, bone
involvement is likely.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr CBC
r ESR and C-reactive protein
r Radiographs
r Blood and wound cultures and sensitivities
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC; WBC may be elevated but often normal
r ESR; elevated in >90% of cases
r C-reactive protein (usually elevated)
r Blood cultures (positive in ∼50% of cases)
Imagingr Plays a central role in evaluation
r Start with plain films; other tests often required
r Radiographs:
– May be normal for the 1st 2–3 wk of symptoms
– Earliest finding is periosteal elevation, followed by
cortical erosions, then new bone formation.
– 40–50% of focal bone loss needed to detect
lucency on radiograph; fewer than 1/3 of cases
have diagnostic findings at 10 days
– Obtain CXR if TB suspected
r MRI:
– Best modality to obtain detailed anatomy and
extension of soft tissue and bone marrow
involvement
– Sensitivity and specificity of ∼90%
– Reveals bone edema, cortical destruction,
periosteal reaction, joint surface damage, and soft
tissue involvement before x-rays
– Effective in early detection (3–5 days from onset
of infection)
– Test of choice to identify vertebral OM and OM in
diabetic foot ulcers
– Occasional false-positive results in trauma,
previous surgical procedures, or neuropathic joint
disease
– Negative study after 1 wk of symptoms rules out
acute OM
r CT:
– Modality of choice when MRI cannot be done
– Reveals bone edema, cortical destruction,
periosteal reaction, small foci of gas or foreign
bodies, joint surface damage, and soft tissue
involvement when plain films not helpful
– Useful in OM of vertebrae, sternum, calcaneus,
pelvic bones
– Useful to surgeons in guiding d ´ ebridement and
biopsy

OSTEOPOROSIS
Daniel Davis rMarian Xu
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Overall decrease in skeletal mass, generally diffuse
r Trabecular bone (especially vertebrae and femur)
affected more commonly and earlier
r Disease begins in adolescence, but fractures do not
usually manifest until age ≥50
r Females affected much more commonly than males,
especially after menopause
ETIOLOGYr Overall increase in resorption over formation of new
bone
r Advanced age is the most important risk factor
r Inadequate dietary calcium an important factor,
especially early in life
r Sedentary lifestyle is a risk factor (weight bearing on
bone favors new bone formation)
r Decrease in estrogen with menopause key factor in
women
r Other risk factors include long-term steroid use,
alcoholism, methotrexate, tobacco use, low body
weight
r Familial or hereditary factor may coexist
Pediatric Considerations
Although disease appears to start in adolescence,
pediatric patients are asymptomatic.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Usually asymptomatic until pathologic fractures
occur
r Fractures with insignificant mechanism or recurrent
fractures are hallmark
r Vertebral column most commonly involved
r Multiple compression fractures of vertebral column
often lead to kyphosis and scoliosis
r Hip fractures (femoral neck and intertrochanteric
fractures) also common
Historyr A suspected fracture with a relatively minor
mechanism or a history of multiple fractures
suggests osteoporosis.
r A family history of osteoporosis is an important risk
factor
Physical Exam
Exam findings are related to the acute fracture rather
than the disease itself.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Fracture without significant mechanism and
identification of risk factors is most important
r Careful neurovascular exam distal to femur or other
extremity fracture
r Rectal tone and postvoid residual should be
determined in patients with vertebral fractures
r Radiographs of suspected fracture may show
osteopenia (late finding in disease)
r Spine films may show old compression fractures
r CT scan should be performed to better evaluate
vertebral fractures:
– Retropulsion, spinal canal compromise is not
always apparent on plain films.
– Make sure CT cuts extend full level above and
below injuries on spine radiographs.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Serum chemistries—such as calcium, parathyroid
hormone, and alkaline phosphatase—may help
differentiate this from other illnesses.
Imagingr Plain films can identify fractures; however, age of
each fracture may be difficult to determine
r Bone scan or CT can help determine age of
fractures, especially in spine
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Bone densitometry can provide prognostic information
and help guide therapy. Dual-energy x-ray
absorptiometry with BMD T-score≤–2.5:
Osteoporosis.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Multiple myeloma or other metastatic tumor
r Osteogenesis imperfecta (usually apparent in
childhood)
r Hyperparathyroidism
r Other demineralizing bone diseases
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Cautions:
r Obtain pre-hospital information on mechanism to
help diagnose pathologic fracture
r Avoid aggressive manipulation or movement of
patient, as this may exacerbate bony injury
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Immobilize fractures
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Fractures are treated with expectation of delayed or
incomplete healing
r Prevention is far more effective than treatment
r Long-term therapy is beneficial (see Medication)
r Use of orthotic back braces and vests should be
arranged in conjunction with orthopedic spine
consultation
r Exercise is also helpful
r Balance must be achieved between osteoporosis risk
and steroid or methotrexate therapy
MEDICATIONr Alendronate: 10 mg/d or 70 mg weekly, alternative
is risedronate 5 mg/d, 35 mg weekly, or 150 mg
monthly
r Zoledronic acid: 5 mg IV yearly
r Raloxifene (selective estrogen receptor modulator):
60 mg PO QD
r Calcium: 1,200 mg daily (total of diet +
supplement)
r Vitamin D: 800 IU/d
r Calcitonin: Nasal spray 200 IU/d
r Denosumab (monoclonal antibody): 60 mg SC every
6m o
r Parathyroid hormone 1–34: 20 μg SC daily
r Estrogen: 0.625 mg/d (with or without
medroxyprogesterone)
Pediatric Considerations
Ensure adequate calcium in diet from early age.

OTITIS EXTERNA
Assaad J. Sayah
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Inflammation or infection of the auricle, auditory
canal, or external surface of the tympanic membrane
(TM):
– Spares the middle ear
– Affects 4/1,000 persons in US
r Also called “swimmer’s ear” due to the usual
history of recent swimming:
– Occasional cases after normal bathing
r Necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa:
– Infection starts at the ear canal and progresses
through periauricular tissue toward the base of
the skull
– Occurs in elderly, diabetic, or other
immunocompromised patients
– Caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa
– Can lead to cellulitis, chondritis, and osteomyelitis
– Associated with 20% mortality
ETIOLOGYr Often precipitated by an abrasion of the ear canal or
maceration of the skin from persisting water or
excessive dryness
r Predisposing factors include:
– History of ear surgery or TM perforation
– Narrow or abnormal canal
– Humidity
– Allergy
– Eczema
– Trauma
– Abnormal cerumen production
r P. aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, streptococcal
species, and rarely fungi
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Recent swimming or prolonged water exposure
r History of diabetes
r History of chemotherapy, prolonged steroid use,
HIV/AIDS, or other processes that compromises
immune system
r Itching of the external ear canal is usually the 1st
symptom
r 1–2 day history of progressive pain
r Ear drainage
r Decreased auditory acuity
r Clogged sensation in ear
Physical Examr Pain in ear or with motion of pinna/tragus
r Swollen, erythematous external ear canal
r Ear drainage
r Decreased auditory acuity
r Pain/swelling in preauricular area
r Necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa:
– Pain, tenderness, swelling in periauricular area
– Headache
– Otorrhea
– Cranial nerve palsy:
◦Facial nerve most affected
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Clinical diagnosis with typical signs/symptoms:
r Pain in ear or with motion of pinna/tragus
r Otoscopic exam
r Swollen, erythematous external ear canal
r Ear drainage
r Cheesy white or gray-green exudate
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr None usually indicated, except when possibility of
necrotizing otitis externa:
– Signs of systemic toxicity or local spread of
infection should be checked
r WBC count
r ESR
r Glucose (check for diabetes)
r Cultures
Imaging
CT/MRI to exclude mastoiditis if the patient has signs
of toxicity or bone involvement
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Remove debris with a soft plastic curette or gentle
irrigation with peroxide/water mix
r Wick placement may be needed to facilitate
medication delivery
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Necrotizing otitis externa
r Otitis media
r Folliculitis from obstruction of sebaceous glands
r Otic foreign bodies
r Herpes zoster infection of the geniculate ganglion
r Parotitis
r Periauricular adenitis
r Mastoiditis
r Dental abscess
r Sinusitis
r Tonsillitis
r Pharyngitis
r Temporomandibular joint pain
r Viral exanthems
Pediatric Considerations
Consider ear canal foreign bodies in children with
purulent drainage from edematous, painful ear canals
TREATMENT
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Clean external ear canal:
– Remove the inflammatory debris by gentle
curettage with a cotton-tipped wire applicator
– Occasional suction with a Frazier suction tip may
be necessary
r Insert a cotton or gauze wick 10–12 mm into the
canal after cleansing if the ear canal is very
edematous
r Management of otitis externa focuses on pain
control, eradication of infection, and prevention of
reoccurrence
MEDICATIONr Most cases respond well to topical treatment:
– Antiseptic, anti-inflammatory, and drying otic
drops eliminate the pathogenic bacteria and allow
for rapid healing of the canal
– Acetic acid solutions such as Domeboro otic (2%
acetic acid): 4–6 drops q4–6h
– Corticosporin otic (hydrocortisone 1%, polymyxin
+ neomycin) suspension: 4 drops to ear canal QID
(use suspensions and not solutions with suspected
TM perforation)
– Ofloxacin: 5 drops BID (drug of choice in
perforated TM)
r Oral antibiotics:
– Administer to patients with cellulitis of the face or
neck, severe edema of the ear canal, concurrent
otitis media, or when the TM cannot be visualized
– Treat diabetics and other immunocompromised
patients with oral ciprofloxacin and follow closely
for symptoms of malignant otitis externa
– Amoxicillin: 500 mg (peds: 40 mg/kg/d) PO TID
– Ciprofloxacin: 500 mg PO BID
r IV antibiotics for patients with necrotizing otitis
externa, severe cellulitis, or septic appearing
r Prophylaxis:
– Apply rubbing alcohol or acetic acid (2%) to keep
the external ear canal dry and prevent recurrence
of infection
r Pain management with acetaminophen or NSAID.
Consider opioids if severe pain
r Surgical d ´ ebridement of granulation tissue and bone
sequestration or drainage of associated abscess may
be necessary in necrotizing otitis externa
COMPLICATIONSr Mastoiditis
r Chondritis of the auricle
r Necrotizing otitis externa
r Osteomyelitis of the base of the skull
r CNS infections

OVARIAN CYST/TORSION
Rene ´e A. King rLynne M. Yancey
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Ovarian cysts:
– Generally asymptomatic until complicated by
hemorrhage, torsion, rupture, or infection
– Follicular cysts:
◦Most common
◦Occur from fetal life to menopause
◦Unilocular; diameter 3–8 cm
◦Thin wall predisposes to rupture, which usually
causes minimal or no bleeding
◦Rupture during ovulation at midcycle is known
as mittelschmerz
– Corpus luteal cysts:
◦Most significant
◦Diameter 3 cm, but usually <10 cm
◦Rapid bleeding from intracystic hemorrhage
causes rupture
◦Rupture is most common just before menses
begins
◦Can cause severe intraperitoneal bleeding
◦Gradual bleeding into cyst or ovary distends
capsule and may cause pain without rupture
r Adnexal torsion:
– 5th most prevalent surgical gynecologic
emergency
– Twisting of vascular pedicle of ovary, fallopian
tube, or paratubal cyst
– Causes adnexal ischemia leading to necrosis
– Occlusion of lymphatics and venous drainage lead
to rapid enlargement of adnexa
– Greatest risk with cysts 8–12 cm
RISK FACTORS
Adnexal torsion:
r Reproductive-age women
r Ovarian cysts, especially >5c m
r Ovarian hyperstimulation
r Tumors: Serous cystadenoma most common;
teratomas
r Pelvic surgery: Tubal ligation; hysterectomy
r Pregnancy
r History of pelvic inflammatory disease
Pregnancy Considerations
Torsion in pregnancy usually occurs in the 1st
trimester, and in vitro fertilization or ovarian induction
are risk factors.
Pediatric Considerations
15% of adnexal torsions occur in children
ALERT
r Anticoagulated patients at increased risk of:
– Hemorrhagic corpus luteal cyst
– Significant bleed from ruptured cyst, including
with ovulation
ETIOLOGYr Ovarian cyst:
– Follicular cysts result from nonrupture of mature
follicle or failure of atresia of immature follicle
– Corpus luteal cysts result from unrestrained
growth in early pregnancy or from normal
intracystic hemorrhage days after ovulation
– Other cysts:
◦Theca lutein
◦Cystic teratoma
◦Endometrioma (chocolate cyst)
r Adnexal torsion:
– Right > left
– Highest frequency in reproductive women
ALERT
Cysts found in postmenopausal women suggest
carcinoma
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Ovarian cyst:
– Abdominal pain
◦Sharp, unilateral
◦Intermittent vs. constant
◦Migration
◦Previous episodes
◦May occur with exercise, intercourse, trauma, or
pelvic exam
– Fever is rare
– Irregular menses (may suggest polycystic ovary
syndrome)
– Infertility
– Pregnancy status
– Previous STDs
– History of breast or GI cancer (may metastasize)
r Adnexal torsion:
– Variable history
– Abdominal pain:
◦Sudden, sharp, colicky
◦Localized vs. diffuse
◦Referred pain to groin or flank
◦May be chronic or recurring with
torsion/detorsion
– Fever
– Nausea/vomiting
– Vaginal bleeding
– UTI symptoms
Physical Examr Ovarian cyst:
– Abdominal tenderness (mild to severe with
peritonitis)
– Adnexal tenderness
– Pelvic mass
– Hemorrhagic shock possible:
◦Usually from corpus luteal cyst rupture
◦Orthostasis, hypotension, tachycardia
r Adnexal torsion:
– Abdominal tenderness (mild to severe)
– Adnexal tenderness
– Adnexal mass

PAGET DISEASE
Anna L. Waterbrook rMatthew C. Kostura
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Paget disease involves resorption of normal bone
and its replacement with fibrous and sclerotic tissue
r Also known as osteitis deformans
r Usually focal, bones most frequently involved
include:
– Pelvis (70%)
– Femur (55%)
– Skull (42%)
– Tibia (32%)
– Spine (53%, lumbar spine)
– Flat bones
r Usually found incidentally and generally
asymptomatic
r Occurs in ∼1–2% of patients >55 yr old
r Incidence increases with age
r Starts with resorptive or osteolytic phase, during
which osteoclasts remove healthy bone
r Hypervascularity begins in resorptive phase:
– Predisposes to hematoma and fracture
r Resorbed bone is eventually replaced by irregular,
dense, disorganized trabecular bone in sclerotic or
osteoplastic phase forming “mosaic pattern”
r Malignant transformation is rare:
– Osteosarcoma is malignancy of concern
– Usually malignant transformation occurs in 1%
r More common in men
r More common in European descent
r Less common in Asian or Scandinavian descent
r Typically involves 1 bone (monostotic)
r May involve a few bones (polyostotic)
ETIOLOGYr Unknown
r Genetic component:
– SQSTM1 mutation seen in many but not all cases
r Environmental influences may also play a role
– Presence of nucleocapsids from measles, canine
distemper, paramyxovirus, or respiratory syncytial
virus may implicate viral cause
– Possible association with rural life and close
contact with farm animals
r May represent vascular hyperplasia with subsequent
inflammation
r Increased nucleoli and intranuclear inclusion bodies
seen in osteoclasts on microscopy
Pediatric Considerations
Generally not seen in children
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Many patients are asymptomatic, with disease
discovered by incidental radiographs or elevated
alkaline phosphatase levels
r Deep, aching bone pain occurs late in the clinical
course
r Pain with weight bearing if femur or tibia
involvement
r Pain worse with rest in nonweight-bearing bones
r Acute (resorptive/osteolytic) phase:
– Pathologic fractures
– Pain from acute lysis, fracture, or resultant arthritis
– Hypercalcemia or renal stones
– Hypervascularity may result in significant bleeding
if affected bone is fractured
– Widespread disease:
◦Increased vascularity and blood flow may result
in high-output cardiac failure
r Secondary (sclerotic/osteoplastic) phase:
– Long-bone involvement may present with swelling
or deformity and gait abnormality
– Skull involvement may cause headaches or
abnormal skull shape (change in hat size)
– Severe skull or spine involvement may result in
CNS compression
– Hearing loss may result from nerve compression or
ossicle involvement
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Diagnosis usually suggested by radiographs
r Thorough neurologic exam must be documented,
especially with vertebral or pelvis involvement
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Alkaline phosphatase is the most dramatic marker of
disease activity
r Calcium and phosphate levels should be checked as
well, but are usually normal
r Hypercalcemia seen in immobilization or presence of
a fracture, but if elevated in an ambulatory patient,
suspect hyperparathyroidism
r EKG if suspect hypercalcemia and CXR with
evidence of high-output cardiac failure
r Increased bone formation may lead to elevations in
urine hydroxyproline or serum osteocalcin or
procollagen fragments
r Alterations in parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels
occur as secondary changes during
resorptive/osteolytic phase (low PTH) and
sclerotic/osteoplastic phase (high PTH)
Imagingr Plain x-rays:
– During resorptive phase, lytic lesions are often not
seen, except in skull, where lesions are well
demarcated (osteoporosis circumscripta)
– Bowing of long bones may occur with resorption
and strength loss
– New bone initially appears irregular and spotty,
and later becomes homogeneous and dense
(“ivory pattern”)
– Excess bone may be deposited along stress lines,
leading to cortical irregularities and thickening
r CT or MRI defines margins and helps evaluate for
neoplasm or hematoma:
– Spiral CT to detect renal calculi
r Radionuclide bone scans useful to evaluate extent
and activity of disease
r Plain films are usually all that is needed in acute
setting to identify/manage fractures
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Primary hyperparathyroidism
r Multiple myeloma
r Hodgkin variants
r Acromegaly
r Osteosarcoma

PAIN (PRINCIPLES/MEDS/COMFORT CARE)
Vincent Bounes
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Unpleasant sensory and emotional experience that
may be secondary to actual or perceived damage to
tissue, the somatosensory system, or a psychogenic
dysfunction.
r It is an individual, subjective, multifactorial
experience influenced by culture, medical history,
beliefs, mood and ability to cope.
EPIDEMIOLOGY
Incidence and Prevalence Estimatesr Most common reason for seeking health care
r Up to 78% of visits to the emergency department.
r Pain is severe for 2/3rds of patients presenting with
pain.
r Chronic pain is present in up to 35% of the
population.
r Prevalence of neuropathic pain is 21.4% in
emergency departments.
ETIOLOGYr Different components of pain can be combined in a
same patient.
r Nociceptive pain:
– Stimulation of peripheral nerve fibers (nociceptors)
that arises from actual or threatened damage to
non-neural tissue.
– Visceral pain:
◦Stimulation of visceral nociceptors
◦Diffuse, difficult to locate, and often referred to
a distant, usually superficial, structure.
◦Sickening, deep, squeezing, dull.
– Deep somatic pain:
◦Stimulation of nociceptors in ligaments, tendons,
bones, blood vessels, fasciae, and muscles
◦Dull, aching, poorly localized pain.
– Superficial pain:
◦Stimulation of nociceptors in the skin or other
superficial tissue.
◦Sharp, well defined, and clearly located.
r Neuropathic pain:
– Exacerbation of normally nonpainful stimuli
(allodynia).
– Paroxysmal episodes likened to electric shocks.
– Continuous sensations include burning or
coldness, “pins and needles” sensations,
numbness and itching.
r Psychogenic pain:
– Pain caused, increased or prolonged by mental,
emotional, or behavioral factors.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr A patient’s self-report is the most reliable measure
of pain.
r Obtain a detailed description of pain:
– Onset
– If caused by an injury, determine the mechanism
of injury
– Localization of pain
– Severity of pain:
◦Mild pain from >0t o≤3/10
◦Moderate pain from >3t o<6/10
◦Severe pain ≥6/10.
– Type of pain
– Duration of pain
– Variations of pain:
◦Daily/weekly/monthly variations
◦Variations caused by physical activities
– Effect of previous analgesic drugs taken before the
consult.
r Acute vs. chronic pain:
– Acute pain:
◦Transitory, usually<30 days
◦Lasting only until the noxious stimulus is
removed or the underlying damage has healed
◦Resolves quickly
– Subacute pain:
◦Lasting 1–6 mo
– Chronic pain:
◦Lasts more than 3–6 mo
◦Pain that extends beyond the expected period of
healing
r Numerical Rating Scale (NRS):
– Patients estimate their pain intensity on a scale
from 0 to 10
r Visual Analog Scale (VAS):
– Patients indicate their pain by a position along a
10 cm continuous line between 2 end points, the
left one representing no pain and the right one
the worst pain they can imagine.

DPL to identify intraperitoneal injuries:
r Check fluid for amylase level.

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Inflammation of pancreas due to activation,
interstitial liberation, and digestion of gland by its
own enzymes
r Acute pancreatitis:
– Exocrine and endocrine function of gland impaired
for weeks to months
– Glandular function will return to normal.
r Chronic pancreatitis:
– Exocrine and endocrine function progressively
deteriorates with resultant steatorrhea and
malabsorption.
– Dysfunction progressive and irreversible
r Pancreatic pseudocyst:
– Cystic collection of fluid with high content of
pancreatic enzymes surrounded by a wall of
fibrous tissue lacking a true epithelial lining
– Localized in parenchyma of pancreas or adjacent
abdominal spaces (lesser peritoneal sac)
– Requires 4–6 wk to form from onset of acute
pancreatitis
ETIOLOGYr Gallstones and alcohol abuse most common causes
of acute pancreatitis (75–80%)
r Alcohol abuse accounts for 70–80% of chronic
pancreatitis.
r Acute:
– Biliary tract disease
– Chronic alcoholism
– Obstruction of pancreatic duct
– Ischemia
– Medications
– Infectious
– Postoperative
– Post-ERCP
– Metabolic diseases
– Trauma
– Scorpion venom
– Penetrating peptic ulcer
– Hereditary
r Chronic:
– Chronic alcoholism
– Obstruction pancreatic duct
– Tropical
– Hereditary
– Shwachman disease
– Enzyme deficiency
– Idiopathic
– Hyperlipedemia
– Hypercalcemia
r Pancreatic pseudocyst:
– Complication in 5–16% of acute pancreatitis;
20–40% of chronic pancreatitis
Pediatric Considerations
Causes mainly viral, trauma, and medications
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Frequency:
– Abdominal pain: 95–100%
– Epigastric tenderness: 95–100%
– Nausea and vomiting: 70–90%
– Low-grade fever: 70–85%
– Hypotension: 20–40%
– Jaundice: 30%
– Grey Turner/Cullen sign: <5%
– Subcutaneous or SQ
r GI:
– Severe, persistent epigastric pain radiating to
back:
◦Colicky or rebound tenderness suggests
nonpancreatic source.
◦Worse when supine
– Nausea, vomiting, and anorexia
– Bowel sounds usually decreased or absent
– Significant GI bleed in patients with acute severe
pancreatitis is uncommon.
– Cullen sign:
◦Bluish discoloration at umbilicus secondary to
hemorrhagic pancreatitis
– Grey Turner sign:
◦Bluish discoloration at flank secondary to
hemorrhagic pancreatitis
r Respiratory:
– Pleuritic chest pain
– Dyspnea
– Lung exam:
◦Left pleural effusion (most common)
◦Atelectasis
◦Pulmonary edema
– Hypoxemia (30%)
r Cardiac:
– Tachycardia
– Hypotension
– Shock
r Neurologic:
– Irritability
– Confusion
– Coma
– Chvostek and Trousseau signs are rare despite lab
evidence of hypocalcemia.
Ranson Criteriar Indicators of morbidity and mortality:
– 0–2 criteria: 2% mortality
– 3 or 4 criteria: 15% mortality
– 5 or 6 criteria: 40% mortality
– 7 or 8 criteria: 100% mortality

– WBC count >16,000 mm3
– Blood glucose >200 mg/dL
– Serum lactate dehydrogenase >350 IU/L
– AST >250 IU/L

– BUN increase >5 mg/dL
– Serum calcium <8 mg/dL

– Estimated fluid sequestration >6L

– Levels >1,000 IU suggest biliary pancreatitis.

– Secreted from various sources

– Assess electrolyte imbalances, ischemia

P
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr If diagnosis is supported by previous events, history
and workup:
– Reassurance and diversion
– Does not require emergent care
r If 1st episode, treat and transport as appropriate to
presentation
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Be calm and reassuring.
r Most panic attacks resolve within 20–30 min
without any treatment.
r Fear may trigger another panic attack.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Patient education, new cognitions:
– Normal response to abnormal alarm
– Physiologic explanations for symptoms
r High-potency benzodiazepines (drugs of choice):
– Clonazepam:
◦Slow for emergency use
◦Long-acting without rapid onset/offset
phenomena
◦Best choice in this class for maintenance therapy
of recurrent panic attacks
– Alprazolam:
◦Rapid onset
◦Rebound anxiety occurs due to short duration
and rapid offset.
◦May lead to escalating doses with continued use
– Lorazepam:
◦Quick onset
◦Advantage of sublingual (SL) use
◦Longer effect and less abrupt offset than
alprazolam
r Avoid low-potency benzodiazepines:
– Diazepam
– Chlordiazepoxide
r Treat recurrent panic attacks and panic disorder with
selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) (or
TCAs), with or without clonazepam:
– Will not work immediately
– Do not need to be started emergently, especially if
there is no clear, established access to follow-up
management
r There are a few small studies on the efficacy of
atypical antipsychotics (e.g., olanzapine,
risperidone) for treatment-resistant panic disorder.
However, data to support this use is limited.
r Discharge therapy:
– Several clonazepam tablets in case of repeated
attacks
ALERT
Rapid offset (withdrawal) of alprazolam may trigger
further attacks.
MEDICATION
First Liner Clonazepam: 0.5 mg PO in the ED; 0.25–0.5 mg PO
BID for initial outpatient therapy
r SSRI:
– To be started as an outpatient
– May require higher doses and longer time to
therapeutic response for panic than for depression
Second Liner Lorazepam: 1 mg PO or SL
r TCA:
– To be started as an outpatient
Pregnancy Considerations
r Limit use of benzodiazepines.
r Risk/benefit discussion about the relative safety of
SSRIs and less anticholinergic TCAs (e.g.,
nortriptyline, desipramine)
r Physiologic and autonomic effects of pregnancy and
postpartum period may trigger attacks in
predisposed women.
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar As medically indicated to rule out organic cause
r Meets criteria for psychiatric admission (suicidal,
homicidal)
Discharge Criteria
Most panic attacks do not require inpatient level of
care.
Issues for Referralr Managed care mental health carve-outs
r Psychopharmacologic and cognitive behavioral
therapy evaluation for repeated attacks, or
interepisode fear or avoidance
r Stigma
r Primary care follow-up may be an acceptable
alternative to specialty, mental health/psychiatry
referral.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Appointment with primary care physician or referral
to mental health specialty treatment
r Avoid precipitants, e.g., caffeine, stimulants, alcohol.

r Panic is “contagious.” Try not to be infected by the
patient’s sense of urgency to stop the symptoms;
they will resolve spontaneously.
r Be calm so as not to add to the patient’s alarm, but
diligent, so patient feels attended to and reassured.
r Cognitive–behavioral therapy (CBT) can start in the
ED with brief explanation of the physiologic cause of
symptoms.
r Be cautious not to start adolescents and young
adults on a lifetime course of benzodiazepines; CBT
( ± SSRI therapy) is associated with good outcomes
and fewer deleterious side effects.
r Avoid the use of alprazolam, especially for ongoing
treatment.

Nicole M. Franks
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr The entrapment of the retracted foreskin proximal to
the glans of the penis
r Leads to lymphatic congestion and venous
obstruction, which may result in arterial compromise
to the glans
r Paraphimosis is a urologic emergency.
ETIOLOGYr A number of conditions of the foreskin may
predispose to paraphimosis, including:
– Phimosis
– Inflammation
– Trauma
– Sexually naive may be unaware of the need to
reduce foreskin after intercourse
r Commonly iatrogenic, from failure to replace the
foreskin after exam, catheterization, or cleaning
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Retracted prepuce (foreskin)
r Pain
r Swollen, edematous glans
r Local cellulitis
r Necrosis of glans in untreated cases
Physical Exam
Exam of the genitalia should include a search for
constricting foreign bodies or constricting bands.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Paraphimosis is a clinical diagnosis with the clinical
findings described earlier.
r Treatment must not be delayed pending diagnostic
lab or radiographic studies.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Imaging
If history suggests penile foreign body, radiographs
may be obtained once the vascular compromise has
been relieved.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Foreign bodies constricting the penile shaft may
mimic paraphimosis; these include:
– Hair tourniquets
– Wire, string, or other materials used for sexual
enhancement or punishment
r Balanoposthitis
r Trauma (zipper injuries)
r Acute idiopathic penile edema
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Patients should be transported promptly; do not
attempt reduction in the field.
r Pre-hospital personnel can be advised to apply an
ice pack to the glans with adequate protection of
the skin.
r Pain control
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Ice can be applied to the glans while preparing to
reduce the prepuce:
– Use the thumb of a glove as an ice-filled condom
to aid in direct application.
r The incarcerated foreskin must be released as soon
as possible to prevent ischemia and necrosis of the
glans.
r The pain associated with reduction techniques must
be managed with some combination of conscious
sedation, adequate analgesia, and local anesthesia.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Medical therapy for paraphimosis involves
reassuring the patient, reducing the preputial
edema, and restoring the prepuce to its original
position and condition.
r The following sequence of procedures should be
followed:
– Paraphimosis can most frequently be reduced
using a penile block and compressing the glans
manually while applying traction on the foreskin.
– Penile block is performed by infiltrating 5 mL of
1% lidocaine without epinephrine in the angle
between the inferior rami of the symphysis pubis:
◦Then use another 5 mL to infiltrate a wheel
along the sides of the penis.
◦This produces a block after 5 min.
– Successful reduction requires steady
circumferential pressure on the distal edema with
simultaneous manual reduction of the foreskin.
– In children, conscious sedation is usually required.
– If manual reduction is unsuccessful, then the
technique of multiple punctures may facilitate
reduction:
◦Make ∼20 holes in the swollen foreskin with a
small sterile needle (26G), allowing expression
of edema fluid, then resume manual reduction.
– If this fails to return the foreskin to its original
position, it will be necessary to incise the
constricting ring of tissue with a dorsal
longitudinal slit in the foreskin after sterile
preparation:
◦If the incision made is too long, after reduction
it may be necessary to suture the incision
transversely with 3.0 absorbable sutures.

PATENT DUCTUS ARTERIOSUS
Steven Lelyveld
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Patent vessel in the fetal heart connects the
pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta.
r Shortly after birth, changes normally provoke
contraction, closure, and fibrosis:
– Sudden increase in the partial pressure of oxygen
– Changes in the synthesis and metabolism of
vasoactive eicosanoids
r In the preterm infant, persistent patency of the
ductus may be a normal life-saving response.
r The patent ductus usually has a normal structural
anatomy.
r Patency results from hypoxia and immaturity.
r In the full-term newborn, patency of the ductus is a
congenital malformation.
r Deficiency of both the mucoid endothelial layer and
the muscular media of the ductus
r As pulmonary vascular resistance falls, aortic blood
is shunted into the pulmonary artery.
r Extent of the shunt reflects the size of the ductus
and the ratio of the pulmonary to systemic vascular
resistances.
r Up to 70% of the left ventricular output may be
shunted through the ductus to the pulmonary
circulation.
r Risk factors:
– Premature birth
– Coexisting cardiac anomalies
– Conditions resulting in hypoxia
– High altitude
– Maternal rubella infection
– Female-to-male ratio, 3:1
ETIOLOGYr Prematurity
r Congenital anomaly
r Hypoxia
r Prostaglandins
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Isolated patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), an
unanticipated event
r PDA, as part of a larger congenital cardiac anomaly,
may be diagnosed by US during pregnancy.
Physical Examr Asymptomatic when the PDA is small, but otherwise
may present with a range of findings.
r Congestive heart failure (CHF), often in 1st day of
life
r Wide pulse pressure
r Prominent apical impulse
r Thrill
r Systolic and continuous murmur.
r Sounds like a humming top or rolling thunder
r Begins soon after onset of the 1st sound, reaches
maximal intensity at the end of systole, and wanes
in late diastole
r Localized to the 2nd left intercostal space or
radiates down the left sternal border toward the
apex or to the left clavicle
r Recurrent pulmonary infections
r Retardation of physical growth
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Establish the diagnosis with imaging studies.
r Rule out complications such as heart failure and
endocarditis.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Unhelpful in making the diagnosis
Imagingr CXR:
– Usually normal in infants
– In children and adults:
◦Increased intrapulmonary markings
◦Calcifications
◦Left ventricle and left atrial enlargement
◦Dilated ascending aorta
◦Dilated pulmonary arteries
r EKG:
– Abnormal if the ductus is large:
◦Left ventricular hypertrophy
◦Right ventricular hypertrophy is a sign of greater
severity.
r Echocardiography:
– Normal if the ductus is small
– Left atrial enlargement
– Size of the ductus can be determined by scanning
from the suprasternal notch.
– Doppler studies will determine aortic to
pulmonary artery flow during diastole.
r Cardiac catheterization:
– Normal or increased right-sided pressure
– Oxygenated blood in the pulmonary artery
confirms left-to-right shunting.
– Injection of contrast into the ascending aorta
shows opacification of the pulmonary arteries.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Venous hum:
– Common insignificant bruit
– Heard in the neck or anterior portion of the chest
– Soft humming sound in systole and diastole
– Decreased by light compression of the jugular
venous system
r Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection to
the innominate vein:
– Continuous murmur like venous hum
r Aorticopulmonary septal defect:
– Murmur is often only systolic.
– Heard at the right sternal border
r Ruptured sinus of Valsalva
r Coronary arteriovenous fistulas
r Anomalous origin of left coronary artery from the
pulmonary artery
r Absence or atresia of pulmonary valve
r Aortic insufficiency with ventricular septal defect
r Peripheral pulmonary stenosis
r Truncus arteriosus

PEDIATRIC TRAUMA
Kevin M. Ban
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Pathophysiology and anatomy of adolescents and
young adults are similar.
r 80% of pediatric trauma is blunt; 80% of
multisystem trauma includes head injury.
r Trauma is the leading cause of death and disability
in children >1 yr in US and Europe.
r Most victims of child abuse are <3 yr. 1/3 of these
patients are <6m o .
ETIOLOGYr Most cases of pediatric trauma are single-system,
minor, blunt injuries.
r Common mechanisms of injury include motor
vehicle collisions and bicycle accidents, struck by a
vehicle as a pedestrian, and fall from height.
r Penetrating injuries are rare in younger children.
r Risk factors include inadequate supervision,
developmental inadequacy of child to perform task,
inadequate attention to task, risk taking, drugs, and
alcohol.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr History is often straightforward and provided by the
child, parents, witnesses, or paramedics. If
inconsistent with injury, consider child abuse.
r Mechanism(s) of injury relatively poor predictor of
injury severity, but may suggest type of injury.
r Variables that increase the likelihood of serious
injuries include handlebar injuries, significant
passenger space intrusion, and failure to use proper
restraint during a motor vehicle collision or helmet
when riding a bike or skateboard.
r AMPLE history includes allergies, medications, past
medical history, time of last meal, and events
leading up to injury.
Physical Examr Primary survey:
– For all children who have sustained a major
trauma, a traditional stepwise ABCDE evaluation
based on assessing the airway, breathing,
circulation, disability, and exposure is appropriate.
r Secondary survey:
– General:
◦Mass-to-surface ratio may impact insensible
water loss and increase the risk of hypothermia.
◦Compensatory mechanisms may delay signs of
hypovolemia. Few findings may be present until
loss of 25–30% of blood volume, at which time
decompensation abruptly occurs.
◦Smaller total blood volume (80 mL/kg)
– Head:
◦Note bulging fontanel, scalp hematomas,
midface instability, auricular and septal
hematomas, lacerations, functional or cosmetic
deformities to the face, and pupillary
abnormalities.
◦Open sutures/fontanelles or multiple skull
fractures may delay the onset of other signs and
symptoms of increased intracranial pressure.
◦Large head/occiput causes cervical spine flexion
when patient is supine on adult backboard.
– Eye/ears, nose, and throat exam:
◦Look for evidence of blood, trauma,
hemotympanum, hyphema, and CSF fluid.
◦Large tongue and tonsillar hypertrophy may
obstruct the airway.
– Neck:
◦Tracheal deviation and posterior neck step-offs
are exceedingly unusual in children.
◦Shorter trachea increases risk of right mainstem
intubation.
◦Cricoid cartilage is narrowest portion of airway
in children <8y r .
◦Children with altered mental status cannot have
their cervical spine precautions cleared in the
ED. These children should remain in a cervical
collar (and be taken off the spinal board) while
in the ED.
◦Pseudosubluxation (anterior displacement of
C-2 on C-3) occurs in 20% of patients.
◦The term spinal cord injury without radiologic
abnormality (SCIWORA) is controversial in the
MRI era.
– Chest:
◦Note the overall work of breathing, grunting,
asymmetric breath sounds, posterior abrasions,
chest wall deformities, and crepitus.
◦Flexible and compliant chest walls make
pulmonary contusions more likely than rib
fractures in young children. Rib fractures may be
a sign of abuse.
◦Diaphragmatic breathing
– Abdomen:
◦Bruising, abrasions, and tenderness
◦Distention is usually caused by gastric air.
◦Liver and spleen relatively large
◦Rib cage covers less of abdomen.
◦Bladder is intra-abdominal in children <2y r .
– Extremities:
◦Palpation and evaluation of joint stability and
tenderness
◦Assess pulses and compartments.
◦Salter–Harris classification of fractures
◦Unique injuries: Greenstick and buckle fractures
– Neurologic exam:
◦Age-appropriate mental status assessment
◦Assess movement of the extremities.
– Skin:
◦Assess for prolonged capillary refill and pallor.
◦Bruising of the ears, dorsa of the feet, or
genitalia may suggest nonaccidental trauma.
– Patterns of injury:
◦Car vs. pedestrian: Waddell triad (femur, torso,
and head injuries)—uncommon
◦Bicycle handlebar injuries may impale child:
Pancreatic or small bowel injury.
◦Lap belt syndrome: Abdominal ecchymoses and
intestinal injury with or without lumbar spine
fracture (chance fracture)
◦Minor trauma history with major injury:
Consider child abuse
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr History and age-appropriate physical exam are the
only essential components to a workup for all
children who present for an evaluation following
trauma.
r Obtaining standard radiographic and lab “trauma
panels” is not evidence based in children.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Lab tests should generally be individualized,
reflecting the patient’s clinical presentation.
r A normal initial hemoglobin and hematocrit do not
rule out a significant hemorrhage but will provide a
baseline value for later comparison; tachycardia may
be only sign of fluid/blood loss early in presentation,
although it is nonspecific for blood loss.
r Initial electrolyte measurement is unnecessary.
r Routine amylase and lipase are not recommended
because of the low incidence of pancreatic injuries;
false-positive tests are common.
r Elevated LFTs should not be used as the sole
determinant in deciding which children should
undergo CT of the abdomen. Patients with AST
>200 IU/L or ALT>125 IU/L who have sustained
abdominal trauma should be considered for CT if
hemodynamically stable. Physical exam should guide
imaging decision.
r Gross hematuria (>50 RBC/HPF) is concerning for
urinary tract injuries, but microscopic hematuria is
not.
r Blood bank specimen for typing in appropriate
patients
r A pregnancy test is indicated for teenage girls.
r Diagnostic peritoneal lavage is rarely indicated with
availability of imaging modalities.

P
Imagingr The traditional “c-spine, chest, pelvis” set of
radiographs is no longer universally obtained;
selective approach is more appropriate.
r Forgo cervical spine radiographs in children who are
awake, alert, cooperative, neurologically intact
without neck pain or midline tenderness on
palpation of the neck, are without pain on range of
motion testing, and are without distracting injury:
– An unconscious child will not be able to have the
cervical spine cleared in the ED and may later
need MRI (less often CT) as an inpatient.
r Chest radiographs indicated for grunting
respirations, hypoxia, asymmetric breath sounds,
dyspnea, crepitus, endotracheal intubation, and
thoracostomy tube or central venous catheter
placement in the internal jugular or subclavian veins
r Pelvic radiographs are seldom indicated. Children
with clinically significant pelvic pain or instability
typically undergo CT of the abdomen and pelvis.
r CT of the head is indicated for abnormal mental
status, focal neurologic deficit, prolonged loss of
consciousness, bulging fontanel, temporal or
parietal scalp hematoma, depressed skull fracture,
and uncontrollable persistent vomiting.
r CT of the abdomen and pelvis is typically indicated
for children with altered mental status, gross
hematuria, abdominal bruising above the ileac
crests, handlebar injuries, and abdominal tenderness
with hemodynamic effect.
r US has limited utility since the presence of free fluid
(i.e., blood) does not always indicate the need for
laparotomy. The usefulness of focused abdominal
sonography for trauma exam in young children
needs further study.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
Nonaccidental trauma should be considered when the
history is inconsistent with the injury.
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Rapid transport to a facility capable of managing the
child’s suspected injuries
r Priorities include stabilization of airway (intubation
by paramedics in the pre-hospital setting is
controversial), breathing, circulation.
r Immobilization of cervical spine and extremity
fractures
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Most traumatized children are stable throughout
their ED course.
r Stabilization may require:
– Cardiorespiratory and pulse oximetry monitoring
– Early oxygen administration
– Placement of 2 large-bore IVs and aggressive fluid
resuscitation with normal saline
– Pain control with morphine
– Labs and radiographs as indicated

Andrew B. Ziller
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Infestation by organisms that live in close
association with host
r Bites are painless
r Signs and symptoms result from host response to
saliva and anticoagulant injected during feeding
r Transmitted by direct contact and fomites (inanimate
objects)
r Head lice are transmitted by head-to-head contact:
– Combs
– Pillows
– Hats
r Head lice are more common in children and females
r Pubic lice are transmitted by sexual contact
r Obligate human parasites cannot survive away from
hosts >7–10 days
ETIOLOGY
Infestation by:
r Pediculus capitis (head louse):
– Most common
– All socioeconomic groups
r Pediculus corporis (body louse):
– Associated with poverty, poor hygiene, and
overcrowding
– Live in clothing and transfer to human host for
feeding
– Can live up to 30 days off of human
– Related to bed bugs
r Phthirus pubis (pubic or crab louse)
Pediatric Considerations
Pubic lice may also indicate sexual abuse in children
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Head lice:
– Dandruff
– Pruritus
– Often asymptomatic
r Body lice:
– Pruritus
– Excoriation particularly at belt lines or seams of
clothing
r Pubic lice:
– Intense pruritus, worse at night
Physical Examr Examine hair for adult lice and nits:
– Nits are cemented on hair shafts and are not
easily removed
– Head lice and pubic lice infestation is confirmed by
differentiating nits from scales, hair casts, and
other easily brushed-off artifacts
– Empty nits are not diagnostic of active infection
r Scalp and posterior neck erythema, scaling, and
excoriated papules:
– May lead to pyoderma, posterior cervical
lymphadenopathy, and bacterial superinfection
r Body lice are observed only in very heavy infestation;
infestation is confirmed by finding nits in clothing
seams:
– Linear excoriations of neck and trunk
– Pus or serum stains on clothing
r Pubic lice:
– Occasional urticaria with typical flare/wheal
formation
– May infest eyelashes and scalp in children
– Characteristic bluish macules (maculae ceruleae)
appear infrequently on trunk and thighs
– Prefer the perineum and pubic areas
– Inguinal adenopathy
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Careful history and physical exam
r Universal precautions
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Nits may be visualized under low-power microscopy
along hair shafts. They are<1 mm long:
– Fluorescent under Wood lamp
r Mature lice are 3–4 mm long
r Pubic louse ∼1 mm long but wider body than head
or body louse
Imaging
No imaging indicated
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Scabies
r Contact or allergic dermatitis
r Seborrheic dermatitis
r Bed bugs (Cimicidae)
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
ALERT
Maintain universal precautions
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Not applicable for routine cases
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Oral antihistamines and topical steroids may help
pruritic symptoms of all lice infestations
r Head lice:
– Topical pediculicidal agents:
◦Permethrin 1% cream rinse (Nix) is a reasonable
agent; it has low toxicity and cost and is ovicidal;
however, resistance is becoming more common
◦Pyrethrin (Rid) also has low toxicity but is less
effective
– All agents require reapplication in 7–10 days if
further adult lice or nits noted
– Remove nits with fine-toothed comb
– Examine all members of household; treat infested
individuals
– Change clothing and machine wash and dry
(using hot cycles) all clothing, towels, linens, and
headgear:
◦Vacuum floors and furniture
◦Wash combs and brushes in hot water for
10–20 min or coat with pediculicide for 15 min
and wash
– Temperature >131◦F (55◦C) for >5 min kills
eggs, nymphs, and mature lice
r Body lice:
– Wash and dry bedding and clothing using hot
cycles
– Apply topical pediculicide cream or lotions from
chin to toes
r Pubic lice:
– Topical pediculicide applied to hairy areas of
chest, axilla, and groin
– Remove nits with fine-toothed comb
– Treat sexual contacts simultaneously
– Wash and dry bedding and clothing using hot
cycles
– Treat eyelash involvement with topical petrolatum
twice daily for 9 days
