PELVIC FRACTURE
Andrew T. LaFree rTheodore C. Chan
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr 3% of all bony fractures
r Pelvis is made up of sacrum and 2 innominate
bones:
– The innominate bones consist of the ilium,
ischium, and pubis
r Boney structures are stabilized by a network of
ligaments, musculature, and other soft tissues in the
pelvic area
r Anterior stability and support are provided by the
symphysis pubis and pubic rami
r Posterior stability and support are provided by the
sacroiliac (SI) complex and pelvic floor
r Pelvis provides protection for lower urinary tract; GI
tract; gynecologic, and vascular, and nervous
structures contained in the region:
– Pelvic fractures have a high associated morbidity
and mortality rate and require urgent diagnosis
and therapy.
r Unstable pelvic fractures are high risk for associated
injuries including:
– Pelvic hemorrhage and hemorrhagic shock
– Intra-abdominal and GI tract injuries
– Genitourinary and urinary tract injuries
– Uterine and vaginal injuries
– Neurologic injuries
– Arterial and venous plexus injuries
ETIOLOGYr 65% of pelvic fractures are caused by vehicular
trauma, including pedestrians struck by automobiles
r 10% caused by falls
r 10% caused by crush injuries
r The remainder caused by athletic, penetrating, or
nontraumatic injuries
r Mortality rate from pelvic fractures is 6–19%:
– Increases with open fractures or evidence of
hemorrhagic shock
r Significant hemorrhage can occur in unstable,
high-energy pelvic fractures (Tile type B and C
fractures):
– Bleeding most common with posterior injuries
involving the vascular plexuses
– Retroperitoneal hematoma may tamponade in the
enclosed pelvic space
Tile Classiﬁcation Systemr Includes stable single bone and avulsion fractures as
well as pelvic ring fractures
r Predicts need for operative repair
r Type A: Stable pelvic ring injuries:
– A1: Avulsion fractures of the innominate bone
(ischial tuberosity, iliac crest)
– A2-1: Iliac wing fractures
– A2-2: Isolated rami fractures; most common pelvic
fracture
– A2-3: 4-pillar anterior ring injuries
– A3: Transverse fractures of sacrum or coccyx
r Type B: Partially stable pelvic ring injury (rotationally
unstable, but vertically stable):
– B1: Unilateral open-book fracture
– B2: Lateral compression injury:
◦B2-1: Ipsilateral double rami fractures and
posterior injury
◦B2-2: Contralateral double rami fractures and
posterior injury (bucket-handle fracture)
◦B2-3: Bilateral type B injuries
r Type C: Unstable pelvic ring injury—rotationally and
vertically unstable, Malgaigne fracture:
– Anterior disruption of symphysis pubis or
2–4 pubic rami with posterior displacement and
instability through sacrum, SI joint, or ileum:
◦C1: Unilateral vertical shear fracture
◦C2: Unilateral vertical shear combined with
contralateral type B injury
◦C3: Bilateral vertical shear fracture
r Acetabular fractures (posterior lip, central/transverse,
anterior column, or posterior column fractures)
Young Classiﬁcation Systemr Based on mechanism of injury
r Only fractures that result in disruption of pelvic ring
included; no single bone, avulsion, or acetabular
fractures
r Predicts chance of associated injuries and mortality
risk:
– LC: Lateral compression
– APC: Anteroposterior compression
– VS: Vertical shear
– CM: Combination of injury patterns
Pediatric Considerations
r Children can have greater hemorrhage
r Nonaccidental trauma is a concern
Pregnancy Considerations
Gravid uterus may be at risk for injury, including
uterine rupture.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Pain, swelling, ecchymosis, tenderness over hips,
groin, perineum, and lower back
r Often presents with other traumatic injuries
including neurologic, intra-abdominal, genitourinary,
perineal, rectal, vaginal, and vascular injury
r Evidence of hemorrhagic shock
r Gross pelvic instability
Historyr History of trauma (fall, vehicular trauma, crush
injuries, athletic injuries)
r Pain on hip movement, ambulation, sitting,
standing, defecation
Physical Examr Ecchymosis, swelling, tenderness over bony
prominences, pubis, perineum, pelvic region, lower
back
r Lower extremities may be shortened or rotated
r Inability to actively or passively perform range of
motion of involved hip
r Tenderness on LC of pelvis, palpation of symphysis
pubis or SI joints
r Gross pelvic instability, deformity, asymmetry in
lower extremity
r Wounds over pelvis or bleeding from rectum,
vagina, or urethra may indicate open fracture
r In hemorrhagic shock:
– Tachycardia, hypotension, narrowed pulse
pressure
– Altered mental status
– Cool and pale extremities
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Pelvic radiograph is the most common initial test
r A single AP view of the pelvis can confirm diagnosis
and should be obtained as early as possible when
fracture suspected:
– Most significant unstable pelvic fractures will be
seen on the single AP view
r Other views include:
– Inlet projection: 30◦ caudal view; allows
visualization of posterior arch
– Outlet projection: 30◦ cephalic angulation; allows
visualization of sacrum
– Judet oblique views: Allow evaluation of
acetabulum
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Type and cross-match
r Hemoglobin/hematocrit, platelet count, and
coagulation studies (prothrombin time, partial
thromboplastin time)
Imagingr CT may further delineate pelvic fracture(s),
retroperitoneal hematoma, visceral injuries:
– CT contrast angiography may delineate source of
bleeding (particularly arterial), but should be
considered only in hemodynamically stable
patients
r Abdominal US focused abdominal sonography for
trauma in patients with significant traumatic injury,
but differentiation of intraperitoneal from
extraperitoneal hemorrhage from pelvic fracture can
be difficult
r MRI indicated for neurologic injury
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Although largely supplanted by US and CT,
diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) remains a rapid
bedside evaluation for intraperitoneal hemorrhage
r Angiography and selective vessel embolization in
the setting of pelvic hemorrhage:
– Particularly for small-vessel arterial bleeding
r Surgery:
– As indicated on the basis of clinical findings and
orthopedic/surgical consult
– Surgical stabilization with pelvic packing
– Direct operative control of pelvic bleeding

can mimic type I fracture on radiograph)

PRE-HOSPITALr IV fluid resuscitation as indicated
r Consider stabilization or immobilization measures
for pelvis
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs of trauma care
r IV fluid resuscitation with blood or crystalloid,
O-negative or type-specific blood if
hemodynamically unstable:
– Avoid using lower extremity IV sites
r Stabilize and immobilize the pelvis to prevent further
injury and decrease bleeding:
– Compression device: Folded sheet with clamp or
commercial compression device wrapped
circumferentially around greater trochanters to
stabilize and compress pelvis
– Pneumatic anti-shock garment (PASG): Use in ED
is controversial, but allows rapid pelvic
immobilization and pelvic compression to slow
bleeding
– External fixator: Requires more time to place than
PASG but “splints” pelvis in a similar manner;
contraindicated in severely comminuted pelvic
fracture
– Placement of a stabilization device should not
interfere with further workup and care (e.g., US,
DPL)
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Determine which pelvic fractures are stable and
which are unstable
r Type A fractures are generally stable
r Type B and C fractures are unstable
r Type A fractures:
– Treated conservatively with bed rest, analgesics,
and comfort measures; management decisions
may be made in conjunction with orthopedics
– For 4-pillar anterior ring injuries, CT should be
obtained to evaluate the posterior pelvis
– Ensure that there are no other breaks in the pelvic
ring
r Type B and C fractures:
– Immediate orthopedics consultation; patient
should remain NPO
– May require ED pelvic stabilization measures
– Assess for pelvic hemorrhage
r Malgaigne fractures:
– Anticipate significant hemorrhage and associated
injuries
r Acetabular fractures:
– Immediate orthopedics consultation; patient
should remain NPO
r Pelvic hemorrhage:
– Mechanical stabilization of unstable pelvic
fractures (usually by application of external pelvic
fixation)
– Angiography and selective vessel embolization
– Direct operative control of pelvic bleeding
r Prioritization of studies: CT, angiography, or surgery:
– In the hemodynamically unstable patient:
◦Open B and C fractures: Surgical exploration
◦Closed fractures: DPL or US can help determine
management in terms of need for immediate
surgical exploration or selective
angiography/embolization
r In the hemodynamically stable patient, the patient
can go to CT for evaluation of the abdomen, pelvis,
and retroperitoneum with external fixation as
appropriate
MEDICATIONr Crystalloid fluids: 2 L IV bolus of normal saline or
lactated Ringer (peds: 20 mL/kg)
r Blood products: 4–6 U cross-matched, type specific,
or O-negative (peds: 10 mL/kg)
FOLLOW-UP

Admission Criteriar Hemodynamic instability, and pelvic hemorrhage to
the ICU
r Type B or C pelvic fracture
r Acetabular fracture
r Other related injuries (e.g., genitourinary,
intra-abdominal, neurologic)
r Intractable pain
Discharge Criteria
Type A pelvic fracture; hemodynamically stable with
no evidence of other injuries
Issues for Referral
Close follow-up should be ensured for discharged
patients.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Discharged patients should be referred to an
orthopedist for follow-up.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Pelvic fractures can be a marker for high-energy
traumatic mechanism and injury:
– Assess for underlying abdominal/pelvic injuries
including GI, genitourinary, vascular, and
neurologic injuries
r In addition to initial resuscitation, immobilization
and stabilization of the pelvis should be considered
for unstable or open fractures or where hemorrhage
is suspected
r Determination of diagnostic/therapeutic pathways

PELVIC INFLAMMATORY DISEASE
Erich Salvacion
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an acute,
community-acquired, sexually transmitted infection
of the upper genital tract, including the uterus,
fallopian tubes, ovaries, or adjacent structures
r Most frequent gynecologic cause for ED visits
(350,000 per year)
r Represents a spectrum of infection:
– No single diagnostic gold standard
– Requires low clinical threshold for considering the
diagnosis and starting empiric antibiotic therapy
r Progressive disease can lead to tubo-ovarian
abscess (TOA)
r Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome is a capsular
inflammation of the liver associated with PID:
– Sharp right upper quadrant abdominal pain
– Worse with inspiration, movement, or coughing
ETIOLOGYr Risk factors:
– Age <25 yr
– Multiple or symptomatic sexual partners
– Previous episode of PID
– Nonbarrier contraception
– Oral contraception
– African American ethnicity
r Most common causes of PID are Chlamydia
trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhea
r Other organisms include groups A and B
streptococci, staphylococci, gram-negative rods
(commonly Klebsiella spp., Escherichia coli, and
Proteus spp.), and anaerobes
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Lower abdominal pain, usually bilateral
r Vaginal discharge
r Abnormal uterine bleeding
r Dysmenorrhea
r Dysuria
r Dyspareunia
r Nausea and vomiting
r Fever and chills
r Proctitis
r Lower abdominal tenderness
r Decreased bowel sounds
r Bilateral adnexal tenderness
r Cervical motion tenderness
r Purulent endocervical discharge
r Adnexal mass or fullness
r Right upper quadrant tenderness
Historyr Lower abdominal pain is the most common
symptom in PID, ranging from subtle to severe pain
r Abdominal pain that worsens during intercourse or
onset of pain shortly after or during menses is
suggestive of PID
r Abdominal pain is usually bilateral and usually
present for ≤2w k
r New vaginal discharge, urethritis, fever, and chills
are common symptoms but are neither sensitive nor
specific for the diagnosis
Pregnancy Considerations
PID is rare during pregnancy, but if present usually
occurs during the 1st trimester before hormonal
changes such as mucus plug formation can protect the
uterus from ascending bacteria.
Physical Examr Only 50% of patients with PID have fever
r Abdominal exam reveals diffuse tenderness worse in
the lower quadrants, usually but not always
symmetric
r Rebound tenderness and decreased bowel sounds
are commonly found
r Right upper quadrant tenderness is suggestive of
perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome) in the
setting of PID
r Pelvic exam can reveal a purulent endocervical
discharge, cervical motion tenderness, or adnexal
tenderness
r If uterine or adnexal tenderness is not prominent,
one must consider other diagnoses
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr History and physical exam including pelvic exam
r Pregnancy test to rule out ectopic pregnancy or
complications of an intrauterine pregnancy
r Cervical culture for N. gonorrhea and C. trachomatis
r Minimum criteria for clinical diagnosis:
– Lower abdominal tenderness or
– Uterine/adnexal tenderness or
– Cervical motion tenderness
r Supportive criteria for diagnosis:
– Fever >38.3◦C (101◦F)
– Abnormal cervical/vaginal discharge
– Intracellular gram-negative diplococci on
endocervical Gram stain
– Leukocytosis >10,000/mm3

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Autoantibody (IgG)-mediated blistering disease of
the skin and mucous membrane:
– Characterized by loss of cell-to-cell adhesion
called acantholysis
r Median age 71 yr
– Reports of disease occurring in neonates through
elderly
r Rare; worldwide incidence 0.7/100,000
r Females > males, 66 vs. 34%
r Pemphix is Greek for bubble or blister
r Pemphigus, specific term for autoantibody disease
against some portion of epidermis
r Pemphigoid: A term describing the group of
syndromes that cause a separation of the epidermis
from the dermis, typically more benign course
r Mortality is highest in those with mucocutaneous
involvement
– If untreated, mortality rates average 60–90%,
with treatment this nears 5%
r 3 major subtypes exist:
– Vulgaris; typically more serious with deeper
mucocutaneous involvement:
◦Accounts for 70–80% of all pemphigus
◦Up to 70% with vulgaris present with oral
lesions, which is often the presenting complaint
◦Autoantibodies to Dsg 1 and 3
◦Affects most races in middle age and elderly
Ashkenazi Jews
– Foliaceus; milder and more superficial cutaneous
lesions:
◦Oral lesions and better prognosis
◦Autoantibodies to Dsg 1 only
– Paraneoplastic pemphigus; often with severe
mucocutaneous involvement
◦Most commonly seen in lymphoreticular
malignancies
Pediatric Considerations
r Pemphigus is rare in neonates and children but may
occur in adolescents
r Early diagnosis and treatment significantly impact
growth, psychological, social, and cultural
development
r Histopathology is identical to adult disease
r Neonates may develop the disease secondary to
transplacental transfer of IgG
r Neonatal pemphigus spontaneously resolves in
several weeks as the maternal antibodies are
catabolized
Pregnancy Considerations
Effective treatment of maternal disease prior to
conception lowers the risk of neonatal transmission
and gestational complications
ETIOLOGYr IgG autoantibodies are directed against
desmosomal cadherins desmoglein 1 and
desmoglein 3 found in all keratinocytes
r Autoantibodies cause histopathologic acantholysis,
cytoskeletal derangements, and apoptosis
r Bullae formation is caused by the loss of cell–cell
adhesion and separation of the keratinocytes
r Immunogenetic predisposition secondary to higher
frequencies of specific human leukocyte antigen
HLA haplotypes including DR4 and DRw6
r Drugs such as penicillamine, captopril, rifampin,
piroxicam, and phenobarbital can trigger
pemphigoid reactions
r Endemic pemphigus foliaceus (fogo selvagem), most
common in South America, may be triggered or
transmitted by bites from flying insects
r Pemphigoid reactions may occur in association with
a neoplasm, usually lymphoma (paraneoplastic
pemphigus)
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Generalized or focal flaccid bullae (blisters) of the
skin and mucosa
r Painful skin erosions with shreds of detached
epithelium
r Painful nonhealing oral, vaginal, or mucosal erosions
r Crusting, partially healing skin erosions from
ruptured bullae
r Hypertrophic, hyperplastic erosive plaques with
pustules in intertriginous areas (pemphigus
vegetans)
r Moist, edematous, exfoliative erosions in seborrheic
areas (pemphigus foliaceus)
r Erythematous, scaly, crusting skin lesions in a malar
distribution (pemphigus erythematosus)
r Lesions usually persist without treatment:
– May heal with post inflammatory
hyperpigmentation
Historyr Typically features mucocutaneous blisters followed
by erosions
r Often appear 1st in mucous membranes with spread
to cutaneous involvement; most commonly to scalp,
chest, axillae, and groin
r Skin lesions are painful flaccid blisters that may
appear anywhere
Physical Exam
Nikolsky sign (separation of the epidermis with lateral
pressure) is characteristic but not diagnostic:
r Poor sensitivity
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Suspected based on clinical presentation
r Biopsy with histologic and immunofluorescence
testing is essential for definitive diagnosis (arrange
with a dermatologist)
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Serum antibody titers, detected by indirect
immunofluorescence, are often used as a marker of
disease activity; however, the ED physician usually
does not order these titers
r ELISA may be used to identify subtypes
Imaging
No diagnostic imaging test exists
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Deep shave or punch biopsy
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Bullous pemphigoid
r Contact dermatitis
r Dermatitis herpetiformis
r Erythema multiforme
r Erysipelas
r Erythroderma
r Toxic epidermal necrolysis
r Epidermolysis bullosa
r Hand, foot, and mouth disease
r Systemic lupus erythematosus
r Systemic vasculitis
r Oral candidiasis
r Herpes simplex gingivostomatitis
r Erosive lichen planus
r Seborrheic dermatitis
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr If severe disease:
– IV access, pulse oximetry monitor, and cardiac
monitor
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr If symptoms of hypotension or sepsis are present, IV
fluid resuscitation should be guided by the Parkland
burn formula
r If signs or symptoms of sepsis are present, initiate
broad-spectrum antibiotic coverage
r In steroid-dependent patients, administer
stress-dose steroids
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Systemic corticosteroids are the mainstay of therapy
r Mild-to-moderate disease should receive PO
prednisone, and intralesional triamcinolone
acetonide may be used
r Severe disease: Conventional high-dose
corticosteroids:
– If severe symptoms are unresponsive to high-dose
PO corticosteroids, consider pulse IV
corticosteroids and admission for plasmapheresis
r Adjuvant immunosuppressive therapy may also be
added to decrease the symptoms associated with
high-dose systemic corticosteroids or in patients
with contraindications to steroid therapy:
– Dapsone, gold, azathioprine, cyclophosphamide,
cyclosporine, methotrexate, mycophenolate, and
IV immunoglobulins

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Traumatic rupture of the corpus cavernosum and the
encompassing tunica albuginea
r May involve the corpus spongiosum and urethra
r Hematoma formation occurs at rupture site.
r Injury is usually unilateral and transverse.
r Most common fracture site is the proximal shaft of

r During erection, pressure within the corpus
cavernosum is maximal, close to arterial pressure,
increasing the volume in each corpus to maximum,
which thins the tunica albuginea, making it
susceptible to rupture.
r Penile erection stretches the spongiosum to the
limit, which limits movement vertically while
allowing lateral movements; this forms a bend at
the base of the penis, making it vulnerable to lateral
swing and rupture of corpus cavernosum.
r 25–30% have associated urethral injury, which may
be partial or complete.
r Caused by blunt trauma to erect penis during:
– Sexual intercourse
– Manipulation
– Fall on erect penis
– Entanglement in clothing
–“ Taghaandan”—Middle Eastern practice of
forcefully bending the erect penis to cause
detumescence
ETIOLOGYr Peyronie disease
r Urethritis in past
r Surgical procedure on corpus cavernosum or trauma
to corpus cavernosum resulting in weak scar tissue

SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Loud popping or crunching sound heard at the time
of injury
r Immediate detumescence
r Severe penile pain
r Deviation of the penis away from the side of injury
r Penile swelling and ecchymosis
r There may be blood at the urethral meatus if there is
a urethral injury.
r May have dysuria, inability to void, or an increase in
the size of the swelling with voiding due to
extravasation of urine

r Sudden painful sensation in erect penis during
sexual intercourse or soon after with loss of erection
r Blood at the urethral meatus after intercourse
r Problems with poor erections after the injury if
presentation is delayed
r Penile deviation with erection
r Urinary retention or weak urinary stream

penis, usually on one side
r Ecchymosis may also involve scrotum.
r Penis flaccid and edematous with angulation away
from the side of tear
r Defect in the penile shaft may be palpable at the
site of the tear.

r Urethrocavernous or urethrocutaneous fistulas may
be present as late complications of a penile fracture.

mucosal defenses

◦Pain radiation to back or shoulder
– Obstruction:

Louisa S. Canham rCarlo L. Rosen
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Pericardial effusion:
– Pericardial sac usually contains 15–40 cc of fluid
– Collection of additional fluid = effusion
r Pericardial tamponade:
– Accumulation of pericardial fluid causes an
elevation of pressure in the pericardial space,
resulting in impairment of ventricular filling and
decreased cardiac output.
– Depends on size and speed of fluid accumulation
– Increase of as little as 80–120 cc of fluid may lead
to a rise in pericardial pressure.
– Up to 70% present in “early tamponade” and
appear clinically stable
– Occurs in 2% of patients with penetrating chest
trauma
ETIOLOGYr Medical causes:
– Pericarditis (20%):
◦90% idiopathic or viral
◦Bacterial, fungal, parasitic, tuberculosis, HIV
– Malignancy (13%):
◦Lymphoma, leukemia, melanoma, breast, lung
◦Metastatic disease, primary malignancy,
postradiation
– Postmyocardial infarction (8%):
◦Acute: 1–3 days after acute myocardial
infarction (AMI)
◦Subacute (Dressler syndrome): Weeks to months
after AMI
◦Incidence reduced with reperfusion therapy
– End-stage renal disease, uremia (6%)
– Autoimmune/collagen vascular disease (5%):
Rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus
erythematosus, scleroderma
– Rheumatic fever
– Radiation therapy
– Myxedema
– Congestive heart failure (CHF), valvular heart
disease
– Drug toxicity (isoniazid, doxorubicin,
procainamide, hydralazine, phenytoin)
– Idiopathic
r Surgical causes:
– Penetrating chest trauma
– Thoracic aortic dissection
– Iatrogenic (cardiac catheterization, postcardiac
surgery, central line placement)
– Blunt trauma rarely causes pericardial effusion.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Beck’s triad = classic presentation of cardiac
tamponade:
– Hypotension
– Muffled heart sounds
– Jugular venous distention
r Dressler syndrome: Pericarditis seen several weeks
after a myocardial infarction:
– Fever
– Chest pain
– Pericardial friction rub
Historyr Past medial history is key:
– History of malignancy?
– Recent viral illness?
– Connective tissue disorder?
– Recent MI?
r History of the present illness:
– Most are asymptomatic.
– Pulmonary symptoms: Dyspnea, cough:
◦Dyspnea is the most common symptom seen in
tamponade (87–88% sensitivity).
– Chest pain is the most common symptom:
◦Usually sharp, pleuritic, relieved by sitting
forward
◦Can be referred to scapula
◦Can also be dull, aching, constrictive
– GI symptoms: Nausea or abdominal pain from
hepatic and visceral congestion or dysphagia from
esophageal compression
– Generalized symptoms: Fatigue, malaise
Physical Examr Signs of shock or right heart failure:
– Tachycardia, hypotension
– Jugular venous distention (may be absent if the
patient is also hypovolemic)
r Pericardial friction rub (100% specific):
– High-pitched “scratchy” sound
– Best heard at left sternal border
– Increased by leaning forward
– Can be transient/intermittent
r Pulsus paradoxus:
– Fall in systolic BP >10 mm Hg with inspiration
– When severe, this can manifest as lack of brachial
or radial pulse during inspiration.
– Sensitive but not specific
r Low-grade fever common; >38◦C is uncommon; if
present, consider purulent pericarditis (can also
result from autoimmune/connective tissue disease).
r Lungs should be clear; if not, consider CHF or
pneumonia.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr ECG
r CXR
r US:
– Echocardiography, including evaluation of aortic
root
– Shock US: Include focused assessment with
sonography in trauma, aorta, pleural effusion, and
pneumothorax views to rule out other causes of
hypotension
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC
r ESR, C-reactive protein:
– Usually elevated in pericarditis
r Cardiac enzymes:
– Consider myocarditis if elevated
r Electrolytes:
– BUN/creatinine in suspected uremic pericarditis
r Coagulation profile:
– Especially in liver failure, anticoagulation, trauma
r Blood cultures if an infectious source is suspected
Imagingr Chest radiograph:
– Cardiomegaly is 89% sensitive for tamponade.
– Can be normal even with effusion if developed
quickly
r Echocardiography:
– 97–100% sensitive, 90–97% specific
– Effusion: Can detect as little as 20–50 cc of
pericardial blood/fluid:
◦Small effusions will only be seen posteriorly.
◦Anterior fat pad may mimic effusion; must also
visualize posterior pericardial space for
diagnosis of effusion.
– Tamponade:
◦Effusions large enough to cause tamponade
should be circumferential.
◦Right atrial or ventricular bowing and eventual
collapse
◦“Sniff” test: During inspiration, the inferior vena
cava will not collapse in patients with
tamponade.
r Chest CT for detecting hemopericardium
r Transesophageal echocardiography
r MRI with gadolinium (for stable patients only)

variation of QRS amplitude (usually only seen with

– Therapeutic for tamponade or large symptomatic
effusion
– Diagnostic for bacterial effusion (to guide
antibiotics) or malignant effusion (for cytology)

– CVP >15 cm H2O suggests tamponade, but may
be normal in the hypovolemic patient.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Noncardiogenic shock:
– Hypovolemic, septic, anaphylactic, spinal
r Other cardiac conditions:
– Myocardial infarction—common misdiagnosis!
– Pericardial constriction (due to pericardial fibrosis)
– CHF
r Pulmonary conditions:
– Pulmonary embolus
– Tension pneumothorax
– Hemothorax
r Other causes:
– Air embolism
– Aortic dissection
– Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm

PRE-HOSPITALr 2 large-bore IV lines
r Start IV fluids.
r Supplemental O2
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Continue pre-hospital measures
r Continuous cardiac monitoring
r In tamponade:
– IV fluid resuscitation with normal saline or blood
– Pericardiocentesis for unstable patients to
decompress the tamponade

unstable:
– Perform pericardiocentesis with placement of an
indwelling catheter for continued drainage:
◦Site of drainage guided by maximum fluid
collection
◦Subxiphoid: 2 cm below and 1 cm to the left of
the xiphoid process, needle aimed at 30–45◦
angle toward the patient’s left shoulder
◦Left parasternal approach: 5th intercostal space
just lateral to sternum, needle inserted
perpendicular to the skin
◦Remove fluid as needed to improve clinical
condition.
r Traumatic pericardial tamponade:
– Consult trauma surgeon immediately.
– Definitive therapy is thoracotomy in the OR.
– If patient is deteriorating despite resuscitation, ED
thoracotomy with pericardotomy is an option.
r Bacterial pericardial effusion:
– Initiate antibiotic therapy to cover gram-negative
and anaerobic organisms and Staphylococcus
aureus.
– May ultimately require partial surgical resection of
the pericardium
r Uremic pericardial effusion:
– Arrange urgent dialysis.
r Dressler syndrome and postirradiation pericardial
effusion:
– Initiate aspirin
r Aortic dissection:
– Immediate cardiothoracic surgical consultation for
operative repair

– Dressler syndrome
– Recent percutaneous intervention

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Inflammation, infection, or infiltration of the
pericardial sac surrounding the heart:
– Pericardial effusion may or may not be present.
r Acute pericarditis:
– Rapid in onset
– Potentially complicated by cardiac tamponade
from effusion
r Constrictive pericarditis:
– Results from chronic inflammation causing
thickening and adherence of the pericardium to
the heart
ETIOLOGYr Idiopathic (most common)
r Viral:
– Echovirus
– Coxsackie
– Adenovirus
– Varicella
– Epstein–Barr virus
– Cytomegalovirus
– Hepatitis B
– Mumps
– HIV
r Bacterial:
– Tuberculosis
– Staphylococcus
– Streptococcus
– Haemophilus
– Salmonella
– Legionella
r Fungal:
– Candida
– Aspergillus
– Histoplasmosis
– Coccidioidomycosis
– Blastomycosis
– Nocardia
r Parasitic:
– Amebiasis
– Toxoplasmosis
– Echinococcosis
r Neoplastic:
– Lung
– Breast
– Lymphoma
r Uremia
r Myocardial infarction:
– Dressler syndrome
r Connective tissue disease:
– Systemic lupus erythematosus
– Rheumatoid arthritis
– Scleroderma
r Radiation
r Chest trauma
r Postpericardiotomy
r Aortic dissection
r Myxedema
r Pancreatitis
r Inflammatory bowel disease
r Amyloidosis
r Drugs:
– Procainamide
– Cromolyn sodium
– Hydralazine
– Dantrolene
– Isoniazid
– Penicillins
– Doxorubicin/daunorubicin
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Chest pain
r Fever
r Mild dyspnea
r Cough
r Hoarseness
r Nausea
r Anorexia
Historyr Chest pain:
– Pain radiating to the ridge of the trapezius from
phrenic irritation
– Central or substernal pain
– Sudden onset
– Sharp
– Pleuritic
– Worse when supine or with cough
– Improved with leaning or sitting forward
r Previous episodes of pericarditis
r History of fever or infection
r History of malignancy or autoimmune disease
Physical Examr Tachypnea
r Tachycardia
r Odynophagia
r Friction rub:
– Heard best at lower left sternal border
– Very specific
– Triphasic rub is classic
– Can have any of these 3 components:
◦Presystolic
◦Systolic
◦Early diastolic
– Intermittent and exacerbated by leaning forward
r Beck triad with the accumulation of pericardial fluid:
– Muffled heart sounds
– Increased venous pressure (distended neck veins)
– Decreased systemic arterial pressure (hypotension)
r Ewart sign:
– Dullness and bronchial breathing between the tip
of the left scapula and the vertebral column
r Pulsus paradoxus:
– Exaggerated decrease (>10 mm Hg) in systolic
pressure with inspiration
r Constrictive pericarditis:
– Signs of both right- and left-sided heart failure
– Pulmonary and peripheral edema
– Ascites
– Hepatic congestion
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr ECG has 4 classic stages
r Stage 1:
– Concave ST-elevations diffusely except aVR and V1
– PR segment depressions with elevation in aVR
r Stage 2:
– Normalization of ST and PR segments
– T-wave flattening
r Stage 3:
– Diffuse T-wave inversions
r Stage 4:
– T-waves normalize, may have some persistent
T-wave inversions
r Atypical changes may include localized ST-elevations
or T-wave inversions
r Myocardial involvement suggested by
intraventricular conduction delay, new bundle
branch block, or Q-waves
r Pericardial effusion suggested by electrical alternans
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC:
– May show leukocytosis
r Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive
protein:
– May be elevated, can follow for resolution
r Cardiac enzymes:
– Helpful in distinguishing pericarditis from
myocardial infarction
– May also be elevated in myopericarditis
Imagingr CXR:
– Most often normal
– May show enlargement of the cardiac silhouette
or calcification of pericardium
– No change in heart size until >250 mL of fluid
has accumulated in the pericardial sac
r Echocardiography:
– Diagnostic method of choice for the detection of
pericardial fluid
– Can detect as little as 15 mL of fluid in the
pericardial sac
– Bedside US good screening tool
r Chest CT:
– Useful for the detection of calcifications or
thickening of the pericardium
– Can help rule out other etiologies

Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Pericardiocentesis:
r Pericardial fluid can help determine underlying
etiology.
r Fluid sent for protein, glucose, culture, cytology,
Gram and acid-fast stains, and fungal smears
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Acute myocardial infarction
r Pulmonary embolism
r Pneumothorax
r Aortic dissection
r Pneumonia
r Empyema
r Cholecystitis
r Pancreatitis
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr ABCs, IV access, O2, monitor
r Consider fluid bolus if no crackles.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs
r Emergent pericardiocentesis:
– For hemodynamic compromise secondary to
cardiac tamponade
– Removal of a small amount of fluid can lead to a
dramatic improvement.
– US guidance if available
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Treatment dependent on the underlying etiology
r Idiopathic, viral, rheumatologic, and post-traumatic:
– NSAID regimens effective
– Corticosteroids reserved for refractory cases
r Bacterial:
– Aggressive treatment with IV antibiotics along
with drainage of the pericardial space
– Search for primary focus of infection.
– Therapy guided by determination of pathogen
from pericardial fluid tests
r Neoplastic:
– Treat underlying malignancy.
r Uremic:
– Intensive 2–6 wk course of dialysis
– Caution should be used if using nonsteroidal
medications.
r Expected course/prognosis:
– Most patients will respond to treatment within
2 wk.
– Most have complete resolution of symptoms.
r Few progress to recurrent episodes with eventual
development of constrictive pericarditis or cardiac
tamponade.
MEDICATIONr Ibuprofen 300–800 mg q6–8h for days to weeks
depending on severity:
– Can also be tapered to prevent recurrence
– Improves coronary blood flow
– GI prophylaxis with 20 mg omeprazole
r Aspirin 800 mg PO q6–8h × 7–10 days:
– Taper off over 3–4 wk
– Omeprazole as with ibuprofen
– Colchicine 1–2 mg × 1 day, then 0.5–1 mg daily
× 3m o
r Colchicine alone: 1–2 mg × 1 day, then 0.5–1 mg
daily × 3 mo:
– Combination with aspirin decreased recurrence
rate
– Lower doses may also be effective.
r Indomethacin 25–50 mg q6h:
– May restrict coronary blood flow
r Prednisone 0.2–0.5 mg/kg daily × 2–4 wk with
taper:
– Used for refractory cases
– For use if aspirin/NSAIDs contraindicated
– Associated with increased rate of recurrence
– Also beneficial in uremic and autoimmune
pericarditis
Pregnancy Considerations
r NSAIDs and aspirin are not teratogenic in 1st 20 wk
of pregnancy
r Glucocorticoids may be used during pregnancy.
r Avoid aspirin and high-dose steroids when
breast-feeding.
r Colchicine is generally contraindicated except with
familial Mediterranean fever.
FOLLOW-UP

Admission Criteriar ICU:
– Hemodynamic instability
– Cardiac tamponade
– Malignant dysrhythmia
– Status postpericardiocentesis
r Telemetry unit:
– Suspicion of myocardial infarction
– Severe pain
– Suspicion of bacterial etiology
– Any high-risk criteria
r High-risk criteria:
– Large effusion (>2 cm total)
– Anticoagulant use
– Malignancy
– Temperature >38◦C
– Traumatic pericarditis
– Immunosuppression
– Pulsus paradoxus
– Slow onset
Discharge Criteriar Mild symptoms in patients without any
hemodynamic compromise
r Close follow-up
r Able to tolerate a regimen of oral medication
r Debate on need for ECG to evaluate for effusion
prior to discharge
Issues for Referral
Follow-up with cardiology:
r Recurrent cases
r Admitted patients
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS

re-evaluation and verification of resolution of
symptoms and absence of complications in 1–2 wk.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Classic history: Viral illness preceding development
of sharp, positional chest pain
r Rub is very specific but not always audible.
r The challenge is distinguishing pericarditis from
acute MI and other etiologies of chest pain.
r Mainstay of therapy is NSAIDs.

Judson J. Merritt rIan R. Grover
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Lunate remains located and in line with the radius
but the distal carpal bones are displaced dorsally
(∼95% of the time) or volarly (∼5% of the time)
r Early surgical treatment is recommended.
r This injury has a high incidence of post-traumatic
arthritis.
ETIOLOGYr Mechanism of injury is usually wrist hyperextension
with ulnar deviation.
r These are high-energy injuries:
– Falls from a height
– Motor vehicle accidents
– Industrial accidents
– Sporting accidents
ALERT
Scaphoid is frequently fractured with perilunate
dislocations.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Severe wrist pain
r Wrist swelling
r Diffuse wrist tenderness
r Paresthesias in the median nerve distribution
Historyr History of a high-energy injury
r Any concomitant injuries
r Pain in the wrist
r May complain of paresthesias in the median nerve
distribution
Physical Examr Wrist swelling
r Possible deformity of the wrist
r Decreased range of motion of the wrist
r Possible decreased sensation in the median nerve
distribution
r Special attention should be paid to skin integrity
because open fractures are common.
r Neurovascular status should be monitored closely,
including 2-point discrimination.
r Check closely for concomitant injuries, specifically of
the upper extremity.
ALERT
Diagnosis is frequently missed on clinical exam.
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Radiographs of the wrist
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Imagingr Radiographic imaging that includes 3 views of the
wrist
r Perilunate dislocation visualized best on the true
lateral view:
– Distal carpal row, specifically the capitate, seen
dorsally (95% of the time) or volarly (5% of the
time) in relation to the lunate
– Lunate is located and in line with the radius
r CT and MRI are not generally needed for diagnosis,
but some orthopedists may request them for
preoperative planning.
Pediatric Considerations
r Wrists are rarely sprained in children.
r Wrist radiographs are difficult to interpret in
pediatric patients.
r Comparison view of the other wrist may be helpful.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Lunate fracture
r Lunate dislocation:
– Dislocation occurs between lunate and distal
radius.
r Scapholunate dissociation and other similar
ligamentous disruptions
r Distal radius fracture
Pediatric Considerations
Consider nonaccidental trauma.
TREATMENT
ALERT
Concern is for concomitant, more serious, injuries.
PRE-HOSPITALr Assess for other injuries
r Immobilize
r Pain control
r Elevate
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Identify other, more serious, associated injuries.
r Immobilize
r Elevate
r Ice
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Pain control
r Procedural sedation for closed reduction:
– Etomidate: 0.1–0.15 mg/kg IV
– Methohexital: 1–1.5 mg/kg IV
– Propofol: 40 mg IV every 10 sec until induction

r Closed reduction of the dislocation should be done
emergently:
– Arm is hung in traction for 10 min with 10–15 lb
of counterweights and the fingers in traps.
– The fingers are then removed from the traps and
manual traction is continued.
– One of the physician’s thumbs is placed volarly
over the lunate and then the injury is recreated
with wrist extension.
– Continued traction is applied to the wrist and then
slow flexion of the wrist is performed, which
usually locates the distal carpal bones.
r Operative fixation to reduce and maintain wrist
stability is required.
r Immobilize wrist using a sugar-tong splint in neutral
position. Obtain postreduction radiograph.
Pediatric Considerations
Although perilunate dislocation is unusual in pediatric
patients, children with wrist pain should be splinted
and referred to a pediatric hand surgeon.
MEDICATIONr Diazepam: 2–5 mg IV q2–4h (peds: Max. dose is
0.25 mg/kg q4h) PRN anxiety
r Fentanyl: 0.05–0.2 mg IV q1h PRN pain
r Hydromorphone: 0.5–1 mg IV q4–6h (peds:
0.015 mg/kg/dose q4–6h) PRN pain
r Lorazepam: 0.5–1 mg IV q1–6h (peds: 0.044 mg/kg
q4–6h) PRN anxiety
r Morphine sulfate: 0.1 mg/kg IV q1h PRN pain
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Open dislocation, presence of multiple trauma, or
other, more serious, injuries
r Inability to reduce dislocation or maintain reduction
r Neurovascular compromise
Discharge Criteriar Closed injuries
r Adequate reduction
r No neurovascular involvement
r Orthopedic follow-up within 2–3 days
Issues for Referral
All patients with perilunate dislocations should be
referred to a hand surgeon for surgical stabilization
and ligament repair.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr All patients with a perilunate dislocation must
follow-up with a hand surgeon for surgical
stabilization and ligament repair.
r Follow-up should be within 2–3 days.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Up to 25% of these injuries are missed on initial
presentation.
r In a patient with wrist pain, swelling, and limited
range of motion, it is important to obtain adequate
x-rays of the wrist and make sure that the lunate
and capitate are located in their fossa on the lateral
wrist x-ray.
r Late presentation of these injuries leads to a very
poor outcome and often requires a salvage
operation.
r Complications include median nerve injury, tendon
problems, complex regional pain syndrome, wrist
instability, and post-traumatic arthritis.
r Even with appropriate treatment, there is a high
incidence of post-traumatic arthritis and loss of grip
strength.

DESCRIPTIONr Collection of pus in supporting structures of teeth:
– Periodontal ligament
– Alveolar bone
r Periodontal pockets result from progression of
periodontal disease and resultant bone loss:
– Food and debris accumulate in periodontal pockets
– Coronal epithelial tissues can reattach to tooth
while bacteria and food debris remain trapped in
pocket, impairing drainage
– Food and debris become secondarily infected in
the setting of impaired drainage
r Complications:
– Osteomyelitis
– Dentocutaneous fistula
– Cavernous sinus thrombosis
– Ludwig angina
– Maxillary sinusitis
– Mediastinitis
– Tooth loss
– Sepsis

r Periodontal abscess is rare in children
r Periapical abscess is more common:
– Originates in pulp
– Associated with caries

r Peptostreptococci
r Viridans group streptococci
r Neisseria species
r Usually polymicrobial

Periodontal abscess is a clinical diagnosis

r Malaise
r Fever
r Facial swelling
Physical Examr Focal swelling or fluctuance of gums and or face
r Tenderness to palpation
r Increased tooth mobility
r Parulis:
– Pimple-like lesion on gingiva, representing
terminal aspect of a sinus tract
– May be seen in chronic abscess

r Heat sensitivity
r Lymphadenopathy
r Trismus is generally absent, unless infection has
spread to muscles of mastication

This is a clinical diagnosis:

Lab
Anaerobic culture of pus:
r Complicated abscess

adjacent structures
r Imaging can confirm and help define extent of

r Performed by dental consultant to verify viability of
tooth
r Performed during follow-up visit with dentist

r Maxillary sinusitis
r Aphthous ulcers

PRE-HOSPITAL

signs of airway compromise are present:

r Transport in sitting position
r Supplemental oxygen

INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Assess for airway patency

– Irrigate cavity with saline

– Clindamycin for penicillin-allergic patients or
patients not responding to penicillin

PERIORBITAL AND ORBITAL CELLULITIS
Shari Schabowski
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Periorbital Cellulitisr An inflammatory, typically infectious condition
affecting the eyelid(s)
r It is anatomically distinguished by its location,
isolated to the tissues anterior to the orbital septum:
– Orbital septum is the connective tissue extension
of the orbital periosteum that is reflected into the
upper and lower eyelids
– Extension to the deep tissues is rare because the
septum represents a nearly impenetrable barrier
but it may be incomplete
r Most commonly presents as a complication of upper
respiratory tract infection (URTI) and sinusitis:
– Swelling is caused by inflammatory edema from
vascular and lymphatic congestion
r May occur as a complication of a localized
inflammation/infection in the eyelid or adjacent
structures:
– Blepharitis
– Hordeolum
– Dacryocystitis
– Surrounding skin disruptions:
r Insect bites
r Minor trauma
r Impetigo or other dermatologic disorders
Orbital Cellulitisr Inflammatory process in the structures deep to the
orbital septum
r Typically occurs secondary to extension from an
adjacent structure:
– Sinusitis:
◦Most commonly ethmoiditis penetrating through
the thin lamina papyracea
– Dental abscess
– Retained foreign body in the orbit
– Puncture wounds
– Orbital fracture
– Postoperative infection
– Hematogenous spread from a remote source due
to valveless orbital veins
– Rare cause—direct extension of periorbital
cellulitis
ETIOLOGY
Periorbital Cellulitisr Streptococcus pneumoniae
r Staphylococcus aureus
r Streptococcus pyogenes
r Moraxella catarrhalis
r Haemophilus influenzae
r Gonococcus – rare
r Consider nonbacterial cause
Orbital Cellulitisr Currently streptococcal and staphylococcal
infections are the most common causes:
– S. pneumoniae, Streptococcus viridans,
S. pyogenes, Streptococcus anginosus, S. aureus
– Anaerobes, Bacteroides, and gram-negatives may
also be seen
r All forms of orbital cellulitis carry a risk of severe
morbidity and possible mortality and are therefore a
true emergency:
– Permanent visual loss may occur
– May extend to subperiosteal space with abscess
formation
– Cavernous sinus thrombosis and CNS infections
may be life threatening
r Fungal infections are an uncommon but an even
more lethal form particularly in the
immunocompromised:
– Cerebrorhino-orbital phycomycosis (CROP)
– Rapidly fatal in 75% of cases:
◦80% of cases occur in patients with a recent
episode of diabetic ketoacidosis
◦Predisposing factor: Severe metabolic acidosis
and immunocompromise
◦Begins in the paranasal sinuses and proliferates
in the blood vessels causing thrombosis and
necrosis
◦Bloody nasal discharge is common
◦May present with evidence of necrosis of the
palate and/or nasal mucosa
Pediatric Considerations
r Routine vaccinations including Hib and
Pneumococcus have dramatically decreased
periorbital and orbital cellulitis, but infections may
still occur with these organisms particularly in
younger children and those without at least 2 Hib
vaccines
r Periorbital cellulitis is overall 5 times more common
and typically occurs in children <5 yr whereas
orbital cellulitis is more common in children over 5 yr
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Periorbital Cellulitis/Orbital Cellulitisr Both present with a unilateral, red, swollen eye:
– Lid swelling may be profound in both
r Differences include:
– Source of inciting infection
– Single vs. both lids involved
– Toxicity, systemic and neurologic symptoms
Orbital CelluLItis
Historyr Preceded by sinusitis in 60–90%, dental infection,
trauma, puncture wound, or recent operation
r Swelling and redness surrounding eye in addition to
eye pain, visual impairment, loss of color vision,
restricted eye movements
r Headache, meningismus, and symptoms of systemic
illness may occur
r Identify complicating medical problems:
– Immunocompromise
– Diabetes
Physical Examr Toxic appearance:
– Fever >39◦C
r Restricted, painful extraocular movements (EOM)
r Afferent pupillary defect
r Conjunctival injection
r Chemosis
r Decreased visual acuity
r Diplopia
r Proptosis
r Meningismus and neurologic findings may be seen.
Periorbital Cellulitis
Historyr Preceded by local skin injury, insect bite, URTI, or
superficial ocular infection
r Ask about vaccination status in young children
r Low-grade fever
r Subacute presentation
Physical Examr Red, swollen eyelid
r Often single lid involvement but can involve both
r Conjunctival injection common
r Low-grade fever common:
– Rare systemic symptoms
r Normal visual acuity
– No symptoms of deep ocular involvement
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Complete eye exam:
– External exam
– Visual acuity
– EOM
– Pupillary exam
– Fundoscopic exam
– Intraocular pressure measurement
r Complete neurologic exam
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Supportive but not diagnostic:
r CBC:
– WBC <15,000 for periorbital cellulitis
– WBC >15,000 may suggest bacteremic
periorbital cellulitis or orbital cellulitis
r Blood culture
r Gram stain and culture of tissue aspirate or swab of
draining purulent material:
– Chocolate agar plate when gonorrhea suspected

DESCRIPTION
Peripheral neuropathy is a general term for peripheral

– Pain and temperature sensation are decreased
with small-fiber neuropathy
– Deep tendon reflexes are decreased secondary to

long-standing motor nerve involvement
– Loss of reflexes secondary to slowing of
conduction along motor nerve efferent limb

– Orthostasis

– Urinary retention
– Impotence

Sally A. Santen rSamantha R. Hauff
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Obstruction of ≥1 of the peripheral arteries
secondary to embolism or thrombus
r Caused by atherosclerosis or embolus
r Patients with PAD may also have coronary artery
and cerebrovascular disease.
r Epidemiology:
– Risks factors (selected):
◦Age
◦Smoking
◦Diabetes
◦Hyperlipidemia
◦HTN
– Associated with morbidity and mortality from
other forms of atherosclerosis (coronary artery
disease, stroke)
– Complications:
◦Aneurysm
◦Thrombosis
◦Ulceration
◦Limb loss
r Chronic arterial insufficiency (CAI):
– Progressive obstructing atherosclerotic disease
causing subacute ischemia and pain (claudication)
– 10% develop critical leg ischemia.
r Acute arterial insufficiency (AAI):
– Caused by arterial thrombosis (50%) or embolism
– Causes acute limb ischemia with signs and
symptoms of the 6 Ps (below)
r Atheroembolism:
– Caused by rupture or partial disruption of an
atherosclerotic plaque (aorta, femoral, iliac)
– Gives rise to cholesterol emboli that shower and
obstruct arteriolar networks
– May be precipitated by invasive arterial
procedures such as cardiac catheterization
ETIOLOGYr Obstruction by atherosclerotic plaques (CAI)
r Arterial thrombosis
r Arterial emboli:
– Cardiac emboli from dysrhythmias, valvular heart
disease, or cardiomyopathy (80%)
– Aneurysms
– Infection
– Tumor
– Vasculitis or foreign body
– Thrombosis of plaques from pre-existing CAI
r Atheroembolism
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr CAI:
– Claudication:
◦Aching pain in the calves (femoropopliteal
occlusion) or buttocks and thighs (aortoiliac
region)
◦Occurs with activity and slowly relieved by rest
or dependent positioning
◦Classic claudication presents in about 1/2 of
patients with PVD.
– Severe disease presents with limb pain at rest:
◦Usually starting in the foot
◦Rapidly progressive claudication or ulceration
r AAI:
– Extremity pain:
◦Sudden onset
◦Gradual increase in severity
◦Starts distally and moves proximally over time
◦Decrease in intensity once ischemic sensory loss
occurs
r Atheroembolism:
– Complaint of cold and painful fingers or toes
– Small atherosclerotic emboli may affect both
extremities.
– Usually related to recent arteriography, vascular or
cardiac surgery
– Multiorgan involvement is common (renal,
mesentery, skin, others)
Physical Exam
ALERT
Sudden onset of pain and pallor in extremity is limb
and life threatening.
r CAI:
– Absent or decreased peripheral pulses
– Delayed capillary refill with cool skin
– Increased venous filling time
– Bruits
– Pallor and dependent rubor of the leg
– Muscle and skin atrophy
– Thickened nails and loss of dorsal hair
– Ulcerations (especially toes or heels) or
gangrene with severe disease
r AAI:
– 6 Ps:
◦Pain (1st, sometimes only symptom)
◦Pallor
◦Pulselessness
◦Poikilothermic
◦Paresthesias (late finding)
◦Paralysis (late finding)
– Identification of a source of a possible embolic
process is crucial (atrial fibrillation,
cardiomegaly).
r Atheroembolism:
– Ischemic and painful digits
– “Blue toe syndrome”
– Livedo reticularis
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr CAI:
– Ankle–brachial index (ankle systolic BP divided by
higher arm systolic BP)
– Bedside test to determine whether CAI is present
(see NEJM video reference)
– Ratio of <0.9 is abnormal and <0.4–5 indicates
severe disease.
– Calcific arteries (diabetes) can have false negative
ABI or elevated ABI (>1.3).
r AAI:
– Physical diagnosis using the 6 Ps
– Those with acute-on-chronic arterial insufficiency
tolerate limb ischemia better than those without
CAI, due to well-developed collateral circulation.
r Atheroembolism:
– Clinical diagnosis: Affected areas painful, tender,
and may be either dusky or necrotic
– Workup may investigate source of emboli with
duplex US, CT angiogram, EKG.

Labr CBC and platelets
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose
r Coagulation studies
r Creatine phosphokinase to evaluate for ischemia.
r Special tests for suspected etiologies:
– Hold blood for hypercoagulable studies
– Sedimentation rate, CRP for vasculitis
– Blood cultures for endocarditis
Imagingr Doppler US:
– Visualizes both venous and arterial systems
– Identifies level of arterial occlusion, as well as
thrombosis and aneurysm
– Sensitivity and specificity >80–90% for occlusion
of vessels proximal to the popliteal vessels
r Plethysmography/segmental pressure
measurements:
– Uses measurements of the volume and character
of blood flow to detect areas of CAI
– Less widely available than US, therefore requires
an experienced technician
– Approximates US in sensitivity and specificity
r Angiography:
– Determines details about the anatomy, including
the level of occlusion, stenosis, and collateral flow
– Useful where the diagnosis of AAI is uncertain or
before emergent bypass grafting
– Advantage is intervention (atherectomy,
angioplasty, or intraluminal thrombolytics) can be
done at the time of diagnosis.
r CT angiogram:
– CT is useful for diagnosis of occlusive aortic
disease or dissection.
– Rapidly available and reliable
– Many centers have moved to CT angiogram as the
1st-line diagnostic tool. The decision for operative
or angiographic intervention is based on the CT
angiogram.
– Requires contrast, therefore may not be 1st line
for patients with renal insufficiency
r MRI:
– Sensitive for evaluation of CAI and dissection
– Disadvantages are that MRI is time consuming
and expensive.

r Arterial dissection
r Deep venous thrombosis
r Venous insufficiency
r Compartment syndrome
r Buerger disease
r Spinal stenosis
r Neuropathy
r Bursitis
r Arthritis
r Reflex sympathetic dystrophy

P
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Maintain hemodynamic stability with fluids.
r Apply cardiac monitor.
r Place the ischemic limb at rest and in a dependent
position.
r Provide oxygen if low oxygen saturation or
pulmonary symptoms.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr IV fluid bolus for hypotension
r EKG, monitor, pulse oximetry
r Supplemental oxygen
r Pain control
r Avoid temperature extremes
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr CAI:
– Antiplatelet therapy with 75 or 325 mg of aspirin
or clopidogrel (75 mg/day) may be used as
1st-line treatment. Dual therapy has not been
shown to improve outcomes, although may be
indicated in other forms of atherosclerosis.
– Other approved drugs include: Cilostazol 100 mg
BID, dipyridamole 200 mg BID, pentoxifylline 400
mg TID
– Revascularization depending on the severity and
location of obstruction:
◦Balloon angioplasty
◦Atherectomy
◦Bypass grafting
– Risk-factor modification:
◦Tobacco cessation
◦Aggressive management of hyperlipidemia,
HTN, diabetes
◦Exercise therapy
r AAI:
– Limit further clot propagation with IV heparin.
– Do not anticoagulate patients suspected of having
an aortic dissection or symptomatic aneurysm.
– Emergent consultation with vascular surgery or
interventional radiology:
◦To determine which diagnostic study is best to
make the diagnosis
◦To begin arrangements for possible operative
therapy or other intervention
◦Options for operative therapy include
thrombectomy, embolectomy, angioplasty,
regional arterial thrombolysis, bypass grafting.
◦Blood flow to the affected limb must be
re-established within 4–6 hr after onset of
ischemic symptoms.
– Complications of AAI include:
◦Compartment syndrome
◦Irreversible ischemia requiring amputation
◦Rhabdomyolysis, renal failure
◦Electrolyte disturbances
r Atheroembolism:
– Treat conservatively if a limited amount of tissue is
involved and renal function is not significantly
compromised.
– No clear therapy for the ischemic digits besides
supportive wound care and analgesia
– Some studies have tried corticosteroids to
decrease inflammation, statins to stabilize plaque,
aspirin, or dipyridamole
– Amputation for irreversibly necrotic toes
– Vascular surgeon referral within 12–24 hr of ED
visit
– Prevent further embolic events by a thorough
investigation and correction of the source of
atheroemboli.

r Cilostazol: 100 mg BID
r Clopidogrel: 75 mg/d
r Heparin: 80 U/kg bolus IV followed by 18 U/h IV
r Pentoxifylline: 400 mg TID

and revascularization.

claudication or ischemic pain at rest:
– To undergo heparinization and angiography to
rule out an acute thrombosis
r Atheroembolism admission indicated with large
areas involved, significant pain, infection, or renal
compromise
Discharge Criteriar Atheroembolism:
– If they have small lesions, adequate pain control,

superinfection, and follow-up within 24 hr
r CAI:
– No evidence of rapid progression, critical leg
ischemia, gangrene, or infection

r Atheroembolism, depending on the origin of the
emboli, may need referral to vascular surgery or to
cardiology.

CAI without acute ischemia and atheroembolism with
minimal involvement should have close follow-up to
evaluate the extent of their disease.

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Suppurative complication of tonsillitis where
infection spreads outside the tonsillar capsule
between the palatine tonsil and pharyngeal muscles
r Most common deep infection of the head and neck
(incidence of 30/100,000 per year)
r In the US, 45,000 cases annually
r Occurs in all ages, more commonly in young adults
(mean age 20–40 yr)
r Occurs most commonly Nov–Dec, April–May
(coincides with highest incidence rates of
streptococcal pharyngitis)
r Complications:
– Airway compromise (uncommon)
– Sepsis (uncommon)
– Recurrence (12–15%)
– Extension to lateral neck or mediastinum
– Spontaneous perforation and aspiration
pneumonitis
– Jugular vein thrombosis (Lemierre syndrome)
– Poststreptococcal sequelae (glomerulonephritis,
rheumatic fever)
– Hemorrhage from extension and erosion into
carotid sheath
– Severe dehydration
– Intracranial extension (meningitis, cavernous sinus
thrombosis, cerebral abscess)
– Dural sinus thrombosis
ETIOLOGYr 2 theories explain the development of peritonsillar
abscess (PTA):
– Direct bacterial invasion into deeper tissues in the
patient with acute pharyngitis
– Acute obstruction and bacterial infection of small
salivary glands (Weber glands) in the superior
tonsil
r Smoking may be a risk factor
r Most common pathogens:
– Group-A Streptococcus
– Staphylococcal species, including
methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
(MRSA)
– Anaerobes (Prevotella, Peptostreptococcus,
Fusobacterium)
– Polymicrobial
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Sore throat
r Fever
r Voice change
r Odynophagia (difficulty swallowing)
r Drooling
r Headache
r Pain radiating to the ear
r Decreased PO intake
r Malaise
Physical Examr Fever
r Trismus
r “Hot potato” voice
r Erythematous tonsils/soft palate
r Inferior and medial displacement of superior pole of
tonsil on affected side
r Uvular deviation away from affected side
r Halitosis
r Cervical lymphadenitis
r Tenderness on ipsilateral side of neck at the angle of
the jaw

PTA, either with additional imaging or physical exam
that may require admission and surgery
r Evaluate and ensure airway patency: Look for stridor,
tripod position, or inability to handle secretions
r Definitive management with either needle aspiration
or incision and drainage (I&D), followed by a course
of antibiotics

examining oropharynx
r May be difficult with severe trismus
Labr Throat culture and monospot (20% incidence of
mononucleosis with PTA)
r CBC and culture of the abscess contents may be
useful in some cases
r Basic metabolic panel may be useful in patients with
decreased oral intake and clinical signs of
dehydration

transducer with a lubricated latex cover can aid in
identification and localization of the abscess
– A cooperative patient can place the transducer at

when the patient has too much trismus to use an
intracavitary probe

– If suspicion for epiglottitis or retropharyngeal

r Chest radiograph:
– With severe respiratory symptoms or draining
abscess
r CT scan of neck:
– If suspicion exists for other deep space infection of
the neck, CT may be indicated
– CT also may be indicated if unable to obtain a

– CT may locate abscess pocket after failed needle

deep space infections (internal jugular vein

TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Rarely associated with airway emergencies, but
diagnosis is likely to be uncertain in transport, so
suction and intubation equipment should be at the
bedside:
r Pulse oximetry, supplemental oxygen
r Cardiac monitor
r IV access
Pediatric Considerations
r PTA occurs in children (<18 yr) in 25–30% of
reported cases (14 cases per 100,000 population)
r Young children may need sedation or general
anesthesia if I&D or aspiration of the abscess is
attempted
r Obtain soft-tissue lateral neck radiograph before
oral exam in young children with symptoms of upper
airway obstruction
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Same as for pre-hospital
r Airway management may be necessary
r Equipment for intubation and cricothyroidotomy
should be available
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Antibiotics should be administered
r IV fluid should be given for dehydration
r Pain control is important
r A single dose of steroids may improve symptoms
r Adequate anesthesia prior to aspiration or I&D
procedures is important:
– Benzocaine spray
– Lidocaine, 1% with 1:100,000 epinephrine
r No clear benefit for one drainage technique over
another:
– Needle drainage:
◦Successful 87–94%
◦Should be performed by a person experienced in
drainage procedure and adept at advanced
airway techniques
◦Less painful, less invasive than I&D
◦The internal carotid artery lies ∼2.5 cm
posterolaterally to the tonsil; sheathing the
aspiration needle to prevent introduction of the
needle to <0.5 cm is prudent
◦The superior pole of the tonsil is the most
common place for maximal fluctuance (followed
by the middle pole and then the inferior pole)
◦Repeat aspiration is necessary in 10%
– I&D:
◦Successful 90–92%
◦An 11- or 15-blade scalpel is used to make stab
incision to area of fluctuance
◦Guard scalpel with trimmed plastic sheath
leaving 1 cm of blade exposed
◦Avoid >0.5 cm depth
◦Medial and superior incisions are safer from the
standpoint of potential injury to the carotid
artery
◦Incision typically made superior to tonsil in area
of soft palate. Incision in the tonsil itself causes
excessive bleeding and may miss the abscess,
which is located in the peritonsillar soft tissue of
the soft palate.
◦Suction should be ready to remove purulent
drainage and blood
◦Packing is not used
– Tonsillectomy (indications in children):
◦Upper airway obstruction
◦Previous episodes of severe recurrent
pharyngitis or PTA
◦Failure of abscess resolution with other drainage
techniques
◦Can be performed immediately or after
resolution of acute infection
MEDICATIONr Length of antibiotic treatment should be 14 days
(<10 day treatment course may be associated with
recurrence)
r Adjunct with steroids can improve symptoms
Intravenous Antibioticsr Ampicillin/Sulbactam (Unasyn), 3 gm q6h
r Penicillin G, 10 million U q6h+ Metronidazole
(Flagyl), 500 mg q6h
r If allergic to Penicillin, Clindamycin, 900 mg q8h
Oral Antibioticsr Amoxicillin/Clavulanic acid (Augmentin), 875 mg
BID
r Penicillin VK, 500 mg q6h + Metronidazole (Flagyl),
500 mg q6h
r Clindamycin, 600 mg BID or 300 mg q6h
Steroidsr Dexamethasone, 10 mg IV/IM/PO single dose
– Pediatrics: 0.6 mg/kg; not to exceed 10 mg
r Methylprednisolone, 2 mg/kg; not to exceed 250 mg
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Airway compromise
r Sepsis
r Altered mental status
r Dehydration and inadequate PO intake
r Extension of infection beyond the PTA (i.e., deep
space neck infections)
Discharge Criteriar Most patients with PTA can be discharged home on
oral antibiotics after abscess drainage
r Must be able to tolerate sufficient oral intake and
antibiotics
Issues for Referralr Referral to an otolaryngologist or surgeon should be
provided
r Tonsillectomy is recommended 6–8 wk following
treatment of the abscess
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Close follow-up recommended in 24–48 hr:
r Treatment failures and recurrences are relatively
common

r Failure to secure the airway early in a severe
infection
r Failure to recognize a more advanced, deep space
infection of the neck
r Knowing the anatomy before performing needle
aspiration or bedside I&D
r Bedside US is a useful adjunct in differentiating and
identifying a PTA vs. peritonsillar cellulitis

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Acute respiratory tract infection spread by small
respiratory droplets
r Bacteria (fimbriae) attach to respiratory epithelial
cells and proliferate, producing toxins:
– Ciliary dysfunction, accumulation of cellular
debris, increased mucus production, lymphocytic
and granulocytic infiltration
r Bronchiolar congestion, obstruction, and necrosis
r Obstruction of the airway due to mucus plug,
leading to hypoxia and hypoventilation
r Increased intrathoracic or intracranial pressure
r Secondary bacterial infection may exacerbate
respiratory distress/failure.
r CNS injury caused by encephalitis, increased
intracranial pressure, and/or hypoxia
r Uncomplicated cases last 6–10 wk; half of the cases
last <6 wk.
r Mortality:
– Mortality greatest in those <1y r
– 1.3% for patients <1m o
– 0.3% in children 2–11 mo
– 90% of deaths are secondary to bacterial
pneumonia
r Epidemiology:
– Incubation period is 6–20 days, usually 7–10 days.
– Mostly young children; 24% in children <6m o
– Increasing incidence in adolescents
– Adults are the primary reservoir
– Peak incidence is late summer/fall
– Preventable with diphtheria–tetanus–pertussis
(Tdap) vaccine
ETIOLOGY
Bordetella pertussis:
r A fastidious, gram-negative, pleomorphic bacillus
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Generally 3 recognized phases with progression:
– Infants may have indistinct stages
r Catarrhal stage:
– 1–2 wk duration
– Rhinorrhea
– Mild cough
– Minimal fever
r Paroxysmal stage:
– 1–6 wk duration
– Classic “whooping” cough, increasing in severity:
◦Coughing spasm that ends with a sudden inflow
of air—the whoop; unremitting paroxysms
– Cyanosis with respiratory distress/failure
– Apnea (infants <6 mo)
– Altered mental status secondary to hypoxia or
encephalitis
r Convalescent stage:
– 2–12 wk duration
– Waning cough
– Improving respiratory status
r Atypical presentations:
– Often atypical in children <6m o
– Partially immunized children have less severe
disease
– Adult manifestations are often only rhinorrhea,
sore throat, persistent cough; often in family
members
Historyr Catarrhal phase:
– Malaise
– Low-grade fever
– Rhinorrhea
– Sore throat
r Paroxysmal phase:
– “Whooping” cough
– Post-tussive cyanosis
– Post-tussive emesis
r “Whooping” sound during paroxysmal phase
r Catarrhal phase:
– Persistent cough
Physical Examr Catarrhal phase:
– Low-grade fever
– Rhinorrhea
– Lacrimation
– Dry cough (late phase)
– Conjunctival inflammation
r Paroxysmal phase:
– Paroxysmal whooping cough
r Convalescent phase:
– Occasional paroxysmal cough
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr The ED diagnosis should be made on clinical grounds
r Attempt to establish a history of a contact
r Observe the paroxysmal cough with the
characteristic whoop
r Use ancillary studies to further support the clinical
diagnosis and exclude complications
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Polymerase chain reaction:
– High sensitivity and specificity
– High sensitivity leads to more false positives
– Best practices for testing with PCR:
◦Test only those with symptoms
◦Testing after 4 weeks of cough or following
antibiotics will increase false negative rate
◦Obtain samples via aspiration or posterior
nasopharyngeal swab to maximize DNA
recovery
– Should be used in conjunction with culture
r Direct immunofluorescence assay of nasopharyngeal
mucus:
– High false-positive rate
r Culture of nasopharynx or cough plate on a
Bordet–Gengou medium:
– Takes 7–12 days
– High specificity
– Low sensitivity
◦Remains the gold standard test
r Serology:
– Useful in later diagnosis
– Perform testing 2–8 weeks after cough onset
r WBC count:
– Leukocytosis (20,000–50,000 cells/mm3) with
marked lymphocytosis
– Normalizes during convalescent phase
– Elevation of WBC and lymphocytosis parallels
severity of cough
r Immunofluorescent and enzyme immunoassays to
exclude respiratory syncytial virus
r Done on either nasal wash or nasopharyngeal swab
(Dacron)
Imaging
CXR:
r Most often normal
r Perihilar infiltrates
r Atelectasis
r Occasionally characteristic “shaggy” right heart
border
r Secondary bacterial pneumonia
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Infection:
– Parallel whooping cough syndrome caused by
Bordetella parapertussis, Chlamydia trachomatis,
Chlamydia pneumoniae, Bordetella
bronchiseptica, or adenovirus
– Pneumonia:
◦Bacteria
◦Mycoplasma
◦Mycobacterium
– Bronchiolitis:
◦Respiratory syncytial virus
◦Influenza
◦Other virus
r Reactive airway disease
r Foreign body
r Cystic fibrosis

r Monitor airway
r Suction

r Suction mucous plugs

recommended for pertussis

– Boostrix: Approved for ages 10 and up

r Apnea

PHALANGEAL INJURIES, FOOT
Taylor Y. Cardall
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr The phalanges of the foot are prone to injury.
r 5th (or small) toe most commonly affected
ETIOLOGYr Usually the result of direct trauma
r Stubbing the toe, kicking a hard surface, or dropping
a heavy object onto toes most common mechanisms
of injury
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
History
History may predict the type of injury found and
should include:
r Time of injury
r Mechanism
r History of previous trauma
r Status of tetanus immunization if laceration is
present
Physical Examr Tenderness, swelling, crepitus, and ecchymosis of
affected digit
r Subungual hematomas are often present.
r Lacerations or crush-type wounds
r Document neurovascular status of the affected digit.
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Radiographs of involved digit
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Imagingr Radiographs of involved digit
r Lateral view may be most sensitive.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Fracture
r Contusion
r Abrasion/laceration
r Dislocation
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Ice to affected digit
r Direct pressure and dressing to any wounds
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Ice to affected digit
r Direct pressure and dressing to any wounds
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Fractures involving the proximal phalanx and
interphalangeal (IP) joint of the hallux:
– Nondisplaced, non–intra-articular fractures may
be placed in a short-leg walking cast with toe
extension for comfort.
– Displaced, non–intra-articular fractures:
r Closed reduction with digital block anesthesia
r Longitudinal traction
r Placement in short-leg walking cast with toe
extension:
– Intra-articular fractures of the hallux merit
orthopedic consult:
◦Frequently treated with open reduction and
internal fixation
r Fractures involving the proximal phalanx and IP joint
of the lesser toes:
– Rarely cause long-term disability
r Nondisplaced fractures:
– Treat with splinting or buddy taping
– Gauze padding between the taped toes to prevent
skin breakdown
r Displaced fractures:
– Closed reduction by digital block anesthesia
– Longitudinal traction
– Buddy taping or splinting
– Hard-sole shoe, weight bearing as tolerated
– Oral analgesics for pain
– Pain usually resolved by 2–3 wk
r IP joint dislocations:
– Closed reduction by digital block anesthesia
– Longitudinal traction with gentle downward
pressure on distal phalanx
– Buddy tape to adjacent toe
– Unstable or unsuccessful reductions require
orthopedic consultation.
– Oral analgesics for pain

PHALANGEAL INJURIES, HAND
Asia M.F. Takeuchi rStephen R. Hayden
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr 1/3 of all traumatic injuries affect the hand.
r Phalanges account for 1 of the most frequently
fractured parts of the skeletal system with the distal
phalanx being the most commonly fractured bone in
the hand.
r Dorsal displacement of the proximal interphalangeal
joint of the finger is the most frequent dislocation.
Pediatric Considerations
Injuries may be more difficult to diagnose in children
who are unable to cooperate for a full exam.
ETIOLOGYr Trauma (commonly work or sports related)
r Infectious sequelae:
– Skin flora: Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococci
– Cat/dog bites: S. aureus and Pasteurella multocida
– Human bites: Eikenella
– Thorns or woody plants puncture: Fungal
– Fresh/salt water exposure: Mycobacterium
marinum and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
r Overuse injury (e.g., “gamekeeper’s thumb”)
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Mechanism of injury:
– Hyperextension injuries most commonly cause
ligamentous injury (e.g., “Jersey finger” which is a
rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon
from its distal attachment) or chip fractures.
– Hyperflexion injury to the tip of digits may cause
“Mallet finger” injury with avulsion fracture at the
insertion of the extensor tendon on the distal
phalanx.
– Crush injuries most commonly cause fractures and
diffuse soft-tissue injury.
r Handedness
r Occupation/hobbies
r Other factors may affect healing (e.g., age, diabetes,
immune suppression, anticoagulation)
Physical Examr Swelling and/or deformity (e.g., amputation,
rotation, shortening, or angulation)
r Skin changes (e.g., ecchymosis, laceration, burn,
pallor) or associated nail injury
r Decreased range of motion or weakness
r Pain or change in sensation in the area of injury
ALERT
Kanavel signs (infectious flexor tenosynovitis)
r Pain along the tendon with passive extension
(early sign)
r Symmetric enlargement of the affected digit
r Slightly flexed finger at rest
r Tenderness along the course of the flexor sheath
(later sign)
r Trigger finger (stenosing flexor tenosynovitis):
r Noninfectious inflammation of the flexor tendon
sheath.
r Painful “snapping” sensation with flexion of the
affected digit.
r May awaken with the finger locked in the palm,
with gradual “unlocking” as the day progresses.
Pediatric Considerations
In an infant with a painful or swollen digit, it is
important to consider a deeply embedded hair
tourniquet that may not be readily obvious on
superficial exam.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Special attention directed at assessing individual
tendon status, neurovascular integrity, and
identifying rotational deformity:
– Isolate and assess each individual joint (PIP , DIP ,
MCP); range with passive motion and against
active resistance
– Normal 2-point discrimination is ∼4–5 mm
– Malrotation can be evaluated by positioning the
fingers with the MCP joints in flexion and the PIP
and DIP in extension:
◦Normally, all fingers are directed toward the
radius and there should be no overlap or
rotation
r Exam conducted 1st to assess function, then under
anesthesia, and finally with tourniquet if needed to
allow a bloodless field for better exam of lacerated
areas.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Consider wound culture if signs of infection present or
if there is concern for flexor tenosynovitis.
Imagingr Plain radiography of involved digits should include
AP , true lateral, and oblique views.
r US can help diagnose tendon tears.
Pediatric Considerations
Open epiphyses make radiographic interpretation less
sensitive.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Tendon laceration/rupture partial/complete
r Complicated open injuries may include several
injuries, and the entire hand should be examined
carefully.
r Beware of lacerations over dorsal
metacarpal–phalangeal areas, which may be “fight
bites” (human bites).
Pediatric Considerations
r Many fractures in children are torus (buckle)
fractures of the phalanges.
r The growth plates are typically weaker than the
surrounding ligaments, thus dislocations are
commonly accompanied by Salter–Harris fractures.
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Reduction of a phalangeal dislocation at the scene
SHOULD NOT be considered UNLESS there will be
an unusually long transport time or there is vascular
or neurologic compromise.
– Reduction may be successful but prompt the
physician to miss significant ligamentous injuries.
r Bleeding should be treated with appropriate direct
pressure dressings.
ALERT
r Amputated digits or tissue should be placed in
clean moist saline gauze, placed in plastic bag,
and then placed in a separate bag with ice.Do not
place digit in direct contact with ice!
r Indications for reimplantation in amputation:
– Thumb
– Single digit between PIP and DIP joints
– Multiple digits
– Amputation in a child
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Remove all rings from injured hand.
r Immobilize the involved areas by proximal-to-distal
splinting.
r Intermittent ice pack application with constant
elevation for the 1st 24 hr.
r Dislocations or severely deformed fractures
producing vascular compromise should be reduced
immediately to a neutral position and immobilized.
