PHALANGEAL INJURIES, HAND
P
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Interphalangeal reduction:
– Dorsal dislocation:
◦Provide longitudinal traction and gently
hyperextend the joint while pushing the base of
the dislocated phalanx into place.
– Volar dislocation:
◦Provide longitudinal traction and gently
hyperflex while pushing the base of the
dislocated phalanx into place.
– Lateral dislocation:
◦Provide longitudinal traction and gently
hyperextend the joint while correcting the ulnar
or radial deformity.
r Interphalangeal immobilization:
– DIP dorsal or lateral finger dislocation:
◦Splint the DIP in full extension while allowing
full range of motion of the PIP joint.
– PIP dorsal or lateral finger dislocation:
◦Apply a dorsal splint with the PIP in 20–30◦ of
flexion.
– Volar finger dislocation:
◦Splint the PIP and DIP in full extension.
r Metacarpophalangeal dislocation:
– Avoid excessive hyperextension or distraction.
Gently distract the affected digit and apply volar
pressure to the base of the dislocated proximal
phalanx.
r Metacarpophalangeal immobilization:
– Finger dislocation: Splint the digit in 90◦ of flexion
at the MCP joint.
– Thumb dislocation: Apply a thumb spica splint
with the MCP joint in 20◦ of flexion.
r Open fracture:
– Immediate referral to a hand surgeon for
treatment within 4–6 hr after trauma.
– Prophylactic antibiotics directed against
gram-positive and gram-negative organisms
should be administered parenterally within 6 hr.
r Closed fracture:
– Distal phalanx:
◦Stable injuries may be splinted with the DIP in
flexion and the PIP free; extend tip of splint
beyond the end of the digit for added
protection; maintain for 3–4 wk.
– Middle phalanx:
◦Nondisplaced stable fractures can be buddy
taped to an adjacent digit.
◦Displaced/angulated fractures may be reduced
(using longitudinal traction with 3-point
pressure to align the fragment) and immobilized
(buddy tape and ulnar/radial gutter splint).
◦Splinting should be done with the wrist in
20–30◦ of extension, the MCP joints in 70–90◦
of flexion, and the PIP and DIP joints flexed
5–10◦.
– Proximal phalanx:
◦A nondisplaced, nonangulated, stable injury can
be buddy taped to an adjacent finger;
ulnar/radial gutter or Burkhalter splint may be
added for comfort.
◦A displaced or angulated fracture may be
reduced by flexing the MCP and PIP joints to
90◦, then using a 3-point reduction technique
to reduce the proximal fragment dorsally and
the distal fragment volarly. Once reduced, the
PIP joint should be extended (to avoid a flexion
contracture), the MCP joint should remain in
70–90◦ of flexion and a radial or ulnar gutter
splint should be placed with the fractured finger
buddy taped to an adjacent finger.
ALERT
No more than 1 or 2 mm of displacement or
shortening is acceptable. Up to 10◦ of angulation is
acceptable but NO amount of rotation is permitted.
r Mallet finger:
– Immobilize the DIP joint in full extension or
slight hyperextension (5–15◦), while allowing
full range of motion of the PIP joint.
–D o not attempt to reduce any displaced
fractures before splinting because any reduction
is unlikely to be maintained without surgery;
refer for urgent orthopedic consult.
r Jersey finger:
– Apply an aluminum splint with the PIP joint and
the DIP joint slightly flexed.
– DIP extension should be avoided until the digit
can be evaluated by a hand specialist (definitive
treatment of complete tendon rupture is
surgery).
r Trigger finger:
– Immobilize by buddy taping to the adjacent
finger for 4–6 wk.
– A metal or thermoplastic finger splint can be
used if buddy taping is unsuccessful.
r Gamekeeper’s thumb:
– Apply ice to the MP joint acutely.
– Immobilize with a thumb spica splint (MP joint
is flexed to 20◦) for 3 wk.
r Subungual hematoma:
– Nail trephination using a heated paper clip,
electric cautery, or an 18G needle.
– This injury does not have to be treated as an
open injury unless there is an underlying tuft
fracture.
r Nail avulsions:
– Clean and repair using fine (e.g., 6-0)
absorbable suture.
– Splint the eponychium and germinal matrix with
the avulsed nail or small piece of gauze or foil to
avoid adhesions.
r Open distal and volar directed fingertip wounds
with no protruding bone and smaller than 1 cm
may be allowed to heal by secondary intention.
MEDICATIONr Evaluate tetanus status and vaccinate per
immunization schedule.
r Digital nerve block should be done with an
anesthetic that does NOT contain epinephrine.
r Antibiotics:
– Not indicated for simple clean wounds
– For grossly contaminated injury, puncture wounds,
or infectious tenosynovitis therapy should be
tailored to specific pathogen exposure (e.g., skin
flora, fresh water, bites)
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITIONr Patients with a stable injury, in an appropriate
splint, may be discharged for orthopedic follow-up
and possible repeat imaging in 1 wk time.
ALERT
Emergent orthopedic consult is required for:
r Amputation
r Open joint injuries or fractures
r Digital neurovascular compromise
r Signs of joint infection or infectious tenosynovitis
r High-pressure injection injury
r Urgent orthopedic consult:
– Unstable fractures (rotational deformity, oblique
or angulated fractures, joint involvement,
epiphyseal injuries)
– Any joint dislocation with tendon rupture
– Digit dislocation that is irreducible
– Unstable joint after attempted dislocation
reduction
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Rotational deformity may not be apparent if finger is
straight, exam under flexion is required.
r Jersey finger (FDP tendon rupture) is often
misdiagnosed as a “jammed” or sprained finger, but
requires more urgent management than these minor
injuries.
r Always check for stability postreduction by having
patient perform active range of motion and checking
a postreduction x-ray.

common finger injuries. Curr Rev Musculoskelet
Med. 2008;1:97–102.

management of open fractures. A critical analysis.
J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2006;88:2739–2748.

PHARYNGITIS
John C. Greenwood rBrian J. Browne
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Inflammation/infection of the pharynx
r 3rd most common complaint for physician visits
r 30 million cases diagnosed annually
r Group A β-hemolytic streptococcus (GAS):
– Streptococcus pyogenes
– Unusual in children <3y ro l d
– Cause of 20–30% of childhood pharyngitis
– Bimodal incidence, highest in ages 5–7 and
12–13 yr
– Cause of 5–15% of adult pharyngitis
– Peak months: January–May; also at the start of
the school year
ETIOLOGYr Viral (most common infectious cause):
– Rhinovirus (20%)
– Coronavirus (>5%)
– Adenovirus (5%)
– Herpes simplex virus (4%)
– Parainfluenza virus (2%)
– Influenza virus (2%)
– Coxsackievirus (<1%)
– Epstein–Barr virus (<1%)
– Acute human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)
r Bacterial:
– GAS (S. pyogenes [15–30%])
– Fusobacterium necrophorum (10%)
– Group C & G β-hemolytic streptococcus (5%)
– Neisseria gonorrhea (<1%)
– Corynebacterium diphtheriae (<1%)
– Arcanobacterium haemolyticum (<1%)
– Chlamydia pneumoniae
– Mycoplasma pneumoniae (<1%)
– Syphilis
– Tuberculosis
r Fungal:
– Candida (thrush)
r Chemical burns
r Foreign bodies
r Inhalants
r Postnasal drip
r Malignancy
r GERD
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Viral:
– Cough
– Rhinorrhea
– Sore throat usually follows
– Have a high suspicion for acute HIV in at-risk
patients presenting with persistent pharyngitis
despite treatment
r Bacterial:
– Sudden-onset sore throat that usually precedes
other symptoms
– Odynophagia
– Fever
– Headache
– Abdominal pain
– Nausea and vomiting
– Uncharacteristic symptoms:
◦Coryza
◦Hoarseness
◦Diarrhea
Physical Examr High-risk features for a serious complication of
pharyngitis:
– Stridor, respiratory distress
– Drooling
– Dysphonia
– Marked neck swelling
– Neurologic dysfunction
r Viral:
– Cough
– Coryza
– Rhinorrhea
– Pharyngeal erythema
– Gingivostomatitis
r GAS:
– Tonsillopharyngeal erythema/exudates
– Soft palatal petechiae
– Beefy red, swollen uvula
– Anterior cervical lymphadenopathy
– Scarlatiniform rash
– Uncharacteristic signs:
◦Conjunctivitis
◦Anterior stomatitis
◦Discrete ulcerative lesions
r Mononucleosis:
– Mistaken for GAS due to similar presentation:
◦Exudative pharyngitis
◦Tender cervical lymphadenopathy
◦Fever
◦Rash
– Other possible exam findings:
◦Hepatosplenomegaly
◦Jaundice
r Diphtheria:
– Consider in nonimmunized patients
– Airway-threatening gray pharyngeal membrane
– Myocarditis (2/3 of patients); clinically evident
cardiac dysfunction (10–25%)
– Cranial and peripheral neuropathies (5%)
r Gonococcal pharyngitis:
– Can be asymptomatic
– Always evaluate children for sexual abuse
– Recurrent episodes of pharyngitis
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Modified Center criteria for the diagnosis of GAS
pharyngitis (most widely used decision rule):
r Criteria (points):
– Absence of cough (+1)
– Tonsillar exudates or swelling (+1)
– Swollen and tender anterior cervical nodes (+1)
– Temperature >38C (+1)
– Age in years:
◦3–14 (+1)
◦15–44 (0)
◦>45 (–1)
r Scoring:
– <1 should not be tested or treated
– 3 is associated with a risk of 28–35%
– >4 is associated with a risk of 51–53%
r Patients with 3 criteria should receive a rapid
antigen detection test (RADT)
r Presumptive treatment without testing has led to
inappropriate use of antibiotics in about 50% of
cases
r Some suggest that patients with a score >4 should
be treated empirically without a RADT
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Throat culture:
– Gold standard
– 24–48 hr for results, will delay treatment
– Necessitates contacting patient/family
– Obtain when Gonococcus is suspected
r GAS RADT:
– Results are available within 30 min
– Treat all patients with (+) RADT results
– Technique: Performed by swabbing the tonsils or
posterior pharynx:
◦Avoid contact with the tongue, buccal mucosa,
and lips
– Sensitivity 85–95%
– Specificity 96–99%:
◦Confirm with conventional throat culture in
children/adolescents with negative RADT
◦Optical immunoassay is extremely accurate;
negative results do not require confirmatory
culture
r Monospot:
– Detects heterophil antibody:
◦Sensitivity:
■ <2 yr old: <30%
■ 2–4 yr old: 75%
■ >5 yr old: 90%
– CBC with peripheral smear: 50% lymphocytes,
10% atypical lymphocytes
– Obtain rapid viral loads if HIV is suspected
Imagingr Lateral neck radiograph for suspected epiglottitis,
retropharyngeal abscess, or foreign body
r Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck is useful to
identify complications such as peritonsilar abscess
and retropharyngeal abscess
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Epiglottitis
r Peritonsillar/retropharyngeal abscess
r Diphtheria
r Mononucleosis
r Lemierre disease
r Ludwig angina
r Candida infection
r Gonorrhea
r Acute HIV infection
r Acute leukemia/lymphoma
r Oropharyngeal cancer
r Foreign body
r Inhalants and chemical burns
r Postnasal drip
r GERD

– Acetaminophen
– Ibuprofen
– Topical analgesics (e.g., Chloraseptic spray)
r GAS infection:
– Often mild and self-limited:
◦Antibiotic therapy accelerates symptom relief
(fever and pain) by 1–2 days
– Goal of antibiotic treatment is to reduce the
incidence of acute rheumatic fever, symptoms, and
suppurative complications
r Antibiotics:
– Penicillin V: Antibiotic of choice for GAS
pharyngitis
– Cephalosporins or macrolides are an acceptable
alternative treatment for nonresponders and
penicillin-allergic patients
r Corticosteroids:
– In conjunction with antibiotics, corticosteroids
have a 3-fold increase in the likelihood of
symptom resolution at 24 hr
– Number needed to treat: 3.3–3.7
– Avoid in diabetics and immunocompromised
patients
r Potential complications of streptococcal infection:
– Suppurative complications:
◦Peritonsillar/retropharyngeal abscess
◦Lemierre disease
◦Otitis media/mastoiditis
– Nonsuppurative complications:
◦Acute rheumatic fever:
■ Rare in industrialized countries, but still the
leading cause of cardiac death within 1st 5
decades of life
■ Sequelae of GAS; not proven in association
with group C or G
◦Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
◦Sydenham chorea
◦Reactive arthritis
◦PANDAS: Pediatric autoimmune
neuropsychiatric disorder associated with
streptococcal infection:
■ Sudden onset of symptoms similar to
obsessive–compulsive disorder
■ Caused by an autoimmune reaction affecting
the basal ganglia
■ Uncommon and controversial
r Diphtheria:
– Goals of therapy:
◦Prevent airway obstruction
◦Treat infection
– Penicillin or macrolide antibiotic
– Complications:
◦Exotoxin-mediated myocarditis and neuritis
(cranial neuropathies)
r Gonococcal pharyngitis:
– 3rd-generation cephalosporin plus macrolide for
possible Chlamydia coinfection

– >27 kg: Benzathine penicillin G (Bicillin LA):

– >12 yr: 250–500 mg PO q6–8h × 10 days
r Amoxicillin:
– 50 mg/kg PO QD, (max. 1 g) × 10 days

– Azithromycin: 20 mg/kg/d × 3 days (max. 500 mg
per dose)
– Erythromycin: 40–50 mg/kg PO div. q6h ×
10 days (max. 500 mg per dose)
r Oral cephalosporins:
– Cephalexin: 20 mg/kg/dose PO BID × 5 days
(max. 500 mg per dose)
r Steroids:
– Dexamethasone: 0.6 mg/kg IM/PO × 1 (max.

– Prednisone: 40–60 mg PO × 1

– Suspected gonococcal pharyngitis:

r Suspected child abuse

Able to tolerate oral intake

r Mononucleosis patients should avoid contact sports

r Use the modified Centor criteria to make the

r Children with negative RADT need follow-up throat

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Phencyclidine (PCP) is a dissociative anesthetic
structurally related to ketamine:
– Causes decreased perception of pain and agitation
r Half-life of 21–24 hr, but may be longer in overdose
r Enterohepatic recirculation—recirculated into the
stomach
ETIOLOGYr Drug of abuse:
– Frequently encountered as an adulterant of
marijuana
r Street names for PCP include:
– Angel dust
– Wicky stick
– Wicky weed
– Wacky weed
–W e t
– Illy
– Embalming fluid
– Sherman
Pediatric Considerations
Exposure in toddlers reported via passive exposure
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr CNS:
– Altered mental status
– Agitation
– Bizarre/violent behavior
– Belligerence
– Coma
– Seizures
– Nystagmus (vertical, horizontal, or rotatory)
r Cardiovascular:
– HTN
– Tachycardia
r Musculoskeletal:
– Traumatic injury (decreased pain perception)
– Rhabdomyolysis (due to vigorous muscular
contraction)
r Vital signs:
– Hyperthermia
History
How was the PCP consumed?
r Smoked with marijuana
r Ingested
Physical Examr Agitation
r Coma
r Hypertension
r Tachycardia
r Diaphoresis
r Nystagmus (vertical, horizontal, or rotatory)
r Hyperthermia
r Vigorous muscular contraction

– Dextromethorphan and ketamine may give false

Labr CBC
r Electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, glucose
r Urinalysis:
– Dip for myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis)

– If urine dip for blood is positive
r Ethanol level

r Extremity/spine radiographs when there is
associated trauma
r CT of the head when there is head trauma/altered
mental status
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Drugs of abuse:
– Cocaine
– Amphetamines
– Designer drugs:
◦Methcathinone (“Cat”)
◦“Ecstasy”
◦“Ice” (methamphetamine)
– Alcohols
– Ketamine
– Sympathomimetics
r Drugs that cause nystagmus:
– Lithium
– Carbamazepine
– Sedative–hypnotics
– Alcohols
– Phenothiazines
– Dextromethorphan

PHENYTOIN POISONING
Michele Zell-Kanter
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Phenytoin follows zero-order pharmacokinetics:
– Small incremental increase in dose can result in a
large increase in plasma concentration.
r Half-life in overdose prolonged; may be up to 70 hr
r Cardiovascular toxicity from IV administration likely
due to the diluent propylene glycol
r Fosphenytoin, a prodrug for parenteral
administration, is metabolized to phenytoin, its
active moiety.
ETIOLOGYr Phenytoin intoxication results from acute, chronic, or
acute-on-chronic administration.
r If the cause of the intoxication is unclear in a patient
receiving chronic phenytoin therapy, consider that
there may have been a:
– Change in the brand of phenytoin
– Change in dosage form
– Drug interaction
– Change in serum albumin
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Level 20–40 μg/mL (or mg/L):
– Nystagmus
– Dizziness
– Ataxia
– Drowsiness
– Nausea/vomiting
– Diplopia
– Slurred speech
r Level 40–90 μg/mL:
– Confusion
– Disorientation
r Level >90 mg/mL:
– Coma
– Respiratory depression
– Paradoxical seizures
r Hypotension/bradycardia with rapid IV
administration:
– Fosphenytoin injection does not contain propylene
glycol
– Hypotension/dysrhythmia unlikely with
fosphenytoin
r Hypersensitivity reaction following chronic use:
– Rash
– Fever
– Neutropenia
– Agranulocytosis
– Hepatitis
– Cholangitis
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Determine the time, route, and amount of ingestion.
r Phenytoin level:
– After oral overdose, the peak plasma
concentration may not be reached until 24 hr or
more post acute ingestion.
– Absorption differs with various oral preparations
and manufacturers
– Repeat levels every 4 hr until levels have peaked
and continue to steadily decline.
– Once levels begin declining, check every 24 hr
until <30 μg/mL.
– Free phenytoin level may be required in patients
who are hypoalbuminemic or patients who are
poor metabolizers.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Fosphenytoin level:
– Measured as phenytoin
– Measure fosphenytoin after conversion to
phenytoin is complete (2 hr post IV infusion or
4 hr post IM injection).
– Prior to complete conversion to phenytoin,
immunoanalytic techniques may overestimate
plasma phenytoin concentrations due to
cross-reactivity with fosphenytoin.
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose:
– Check for anion gap metabolic acidosis due to
coingestant, seizure activity, from propylene glycol
in the IV formulation
– Determine glucose with altered mental status.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Intoxication with other CNS depressants
r Guillain–Barr ´ e syndrome
r Botulism
r Posterior fossa tumor
r Acute cerebellitis

PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA
David N. Zull
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Pheochromocytoma (pheo) is a catecholamine-
producing tumor arising from the chromaffin tissues
of the sympathetic nervous system.
r Origin from the adrenal medulla or sympathetic
ganglia:
– 80% solitary adrenal (usually the right side)
– 10% bilateral (usually inherited form)
– 10% extra-adrenal in location:
◦Abdominal, within mesenteric ganglia (86%)
◦Thorax (10%), neck (3%), bladder (1%)
– 10% malignant (usually inherited form)
r Incidence:
– 0.2–0.4% of hypertensive patients, but higher
proportion of patients with severe hypertension
– 2–8/million population per year
– Peaks in decades 3–5, 10% in children
– Male = female
– In about 1/2 of the cases, the diagnosis is made
postmortem.
– 10% asymptomatic, incidental on CT
r Genetics:
– Inherited form 25%, autosomal dominant
– Usually associated with multiple endocrine
neoplasia (MEN) 2A, less so with MEN 2B or von
Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease:
◦MEN 2A (medullary thyroid carcinoma [CA],
pheo, and hyperparathyroidism)
◦MEN 2B (medullary thyroid CA, pheo, oral
mucosal neuromas, skeletal and bony
abnormalities)
◦VHL (hemangioblastomas of retina and CNS,
pancreas and renal cysts, and pheo
– Other associated diseases: Neurofibromatosis,
tuberous sclerosis, Sturge–Weber syndrome,
paragangliomas of the neck
ETIOLOGYr The tumor synthesizes and stores catecholamines in
the same manner as the normal adrenal medulla.
r Tumors predominantly secrete norepinephrine, and
to a lesser extent epinephrine (some tumors are
epinephrine predominant, in which hypotensive
episodes are characteristic)
r Paroxysmal release of catecholamines:
– Spontaneously due to changes in blood flow or
tumor necrosis
– Direct pressure on the gland from external forces
(trauma, exercise)
– Precipitation of release (opiates, glucagon,
metoclopramide, steroids, foods with tyramine,
iodinated contrast media)
– Augmentation of catecholamine effect (tricyclic
antidepressants [TCAs], β-blockers,
sympathomimetics)
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Hypertension, moderate to severe, refractory to
treatment:
– 40%: Paroxysms with normal BP between
episodes
– 30%: Sustained hypertension with paroxysms
– 30%: Sustained hypertension without paroxysms
– Sometimes normotensive in familial forms and
small tumors: <5%
r Paroxysmal symptoms
– Sudden onset, gradual resolution
– Duration: Minutes to hours (average 20 min)
– Intervals: Hours to months (average weekly)
– Increasing frequency, duration, and severity with
time
r Clinical characteristics of paroxysms
– Hypertensive crisis or urgency
– Headache – abrupt, throbbing, bilateral
– Tachycardia/palpitations
– Profuse diaphoresis/pallor
– Apprehension/anxiety/tremulous
– Shock associated with trauma, surgery,
parturition, anesthesia
r Acute crisis
– Prolonged (>24hr) severe paroxysm
– Severe HTN or shock, hyperpyrexia
– Multiorgan failure/lactic acidosis
– Pulmonary edema due to cardiomyopathy (dilated,
hypertrophic or Takotsubo)
– Stroke (SAH, PRES, RCVS, embolic)
– Severe headache/encephalopathy
– Chest pain (MI/dissection)
– Acute abdomen
◦Hemorrhagic tumor necrosis
◦Mesenteric infarction
r Chronic symptoms
– Chest pains/palpitations
– Orthostasis (decreased plasma volume and
blunted sympathetic reflexes)
– Constipation can be severe, leading to ileus or
pseudo-obstruction (catecholamines inhibit
peristalsis)

– 1 mg IV test dose
– 2.5–5 mg IV bolus given at 1 mg/min repeat bolus
every 5–15 min to BP control. Follow by infusion
– Infusion starting at 0.1 mg/min titrated up to 1
mg/min

DESCRIPTIONr True phimosis is the pathologic inability to retract
the foreskin over the glans of the penis as a result of
scarring.
r The inability to retract a normal, supple foreskin is
not true phimosis.
r The foreskin is rarely retractable at birth due to
normal adhesions between the glans and the inner
prepuce.
r ∼90% are retractable by 3 yr of age, and 99% are
retractable by 17 yr, as the epithelial cells that
comprise smegma are shed.
r Parents should be instructed not to forcibly retract
the foreskin.
ETIOLOGY
Possible causes of true phimosis include:
r Trauma from forcible retraction of the foreskin
r Repetitive bouts of diaper dermatitis
r Recurrent balanoposthitis
r Poor hygiene
r Poorly performed circumcision
r Congenital anomalies

r Poor urinary stream
r Whitish, narrowed preputial opening of the foreskin
r Edema, erythema, and tenderness of prepuce
r Balanoposthitis (inflammation of the glans and
foreskin)
r Ballooning of foreskin on urination in severe cases
Physical Exam
Exam should include an evaluation for potential
complications:
r Obstruction and vascular compromise of glans
r Occur only in the most extreme cases

r In patients with severe stenosis, the complication of
an obstructive uropathy may occur. This should be
investigated by:
– Evaluation of kidney function:
◦BUN and creatinine
– Renal sonogram
r Phimosis secondary to recurrent balanoposthitis
should prompt a workup for diabetes mellitus:
– Urinalysis, serum glucose, or glycosylated
hemoglobin (Hgb A1C)

r Balanoposthitis without phimosis

be instructed not to attempt retraction of the
foreskin prior to medical evaluation.
r Unwarranted attempts may traumatize a normal,
nonretractable prepuce or convert the situation to a
more emergent paraphimosis.

None required in most cases

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Hemorrhage at the decidual–placental interface
leading to complete or partial separation of the
normally implanted placenta before delivery of the
fetus
r Incidence/prevalence:
– ∼1% of all pregnancies
– 30% of bleeding episodes in the 2nd half of
pregnancy
– 15% of all fetal deaths
– Neonatal death in 10–30% of cases
– 6% of all maternal mortality
r Synonym(s): Abruptio placentae, accidental
hemorrhage (in UK)
ETIOLOGYr Primary cause unknown
r Vascular injury with dissection of blood into the
decidua basalis or mechanical shearing between the
placenta and uterus leading to bleeding and clot
formation
r More severe cases lead to:
– Development of disseminated intravascular
coagulation (DIC)
– Maternal–fetal compromise
r Research suggests that the majority of abruptions
are due to chronic processes:
– Inflammatory changes in the placenta
– Manifestation of ischemic placental disease
r Acute abruption can occur due to:
– Trauma
– Rapid uterine decompression
– Placenta implantation over a uterine anomaly or
fibroid
r Multiple known risk factors:
– Previous abruption (10–20% recurrence risk)
– Maternal hypertension (>140/90) and
preeclampsia
– Increased parity and maternal age
– Multiple gestation
– Fibroids or other uterine/placental abnormalities
– Tobacco use
– Cocaine abuse
– Trauma
– Premature rupture of membranes, particularly if
associated with chorioamnionitis or
oligohydramnios
– Rapid uterine decompression:
◦Polyhydramnios with membrane rupture
◦Rapid delivery of 1st twin
– Elevated 2nd trimester maternal serum
α-fetoprotein
– Thrombophilias
– Maternal race:
◦More common among African American and
Caucasian women
◦Incidence increasing more rapidly among
African American women

SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr 20+ wk of pregnancy
r Vaginal bleeding (>80%, usually painful)
r Abdominal or back pain (>50%)
r Uterine cramps, tenderness, frequent contractions,
or tetany
r Nausea, vomiting
r Otherwise unexplained preterm labor
r History of recent trauma should be elicited
r Recent drug use, particularly cocaine or other
sympathomimetics
r Prior abruption or other risk factors
r Estimated gestational age
r Prenatal care history
Physical Examr Signs of hypotensive shock may be present
r Uterine tenderness frequently present
r Vaginal bleeding (absent in 20–25%)
r Petechiae, bleeding, and other signs of DIC
r Decreased fetal heart tones and movement
r Fetal bradycardia or nonreassuring fetal heart rate
tracings

r Sterile vaginal exam must be performed with
caution to avoid tissue injury, especially if placenta
previa suspected:
– Assess for presence of amniotic fluid (nitrazine
paper turns blue; ferning of fluid on glass slide)
– Evaluate for vaginal or cervical lacerations

r Blood type, Rh, and cross-match
r Rapid hemoglobin determination
r Determine fetal heart tones by Doppler
r Fetal monitoring to detect signs of early fetal distress
r Uterine tocographic monitoring

Labr Blood type and Rh
r CBC
r PT/PTT
r Fibrinogen levels (normally 450 in latter half of

r Fibrinogen <200 mg/dL and platelets
<100,000/μL highly suggestive of abruption
r Kleihauer–Betke if mother Rh-negative (significant

traumatic abruption)

r If abdomen/pelvis CT scan done as part of maternal

visible (must ask the radiologist to evaluate

r Bleeding during labor
r Vaginal or cervical lacerations
r Uterine rupture
r Preterm labor
r Ovarian torsion
r Pyelonephritis
r Cholelithiasis/cholecystitis
r Appendicitis
r Other blunt intra-abdominal or pelvic injuries

PLACENTA PREVIA
Roneet Lev
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Placental tissue overlying or proximate to the
internal cervical os
r Uterine enlargement and cervical dilation cause
placental vessels near the cervix to tear, resulting in
vaginal bleeding
r >90% of placenta previa diagnosed before
20 weeks will migrate and have normal placental
location at term
r If placenta covers the internal os by >20 mm, then
previa is expected at birth
r Increased amount of placental overlap
(>15–23 mm) predicts placenta previa present at
birth
r Causes 20% of all antepartum hemorrhage
r Classifications:
– Complete placenta previa: Cervical os is
completely covered by placenta
– Partial placenta previa: Cervical os is partially
covered by placenta
– Marginal placenta previa: Edge of placenta is at
margin of cervical os
– Low-lying placenta: Placenta edge is within 2 cm
to cervical os
ETIOLOGYr Unknown etiology
r Incidence: 4/1,000 births = 0.4% of pregnancies at
term
r Maternal mortality: 0.03%
r Perinatal morbidity and mortality: Triple, due to
preterm delivery
r Factors affecting location of implantation:
– Increased number of curettages from spontaneous
or induced abortions
– Abnormal endometrial vascularization
– Delayed ovulation
r Risk factors:
– Multiparity (5% grand multiparous patients vs.
0.2% nulliparous)
– Multiple gestation
– Prior C-section (up to 3× increase, increases with
number or prior C-sections)
– Increased maternal age (0.7% age <19 yr, 1%
age ≥35 yr)
– Previous placenta previa (4–8% recurrence)
– Smoking (2–4 times increase)
– Male fetus (14% increase)
– Assisted fertilization
– Residence at higher altitude
– Asian maternal race
– Unexplained elevated maternal serum alpha fetal
protein (MSAFP)
r Associated conditions:
– Congenital anomalies
– Abnormal fetal presentation
– Preterm premature rupture of the membranes
– Amniotic fluid embolism; associated with
pathologies of the placenta
– Vasa previa: Fetal vessels course through
membranes and cover os
– Placenta accreta, increta, percreta (growth of
placenta into uterine wall) occur in 5–10% of
patients with placenta previa; sustained bleeding
may require C-section hysterectomy
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Painless vaginal bleeding in pregnancy after 20 wk is
placenta previa until proven otherwise
Historyr Painless bright red vaginal bleeding in 70%
r Uterine contraction in 20%
r Common incidental finding on US in 2nd trimester
(6% at 16–18 wk)
r 1st episode of bleeding typically occurs at 27–32 wk
r Bleeding may range from minor to massive; number
of bleeding episodes does not correlate with degree
of placenta previa
r Inciting factors—usually no cause; recent
intercourse or heavy exercise may contribute
r Initial bleeding is often self-limited and not lethal,
but often recurs
Physical Examr Never do a digital exam or instrument probe of the
cervix in 2nd-trimester vaginal bleeding until
placenta previa is ruled out
r Sterile speculum exam can be safely performed prior
to US to identify if blood is from the os, a vaginal
lesion, or hemorrhoids
r Blood seen at patient’s feet is a sign of heavy
bleeding
r Hypotension and tachycardia may indicate
hemorrhagic shock
r Fetal heart tones should be monitored along with
other vital signs
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Vaginal ultrasonography is the diagnostic procedure of
choice
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC, platelets
r Type and screen; upgrade to cross-match if
transfusion is indicated
r Kleihauer–Betke (KB)—detects >5 mL of fetal cells
in maternal circulation (it takes only 0.1 mL to
sensitize mother if Rh negative)
r If coagulopathy suspected (rare): Prothrombin
time/partial thromboplastin time, fibrin-split
products, fibrinogen (<300 mg/dL is abnormal)
r Rh status
Imagingr Transabdominal US: 93–98% accurate:
– False negative: Obesity, posterior or lateral
placenta, fetal head over cervical os
– False positive: Overdistended bladder
– No sufficient accuracy for placenta previa position,
need to obtain transvaginal US if placenta previa
is detected or uncertain findings
r Transvaginal US: 100% accurate:
– Vaginal probe does not exacerbate bleeding
r Color flow Doppler US: Used to determine placenta
accreta
r MRI: May be useful in evaluating placental
abnormalities such as accreta and percreta
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Placenta abruption (may occur concurrently)
r Uterine rupture
r Fetal vessel rupture
r Cervical/vaginal trauma
r Cervical/vaginal lesions
r Bleeding disorder
r Spontaneous abortion
r “Bloody show” of labor

P
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Patient with vaginal bleeding at >24 wk should be
transported to a facility that can handle high risk
and premature delivery
r Place patient in left lateral recumbent position if
hypotensive in 2nd half of pregnancy
r O2 and IV as with other patients
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Resuscitation for hemorrhagic shock as with any
source with monitoring of fetus and higher cut off of
blood transfusion
r ABCs
r 2 large-bore IVs with normal saline (NS) or lactated
Ringer (LR) for resuscitation
r Left lateral recumbent position if hypotensive in 2nd
half of pregnancy
r Fluid resuscitation
r Blood transfusion for hematocrit (Hct) <30 or
hypotension not responding to fluids
r Fresh-frozen plasma if coagulopathy
r Fetal monitoring (heart rate <120 or >160 bpm is
abnormal)
r Immediate OB consultation for symptomatic patients
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Emergent OB consultation for patients with active
bleeding
r Volume resuscitation with 2 large-bore IVs with NS
or LR
r Blood transfusion to keep Hct 30–35%
r RhoGAM if mother is Rh negative
r Fetal monitoring
r Keep NPO and on bed rest until considered stable by
OB
r Magnesium sulfate only for contractions of preterm
labor when delivery is not recommended
r Antenatal steroids (betamethasone) at 24–34 wk to
stimulate prenatal lung maturity
r Emergency C-section or delivery for continued
bleeding or fetal compromise
MEDICATIONr RhoGAM: 1 vial (300 μg) IM if not already given at
28 wk; may need >1 vial if KB indicates >15 mL of
fetal RBS
r Magnesium sulfate: 6 g IV over 20 min, then
2–4 g/h; adjust to contractions
r Betamethasone: 12 mg IM q24h × 2 doses
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Active bleeding placental previa is a potential
obstetric emergency, and all patients should be
admitted
r Select patients may be managed on outpatient basis
if bleeding is resolved. In consultation with OB
Discharge Criteriar Asymptomatic patients
– Bed rest is not necessary. Avoid strenuous physical
activity. Report bleeding or contractions
– <20 wk and placenta not over the os: No special
follow up necessary
– <20 wk and placenta 0–20 mm: Repeat US at
28 wk
– Placenta >20 mm over os is unlikely to resolve.
C-section at 36–37 wk
– Pelvic rest (no intercourse or tampons in vagina) if
placenta previa found after 28 wk or at any time if
associated with bleeding
r 70% of patients will have a 2nd episode of bleeding
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Patients with incidental finding of placenta previa
found at <20 wk will need outpatient US to
determine migration of placenta
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Do not perform digital vaginal exam if suspect
vaginal bleeding after 2nd trimester. Do US first
r Sterile speculum exam and transvaginal US are safe
and do not increase bleeding
r Painless vaginal bleeding after 20 wk is placenta
previa until proven otherwise
r Painful vaginal bleeding after 20 wk is placental
abruption until proven otherwise
r The 2 above conditions can occur simultaneously

PLANT POISONING
Patrick M. Lank
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Plant exposure is 1 of the most common reasons to
contact the poison center
r Majority of cases involve unintentional ingestion in
children <6 yr old.
ETIOLOGY
Identification of ingested plant species should be
attempted whenever possible.
Plants with Anticholinergic Propertiesr Genera include Atropa, Datura, Hyoscyamus,
Solandra, and Solanum.
r Common names of anticholinergic plants include
Jimson weed, deadly nightshade, henbane, and
angel trumpet.
r Competitive antagonists of acetylcholine at the
muscarinic acetylcholine receptor
Plants with Cardiac Glycosidesr Genera include Digitalis, Nerium, Thevetia, and
Helleborus.
r Common names of cardiac glycoside plants include
foxglove, oleander, yellow oleander, lily of the valley,
and hellebore/Christmas rose
r Inhibit Na+/K+-ATPase:
– See separate chapter on Digoxin Poisoning
Plants with Nicotine-like Alkaloidsr Genera include Nicotiana, Caulophyllum, and
Conium
r Common names of plants containing nicotine
include tobacco, blue cohosh, and poison hemlock.
r Direct-acting agonists at the nicotinic acetylcholine
receptor
Plants with Cyanogenic Compoundsr Genera include Hydrangea, Malus, Prunus,
Sambucus
r Common names of plants containing cyanogenic
compounds (in some part of the plant) include
apricot, cherry, peach, plum, apple, cassava, and
elderberry
r Metabolized to cyanide, which interferes with
electron transport chain and leads to cellular
poisoning
Plants with Calcium Oxalate Crystalsr Genera include Alocasia, Dieffenbachia, and
Philodendron as well as many others
r Common names for calcium oxalate–containing
plants include elephant’s ear, dumb cane, and
mother-in-law’s tongue
r Clinical manifestations occur after release of
intracellular calcium oxalate crystals:
– Local tissue exposure to calcium oxalate crystals
leads to inflammatory response.
Plants with Pyrrolizidine Alkaloidsr Genera include Crotalaria, Heliotropium, Senecio,
and Sesbania
r Common names of plants with pyrrolizidine
alkaloids include scorpion’s tail, ragwort, groundsel,
and rattlebox
r Metabolized to highly reactive pyrroles, which are
directly hepatotoxic acutely and lead to hepatic
vascular proliferation and veno-occlusive disease
chronically.
Plants with Sodium Channel Activityr Genera include Aconitum, Delphinium, Leucothoe,
Lyonia, Pernettya, Pieris, Rhododendron,
Schoenocaulon, Veratrum, and Zigadenus
r Common names of plants with aconitine, veratrum
alkaloids, and zygacine, all sodium channel openers,
include: Aconite (monkshood, wolfsbane,
delphinium), veratrum (false hellebore), and
zygacine (death camas)
r Common names of plants with grayanotoxins, which
have variable effects on sodium channels, include
sweet bells, rhododendron, azalea, and
lily-of-the-valley bush
r Variable sodium channel effects depending on toxin,
although most lead to prolonged sodium channel
influx.
Plants with Toxalbuminsr Genera include Abrus, Jatropha, Phoradendron,
Ricinus, Robinia, Wisteria
r Common names of plants with toxalbumins include
rosary pea, mistletoe, and castor bean
r Cause direct cellular toxicity by interfering with
ribosomal function
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Anticholinergicr Dry, warm, and flushed skin
r Absent bowel sounds
r Urinary retention
r Agitated delirium
Cardioactive Steroidsr Digoxin-like toxicity
r Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting
r Multiple cardiac effects, ranging from junctional
bradycardia to v-tach/v-fib
r ± hyperkalemia
Nicotine-like Alkaloidsr Hypertension
r Tachycardia→ bradycardia (late)
r Diaphoresis
r Salivation
r Vomiting
r Fasciculations
r Muscle weakness
Cyanogenic Compoundsr Potentially delayed (unlike cyanide gas)
r Initial symptoms:
– Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting
– Lethargy
– Diaphoresis
r Followed by:
– Altered mental status
– Lactic acidosis
– Seizures
– Cardiovascular collapse
– Multiorgan system failure
Calcium Oxalate Crystalsr Oropharyngeal burning pain and swelling (after
biting or chewing)
r Ocular exposure results in keratoconjunctivitis
r Dermal irritation after dermal contact
Pyrrolizidine Alkaloidsr Acutely causes hepatitis
r Chronic exposure may lead to hepatic
veno-occlusive disease
Sodium Channel Activatorsr Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting
r CNS: Progress from paresthesias to depressed
mental status, respiratory depression, coma, and
seizures.
r CV: Bradycardia with atrioventricular blocks,
progressing to tachydysrhythmias
Toxalbuminsr Effects depend on plant (e.g., mistletoe is rarely
toxic, whereas ricin can be deadly) and route of
exposure
r Gastroenteritis, diarrhea, or abdominal pain if
ingested
r Localized pulmonary effects if inhaled
r Diffuse organ dysfunction if injected
Pediatric Considerations
r Often present with lip, tongue, and oropharyngeal
irritation and swelling from oxalate
crystal–containing plants:
– Potential for airway compromise
r Usually consume leaves, seeds, and berries
r Nicotine group: 1 or 2 cigarettes potentially lethal
r Jimson weed:
– Seeds highly concentrated
– 100 seeds equal 6 mg of atropine
– Lethal at 4–5 g of leaf
r Yellow oleander:
– 2 leaves lethal in 12.5 kg child
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Identification of ingested material
r Workup depends on plant ingested
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose, liver function
tests
r ABG/VBG for blood pH determination
r Digoxin level for cardiac glycoside plants
r Lactic acid for cyanogenic plants
Imagingr ECG
r CXR
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Altered mental status:
– Drug use/alcohol
– Seizures
– Trauma
– Cerebrovascular accident
– Hypoglycemia
r Digoxin toxicity
r Gastroenteritis
r Agents causing metabolic acidosis (see Acidosis
chapter)
r Cardiotoxic drugs

PLANT POISONING
P
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Examples of common nontoxic houseplants:
– African violet
– Bird of paradise
– Ficus
– Gardenia
– Grape ivy
– Orchids
– Poinsettia (despite reputation)
– Rubber tree
– Spider plant
– Wandering Jew
– Wax plant
– Zebra plant
r Collect seeds, leaves, spores in paper bag.
r Contact local botanist.
r Syrup of ipecac is not recommended
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Airway, breathing, and circulation management
(ABCs)
r 0.9% normal saline IV:
– Aggressive volume replacement for
dehydration/hypotension
– Initiate pressors for hypotension unresponsive to
fluids
r Cardiac monitoring
r Supportive care for most ingestions
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Supportive care
r Rare plants necessitate focused/antidotal therapy
Anticholinergicr Benzodiazepines for agitation
r Consider physostigmine for severe agitated delirium
Cardioactive Steroids
Digoxin-specific Fab indicated in:
r Significant bradycardia
r Tachydysrhythmia
r Hyperkalemia
Nicotine-like Alkaloidsr Parenteral short-acting antihypertensives such as
nitroprusside for hypertensive crisis
r Treat seizures with benzodiazepines.
Cyanogenic Compoundsr Correction of electrolyte abnormalities
r Hydroxocobalamin or prepackaged cyanide antidote
kit if severe lactic acidosis or hemodynamic
compromise
Calcium Oxalate Crystalsr For mild symptoms, popsicles may decrease burning
r Viscous lidocaine and analgesics for more severe
oral exposure
r Copious irrigation for ocular, oropharyngeal, and
dermal exposure
Pyrrolizidine Alkaloidsr Supportive care
r Removal from source. Pyrrolizidine alkaloids have
been found in herbal medication products as well as
food contaminants
r Liver-specific management in conjunction with
hepatologist
Sodium Channel Activatorsr Atropine for bradycardia and atrioventricular blocks
r Normal saline bolus for hypotension, or vasopressor
therapy if normal saline fails
Toxalbumins
Supportive care based on clinical symptoms: Replace
GI losses with intravenous fluids, replete electrolytes.
MEDICATIONr Atropine: 0.5 mg (peds: 0.02 mg/kg) IV , repeat
0.5–1 mg IV
r Cyanide antidote kit:
– Inhale amyl nitrite ampule for 30 sec every minute
until sodium nitrite given.
– Sodium nitrite: 10 mL of 3% solution or 300 mg
IV over 3–5 min (peds: 0.15–0.33 mL/kg):
◦Monitor methemoglobin levels to keep <30%.
– Sodium thiosulfate: 50 mL IV of 25% solution or
12.5 g (peds: 1.65 mL/kg)
r Digoxin Fab fragments: Empiric dose 5–10 vials
r Hydroxocobalamin: 5 g IV for adults; 70 mg/kg not
to exceed 5 g IV for pediatrics
r Magnesium: 2–4 g IV
r Physostigmine: 0.5–2 mg IV
r Sodium bicarbonate 8.4%: 1 amp IV push until
narrowing of QRS complex
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Dysrhythmias for cardiac monitoring
r Intractable vomiting
r Refractory hypotension
r Evidence of end-organ damage (e.g., hepatic
dysfunction, acidosis) or concern for potential for
end-organ damage
r Altered mental status
Discharge Criteriar Baseline mental status
r Tolerating oral fluids
r Normal cardiac activity
r Delayed sequelae not anticipated
Pediatric Considerations
Lower threshold to admit children:
r Tend to eat more concentrated parts of plants
r Lower lethal dose
r Symptoms less specific
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Follow-up with medical toxicologist or primary care
physician
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Death from unintentional plant exposures is rare.
r Intentional exposures from herbal remedies,
attempted abuse or therapeutic misadventures can
be deadly.
r Contact your regional poison center if concerned
about a patient ingesting a potentially poisonous
plant: 1-800-222-1222

PLEURAL EFFUSION
Sierra Beck rSteven M. Lindsey
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Normal conditions:
– Pleural space contains 0.1–0.2 mL/kg (30 mL in
an adult) of clear, low-protein fluid that facilitates
movement of the pulmonary parenchyma within
the thoracic space.
– Fluid formation and reabsorption are governed by
hydrostatic and oncotic forces.
– Normally, the sum of these forces results in
movement of fluid into the pleural space from the
parietal surface and reabsorption at the visceral
surface.
– Lymphatics help remove any excess fluid.
r Alteration of any of the above factors results in
abnormal fluid accumulation.
r Classification:
– Transudative effusion:
◦An ultrafiltrate of serum, containing low protein
and cells
◦Results from increase in hydrostatic pressure
and/or decrease in oncotic pressure
◦Pleural surface is not involved in the primary
pathologic process.
– Exudative effusion:
◦Contains high protein and cells
◦Results from pathologic disease of the pleural
surface leading to membrane permeability
and/or disruption of lymphatic reabsorption
ETIOLOGYr Transudative effusions:
– Congestive heart failure (CHF)
– Peritoneal dialysis
– Cirrhosis with ascites
– Pulmonary embolism
– Acute atelectasis
– Nephrotic syndrome
– Myxedema
– Hypoproteinemia
– Superior vena cava syndrome
– Meigs syndrome:
◦Triad of ascites, benign ovarian tumor, and
pleural effusion
r Exudative effusions:
– Pulmonary or pleural infection:
◦Bacterial, viral, fungal, tuberculosis (TB),
parasitic
– Primary lung cancer
– Mesothelioma
– Metastasis (often from breast cancer, ovarian
cancer, or lymphoma)
– Pericarditis
– Pulmonary embolism
r Intra-abdominal disorders:
– Pancreatitis, hepatitis, cholecystitis
– Subdiaphragmatic abscess
– Esophageal rupture
– Peritonitis
– Meigs syndrome
r Rheumatologic disease:
– Systemic lupus erythematosus
– Rheumatoid arthritis
– Sarcoidosis
r Trauma:
– Hemothorax
– Chylothorax
r Drugs:
– Drug-induced lupus
– Nitrofurantoin, methysergide, dantrolene,
amiodarone, bromocriptine
– Crack cocaine
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Small effusions are often asymptomatic.
r Dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and/or cough
r Tachypnea, hypoxia, decreased breath sounds,
and/or dullness to percussion
Historyr Underlying primary pathologic process (CHF ,
pneumonia, pulmonary embolus, pancreatitis) is
often the source of complaints.
r Dyspnea on exertion or at rest
r Cough with large effusion
r Pleuritic chest pain with inflammation of pleura
r Empyema: Fever, fatigue, weight loss
Physical Examr Decreased breath sounds
r Decreased tactile fremitus
r Increased egophony for large effusions
r Dullness to chest percussion
r Pleural friction rub
r Examine for the primary cause of pleural effusion.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Cardiac monitor and pulse oximetry
r CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation
panel
r Chest radiography
r Search for underlying cause
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC
r Electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, glucose, serum lactate
dehydrogenase (LDH), serum protein
r Pulse oximetry or arterial blood gas
r Coagulation panel
r Pleural fluid analysis to determine if transudative or
exudative effusion:
– Check pleural protein and LDH levels.
– Light criteria: Fluid is likely exudative if 1 or more
of the following criteria are met:
◦Pleural fluid protein/serum protein >0.5
◦Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH >0.6
◦Pleural fluid LDH >2/3 upper limit of normal
serum LDH
r If effusion is transudative, no further fluid analysis is
usually necessary.
r Determining etiology of exudative effusion:
– Initial testing: Cell count with differential, Gram
stain and culture, acid fast bacilli stain, pH,
glucose, and cytology
– Based on clinical scenario consider: Triglycerides,
amylase, albumin, creatinine, adenosine
deaminase, and tumor markers.
– RBC and Hct:
◦5,000–100,000/mm3 nonspecific
◦>100,000/mm3 suggestive of malignancy,
trauma, or pulmonary embolus
◦Pleural fluid Hct >0.5 serum Hct is by definition
a hemothorax.
◦Other causes: Malignancy, TB, aortic rupture
◦Heparinize and chill hemorrhagic samples to be
sent for cytology.
– WBC:
◦1,000–10,000/mm3 nonspecific
◦>10,000/mm3 suggestive of parapneumonic
effusion, empyema, pancreatitis, rheumatologic,
malignancy, or TB
– Glucose:
◦Glucose <60 mg/dL suggestive of complicated
parapneumonic effusion/empyema, malignancy,
esophageal rupture, or rheumatologic disease
– Triglyceride:
◦Triglycerides>100 mg/dL suggestive of
chylothorax, disruption of thoracic duct
– Amylase:
◦Amylase >200 IU/L suggestive of pancreatitis,
esophageal rupture, malignancy, TB, or
empyema
– pH:
◦Send in a chilled heparinized arterial blood gas
syringe.
◦pH < 7 suggests complicated parapneumonic
effusion or empyema
– Cytology identifies malignant cells.
Imagingr Chest radiograph:
– Upright chest film:
◦Blunting of the costophrenic angle
◦Requires at least 200–250 mL of fluid
◦Presence of subpulmonic effusions may be
indicated by loss of supradiaphragmatic vascular
markings or an increased space between the
gastric bubble and pulmonary parenchyma.
– Lateral decubitus film:
◦Can identify as little as 5–10 mL of fluid.
◦Suspect a loculated effusion or alternative
diagnosis if effusion fails to layer.
r US:
– Has similar sensitivity to lateral decubitus film and
can detect as little as 5–10 mL of fluid.
– Can differentiate simple effusions from loculated
fluid collections.
– Improves patient safety and decreases risk of
pneumothorax for thoracentesis
r CT chest with IV contrast:
– Most sensitive study for detecting pleural fluid
collections and identifying loculated effusions.
– Useful for determination of underlying lung
process such as masses and pleural thickening
ALERT
r Consider pulmonary embolism as a cause of
unexplained pleural effusion
r Obtain lateral decubitus films, or bedside US prior
to performing thoracentesis to avoid misdiagnosis
and procedural complications.

PLEURAL EFFUSION
P
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Diagnostic/therapeutic ED thoracentesis:
r Indication:
– Diagnose new effusion in a toxic patient.
– Relieve symptomatic dyspnea caused by large
effusions.
– Diagnostic thoracentesis in a stable patient can be
deferred until after the patient has been admitted.
r No absolute contraindications.
r Relative contraindications:
– Platelets <50,000/mm3
– Prothrombin and partial thromboplastin time >2
× normal level
– Serum creatinine >6
r Correct coagulopathy if present.
r Position patient upright with arms crossed in front
to elevate scapula.
r Identify superior border of effusion with US,
percussion, or egophony.
r Mark area 1 interspace below this in the posterior
axillary line or the midscapular line.
r Prepare area with Betadine, dry, and drape for
sterile field.
r Anesthetize with 2% lidocaine.
r Attach 3-way stopcock between needle and syringe.
Enter superior border of rib with needle bevel down,
aspirating while advancing.
r Use 20G needle for diagnostic aspiration.
r Use 16G–18G needle/catheter (commercial kit) for
therapeutic aspiration.
r Advance catheter once pleural space entered.
r Minimum of 100 cc required for basic studies
(protein, LDH, cell count, Gram stain and
culture)—more for cytology/additional studies.
r Avoid withdrawing >1,500 cc to prevent
re-expansion pulmonary edema.
r Intraprocedural chest pain may indicate trapped
lung or pneumothorax; stop procedure and obtain
chest radiograph.
r After obtaining fluid, withdraw needle, apply
pressure, dress, and obtain post procedural chest
radiograph for pneumothorax.
r Indications for tube thoracostomy:
– Loculated effusion
– Aspiration of pus
– Complicated parapneumonic effusion with pH
< 7, or pleural glucose <60 mg/dL, or positive
pleural Gram stain or culture
– Hemothorax
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Intraparenchymal densities:
– Lobar collapse
– Mass, tumor, infiltrative disease
– Pneumonia
r Pleural densities:
– Pleural scaring
– Mesothelioma, metastatic disease
r Other:
– Herniated abdominal contents
– Paralyzed diaphragm
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
IV access, high-flow oxygen, cardiac monitor, and
pulse oximeter.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs
r High-flow oxygen for shortness of breath
r Emergent thoracentesis for significant respiratory
compromise.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Identify and treat underlying pathologic process
r Surgical consult for tube thoracostomy if empyema
found.
r Consult interventional radiology or pulmonology for
loculated effusions.
MEDICATIONr CHF: Diuresis
r Parapneumonic effusion: Antibiotics
r Pulmonary embolism: Anticoagulation:
– Bloody effusion is not a contraindication to
anticoagulation.
r Rheumatologic disease: NSAIDs and steroids
r Loculated effusion: Injection of streptokinase or
urokinase into pleural space by thoracic surgeon or
pulmonologist
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Respiratory compromise
r Unknown cause of the effusion
r Primary process requires hospitalization
r Presence or suspected parapneumonic effusion or
empyema
r Observation for 6 hr or admission for potential
complications of thoracentesis:
– Pneumothorax
– Re-expansion pulmonary edema
r ICU admission for severe hemodynamic and
respiratory compromise
Discharge Criteriar Source of the pleural effusion is known.
r No evidence of respiratory compromise exists.
r Majority of effusions will resolve if the primary
process is treated appropriately.
r Patient must be reliable and have access to a
telephone, a supportive social environment, and
adequate follow-up.
Issues for Referral
Arrange appropriate follow-up with oncologist or
pulmonologist prior to discharge.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Patients should be instructed to return to the ED for
worsening dyspnea, fever/chills, or other symptoms of
respiratory distress.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r The most common causes of pleural effusion are
CHF , pneumonia, and malignancy.
r Identify and treat the underlying cause of the pleural
effusion.
r Bedside US can help characterize the effusion and
reduce the risk of pneumothorax with thoracentesis.
r Failure to identify fatal causes of pleural effusion
such as pulmonary embolism, esophageal rupture,
or hemothorax
r Failure to drain large effusions that are causing
respiratory or circulatory compromise
ADDITIONAL READING

Clinical Procedures in Emergency Medicine. 5th ed.
Philadelphia, PA: Saunders Elsevier; 2009.

Pneumothorax following thoracentesis: A systematic
review and meta-analysis. Arch Intern Med. 2010;
170(4):332–339.

Practice. 7th ed. Philadelphia, PA: Mosby Elsevier;

PNEUMOCYSTIS PNEUMONIA
Alan M. Kumar
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Originally called Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia,
then renamed Pneumocystis jirovecii but still
referred to as PCP
r Most common opportunistic infection in patients
with HIV , even with PCP prophylaxis and
antiretroviral therapy
r Believed to be transmitted by respiratory-aerosol
route:
– Cysts colonize respiratory tract.
– Cysts rupture and multiple trophozoites release
and form foamy exudate in alveoli.
r Most cases are believed to represent reactivation of
latent disease, although person-to-person
transmission suggested.
r Actual mode of transmission is unclear.
ETIOLOGYr Pneumocystis is classified as a fungus.
r Pneumocystis occurs in hosts with altered cellular
immunity:
– HIV infection (most common, especially when CD4
count <200 cells/mm3)
– Cancer
– Corticosteroid treatment
– Organ transplantation
– Malnutrition
Pediatric Considerations
PCP in children is typically more severe.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Subacute presentation
r Up to 7% of patients can be asymptomatic.
r Patients on inhaled pentamidine prophylaxis may
have milder symptoms:
– Increased incidence of pneumothorax
– Increased incidence of extrapulmonary disease
Historyr Fever
r Cough with none or minimal amount of white
sputum
r Dyspnea on exertion or at rest:
– Progressive over days (most common in
non–HIV-immunocompromised hosts)
– Indolent, developing over weeks to months (more
common in HIV-positive hosts)
– Oxygen desaturation with exercise
r Chills
r Fatigue
r Weight loss
r Chest pain
Physical Examr Tachypnea
r Tachycardia
r Crackles and rhonchi on lung exam
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr CBC
r Electrolytes
r Arterial blood gas (ABG)
r Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
r Blood cultures
r Chest x-ray
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr ABG:
– Obtain in all cases of PCP .
– Calculate the alveolar–arterial (A–a) gradient
(usually increased).
– Adjunctive corticosteroid therapy for A–a gradient
>35 mm Hg or PaO2 <70 mm Hg
r LDH:
– Elevated in HIV-positive patients with PCP
compared to non-PCP pneumonia
– Higher levels correlate with poorer prognosis.
Imagingr Chest radiograph:
– Classically reveals bilateral interstitial or central
alveolar infiltrates
– Radiograph normal in up to 25% of patients with
PCP
– Early or mild infection associated with decreased
sensitivity
– Atypical presentations include:
◦Lobar infiltrates
◦Cysts
◦Pneumothoraces
◦Pleural effusions
◦Nodular infiltrates
– Prophylaxis with aerosolized pentamidine is a risk
factor for developing predominantly upper lobe.
– Chest radiograph abnormalities can persist for
months after treatment.
r High-resolution chest CT:
– High sensitivity for PCP in HIV-positive patients.
– Reveals patchy ground-glass attenuation
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Induced sputum:
– Definitive diagnosis requires presence of
Pneumocystis organisms in an appropriately
stained respiratory specimen.
– Specificity approaches 100%, but sensitivity
depends on quality of induced sputum and lab
expertise.
– Less sensitive in patients on inhaled pentamidine
prophylaxis and non–HIV-positive patients
r Bronchoalveolar lavage:
– Perform if the induced sputum is nondiagnostic
and the suspicion for PCP is still high.
– Sensitivity 80–100%
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
Constellation of dyspnea, fever, diffuse radiographic
infiltrates, minimal or nonproductive cough, and slow
progressive course suggests atypical cause of the
pneumonia:
r Chlamydia pneumoniae
r Legionella
r Mycoplasma
r Tuberculosis
r Viral pneumonia (especially cytomegalovirus)
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Provide supplemental oxygen for symptomatic
patients.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs
r Provide adequate oxygenation with nasal cannula
up to 100% nonrebreather.
r Perform endotracheal intubation in those with
refractory hypoxemia despite maximal oxygenation
or hypercarbic respiratory failure.
r At least 500–1,000 cc 0.9% normal saline IV bolus
for hypotension, sepsis, dehydration

P
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Initiate antibiotics:
– IV Bactrim is the first-line agent.
– IV pentamidine for those who cannot tolerate
Bactrim
– Oral therapy is an option for well-appearing
patients.
– Alternative regimens include
trimethoprim–dapsone, clindamycin–primaquine,
and atovaquone.
– Continue antibiotics for 21 days.
r Adjunctive corticosteroids in patients with A–a
gradient >35 mm Hg or PaO2 <70 mm Hg:
– Must start within 1st 72 hr of treatment
r Isolate suspected PCP patients from others who are
immunocompromised.
MEDICATIONr Atovaquone: 750 mg (peds: Dosing not established)
PO q12h
r Clindamycin/primaquine: Clindamycin 900 mg
(peds: Dosing not established) IV q8h or
300–450 mg PO q6h and primaquine 15–30 mg
(peds: Dosing not established) PO per day
r Pentamidine: 4 mg/kg/24h IV over 1 hr (peds:
3–4 mg/kg IM or IV once/day for 21 days)
r Prednisone: 40 mg (peds: Dosing not established)
PO q12h for 5 days, 40 mg PO per day for 5 days,
then 20 mg PO per day for 11 days (IV
methylprednisolone at 75% of the prednisone dose
may be substituted)
r Trimethoprim/dapsone: Trimethoprim 15–20 mg/kg/
d IV div. q8h + dapsone 100 mg PO per day (peds:
Dosing not established)
r Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim):
Trimethoprim 15–20 mg/kg/d IV div. q6h and
sulfamethoxazole 100 mg/kg/d IV div. q6h (peds:
Dosing same)
Pediatric Considerations
r Treatment of choice is IV
trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, followed by IV
pentamidine.
r Dosing for alternative medications not yet
established (consult pediatric infectious disease
specialist).
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Moderate to severe disease (PaO2 <70 mm Hg or
A–a gradient >35 mm Hg)
r Inability to digest medications
r Inability to return for careful follow-up
Discharge Criteriar Nontoxic clinical appearance
r Mild disease state (no hypoxemia or A–a gradient)
r Ability to tolerate medications
r Close follow-up arranged
r If results of induced sputum are not available, add
macrolide to empirical regimen.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Close follow-up must be arranged with infectious
disease specialist to allow for outpatient
management.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Include PCP in differential diagnosis in any patient
presenting with shortness of breath who is
immunocompromised or is suspected of having
undiagnosed HIV .
r Patients considered for PCP are also more likely to
have TB or atypical bacterial pneumonia.
r Well-appearing patients with low oxygen
saturations are at higher risk for complications.

PNEUMOMEDIASTINUM
Matthew D. Bitner
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Presence of free air or gas within the mediastinum
(mediastinal emphysema)
r May originate from esophagus, lungs, or bronchial
tree (aerodigestive process)
r May occur spontaneously (primary
pneumomediastinum) or as result of trauma,
surgery, or other pathologic processes (secondary
pneumomediastinum)
r Spontaneous pneumomediastinum:
– Caused by extrapleural tracheobronchial injury:
◦Increased intra-alveolar pressure, low
perivascular pressures, or both
◦Terminal alveolar rupture into the lung
interstitium and bronchovascular tissue sheath
◦Dissection of air into the hilum and subsequently
the mediastinum along a pressure gradient
◦Mediastinal air then dissects into the fascial
planes, most commonly into the tissues of the
neck.
– Often in setting of a Valsalva maneuver, forceful
vomiting, in association with bronchospasm or
inhalational drug use
– Men > women (2:1 in some series)
– Young > old (most common in 2nd/3rd decades
of life in most series)
– Pediatric patients have a bimodal age distribution
of peak incidence (<7 and 13–17 yr)
r Relatively rare, 1/30,000–50,000 hospital
admissions
ETIOLOGYr Primary or spontaneous pneumomediastinum:
– Associated with forced Valsalva maneuvers:
◦Forceful vomiting
◦Forceful straining during exercise
◦Straining during defecation
◦Coughing/sneezing
◦Intense screaming
◦Labor and delivery
◦Playing wind instruments
◦Pulmonary function testing
◦Anorexia nervosa
◦Obesity
◦Pre-existing lung disorders (interstitial lung
disease, pulmonary fibrosis, pneumonitis)
◦Illicit inhalation drug use (marijuana, cocaine,
methamphetamine)
◦Tobacco abuse
– A majority of cases will have no identified
precipitating event/cause
– Has been rarely described after dental
extraction/procedures.
r Secondary pneumomediastinum:
– Secondary to thoracic barotrauma
– Common traumatic mechanisms:
◦Motor vehicle collision
◦Fall
◦Blows to chest or neck
◦Recent esophageal/tracheobronchial
instrumentation
– Positive-pressure ventilation
– Esophageal rupture (Boerhaave syndrome)
– In association with mediastinal infection caused
by gas-forming organisms
r Tension pneumomediastinum:
– Rare but life-threatening event
– Usually in patients on positive-pressure ventilation
r May be associated with pneumopericardium and/or
extension of a pneumothorax/tension pneumothorax
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Chest pain (most common symptom in multiple
series):
– Sharp
– Pleuritic
– Retrosternal
– Radiating to back and arms
– Often positional
r Dyspnea
r Neck pain:
– Occurs in association with dissection of air into
soft tissues of neck
– Often described as “neck swelling,” “neck pain,”
“throat pain,” or “difficulty swallowing”
r SC emphysema:
– Most commonly located at the supraclavicular
area and anterior neck
r Dysphagia/odynophagia
r Dysphonia/hoarseness
r Hamman crunch: Presence of a precordial crinkling
or crepitance during systole:
– Uncommon but pathognomonic
– Best heard with patient in left lateral decubitus
position
r Meckler triad (esophageal rupture): Vomiting, lower
chest pain, and cervical SC emphysema following
overindulgence of food or alcohol
Historyr Inhalational drug use
r Asthma exacerbation
r Pre-existing lung disorders
r Forceful vomiting (such as in diabetic ketoacidosis
[DKA], or hyperemesis)
r Preceding strenuous athletic activity
Physical Examr SC emphysema
r Hamman crunch
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Exclude secondary causes, notably esophageal
rupture.
r Chest radiography
r Chest CT (if high index of suspicion)
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
CBC if there is suspicion of mediastinitis (the most
concerning consequence of esophageal rupture, with
high morbidity and mortality)
Imagingr CXR:
– Most valuable initial test
– Important to include lateral view because
mediastinal air is often missed on
posterior–anterior view
– Aids in excluding pneumothorax,
pneumopericardium
– Identification of a pleural effusion or parenchymal
infiltrate may suggest an esophageal rupture.
– Negative in up to 30–35% of cases
– Spinnaker sail sign or “angel wing” sign
(produced by air lifting the thymus off the heart
and major vessels)
– Continuous diaphragm sign (air collecting
between the diaphragm and the pericardium)
– SC or superior mediastinal emphysema
r Chest CT:
– Imaging test of choice if suspicion is high but CXR
is negative (CXR has high false-negative rate)
r Esophagram with water-soluble contrast material:
– Study of choice to exclude diagnosis of
esophageal rupture
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Esophagoscopy:
– Limited usefulness (overutilized)
– May be used to further delineate injuries identified
with CT and/or esophagram
r Laryngoscopy/bronchoscopy:
– Limited usefulness (overutilized)
– May be used to exclude diagnosis of
laryngeal/tracheobronchial injury
r Pericardiocentesis:
– Only in the setting of tension pneumopericardium
in the crashing patient
r Tube thoracostomy:
– Only in the setting of concomitant pneumothorax
of sufficient size, or one that is rapidly progressing
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Aortic dissection
r Coronary ischemia
r Esophageal diverticula
r Esophageal webs
r Mediastinitis
r Myocarditis
r Pericarditis
r Pneumonia
r Pneumopericardium
r Pneumothorax/tension pneumothorax
r Pulmonary embolus
r Schatzki rings

TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Resuscitation of the acutely ill patient (as in the
patient with septic mediastinitis)
r In the appropriate setting, standard care of the
trauma patient
r Withhold PO intake
r Rapid patient evolution and transport to an
appropriate facility
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr IV access
r Oxygen
r Cardiac monitoring
r Pulse oximetry
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Spontaneous pneumomediastinum:
– Usually a benign, self-limiting condition
– Does not require specific treatment
– Efforts should focus on pain relief and reassurance
once diagnosis is confirmed.
– High-flow oxygen may facilitate the reabsorption
of nitrogen and provide comfort.
– Withhold PO intake if suspected esophageal
source (pending diagnostic studies)
– Condition is self-limiting and may be expected to
resolve over 2–5 days.
r Secondary pneumomediastinum:
– Once diagnosis is made, direct invasive diagnostic
modalities toward the most likely underlying cause
(esophagoscopy, laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy).
– Direct therapy toward underlying cause.
MEDICATIONr Treat underlying cause aggressively (e.g., asthma
exacerbation or DKA).
r Oxygen 15 L via nonrebreather mask
r Analgesia (non-narcotic and narcotic as necessary)
r Antibiotics have limited use, but in the setting of
concern for mediastinitis use broad-spectrum
coverage to include GI flora, resistant organisms,
and Pseudomonas:
– Vancomycin 10–15 mg/kg IV q12h and
– Piperacillin/tazobactam 3.375–4.5 g IV q6h and
– Clindamycin 600–900 mg IV q8h or
Metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Secondary pneumomediastinum
r Associated pneumothorax
r Possibility of esophageal rupture has not been
excluded
r Abnormal vital signs
r Ill/toxic-appearing patient
r Intractable pain
r Underlying disorder requires admission (asthma
exacerbation, exacerbation of lung disorder, DKA).
r Social situation prevents compliance or follow-up
r Extremes of age (pediatric and elderly)
r Immunosuppression
r Failure of outpatient management
Discharge Criteriar Spontaneous pneumomediastinum
r Normal vital signs
r No pneumothorax
r No significant comorbidities
r Period of observation in the ED with resolution of
symptoms
r Close outpatient follow-up
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Patients should be followed up for re-evaluation of
clinical symptoms and imaging for resolution of the
process.
r Recurrent spontaneous pneumomediastinum may
warrant cardiothoracic consultation for further
diagnostic evaluation (invasive studies).
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Ensure that underlying causes are excluded.
r Be aware of typical presenting features (chest pain,
dyspnea, and neck swelling), pre-existing
conditions, and precipitating factors associated with
pneumomediastinum.
r Hamman crunch is pathognomonic but not
commonly seen.
r Remember Meckler triad:
– Vomiting
– Lower chest pain
– Cervical SC emphysema

patients. J Trauma. 2008;65(6):1340–1345.

pneumomediastinum. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg.

PNEUMONIA, ADULT
Jason C. Imperato
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Epidemiology:
– 7th leading cause of death and leading cause
from infectious disease in US
r Highest mortality in elderly and patients with the
following coexisting conditions:
– Chronic heart, lung, liver, and kidney disease
– Diabetes mellitus
– Alcoholism
– Malignancy
– Asplenia
– Immunosuppression
– Use of antimicrobials within last 3 mo
r Classifications:
– Source based:
◦Community acquired (CAP)
◦Health care associated (HCAP)
◦Hospital acquired (HAP)
◦Ventilator associated (VAP)
– Symptom based:
◦Typical
◦Atypical
r Complications:
– Bacteremia
– Sepsis
– Abscess
– Empyema
– Respiratory failure
ETIOLOGYr CAP (typicals):
– Streptococcus pneumoniae
– Haemophilus influenzae
– Klebsiella pneumoniae
– Moraxella catarrhalis
– Streptococcus pyogenes
– Staphylococcus aureus
r CAP (atypicals):
– Mycoplasma pneumoniae
– Chlamydophila pneumoniae
– Legionella pneumophila
– Viral
r HCAP/HAP/VAP:
– Gram negatives (Pseudomonas,
Stenotrophomonas)
– Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA)
r Immunosuppressed:
– Mycobacterium tuberculosis
– Pneumocystis jirovecii
r Aspiration:
– Chemical pneumonitis ± oral and gastric
anaerobes
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Typical:
– Acute onset
– Fever
– Chills
– Rigors
– Cough
– Purulent sputum
– Shortness of breath
– Pleuritic chest pain
r Atypical:
– Subacute onset
– Viral prodrome
– Nonproductive cough
– Low-grade fever
– Headache
– Myalgias
– Malaise
– Absence of pleurisy and rigors
Physical Examr Vital signs:
– Tachypnea
– Tachycardia
– Hypoxia
– Fever
r Pulmonary exam:
– Dullness to percussion
– Tactile fremitus
– Egophony
– Rales
– Rhonchi
– Decreased breath sounds
r Note that pneumonia may be present in the absence
of the above signs of consolidation.
Geriatric Considerations
r Elderly patients have higher morbidity and mortality
from pneumonia.
r Atypical presentations are more common.
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Combination of clinical and radiographic diagnosis
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr General:
– CBC with differential
– Serum chemistry
r Others:
– Blood cultures (ICU only)
– Sputum cultures and Gram stain (ICU only)
– Urine antigen tests forS. pneumoniae & Legionella
– C-reactive protein possibly helpful
– Lactate may be helpful
– Influenza viral test
Imaging
Chest radiograph:
r General:
– Findings are nonspecific for particular infectious
etiologies.

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Mechanism is often unknown.
r Source is oropharyngeal aspiration (most common)
or hematogenous.
r Distribution depends on the organism: Interstitial
(Mycoplasma pneumoniae, virus), lobar
(Streptococcus pneumoniae), abscesses
(Staphylococcus aureus), or diffuse (Pneumocystis
carinii)
ETIOLOGYr <2 wk:
– Group B Streptococcus species
– Enteric gram-negative organisms
– Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)
– Herpes simplex virus
– S. aureus
r 2 wk–3 mo:
– Chlamydia trachomatis
– Parainfluenza virus
– RSV
– S. pneumoniae
– S. aureus
– H. influenza
– Bordetella pertussis
r 3 mo–8 yr:
– Viral (predominate):
◦RSV
◦Parainfluenza virus
◦Influenza virus
◦Adenovirus
– S. pneumoniae
– H. influenza in unimmunized children
– Group A streptococcus
– S. aureus
– B. pertussis
r >8 yr:
– M. pneumoniae most common
– Viral
– S. pneumoniae
r Recent immigrants from developing countries:
– Mycoplasma tuberculosis
– H. influenza
– B. pertussis
r Immunocompromised (e.g., HIV , cancer):
– P. carinii
– Mycoplasma avium complex
– M. tuberculosis
– Klebsiella pneumoniae
– Pseudomonas aeruginosa
r Less common:
– Fungal (coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis)
– Rickettsia (Q fever)
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr General (in all ages):
– Cough
– Rales
– Fever
– Hypoxia
– Tachycardia
– Tachypnea, retractions, grunting
– Rash (up to 10% of cases); usually maculopapular
– Nonspecific symptoms of toxicity
– Pulmonary exam:
◦Decreased breath sounds, ventilation
◦Dullness to percussion
◦Wheezing, ronchi, rales
r Infants <6 mo:
– Altered behavior: Listless, irritable
– Apnea (esp. RSV in premature infants)
– Conjunctivitis (Chlamydia <1 mo old)
– Cyanosis
– Grunting
– Poor feeding
– Temperature instability
(hypothermia/hyperthermia)
– Vomiting, often with coughing
– Cough
– Nasal congestion
– Nasal flaring
– Wheezing
– Staccato cough (Chlamydia)
r Children >5 yr:
– Pleuritic chest pain
– Productive cough
– Rigors, chills

r Past medical history include immune status
r Exposures
r Progression of signs and symptoms
Physical Examr Pulmonary exam may be helpful, particularly in
children >5y r .
r Peripheral and central cyanosis should be assessed.
r Evidence of respiratory compromise, distress, failure
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Pulse oximetry
r Chest radiograph:
– Gold standard for diagnosis
– Should be ordered for patients with signs of lower
respiratory tract infection and patients <36 mo
old with marked leukocytosis or neutrophilia
(WBC >15,000 or absolute neutrophil count
[ANC] >9,000).
– Much overlap between viral and bacterial findings
– Viral and M. pneumoniae tend to show interstitial
infiltrates, often perihilar and peribronchial.
– Bacterial pneumonias may show focal lobar
consolidation, focal alveolar infiltrates, and
possibly effusion or pneumatocele.
– Round pneumonia pathognomonic of S.
pneumonia
– Lateral decubitus films may aid in demonstrating
effusion.

Labr CBC with differential:
– Patients with bacteremia tend to have
leukocytosis with left shift.
– Sensitivity and specificity are poor.
– Patients with WBC ≥20,000 or ANC >9,000 are
at increased risk of pneumococcal bacteremia.
– B. pertussis usually has elevated WBC with
lymphocytosis.
r Blood culture:
– Low yield (<10–20%)
– Recommended in children <36 mo
– Probably worthwhile in toxic patients requiring
hospitalization
r Arterial blood gas may be useful in determining
degree of respiratory insufficiency in critically ill
patients.
r Electrolytes to exclude syndrome of inappropriate
antidiuretic hormone secretion and in hypotensive
children
r Sputum for Gram stain and culture may be obtained
in older children with suspected bacterial infection.

– Useful if suspecting this organism
– More likely positive with severe illness
r Nasopharyngeal washes for direct fluorescent
antibody and culture:
– Identify RSV ,C. trachomatis, and B. pertussis
infections
Imaging
Chest radiographs are still the imaging modality of
choice:
r Posteroanterior and lateral films should be obtained
whenever possible.
r CT provides additional detail and better
identification of underlying lung pathology but adds
little as an initial testing modality.

Pleural fluid (if present) for culture, Gram stain,

– Foreign body
– Hydrocarbon
r Congestive heart failure
r Congenital:
– Cystic fibrosis
– Sequestered lobe
– Congenital lobe absence
– Hemangioma
r Neoplasm

PNEUMOTHORAX
William Porcaro
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Presence of free air in the intrapleural space
r Spontaneous pneumothorax is due to atraumatic
rupture of alveolus, bronchiole, or bleb.
r Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (2/3 of
incidences):
– No underlying pulmonary pathology present
– Rupture of small subpleural cyst or bleb
– Primarily young, healthy patients (20–40 yr old)
with tall, thin body habitus
– Risk factors: Smoking, family history, Marfan
syndrome, homocystinuria, thoracic endometriosis
r Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax from
underlying pulmonary pathology (see Etiology)
r Tension pneumothorax:
– Air continues to enter pleural space through
bronchoalveolar disruption and becomes trapped
via “ball-valve” mechanism.
– Intrapleural pressure increases.
– Venous return to right heart decreases, resulting in
decrease in cardiac output.
– Mediastinum shifts toward uninvolved side,
mechanically interfering with right atrial filling.
– Ventilation compromise and ventilation/perfusion
mismatch result in hypoxemia
ETIOLOGYr Idiopathic
r Airway disease:
– Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
– Asthma
– Cystic fibrosis
r Infections:
– Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia
–T B
– Fungal pneumonia
– Pneumocystis carinii
r Neoplasm
r Interstitial lung disease:
– Sarcoidosis
– Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
– Lymphangiomyomatosis
– Tuberous sclerosis
– Pneumoconioses
r Connective tissue diseases
r Pulmonary infarction
r Endometriosis
r Blunt chest trauma
r Penetrating trauma to neck or trunk
r Iatrogenic:
– Central line placement
– Other vascular access procedures
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Severity of symptoms is generally proportional to
size of the pneumothorax.
r Chest pain on the ipsilateral side:
– Sharp, pleuritic pain
– Sudden onset
– Dull ache in delayed presentations
r Shortness of breath
r Rarely cough, asymptomatic, or generalized malaise
Physical Examr Tachypnea
r Heart rate <120 bpm generally seen in simple
spontaneous pneumothoraces
r Jugular venous distention and tracheal deviation to
the contralateral side may be evident in tension
pneumothorax.
r Cardiac and pulmonary exam:
– Asymmetric decreased breath sounds
– Hyperresonance to percussion of ipsilateral side
r Tension pneumothorax:
– Hypotension
– Tachycardia, heart rate>120 bpm
– Diaphoresis
– Cyanosis
– Cardiovascular collapse
– Tracheal deviation
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Imaging is mainstay of the workup
r DO NOT delay chest decompression if the patient is
hemodynamically unstable and there is sufficient
clinical evidence of pneumothorax.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Arterial blood gas offers little over oxygen saturation.
Imagingr Chest radiograph:
– Upright chest radiograph
r Patients unable to tolerate upright chest radiograph
can be taken in decubitus position with the
suspected side up:
– Absence of lung markings distal or peripheral to
the visceral pleural white line
– Displacement of mediastinum or anterior junction
line
– Deep sulcus sign
r On frontal view, larger lateral costodiaphragmatic
recess than on opposite side
r Diaphragm may be inverted on the side with deep
sulcus:
– A rough estimate of pneumothorax size is
sufficient to make clinical decisions.
r Expiratory film:
– May demonstrate small pneumothorax but has
not been shown to increase yield of detection
r Chest CT:
– Very sensitive for small pneumothorax but has
little practical advantage over chest radiograph
r US:
– User experience required
– Rapid at bedside
– Lack of lung sliding and comet-tail artifact
signifies pneumothorax.
– M-mode confirms pneumothorax with smooth
lines above and below pleural line.
– With experience, sensitivity surpasses chest
radiograph
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
ECG:
r Often necessary to rule out cardiac etiologies of
chest pain
r Nonspecific changes include T-wave inversion, left
axis deviation, and decreased R-wave amplitude.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Acute abdominal processes
r Aortic aneurysm or dissection
r Asthma exacerbation
r Chest wall pain
r COPD exacerbation
r Myocardial infarction
r Pericarditis
r Pleuritis
r Pneumomediastinum
r Pulmonary embolus
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
ALERT
Unstable patients with a suspected tension
pneumothorax require immediate needle
thoracostomy.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Cardiac monitor
r Pulse oximetry
r Oxygen 100% via nonrebreather face mask
r IV access
r Suspected tension pneumothorax requires either
immediate needle thoracostomy or tube
thoracostomy.
r Needle thoracostomy:
– Immediate placement indicated in unstable
patients with a tension pneumothorax
– 14G–18G angiocatheter in the 2nd intercostal
space at midclavicular line or 4th or 5th
intercostal space at anterior axillary line
– NOTE: The length of most standard angiocatheters
is too short to penetrate the pleural cavity in
moderate to large framed patients – longer,
purpose-specific catheters may be required
