PROSTATITIS
Nicole M. Franks
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Acute (bacterial) prostatitis:
– Acute febrile illness
– Systemic symptoms may appear days before
localizing urinary symptoms appear.
– Patients may appear toxic and usually have a
concurrent cystitis.
r Prostatic abscess:
– Once common after acute prostatitis, now rare
except in immunocompromised patients
– Fever, rectal pain, and leukocytosis despite
treatment
– Fluctuant mass on rectal exam
r Chronic bacterial prostatitis:
– ∼10% of cases of prostatitis
– Most common cause of recurrent UTI in men
– WBC and bacteria may be present in expressed
prostatic secretions (EPS).
r Chronic nonbacterial prostatitis (also called
prostatosis):
– Same symptoms as chronic bacterial prostatitis
but unable to culture organisms from urine or EPS
r Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CPPS):
– Symptoms referable to the prostate
– No inflammatory cells are found
– No bacteria cultured from the urine or EPS
ETIOLOGYr Usually a single-organism bacterial infection of the
prostate
r Acute prostatitis:
– Age <35 yr:
◦Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia
trachomatis are usual etiologies.
– Age ≥35 yr:
◦Enterobacteriaceae or Escherichia coli (usual),
Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, and
Proteus also seen
– Rarely may be caused by Salmonella, Clostridia,
tuberculosis, or fungi.
– Cryptococcus neoformans in AIDS patients
r Chronic bacterial prostatitis:
– Enterobacteriaceae (80%), Enterococcus (15%),
and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
r Chronic nonbacterial prostatitis:
– Possible role for Chlamydia, Ureaplasma
urealyticum, Trichomonas vaginalis, and
Mycoplasma hominis
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Irritative voiding symptoms:
– Frequency, urgency, dysuria
r Low back pain
r Perineal, suprapubic, or testicular pain
r Bladder outlet obstruction and urinary retention
r Ejaculatory symptoms such as hematospermia
r Acute prostatitis:
– Fever, chills
– Malaise
– Arthralgias or myalgias
r Primary symptom in chronic prostatitis is relapsing
dysuria.
Physical Examr Acute prostatitis:
– Exquisitely prostate tenderness
– Warm, swollen
– Firm or boggy prostate
– Acutely inflamed prostate should not be
massaged because that may precipitate
hematogenous spread of organisms.
r In chronic prostatitis, the exam is usually normal.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Urinalysis (with microscopy) and culture
r Acute prostatitis:
– CBC, electrolytes, and blood cultures may be
helpful in the acutely ill patient.
–I f <35 yr old or suspected sexual transmission,
test for syphilis:
◦Venereal Disease Research Lab or rapid plasma
reagin
r Chronic prostatitis/CPPS:
– Prostatic massage between voiding may be used
to capture EPS for Gram stain and culture if
organism or white cells not present in the urine.
Imagingr Not indicated in acute prostatitis
r If prostatic abscess suspected, transrectal US or
pelvic CT with IV and rectal contrast will confirm
diagnosis.
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Not applicable in ED
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Benign prostatic hyperplasia
r Cystitis
r Epididymitis
r Orchitis
r Perirectal/perianal abscess
r Proctitis
r Prostatic carcinoma
r Prostatic infarction
r Pyelonephritis
r Seminal vesiculitis
r Urethritis
r Urolithiasis
r Vesicular calculi
r Other causes of lower back pain (strain, disc
disease, sacroiliac joint disease, etc.)
TREATMENT
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Initial resuscitative measures as indicated
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Prostatic abscess requires urgent urologic
consultation and transrectal US-guided aspiration.
r Antibiotic therapy should be initiated in ED (see
Medications).
r Urinary tract instrumentation should be avoided:
– If patient has painful urinary retention in acute
prostatitis, suprapubic needle aspiration or
suprapubic catheter placement should be
performed.
r Many patients will benefit from IV fluid.
r Pain control with NSAIDs and narcotic analgesics as
needed
r Stool softeners
r Bed rest
r Irritative voiding symptoms may persist for months
after antibiotic therapy and may be treated with
NSAIDs.

– Doxazosin: 1 mg PO (immediate release) every day
– Peripheral β-adrenergic blocking agents have

– Terazosin: 1 mg PO qhs

– Patients who appear ill or toxic
– Hypotension
– Urinary retention

– Admission generally not warranted unless patient

– Patient must be nontoxic.
– Able to take fluids and oral medications (analgesia

PRURITUS
Christine Tsien Silvers
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Unpleasant sensation that provokes a desire to
scratch
r Mediated by unmyelinated C fibers in upper portion
of dermis:
– Transmitted to dorsal horn of spinal cord
– Via spinothalamic tract to cerebral cortex
r Peripheral mediators (e.g., histamine and peptides
such as substance P that release histamine)
stimulate C fibers and induce itching
r Prostaglandins (PGE2, PGH2) lower threshold to
pruritus
r Opiates cause pruritus by acting on central receptors
r No single pharmacologic agent effectively treats all
causes of pruritus
r “Itch–scratch–itch” cycle:
– Itching triggers scratching
– Scratching damages skin and stimulates nerve
endings, thereby producing even greater itching
ETIOLOGY
4 categories in proposed itch classification:
r Pruritoceptive: Generated in the skin from localized
irritation or inflammation
r Neurogenic: Generated in the CNS due to circulating
pruritogens
r Neuropathic: Due to CNS or PNS lesions
r Psychogenic
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Onset:
– Shortly after freshwater bathing in swimmer’s itch
– More intense at night with scabies
– Paroxysmal with multiple sclerosis
– With sudden changes in temperature in
polycythemia vera
r Character: Paroxysmal, burning, pricking
r Time of occurrence, duration
r Severity; impact on quality of life
r With or without skin lesions
r Anatomic area (e.g., exposed skin only)
r Exacerbating or alleviating factors (e.g., water, heat,
dryness, dampness, coolness)
r Medications
r New products (e.g., soap, cosmetics, laundry
detergents, fabric softeners)
r Age
r Family history of atopic dermatitis or skin disease
r Personal history of allergies or asthma
r Pruritus in other family members
r Systemic or associated symptoms (e.g., night
sweats, fever, tremors, weight loss, fatigue, jaundice,
anemia, neurologic symptoms)
r Sexual history, history of HIV or AIDS
r Social: Occupation, hobbies, pets, travel
Physical Examr Dermatologic:
– Absence of rash
– Diffuse or localized rash
– Location: Genitals, interdigital webs, axilla, wrists,
etc.
– Generalized morbilliform eruptions
– Discrete weeping patches with vesicles
– Dry skin
– Jaundice
– Follicular (around the hair)
– Nonfollicular (e.g., insect bites, scabies)
– Primary lesions:
◦Papular, pustular, urticarial, or polymorphic
– Secondary lesions:
◦Excoriations
◦Lichenification
◦Hyperpigmentation
◦Prurigo papules: Thickened papular areas of skin
from constant rubbing
r Psychogenic: Constant rubbing in areas patient can
readily reach
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Detailed history is key in the ED workup
r Physical exam to characterize skin lesions
r Look for evidence of systemic disease
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab

PSORIASIS
Allison Tadros rErica B. Shaver
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Chronic, noncontagious, inflammatory skin condition
r Disease of hyperproliferation
r Recently classified as an autoimmune disease
r Presents with erythematous plaques with silver
scaling
r Most commonly affects the elbows, knees, lumbar
area, gluteal cleft, and glans penis
r Up to 1/3 of patients develop associated arthritis
and 10% have ocular manifestations
r Course is unpredictable; marked variability in
severity over time and remissions may be seen
r Exact cause unclear: triggers may be infectious,
stressors, medications, or trauma
r Tends to show improvement in summer months,
possibly related to UV exposure
r Associated with metabolic syndrome
r Caucasians and atopics most affected
r 2 peaks of onset: between ages 20–30 and 50–60
r Affects 2.2% of US population, slightly higher
incidence in females
r Rare cause of mortality, but at least 100 deaths
annually in US related to severe disease and/or
treatment adverse effects
r Several clinical presentations:
– Plaque-type psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris):
◦Most common form (75–80%) with
erythematous, raised plaques with
well-demarcated borders distributed over the
scalp, back, and extensor side of the knees and
elbows
– Guttate psoriasis:
◦Abrupt appearance of multiple, discrete,
salmon-colored, “drop-like” papules with a fine
scale in a patient with no prior history of
psoriasis
◦Most commonly seen on the trunk and proximal
extremities
◦Often preceded by a streptococcal infection and
resolves spontaneously
– Pustular psoriasis:
◦Occasionally isolated to the palms and soles, but
can present as widespread erythema, scaling,
and sheets of superficial pustules with erosions
◦Patient may appear toxic and have other
systemic symptoms, like malaise, fever, and
diarrhea
◦Potentially severe and life threatening and
treated as an inpatient if generalized
– Erythrodermic psoriasis:
◦Generalized erythema and pruritis with a fine
scale
◦Increased risk for infection, dehydration
◦Often treated as inpatients
– Nail psoriasis
◦Pitting over the nail plate or change in nail bed
◦Nail changes in up to 50% of patients
– Inverse flexural psoriasis:
◦A variant that causes lesions in flexural areas
and in skin folds that do not exhibit scaling due
to moisture in these areas
– HIV-induced psoriasis:
◦May be the first manifestation of AIDS, more
frequent and severe in HIV population
r Genetics:
– There is a genetic predisposition and gene loci
have been identified
– 40% of patients with psoriasis have a family
history in a 1st degree relative
ETIOLOGYr Typical findings of erythema and scaling are the
result of increased number of epidermal stem cells
and keratinocyte hyperproliferation, shortened cell
cycles, inflammatory infiltrates, and vascular changes
r Triggers include:
– Drugs:
◦Lithium
◦β-blockers
◦Antimalarials
◦Steroid withdrawal
◦NSAIDs
◦Alcohol
◦Potassium iodide
– Infections:
◦Streptococcal pharyngitis
◦HIV
◦Staph
– Local trauma:
◦Frostbite
◦Sunburn
◦Recent skin trauma (Koebner phenomenon)
– Stress: Emotional and physical
– Winter:
◦Low light exposure
◦Dry weather
– Cigarette smoking
– Elevated BMI
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Long standing area of scaling erythema
r May give a history of previous diagnosis of psoriasis
r May be mildly pruritic
r May relate to one of the above triggers
r Specific location of lesions
r Family history of the disease
r History of improvement with sun exposure, or if
recurrent, success of prior regimens
r Systemic symptoms like fevers or joint pains
Physical Examr The classic skin lesion is a round, red patch with a
central plaque of silvery, white scale that appears on
extensor surfaces
r Redness and scaling around the umbilicus is highly
suggestive of psoriasis
r Positive Auspitz sign:
– Erythema and punctate bleeding when scales are
removed
r In dark-skinned patients lesions may be grey
r Scalp lesions may be confused with seborrhea:
– Lesions that extend beyond the hair borders
indicate psoriasis
r Stippling and pitting of nail and onycholysis:
– Yellow or brown band across the nail may help
differentiate psoriasis (+ band) from
onychomycosis (– band)
r Patients with plaque psoriasis may have
concomitant psoriatic arthritis:
– Often affects the DIP joints of the hands and feet
r Asymmetric oligoarticular arthritis:
– Present in 70% of these patients
– Swelling of the juxta-articular tissue
– “Sausage-shape” to the affected digits
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr The diagnosis is clinical
r Rarely, a biopsy is necessary to confirm the
diagnosis or rule out other conditions
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr No lab test confirms the diagnosis
r Elevated sedimentation rate in erythrodermic and
pustular forms
r Positive streptococcal cultures and titers with
guttate psoriasis
r Hypocalcemia and leukocytosis in pustular disease
r Negative rheumatoid factor
r Uric acid may be elevated
r If starting medications, consider checking baseline
CBC, LFTs, and renal function, as well as TB
screening
Imagingr Plain radiographs of the hands or feet may be
abnormal with psoriatic arthritis
r Sacroiliitis and ankylosing spondylitis may also be
seen on radiographs
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
Best thought of by region
r Scalp: Seborrhea
r Flexure creases:
– Candidiasis
– Intertrigo
– Eczema
r Nails: Onychomycosis
r Trunk and extremities:
– Nummular eczema
– Pityriasis rosea or rubra pilaris
– Tinea
– Systemic lupus erythematosus
– Syphilis
– Lichen simplex chronicus
– Atopy, drug eruption
– Mycosis fungoides
– Squamous cell carcinoma

TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Maintain universal precautions
r IV access and pain control as necessary
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr General resuscitation efforts aimed at correcting
fluid and electrolyte abnormalities
r Treating sepsis if present:
– Cultures of lesions, blood, and urine
r Systemic steroids should not be used as they may
predispose to severe complications
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Patients should be educated on the chronic nature
of psoriasis and that there is no cure even with
treatment
r Treatments can be expensive and compliance is
often poor
r Some patients may decline treatment in milder cases
r 3 basic types of treatment for psoriasis:
– Topical therapy
– Systemic therapy
– Phototherapy
r Topical therapy is the most commonly prescribed
treatment modality from the ED
r Systemic therapy is usually employed only after
failure of topical and phototherapy and in
conjunction with a dermatologist
r Exceptions where systemic therapy may be used:
– Generalized pustular psoriasis
– Very active psoriatic arthritis
– Psoriasis that is considered severely disabling
r Phototherapy is not an ED treatment modality
r Dermatology consult should be obtained in severe
cases
MEDICATIONr Mild to moderate disease:
– Usually topical treatment only
– No single topical agent works best for all patients.
– Emollients:
◦Works well for limited plaque psoriasis
◦Greasier choices work best, but may be poorly
tolerated by patients.
– Topical steroids
◦Major form of therapy for those with limited
disease
◦Can be used as monotherapy, 1–2 times a day,
or in combination with emollients
◦Once improvement is achieved, consider
tapering use
◦May need to rotate drugs
◦Occlusive dressing improves efficacy
– Salicylic acid
◦Topical keratolytic agent
◦Precaution if already on systemic aspirin
– Coal-tar preparations:
◦Usually used with topical steroids
◦Newer forms are less messy
– Vitamin D analogs:
◦Calcipotriene and calcitriol
– Tazarotene
◦Topical retinoid, 0.1% cream
◦Pregnancy class X
– Tacrolimus
◦Topical treatment for inverse psoriasis or facial
lesions
r Is steroid sparing and reduces risk of atrophy from
steroids
r Moderate to severe disease:
– The above-named agents may be employed along
with phototherapy and systemic medications
– Phototherapy:
◦UV radiation is thought to have antiproliferative
and anti-inflammatory effects
◦Ultraviolet B light is usually combined with ≥1
topical agents and has reports of 80% remission
◦Ultraviolet B may be used alone in guttate
psoriasis
◦Psoralen ultraviolet A (PUVA) light therapy
combines a systemic agent (psoralen) that
sensitizes the skin to UVA light
◦Therapy is usually given 2–3 times per week
– Systemic agents: May be used in various
combinations with the above modalities:
◦Should not be initiated without dermatology
consultation
◦Methotrexate (immunosuppressant): Assess
renal, liver, and hematologic function prior to
therapy; not to be used during pregnancy
◦Retinoids: May cause dryness, scaling, redness,
and tenderness of the skin
◦Systemic corticosteroids: Not favorable due to
iatrogenic Cushing syndrome; it may have a role
in acute erythrodermic psoriasis if patient is
extremely ill
◦Cyclosporine: Use in conjunction with
dermatology consult
– Injectable immunosuppressants: Etanercept and
Alefacept
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteria
ALERT
Acute erythroderma and acute pustular psoriasis
warrant admission for supportive therapy and
systemic treatment, as noted above.
Discharge Criteriar Advise patients that the disease is not contagious
r Warn patients to avoid skin trauma and sunburns
r Educate the patient on avoiding medications that
trigger relapses
r Refer patients to the National Psoriasis Foundation,
www.psoriasis.org
Pediatric Considerations
r About 10–15% of cases occur ≤age 10
r Involvement of face and flexural areas more
common; pustular and erythrodermic less common
r May have significant psychosocial impact on this
population
Pregnancy Considerations
Many of the drugs used to treat psoriasis are
contraindicated in pregnancy
Issues for Referralr Referral to dermatology is indicated for most
patients with psoriasis
r Patients with psoriasis may also need referral to
primary care doctor and/or psychiatry to cope with
impaired quality of life
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Follow-up with dermatology and/or primary care
doctor to evaluate efficacy of treatment
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Patients with pustular psoriasis are at risk for severe
systemic infections
r Patients with erythrodermic psoriasis are at risk for
dehydration and may need to be treated similarly to
a major burn patient
r Improvement occurs in weeks, not days

Danielle B. Kushner rRohn S. Friedman
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Psychiatric “civil commitment”: The
state-sanctioned involuntary hospitalization of
mentally disordered individual
r Voluntary psychiatry hospitalization: Voluntary
psychiatric admission of competent adult who
agrees to hospitalization
r Commitment criteria (review specific laws in your
state):
– Individual is mentally ill (many states exclude
mental retardation, antisocial behavior, medical
illness, and substance abuse)
– Likelihood of serious harm defined as:
◦Substantial risk of physical harm to self
◦Substantial risk of physical harm to other
persons
◦“Gravely disabled”: Inability to care for basic
needs, including food, clothing, shelter, medical
care, and safety
– No less-restrictive alternative to hospitalization
would attenuate risk
r 2 stages of commitment:
– Emergency detention and admission (sometimes
called emergency hold)—an emergency admission
with minimum of legal process. Usually 72 hr
– Longer-term commitment—requires judicial
approval of continued confinement in an
adversarial proceeding where patient may have
legal representation
ETIOLOGYr Underlying genetic/biologic predisposition to
psychiatric illness
r Precipitating psychosocial events can trigger onset
or worsening of symptoms
r Substance abuse can worsen symptoms or lead to
disinhibition causing worsening safety concerns
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Recent change in behavior or thinking
r Psychotic symptoms
– Hallucinations
– Delusions
– Disorganized thought
r Panic, anxiety, or agitation
r Depressed mood
r Neurovegetative symptoms (disturbance of sleep,
appetite, libido, energy, concentration, energy,
psychomotor state)
r Manic symptoms (elevated or irritable mood,
grandiosity, racing thoughts, excessive involvement
in pleasurable activities at high potential risk)
r Specific evidence of commitment criteria:
– Actual or threatened violence toward self
– Actual or threatened violence toward others
– Inability to care for self or protect self in the
community
r Past psychiatric diagnoses, treatment,
hospitalizations, history of harm to self or others
r Medication compliance
r Drugs of abuse: Amount and time of last use
r Access to weapons
Physical Examr Signs of toxidromes/overdose
– Slurred speech, ataxia (alcohol intoxication)
– Tremor, nystagmus, diaphoresis, tachycardia
(alcohol withdrawal)
– Dilated pupils, piloerection, rhinnorhea (opiate
withdrawal)
– Hyperreflexia, myoclonus, diaphoresis, dilated
pupils (serotonin syndrome)
r Signs of self-injury (scars, fresh wounds)
r Hypoactivity, rigidity, catalepsy, posturing
(catatonia, NMS)
r Mental status exam
– Expansive, irritable, or depressed mood
– Disordered thought process, loose associations
– Hallucinations
– Delusions
– Suicidal ideation (active vs. passive), intent, or
plan
– Homicidal ideation (identified target, intent, plan)
– Impaired cognition (delirium, dementia)
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Thorough medical evaluation to rule out medical
causes of change in thinking or behavior
r Psychiatric evaluation to clarify diagnosis and need
for hospital level of care
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Basic screening labs for medical clearance as
indicated by history and physical:
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose
r Liver function tests
r CBC and differential
r Toxicology screens and medication levels
r Urinalysis if infection suspected
r TFTs
Imaging
CT or MRI of head if injury or structural CNS pathology
suspected
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr EEG if seizure/postictal state suspected
– Repetitive pattern
– Aura usually somatosensory psychiatric autonomic
symptoms
– Postictal period of either confusion or dysphasia
r LP
– Fever or nuchal rigidity
– Seizures
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Substance intoxication or withdrawal
r Delirium
r Dementia
r Traumatic brain injury/subdural
r Temporal lobe seizures
r Encephalitis
r Meningitis
r Antisocial behavior (patient feigning psychiatric
symptoms, homicidal or suicidal ideation to obtain
medications or shelter or avoid arrest)
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Patient or concerned family may call the ED and
describe an emergency circumstance
r Depending on state, police, social worker,
psychologist, or psychiatrist can send patient to ED
for emergent assessment and possible involuntary
hospitalization
r EMTs can restrain and bring patient to hospital
involuntarily with appropriate legal paperwork
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Ensure patient and staff safety
– Make sure patient does not have weapon or
medications
– Room without hazards (sharps, medications, etc)
– Constant observation to prevent elopement
r Assess for overdose or self-injury requiring
immediate treatment
r Ensure that proper legal paperwork is in place to
hold patient in the ED
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Medical workup and clearance
r Psychiatric consultation, if available
r Determine if patient requires psychiatric
hospitalization.
r Restrain patients at risk of harming themselves or
others, using least restrictive means required to
maintain safety:
– Nurse or security guard standing outside room
– Pharmacologic restraint given PO, IM, or IV
– Physical restraints
r Continue patient’s confirmed home medications if
appropriate
r Offer symptomatic medications such as antianxiety,
antipsychotic, or sleep aid as needed
r Treat alcohol or drug withdrawal as needed

PSYCHIATRIC COMMITMENT
P
MEDICATIONr First line is Olanzapine 5–10 mg PO/IM OR
haloperidol 5 mg IM with lorazepam 2 mg IM and
benztropine 1 mg IM.
r First Line for EtOH/BZP withdrawal:
– Diazepam 5–10 mg PO q1h prn (monitored with
standardized symptoms assessment such as CIWA
scale)
r 1st line for delirium not associated with alcohol
withdrawal or anticholinergic excess:
– Haloperidol 1–2 mg PO/IM/IV
r 1st line for agitation not associated with psychosis,
delirium, or alcohol withdrawal:
– Lorazepam 1 mg PO/IM/IV
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Danger to self
r Danger to others
r Severely disabled and unable to care for self/protect
self in community
r Follow commitment process for your state
Discharge Criteriar Patients may be discharged after medical and
psychiatric evaluation if they:
– Can care for themselves adequately and
– The risk of harm to self or others is assessed to be
safely manageable in a less-restrictive alternative,
such as a partial hospital, a crisis
stabilization/observation unit, or outpatient
treatment
Issues for Referralr Patient with acute psychiatric illness who does not
meet the criteria for hospitalization usually requires
1 or more of the following:
– Crisis stabilization or observation unit
– Partial hospitalization, day program, or intensive
outpatient program referral
– Psychiatrist and/or therapist follow-up
appointment within 3–5 days
– Crisis Line phone number
r Patient may need to call insurer for list of or referral
to outpatient providers covered by his or her
insurance and may need a prior authorization
FOLLOW-UP
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Patient instructed to return to ED if feels unsafe, has
increasing suicidal/homicidal thoughts, or other
symptoms worsen
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Psychiatric civil commitment involves involuntary
hospitalization due to mental illness and 1 of the
following:
– Substantial risk of harm to self
– Substantial risk of harm to others
– Inability to care for/protect self
r The details vary by state, so you need to know the
specifics of your jurisdiction:
– Mental retardation, antisocial behavior, organic
causes such as dementia or delirium, and
substance abuse may not qualify as a mental
illness for which a person can be committed
– The definition of the 3rd criterion for commitment
(“gravely disabled,” unable to care for or protect
self, or in need of treatment) varies
– Time frames and procedures differ
r Need to complete thorough psychiatric and medical
evaluation to evaluate causes of change in patient’s
behavior
r Physician must weigh the ethical considerations
inherent in involuntary hospitalization, balancing
patient rights against the safety of patient or others.
ADDITIONAL READING
r Gutheil TG, Appelbaum PS. Clinical Handbook of
Psychiatry and the Law. 4th ed. Philadelphia, PA:
Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2007.
r Melton GB, Petrila J, Poythress NG, et al.

r Nordstrom K, Zun LS, Wilson MP, et al. Medical

for emergency psychiatry project Beta medical

13(1):3–10.
r Wilson MP, Pepper D, Currier GW, et al. The
psychopharmacology of agitation: Consensus

psychiatry project Beta psychopharmacology
workgroup. West J Emerg Med. 2012;13(1):26–34.

PSYCHOSIS, ACUTE
Celeste N. Nadal rSerena A. Fernandes
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Disorder of brain function characterized by loss of
contact with reality, abnormal perceptions,
disorganization of emotions, thought, and behavior
r Dopamine pathways are strongly implicated
r May be secondary to psychiatric or medical,
nonpsychiatric causes
r Medical causes of psychosis can be secondary to
focal or systemic medical insults, neurologic
impairment, or pharmacologic agents
ETIOLOGY
Medical, Nonpsychiatricr Neurologic disease:
– Head injury (history of)
– Dementias (Alzheimer, Lewy body)
– Cerebrovascular accident
– Seizures
– Space occupying lesions (neoplasm, malignancy,
abscesses, cysts)
– Hydrocephalus
– Migraines
– Demyelinating diseases (multiple sclerosis)
– Neuropsychiatric disorders (Parkinson,
Huntington, Wilson disease)
r Infectious disease:
– Any focal infection (UTI, PNA, cellulitis)
– HIV infection
– Neurosyphilis
– Lyme disease
– Encephalitis, meningitis or cerebritis:
◦Bacterial (TB, Lyme)
◦Viral (HSV , CMV , EBV)
◦Fungal (Cryptococcus)
◦Prion diseases
r Metabolic:
– Electrolyte imbalance
– Hypoxia
– Hypoglycemia
– Hypercarbia
– Porphyria
– Intoxication or withdrawal syndrome
– Organ failure:
◦Liver (hepatic encephalopathy)
◦Renal
◦Cardiac (CHF , arrhythmias)
r Endocrine:
– Thyroid disease
– Parathyroid disease
– Cushing syndrome
– Addison disease
r Nutritional deficiencies:
– Niacin
– Thiamine
– Vitamin B12 and folate
r Autoimmune disease:
– SLE
– Paraneoplastic syndrome
– Myasthenia gravis
Pharmacologicr Medications:
– All medications can cause psychosis
– Sedative–hypnotics: Benzodiazepines (lorazepam,
diazepam, alprazolam), barbiturates (butalbital),
other (zolpidem)
– Anticholinergic and antihistaminergic agents
(diphenhydramine, cimetidine)
– Steroids (prednisone)
– Antiepileptic agents
– Antiparkinsonian agents (amantadine, levodopa)
– Cardiovascular agents (digoxin, reserpine)
– Anti-infectious medications: Antibiotics (isoniazid,
rifampin, fluoroquinolones, TMP/SMX), antivirals
(oseltamivir, interferon), antiparasitics
(metronidazole)
– Chemotherapeutic agents (vincristine)
– Muscle relaxants (dicyclomine, carisoprodol)
r Substances associated with intoxication:
– Alcohol
– Amphetamines
– Cocaine
– Opioids
– Hallucinogens
– Cannabis
– Sedative–hypnotics
– Other: LSD, MDMA, PCP , ketamine
r Substances associated with withdrawal:
– Alcohol and sedative–hypnotics
r Toxins (heavy metals, organophosphates, carbon
monoxide)
Psychiatricr Brief psychotic disorder:
– Abrupt onset, usually due to psychosocial
stressors, lasting <1m o
r Delusional disorder:
– Circumscribed delusions
r Schizophreniform disorder:
– Symptoms present 1–6 mo
r Schizophrenia
r Schizoaffective disorder
r Mood disorder with psychotic features
r Postpartum psychosis
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Delusions are fixed, false beliefs that are:
– Impervious to outside logic
– Often persecutory, religious, or somatic content
r Hallucinations:
– Sensory experiences in the absence of external
stimuli
– Can involve any sensory modality; auditory and
visual are most common.
r Thought disorder:
– Disorganized speech ranging from odd,
idiosyncratic logic (loose associations) to
incoherence (neologisms, word salad) or poverty
of content
r Disorganized or catatonic behavior:
– Odd, stereotyped behavior (waxy flexibility,
echopraxia)
r Negative symptoms:
– Flattened affect
– Apathy
– Anhedonia
– Social isolation
r Features suggesting a nonpsychiatric etiology:
– Sudden onset
– >30 yr old
– Fluctuating course
– Focal neurologic symptoms
– Abnormal vital signs
– Visual, olfactory, gustatory or tactile hallucinations
– Impairment of orientation, attention, or cognitive
function
Historyr Screen for psychosis, including onset, duration,
triggers, and content:
– Delusions:
◦“Do you feel anyone is trying to harm you or
that you are being followed?”
◦“Is anyone trying to send you messages, steal,
control, or block your thinking?”
– Hallucinations:
◦“Do you ever see or hear things that other
people cannot see or hear?”
◦“Do you ever hear voices telling you to do things
such as to harm yourself or to harm others?”
r Suicidal or homicidal behavior or threats
r Past medical and psychiatric history
r Social situation and ability to care for self
r Recent use, increase or cessation of medications,
drugs, or alcohol
r Obtain history from friends, family, and treaters
Physical Exam
Look for signs of a medical etiology:
r Vital signs
r Eye exam (pupils, EOM, fundi)
r General exam with particular attention to the signs
and symptoms of endocrine, liver, and renal disease
r Neurologic exam, including cognitive exam
r Careful assessment for signs of delirium
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
The workup is case specific and primarily based on the
suspected etiology
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose, calcium
r Toxicology screen
r CBC with differential
r TSH
r Urinalysis
r Further specific studies should be guided by the
suspected underlying etiologies

PSYCHOSIS, ACUTE
P
Imaging
Consider head imaging for new-onset psychotic
symptoms of unclear etiology, especially in setting of
focal neurologic symptoms.
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
When clinically warranted consider:
r Lumbar puncture
r EEG
r EKG (monitor QT)
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
See Etiology.
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Patients can display unpredictable and violent
behavior toward themselves and others
r Patients may require police presence or restraints to
maintain safety
r Local laws vary regarding involuntary restraint
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Safety of patient and staff is paramount and may
require presence of security
r Behavioral interventions should be used first
– Provide a calm, containing environment
– Remove all potentially dangerous items
– Use a reassuring voice and calm demeanor to set
boundaries and verbally redirect
r If safety is a concern, patient needs to be under
constant observation
r Physical or chemical restraints as necessary
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr If a nonpsychiatric etiology is suspected, identify and
treat underlying medical condition
r If a psychiatric etiology is suspected, consider
psychiatric consultation or referral
r Acute agitation is reduced with antipsychotics:
– Encourage voluntary PO medications prior to IM
administration
– Avoid polypharmacy
r Rapid tranquilization may be achieved with the
addition of a benzodiazepine
r Monitor for and treat adverse effects from
antipsychotic medications:
– Extrapyramidal symptoms (dystonia, akathisia,
pseudoparkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia)
– Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a
life-threatening complication:
◦Characterized by hyperthermia, muscle rigidity,
autonomic instability, and altered consciousness
MEDICATIONr 1st line antipsychotics:
– Haloperidol: 2–10 mg PO/IV/IM, repeat
q20–60min prn to max. 100 mg/d; elderly
0.5–2 mg/dose
◦Commonly augmented with lorazepam
r 2nd line antipsychotics:
– Aripiprazole: 2–15 mg PO/IM, may repeat q2h prn
to max. 30 mg/d
– Chlorpromazine: 25 mg PO/IM, repeat 25–50 mg
q60min prn to max. 1,000 mg/d. Caution:
Sedating, postural hypotension, do not use in
elderly
– Olanzapine: 2.5–20 mg PO/IM, may repeat dose
q2–4h prn to max. 20 mg/d; elderly
2.5–5 mg/dose. Caution: Concurrent use of IM
olanzapine and IV benzodiazepines may increase
risk of cardiopulmonary collapse
– Risperidone: 1–2 mg PO, may repeat 2 times;
elderly 0.25–0.5 mg/dose. Caution: Orthostatic
hypotension
– Quetiapine: 25–50 mg PO BID, increase by
100 mg/d to max. 800 mg/d; elderly
12.5–25 mg/dose, increase by 25–50 mg/d
– Ziprasidone: 20–40 mg PO BID, max. 80 mg PO
BID; 10 mg IM q2h or 20 mg IM q4h prn to max.
40 mg/d IM, no more than 3 days. Caution:
Monitor QT
r Benzodiazepines:
– Lorazepam to augment tranquilization: 1–2 mg
PO/IM/IV; elderly 0.25–0.5 mg PO/IM/IV
Geriatric Considerations
Black box warning: Elderly patients with
dementia-related psychoses treated with antipsychotic
drugs are at increased risk of death.
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar If nonpsychiatric etiology, admit to appropriate
medical service
r If psychiatric etiology and patient is medically stable,
patient may require admission to a psychiatric
hospital if patient:
– Is a danger to self or others
– Is gravely disabled and unable to care for self due
to psychosis
– Has new-onset psychosis and medical etiology has
been ruled out
r Criteria for involuntary hospitalization vary
Discharge Criteriar Patient is not a danger to self or others and is able
to perform activities of daily living
r Psychotic symptoms resolved after causative medical
issue addressed and patient is medically stable for
discharge
Issues for Referral
Consider psychiatric consultation for complicated
cases or for psychiatric admission.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Plan appropriate outpatient medical follow-up
r In patients with psychiatric disorders not requiring
admission, plan outpatient psychiatric follow-up
within 1 wk
r Consider referral for detoxification in patients with
problems related to substance use
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Psychotic symptoms should be evaluated for
treatable medical causes and not assumed to be
solely psychiatric in nature even in patients with
known mental illness
r Visual, olfactory, gustatory, or tactile hallucinations
should prompt medical workup
r Avoid using IM olanzapine with IV benzodiazepines
as this increases risk for cardiopulmonary collapse
r Patients who have recently started or increased their
antipsychotics who present with fever, rigidity,
autonomic instability, and mental status changes
should be assessed for neuroleptic malignant
syndrome
ADDITIONAL READING

BMJ. 2007;334(7595):686–692.
r Mathias M, Lubman DI, Hides L. Substance-induced
psychosis: A diagnostic conundrum. J Clin
Psychiatry. 2008;69:358–367.

Consensus statement of the american association
for emergency psychiatry project Beta medical
evaluation workgroup. West J Emerg Med.

psychopharmacology of agitation: Consensus
statement of the american association for emergency
psychiatry project Beta medical evaluation
workgroup. West J Emerg Med. 2012;13(1):26–34.

PSYCHOSIS, MEDICAL VS. PSYCHIATRIC
Richard E. Wolfe
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Mental derangement involving hallucinations,
delusions, or grossly disorganized behavior resulting in
loss of contact with reality
r Complex and poorly understood pathophysiology
r An excess in dopaminergic signaling may be a
contributing factor
r Psychosis ranges from a relatively mild derangement
to catatonia
r CNS impairment leading to a psychotic presentation
may be due to:
– Neurologic disorders
– Metabolic conditions
– Toxins or drug effects
– Infections
r Higher risk for underlying psychiatric disorder:
– Hallucinations and illusions incorporated into
delusional system
– Late adolescence/early adulthood
– Normal orientation
r Higher risk for underlying medical disorder:
– Middle- to late-life presentation
– Acute onset
– History of substance abuse
– No pre-existing psychiatric history
– Absence of a family history of major mental illness
– Presence of pre-existing medical disorders
– Lower socioeconomic level
– Recent memory loss
– Disorientation or distractibility
– Abnormal vital signs
– Visual hallucinations:
◦Delirium
◦Dementia
◦Migraines
◦Dopamine agonist therapy (i.e., carbidopa)
◦Posterior cerebral infarcts
◦Narcolepsy
ETIOLOGYr Neurologic:
– Head trauma
– Space-occupying lesions
– Cerebrovascular accident
– Seizure disorders
– Hydrocephalus
r Neuropsychiatric disorders: (Parkinson, Huntington,
Alzheimer, Pick, Wilson disease)
r Infectious:
– Focal infections in the elderly (UTI, pneumonia)
– HIV
– Neurosyphilis
– Encephalitis
– Lyme disease: Neuroborreliosis
– Parasites:
◦Cerebral malaria
◦Neurocysticercosis
◦Schistosomiasis
◦Toxoplasmosis
◦Trypanosomiasis
r Metabolic:
– Electrolyte imbalance
– Hypoglycemia
– Hypoxia
– Porphyria
– Withdrawal syndromes
r Endocrine:
– Thyroid disorders
– Parathyroid disorders
– Diabetes mellitus
– Pituitary abnormalities
– Adrenal abnormalities
r End-organ failure:
– Cardiac/respiratory
– Renal
– Hepatic
r Nutritional deficiencies:
– Pernicious anemia
– Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome
– Pellagra
– Pyridoxine deficiency
r Autoimmune disorders:
– Systemic lupus erythematosus
– Sarcoidosis
– Myasthenia gravis
– Paraneoplastic syndromes
r Demyelinating disease:
– Multiple sclerosis
– Leukodystrophies
r Postoperative states:
– Delirium
r Intoxicants:
– Alcohol
– Benzodiazepines
– Barbiturates
– Stimulants (cocaine, amphetamines)
– Hallucinogens
– Opiates
– Anticholinergic compounds
– Inhalants
– Cannabis
r Toxins:
– Bromide
– Carbon monoxide
– Heavy metals
– Organic phosphates
r Medication side effects:
– Corticosteroids
– Anticholinergics
– Sedative–hypnotics
r Psychiatric:
– Antidepressants
– Antipsychotics
– Lithium carbonate
r Antiparkinsonian drugs
r Anticonvulsants
r Antibiotics (quinolones, isoniazid)
r Antihypertensive agents
r Cardiac (digitalis, lidocaine, propranolol,
procainamide)
r Interferon
r Muscle relaxants
r Over-the-counter medications:
– Pseudoephedrine
– Antihistamines
r Psychiatric:
– Schizophrenia
– Schizoaffective disorder
– Delusional disorder
– Bipolar disorder with psychotic features
– Major depression with psychotic features
– Stress reactions including post-traumatic stress
disorder
– Narcolepsy (hallucinations at edge of sleep/wake
cycle)
– Postpartum psychosis
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Psychosis characterized by:
– Impaired reality testing
– Inappropriate affect
– Poor impulse control
r Focal and diffuse CNS impairment may result in
derangements of:
– Perception
– Thought content
– Thought process
r Hallucinations:
– Sensory perception that has the compelling sense
of reality of a true perception without external
stimulation of the relevant sensory organ
r Delusions
– Beliefs held with certainty, incorrigibility, and
impossibility
– Categorized by type and theme:
◦Bizarre or nonbizarre
◦Mood congruent or neutral
◦Persecutory or grandiose
◦Primary or secondary
r Thought disorder
r Affective symptoms may include mania, depression,
or catatonia.
Historyr Time course: Acute, episodic, chronic
r Collateral from family or outpatient providers
r Substance use
r Medications and medication adherence
r Family history
r Associated symptoms: Fever, weight loss, appetite,
recent surgery and trauma
Physical Examr Vital signs
r Neurologic exam:
– Cognitive exam: Attention and orientation
– Motor exam: Tone, abnormal movements
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Detailed history and physical exam, including
neurologic exam

P
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Low likelihood of clinically significant findings if
there is a past history of psychosis, a benign history,
and normal physical exam
r 1st line:
– CBC
– Electrolytes including calcium, BUN/creatinine,
glucose
– Urine and serum toxicology screen
– Urinalysis
– Liver function tests
– Thyroid function tests
– Vitamin B12 and folate
r 2nd line guided by history and physical findings:
– Ammonia level
– HIV testing
– Fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (to
rule out neurosyphilis; rapid plasmin reagin not
sufficient as screen)
– Ceruloplasmin
– Urine heavy metals
– ESR, C-reactive protein, antinuclear antibody
Imagingr Routine CT or MRI scans are of little benefit
r Indications:
– History or exam suggests a neurologic disorder
– 1st-episode psychosis, 50 yr and older
r No clear clinically relevant benefit for MRI over CT
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr EKG with attention to corrected QT interval
r Not recommended for routine screening:
– Lumbar puncture
– EEG
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Martha Mitchell effect:
– Process by which a clinician mistakes the patient’s
perception of real events as delusional
r Locked-in syndrome
r Periodic paralysis
r Conversion disorder
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Ensure safety of patient, bystanders, and medical
personnel.
r Monitor vital signs, check finger stick.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Safety
r Evaluation
r Check O2 saturation and serum glucose
r If uncooperative and dangerous, control behavior
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Treat underlying medical illness or substance abuse
disorder.
r Control psychotic behavior with psychotropic
medications
r Check for prolonged QT before administering
neuroleptic agents
r Haloperidol in combination with lorazepam:
– Safe, fast; least disruptive of ongoing medical
exam of patient
r Atypical neuroleptics:
– Few extrapyramidal side effects
– Olanzapine and ziprasidone can be given IM
– Olanzapine (Zydis) and Risperdal M-tab are
available in dissolving wafer preparations.
– Avoid IM lorazepam with IM olanzapine due to
risk of respiratory depression.
MEDICATION
First Liner Haloperidol 2–10 mg IM or IV with lorazepam
0.5–2 mg IM or IV
Second Liner Neuroleptics:
– Olanzapine: 5–10 mg PO, SL, or IM
– Risperidone: 1–2 mg PO or SL
– Quetiapine: 25–100 mg PO
r Benzodiazepines:
– Diazepam: 5–10 mg IV
Geriatric Considerations
r Increased mortality risk in patients >65 yr on typical
and atypical antipsychotics
r Start with lower doses (Haloperidol 2 mg IV),
Olanzapine 2.5–5 mg PO, SL, or IM).
r Use benzodiazepines cautiously, given risk of
disinhibition; avoid in delirious patients.
Pregnancy Considerations
Best evidence of safety of antipsychotic use in
pregnancy is for 1st-generation (typical) antipsychotics
such as haloperidol.
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar If primarily medical etiology, admission to medical
service, criteria dictated by specific medical condition
r If primarily psychiatric etiology (e.g., schizophrenia),
admit to psychiatric service if:
– Danger to self or others
– Inability to care for self
– Deranged thought pattern that can be threat to
self or others
– 1st episode: Evaluation and stabilization
– Laws for involuntary hospitalization vary by state.
Discharge Criteriar Stable medical condition
r Not suicidal/homicidal
r Able to care for self
r Capable of making medical decisions
Issues for Referralr Insurance coverage determines inpatient and
outpatient psychiatric disposition options.
r Case management or social services necessary for
psychiatric disposition.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr If psychosis is primarily psychiatric, confirm
follow-up appointment with mental health provider
within 1–2 wk.
r Reassess risk/benefit of continuing on antipsychotic
medication at follow-up.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Patients with psychosis may not be able to explain
their symptoms in a typical way. Get collateral and
maintain a high degree of suspicion.
r Important to rule out organic causes prior to
ascribing psychosis to a psychiatric disorder.

PULMONARY CONTUSION
Douglas W. Lowery-North
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Transfer of kinetic energy to the lung, causing direct
damage to the lung parenchyma, resulting in both
hemorrhage and edema in the absence of a
pulmonary laceration
r Mortality rate is 10–25%.
r Independent risk factor for:
– Acute respiratory distress syndrome
– Pneumonia
– Long-term respiratory dysfunction
PATHOPHYSIOLOGYr Development of pulmonary contusion:
– Takes place in 2 stages:
◦1st stage, which is related to the direct injury,
results in disruption of the alveolocapillary
membrane, which leads to extravasation of
blood into the interstitial and alveolar space.
◦2nd stage is related to the indirect worsening of
the injury as a result of measures that occur
during the resuscitation of the patient, in
particular, administration of IV fluids.
r Leads to:
– Increased intrapulmonary shunting
– Increased resistance to airflow
– Decreased lung compliance
– Increased respiratory work
– Hypoxemia and acidosis
– Respiratory failure
ETIOLOGYr Blunt or penetrating thoracic trauma
r Sudden deceleration–compression
r Fall from height
r Motor vehicle accident
r Assault
r Missile
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Blunt or penetrating thoracic trauma by any
mechanism
r Mechanism as described by patient, family or
emergency medical services personnel:
– Seat belt use
– Steering wheel damage
– Air bag deployment
r Chest pain
r Dyspnea
r Hemoptysis
Physical Examr Auscultation:
– Initially normal or diminished breath sounds
– Progresses to crackles, rales, absent breath sounds
r Localized ecchymosis, edema, erythema, and
tenderness of chest wall
r Bony deformities, crepitus, point tenderness, and
paradoxical movements associated with rib fractures
r Ecchymosis from seat belt, aka “seat belt sign”
r Ecchymosis from steering wheel impact
r Splinting respirations
r Cyanosis, tachycardia, hypotension
r Dyspnea, tachypnea
ALERT
Insidious onset increasing 6–12 hr post injury
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
CXR:
r Radiographic findings may not appear until 6–12 hr
post injury.
r Patchy alveolar infiltrates to frank consolidation.
r Associated intrathoracic injury:
– Rib fractures
– Pneumothorax, hemothorax
– Widened mediastinal silhouette
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Arterial blood gas may reveal hypoxemia and elevated
alveolar–arterial gradient.
Imagingr Chest radiograph:
– Percentage of contusion can help predict the need
for intubation:
◦<18%: Usually will not need intubation
◦>28%: Usually leads to intubation
r Thoracic CT is useful in detecting pulmonary injury
and associated intrathoracic injuries not identified
on CXR:
– Studies that have shown injury size on CT can also
assist with prognosis.
– >20% of the total lung volume is predictive of
the need of assisted ventilation.
r US has been studied and could prove to be a fast,
sensitive method for diagnosing pulmonary
contusion.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Adult respiratory distress syndrome
r CHF
r Hemothorax
r Noncardiogenic causes of pulmonary edema
r Pneumonia, abscess, or other infectious process
r Pneumothorax
r Pulmonary laceration, infarction, or embolism
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Thoracic trauma with significant mechanism or
pre-existing pulmonary disease should be routed to
the nearest available trauma center.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Manage airway and resuscitate as indicated.
– Stabilize associated chest wall injuries (open
chest, flail chest)
r IV line, O2, continuous cardiac monitoring, and
pulse oximetry
r Control airway:
– Endotracheal intubation indications:
◦Severe hypoxemia (PaO2 <60 mm Hg on room
air,<80 mm Hg on O2)
◦Significant underlying lung disease
◦Impending respiratory failure
– Early intubation and institution of positive end
expiratory pressure:
◦Correct hypoxemia and acidosis.
◦Decrease the work of breathing.

ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Maintain adequate oxygenation and ventilation.
r Monitor O2 saturation and respiratory rate.
r In conscious and alert patients, O2 administration
via face mask is 1st-line therapy.
r If patient cannot maintain a PaO2 >80 mm Hg on
high-flow oxygen:
– Continuous positive airway pressure via mask
– Nasal bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP)
– Early endotracheal intubation and mechanical
ventilation
r In patients with severe unilateral injuries with
significant hemoptysis or air leaks, consider selective
bronchial intubation.
ALERT
r Avoid excessive fluid administration:
– IV crystalloid administration needed for
resuscitation must be balanced with the risk of
increasing interstitial pulmonary edema.
r Frequent re-exam and serial chest radiographs are
required to monitor alveolar fluid accumulation.
r Mental status must be appropriate and patient
must be alert and cooperative for BiPAP/CPAP:
– Often this is only a temporizing intervention and
should not delay intubation in worsening
patients.
MEDICATIONr Adequate pain control is key for optimal outcome.
r Steroids have no proven benefit.
r Prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated.
Pediatric Considerations
Increased pliability of the chest wall increases the
frequency of pulmonary contusions.
Geriatric Considerations
r Suboptimal cardiopulmonary reserve in combination
with large-volume fluid resuscitation increases the
likelihood of worsening of pulmonary contusions in
the elderly.
r Pulmonary contusion has been identified as a
marker for bad outcomes in elderly patients with
isolated blunt chest trauma.
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteria
Patients with pulmonary contusion must be admitted
to the hospital for observation in anticipation of
delayed-onset respiratory compromise.
Discharge Criteriar Patients with minimal chest trauma
r No evidence of respiratory distress or hypoxemia:
– Normal respiratory rate
– Reassuring pulse oximetry
– Negative chest radiograph
r Strict return criteria should be discussed with the
patient prior to discharge:
– Shortness of breath
– Hemoptysis
– Inadequate pain control or increased pain
– Cough
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Avoid underestimating the severity of pulmonary
injury based on initial chest x-ray.
r Failure to recognize this injury in the ED can lead to
unexpected deterioration.
r Comorbid conditions such as chronic lung disease
and renal failure increase the likelihood of requiring
mechanical ventilation.
r Careful monitoring and reassessment is key.

PULMONARY EDEMA
Timothy C. Peck rShamai A. Grossman
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Imbalance in Starling forces causes an accumulation of
alveolar fluid secondary to leakage from pulmonary
capillaries into the interstitium and alveoli of the
lungs.
r Cardiogenic:
– Abnormality in cardiac function leading to
inadequate tissue perfusion
– Acute decompensated cardiac failure: Acute fluid
overload in the setting of chronic HF
– Acute vascular failure: Decreased contractility and
increased vascular resistance
r Noncardiogenic:
– Increased alveolar–capillary membrane
permeability, and accumulation of fluid in the
alveoli without a cardiac etiology
– Acute lung injury: Lower severity
– Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS):
PaO2/FiO2 ratio of ≤200 mm Hg
r New York Heart Association classification:
– Class I: Not limited in normal physical activity by
symptoms
– Class II: Ordinary physical activity results in
fatigue, dyspnea, or other symptoms
– Class III: Marked limitation in normal activity
– Class IV: Symptoms at rest or with any activity
r Epidemiology:
– 5.8 million patients in US
– Increases with increasing age and affects 10% of
population >75 yr.
– 30–40% of patients with HF are hospitalized
every year.
– 11% 1 mo mortality after AHF admission
ETIOLOGYr Cardiogenic etiologies:
– Contractile dysfunction:
◦Ischemic heart disease
◦Idiopathic cardiomyopathy
◦Myocarditis
– Systolic pressure overload:
◦Aortic stenosis
◦Systemic hypertension
– Systolic volume overload:
◦Aortic regurgitation
◦Mitral regurgitation
– Restricted diastolic filling:
◦Mitral stenosis
◦Left atrial myxoma
◦Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
– High-output states:
◦Hyperthyroidism
◦Anemia
◦Arteriovenous fistula
◦Wet beriberi
– Congenital heart disease
– Endocarditis
– Rheumatic heart disease
r Noncardiogenic etiologies:
– Sepsis
– Acute pulmonary infection, aspiration
– Inhalation injuries
– Aspiration
– Near drowning
– Disseminated intravascular coagulation
– Pancreatitis
– Pulmonary contusion
– Severe (nonthoracic) trauma
– Cardiopulmonary bypass
– Uremia
– High-altitude pulmonary edema
– Neurogenic pulmonary edema
– Narcotic overdose
– Salicylate overdose
– Pulmonary embolism
– Fat embolism
– Transfusion-related acute lung injury
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Risk factors:
– Prior CHF diagnosis
– History of coronary artery disease or myocardial
infarction
– Diabetes
– Severe systemic illness
r Symptoms:
– Dyspnea on exertion progressing to dyspnea at
rest
– Orthopnea
– Peripheral edema
– Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
– Acute weight gain
– Weakness/fatigue
– Cough
Physical Examr Vital signs
– May be hypertensive or hypotensive
– Tachypnea
– Low oxygen saturation
r General
– Diaphoresis
– Cold, ashen, or cyanotic skin
r Respiratory:
– Rales
– Wheezes
– Accessory muscle use
r Cardiovascular
– Tachycardia
– Jugular venous distention
– Increased P2, S3, S4
– Hepatojugular reflex
r Extremities
– Peripheral edema
r Noncardiogenic
– Similar pulmonary but rarely peripheral signs
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr ECG to evaluate for cardiac ischemia and
dysrhythmias.
r Chest x-ray to confirm the diagnosis and assessing
illness severity.
r Labs: B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), cardiac
enzymes, and creatinine
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr BNP:
– Lab parameter for the detection and follow-up of
heart failure:
◦<100 pg/mL: CHF unlikely
◦100–500 pg/mL: Indeterminate
◦>500 pg/mL: Most consistent with CHF
– May not be elevated in very acute CHF or
ventricular inflow obstruction
– May be falsely elevated in patients with renal
failure undergoing dialysis due to LVH
r N-terminal pro-BNP:
– Similar test characteristics to BNP
r Cardiac troponins:
– May be elevated due to myocardial ischemia
causing AHF or as result of AHF’s effects on
cardiac myocytes
– Elevated in 20% of AHF episodes
– Strong negative prognostic factor
r Serum chemistry panel:
– Creatinine elevation:
◦Predicts all-cause mortality in chronic heart
failure
◦Indication of acute end-organ hypoperfusion
◦Indication for admission or observation
– Hyponatremia: Marker of severe HF
– Electrolyte abnormalities are common due to
various HF treatments.
r Elevated alanine aminotransferase, aspartate
aminotransferase, or bilirubin suggests congestive
hepatopathy.
r Serum lipase if pancreatitis is suspected as the
underlying cause
r Arterial blood gas: Evaluates hypoxemia,
ventilation/perfusion mismatch, hypercapnia, and
acidosis.
Imagingr CXR:
– Pulmonary redistribution: Cephalization of vessels
– Cardiomegaly: Cardiac silhouette >50% of
thoracic width on PA exam only
– Interstitial edema:
◦Pleural effusions
◦Kerley B lines
– Bilateral perihilar alveolar edema producing a
characteristic butterfly pattern
– Noncardiogenic: Bilateral interstitial or alveolar
infiltrates in a homogeneous pattern, typically
without enlarged heart shadow
– Radiographs are often normal in the 1st 12 hr of
the disease process.

– Measures cardiac output
r Bedside ultrasonography:
– Bilateral B-lines: Comet-tail artifacts arising from

decrease in intensity on both the left and the right
thorax
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr COPD exacerbation
r Pneumonia
r Asthma
r Pulmonary embolism
r Pericardial tamponade
r Pneumothorax
r Pleural effusion
r Anaphylaxis
r Acidosis
r Hyperventilation syndrome
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr IV access
r Supplemental oxygen
r 100% nonrebreather mask
r Cardiac monitor
r Pulse oximetry
r Sublingual nitrates
r If bag valve mask is needed, should use PEEP valve
if available
r Endotracheal intubation in severe cases.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Assess and gain control of airway, breathing, and
circulation.
r Noninvasive ventilation or endotracheal intubation
for impending respiratory failure.
r IV access
r Supplemental oxygen
r Cardiac monitor
r Pulse oximetry
r Place patient in an upright position.
r Inotropic therapy for hypotensive patient with signs
of end-organ dysfunction
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Treatment decisions should be based on the
underlying cause of pulmonary edema.
r Supplemental O2
r Volume restriction
r Urine output monitoring with or without urinary
catheter
r BiPAP/CPAP:
– Improves oxygenation, reduces respiratory work,
decreases left ventricular afterload
– Reduces need for intubation, length of stay, and
mortality
– Efficacy of BiPAP = CPAP
r Noncardiogenic causes: Frequently require
positive-pressure ventilation:
– Low-volume ventilation recommended (6 mL/kg)
r Positive-end expiratory pressure: Most useful
strategy for oxygenation
r Hypotensive patients:
– Avoid nitrates, angiotensin-converting enzyme
inhibitors (ACEIs), and morphine.
– Initiate inotropes:
◦Dobutamine, Dopamine, Norepinephrine, or
Milrinone
– Direct cardioversion for new onset unstable atrial
fibrillation
r Normotensive or hypertensive patients:
– Nitrates (nitroglycerin vs. nitroprusside)
– Diuretics (furosemide vs. bumetanide) may be
most effective after initial stabilization
r Noncardiogenic: Treat underlying cause.

suspected
r Bumetanide: 1–3 mg IV
r Captopril: 6.25 mg SL
r Dobutamine: 2–10 μg/kg/min IV , titrate. May lower
BP due to vasodilatory effects.
r Dopamine: 2 × 20 μg/kg/min IV; titrate
r Enalapril: 0.625–1.25 mg IV
r Furosemide: 20–80 mg IV
r Torsemide: 10–20 mg IV
r Milrinone: 50 μg/kg IV; titrate; inotropic effects
comparable to dobutamine
r Nitroglycerin: 0.4 mg SL; 1–2 in; 5–20 μg/min IV
and titrate; Nitropaste is not preferred as it is more
difficult to titrate and to use in diaphoretic patients.
r Nitroprusside: 0.25–0.3 μg/kg/min, titrate up by
0.5 μg/kg/min q2–3 min until desired effect
r Norepinephrine: 2–12 μg/min IV; titrate
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar ICU:
– Positive-pressure ventilation
– Inotropic support
– Acute cardiac ischemia or infarction
– ARDS
r Monitored unit:
– New-onset pulmonary edema
– Electrocardiographic changes
– Patients presenting with risk factors for mortality,
including advanced age, renal dysfunction,
hypotension, digoxin use, and anemia
Discharge Criteriar Most patients with pulmonary edema should be
admitted or observed for 24 hr.
r Patients with mild underlying disease and a mild
exacerbation that responds fully to ED management
and have no risk factors for in-house mortality (see
above) may be discharged.
r Ensure close outpatient follow-up.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Contact patient’s primary physician and/or
cardiologist to establish close follow-up.
r Continue diuresis.
r Low-salt diet
r Daily weights
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Nitrates, SL and IV , are 1st-line therapy to reduce
preload.
r BNP can reliably differentiate between AHF
syndromes and other causes of dyspnea.
r AHF chest radiography findings can be absent early
in disease course.
r Aggressive, early treatment of normotensive and
hypertensive patients with nitrates, diuretics, and
ACEIs can rapidly reverse the clinical course.
r Positive-pressure ventilation is an essential
intervention in noncardiogenic pulmonary edema
and can reduce rates of intubation and mortality in
AHF .

PULMONARY EMBOLISM
Alan M. Kumar
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr The majority of pulmonary embolisms (PEs) arise
from thrombi in the deep veins of the lower
extremities and pelvis.
r Thrombi also originate in renal and upper extremity
veins.
r After traveling to lungs, the size of the thrombus
determines signs and symptoms.
ETIOLOGYr Most patients with PE have identifiable risk factor:
– Recent surgery
– Pregnancy
– Previous deep vein thrombosis (DVT)/PE
– Stroke or recent paraplegia
– Malignancy
– Age >50 yr
– Obesity
– Smoking
– Oral contraceptives
– Major trauma
r Hematologic risk factors:
– Factor 5 Leiden
– Protein C or S deficiency
– Antithrombin III deficiency
– Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome
– Lupus anticoagulant
Pediatric Considerations
r Thromboembolic disease is quite rare.
r Risk factors in children:
– Presence of central venous catheter
– Immobility
– Heart disease
– Trauma
– Malignancy
– Surgery
– Infection
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Variability in signs and symptoms make diagnosis
difficult
r Most common:
– Dyspnea
– Pleuritic chest pain
– Tachypnea
r General:
– Fevers (rarely >102◦F)
– Diaphoresis
r Pulmonary:
– Cough
– Hemoptysis (rarely massive)
– Rales
r Cardiovascular:
– Tachycardia
– Syncope
– Murmur
r Extremities:
– Cyanosis
– Evidence of thrombophlebitis
– Lower-extremity edema
r Abdominal pain
r Symptoms similar in elderly but typically more subtle
if age <40 yr
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Routine labs are nonspecific.
r CXR:
– Used to rule out other causes
– Most common findings with PE:
◦Normal
◦Nonspecific parenchymal abnormality
◦Atelectasis
– Other findings with PE:
◦Pleural effusions
◦Pleural-based opacities (Hampton hump)
◦Elevated hemidiaphragm
◦Local oligemia (Westermark sign)
r ECG:
– To rule out cardiac etiology
– Usually normal in PE
– Other findings include:
◦Nonspecific ST–T-wave changes (most common
abnormality)
◦Sinus tachycardia
◦Left axis deviation
◦Right bundle branch block pattern
◦S1Q3T3 pattern is uncommon and not specific
enough to rule in/out diagnosis.
r Modified Wells criteria:
– Popular decision rule that can assist with risk
stratification in combination with D-dimer
– Each criterion is given numeric value and if total
value <4, along with negative D-dimer, risk of PE
is <2%:
◦Clinical signs/symptoms of DVT: 3 pts
◦PE is no. 1 diagnosis: 3 pts
◦Heart rate >100 bpm: 1.5 pts
◦Surgery or immobilization for 3 days within last
4 wk: 1.5 pts
◦Previous PE or DVT: 1.5 pts
◦Hemoptysis: 1 pt
◦Malignancy with treatment within last 6 mo:
1p t
r Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria (PERC)
– Useful in low prevalence setting (ED) in
combination with low clinical suspicion.
◦Age <50 yr
◦Heart rate <100 bpm
◦O2 saturation ≥95%
◦No hemoptysis
◦No estrogen use
◦No prior DVT or PE
◦No unilateral leg swelling
◦No surgery or trauma requiring hospitalization
within the past 4 wk
– <1% risk for PE/DVT in 45 days if PERC score 0
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Arterial blood gas:
– Can show hypoxemia, hypocapnia, respiratory
alkalosis, or increased alveolar–arterial (A–a)
gradient
– PE still possible with normal A–a gradient
– Does not aid in diagnosis of PE
r CBC:
– Anemia may be contributing factor to dyspnea.
r D-dimer enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay:
– D-dimers are detectable at levels >500 ng/mL in
nearly all patients with PE.
– High sensitivity (close to 100%) with low
specificity for PE
– Almost always elevated in patients with
malignancy or surgery within the last 3 mo
– Multiple studies confirm that negative
enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay D-dimer in
combination with low clinical suspicion effectively
rules out PE.
Imagingr Spiral chest CT with IV contrast:
– Has ability to also detect alternative pulmonary

◦Diminished production
◦Altered distribution
◦Increased destruction
◦Abnormal function

– Generally due to vasculitis:
◦Autoimmune, small-vessel leukocytoclastic
vasculitis
◦Hypersensitivity to various antigens
◦Formation of circulating immune complexes
deposited in walls of postcapillary venules;
activate complement that is chemotactic for
polymorphonuclear leukocytes

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Complication of a lower UTI by bacterial ascension
into the upper urinary tract
r Primarily a clinical diagnosis
r Incidence lower in males in every age group
r Male/female ratio:
– 1:10 in 1st years of life
– 1:5 in children
– 1:50 in reproductive years
– 1:1 in 5th decade and later
r Bilateral infection in up to 25% of cases, hence no
lateralizing signs (in some studies)

– Escherichia coli 80–95% predominates
– Uropathogens:
◦Klebsiella species
◦Citrobacter species
◦Enterobacter species
– Others:
◦Staphylococcus saprophyticus 5–15%
◦Proteus mirabilis
◦Serratia species
◦Pseudomonas species
◦Staphylococcus aureus (increasing)
r Predisposing factors (consider complicated
infections):
– Recent instrumentation:
◦Catheterization
◦Cystoscopy
– Urinary retention:
◦Mechanical (see Obstruction below)
◦Medications (e.g., anticholinergics)
◦Other infections (e.g., herpes simplex)
– Urinary obstruction:
◦Stricture
◦Renal calculi
◦Prostatic hypertrophy
– Anatomic abnormalities:
◦Hypospadias
◦Ureteral ectopia
◦Bifid ureter
◦Renal scarring
◦Ureterovesicular reflux (UVR)
◦Posterior urethral valves
– Neurologic conditions:
◦Neurogenic bladder
◦Spinal cord injury

– Previous UTIs (in childhood, >3 in last year)
– Recent pyelonephritis (within 1 yr)
– Diabetes mellitus
– Immunosuppression
– Pregnancy

SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Dysuria, urgency, frequency
r Back, flank, or abdominal pain
r Fever, chills
r Arthralgias, myalgias, malaise
r Nausea and/or vomiting
r Costovertebral angle/suprapubic tenderness
r Ill/toxic appearing
r Dehydration

– Invasion of upper urinary tract without clinical
symptoms:
◦Suspect in lower UTI that does not resolve with
standard treatment.

may be only symptom in infants.
r Enuresis in previously toilet-trained child

immunocompromised (hematogenous spread)
r Renal scarring:
– More common sequelae in young children than in
adults
r Group B streptococci
r Etiologic agents in neonates

mental status may predominate.

– Clean-catch or catheterized urine specimen;
catheterized specimen if:
◦Vaginal discharge or bleeding
◦Contaminated specimen

nitrites:
◦If not present, consider alternate diagnosis.
◦Nitrite represents a gram-negative pathogens
are present that is converting dietary nitrates to
nitrites.
◦Note that some uropathogens such as
Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, and
S. Saprophyticus are not nitrate reducers
– Hematuria:
◦White cell cast: Renal origin of pyuria

– Obtain in:
◦Suspected pyelonephritis
◦Unclear diagnosis
◦Treatment failures, recurrent infections
◦High clinical suspicion, with negative UA
– >100,000 colony-forming units (CFU)/mL is
positive.

◦Early infection
◦Clinical scenario consistent with UTI
◦Catheter or suprapubic specimen
◦Males

– Leukocytosis
– Does not rule in or out upper tract infection

cultures do not correlate with more severe disease.
– Bacteria identified more readily on urine culture

◦Renal/perinephric abscess
◦Intraparenchymal gas formation

◦Renal failure (lack of iodinated contrast)

– Within 48 hr if no clinical improvement
– Within 3–6 wk if clinical improvement

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Postnatal hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the circular
smooth muscle cell layer causing a thickened pylorus
and antrum leading to progressive gastric outlet
obstruction
r Neuronal nitric oxide synthase (NOS-1) may be a
genetic susceptibility locus.
r Administration of erythromycin in infants during 1st
2 wk of life may increase risk of hypertrophic pyloric
stenosis.
r Jaundice due to transient glucuronyl transferase
deficiency
r Adult: Caused by peptic ulcer disease
ETIOLOGYr Most common cause of GI obstruction in infants;
incidence 1/150 males, 1/750 females (average:
3/1,000 live births)
r Males affected 5× more commonly than females;
firstborn most common
r Familial, 15%:
– Child of affected parent has 7% incidence.
– Recurrence risk in subsequent male children is
10%; 2% in females.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Vomiting:
– Gradual onset, usually beginning at around
3–6 wk of age; rarely after 12 wk of age
– Progressive, usually becoming projectile
– Nonbilious
– May be blood tinged (secondary to esophagitis,
gastritis, gastric ulceration)
– Progressively worsening
– Postprandial
r Represents the hypertrophied pylorus:
– Confirms diagnosis
r Constipation or small amount of stools
r “Lean and hungry” infant early in course;
dehydrated and uninterested in feeding late in
course; failure to thrive
r Variable dehydration and wasting depending on
duration of symptoms
r Jaundice in 8% of children
r Adult presents with vomiting, anorexia, early satiety,
and epigastric pain.
Physical Examr Often normal unless a relaxed abdomen
r May feel olive-shaped mass at lateral margin of the
right rectus abdominis muscle in the right upper
quadrant (80% of patients), often after vomiting:
– Best felt immediately after vomiting or after the
stomach is emptied via gastric suction as the
dilated body of the stomach overlies the pylorus
– Represents the hypertrophied pylorus:
◦Helps confirm diagnosis
◦Peristaltic waves moving from the left to right in
the left upper quadrant, seen best after feeding
or just prior to vomiting

If “olive” palpable, further diagnostic evaluation may
be unnecessary and surgical consultation should be
sought; otherwise, imaging studies are indicated.

– Hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis
– Normal electrolytes do not exclude the diagnosis.

r CBC if blood in emesis
r Urinalysis for hydration

– Study of choice
– US diagnosis hinges on identification and
measurement of pyloric muscle mass (3 mm ring
thickness, 1.5 cm pylorus channel or muscle
length, and 10–14 mm pylorus diameter) and
observation of fluid movement through the
pylorus.

a narrowed gastric outlet

– Remove contrast from the stomach after the study
to prevent aspiration.

– Not diagnostic; rarely helpful
– Dilated stomach and no air distal to the pylorus
– Most useful with other views to begin evaluation
for other abdominal pathology

Jason A. Tracy
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
A disorder of myocardial repolarization characterized
by a prolonged QT interval on the electrocardiogram
r The pathophysiology is complex and incompletely
understood:
– Alteration in cardiac sodium, potassium, or
calcium ion flow
– Imbalance in the sympathetic innervation of the
heart
r Prolonged ventricular repolarization results in
lengthening of QT interval on surface ECG:
– “Pause-dependent” lengthening due to
short–long–short sequence in which a sinus beat
is followed by an extrasystole (short), then a
postextrasystolic pause (long), concluding with a
ventricular extrasystole (short)
– “Adrenergic-dependent” pauses found in
congenital cases
r Symptoms often preceded by vigorous exercise,
emotional stress, or loud noise.
r Nocturnal bradycardia can lengthen QT interval,
causing sleep-related symptoms.
r Re-entrant rhythm can lead to torsades de pointes,
ventricular tachycardia, and ventricular fibrillation.
r Hemodynamic compromise following dysrhythmia
leads to syncope or death.
r Independent risk factor for sudden cardiac death.
RISK FACTORS
Geneticsr 10 genes linked to long QT syndrome:
– Autosomal recessive form associated with
deafness (Jervell and Lange–Nielsen syndromes)
– Autosomal dominant form not associated with
deafness (Romano–Ward syndrome)
– Adrenergic stimulation (fright, exertion, delirium
tremens, and loud auditory stimulus) becomes
prodysrhythmic in certain genotypes, while
sleep-related symptoms are found in others.
r 10–15% of carriers have baseline normal QTc.
r Death occurs in 1–2% of untreated patients per
year.
– Drug-induced QT prolongation may also have a
genetic background.
– Congenital form occurs in 1 in 3,000–5,000, with
mortality of 6% by age 40 yr.
Pediatric Considerations
r Diagnosis suspected in the young with syncope,
cardiac arrest, or sudden death
r Syncope following emotional stress or exercise
suggestive
r Death occurs without preceding symptoms in 10%
of pediatric patients.
ETIOLOGYr Drugs:
– Complete list at www.QTDrugs.org
– Class Ia antidysrhythmics—quinidine,
procainamide, disopyramide
– Class III antidysrhythmics—sotalol, ibutilide,
amiodarone
– Antibiotics—erythromycin, pentamidine,
chloroquine, trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole
– Antifungal agents—ketoconazole, itraconazole
– Psychotropic drugs—phenothiazines, haloperidol,
risperidone, STCAs
– Cisapride
– Antihistamines
– Organophosphates
– Narcotics—methadone

– Hypokalemia
– Hypomagnesemia
– Hypocalcemia

– Bradyarrhythmias
– Arteriovenous block
– Mitral valve prolapse
– Myocarditis
– Myocardial ischemia
r CNS
– Subarachnoid hemorrhage
– Stroke
r Congenital (idiopathic)
r Other

– Anorexia nervosa
– Hypothyroidism
– Hypothermia

SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Palpitations
r Light-headedness
r Dizziness
Historyr Syncope
r Near syncope
r Seizure
r Family history of syncope or sudden death
r Congenital deafness
r Medication use

r ECG
r QTc (QT corrected for heart rate) >0.44 sec in men
and >0.46 sec in women
r QT measured from beginning of quasi-random
signal to end of T wave:
– Measured best in the limb leads and should be
averaged over 3–5 beats
– There is no expert consensus on best heart rate
correction (QTc) formula.
– Bazett formula (QT divided by square root of RR
interval) is most commonly used
– Increase in QT variability

in suspected cases

forms

Herbert Neil Wigder r Ashley Alwood r Matthew A. Kippenhand
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
CNS infectious disease of mammals caused by the
rabies virus:
r Highest case fatality rate of any known infectious
disease
ETIOLOGYr Epidemiology:
– 30,000–70,000 people die/yr worldwide
– Especially common in Southeast Asia, Philippines,
Africa, South America, and Indian subcontinent
– US has 2–3 human cases per year.
– Most clinical cases in US from foreign travel and
bat exposures
– Raccoons, skunks, foxes, bats, dogs, woodchucks,
groundhogs are reservoirs.
– In US bats are the most common reservoir while
abroad dogs are more common.
– Squirrels, rats, mice, hamsters, guinea pigs,
gerbils, chipmunks, and rabbits can also be
infected but there has never been a reported case
of human transmission.
r Pathophysiology:
– Negative-stranded RNA genome, family
Rhabdoviridae, genus Lyssavirus
– Mode of transmission:
◦Contact with infected saliva of host
◦Bite: Most common
◦Nonbite: Saliva or bat aerosol exposure to an
open wound or mucous membrane
◦Transplant procedures are the only
well-documented person-to-person transmission
◦Not considered a transmission risk: Petting rabid
animal or contact with the blood, urine, or feces
of a rabid animal
– Progression after infection:
◦Virus multiplies in local tissue and is taken up
into muscle through n-acetylcholine receptors.
◦Virus enters peripheral nerves and is transported
to CNS via retrograde axoplasmic flow at ∼1–4
inches per day
◦Once in CNS, rapid replication and
dissemination cause encephalitis.
◦Centrifugal spread of virus to peripheral nerves,
including salivary glands
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Once a patient exhibits clinical signs course is
almost universally fatal.
r 5 stages: Incubation, prodrome, encephalitis, coma,
death (or recovery):
– Incubation: 1–3 mo (range 10 days to 1 yr):
◦Virus amplifies in peripheral tissues
◦Time depends on amount inoculated and
proximity to CNS, thus shorter incubation for
head or neck bites
– Prodrome: 1–7 days:
◦Nonspecific symptoms: Fever, headache,
malaise, myalgias, anorexia, sore throat,
nausea, and vomiting
◦Paresthesias or fasciculations around bite site
give clue to diagnosis.
– Encephalitis (classic form): 2–7 days:
◦Anxiety, agitation, hallucinations, confusion or
delirium, muscle spasms, opisthotonos, and
seizure
◦Aerophobia (pathognomonic): Pharyngeal
spasm from draft of air
◦Hydrophobia (pathognomonic): Violent
involuntary muscle contraction of diaphragm,
pharyngeal, laryngeal, and accessory respiratory
muscles when attempting to swallow (seen in
up to half of cases)
◦Dysrhythmias, myocarditis, autonomic
instability, and fevers
◦Brainstem involvement: Diplopia, facial paralysis
– Coma:
◦Apnea from respiratory center involvement,
vascular collapse, flaccid paralysis, adult
respiratory distress syndrome, syndrome of
inappropriate diuretic hormone
◦Most die within 2 wk
– Death (or recovery):
◦Almost universally fatal if no pre- or
postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) given
◦Rare case reports of survival without prophylaxis
◦Known survivors have some residual neurologic
deficits
r 3 manifestations of disease:
– Classic or encephalitic rabies accounts for ∼80%
of cases. See above.
– Paralytic rabies (∼20%): Ascending paralysis
mimicking Guillain–Barr ´ e syndrome
– Atypical rabies (<1%): Seen with bat-associated
rabies. Characterized by neuropathic pain, sensory
or motor deficits, choreiform movements,
myoclonus, and seizures

history (e.g., child or intoxicated): Assume exposure
r Travel to endemic areas with associated dog
exposure

handling of the animal prior to bite is considered a
provoked attack.

r A bat bite wound often not visible on exam
r Altered mental status, seizures, encephalopathy
r Percussion myoedema: Muscle mounds at
percussion site
r Autonomic manifestations: Dilated pupils,
perspiration, hypersalivation, orthostatic
hypotension

– Virus isolation in cell culture

– Mildly elevated WBC and protein, normal glucose
