BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Occurs between 6 mo and 5 yr of age associated
with fever:
– No evidence of intracranial infection or other
defined CNS primary cause
– Average age of onset is 18–22 mo
– Children with previous nonfebrile seizures
excluded
r Most common pediatric convulsive disorder:
– Affects 2–4% of young children in US
r Occurs in normal children with a systemic viral illness
r High-risk children:
– History of febrile seizure in immediate family
members
– Delayed neurologic development
– Males
r Subgroups:
– Simple febrile seizures:
◦Brief, self-limited lasting <10–15 min, resolve
spontaneously
◦Generalized without any focal features
– Complex febrile seizures:
◦Duration >15 min
◦Focal features
◦More than 1 seizure within a 24-hr period
r Risk of recurrence:
– One-third of cases
– Early age of onset, history of febrile or afebrile
seizures in 1st-degree relatives, and temperature
<40◦C during initial seizure increase the
likelihood of recurrence
r Risk of subsequent epilepsy:
– Greatest for those with prior abnormal neurologic
development, a complex (>15 min) 1st febrile
seizure, a focal seizure, or a family history of
afebrile seizures
– Only slightly greater than the general population if
1st febrile seizure is simple and neurologic
development normal
– Not affected by the use of prophylactic
medications
ALERT
Because this is usually self-limited, intervention
must be individualized in relation to airway,
breathing, and seizure management
ETIOLOGY
Common childhood infections:
r Upper respiratory illnesses
r Otitis media
r Roseola
r GI infections
r Shigella gastroenteritis
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Fever
r Seizure may occur concurrent with recognition of
the febrile illness
r Seizure
r Generalized tonic–clonic seizure most common:
– Tonic phase:
◦Muscular rigidity
◦Apnea and incontinence
◦Self-limited and last only a few minutes
– Other seizure types:
◦Staring with stiffness
◦Limpness
◦Jerking movements without prior stiffening
Historyr Careful history and physical exam help confirm
diagnosis and rule out other etiologies
r Symptoms/evidence of infectious illness
r Duration and pattern of fever
r Medication exposure/toxin
r Recent immunizations
r Trauma/occult trauma
r Growth pattern and developmental level
r Family history of seizures
r Complete description of seizure
Physical Examr Reducing temperature may be useful in evaluation;
give antipyretics early
r Evidence of infectious illness-rash, ear infection,
respiratory infection, diarrhea, etc.
r Careful neurologic exam including mental status
r Presence of meningismus, bulging fontanelle, nuchal
rigidity, etc.
r Evidence of focal deficit or increased ICP
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Routine lab studies not indicated
r Evaluate for a source of fever if serious bacterial
infection is suspected:
– WBC
–U A
– Blood and urine cultures
r Lumbar puncture:
– Not routinely indicated
– Indications 12–18 mo of age:
◦History or irritability, decreased feeding, lethargy
◦Consider if deficient in Haemophilus influenzae
type b or Streptococcus pneumoniae
immunizations
◦Physical signs of meningitis and/or history
consistent with meningitis
◦Complex seizure
◦Prolonged postictal state
◦Prior antibiotics altering presentation
◦Abnormal mentation after postictal state
– Indications >18 mo old:
◦Signs/symptoms of CNS infection present
◦Electrolytes and bedside glucose in infants and
children with vomiting or diarrhea
r EEG:
– Not helpful in the initial evaluation of febrile
seizures
– May be indicated if developmental delay,
underlying neurologic abnormality, or focal seizure
– Does not help predict recurrences or risk for later
epilepsy
r Anticonvulsant levels
r Toxicology studies of blood and urine if history and
physical exam suggestive
Imagingr Chest radiograph only in patients with significant
respiratory symptoms or pertinent findings on
physical exam
r Head CT:
– Indicated with traumatic injuries, focal neurologic
findings, or inability to exclude elevated
intracranial pressure
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Febrile delirium
r Febrile shivering with pallor and perioral cyanosis
r Breath-holding spell during febrile event
r Acute life-threatening event
r Other causes of seizure:
– Afebrile seizure occurring during febrile event
– Sudden discontinuance of anticonvulsants
– Infection:
◦Meningitis/encephalitis
◦Acute gastroenteritis, often with dehydration
– Head trauma
– Toxicologic:
◦Anticholinergics
◦Sympathomimetics
◦Other
– Hypoxia
– Metabolic disease
– Intracranial masses
– CNS vascular lesions
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Protect the airway
r Oxygen
r Support breathing as needed
r Cautions:
– Keep child from incurring injury while actively
convulsing
– Respiratory insufficiency and apnea occur
secondary to overaggressive treatment with
benzodiazepines
– Simple febrile seizures are self-limited and
generally require no anticonvulsant therapy or
ventilatory support

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Presence of an infection with an associated systemic
inflammatory response
r The systemic inflammatory response syndrome
(SIRS) is composed of 4 criteria:
– Temperature >38◦Co r<36 ◦C
– Heart rate >90 bpm
– Respiratory rate >20/min or PaCO2 <32 mm Hg
– WBC >12,000/mm3, <4,000/mm3,o r>10%
band forms
r Sepsis = infection with ≥2 SIRS criteria:
– Release of chemical messengers by the
inflammatory response
– Macrocirculatory failure through decreased
cardiac output or decreased perfusion pressure
– Microcirculatory failure through impaired vascular
autoregulatory mechanisms and functional
shunting of oxygen
– Cytopathic hypoxia and mitochondrial dysfunction
r Hemodynamic changes result from the inflammatory
response:
– Elevated cardiac output in response to
vasodilatation
– Later myocardial depression:
r Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS):
– Adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
– Acute tubular necrosis and kidney failure
– Hepatic injury and failure
– Disseminated intravascular coagulation
r Sepsis should be viewed as a continuum of severity
from a proinflammatory response to organ
dysfunction and tissue hypoperfusion:
– Severe sepsis: Sepsis with at least 1 of the
following organ dysfunctions:
◦Acidosis
◦Renal dysfunction
◦Acute change in mental status
◦Pulmonary dysfunction
◦Hypotension
◦Thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy
◦Liver dysfunction
– Septic shock: Sepsis-induced hypotension despite
fluid resuscitation:
◦Systolic BP <90 mm Hg or reduction of
>40 mm Hg from baseline
r Sepsis is the 10th leading cause of death in US:
– In-hospital mortality for septic shock is ∼30%
ETIOLOGYr Gram-negative bacteria most common:
– Escherichia coli
– Pseudomonas aeruginosa
– Rickettsiae
– Legionella spp.
r Gram-positive bacteria:
– Enterococcus spp.
– Staphylococcus aureus
– Streptococcus pneumoniae
r Fungi (Candida species)
r Viruses
Pediatric Considerations
r Children with a minor infection may have many of
the findings of SIRS.
r Major causes of pediatric bacterial sepsis:
– Neisseria meningitidis
– Streptococcal pneumonia
– Haemophilus influenzae
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Question for signs of infection and a systemic
inflammatory response:
– Fever
– Dyspnea
– Altered mental status:
◦Change in mental status
◦Confusion
◦Delirium
– Nausea and vomiting
r Look for a source of the infection:
– Cough, shortness of breath
– Abdominal pain
– Diarrhea
– Dysuria/frequency
r Past history should highlight risk factors and
immunosuppressive states:
– Underlying terminal illness
– Recent chemotherapy
– Malignancy
– History of a splenectomy
– HIV
– Diabetes
– Nursing home resident
Physical Examr An elevated respiratory rate is an early warning sign
of sepsis and occurs without underlying pulmonary
pathology or acidosis.
r BP is often normal early in sepsis.
r Hypotension when septic shock occurs
r Extremities are often warmed and flushed despite
hypotension.
r Look for a source of the infection:
– Abdominal exam
– Rectal exam to assess for an abscess
– Chest exam for signs of pneumonia
– Any rash is important:
◦Localized erythema with lymphangitis
(streptococcal or staphylococcal cellulitis)
◦Rash involving palms of hands and soles of feet
(rickettsial infection)
◦Petechiae scattered on the torso and extremities
(meningococcemia)
◦Ecthyma gangrenosum (pseudomonas
septicemia)
◦Round, indurated, painless lesion with
surrounding erythema and central necrotic black
eschar
– Decubitus ulcers
– Indwelling catheter:
r CNS infections:
– Coma
– Neck stiffness (meningitis)
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Serum lactate should be done early in the course to
assess severity and need for goal-directed therapy
r Blood cultures prior to antibiotics:
– Broad spectrum of lab tests and imaging studies
to locate the source of the infection and assess for
MOF .
– Placement of a central line with an ScvO2 catheter
may be used to adjust therapy.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Serum lactate:
– >4 mmol/L defines severe sepsis
– Normal lactate does not rule out septic shock
r CBC with differential:
– Leukocytosis is insensitive and nonspecific
– Neutrophil count <500 cells/mm3 should prompt
isolation and empiric IV antibiotics in
chemotherapy patients.
– >5% bands on a peripheral smear is an imperfect
indicator of infection.
– Hematocrit:
◦Patients should be maintained with a
hematocrit >30% and hemoglobin >10 g/dL.
– Platelets:
◦May be elevated in the presence of infection or
sepsis-induced volume depletion
◦Low platelet count is a significant predictor of
bacteremia and death.
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose:
r Ca, Mg, pH
r C-reactive protein
r Cortisol level
r INR/prothrombin time/partial thromboplastin time
r Liver function tests
r ABG or VBG:
– Mixed acid–base abnormalities: Respiratory
alkalosis with metabolic acidosis
– VBG correlates very closely with ABG, except for
SaO2
r Blood cultures:
– From 2 different sites
– 1 may be drawn through an indwelling central line
(i.e., Broviac).
r Urine analysis and culture
Imagingr CXR:
– Determine whether pneumonia is the infectious
source.
– Fluffy, bilateral infiltrates may indicate that ARDS
is already present.
– Free air under the diaphragm indicates the source
of the infection in intraperitoneal and a surgical
intervention is mandatory.
r Soft tissue plain films:
– Indicated if extremity erythema or severe pain
– Air in the soft tissues associated with necrotizing
or gas-forming infection
r Imaging studies to locate the source of the infection
based on the presentation:
– CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
– Abdominal US for gallbladder disease
– Transthoracic or transesophageal echocardiogram

BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Constellation of signs and symptoms from excessive
stimulation of central and peripheral serotonergic
receptors
r Spectrum of symptoms may range from mild and
subtle findings to severe and sometimes fatal toxicity
r Results from use of serotonergic agents, alone or in
combination with other serotonergic agents (may be
therapeutic, intentional overdose, recreational, drug
interactions)
r Classic triad:
– Autonomic dysfunction: Hyperthermia,
diaphoresis, tachycardia, and hypertension
– Cognitive changes: Confusion, agitation,
hallucinations, decreased responsiveness
– Neuromuscular excitability: Hyperreflexia,
myoclonus, tremors

Incidence and Prevalence Estimatesr SSRIs implicated most often, alone or in
combination with other drugs
r Incidence higher in females but fatalities greater in
males
r Highest incidence in ages 19–39
r Most fatalities from drug/drug interactions or
recreational abuse
ETIOLOGYr Serotonin produced by metabolism of L-tryptophan
r Exerts action on 5-hydroxytryptophan (5-HT)
receptors of which there are 7 types located in
central and peripheral nervous systems:
– Influences sleep and temperature regulation,
affective behavior, food intake, migraines, emesis,
sexual behavior, nociception, motor tone, GI
motility, and vascular tone
r Extensive list of serotonergic agents, with psychiatric
meds most common (SSRIs, SNRIs):
– Examples: Citalopram, desvenlafaxine, duloxetine,
escitalopram, fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, paroxetine,
sertraline, trazodone, venlafaxine
r Other serotonergic agents include (not exhaustive):
– Buspirone, cocaine, dextromethorphan, fentanyl,
lithium, MAOIs, MDMA (ecstasy), meperidine,
methadone, metoclopramide, ondansetron,
selegiline, St. John’s wort, TCAs, tramadol,
triptans (controversial)

SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS

– Family, friends, EMS personnel, may provide
additional information
r Patient medication list: Prescribed medications,
over-the-counter medications, herbal supplements
r Medical history:
– Seizures, migraines, attention deficit/hyperactivity
disorder, Parkinson, recent illnesses
r Psychiatric history
r Illicit drug abuse history
r Onset of symptoms:
– Mental status/behavioral changes, development of
hyperthermia, muscular rigidity/clonus
Physical Examr Vital signs:
– Hyperthermia
– Tachycardia
– Hypertension or hypotension (may evolve into
frank shock and cardiovascular collapse)
r Dermatologic:
– Diaphoresis, normal color
r GI:
– Hyperactive bowel sounds
– Diarrhea
r Mental status/neurologic:
– Agitation
– Altered mental status
– Ocular clonus
– Hallucinations
– Waxing/waning delirium

– Clonus: Most helpful finding in diagnosis, greater
in lower extremities
– Hypertonicity and rigidity, greater in lower
extremities
– Hyperreflexia, greater in lower extremities

diagnosis

taken/been on a serotonergic agent and 1 of the

– Inducible clonus plus agitation or diaphoresis
– Ocular clonus plus agitation or diaphoresis

coingestants

r Total CK
r Cell count, blood/urine cultures if infectious process
suspected

r EKG:
– Evaluate QRS/QT intervals, dysrhythmias

inflammatory response:
– C3a and C5a act as anaphylatoxins.
– C5a is strongly chemotactic for neutrophils.

Specific legal definition varies from state to state:

between the penis and vulva or penis and anus

penis, vulva, or anus

groin, inner thigh, or buttocks

women, 5% in men
r 72% of female rape victims are raped by someone
they know; however, men are primarily raped and
physically assaulted by strangers and acquaintances,
not intimate partners.
r Women who are disabled, pregnant, or attempting
to leave their abusers are at increased risk of
intimate partner rape.
r Prevalence of sexual assault in men is higher in
those who are gay, bisexual, veterans, prison
inmates or seeking mental health services
r Nearly 25% of women and 7% of men have been
raped or sexually assaulted by a current or former
partner.

– Most will reveal the history only in response to
direct questions.
r Tachycardia or pounding heart beat
r Headaches
r Nausea
r Back pain
r Skin problems
r Menstrual symptoms
r Sudden weight change
r Sleeping disorders
r Abdominal pain
r Trouble breathing

– Of those with injuries, 70% report no injury at
presentation.

– Vulvar trauma
– Laceration of vaginal wall (more common in
younger patients, near introitus)
– Multiple contusions
– Abrasions
– Human bite
– Lacerations or puncture wound to extremity
– Burns

happened.

– Number of assailants
– Types of penetration: Vaginal, oral, rectal
– Assailant ejaculation: Ask if assailant used

◦Bathed
◦Urinated
◦Defecated
◦Eaten
◦Tampon use

12 hr in vagina

reporting to police.
r Female chaperone required if male physician

with patient’s consent.

– Staining
– Tears
– Mud
– Leaves

place all clothes in paper bag.

r Only the patient should handle the clothing.

– Lacerations
– Bites
– Scratches
– Foreign bodies
– Ecchymosis
– Dried semen on skin

– Scalp or pubic hair samples

pace.
r Allow advocate to stay with patient during exam

SHOCK
Nathan Shapiro rChristopher M. Fischer
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Inadequate supply of blood flow to tissues to meet
the demands of the tissues
r Tissue oxygen requirements are not fulfilled.
r Toxic metabolites are not removed.
r If untreated, inevitable progression from inadequate
perfusion to organ dysfunction and ultimately to
death.
r Major categories of shock:
– Hypovolemic shock:
◦Decreased blood volume
◦Suspect hemorrhage if acute onset
◦Severe dehydration if progressive onset and
elevated hematocrit, BUN, and creatinine
– Obstructive (cardiogenic) shock:
◦Decreased cardiac output and tissue hypoxia
with adequate intravascular volume and
myocardial dysfunction
◦Venous congestion with increase in central
venous pressure
◦Compensatory increase in SVR
◦May be caused by cardiac dysfunction,
obstruction to inflow of blood to the heart, or
obstruction to outflow of blood from the heart
– Septic shock:
◦An initial infectious insult overwhelms the
immune system.
◦Biochemical messengers (cytokines,
leukotrienes, histamines, prostaglandins) cause
vessel dilatation.
◦Capillary endothelium becomes disrupted and
the vessels leak.
◦Drop in SVR leads to inadequate tissue
perfusion.
◦Secondarily, decreased cardiac output from
“cardiac stun” resulting in cold septic shock
– Neurogenic shock:
◦Spinal cord insults disrupt sympathetic
stimulation to vessels.
◦Loss of sympathetic tone causes arteriodilating
and vasodilatation.
◦Lesions proximal to T4 disrupt sympathetic,
spares vagal innervation causing bradycardia.
– Anaphylactic shock:
◦An antigen stimulates the allergic reaction.
◦Mast cells degranulate.
◦Histamine releases, along with autocoids,
stimulate an anaphylaxis cascade.
◦Vascular smooth muscle relaxes.
◦Capillary endothelium leaks.
◦Drop in SVR leads to inadequate tissue
perfusion.
– Pharmacologic agents may cause shock through
smooth muscle dilation or myocardial depression.
ETIOLOGYr Hypovolemic shock:
– Abdominal trauma, blunt or penetrating
– Abortion—complete, partial, or inevitable
– Anemia—chronic or acute
– Aneurysms—abdominal, thoracic, dissecting
– Aortogastric fistula
– Arteriovenous malformations
– Blunt trauma
– Burns
– Diabetes
– Diarrhea
– Diuretics
– Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
– Epistaxis
– Fractures (especially long bones)
– Hemoptysis
– GI bleed
– Mallory–Weiss tear
– Penetrating trauma
– Placenta previa
– Postpartum hemorrhage
– Retroperitoneal bleed
– Severe ascites
– Splenic rupture
r Toxic epidermal necrolysis:
– Vascular injuries
– Vomiting
r Cardiogenic shock:
– Cardiomyopathy
– Conduction abnormalities and arrhythmias
–M I
– Myocardial contusion
– Myocarditis
– Pericardial tamponade
– Pulmonary embolus
– Tension pneumothorax
– Valvular insufficiency
– Ventricular septal defect
r Vasogenic shock:
– Acute respiratory distress syndrome
– Bacterial infection
– Bowel perforation
– Cellulitis
– Cholangitis
– Cholecystitis
– Endocarditis
– Endometritis
– Fungemia
– Infected indwelling prosthetic device
– Intra-abdominal infection or abscess
– Mediastinitis
– Meningitis
– Myometritis
– Pelvic inflammatory disease
– Peritonitis
– Pyelonephritis
– Pharyngitis
– Pneumonia
– Septic arthritis
– Thrombophlebitis
– Tubo-ovarian abscess
– Urosepsis
r Anaphylactic:
– Drug reaction (most commonly to aspirin,
β-lactam antibiotics)
– Exercise (rare)
– Food allergy (peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish, fish,
milk, eggs, soy, and wheat account for 90% of
food-related anaphylaxis)
– Insect sting
– Latex
– Radiographic contrast materials
– Synthetic products

– Antihypertensives
– Antidepressants
– Benzodiazepines
– Cholinergics
– Digoxin
– Narcotics
– Nitrates
r Neurogenic:
– Spinal cord injury

SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Generalized shock:
r Hypotension
r Decreased peripheral pulses
r Tachycardia
r Tachypnea
r Decreased urine output
r Diaphoresis
r Obtundation
r Lethargy

factors

cellulitis and urticarial rash, etc.)

shock state:
– Hypovolemic (classic symptoms):
◦Neck veins are flat.
◦Mucous membranes are dry.
◦Extremities are cold.
– Cardiogenic shock (classic symptoms):
◦Jugular venous distension is present.
◦Mucous membranes are moist.
◦Extremities are cold.
– Early septic shock (classic symptoms):
◦Neck veins are flat.
◦Mucous membranes are dry.
◦Extremities are warm.
◦During late shock, extremities may become cold
and mottled.

r WBC:
– High: Nonspecific marker of infection
– Low: Neutropenic infections
r Electrolytes
r Blood glucose:
– High: Diabetic ketoacidosis or septic shock
– Low: Pediatric sepsis
r Prothrombin time/partial thromboplastin time
r Cardiac enzymes
r Urinalysis
r β-human chorionic gonadotropin
r Lactic acid level:
– Good surrogate marker of shock state
Imagingr CXR
r ECG
r Abdominal US
r CT abdomen:
– Requires that the patient 1st be stabilized
– In the setting of abdominal trauma and in search
for suspicion of abdominal infection
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
EKG:
r Assess for ischemia and other disorders of cardiac
muscle:
r Electrical alternans or low voltage with cardiac
tamponade
r Right-heart strain with pulmonary embolism
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr ABCs per standard protocol
r Fluid resuscitation as warranted
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Large-bore IV access:
– When possible, central venous access and
monitoring
r Fluid resuscitation in noncardiogenic shock patients
r Control bleeding with direct pressure measures.
r Stabilization of a fractured pelvis with sheet or
commercial device or external fixation
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Hypovolemic shock:
– Identify source of volume depletion
– Aggressive fluid resuscitation keeping systolic
blood pressure (SBP) >100 mm Hg until definitive
treatment
– 2–3 L crystalloid initially
– Packed RBCs if 2–3 L crystalloids do not improve
SBP
– Identify source of bleeding and rapidly move
toward definitive treatment.
– Thoracotomy and aortic cross-clamping in
refractory shock with penetrating torso trauma
r Cardiogenic shock:
– Ease work of breathing with intubation
– Insult-specific therapy (e.g., thrombolytics for MI,
pericardiocentesis for pericardial tamponade)
– Treat dysrhythmias.
– Vasopressors (norepinephrine or dopamine) as
needed
r Septic shock:
– Aggressive crystalloid fluid resuscitation
– Titrate fluid to urine output >30 cc/hr
– Blood product transfusion to maintain HCT
30–35%
– Early antimicrobial therapy
– Inotropic support as needed
– Norepinephrine as preferred 1st-line infusion
r Anaphylactic shock:
– Intubation for airway compromise
– Epinephrine
– Subcutaneous in noncritical settings
– IV drip for immediate life threats or refractory
hypotension
– H1 blockers (diphenhydramine)
– H2 blockers (cimetidine)
– Corticosteroids (hydrocortisone or
methylprednisolone)
– Nebulized β2-antagonists for bronchospasm
– Patients taking β-blockers may be more likely to
experience severe symptoms of anaphylaxis
r Pharmacologic shock:
– Decontamination of overdoses with charcoal
– Inotropic agents as needed
– Drug-specific antidotes
r Neurogenic shock:
– Supportive therapy
– Traction and fracture stabilization
– Corticosteroids

r Calcium gluconate: 100–1,000 mg IV at
0.5–2 mL/min
r Cimetidine: 300 mg IV
r Diphenhydramine: 50–100 mg IV over 3 min
r Dobutamine: 5–40 μg/kg/min IV:
– Dopaminergic: 1–3 μg/kg/min IV
– β-effects: 3–10 μg/kg/min IV
– α/β-effects: 10–20 μg/kg/min IV
– α-effects: 20 μg/kg/min IV
r Epinephrine:
– 1–4 μg/min IV infusion
– Endotracheal 1 mg (10 mL of 1:10,000) once
followed by 5 quick insufflations
– Place 1 mg in 250 mL D5W = 4 μg/mL
r Glucagon: 1–5 mg IV bolus initial, then 1–20 mg/h
infusion

r Methylprednisolone: 1–2 mg/kg IV

1–2 μg/kg/min IV
r Phenylephrine: 40–180 μg/min IV

– All patients with persistent shock need ICU
monitoring.

admitted to non-ICU setting (e.g., tension
pneumothorax that has been decompressed and
chest tube placed).
Discharge Criteria
Patients who are in shock should not be discharged
home from the ED.
Issues for Referralr Traumatic hypovolemic shock (hemorrhagic shock)
patients may require a trauma center.
r Patients with cardiogenic shock due to MI may
require cardiac catheterization or additional cardiac
surgery support.
r Septic shock due to necrotizing fasciitis may require
advanced surgical support.
r Neurogenic shock with spinal cord injury will require

r Identify the etiology of shock.
r Aggressively resuscitate the patient, 1st with IV
fluids and next with vasopressor support to
minimize hypoxic exposure.

SHOULDER DISLOCATION
Doodnauth Hiraman rWallace A. Carter
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Shoulder is a very dynamic joint, prone to injury.
r Anterior dislocation (90–96%):
– Injury is from direct or indirect forces on the
abducted and externally rotated arm.
– Injury may also result from a direct blow to
posterolateral aspect of shoulder.
r Posterior dislocation:
– Often missed
– Forces on the adducted and internally rotated arm
result in posterior dislocation of humeral head in
relation to glenoid fossa.
– Most common mechanism is seizure and sudden
contraction of all the posterior muscle groups.
– Other mechanisms include electrocution and
direct blow to anterior shoulder.
r Inferior dislocation (rare):
– Luxatio erecta
– Hyperabduction of arm, tear of rotator cuff, and
rotation of arm 180◦ above head
– Commonly seen after a fall from a height:
◦Arm has struck object on descent and is thrust
above the head.
– Often accompanied by neurovascular injury and
fracture
Pediatric Considerations
Dislocation is rare in children: Epiphyseal fractures
must be suspected.
Geriatric Considerations
Dislocation is often accompanied by fracture.
ETIOLOGYr Falls from height
r Impact injuries
r Distraction injuries of upper arm
r Seizures
r Electrocution
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Severe pain in the affected shoulder
r Anterior dislocation:
– Shoulder is squared off.
– Prominent acromion process and palpable anterior
fullness
– Arm is held in slight abduction and external
rotation.
r Posterior dislocation:
– Coracoid process is prominent, with a palpable
posterior bulge.
– Arm is held in slight adduction and internal
rotation.
r Inferior dislocation (luxatio erecta):
– Rare but easy to identify
– Arm is shortened and fixed above head as if raised
to ask a question.
r Head of humerus may be palpable on the lateral
chest wall.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Evaluate neurovascular status of distal arm.
r Retest neurovascular status after any manipulation.
r Dislocation requires prompt treatment:
– Incidence of post-traumatic arthritis increases with
time dislocation is untreated.
– Plain films of the shoulder should be obtained
immediately.
– Even in clinically obvious cases, films should be
obtained before manipulation, unless a significant
delay will result.
– An impacted humeral head fracture may be
converted to a displaced humeral head fracture if
manipulated.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Imagingr At least 2 views should be obtained:
– Anteroposterior (AP):
◦To visualize dislocation or fracture
– Trans-scapular Y or axillary view:
◦To visualize if anterior or posterior
r Anterior dislocation:
– Posterolateral compression fracture of the humeral
head (Hill–Sachs deformity)
– Corresponding lesion on anterior glenoid rim is
the Bankart lesion:
◦These do not require treatment.
– Fractures of the greater tuberosity of the humeral
head are seen in 15–35%:
◦If there is >1 cm displacement after reduction,
surgical intervention may be necessary.
r Posterior dislocation:
– Often missed on AP film
r Degree of overlap on radiographic film is smaller and
displaced superiorly, producing the meniscus sign.
r Rotated humerus yields “light bulb on a stick”
finding on AP view:
– Reverse Hill-Sachs deformity from compression
fracture of the anterior medial humeral head may
also be seen.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Fracture of the humeral head
r Fracture of the humeral shaft
r Acromioclavicular injury
r Septic shoulder joint
r Hemarthrosis in shoulder joint
r Scapular fracture
r Cervical spine injury
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Neurovascular injury should be identified and the arm
splinted in the position of most comfort.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Airway management and resuscitate as indicated.
r Exclude more serious injuries, especially in
multitrauma patient.
r Ensure no injury to axillary nerve or vessels.

S
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Adequate analgesia and muscle relaxation are
essential for successful reduction:
– Procedural sedation with a short-acting opioid
and a benzodiazepine OR
– Methohexital or etomidate alone
– In the cooperative patient, intra-articular block
only (20 cc of lidocaine 1% or bupivacaine 0.5%)
into shoulder joint
r Anterior dislocation reduction techniques:
– Scapular manipulation:
◦Patient seated, traction to arm in horizontal
plane, countertraction with other hand on
clavicle
◦2nd person adducts tip of scapula medially,
moving glenoid fossa
– Stimson:
◦Patient in prone position with arm dangling over
side, hang 10–15 lb around wrist; muscle
fatigued over 20–30 min
◦Can concurrently use scapular manipulation
◦Only 1 person required
– Traction/countertraction:
◦Patient in supine position with continuous
longitudinal traction to affected arm
◦Countertraction from sheet wrapped around
chest
◦Arm internally or externally rotated if
unsuccessful after several minutes
– External rotation:
◦Patient supine; elbow at 90◦; gentle, slow
external rotation of arm
◦Should be done slowly and with cooperative
patient
r Posterior dislocation reduction techniques:
– May use Stimson or traction/countertraction
techniques with manipulation of humeral head
anteriorly
r Inferior dislocation (luxatio erecta) reduction
techniques:
– Patient in supine position; gentle longitudinal
traction to distract humeral head
– Gentle countertraction with sheet draped over
trapezius and chest
– Arm slowly rotated from 180–0◦
r Postreduction care:
– Postreduction films
– Place in sling and swath or shoulder immobilizer
immediately after reduction.
– Shoulder should remain immobilized for 2–3 wk in
young patients.
– Immobilization time should be less in older
patients to avoid frozen shoulder.

used)

preservative-free formulation.

reduction under general anesthesia or open

r Patients with neurovascular compromise

appropriate immobilizer and with orthopedic

SICK SINUS SYNDROME
David F. M. Brown rNirma D. Bustamante
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Collective term used to describe dysfunction in the
sinus node’s automaticity and impulse generation
r Mechanism:
– Caused by progressive degeneration of the
intrinsic functions of the sinoatrial (SA) node
– Characterized by periods of unexplained sinus
node dysfunction leading to bradyarrhythmias,
often without appropriate atrial or junctional
escape rhythms
r Syndrome includes:
– Chronic SA nodal dysfunction
– Frequently depressed pacemakers
– Arteriovenous nodal conduction disturbances
– Sluggish return of SA nodal activity after DC
cardioversion
r Presents in all age groups (mean age >65 yr)
r Male/female ratio is 1:1
ETIOLOGYr Intrinsic causes:
– Most common cause: Idiopathic degenerative
fibrosis of sinus node
– Coronary artery or SA nodal artery disease
– Cardiomyopathy
– Ion channel mutations/familial SSS
– Leukemia and metastatic disease
– Infiltrative cardiac or collagen vascular disease,
including amyloidosis
– Surgical trauma
r Inflammatory diseases:
– Rheumatic heart disease
– Chagas disease
– Pericarditis and myocarditis
r Extrinsic causes (not true SSS but similar
presentation):
– Drugs:
◦β-blockers, calcium channel blockers, clonidine
◦Digoxin, amiodarone
◦Lithium, phenytoin
– Autonomically mediated syndromes
(cholinesterase deficiency)
– Hyperkalemia/hypokalemia
– Hypothyroidism
– Hypothermia
– Hypoglycemia
– Sepsis/infection
Pediatric Considerations
Associated with congenital abnormalities and
subsequent surgical repair, as well as with congenital
SA nodal artery deficiency
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Symptoms represent CNS hypoperfusion from
bradydysrhythmia or traditional cardiovascular
presentations
Historyr Asymptomatic
r Palpitations/fatigue
r Syncope/presyncope/dizziness
r Anginal equivalents (chest pain/SOB)
r Activity intolerance
r Sudden death
Physical Examr Bradycardia
r Alternating bradycardia and atrial tachycardia
r Altered mental status
r Cyanosis
r Transient ischemic attack/stroke
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Ascertaining etiology
r 12-lead EKG
r CXR
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Serum electrolytes (including magnesium and
calcium)
r Cardiac markers
r Digoxin level, if appropriate
r Thyroid function testing
Imaging
EKG:
r Most common finding: Chronic, inappropriate sinus
bradycardia
r Sinus pauses or SA block
r Atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response
r Prolonged pauses after cardioversion or carotid
massage
r Bradyarrhythmias may alternate with
supraventricular tachydysrhythmia.
r Tachy–brady syndrome: Bursts of atrial tachycardia
interspersed with bradycardia
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Most electrophysiologic studies are no longer
recommended due to poor sensitivity and specificity.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Other bradydysrhythmias
r Other tachyarrhythmias: In particular, be careful to
distinguish SSS from atrial fibrillation, because DC
cardioversion or the use of nodal agents in presumed
Afib can be harmful if SA node dysfunction coexists.
r Electrolyte derangements
r Medication toxicity: β-blockers, calcium channel
blockers, clonidine, digoxin
r Excessive vagal tone
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Advanced life support transport
r Oxygen supplementation
r Cardiac monitoring
r Atropine if bradycardic and hemodynamically
unstable
r Transcutaneous pacing for unstable patients
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Atropine if a bradydysrhythmia is causing unstable
signs/symptoms: Angina, mental confusion, or
hypotension
r Transcutaneous pacing if atropine unsuccessful
r If this fails, emergent transvenous pacing
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURES
Supraventricular tachydysrhythmia alternating with
bradycardia:
r Unstable:
– Cardiovert
– Anticipate subsequent profound bradycardia
r Stable patients:
– Cardiac monitoring
r Digoxin, diltiazem, verapamil, or magnesium can be
used for tachydysrhythmia
r Any medication may cause profound bradycardia
r Bradycardia:
– Discontinuation of medications that alter sinus
node function
– Correct reversible causes of SA nodal depression:
O2, warming, glucose
ALERT
Rewarming is critical in hypothermia as atropine
may cause myocardial instability:
r Anticoagulate patients with atrial fibrillation and
tachy–brady syndrome.

SICKLE CELL DISEASE
Steven H. Bowman r Marcus E. Emebo r Mary E. Johnson
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Sickle cell disease (SCD) is an autosomal recessive
hemoglobinopathy characterized by abnormal
hemoglobin (HbS) which polymerizes under stress
and deforms RBCs, resulting in hemolysis,
vaso-occlusion, and subsequent tissue
ischemia/infarction
r HbS production secondary to a single amino acid
substitution in hemoglobin gene
r Occurs in people of African, Mediterranean, Middle
Eastern, and Asian descent; areas where malaria is
endemic
r Severity variable even among the same phenotype
r Genotypes and severity in African Americans:
– HbSS, severe
– HbSC, mild to moderate severity
– HbSβ-thalassemia, mild to moderate severity
– HbAS, sickle cell trait:
◦No manifestation of disease
◦At risk for sudden death with extreme physical
exertion, severe hypoxia, severe dehydration, or
maternal labor
r Chronic hemolytic anemia associated with
progressive vasculopathy manifested by systemic
and pulmonary hypertension, cholelithiasis,
cutaneous leg ulcers, and priapism
r Acute vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC) can occur in
essentially any organ systems:
– Bone/joint crises:
◦Vaso-occlusion of bone microvasculature causes
infarction
◦Long bones, ribs, sternum, spine, and pelvis
affected
◦Dactylitis, or “hand–foot syndrome,” occurs at
ages 6–24 mo
– Acute chest syndrome:
◦Vaso-occlusion of pulmonary vasculature
◦Fat embolism from infarcted bone marrow
and/or infections (viral or bacterial) may
contribute
◦Associated Chlamydia pneumoniae and
Mycoplasma pneumoniae isolated in sputum
and Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteremia
◦High mortality (2–14%)
◦50% of sickle cell patients will experience at
least 1 episode
◦Radiographic pulmonary infiltrate with fever and
respiratory symptoms makes it difficult to
distinguish from pneumonia
◦More common in children
– Splenic sequestration:
◦Splenic sinusoids become congested with
sickled RBCs, obstructing outflow
◦Estimated 6–17% of SCD deaths
◦Circulatory collapse may be rapidly fatal
◦More common in children <5y ro l d
– Aplastic crisis:
◦Bone marrow suppression usually occurs
secondary to viral infection, most commonly
Parvovirus B19
◦Hallmark acute anemia with low reticulocyte
count
◦Acute bone marrow suppression significantly
worsens chronic anemia
◦Generally self-limited
◦More common in children
– Cerebrovascular accident/transient ischemic attack
(CVA/TIA):
◦Secondary to vaso-occlusion by sickled cells and
thromboembolism in children and older
patients, respectively
◦Children with SCD have a 300-fold increased
risk of CVA/TIA
◦Most events occur before the age of 10 and
after the age of 29 yr
– Bacterial infection:
◦Sepsis is the leading cause of death in patients
with SCD
◦Increased risk of bacteremia, meningitis, and
osteomyelitis
◦Impaired splenic function impairs ability to fight
encapsulated organisms
◦S. pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae,
Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and
Salmonella are leading organisms
◦Children <5 yr of age have 400-fold increase in
pneumococcal infections.
– Priapism:
◦Painful, sustained, unwanted erection >3h r
◦More commonly low-flow (ischemic) priapism
than high-flow (nonischemic)
Pediatric Considerations
r Acute sickle cell complications in children carry high
morbidity and should be screened for aggressively
r Infections commonly precipitate crisis
r Confirm immunization history (pneumococcal and H.
influenzae type b)
r Determine if child is receiving prophylactic penicillin,
normally indicated in children ≤5y ro l d
r Overwhelming infection highest in children <3y ro f
age
Pregnancy Considerations
r Variable frequency of crisis episodes, not uncommon
for increased frequency
r Anemia is more profound
r Increased rates of hypertensive disorders of
pregnancy, asymptomatic bacterial infections, UTI,
and pyelonephritis leading to septicemia
r Increased risk of spontaneous abortions, antepartum
bleeding, and premature rupture of membranes
r Increased risk of preterm labor, intrauterine growth
restriction, and low birth weight
ETIOLOGY
Common crisis precipitants:
r Infection (bacterial and viral)
r Dehydration
r Hypoxemia
r Acidosis
r Emotional stress
r Surgery/trauma
r Weather changes
r Pregnancy
r Toxins
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr May present with either:
– Pain crisis
– Complications of the disease
– Combination of above
r May not demonstrate usually autonomic signs of
acute pain
r Sickle cell pain crisis:
– Bone/joint crisis:
◦Pain in extremities, back, sternum, or joints
◦Variable extremity and joint swelling/warmth
◦Hand–foot syndrome in infants; swelling in
hands and feet and a reluctance to walk or use
hands
– Abdominal crisis:
◦Abdominal pain without peritonitis
◦Variable nausea, vomiting, diarrhea
– Priapism: Prolonged painful erection
r Complications/progression of disease:
– Acute chest syndrome:
◦Chest pain
◦Fever
◦New pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiographs
◦Respiratory symptoms
◦Hypoxemia
– Splenic sequestration crisis:
◦Abdominal pain, splenomegaly
◦Fatigue, lethargy, pallor
◦Hypotension, tachycardia, syncope, shock
– Aplastic crisis:
◦Variable fever, headache, nausea, vomiting
◦Fatigue, pallor, tachycardia
– CVA/TIA:
◦Focal neurologic deficit
◦Mental status changes
◦Seizure
Historyr Genotype
r Onset of current symptoms
r Previous crises
r Immunizations
r Surgical history
r Determine typical vs. atypical crisis
Physical Exam
Conduct a thorough physical exam:
r Vital signs: BP , HR, temperature, O2 saturation
r General appearance: Jaundice, pallor
r Cardiopulmonary exam:
– Rales, wheezing, tachypnea
– Peripheral edema, elevated JVD
– Gallops, murmurs
r Abdominal exam:
– Organomegaly, tenderness, peritonitis
r Musculoskeletal exam
– Erythema on extremities
– Warm, swollen hands and feet in children
r Neurologic exam:
– Focal neurologic impairment
– Cranial nerve palsy

SICKLE CELL DISEASE
S
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Conduct a thorough physical exam, with focus on
signs of infection or ischemia.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC:
– Compare Hb with prior values if available
– Leukocytosis is common and does not necessarily
indicate infection
r Reticulocyte count is generally elevated in SCD
individuals, and decreased with aplastic crisis
r Complete metabolic panel (CMP):
– Be aware that creatinine may appear normal
despite baseline chronic renal dysfunction
– Elevated total bilirubin levels may indicate
intravascular hemolysis
r Markers of hemolysis (total bilirubin, haptoglobin,
and LDH) may be present at variable degrees
r Serial arterial blood gases and A–a gradients helpful
in acute chest syndrome
r Cultures: Blood, urine, throat, and CSF (if indicated)
r Type and screen (or cross)
r Urine pregnancy test in women
Imagingr Radiographs should be directed to confirm
diagnosis:
– Chest radiograph if pneumonia or acute chest
syndrome suspected
– Extremity radiographs if osteomyelitis suspected
r IV contrast may exacerbate or precipitate a crisis
r Head CT/MRI to evaluate stroke
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Lumbar puncture if CNS infection or subarachnoid
hemorrhage is suspected
r Arthrocentesis for acute arthritis
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Sickle cell crises may mimic or obscure more serious
underlying pathology (e.g., acute abdomen, MI, PE,
nephrolithiasis)
r Suspect other diagnoses if pain is more severe or
atypical
TREATMENT
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Identify and treat high morbidity complications
r Establish venous access
r Assess pain and initiate therapy
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Choice of analgesics dependent on patient, severity
of presentation, and prior agents:
– Reassess pain frequently (e.g., every 15–30 min)
and titrate until improvement
– IV opiates (e.g., morphine, hydromorphone,
fentanyl) 1st line, consider adjunct agents
– Adjuncts: Acetaminophen, NSAIDs (use with
caution given impaired renal function)
– Caution with meperidine as metabolites may
accumulate and pose seizure risk
– If no venous access, PO and subcutaneous
analgesics preferred over IM
r Hydration:
– Oral hydration if patient tolerating po
– Parenteral IV solution 0.45% NS for adults and
children or 0.2% NS for infants
– Avoid over-hydration, at risk for:
◦Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis which
promotes RBC sickling
◦Atelectasis which precipitates acute chest
syndrome
r Complication-specific therapy:
– Acute chest syndrome:
◦Oxygen, bronchodilators, incentive spirometer
◦Consider exchange transfusion for worsening
respiratory symptoms, hypoxemia, and
increasing A–a gradient
– Splenic sequestration:
◦Simple transfusion, promotes remobilization of
RBCs
◦Be aware risk of precipitating VOC after raising
Hb levels
◦Ideal treatment is prevention: Chronic
transfusions, splenectomy
– Aplastic crisis:
◦Simple transfusion
◦Isolation from pregnant healthcare workers
– Priapism:
◦1st line: Intracavernosal aspiration with
α-adrenergic agonist (e.g., epinephrine,
terbutaline) irrigation
◦2nd line: Exchange transfusion if failed
aspiration
– Empiric antibiotics: Sepsis, pneumonia, and
osteomyelitis
– Exchange transfusion may be required for
complications such as CVA and priapism
r Consultations:
– Hematology especially if exchange transfusion
required
– Neurology/neurosurgery for acute CNS events
– Urology for priapism
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Refractory pain
r Complications: Acute chest syndrome, sequestration
crisis, aplastic crisis, CVA/TIA, refractory priapism
r Signs of bacterial infection or fever of undetermined
etiology
r Symptomatic anemia
r ICU admission for hemodynamic instability,
worsening hypoxemia in acute chest syndrome, and
severe acute CNS events.
Discharge Criteriar Resolution of pain crisis
r No indications for admission
r Follow-up arranged with hematologist
Issues for Referral
Meticulous primary care can limit the frequency and
severity of pain crises.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
If discharged, patient should see PCP or hematologist
in 1–2 days.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Distinguish typical sickle cell crisis from acute
life-threatening complications
r Treat pain aggressively with appropriately selected
and administered analgesic agents
r Patients with acute pain may not demonstrate
typical signs, such as tachycardia or diaphoresis

SINUSITIS (RHINOSINUSITIS)
Cory A. Siebe rMaria E. Moreira
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Inflammation of mucous membranes lining the
paranasal sinuses and nasal passages with or
without fluid collection in the sinus cavities
r Classifications:
– Acute: Signs and symptoms for <4w k
– Subacute: Signs and symptoms for 4–8 wk
– Chronic: Signs and symptoms for >8 wk in spite
of antibiotic treatment
– Recurrent: 3 or more episodes per year
ETIOLOGYr Acute rhinosinusitis pathophysiology:
– Viral upper respiratory infection or allergies causes
mucous membrane inflammation
– Inflammation causes obstruction of sinus ostia,
decreased mucociliary clearance, and thickening of
secretions
– Viruses are the primary cause, but 0.5–2.2%
develop into bacterial infection after bacteria
become trapped and multiply, resulting in
suppuration
– Nosocomial rhinosinusitis associated with
nasogastric and nasotracheal tubes
– Immunocompromised patients at higher risk for
rhinosinusitis
r Subacute and chronic rhinosinusitis
pathophysiology:
– Multifactorial, role of bacteria remains elusive
– Allergic inflammation causing narrowed ostia and
blocked drainage
– Immune dysfunction leading to increased
infectious risk
– Impaired ciliary function leading to decreased
mucous clearance
– Odontogenic infection causing maxillary sinusitis
– Fungus ball
– Anatomical obstruction or polyps obstructing
sinus ostia
r Microbiology:
– Acute rhinosinusitis:
◦Nontypable Haemophilus influenzae
◦Streptococcus pneumoniae
◦Moraxella catarrhalis
◦Staphylococcus aureus
◦Anaerobes
◦Viruses: Parainfluenza, adenovirus, rhinovirus,
influenza
– Chronic rhinosinusitis:
◦Same as acute, often polymicrobial, with
increasing anaerobes and gram negatives
– Nosocomial rhinosinusitis:
◦S. aureus
◦Streptococcal species
◦Pseudomonas
◦Klebsiella
– Immunocompromised patients with rhinosinusitis:
◦Bacteria as above
◦Fungal pathogens (Aspergillus)
Pediatric Considerations
r Nontypable H. influenzae more common than
S. pneumoniae as cause of acute bacterial
rhinosinusitis in children
r Ethmoid and maxillary sinuses present at birth
r Frontal and sphenoid sinuses do not emerge until
age 6–7 yr
r Rhinosinusitis more common in children
r Periorbital/orbital cellulitis is a common complication
of ethmoid rhinosinusitis in children:
– Periorbital swelling, fever, ptosis, proptosis, and
painful or decreased extraocular movements
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Facial–dental pain, headache, halitosis, hyposmia,
cough
r Purulent nasal discharge and postnasal drainage
r Fever
r Frontal sinusitis:
– Pain of the lower forehead
– Pain worsened when lying on the back; improves
when upright
r Maxillary sinusitis:
– Malar facial pain
– Maxillary dental pain
– Referred ear pain
– Pain worsens with head upright or bending
forward and improves with reclining
r Ethmoid sinusitis:
– Retro-orbital pain
– Periorbital edema
r Sphenoid sinusitis (very uncommon):
– Pain over the occiput or mastoid
– Pain worse when lying on back or bending forward
Historyr Acute viral rhinosinusitis:
– Symptoms typically resolve in 7–10 days
r Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis needing antibiotic
treatment can present in 3 different patterns:
– Pattern 1: Persistent symptoms lasting >10 days
without improvement
– Pattern 2: Severe symptoms or:
◦Temperature ≥39◦C and purulent nasal
discharge for 3–4 days at the beginning of
illness
– Pattern 3: Worsening symptoms:
◦Return of symptoms after a 5–6- day duration of
upper respiratory infection that was improving
r Other important history:
– Symptom history and time course
– Allergy history
– Recent NG or NT tube placement
– Immunocompromised state
Physical Examr Vital signs, toxic/nontoxic appearance
r Edema of the nasal mucous membranes and
turbinates
r Purulence in the nares or posterior pharynx
r Warmth, tenderness, or cellulitis over sinus
r Sinus tenderness on palpation
r Periorbital edema
r Failure of transillumination of maxillary sinuses:
– Observed through the palate
r Dental exam revealing abscess or tenderness of
maxillary teeth
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Clinical diagnosis based on history and physical
exam
r Determine if patient fits pattern of acute bacterial
rhinosinusitis that should be treated with antibiotics
(see “History”)
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Lab studies not helpful for diagnosis or management
Imagingr Imaging unnecessary in uncomplicated cases
r Plain-film radiography:
– Normal films do not exclude bacterial cause
– Waters view can be ordered, but has moderate
sensitivity in diagnosing maxillary sinus
abnormality and poor sensitivity in diagnosing
lesions in other sinuses
– Odontogenic maxillary sinusitis may be missed by
dental exam and panorex films, but is apparent as
periapical lucency on cone beam CT or sinus CT
r CT:
– Preferred if imaging is necessary
– Warranted in patients with complicated
rhinosinusitis, severe headache, seizures, focal
neurologic deficits, periorbital edema, or
abnormal intraocular muscle function
– IV contrast if concern for osteomyelitis or abscess
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Sinus aspirate culture:
– Gold standard for making a microbial diagnosis
but not routinely performed
r Culture of discharge may have benefit but remains
unstudied and is not typically performed
r Functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS):
– Restores physiologic sinus drainage
Pediatric Considerations
FESS is a safe and effective treatment in children

S
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Uncomplicated viral or allergic rhinitis
r Otitis media
r Dacryocystitis
r Migraine and cluster headache
r Dental pain
r Trigeminal neuralgia
r Temporomandibular joint disorders
r Giant cell arteritis/temporal arteritis
r Rhinitis medicamentosa (decongestants, β-blockers,
antihypertensives, birth control pills)
r Nasal polyp, tumor, or foreign body
r CNS infection
r Granulomatous or ciliary disease
r Aspergillosis
r Rhinocerebral mucormycosis:
– Rare rapidly progressive fungal infection
– Occurs in diabetics and the immunocompromised
– Orbital/facial pain out of proportion to exam
– Lethargy, headache in a systemically ill-appearing
patient
– Black eschar or pale area on the palate or nasal
mucosa
Pregnancy Considerations
r Rhinitis of pregnancy:
– Estrogen has cholinergic effect on mucosa
– Worse during 3rd trimester
– Resolves within 2 wk postpartum
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
No special considerations
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Toxic-appearing patients may require airway
management and fluid resuscitation.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Identifying rhinosinusitis needing antibiotics
r Counseling and reassurance to patients requesting
antibiotics for mild symptoms <10 days duration
MEDICATIONr Nonantibiotic therapies:
– Pain control
– Saline nasal irrigation may be beneficial
– Oral corticosteroids as adjunctive to oral
antibiotics are effective, but data limited
– Intranasal steroids recommended as adjunct to
antibiotics primarily in those with allergies:
◦Beclomethasone dipropionate: 1 spray per
nostril QD/TID/BID
◦Dexamethasone sodium phosphate: 2 sprays
per nostril BID/TID
– Antihistamines recommended for patients with
underlying allergy
– Nasal or oral decongestants not recommended
(phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine, oxymetazoline)
– Expectorants may be helpful:
◦Guaifenesin:
■ Adult: 200–400 mg PO; not >2.4 g/24 h
■ Peds 2–5 yr: 50–100 mg PO; not >600
mg/24 h;
■ Peds 6–11 yr: 100–200 mg PO; not
>1.2 g/24 h
r Antibiotics:
– Amoxicillin–clavulanate: 250–500 mg PO TID or
875 mg PO BID (peds: 40 mg/kg/d, based on the
amoxicillin component)
– If high risk (systemic toxicity w/fever ≥39◦C,
attendance at daycare, age <2o r>65 yr, recent
hospitalization, abx use in last month, or
immunocompromised) use amoxicillin–
clavulanate: 2 g PO BID (peds: 90 mg/kg/d, based
on amoxicillin component)
– Doxycycline: 100 mg PO BID (alternative for initial
empiric therapy in adults)
r 2nd- and 3rd-generation oral cephalosporins no
longer recommended for empiric monotherapy due
to resistance among S. pneumoniae. Can use
following combination:
– Cefpodoxime: 200–400 mg PO BID (peds:
10 mg/kg/d PO BID) or
– Cefuroxime: 250–500 mg PO BID (peds:
15 mg/kg/d PO BID) +
– Clindamycin: 150–300 mg PO q6h (peds:
8–16 mg/kg/d PO split q6–8h, MRSA-suspected
use 40 mg/kg/d PO split q6–8h)
r Macrolides (clarithromycin and azithromycin) not
recommended due to high rates of resistance
amongst S. pneumoniae (30%)
r Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) not
recommended due to high rates of resistance among
S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae (30–40%)
r Type 1 penicillin allergy:
– Levofloxacin: 500 mg PO per day (peds: 8 mg/kg)
children under 50 kg max. dose 250 mg/d.
Children over 50 kg max. dose 500 mg/d.
– Moxifloxacin: 400 mg PO per day (adult)
r If symptoms not improved after 3–5 days of 1
antibiotic, switch to another antibiotic
r Recommended duration of therapy:
– Acute: 10–14 days in children; 5–7 days in adults
– Chronic: 3–6-wk course of antibiotics
(controversial), douche, and nasal steroids
First Line
Supportive care
Second Line
Antibiotics
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Evidence of spread of infection beyond the sinus
cavity or toxic-appearing patients
r Immunocompromised/diabetic patients with
extensive infection
r Multiple sinus or frontal sinus involvement
r Extremes of age
r Severe comorbidity
r ENT evaluation and aspiration if patient is severely
ill, immunocompromised, or has pansinusitis and is
ill-appearing
Discharge Criteria
Most cases of uncomplicated rhinosinusitis may be
managed on an outpatient basis.
Issues for Referralr Complications of acute infection
r Immunocompromised patients
r Chronic rhinosinusitis or nasal polyps
r Concerns for osteomyelitis, CNS infection, or abscess
r Acute rhinosinusitis–aspergillosis
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
If patient has no relief with initial treatment and
nonantibiotic therapies, follow up with PCP or ENT.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Patients presenting with <10 days of mild
symptoms should be treated with supportive care
r Patients presenting with ≥10 days of symptoms,
severe symptoms at 4–5 days with fever, or
worsening after initial improvement can be
diagnosed with acute bacterial rhinosinusitis and
should be treated with antibiotics
r Term rhinosinusitis preferred, since inflammation of
sinuses rarely occurs without inflammation of the
nasal mucosa

SKIN CANCER
John J. D’Angelo
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Most common cancer in US
r Increasing incidence
r 1 in 6 will have skin cancer during their lifetime
r Actinic keratosis:
– Premalignant lesion
– Thickened scaly growth caused by sunlight or
other artificial light source
– Found on areas of body with high sun exposure
– 0.1–10% may transform into squamous cell
carcinoma (SCC)
r Nonmelanoma skin cancer:
– Less commonly fatal
– Fast growing
– May be destructive if left untreated
– Basal cell carcinoma (BCC):
◦Cells arise from epidermis
◦Most common skin cancer
◦Account for 75% of all nonmelanoma skin
cancers
◦Male > female, 3:2.
◦Locally invasive without risk of distant
metastasis
◦Most important risk factor is sun exposure
◦More common in fair-skinned patients
◦Most lesions are on the head and neck
– SCC:
◦2nd most common skin cancer
◦20% of cases of skin cancer
◦Most arise from precancerous actinic keratosis
lesions
◦Male > female
◦Most important risk factor is sun exposure,
especially sunburn
◦70% occur on head and neck
◦More common in older, fair-skinned patients
◦Risk of regional lymph node and distant
metastasis
◦SCC lesions of mucosal surfaces are more
aggressive
r Melanoma:
– 5% of all diagnosed skin cancer in US
– 62,000 new cases in 2008
– 15% are fatal
– 75% of skin cancer cause deaths
– Arises from melanin-producing cells
– Most important risk factor is sun exposure,
especially sunburn
– Additional risk factors:
◦Fair skin; blond/red hair
◦Multiple common melanocytic nevi
◦Atypical nevi
◦Immunosuppression
◦Positive family history
◦History of nonmelanoma skin cancer (BCC or
SCC)
◦≥5 sunburns in early life doubles the risk for
malignant melanoma
– Risk of regional lymph node and distant metastasis
ETIOLOGYr UV irradiation:
– Both UVA and UVB rays
– Sun exposure
– Tanning beds
r SCC often associated with human papilloma virus
(HPV)
r Immunosuppression may predispose to SCC
r Vitamin D metabolism may play a role
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Actinic keratosis:
– Rough, pink, circumscribed lesions <1c mi n
diameter
– A lesion may have both actinic keratosis and SCC
r BCC:
– May be single or multiple
– Usually painless
– Usually appears in sun-exposed areas of skin
– Erosion or bleeding with mild trauma may be 1st
symptoms
– Nodular BCC:
◦Most common
◦Waxy or pearly papule, possibly with
telangiectasia
◦Well-demarcated borders
◦May have central ulceration
– Pigmented BCC:
◦Similar to nodular BCC with brown, blue, or
black coloration
◦Often mistaken for superficial spreading or
nodular melanoma
– Cystic BCC:
◦Bluish/gray cystic nodules
◦May be mistaken for benign cysts
– Superficial BCC:
◦Scaly patch-like or papule surrounded by small,
clear micropapules
◦Pink, red, or brown
– Micronodular BCC:
◦Well-defined border
◦Aggressive
◦Rarely with ulceration
– Morpheaform BCC:
◦Poorly defined borders
◦May appear “scar like”
◦Aggressive
◦Ulceration and bleeding are rare
r SCC:
– Characteristic lesion is raised, firm, keratotic
papule or plaque
– Often enlarging
– Usually asymptomatic but may be ulcerated and
painful as invasion occurs
– Ulcers often crust and ooze
– Cranial nerve involvement may indicate an
aggressive tumor with perineural invasion:
◦Facial numbness, asymmetry, weakness, or pain
r Melanoma:
– Pigmented skin lesion:
◦2% will be amelanotic
– Features suggestive of melanoma (the ABCDEs of
melanoma):
◦Asymmetry (not regularly round or oval)
◦Border irregularity (notched or poorly defined)
◦Bleeding (spontaneous)
◦Color variegation (shades or combinations of
brown, tan, red, white, or blue-black)
◦Diameter >6m m
◦Elevation/Enlargement
– Lesions rarely symptomatic unless ulcerated
– Superficial spreading melanoma:
◦70% of all malignant melanomas
◦May have a wide variety of colors
◦Often arise from dysplastic nevus
◦Usually <3c m
◦Slight elevation and induration is common
◦Often have satellite lesions
– Nodular melanoma:
◦10–15% of melanomas
◦The most symmetric of the different melanomas
◦Dark brown or black
◦Often exophytic
– Lentigo maligna melanomas (LMM):
◦Always starts as lentigo maligna, a macular
insitu malignancy which is an evolving lesion of
melanoma
◦LMM occurs after the lesion begins vertical
growth into the dermis – typically indicated by
papular or nodular areas
◦Irregular shape and multiple colors
– Acral lentiginous melanoma:
◦Equal among black and white patients
◦Most common form of melanoma found in
Asians and African Americans
◦Occur on palms, soles, and subungual region
with predilection for soles of feet
◦May be mistaken for subungual hematoma
◦Involvement of the proximal nail fold
(Hutchinson sign) is an indicator of melanoma
– Mucosal lentiginous melanoma:
◦Develops from mucosal epithelium in
respiratory, GI, and GU tracts
◦Often diagnosed at a later stage of disease
◦Very rare
– Metastatic melanoma:
◦Presentation related to affected organ system
◦Lymphangitic spread with local to regional
lymphadenopathy
◦Typical visceral sites of hematogenous spread
include liver, lung, bone, brain, and intestines

SLEEP APNEA
Ajay Bhatt
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Disorder characterized by cessation of breathing
during sleep:
– Defined as apneic episodes >10 sec with brief
EEG arousals or >3% oxygenation desaturation
r Risk factors:
– Obesity
– Male
– >40 yr of age
– Upper airway anomalies
– Myxedema (hypothyroidism)
– Alcohol/sedative abuse
– Smoking
r Associated illness:
– Various dysrhythmias, particularly atrial fibrillation
and bradyarrhythmia
– Right and left heart failure
–M I
– Stroke
– Motor vehicle accidents
– Hypertension poorly controlled by medical
therapies
EPIDEMIOLOGYr Affects about 9% of middle-aged men and 4% of
middle-aged women
r 80% of moderate or severe cases undiagnosed in
middle-aged adults
ETIOLOGY
3 classifications of sleep apnea:
r Obstructive (84%) is due to upper airway closure
despite intact respiratory drive:
– Also known as Pickwickian syndrome
– Pharyngeal airway is narrowed
r Central (0.4%) is due to lack of respiratory effort
despite patent upper airway.
r Complex (15%) is due to a combination of
obstructive and central sleep apnea.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Excessive daytime sleepiness
r Snoring
r Irritability
Historyr Significant other apnea report
r Difficulty sleeping
r Decreased attention/concentration
r Depression
r Decreased libido/impotence
Physical Examr Hypertension, hypoxemia
r Obesity
r Craniofacial anomalies
r Macroglossia
r Enlarged tonsils
r Elevated jugular veins (secondary to pulmonary
hypertension)
r Large neck circumference
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Pulse oximetry
r ECG
r Chest radiograph
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
ABG is the best test to demonstrate hypercarbia and
hypoxemia.
Imagingr Consider lateral neck soft tissue radiograph to rule
out other etiologies of upper airway obstruction.
r Chest radiograph to assess other etiologies of
hypoxemia
r Chest CT rarely indicated
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Polysomnogram (PSG) is required for diagnosis:
r >5 apneic episodes per hour
r Not a consideration for ED management
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Asthma
r Cheyne–Stokes breathing
r COPD
r Diaphragmatic paralysis
r High altitude–induced periodic breathing
r Hypothyroidism
r Left heart failure
r Narcolepsy
r Obesity hyperventilation syndrome
r Primary pulmonary hypertension
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Caution not to overventilate patient with chronic CO
retention
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Chin lift/jaw thrust maneuver, oxygen as needed, oral
or nasal airway devices
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Proper technique is required for airway
management:
– Supplemental oxygen as needed
– Bag-valve-mask ventilation may be difficult:
◦Consider the use of nasal and oral airways
◦2-person technique to ensure a good seal
r Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is the
standard of treatment:
– Acts as a pneumatic splint by maintaining upper
airway patency
– BiPAP is an alternative for patients requiring high
pressures or with comorbid breathing disorders.
– Long-term CPAP therapy decreases BP , insulin
resistance, metabolic syndrome, and risk of
cardiovascular disease.
ALERT
Endotracheal intubationr Higher prevalence of difficult intubation:
– Patients frequently have higher Mallampati
scores.
– Excess pharyngeal tissue in lateral walls often
obstructs airway visualization.
– Patients have overall lower arterial oxygen
saturation.
r Plan and consider several methods of definitive
airway control:
– Have alternative devices (laryngeal mask airway,
bougie) available.
– Be prepared to perform cricothyroidotomy if
necessary.
r Use neuromuscular blockade only if successful
oral intubation is reasonably likely and bag-mask
ventilation is easy.
r Positive end-expiratory pressure for ventilated
patients

SLIPPED CAPITAL FEMORAL EPIPHYSIS
Virag Shah
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Femoral epiphysis translates (slips) posteriorly and
inferiorly relative to the femoral head/neck
r Classification systems:
– Degree of femoral head “slip” as a percentage of
femoral neck diameter:
◦(Mild, grade 1) <33.3%
◦(Moderate, grade 2) 33.3–50%
◦(Severe, grade 3) >50%
– Temporal:
◦Acute: <3 wk of symptoms
◦Chronic: >3 wk of symptoms
◦Acute on chronic: >3 wk of symptoms, now
with acute pain
– Stability:
◦Stable: Bears weight w/or w/o crutches
◦Unstable: Unable to bear weight
r Epidemiology:
– Peak age: 12–14 yr (boys), 11–12 yr (girls)
– Male > female (1.6:1)
– Bilateral slips: 20% at presentation; additional
20–40% progress to bilateral
– Atypical SCFE: Endocrinopathy associated:
◦Patient may be <10 yr age, >16 yr age, or
weight <50th percentile
◦High risk of bilateral SCFE (up to 100%)
ETIOLOGYr Proximal physis position changes in adolescence
from horizontal to oblique; hence hip forces shift
from “compression” to “shear”
r Shear force > strength of femoral physis
r Weakest point of physis = zone of hypertrophy
r Risk factors:
– Obesity: May contribute to shear forces
– Down syndrome
– Endocrinopathy such as hypothyroidism, growth
hormone deficiency, renal osteodystrophy (2◦
hyperparathyroidism): May contribute to growth
plate weakening
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Determine chronicity of symptoms and whether or
not the patient can bear weight
r Pain in the knee, thigh, groin, or hip (referred pain
from the obturator nerve):
– Vague and dull for weeks in chronic SCFE
– Severe and sudden onset in acute SCFE, often in
the setting of trauma
Physical Examr If stable, presents with limp or exertional limp
r If unstable (patient cannot ambulate), avoid further
ambulation attempts
r Commonly presents with leg externally rotated
r Restricted internal rotation, abduction, and flexion
(cannot touch thigh to abdomen)
r Anterior hip joint tenderness
r Test: Apply gentle passive hip flexion → if hip
externally rotates + abducts → highly suggestive of
SCFE
r Gait:
– Antalgic (patient takes short steps on affected side
to minimize weight-bearing during “stance”
phase of gait)
– Trendelenburg (shift of torso over affected hip;
sign of moderate/severe slip)
– Waddling (sign of bilateral SCFE)
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Plain radiographs:
– Further imaging with aid from consultant
r Orthopedic consultation
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr If no diagnostic radiographic abnormality, the
practitioner may consider the following to help risk
stratify possible alternative diagnoses:
– CBC with differential, sedimentation rate,
C-reactive protein
r If endocrinopathy suspected, consider thyroid
function testing
Imagingr Both hips should be imaged for comparison
r Some clinicians prefer cross-table lateral view in
acute SCFE instead of frog-leg view (theoretical risk
of worsening displacement)
r Anteroposterior radiograph:
– Widened or irregular physis
– Bird’s beak appearance of the epiphysis
“slipping” off of the femoral head
– Klein line: Parallel line drawn from superior border
of the femoral neck; line intersects the epiphysis in
normal patient
r Lateral radiograph (frog-leg or cross-table)
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
If septic hip is suspected, aspiration and fluid analysis
may be needed to exclude.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Legg–Calv ´ e–Perthes:
– Typically seen in 4–9-yr-old age range
r Septic arthritis of hip
r Osteomyelitis
r Toxic synovitis
r Femur or pelvic fractures
r Inguinal or femoral hernia

SMALL-BOWEL INJURY
Barry J. Knapp
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
2 general causes:
r Blunt visceral trauma
r Penetrating: Visceral injury (96% of gunshot
wounds, 50% of stabbings)—serosal tear, bowel
wall hematoma, perforation, bowel transection,
mesenteric hematoma/vascular injury
ETIOLOGYr Blunt:
– 3rd most commonly injured organ (5–10% of all
blunt trauma victims)
– Motor vehicle accidents
– Nonvehicular trauma: Abuse/assault, bicycle
handlebars, large-animal kick
– Blast victims
r Mortality rate from small-bowel injury is 33%.
r Mesenteric tears may initially be asymptomatic:
– Deceleration injury at fixed points (e.g., ligament
of Treitz)
– Shearing mechanisms near fixed points (e.g.,
ileocecal junction, adhesions)
– Compressive force against anterior spine
– Bursting or “blowout” at antimesenteric margin
from sudden closed-loop intraluminal pressure rise
r Associated injuries:
– Liver and splenic lacerations; thoracic and pelvic
fractures
– Seatbelt syndrome: Abdominal wall ecchymosis,
small-bowel injury; Chance fracture of L1, L3
r Penetrating:
– Small bowel is the 2nd most commonly injured
organ (32%) in anterior abdominal stabbing.
– Small-bowel injury is most common in gunshot
wounds (49%).
Pediatric Considerations
r Blunt:
– Less common in children (1–8% of all blunt
pediatric trauma)
– Lower chance of intestinal injury in vehicular
accidents when both shoulder and lap belts are
worn.
– Be cautious of nonpenetrating trauma: Airgun
accidents at close range (<10 ft)
– Consider the possibility of nonaccidental trauma.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Physical signs and symptoms are unreliable
r Delays in diagnosis are common
r Presence of a “seatbelt sign” doubles the risk for
small-bowel injury.
r Initial presentation may be mild:
– Uniformly, patients will progress to serious
signs/symptoms.
r Delays in diagnosis add to morbidity and mortality:
– Mortality is 2% when diagnosis is made within
8 hr; 31% when made after 24 hr.
Historyr History of blunt or penetrating abdominal trauma
r Must consider in ill children without a definite
history of trauma (child abuse)
Physical Examr In awake, alert patients look for:
– Abdominal tenderness (87–98%)
– Abdominal pain (85%)
– Peritoneal signs (67%)
r Many patients will have:
– Abdominal wall bruising (54%)
– Hypotension (38%)
– Guaiac-positive rectal exam (5%)
r Small-bowel injury may initially be obscured by
abnormal mental status, severe associated injuries.
r Small-bowel injury not initially apparent may be
indicated by:
– Progressive abdominal pain
– Intestinal obstruction
– Decreased urine output
– Tachycardia
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Initial physical exam should note all wounds and
areas of tenderness.
r CT for all medically stable patients
r For patients with a negative CT scan in which there
is high suspicion of bowel injury, further evaluation
or serial exams are indicated.
r For medically unstable patients, diagnostic
peritoneal lavage (DPL) is superior to US in
determining presence of a hollow viscus injury.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr No diagnostic test has proven highly sensitive in the
prediction of small-bowel injury.
r Serum amylase, lipase, and liver function tests have
poor sensitivity for acute injury.
Imagingr Plain radiography of chest/abdomen:
– Not useful for small-bowel injury
– Incidence of pneumoperitoneum visible on plain
radiograph is only 8%.
r CT:
– Diagnostic standard for solid-organ injury and
head trauma but is less sensitive for hollow viscus
injuries
– Newest-generation helical CT scanners have a
sensitivity of 88% and a specificity of 99%.
– The benefits of oral contrast are controversial; it is
acceptable to use IV contrast only
– Blunt trauma:
◦Used in stable patients
◦Indications for CT in blunt trauma include
abdominal tenderness, hypotension, altered
mental status (GCS <14), costal margin
tenderness, abnormal CXR, HCT <30% and
hematuria
◦Specific signs for small-bowel injury on CT are
pneumoperitoneum (sensitivity 50–75%) and
extravasation of contrast (sensitivity 12%).
◦Signs on CT suggestive of small-bowel injury
include unexplained free intraperitoneal fluid
(most sensitive 93%), thickened bowel wall
>3 mm (61% sensitive), intramural hematomas
(75–88% sensitive), interloop fluid, mesenteric
streaking.
– Penetrating: CT is not recommended because
sensitivity is only 14%; false-negative result rate is
18%.
r US: Not sensitive in hollow viscus injury because air
in bowel makes visualization difficult
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr DPL:
– Invasive but may be helpful in unstable patients or
in patients with clinically suspicious but
nondiagnostic abdominal CT
– Sensitive for hemoperitoneum but not source of
bleeding
– Positive if RBC count of >100,000/mm3
– Lavage amylase >20 IU/L and leukocyte count
>500/mm3 (late markers of small-bowel injury)
– Lavage microscopy for succus/vegetable
matter/feces is specific for small-bowel injury but
not sensitive.
– Lavage alkaline phosphatase (>3 IU/L) is reported
to be a useful immediate marker of small-bowel
injury.
r Laparoscopy: Plays a key role in diagnosing
small-bowel injury in stable patients with
progressive signs or symptoms

S
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Hemoperitoneum owing to vascular insult
r Solid visceral organ injury or gastric/colon/rectum
perforation
r Vertebral injury and associated ileus
Pediatric Considerations
Delay in diagnosis of 1–2 days is common and
increases morbidity.
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
ALERT
r Patients should be transported to the nearest
trauma center.
r Do not attempt to replace eviscerated abdominal
contents; cover with moist gauze, blanket, and
transport.
r Do not remove impaled objects in the abdomen;
stabilize the object with gauze and tape and
transport.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Standard advanced trauma life support protocols,
including airway, breathing, and circulation
management
r Aggressive fluid resuscitation, central line suggested
with pressure infusion of warmed IV fluid (lactated
Ringer solution or normal saline)
r Cover eviscerated small bowel with moist gauze; do
not remove impaled foreign body in ED.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Immediate transfer to OR is required for patients
with an indication for laparotomy:
– Evisceration
– Abdominal pain with hypotension
– Positive DPL or abdominal CT
– Thoracic abdominal herniation visualized on chest
radiograph
– Impaled foreign body
– Penetrating gunshot wound to the abdomen
– Tetanus and antibiotic prophylaxis should be given
for penetrating abdominal wounds and blunt
injury requiring surgical exploration.
r Local wound exploration is safe for abdominal stab
wounds.
r Serial abdominal exams and observation for
otherwise stable patients
r Judicious analgesia as BP permits after diagnosis is
established
MEDICATIONr Cefotetan (Cefotan): 1–2 g (peds: 20 mg/kg) IV
q12h or
r Cefoxitin (Mefoxin): 1–2 g (peds: 40 mg/kg) IV q6h
or
r Ceftizoxime (Cefizox): 1–2 g (peds: 50 mg/kg) IV
q8–12h +
r Metronidazole: 500 mg (peds: 7.5 mg/kg) IV q6h
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Indication for laparotomy
r Abnormal mental status/intoxication with
abdominal injury
r Presence of abdominal pain, tenderness (even with
a negative workup) mandates admission for
observation and serial exams.
r Stab and gunshot wounds that violate the
abdominal fascia, positive DPL, or worsening
findings on clinical exam
Discharge Criteriar Minimal mechanism blunt trauma in a sober patient
with normal exam result who has no abdominal
pain and will receive adequate follow-up
r Explicit discharge instructions to return for
worsening signs/symptoms are important to identify
those with unsuspected injury.
r Penetrating wounds that do not violate abdominal
fascia
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Discharged patients who develop abdominal
complaints should return promptly to the ED.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Small-bowel injury should be considered in any
blunt/penetrating abdominal trauma victim.
r Initial presentation of patients with small-bowel
injuries may be unimpressive.
r Presence of a “seat belt sign” doubles the risk for
small-bowel injury.
r CT scanning may miss a significant percentage of
small-bowel injuries.
r Observation and serial exams are an important
aspect of detecting occult injuries.

SMOKE INHALATION
Trevonne M. Thompson
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Suspect smoke inhalation in anyone involved in a
fire within a closed space or with a history of loss of
consciousness.
r May cause direct injury to the upper (supraglottic)
airway structures
r May cause chemical/irritant effect to lower airway
structures
r May cause systemic toxicity from inhaled substances
ETIOLOGYr Direct heat injury from heated gases/smoke:
– Limited to supraglottic structures because of the
heat-dissipating properties of the upper airway
r Irritant effect from smoke components
r Systemic toxicity from inhaled cellular toxins:
– Carbon monoxide
– Hydrogen cyanide
ALERT
Inhalation of steam can be rapidly fatal:
r Steam has ∼4,000 times the heat-carrying
capacity of hot air.
r Can rapidly cause obstructive glottic edema,
thermally induced tracheitis, and hemorrhagic
edema of the bronchial mucosa
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Exposure to a fire or heavy smoke
r Typically in a confined space
r Maintain high index of suspicion with history of loss
of consciousness
Physical Examr May have a normal physical exam with symptoms
developing during the 24-hr interval following
exposure
r Upper airway (supraglottic):
– Nasopharyngeal irritation
– Hoarseness
– Stridor
– Cough
r Lower airway:
– Chest discomfort
– Hemoptysis
– Bronchospasm
– Bronchorrhea
r May have symptoms and signs of carbon monoxide
and/or cyanide toxicity
ALERT
The following signs are suggestive of significant
inhalation injury:
r Facial and upper cervical burns
r Carbonaceous sputum
r Singed eyebrows and nasal vibrissae
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Pulse oximetry:
– May be falsely elevated in cases of carbon
monoxide exposure
r ABG measurement:
– Hypoxia
– Metabolic acidosis in cases of carbon monoxide or
hydrogen cyanide
r Chest radiography:
– Initial radiograph typically normal
– May show signs of pulmonary injury over the next
24 hr
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose
r CBC
r Coagulation profile
r Creatine phosphokinase when indicated in burn
patients
r Carboxyhemoglobin to evaluate for potential carbon
monoxide exposure
r Cyanide level:
– In suspected cases of cyanide exposure, do not
wait for the level before initiating therapy.
– May send lactate level as a marker of cyanide
toxicity
r Pregnancy test
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Peak expiratory flow rate:
– Low peak flow associated with more severe injury
r PaO2/FiO2 ratio:
– A ratio of <300 after initial resuscitation is
associated with the development of respiratory
failure.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Irritant gas exposure
r Asphyxiant gas exposure
r Cardiogenic pulmonary edema
r COPD exacerbation
r Asthma exacerbation
r Pneumonia
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr 100% oxygen by face mask
r Intubation for patients with agonal breathing
r Rapid transport to ED for those with stridor:
– May need advanced airway management
r Albuterol nebulizer therapy for bronchospasm
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr 100% oxygen via face mask
r Intubation:
– Respiratory distress
r Drooling
r Stridor:
– Refractory hypoxia
– CNS depression
– Significant facial/upper airway burns
r Establish IV access.
