THORACIC OUTLET SYNDROME
T
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Consider a coagulation workup for either venous or
arterial TOS.
Imagingr Perform as outpatient except in case of
limb-threatening ischemia and/or suspicion of
venous thrombus
r CXR:
– Assess for anatomic abnormalities: 1st rib, cervical
rib, clavicle deformity:
◦Without an abnormality, ATOS is very unlikely.
– Pulmonary disease
r Cervical spine series:
– Fracture
– Scoliosis
r US can diagnose venous thrombosis
r Duplex scanning is the best way to screen for
subclavian artery aneurysm or stenosis, which, if
present, can lead to arteriography
r Arteriogram:
– Usually used to help a surgeon plan reconstruction
– Indications include:
◦Decreased radial pulse
◦BP is 20 mm Hg less than the opposite limb.
◦Suspected subclavian stenosis
◦Bruit or abnormal supraclavicular pulsations or
pulsating mass
◦Peripheral emboli in the upper extremity
r Venography:
– Indicated if edema, peripheral unilateral cyanosis,
or distended thoracic and extremity veins
r NTOS:
– No gold standard test: Diagnosis remains mostly
clinical.
– Electromyography and nerve conduction velocity
tests are often normal.
r MRI may be required to assess for spinal cord
disease, herniated cervical disk, or assessing for
pancoast tumor.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Cardiac ischemia
r Cervical spondylosis or disk disease
r Carpal tunnel syndrome or nerve entrapments
r Pancoast tumor; other neck/mediastinum
malignancies
r Neuritis
r Myositis
r Raynaud disease
r Multiple sclerosis or degenerative spinal cord disease
r Shoulder inflammatory diseases: Arthritis, rotator
cuff injury, bicipital tendonitis
r Atherosclerotic or thromboembolic disease
TREATMENT
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Heparinization if signs of arterial or venous
thrombosis
r Vascular surgery consult for signs of ischemia and
for catheter-directed thrombolysis if needed:
– Anticoagulation and thrombolysis followed by
surgical decompression is required for thrombosis
r Initial management:
– The majority improve with conservative treatment
consisting of physical therapy and medications for
symptomatic relief.
r Surgery reserved for failure of medical therapy:
– Often required for vascular forms
– People with NTOS often undergo more extensive
evaluation and medical management prior to
surgical intervention
– 70–90% of patients experience some to complete
relief postoperatively.
MEDICATIONr Cyclobenzaprine: 10 mg PO TID
r Diazepam: 5 mg PO TID
r Ibuprofen: 800 mg PO TID
r Methocarbamol: 1,000–1,500 mg PO TID
r Soothing liniments or ointments
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Ischemia
r Venous thrombosis
r Arterial thrombosis
r Arterial aneurysm or stenosis
r Intractable pain
Discharge Criteriar Nonlimb-threatening neurologic findings
r Absence of arterial or venous thrombosis
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Vascular, neurologic, or orthopedic consultation is
indicated according to the pathologic condition.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r 3 types of TOS: Neurogenic, arterial, and venous:
– Neurogenic is most common in adults.
– ATOS and VTOS are the more common types in
children and adolescents.
r VTOS is the only type that has arm swelling and
edema.
r Both NTOS and ATOS have hand coldness and pallor,
but for different reasons.
r May have a history of repetitive use or trauma
r Exam or imaging may reveal a congenital
abnormality such as a cervical rib.

THROMBOTIC THROMBOCYTOPENIC PURPURA
Hany Y. Atallah
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is a
severe disorder of abnormal clotting affecting
multiple organ systems.
r Classically characterized by pentad of:
– Thrombocytopenia
– Hemolytic anemia
– Mild renal dysfunction
– Neurologic signs
– Fever
r Uncommon to see all 5 features in 1 patient; if
present, severe end-organ damage or ischemia has
likely taken place.
r Thrombocytopenia and hemolytic anemia are the
most common features.
r Associated with acquired or congenital deficiency of
plasma von Willebrand factor–cleaving protease
(VWFcp)
r Patients who present with severe neurologic
abnormalities with acute renal failure are best
described by the comprehensive term TTP-HUS
Classic Courser Acute onset
r Fulminant course lasting days to a few months
r Nearly always fatal without treatment:
– >90% mortality without treatment
– Reverses to >90% survival with modern
treatment
r Clinical presentations include:
– Idiopathic
– Familial, chronic, or relapsing
– Drug induced:
◦Allergic or immune mediated (quinine,
ticlopidine, clopidogrel)
◦Dose-related toxicity (mitomycin C, cyclosporine)
– Pregnancy, postpartum associated:
◦10–25% of cases
– Bone marrow transplantation associated
– Infection
r More common in the 3rd–6th decades of life
r Uncommon in pediatric or geriatric populations
r Women affected about twice as frequently as men
ETIOLOGYr Unknown primary stimulant; possibly systemic
endothelial cell damage results inactivation of
coagulation pathway
r Platelet aggregation and fibrin deposition occurring
in arterioles and capillaries leading to microthrombi
and obstruction to blood flow
r Platelet aggregation leads to:
– Consumption of platelets
– Widespread microvascular hyaline thrombotic
lesions
r Microvasculature obstruction with platelet
aggregates leads to:
– Red cell hemolysis
– Accumulation of heme breakdown products
– Anemia
r End-organ ischemia results from diffuse thrombosis
in small vessels:
– Most common in heart, brain, kidney, pancreas,
and adrenal glands
r Deficiency of vWFcp causes failure of control of
coagulation pathway.
RISK FACTORS
Geneticsr Some cases are genetic/familial.
r VWFcp was recently identified as new member of
ADAMTS family and designated ADAMTS13.
r Mutations in ADAMTS13 gene cause autosomal
recessive form of chronic relapsing TTP .
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
5 major clinical features: Classic pentad
r Thrombocytopenia:
– Platelet count <20,000/mm3
r Microangiopathic and hemolytic anemia:
–H b <10 g/dL (<6 g/dL in 40%)
r Neurologic symptoms:
– Presenting complaint in 60%, occur in 90%
– Typically fluctuating
– Headache
– Altered mentation (confusion, stupor, coma)
– Behavioral or personality changes
– Focal sensory or motor deficits or aphasia
– Seizures
– Spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage
r Renal insufficiency:
– Usually mild
– Creatinine <3 mg/dL
r Fever:
– Occurs in acute episodes and prodromal
syndromes
– Fever is the least common feature
r Rare for all components of pentad to be present in
the same individual
Historyr General:
– Weakness
– Fatigue
– Fever
– Malaise
r Hemorrhage:
– Easy bruising
– Epistaxis
– Menorrhagia
– GI bleeding
– Loss or change in vision
r GI complaints:
– Anorexia
– Diarrhea
– Abdominal pain
r Neurologic:
– Headache
– Confusion
– Seizure
– Behavioral or personality changes
– Focal sensory or motor deficits or aphasia
Physical Examr Purpura
r GI hemorrhage
r Epistaxis
r Jaundice
r Shock
r Altered mental status
r Focal sensory or motor deficits
r Pulmonary infiltrates and edema
r Alteration of vision, retinal hemorrhage/detachment.
r Abnormalities of cardiac conduction
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Clinical Diagnosisr Because of success of treatment, base diagnosis on:
– Identification of 2 major findings:
◦Thrombocytopenia
◦Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
– Exclude other major differential diagnoses.
r Comprehensive history and physical exam with
directed lab testing
r Identify possible drug-associated disease and avoid
re-exposure.
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC/platelet count/reticulocyte count:
– Anemia: Hemoglobin <10 g/dL
– Thrombocytopenia <20,000/mm3
– Increased reticulocyte count
r Coagulation studies:
– Normal
r Peripheral blood smear:
– Macroangiopathic changes
– Schistocytes
– Helmet cells
– Nucleated RBCs
r Coombs test:
– Negative direct Coombs test
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose:
– Mild elevation of BUN, creatinine
– Hyperkalemia owing to RBC lysis
r Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH):
– Elevated 5–10 times due to hemolysis and tissue
ischemia
r Bilirubin:
– Increased unconjugated bilirubin
r Urinalysis:
– Hematuria (microscopic to gross)
r ADAMTS13 assay may be used to distinguish
chronic recurring TTP , TTP secondary to presence of
ADAMTS13 inhibitor, and hemolytic-uremic
syndrome (HUS):
– ADAMTS13 deficiency does not detect all patients
who may respond to plasma exchange
transfusions.
Imagingr CT head:
– To rule out intracranial hemorrhage

THROMBOTIC THROMBOCYTOPENIC PURPURA
T
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Biopsy:
– Confirms diagnosis
– Reveals hyaline lesions in small vessels
– Contraindicated during fulminant presentation
(hemorrhage risk)
r EEG:
– To predict need for anticonvulsant therapy
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr HUS:
– Triad of thrombocytopenia, schistocytosis, and
renal dysfunction
– Neurologic symptoms unusual
– Often preceded by infectious prodrome and
diarrhea
r Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC):
– Causes deposition of fibrin in microvasculature
and not hyaline
– Coagulation studies abnormal
r Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP):
– No evidence of hemolysis
– LDH and bilirubin normal
r Pregnancy-related thrombocytopenia:
– Preeclampsia, eclampsia
– Pregnancy-associated hemolysis
– HELLP (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low
platelets)
r Evans syndrome:
– Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
– Prominence of microspherocytes rather than
schistocytes
– Positive direct Coombs test
r Malignant hypertension
r Bacterial sepsis
r Subacute bacterial endocarditis
r Autoimmune disorders (e.g., systemic lupus
erythematosus [SLE])
r Disseminated malignancy
r Heparin-associated thrombocytopenia
r Prosthetic valves or severely calcified aortic stenosis
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr ABCs
r Evaluate for other possible causes of altered mental
status (hypoglycemia, overdose)
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr ABCs
r 0.9% normal saline (NS) IV fluid resuscitation for
shock or GI hemorrhage
r RBC transfusions:
– For significant anemia or bleeding complications
r Platelet transfusions:
– Reserve for life-threatening hemorrhage (e.g.,
CNS bleeds) or required invasive procedures
– May aggravate the thrombotic, microvascular
obstructive process and worsen the end-organ
ischemia and shock
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) or fresh unfrozen plasma:
– Initiated as bridge to exchange transfusions on
diagnosis of TTP
– Success rate approaching 64%
– Provides a platelet-antiaggregating factor absent
or diminished in patient’s own serum
– Used prophylactically to prevent recurrence in
chronic relapsing variant
r Plasma exchange transfusions:
– Most important component of treatment
– Combination of plasmapheresis and FFP infusion
– Plasmapheresis removes:
◦Immune complexes responsible for endothelial
damage and initiation of TTP
◦Circulating proaggregation factors promoting
platelet aggregation
– Perform daily until:
◦Platelet count normalizes
◦Neurologic symptoms improve
◦LDH normalizes
– Improvement of renal function may lag behind
other findings.
– Taper frequency based on empiric judgment of
response; may need to resume if relapse occurs.
– Complications include:
◦Allergy or serum sickness
◦Secondary infection
◦Hypotension
r Corticosteroids:
– Unproven therapeutic benefit
– May limit immunologically mediated endothelial
damage and decrease splenic sequestration of
platelets and damaged RBCs
– Supportive benefit if adrenal glands damaged
through hemorrhage or ischemia
r Antiplatelet or immunosuppressive drugs:
– Aspirin and dipyridamole most commonly used
– Use of sulfapyrazine, dextran, and vincristine has
been reported.
– Used with variable effectiveness
– Can worsen bleeding complications
r Splenectomy:
– Historically recommended
– Of uncertain efficacy
r Dialysis:
– For renal failure
MEDICATIONr Aspirin: 325–650 mg PO q4–6h
r Dipyridamole: 75–100 mg PO QID
r FFP:
– Plasma infusion: 30 mL/kg/d (75–100 mL/h)
– Plasma exchange transfusion: 3–4 L/d
r Methylprednisolone: 0.75 mg/kg q12h
r Prednisone: 1–2 mg/kg/d (high dose up to
200 mg/d)
r Rituximab: 375 mg/m2 IV once per week for
4–8 doses
r Vincristine: 1.4 mg/m2 once per week IV
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Newly diagnosed serious platelet disorder, especially
with bleeding complications or altered mental status
or renal dysfunction
r ICU admission for TTP with active bleeding or
neurologic findings:
– Transport to tertiary care center with appropriate
specialty care facilities.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONS
Patients with known disease and found to be stable
may follow up with a hematologist.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r TTP can be confused with HELLP syndrome in
pregnant females.
r Because of the high mortality of untreated TTP ,
recognition of the disease and initiation of
treatment is key.
ADDITIONAL READING

thrombocytopenic purpura. N Engl J Med. 2006;354:
1927–1935.

thrombocytopenic purpura: 2010. Blood 2010;116:
4060–4069.

therapy for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: A
proposed study of the Transfusion Medicine/
Hemostasis Clinical Trials Network with a systematic
review of rituximab therapy for immune-mediated
disorders. J Clin Apher. 2006;21:49–56.

of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Curr Opin
Hematol. 2008;15(5):445–450.

THUMB FRACTURE
Daniel R. Lasoff rLeslie C. Oyama
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Distal phalangeal fractures:
– Blunt trauma, hyperextension of the thumb, axial
loading of the thumb, and crush injuries.
– Tuft fracture is a similar fracture in other digits, in
which the distal phalanx is crushed and/or
fragmented.
– It may be open or closed and associated with nail
bed injury.
– Severe nail bed injury, intra-articular,
displaced/angulated fractures, or tendon injuries
warrant orthopedics’ consultation.
– Noncomplex tuft fractures can be splinted and
treated as soft tissue injuries.
r Proximal phalangeal fractures and thumb
metacarpal fractures:
– Blunt trauma to the thumb:
◦Axial loading of the thumb with the
metacarpophalangeal (MP) joint partially flexed,
the hand closed or the thumb MP joint
otherwise stabilized
– Bennett fracture (type I):
◦Intra-articular fracture/dislocation at the base of
the metacarpal where the ulnar aspect of the
metacarpal maintains its attachment.
– Rolando fracture (type II):
◦Comminuted Y- or T-shaped intra-articular
fracture of the base of the 1st metacarpal.
◦Similar to a comminuted Bennett, these can be
much more complex with multiple comminuted
fractures.
– Type III fractures
◦Extra-articular metacarpal fractures. Tend to be
transverse or less commonly oblique.
ETIOLOGYr Falls, hyperflexion, hyperextension
r Motor vehicle accidents
r Sports, especially downhill or alpine skiing
r Basketball
r Baseball
r Football
r Rugby
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Pain, swelling, and deformity of the thumb
r Exam should include the thenar eminence for pain
or deformity.
r The thumb may be rotated distal to the fracture site.
r The base of the thumb may appear radially deviated
relative to the rest of the hand in the resting
position.
r Occasionally, there may be damage to the thumb
digital nerves.
Pediatric Considerations
r Fractures to the thumb sometimes occur in children.
r Consider nonaccidental trauma.
r Do not neglect appropriate pain management in
children.
Physical Examr Immobilize the thumb pending definitive evaluation.
r Neurovascular exam with 2-point discrimination.
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Radiography as noted below
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Imagingr Plain radiography of affected areas
r Avoid testing stress of thumb MP joint, as in testing
for gamekeeper thumb, until all plain radiography is
complete.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Extra-articular fracture of the base of the thumb
metacarpal
r Scaphoid fracture
r Gamekeeper thumb: Ulnar collateral ligamentous
injury
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Dress open wounds.
r Immobilize hand and wrist with thumb in neutral
position.
r Elevate and apply cold to reduce swelling.
r Age-appropriate social management
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Immobilize thumb pending definitive evaluation.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Thumb spica splint with the thumb in neutral
position, as if holding a beverage can
r Splint instructions should be provided to patient.
r Angulated extra-articular fractures of the 1st
metacarpal require reduction. Can tolerate up to 30◦
of angulation. Angulation >30◦ requires another
attempt at reduction or orthopedics’ consultation.
r Distal phalangeal fractures require DIP splint in
extension for 3–4 wk.
MEDICATION
Pain control with oral analgesic preparations

TIBIAL PLATEAU FRACTURE
Sarah V. Espinoza rLeslie C. Oyama
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Synonym: Tibial condylar fracture
r Fracture or depression of the proximal tibial
articulating surface
r Valgus or varus force applied in combination with
axial loading onto tibial plateau
Schatzker Classiﬁcation of Plateau
Fracturesr Type 1:
– Split fracture of the lateral tibial plateau without
depression of the plateau
r Type 2:
– Split fracture and depression of lateral tibial
plateau
– Associated with lateral meniscus injury
r Type 3:
– Central depression of the lateral plateau
– Injuries may be unstable
r Type 4:
– Split of the medial tibial plateau
– Can cause damage to other structures:
◦Popliteal vessels
◦Peroneal nerve
◦MCL
◦Lateral meniscus
◦Lateral collateral ligament
◦Cruciate ligaments
◦Tibial spines
◦Compartment syndrome
r Type 5:
– Bicondylar tibial plateau fracture
– Same associated injuries as type 4
r Type 6:
– Bicondylar, grossly comminuted fracture of the
plateau
– Diaphyseal–metaphyseal dissociation
– Same associated injuries as types 4 and 5
ETIOLOGYr Mechanism of injury:
– Types 1 & 2 from a valgus force with axial loading,
generally a low-energy injury
◦Associated with contact sports, twisting motions
(e.g., skiing) or classically, pedestrians struck by
a vehicle bumper
– Type 3 are low-energy injuries in osteopenic bone
– Types 4–6 are high-energy injuries usually from
motor vehicle/cycle collisions and falls from height
causing medial plateau fractures
◦Associated with neurovascular injuries
r Age associated
– Type 1: Younger patients with cancellous bone of
the plateau resists depression.
– Types 2 & 3: Depression fractures seen in
osteopenic older bones

Tibia
r 80% have associated fibular fractures
r Open (24% are open) vs. closed
r Extent of soft tissue damage
r Gustilo–Anderson classification of open fractures:
– Type I:
◦Wound <1c m
◦Little soft tissue damage
◦No crush injury
– Type II:
◦Wound >1c m
◦Moderate soft tissue damage
◦Little or no devitalized soft tissue
– Type III—severe soft tissue injury:
◦A—adequate soft tissue coverage of bone
◦B—tissue loss/periosteal stripping
◦C—neurovascular injury requiring surgery
r Anatomic location:
– Proximal, middle, or distal 3rd
– Articular extension
r Displacement
r Degree of shortening
r Angulation
r Configuration:
– Spiral, transverse, or oblique
– Comminuted, with butterfly fragment or multiple
fragments
Fibula
r Proximal:
– Associated with peroneal nerve injury
– Disruption of ankle syndesmosis (Maisonneuve

r Middle
r Distal
Pediatric Considerations
r 3rd most common long bone fracture in children
r 2nd most common long bone fracture in
nonaccidental trauma (usually apophyseal or
metaphyseal corner)
r Nonphyseal fracture patterns:
– Compression (torus): Distal metaphysis
– Incomplete tension–compression (greenstick)
– Plastic/bowing deformity of fibula may occur.
– Complete fractures
r Physeal fracture patterns:
– Tibial shaft fractures may extend to the physis in

ETIOLOGYr High- vs. low-energy injury
r Amount of soft tissue injury is prognostic and
determined by the degree of energy involved.
r Indirect force—frequently low-energy trauma:
– Rotary and compressive forces often result in
oblique and spiral fractures.
r Skiing, fall, child abuse
r Direct force—high-energy trauma:
– Direct blow to leg often results in transverse and
comminuted fractures.
r Pedestrian vs. auto, motor vehicle crash (MVC):
– Bending force over a fulcrum often produces
comminution with a wedge-shaped butterfly
fragment.
r Skier’s boot top, football tackle, MVC

r Bicycle spoke injury:
– Foot and lower leg get caught between frame and
wheel spoke
– Crush injury is the primary problem.

often deceiving:

– Orthopedic surgery consultation should be
obtained for all spoke-injury patients with
associated fractures.
r Toddler fracture:
– Spiral fracture involving the distal 3rd of the tibia
with intact fibula secondary to rotational force
(turning on planted foot)
– Age range is 9 mo–6 yr, most often when learning
to walk.
– Fractures in midshaft or more transverse are
suggestive of nonaccidental trauma.

r Pain is usually immediate, severe, and well localized

nerve as it wraps around the fibular head
r Compartment syndrome

r Rely on parents for historical information.
r Child may present limping with no obvious
deformity.

r Careful neurovascular exam (compare with
contralateral side)
r Examine for associated injuries.
r Completely expose patient and put into gown.
r Assessment for compartment syndrome

r Compartment syndrome
r Occurs in 8% of diaphyseal fractures, more
common in younger patients
r Relatively common complication of tibial fractures
and may not appear until 24 hr after injury
r Pain disproportionate to that expected
r Patient may have swollen, tight compartment, but
does not always have pain on palpation of
compartment.
r Pain on passive stretch of foot, toes
r Sensory deficit
r Motor weakness is a late finding.
r Pulselessness is not a sign of compartment
syndrome:

compartment syndrome unless there is

– Posterior tibial and peroneal arteries

TICK BITE
Jonathan A. Edlow
BASICS
DESCRIPTION
Even in high endemic areas for tick-borne diseases,
the risk of infection with a tick-borne pathogen is very
low. After a tick bite, patient concerns include:
r Tick removal
r Local effect of the bite
r Possibility of acquiring a tick-borne illness:
– Fear of contracting Lyme disease
– Desire to be tested or treated for Lyme
ETIOLOGYr Specific tick-borne infections are discussed in other
chapters.
r Tick bite can be from different species of ticks of 2
major types:
– Soft ticks (Ornithodoros):
◦Cause tick-borne relapsing fever
◦Only feed for minutes and therefore almost
never provoke a visit to the ED
– Hard ticks—especially Ixodes and Dermacentor:
◦Feed for several days to a week and therefore,
more likely to be noticed by patient and lead to
an ED visit
r Lyme disease transmission:
– Species of tick, stage of development, duration of
attachment, and geography may all play a role in
the possibility of developing Lyme disease.
– Most cases of Lyme are associated with bites from
nymphal Ixodes scapularis ticks.
– Most cases of Lyme are transmitted only after the
tick has been attached for 24–48 hr:
◦Degree of engorgement is a marker for duration
of attachment.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Tick is attached to skin.
Historyr The patient usually has made the diagnosis
themselves, although sometimes they mistake the
tick for skin tags or other skin lesions.
r Ask regarding duration of tick attachment, as this
may influence the decision to prescribe antibiotic
prophylaxis.
Physical Exam
Directly examine the skin and the tick:
r Try to identify the tick species.
r Estimate degree of engorgement.
ALERT
r Some tick-borne infections are potentially fatal.
Because there are no confirmatory diagnostic tests
that are available in real time, they must be
diagnosed based on history, physical, and
epidemiologic context.
r Because the drug of choice for some of these
infections—doxycycline—is not usually prescribed
for empiric therapy for acutely ill febrile patients,
ask about the potential for tick bites in the history
of febrile patients and consider using this drug in
the appropriate settings.
ESSENTIAL WORKUP
Accurate history and physical exam searching for
presence of tick
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Testing for Lyme disease is not indicated:
– Such antibody testing would only reflect prior
exposure to Borrelia burgdorferi
– No treatment implications whatsoever for the
current bite
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Testing of the tick itself is not recommended.
r See treatment for tick removal.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Tick-borne diseases in North America:
– Lyme disease
– Other Lyme-like diseases such as Southern
tick-associated rash illness (STARI) and Borrelia
miyamotoi infection
– Babesiosis
– Anaplasmosis (formerly ehrlichiosis)
– Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF)
– Relapsing fever
– Tularemia
– Colorado tick fever
– Q-fever
– Tick-borne encephalitis (Powassan fever)
– Tick paralysis
r Additional tick-borne diseases found in Europe:
– Tick-borne encephalitis
– Boutonneuse fever (Rickettsia conorii)
– Other spotted fever rickettsiae

T
TREATMENT
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Remove tick:
r Early removal reduces the likelihood of transmission
of tick-borne infections.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Tick removal method:
– Grasp the tick with very fine forceps, as close to
the skin as possible, and gently lift up over
30–120 sec.
– Most ticks will come out.
– Do not to squeeze the tick, which could inject
infectious materials into the patient’s skin.
– If mouthparts are left in the skin, although this
could lead to local infection or foreign body
reaction, it has no implications for transmission of
tick-borne diseases.
r Another described method:
– Inject an intradermal wheal of lidocaine with
epinephrine beneath the tick.
– Tick may crawl out of its own accord.
r Methods not to use include:
– Burning the tick with a match
– Covering it with petroleum jelly or other noxious
agents
r Lyme disease prophylaxis:
– Indicated if the tick is an engorged I. scapularis
nymph is found within 72 hr of the bite, or if the
physician decides to prophylax
– Doxycycline 200 mg for 1 dose
– For children, there is no studied single-dose
regimen:
◦Prescribe amoxicillin (25–50 mg/kg) for 10 days
in divided doses.
◦No data support prophylactic antibiotics for
other tick-borne diseases.
Pediatric Considerations
r Several studies used 10 days of amoxicillin in
children for prevention of Lyme disease.
r No patients in the treated groups developed Lyme or
seroconverted.
r Tick paralysis is a rare disease but usually occurs in
children, especially in girls with long hair; never
diagnose Guillain–Barr ´ e syndrome without doing a
thorough inspection of the entire body, especially
the scalp, for ticks.
Pregnancy Considerations
Although there are no high quality data on antibiotic
prophylaxis for Lyme disease in pregnant women,
some authors recommend having a very low threshold
for treating pregnant women with tick bites (using
amoxicillin).
MEDICATIONr Amoxicillin: 25–50 mg/kg in div. doses TID for
14–21 days
r Doxycycline: 200 mg PO for 1 dose
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Tick bite with symptoms or signs of tick paralysis or
in patients who have an established tick-borne
disease which is severe (e.g., hypotension or sepsis)
r Tick bite leading to systemic infection sufficiently
severe to require admission (e.g., RMSF ,
anaplasmosis, babesiosis [especially in a
splenectomized patient]).
Discharge Criteria
All other patients, the vast majority, are safely
discharged.
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Follow-up with primary care physicians if there are
issues regarding local bacterial infection from the
bite (cellulites) or subsequent symptoms and signs
of 1 of the tick-borne infections listed above.
r Seek medical attention in the event of a febrile
illness and to report the history of the tick bite to
that physician.
r Patients who have been bitten by ticks should be
counseled about future tick bite prevention,
including potential use of DEET to the skin and
permethrin-treated clothing.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Early tick removal reduces the likelihood of
transmission of tick-borne infections.
r Lyme disease prophylaxis is indicated if the tick is an
engorged I. scapularis nymph.
r Consider babesiosis in splenectomized patients
presenting with fever.

r Requires keratin for growth, so does not involve
mucosa
r Named for location of infection
ETIOLOGYr Dermatophytes:
– Microsporum
– Trichophyton
– Epidermophyton
– Malassezia furfur, a yeast, is the etiologic agent of
tinea versicolor (not a true tinea)
r Trauma or maceration of the skin may allow fungal
entry into skin
r Transmission may be person to person, animal to
person, or soil to person
Pediatric Considerations
r Fungi can be spread from toys and brushes
r Tinea unguium is rare in children and is associated
with:
– Down syndrome
– Immunosuppression
– Tinea pedis or capitis
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Tinea capitis:
– Children are predominately affected
– Most contagious dermatophytosis
– Alopecia, dandruff-like scaling
– Kerion:
◦Boggy, inflammatory mass that exudes pus and
causes cervical lymphadenopathy
– “Black dots” from infected hairs broken off at the
scalp
r Tinea corporis (“ringworm”):
– Arms, legs, and trunk
– Sharply marginated, annular lesion with raised
margins and central clearing
– Hair follicle involvement may produce indurated
papules and pustules
– Lesions may be single, multiple, or concentric
– Pets are often a vector
r Tinea cruris (“jock itch”):
– Erythematous, scaly, marginated patches involving
the perineum, thighs, and buttocks
– Associated with heat, humidity, and tight-fitting
undergarments
– Unlike the case in candidiasis, the scrotum and
penis are spared
r Tinea pedis (“athlete’s foot”):
– Scaling, maceration, fissuring between the toes
– Risk factors:
◦Advanced age
◦Immunocompromised status
◦Hot, humid climates
◦Infrequent changing of socks
– More common in adults than children
– Most common tinea infection in US
– “Trichophytid” reaction:
◦Vesicular eruption remote from infection
◦Involving hands, mimics dyshidrotic eczema
r Tinea unguium:
– 1 type of onychomycosis
– Yellow or brown discoloration with thickening and
debris under the nails
– Onycholysis: Loosening of the nail from bed
– May involve the plantar surface of the foot
r Tinea versicolor (not true tinea):
– Most common in warm months
– Round or oval superficial brown, yellow, or
hypopigmented macules that may coalesce
– Upper trunk, arms, and neck
– Facial involvement is common in children
Historyr Time of onset from inoculation to visible skin
changes is about 2 wk
r Main symptom is itching:
– Hair loss with tinea capitis
r Participation in contact sports or contacts with
similar skin disease
Physical Examr Tinea capitis: Alopecia, broken hairs at scalp surface
r Tinea corporis: Areas of exposed skin typically
involved with annular scaly plaques, raised edges,
may have pustules and vesicles
r Tinea cruris: Erythematous lesions on groin and
pubic region with central clearing and raised edges
r Tinea pedis: Scaling, maceration, and fissuring of
toe webs, often only 1 foot affected
r Tinea unguium: Separation of nail plate from nail
bed with thickened, discolored, broken nails
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Diagnose by clinical exam
r If diagnosis is in doubt, confirm with microscopy
before starting oral antifungals because of possible
side effects
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Lab
Fungal cultures are slow growing and should not be
routinely done
Imaging
Generally not indicated
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Wood lamp is insensitive:
– Trichophyton, the most common cause of tinea
infections, does NOT fluoresce
– Microsporum fluoresces bright green
– Malassezia (tinea versicolor) fluoresces yellow to
yellow-green
– Erythrasma (nontinea corynebacterial infection)
will fluoresce coral red
r Microscopy:
– Cleanse area with 70% ethanol
– Scrape active margin of lesion with no. 10 or no.
15 scalpel blades
– Place scrapings on a glass slide, add a drop of
10–20% potassium hydroxide solution, and cover
with a coverslip
– The presence of septate hyphae confirms
dermatophyte infection
– Budding yeasts and short hyphae (“spaghetti and
meatballs”) confirms Malassezia
Pediatric Considerations
r Methods to obtain fungal elements for culture or
microscopy:
– Brushing the hair with a toothbrush
– Rolling a moistened cotton swab
– Collecting skin cells with transparent tape
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Tinea capitis: Impetigo, pediculosis, alopecia areata,
seborrheic dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, and
psoriasis
r Tinea corporis: Impetigo, herpes simplex, Lyme
disease, verruca vulgaris, psoriasis, nummular
eczema, granuloma annulare, herald patch of
pityriasis rosea, erythema multiforme, urticaria,
seborrheic dermatitis, and secondary syphilis
r Tinea cruris: Impetigo, seborrheic dermatitis,
psoriasis, candidal infection, irritant and allergic
contact dermatitis, and erythrasma
r Tinea pedis: Scabies, erythrasma, Candida, allergic
and contact dermatitis, and psoriasis
r Tinea unguium: Psoriasis, dermatitis, lichen planus,
and congenital nail dystrophy
r Tinea versicolor: Vitiligo, secondary syphilis

T
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITAL
Maintain universal precautions.
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY
Only in immunocompromised or septic patients
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Improvement usually occurs within 1–2 wk of
treatment; hair and nail tinea require longer
treatment of 3–6 mo
r Topical antifungals do not penetrate hair/nails:
– Use in conjunction with systemic agent for tinea
capitis or unguium.
r Tinea capitis:
– Terbinafine is now considered the drug of choice
by most:
◦Pill form may be crushed in food
– Newer oral antifungals, including terbinafine,
itraconazole, and fluconazole, are preferred:
◦Retained in tissues longer
◦Allows for shorter treatment courses without a
decrease in efficacy
◦Improved compliance
– Selenium sulfide or ketoconazole shampoo
reduces transmissibility
– Kerion may respond more rapidly with addition of
prednisone (peds: 1 mg/kg PO QD for 2 wk)
ALERT
Terbinafine may be less effective than griseofulvin
against Microsporum species causing tinea capitis;
however, Trichophyton species are the predominant
causative organism in children:r Tinea corporis, cruris, and pedis:
– Topical terbinafine or imidazoles (ketoconazole,
miconazole, and clotrimazole) are 1st-line
agents:
◦Topical terbinafine has been shown to be as
effective as or more effective than the
imidazoles, with a shorter course
– Oral therapy may be necessary for cases
resistant to topical treatment or for
immunocompromised patients
– Keep the area dry (talc powders) and frequently
change socks and underclothes
r Tinea unguium:
– Requires oral therapy and longer course than
other tinea infections
– Terbinafine had a slightly higher cure rate than
imidazoles (ketoconazole, miconazole, and
clotrimazole) or griseofulvin in a meta-analysis
– Ciclopirox 8% nail lacquer approved for
treatment but has low cure rates:
◦May enhance oral therapy
r Tinea versicolor:
– Topicals are 1st-line therapy:
◦Selenium sulfide 2.5% shampoo was as
effective as topical ketoconazole
– Oral ketoconazole, itraconazole, or fluconazole
have been used with cure rates up to 97% but
are not as safe as topicals
MEDICATIONr Ciclopirox 8% nail lacquer: Apply to the affected
nails daily, max. 48 wk; remove with alcohol every
7 days (peds: Same).
r Clotrimazole: Apply 1% cream to affected area BID
for 4–6 wk (peds: Same).
r Fluconazole: Tinea unguium—150–300 mg/wk
pulse therapy for 3–6 mo for fingernails, 6–12 mo
for toenails; tinea corporis, cruris, and pedis: 150
mg PO weekly for 4–6 wk; tinea versicolor: 400 mg
PO single dose (peds: 6 mg/kg/d for 3–6 wk for
tinea capitis)
r Griseofulvin: Tinea capitis, corporis, cruris—500 mg
PO QD for 4–6 wk (peds: 10–20 mg/kg up to
500 mg PO QD until the hair regrows, usually
6–8 wk)
r Itraconazole: Tinea capitis: Adults and peds:
3–5 mg/kg PO QD for 2–4 wk; tinea unguium:
200 mg PO QD for 3 mo; tinea versicolor: 400 mg
PO QD for 3–7 days; contraindicated in CHF
r Ketoconazole: 2% topical cream QD for 4–6 wk;
tinea capitis, corporis, cruris, pedis—200 mg PO QD
for 4 wk (peds: 3.3–6.6 mg/kg PO QD for 4 wk);
tinea versicolor—400 mg PO ×1 or 200 mg QD for
7 days (contraindicated with terfenadine and
astemizole); soda increases absorption 65%
r Miconazole: Apply cream to affected area BID for
4–6 wk (peds: Same)
r Selenium sulfide: 2.5% shampoo to affected area
for 10 min for 1–2 wk (peds: Same)
r Terbinafine: 1% topical cream BID for 4–6 wk for
tinea pedis QD for tinea corporis and tinea cruris;
tinea unguium—250 mg PO QD for 6 wk for
fingernails, 12 wk for toenails (peds: <20 kg,
67.5 mg/d; 20–40 kg, 125 mg/d; >40 kg,
250 mg/d at same interval as adult); tinea pedis:
250 mg PO per day for 2 wk; tinea capitis:
250 mg/d for 4 wk (dose by weight as for tinea
unguium for 4 wk)
r Tolnaftate: Apply 1% cream/powder/solution to the
affected area BID for 4–6 wk (peds: Same)
ALERT
r The oral antifungals may rarely cause
hepatotoxicity; consider checking liver
transaminases prior to initiating therapy
Pediatric Considerations
Topical preparations are preferred when possible
Pregnancy Considerations
r Few studies addressing the use of antifungal
medications during pregnancy in humans
r Some of the imidazoles have shown adverse effects
in animals – class C (fluconazole, itraconazole,
ketoconazole)
r Clotrimazole, miconazole, and terbinafine are class
B drugs
r Weigh risk: Benefit as elective antifungal therapy
generally not recommended.
First Liner Tinea capitis: Terbinafine
r Tinea corporis, cruris, pedis: Topical terbinafine or
imidazoles (ketoconazole, miconazole, and
clotrimazole)
r Tinea versicolor: Selenium sulfide shampoo and
topical ketoconazole
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Invasive disease in immunocompromised host
r Kerion with secondary bacterial infection
Discharge Criteriar Most patients may be managed as outpatients
r Children may return to school once appropriate
treatment has been initiated
Issues for Referral
Patients started on oral antifungals should be referred
for follow-up to monitor therapy and advised
regarding symptoms of hepatitis
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Monitor for bacterial superinfection, cellulitis,
generalized invasive infection:
– Especially in immunocompromised (diabetics, HIV
patients)
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Tinea capitis is the most common pediatric
dermatophyte infection
r Itching is the main symptom in most forms of tinea,
with associated hair loss in tinea capitis
r Cellulitis frequently complicates of tinea pedis
r Relapse of tinea pedis/cruris is common
– Patients should wash or replace contaminated
socks/towels/footwear

TOLUENE POISONING
Michael E. Nelson
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Prototypical volatile hydrocarbon
r Clear, colorless liquid with sweet odor
ETIOLOGYr Abused for its euphoric effect
r Occupational exposures
r Used as organic solvent found in:
– Oil paints and stains
– Paint thinners
– Glues, inks, dyes, correction fluid
– Coolants
– Petroleum products
– Aerosolized household products
– Degreasers
r Production and use of gasoline is largest source of
exposure
Pediatric Considerations
r Prevalent in adolescent age group:
– Inexpensive “high” with readily available sources
– Many psychosocial problems
r May develop chronic neurologic dysfunction
r Mechanism:
– Rapidly absorbed by inhalation
– Readily crosses blood–brain barrier, reaching high
concentrations in brain
– May sensitize myocardium to dysrhythmogenic
effect of catecholamines
– Inhibits myocardial voltage-gated sodium channels
and inward rectifying potassium channels
– Alveolar excretion and liver metabolism
r Methods of intoxication:
– Sniffing: Simple inhalation of substance directly
from container
– Huffing: Vapors inhaled through cloth saturated
with substance
– Bagging: Vapors inhaled from bag containing
substance
r Toxic range:
– 100 ppm: Impairment of psychomotor and
perceptual performance
– 500–800 ppm: Headache, drowsiness, nausea,
weakness, and confusion, potential lethal ranges
– >800 ppm: Convulsions, ataxia, staggering gait
– 10,000–30,000 ppm: Anesthesia within 1 min
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Acute:
– Neurologic:
◦Depression
◦Euphoria
◦Ataxia
◦Dizziness
◦Seizures
– Cardiac:
◦Fatal dysrhythmias
– Pulmonary:
◦Chemical pneumonitis
◦Pulmonary edema
– Electrolytes:
◦Hypokalemia
◦Hypocalcemia
◦Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, likely from
hippuric acid metabolite
– GI:
◦Abdominal pain
◦Nausea, vomiting
◦Hematemesis
– Renal:
◦Distal renal tubular acidosis
◦Hematuria
◦Proteinuria
– Musculoskeletal:
◦Diffuse weakness
r Chronic:
– Neurologic:
◦Peripheral neuropathy (diffuse demyelination)
◦Leukoencephalopathy
◦Cerebral/cerebellar atrophy
◦Optic atrophy
◦Dementia
◦Cognitive/neurobehavioral abnormalities
– Cardiac:
◦Dysrhythmias
◦Dilated cardiomyopathy
– Renal:
◦Distal renal tubular acidosis
◦Renal failure
◦Fanconi syndrome
– Musculoskeletal:
◦Rhabdomyolysis
– Psychiatric:
◦Addiction/withdrawal
Pregnancy Considerations
r Fetal solvent syndrome reported from mothers who
chronically abused toluene while pregnant,
resembles fetal alcohol syndrome
r Infant more likely premature, low birth weight,
microcephaly, and developmental delay
Historyr Detailed history of sniffing, huffing, bagging, or
other abuse of paints/solvents
r Occupational exposures
Physical Examr Presence of agent on lips, nose, or clothes (metallic
paint has highest concentration)
r Perioral eczematous dermatitis from chronic huffing
or bagging
r Odor of agents
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Detailed physical exam
r CXR for suspected pneumonitis
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose:
– Hypokalemia
– Normal or high anion gap metabolic acidosis
– Hyperchloremia
– Impaired renal function
– Severe hypocalcemia/hypophosphatemia
r Urinalysis:
– Check for myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis)
– Hematuria and protein often present
r Creatinine kinase if suspect rhabdomyolysis
r Alcohol level—often coingestant
r Liver enzymes, prothrombin time (PT), partial
thromboplastin time (PTT), INR, as may cause
hepatotoxicity
r Urine for hippuric acid (metabolite of toluene):
– Confirms exposure but does not correlate with
systemic effects
r Serum levels only detectable for short time after
exposure
Imagingr EKG:
– For atrial and ventricular dysrhythmias
r CXR:
– Indicated if dyspnea or low oxygen saturation
– Chemical pneumonitis
r CT head:
– For altered mental status/chronic exposure
– Cerebral/cerebellar atrophy, white matter
hypodensity

TOOTHACHE
Franklin D. Friedman
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Tooth pain is caused by irritation of the root nerves
located in pulpal tissue:
– The pulp is the tooth’s center and its
neurovascular supply
r Other etiologies, both inside the mouth and referred
to the oral cavity, may cause oral pain
ETIOLOGYr Dental:
– Dental caries (hard structures demineralized by
bacteria)
– Pulpitis (inflamed pulp secondary to infection)
– Reversible pulpitis is mild inflammation of the
tooth pulp caused by caries encroaching on the
pulp
– Irreversible pulpitis is the result of an untreated
carious lesion causing severe inflammation of the
pulp and severe, persistent, poorly localized
discomfort
– Periapical abscess (necrotic pulp and subsequent
abscess)
– Postextraction pain (dry socket, infection)
– Cracked-tooth syndrome (pain, cold sensitivity,
crack difficult to visualize)
r Periodontal disease:
– Gingivitis and periodontitis (gingivitis with loss of
periodontal ligament attachment)
– Periodontal abscess (gum boil)
– Pericoronitis (gingival inflammation from
malerupted tooth)
– Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (gingival
pain, ulcers with/without pseudomembranes)
– Denture stomatitis
– Herpetic gingivostomatitis
– Aphthous ulcers (canker sores)
– Traumatic ulcers
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Tooth pain:
– May be referred to jaw, ear, face, eye, and neck
(sensory distribution of 5th cranial nerve)
– Pain often associated with chewing, changes in
temperature, and recumbency
r Malodorous breath
r Fever and chills
r Foul taste in mouth
r Associated symptoms
r Duration of symptoms
r Treatments that have already been tried
Physical Examr Dental decay
r Facial swelling or erythema
r Trismus:
– Decreased maximal interincisal opening (normal
opening, 35–50 mm)
r Inspect and palpate lips, salivary glands, floor of the
mouth, lymph nodes of the neck
r Assess voice changes
r Identify periodontal abscess
r Evaluate for deep-space infection
r Examine face for swelling, redness, tenderness, and
increased warmth
r Examine neck for adenopathy and stiffness
r Teeth should be percussed for tenderness and
mobility
r Teeth should be examined for fracture and missing
teeth
r Dental numeric system used in adults:
– Maxillary: Right to left 1–16; mandibular: Left to
right 17–32 (peds: A–J and K–T)
– Alternatively identification of teeth by their
location is also appropriate (i.e., left rearmost,
upper molar)
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Obtain appropriate medical and dental history
r Ask about drug allergies, especially antibiotics and
analgesics, and current medications
r Assess need for predental procedure antibiotic
prophylaxis:
– Rheumatic fever
– Cardiac valve replacements
– Orthopedic joint replacements
– Mitral valve prolapse or valvular heart disease
r If physical exam conflicts with patient’s history and
intraoral source of pain is not apparent consider
other sources of pain:
– Nonodontogenic etiologies of pain
– Factitious pain/drug-seeking behavior

Labr No lab tests needed except in patients with signs of
systemic toxicity and those patients with perceptible
deep-space infection
r As with any other infection with symptoms of
systemic toxicity, consider CBC, blood cultures,
markers of inflammation like ESR or CRP
Imagingr Panoramic and periapical radiograph views if
suspicion exists about dental infection or fracture
r CT or MRI to evaluate deeper infections
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
A local or regional dental nerve block may sometimes
offer both therapeutic and diagnostic benefit

r Otitis media
r Pharyngitis
r Peritonsillar abscess
r Temporomandibular joint syndrome:
– Usually presents with pain around the ear
r Trigeminal neuralgia
r Vascular headache
r Herpes zoster
r Cardiac ischemia

– Most prevalent
– Self-limited, symptoms resolve in 1 to 2 wk
– Cervical spine disease
– Fracture
– Dislocation, subluxation
– Infections
– Spondylosis
– Tumor
– Scar tissue–producing injuries

– Lymphadenitis
– Tuberculosis
– Myasthenia gravis
– Neuritis of the auriculotemporal branch of the
trigeminal nerve

– Nasopharyngeal abscess
– Retropharyngeal abscess
– Cervical adenitis
– Tonsillitis
– Meningitis
– Mastoiditis
– Sinusitis

suppress tremor)
r Ocular muscle palsy
Central

– Female > male

– Generalized tardive dystonia
– Wilson disease
– λ-Dopa therapy
– Acute (neuroleptic drugs)
– Strychnine poisoning

– Hemivertebrae
– Spina bifida

– Cervical adenitis

– Pharyngitis
– Mastoiditis

– Syrinx with spinal cord tumor

– Clavicular fractures
– Pneumomediastinum

Compensatory

r Congenital nystagmus
r Posterior fossa tumor
Central
Dystonias:

r Drug induced
r Cerebral palsy

SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Intermittent painful spasms of sternocleidomastoid

TOXIC EPIDERMAL NECROLYSIS
Andrew K. Chang rAndrew E. Chertoff
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr One of the most fulminant and potentially fatal of all
dermatologic disorders
r Skin sloughing at the dermal–epidermal interface
results in the equivalent of a 2nd-degree burn
r Can affect up to 100% of total body surface area
(BSA)
r May extend to involve:
– GI mucosa
– Respiratory mucosa
– Genitourinary/renal epithelium
r Mechanism unclear, research indicates immunologic,
cytotoxic, and delayed hypersensitivity may be
involved as well as genetic susceptibility
r Current classification system proposes 3 categories
within the spectrum of Stevens–Johnson syndrome
(SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), distinct
from erythema multiforme major and based on
percentage of total BSA:
– SJS: <10% of BSA
– SJS–TEN overlap syndrome: 10–30% of BSA
– TEN: >30% of BSA, can affect up to 100% BSA
r More common in older patients and
immunocompromised patients
r Mortality rate is about 30%, usually due to
secondary sepsis from Staphylococcus aureus and
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
r Synonym(s):
– Lyell syndrome
– Fixed drug necrolysis
– Epidermolysis necroticans combustiformis
– Epidermolysis bullosa
ETIOLOGYr Dose-independent drug reactions are the usual
cause of TEN:
– Drugs introduced within previous 1–3 wk are
most likely candidates
– Frequently implicated drugs include:
◦Sulfonamide and PCN antibiotics
◦Anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin,
phenobarbital, lamotrigine)
◦NSAIDs (oxicams, pyrazoles, sulindac),
◦Allopurinol
◦Corticosteroids
◦Antiretroviral drugs
r Other rare causes: Infections, graft-versus-host
disease, vaccinations, idiopathic cases (combined
<4%)
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
Historyr Prodrome: Influenza like, one to several days of
fever, malaise, pruritus, cutaneous tenderness,
erythema, anorexia, myalgias, arthralgias
r Mucous membranes are commonly affected 1–3
days before skin lesions appear (oropharynx, eyes,
genitalia, anus, esophageal and intestinal mucosae,
respiratory epithelium) leading to conjunctivitis,
esophagitis, pharyngitis, GI bleeding, vomiting,
diarrhea, dysuria, cough, dyspnea
Physical Examr Skin:
– Rash usually begins on face (scalp usually spared)
and trunk as erythematous macules, irregular
target-like bullae, or diffuse, ill-defined erythema;
initially may have pain at sites out of proportion to
exam
– Widespread epidermolysis, denuding of skin
surfaces, flaccid bullae, and sheet-like sloughing
of epidermis generally progress over 3–4 days but
can progress rapidly over hours
– Nikolsky sign: With lateral pressure, the skin
denudes and sloughs from separation of epidermis
from dermis
r Mucous membranes involved in >90% of cases,
initial swelling and erythema followed by blistering
and ulceration
r Ocular lesions (pseudomembranes, synechiae or
adhesions, keratitis, corneal erosions)
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Diagnosis is made clinically:
– Based on history and characteristic skin and
mucous membrane lesions
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr No confirmatory lab tests exist
r CBC: Normocytic anemia, leukocytosis,
lymphopenia/neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia
may be present
r ESR may be elevated as a result of systemic
inflammation
r Serum chemistry: Electrolyte derangements if
extensive fluid losses:
– Prerenal azotemia
– Serum bicarbonate <20 associated with 40×
higher mortality
r LFTs: Elevated transaminases, low total protein and
albumin
r UA may show hematuria (urethral–mucosal erosion,
glomerulonephritis) or casts (acute tubular necrosis)
r Wound/skin cultures and blood cultures
r Serum granulysin (an implicated cytotoxin)
Imaging
Chest radiograph should be obtained
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgeryr Severity of illness score for TEN (SCORTEN): Each
risk factor earns 1 point, a higher score means a
poorer prognosis:
– Age >40 yr
– Malignancy
– Tachycardia >120/min
– Initial percentage of epidermal detachment>10%
– BUN >27 mg/dL
– Serum glucose level >252 mg/dL
– Serum bicarbonate level <20 mEq/L
r Biopsy may be performed by consulting
dermatologist to rule out autoimmune bullous
diseases, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, and
other diagnoses:
– Results not immediately available to ED physician
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS)
r Erythema multiforme major (EMM):
– Differentiation of SJS/TEN from EMM:
– Immunopathologically distinct
– Etiology: SJS/TEN is mainly drug-induced,
mechanism uncertain; EMM both infection and
drug-induced, mechanism type IV hypersensitivity
– Lesions:
◦TEN: Widely distributed, mainly on the trunk
and face, nonspecific, target-like lesions that
often are confluent and too numerous to count,
then desquamation
◦EMM: Limited in number, symmetric and acral
distribution, typical target type (at least 3
concentric rings) with or without blisters
– Prognosis: EMM is usually benign; recurrence of
disease is common (30%)
r Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS):
– Differentiation of TEN from SSSS:
– Age: TEN: Primarily adults (but may occur in
children); SSSS: Primarily affects children
– Etiology:
◦TEN most often represents an idiosyncratic,
drug-induced, dose-independent reaction and
hence does not require treatment with
antibiotics
◦SSSS results from infection and requires
antibiotics
– Pain: TEN, painful; SSSS, painless
– Mucous membranes: Involved with TEN; spared
with SSSS
– Skin cleavage: Dermal–epidermal junction in TEN;
intraepidermally in SSSS (both can produce a
positive Nikolsky sign)
r Autoimmune bullous diseases (pemphigus vulgaris,
bullous pemphigoid)
r Scarlet fever
r Toxic shock syndrome
r Chemical or thermal scalds
r Hypersensitivity vasculitis
r Kawasaki syndrome

T
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr Transport to facility with burn center
r Care during transport should be gentle to avoid skin
trauma
r IV catheter should be avoided for short transport if
hemodynamically stable (more sterile conditions in
ED)
r Avoid using adhesive materials
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr If intubation or nasogastric tube is required, gentle
technique must be used to minimize mucosal
damage
r Meticulous sterile technique
r Peripheral IV line is preferred over central line to
decrease risk of sepsis
r Cardiac monitor, pulse oximeter, nasogastric tube,
Foley catheter
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Identify and stop any causative medication
r Aggressive fluid resuscitation and electrolyte
management as in burn care (Parkland formula):
– Urine output should target a rate of
0.5–1 mL/kg/hr.
r Warming measures and frequent core temperature
evaluation are important
r If available, cover with biologic dressings (e.g.,
Biobrane):
– Reduces pain, decreases caloric and evaporative
losses, and facilitates healing
r Antibiotic drops for eyes
r Petroleum jelly application to lips
r Prevention of peptic stress ulcers
r Topical antibiotics, including silver nitrate, are
unproven but may be applied with the exception of
silver sulfadiazine (sulfonamide derivative).
r Timely admission to burn unit/ICU
r Ophthalmology consultation is required for eye
involvement (evaluation and removal of
pseudomembranes and adhesions)
MEDICATION
There are no established treatment regimens;
however, there are several suggested guidelines:
r Pain should be controlled with IV opiates
r Antibiotics should be used when documented signs
of sepsis are present or for sudden deterioration in
the clinical setting; coverage should include
gram-positive, gram-negative (including
P. aeruginosa), and aerobic organisms
r Antihistamines can be used for pruritus
r Anticoagulation should be considered while patients
are nonambulatory for prevention of
thromboembolic events
r Systemic corticosteroids continue to be
controversial:
– Retrospective studies show no benefit and
suggest greater risk of death from infection
r IVIG should be started 48–72 hr after bulla
formation but can be helpful after 72 hr
r The following experimental therapies are under
investigation:
– Plasmapheresis
– Cyclosporine
– Cyclophosphamide
– N-acetylcysteine
– Anti-TNF-α antibodies (i.e., Infliximab) but
Thalidomide contraindicated (harm shown)
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteria
All patients with suspected TEN should be admitted to
a burn unit (if burn unit is unavailable and transfer is
not possible, then admit to ICU)
Issues for Referralr Transfer to facility with burn unit has been shown to
improve patient outcome
r Dermatology should be called to help confirm the
diagnosis
r Ophthalmology should be called to evaluate and
prevent corneal ulcerations and adhesions
r Surgery or plastic surgery should evaluate the need
for wound d ´ ebridement.
r Respiratory therapy should initiate pulmonary toilet
in the setting of pulmonary mucosal sloughing.
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Burn units and ICUs offer the best management
settings
r Remember to educate patients on medications
(including combinations, medications, and
structurally similar medications)
r Aggressive fluid hydration is essential

TOXIC SHOCK SYNDROME
Michelle J. Sergel rKristopher Wnek
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a severe, acute
life-threatening illness
r Etiologic organisms:
– Staphylococcus aureus, more common (TSS)
– Group A streptococcus or GAS, less common
(Streptococcal TSS or STSS)
r S. aureus produce structurally similar toxins:
– Toxic shock syndrome toxin (TSST-1)
– Enterotoxin B (SEB)
– Enterotoxin C (SEC)
r GAS pyrogenic exotoxins:
– Exotoxin A (SPEA)
– Exotoxin B (SPEB)
r Exotoxins act as superantigens causing
overwhelming immune response:
– Massive cytokine production
– Induce fever directly at the hypothalamus or
indirectly via interleukin-1 (IL-1) and tumor
necrosis factor (TNF) production
– Enhance delayed hypersensitivity
– Suppress neutrophil migration and
immunoglobulin
– Enhance host susceptibility to endotoxins
r Massive vasodilation occurs
– Serum protein and fluid shifts leading to
hypotension
ETIOLOGYr Initial cases described in young healthy menstruating
females due to highly absorbent tampons
– Changes made in tampon composition to
decrease incidence
r Approximately one-half of reported TSS cases are
nonmenstrual:
– Surgical wounds
– Postpartum wound infections
– Mastitis
– Septorhinoplasty
– Sinusitis
– Osteomyelitis
– Arthritis
– Burns
– Nasal packing (nasal tampons)
– Cutaneous and subcutaneous lesions
r Nonmenstrual cases predominantly due to SEB and
SEC producing S. aureus
r 30–50% of healthy adults and children carry
S. aureus in the nasal vestibule, vagina, rectum
and/or on the skin
r GAS infections often begin within 24–72 hr at the
site of minor trauma, often without a visible in skin
r Despite increased incidence of Methicillin-resistant
S. aureus (MRSA) infections, a recent study reported
MRSA only accounting for 7% of cases
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
TSS Criteria for Diagnosisr CDC case definition:
– Fever >38.9◦C (102◦F)
– Hypotension (systolic BP <90 mm Hg) or shock
– Diffuse, blanching nonpruritic macular
erythroderma rash
– Subsequent desquamation 1–2 wk after the onset
of illness (particularly involving palms and soles)
– Multisystem involvement—at least 3 of the
following should be present:
◦GI: Profuse diarrhea or vomiting at onset of
illness
◦Musculoskeletal: Severe myalgias or greater
than a 2-fold increase in creatine
phosphokinase (CPK)
◦Mucosal inflammation: Conjunctival, vaginal, or
pharyngeal hyperemia
◦Renal: Increase in BUN or creatinine >2 times
normal upper limit or sterile pyuria without
evidence of infection
◦Hepatic: Total bilirubin or transaminases >2
times normal upper limit
◦Hematologic: Thrombocytopenia
<100,000/mm3
◦CNS: Disorientation, confusion, or hallucinations
– Negative results on the following tests, if
obtained: Throat, or CSF cultures, rise in titer to
Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF),
leptospirosis, or rubeola
Streptococcal TSS (STSS) Criteria for
Diagnosisr CDC case definition:
– Isolation of GAS from a normally sterile site
– Hypotension
– Plus 2 or more of the following:
◦Renal impairment (creatinine >2)
◦Coagulopathy
◦Liver involvement (>2 times the upper limit of
normal for transaminases or bilirubin)
◦ARDS
◦Erythematous macular rash, may desquamate
◦Soft tissue necrosis
Otherr Tachycardia frequently present
r Can rapidly progress to multisystem dysfunction
(ARDS or DIC)
r STSS often presents with diffuse or localized
pain—abrupt in onset and severe
r Pain precedes physical findings
r Nearly 80% of patients with STSS have clinical signs
of soft tissue infection
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Clinical diagnosis using diagnostic criteria in the
absence of other attributable illness
r Thorough history and physical exam
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr CBC:
– Leukocytosis or leukopenia, marked bandemia
common
r Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose:
– Elevated BUN and creatinine common
r Calcium, magnesium:
– Hypocalcemia/hypomagnesemia often present
r Urinalysis:
– Normal or sterile pyuria without evidence of
infection
r CPK:
– 2-fold increase
r Hepatic function:
– Elevated total bilirubin, AST, ALT
r Prothrombin time (PT), partial thromboplastin time
(PTT), platelets:
– Thrombocytopenia <100,000 platelets/mm3
r Culture the site of injury/infection if possible
r Blood, urine, throat, and CSF cultures as indicated:
– The case definition does not require a positive
blood culture for S. aureus, but does for
Streptococcus organisms.
r Serology for RMSF , rubeola, and leptospirosis
r Hepatitis B surface antigen
Imagingr Chest x-ray – to rule out other sources of systemic
illness
r Consider x-ray or CT scan if localized pain is
concerning for abscess or necrotizing infection
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome:
– In children <5y ro fa g e
– Initial macular rash followed by the formation of
ill-defined bullae that can be rubbed off revealing
a shiny, moist epidermis (positive Nikolsky sign)
r Scarlet fever:
– Preceding streptococcal pharyngitis
– Rash begins on the upper chest, neck, and back
spreading to the remainder of the trunk, sparing
the palms and soles
– Hypotension absent
r Kawasaki disease:
– Fever, conjunctival hyperemia, and erythema of
the mucous membranes
– Not associated with renal failure, hypotension, or
thrombocytopenia
r Stevens–Johnson syndrome:
– Severe multisystem involvement
– Mucosal involvement of the mouth, conjunctivae,
vagina, anus, and urethral meatus
r Leptospirosis:
– Transmitted through contact with infected animals
– Fever, headache, severe myalgias, and conjunctival
suffusion
– Truncal rash that only desquamates in children
r RMSF:
– Rash is pink and macular, beginning on the wrists,
palms, ankles, and soles spreading to the trunk
and face
– Petechiae appear after 4 days
r Meningococcemia:
– Meningismus present
– Rash is petechial

TOXIC SHOCK SYNDROME
T
TREATMENT
PRE-HOSPITALr ABCs
r IV access
r IV fluids for hypotension
INITIAL STABILIZATIONr Again, ABCs
r Aggressive management of circulatory shock
– IV fluids
– Pressors
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURES
Hypotensionr Aggressive fluid replacement
– The 1st 24 hr may require 4–20 L of crystalloid
and/or fresh frozen plasma (colloid)
– Caution: Large amounts of IV fluids and pressors
used to treat refractory hypotension can result in
rapid onset pulmonary edema
– Pressors (dopamine/norepinephrine) if fluid
correction fails to restore normal arterial pressure
Infection Managementr Search for and treat the focus of infection
r Remove the source of infection (e.g., tampon, nasal
or wound packing)
r Early surgical/gynecologic consultation if drainage or
d´ebridement of infectious sites necessary
r Antibiotics
– Recommended to reduce recurrence, but have not
been shown to alter the course of the initial
infection
– Clindamycin and linezolid are potent suppressers
of bacterial toxin synthesis
– Clindamycin or linezolid + vancomycin for TSS
– Linezolid + vancomycin for TSS with extensive
infection
– If TSS due to known methicillin-susceptible
S. aureus then clindamycin + oxacillin or nafcillin
– Clindamycin + imipenem or meropenem or
ticarcillin–clavulanate or piperacillin–tazobactam
for STSS
r IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) treatment:
– May be efficacious in streptococcal toxic shock,
but no controlled trials have proven efficacy in
staphylococcal TSS.
– May initiate if no response to fluids, pressors, and
antibiotics in patients with pulmonary edema and
hypotension
MEDICATIONr Clindamycin: 600–900 mg (peds: 20–40 mg/kg/
24 h) IV q6–8h
r Dopamine: 2–20 μg/kg/min IV , titrate to BP
r Linezolid: 600 mg (peds: 10 mg/kg/12 h) IV q12h
r Meropenem: 1 g IV q8h
r Nafcillin: 1.5 g (peds: 100 mg/kg/24 h) IV q4h
r Norepinephrine: 0.01–3 mcg/kg/min IV , titrate to BP
r Oxacillin: 1–2 g (peds: 50–100 mg/kg/24 h) IV q4h
r Piperacillin–tazobactam: 4.5 g q6h
r Ticarcillin–clavulanate: 3.1 g q4h
r Vancomycin: 30 mg/kg QD IV div. in 2 doses (peds:
40 mg/kg QD IV div. in 4 doses)
r Staphylococcal TSS: IVIG, 400 mg/kg over several
hours
r Streptococcal TSS: IVIG 1 g/kg on day 1 then
0.5 g/kg on days 2 and 3
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Cases necessitate admission
r ICU admission for critically ill or those in shock
Discharge Criteria
None
Issues for Referral
Early surgical/gynecologic consultation if drainage or
d´ebridement is needed
FOLLOW-UP RECOMMENDATIONSr Patients who are bacteremic are treated for a
minimum of 14 days:
– Depending on the clinical course
– Continue treatment for 14 days from the last
positive culture.
r Screening for S. aureus nasal carriage in patient
with S. aureus TSS and eradication of the carrier
state with mupirocin
PEARLS AND PITFALLS
r Consider the diagnoses of staphylococcal TSS and
GAS TSS
r Ensure adequate supportive care for hypotension in
TSS
r Prompt and aggressive exploration and d ´ ebridement
of suspected deep-seated infection
r Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics including
clindamycin or linezolid is recommended

TOXOPLASMOSIS
Roger M. Barkin
BASICS
DESCRIPTIONr Toxoplasma gondii—intracellular protozoan
parasite:
– 3 forms:
◦Tachyzoite: Asexual invasive form
◦Tissue cyst: Persists in tissues of infected hosts
during chronic phase
◦Oocyst: Contains sporozoites and produced
during sexual cycle in cat intestine
r Transmission:
– Ingesting tissue cysts or oocysts:
◦Ingesting undercooked meat
◦Vegetables contaminated with oocysts
◦Contact with cat feces, through cat or soil
– Transplacental
– Blood product
– Organ transplantation
ETIOLOGYr 70% of adults seropositive
r Asymptomatic in most immunocompetent patients
r Worldwide; cats are the common host
r Incubation is 7 days with a range of 4–21 days
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS
4 types of infection
Immunocompromised Host
r CNS:
– Subacute presentation (90%)
– Encephalitis
– Headache
– Altered mental status
– Fever
– Seizures
– Cranial nerve palsies
– Spinal cord lesions
– Cerebellar signs
– Meningitis-like symptoms
– Movement disorders
– Neuropsychological symptoms:
◦Psychosis
◦Paranoia
◦Dementia
◦Anxiety
◦Agitation
r Pulmonary:
– Pneumonitis
– Prolonged febrile illness
– Nonproductive cough
– Dyspnea
Immunocompetent Host
r 90% are asymptomatic
r Lymphadenopathy, usually cervical
r Fever
r Malaise
r Mononucleosis-like syndrome with macular rash and
hepatosplenomegaly
r Headache
r Sore throat
r Night sweats
r Maculopapular rash
r Urticaria
r Usually, self-limited process; resolves in 2–12 mo
r Rarely presents with pneumonitis or encephalitis
Ocular Toxoplasmosis
r Blurred vision
r Scotoma
r Pain
r Photophobia
r Retina:
– Small clusters of yellow-white cotton-like patches
– Chorioretinitis; affects 85% of young adults with
untreated congenital infection
Congenital Toxoplasmosis
r Results from an asymptomatic acute infection during
pregnancy
r 1st trimester:
– Spontaneous abortion
– Stillbirth
– Severe disease up to 25% of the time
r 2nd or 3rd trimester:
– 50–60% chance of acquiring congenital
toxoplasmosis
– 2% fatal
r Most asymptomatic at birth
r Delayed onset. 70–90% asymptomatic at birth:
– CNS disease
– Ocular disease (blindness months to years later)
– Lymphadenopathy
– Hepatosplenomegaly
– At birth, may have maculopapular rash,
lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly,
jaundice, thrombocytopenia
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Diagnose via:
– Isolation of organism:
◦Blood
◦CSF for encephalitis
◦Bronchoalveolar lavage for pneumonitis
◦Amniotic fluid
◦Aqueous humor
– Detection of tachyzoites in tissues or body fluids
– Demonstrating characteristic lymph node
pathology
r Thorough ocular exam:
– Retinal exam
– Visual acuity
DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION
Labr LDH >600/UL associated with toxoplasmosis
r CBC:
– Atypical lymphocytes
r ABG/pulse oximetry for pulmonary symptoms
r IgG antibodies:
– High number of false-positive and false-negative
results
– Common tests:
◦Sabin–Feldman dye test
◦Indirect fluorescent antibody
◦Agglutination
◦Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay test
r Immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies:
– Absence excludes diagnosis in immunocompetent
host
– Reference labs may be helpful, such as Remington
(650-853-4828 Toxoplasma Serology Laboratory)
(www.pamf.org/serology)
– Diagnoses acute infection
– Appear in 5 days
– Disappear in weeks to months
– Neonatal testing differentiates from maternal
infection
Imagingr Chest radiograph for pulmonary symptoms:
– Pneumonitis associated with reticulonodular
pattern
r CT head with contrast:
– Multiple bilateral hypodense ring-enhancing
lesions
r MRI brain:
– High signal abnormalities on T2-weighted images
r Serial fetal ultrasonography can be useful in
exploring congenital infection of the CNS or other
signs.
Diagnostic Procedures/Surgery
Brain biopsy for encephalitis—definitive diagnosis
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Cryptococcal meningitis
r CNS lymphoma
r Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia
r Cytomegalovirus retinitis
r Mycobacterial infection

TOXOPLASMOSIS
T
TREATMENT
INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Treat seizures in standard fashion with diazepam
and phenytoin.
r Initiate oxygen if hypoxia due to pneumonitis.
ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURES
Immunocompetent
Toxoplasmic lymphadenitis:
r No antibiotics unless symptoms severe and
persistent
r Treat symptomatic patients with pyrimethamine and
folinic acid plus sulfadiazine or clindamycin for
3–4 wk
r Clindamycin may be a useful alternative to
sulfadiazine because of the side effects of the latter
and in those who are hypersensitive to sulfa
r Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine (Eon Labs
800-526-0225) is available as a combination drug.
r Corticosteroids may be useful for ocular
complications and CNS disease.
r Reassess to determine if longer therapy needed.
Immunocompromisedr Confirmed acute infection by serology/symptoms:
– Treat with pyrimethamine and folinic acid +
sulfadiazine or clindamycin for 4–6 wk after
resolution of symptoms.
– Alternative medications:
◦Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole
◦Pyrimethamine and folinic acid + dapsone
r CNS symptoms + a lesion on CT or MRI:
– Treat empirically with pyrimethamine and folinic
acid + sulfadiazine or clindamycin.
– Brain biopsy or CSF to confirm diagnosis
– Administer anticonvulsants only if confirmed prior
seizures:
◦Poorer outcome for patients on anticonvulsants
r Chronic asymptomatic infection:
– No therapy required
– Prophylaxis options for toxoplasmosis in AIDS and
immunosuppressed patients:
◦Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole; lifelong
prophylaxis should be considered in HIV
patients after consultation.
◦Pyrimethamine (75 mg/wk) and dapsone (200
mg/wk) and leucovorin 10–25 mg with each
dose pyrimethamine
Ocularr Treat with pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine for 1 mo.
r May add clindamycin
r Administer systemic steroids with macular or optic
nerve involvement.
Acute Acquired Infection in Pregnancyr Initially treat with spiramycin pending confirmatory
tests and consultation (FDA, Division of Special
Pathograns and Transplant Drug Products
301-796-1600 or CDC at 404-718-4745).
r After the infection is documented, initiate treatment
after consultation:
– Spiramycin in the 1st 17 wk
– Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine after 17 wk
r Spiramycin may reduce congenital transmission but
does not treat fetus if infection is in placenta;
maternal therapy may decrease severity of
congenital disease.
r Treat congenital infection with sulfadiazine,
pyrimethamine, and folinic acid for 12 mo.
r Prevention of exposure in seronegative pregnant
women is important when contacting cats or their
excrement.
MEDICATIONr Clindamycin:
– 600 mg (peds: 20–40 mg/kg/24 h) IV q6h
– 300 mg (peds: 8–20 mg/kg/24 h) PO q6h
– Useful if patient hypersensitive to sulfa
r Dapsone: 50 mg PO per day or 200 mg PO per week
(child >1 mo: 2 mg/kg PO per day)
r Folinic acid: 5–25 mg PO daily in conjunction with
pyrimethamine therapy
r Pyrimethamine: 100 mg BID on 1st day loading
dose, then 25–50 mg PO per day
r Spiramycin: FDA authorization required
r Sulfadiazine: 500 mg–2 g (peds: 100–200 mg/kg/
24 h div. BID) PO q6h
r Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole: 5 mg/kg of
trimethoprim component IV or PO q12h
FOLLOW-UP
DISPOSITION
Admission Criteriar Acute infection with severe systemic symptoms
r Immunocompromised patients with:
– Toxoplasmosis encephalitis
– Pneumonitis
– Sepsis
Discharge Criteriar Immunocompetent patients with:
– Mild symptoms
– Ocular
r Maternal/congenital infection with mild symptoms
Issues for Referral
Infectious disease consultant

Report of the Committee on Infectious Diseases. Elk
Grove, IL: AAP; 2012.
r Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Guidelines for prevention and treatment of
opportunistic infections in HIV infected adults and
adolescents. MMWR. 2009;58:1–207.
http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/pdf/rr/rr58e324.pdf.

Toxoplasma gondii infection in the United States.
Clin Infect Dis. 2009;49:878–884.

for prevention and treatment of opportunistic
infections in HIV-infected adults and adolescents:
Recommendations from CDC, the National Institutes

Infectious Diseases Society of America. MMWR
Recomm Rep. 2009;58:1–207.

TRANSFUSION COMPLICATIONS
Philip Shayne
BASICS
EPIDEMIOLOGYr Of 39 million hospital discharges in US, 5.8%
(2.3 million) were associated with blood
transfusions (2004).
r In 2011 there were 30 deaths in US fully
attributable to transfusion complications.
r Some type of transfusion reaction occurs in 2% of
units transfused within 24 hr of use.
r Noninfectious complications:
– Febrile nonhemolytic reaction: RBCs 1 in 500
transfusions, platelets 1 in 900
– Allergic reaction (nonanaphylactic): 1 in 3 to 1 in
300
– Anaphylaxis: 1 in 20,000 to 1 in 50,000
– Acute hemolytic reaction: 1 in 38,000 to 1 in
70,000
– Delayed hemolytic reaction: 1 in 4,000 to 1 in
11,000
– Transfusion-associated circulatory overload
(TACO): 1 in 100, but as high as 10% in
susceptible populations
– Alloimmunization: 1 in 10 to 1 in 100
– Graft-versus-host disease: 1 in 400,000; rare but
has >90% mortality.
– Transfusion-related lung injury (TRALI): 1 in 5,000
to 1 in 190,000; represents 13% of reported
transfusion-related deaths
– Iron overload: Unknown incidence, depends on
volume of blood, often occurs after >100 RBC
units
– Hypocalcemia: Unknown incidence
– Hyperkalemia: Unknown incidence
r Infectious complications:
– Bacterial contamination: RBCs 1 in 65,000 to 1 in
500,000; platelets 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 10,000:
◦Most common bacterial agents: Yersinia
enterocolitica, Pseudomonas spp, Serratia spp.
◦Leading cause of mortality among infectious
complications; 17–22% of all cases
– Hepatitis C: 1 in 1.6 million
– Hepatitis B: 1 in 100,000 to 1 in 400,000
– HTLV I and II: 1 in 500,000 to 1 in 3 million
– HIV: 1 in 1.4 million to 1 in 4.7 million
– HAV: 1 in 1,000,000
– B19 parvovirus: 1 in 40,000; post-transfusion
anemia rare with scattered case reports
– Parasites: Babesia and malaria: <1 in 1 million
– Parasites: Trypanosoma cruzi: 1 in 42,000
– Case reports of Epstein–Barr virus, Lyme disease,
brucellosis, human herpesvirus, Creutzfeldt–Jakob
disease
Acute Intravascular Hemolytic
Transfusion Reactionr Mortality and morbidity correlate with amount of
incompatible blood transfused (symptoms can occur
with exposure to as little as 5–20 mL)
r Occurs immediately from:
– ABO incompatibility
– Blood type identification error
– Incompatible transfused cells immediately
destroyed by antibodies
r Intravascular hemolysis causing activation of
coagulation system, leading to inflammation, shock,
and DIC
r Mediators (cytokines) released during inflammatory
response
r Renal failure:
– Cytokines cause local release of endothelin in
kidney, causing vasoconstriction.
– Leads to parenchymal ischemia and acute renal
failure
r Respiratory failure owing to pulmonary edema/adult
ARDS:
– Free hemoglobin (Hb) causes vasoconstriction in
pulmonary vasculature.
Other Transfusion-related
Complicationsr Hemolysis because of Rh incompatibility:
– Mild, self-limiting
– 1:200 U transfused
r Febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction:
– Most common transfusion reaction, diagnosis of
exclusion.
– Temperature increases at least 1◦C with chills
within 6 hr
– Antigen–antibody reaction to transfused blood
components (WBCs, platelets, plasma)
– Usually mild
– Occurs more often with multiparous women or
multiple transfusions
– Recurs in 15% of patients
– Acetaminophen may be used prophylactically; its
use as premedication is controversial, though not
harmful.
r Allergic transfusion reaction:
– Occurs in 1% of transfusions
– Usually seen with immunoglobulin A
(IgA)–deficient patients
– Urticaria alone is not a reason to stop transfusion.
– Antihistamine may be used as therapy or
prophylactically.
r Premedicating with acetaminophen and
diphenhydramine found to have no effect on
incidence of transfusion reaction compared with
placebo in some trials.
Delayed Reactionsr Infection:
– HIV , hepatitis B, hepatitis C
◦Blood screened for viruses
◦Blood treated to inactivate viruses
◦Blood donors with recent history of travel or
poor health are deferred from donating.
r Delayed extravascular hemolytic reaction:
– Occurs 7–10 days after transfusion
– Antigen–antibody reaction that develops after
transfusion
– Coombs test positive
– Usually asymptomatic
– Blood bank analysis detects antibody
r Electrolyte imbalance:
– Hypocalcemia: Calcium binds to citrate
– Hyper/hypokalemia: Citrate metabolized to
bicarbonate, which drives potassium
intracellularly; prolonged storage of blood may
cause hemolysis and hyperkalemia
r Graft-versus-host disease:
– Fatal in >90%
– Immunologically competent lymphocytes
transfused into immunocompetent host
– Host unable to destroy new WBCs
– Donor WBCs recognize host as foreign and attack
host’s tissues.
r Anaphylactic reaction:
– Can occur with <10 mL of exposure
– Generalized flushing, urticaria, laryngeal edema,
bronchospasm, profound hypotension, shock, or
cardiac arrest.
– Treat with subcutaneous epinephrine, supportive
hemodynamic and respiratory care.
r TRALI:
– Symptoms typically begin with 6 hr of transfusion.
– Acute onset of respiratory distress, bilateral
pulmonary edema, fever, tachycardia,
hypotension, with normal cardiac function
– 3rd most common cause of fatal transfusion
– Difficult to distinguish from ARDS and TACO;
often misdiagnosed and underreported
– Provide supportive care.
– Disease is typically self-limited within 96 hr.
– Mortality is 5–10%.
– Diuretics contraindicated
Pediatric Considerations
Blood can be transfused through 22G peripheral
catheter under pressure (but <300 mm Hg) with
minimal hemolysis.
DIAGNOSIS
SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr General:
– Fevers
– Chills
– Burning at infusion site
– Urticaria/pruritus/skin erythema
r Pulmonary:
– Dyspnea
– Bronchospasm
– Respiratory distress/failure
r Cardiovascular:
– Tachycardia
– Hypotension
– Substernal chest pain/tightness
r GI:
– Nausea
– Vomiting
– Diarrhea
r Hematologic:
– Bleeding
– Hemoglobinuria
– Oozing from surgical wounds
– Jaundice
– DIC
r Miscellaneous:
– Low back pain
– Renal failure (oliguria/anuria)
– Classic triad of fever, flank pain, and red-brown
urine of acute hemolytic reactions is rarely seen.
ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Recognize clinical findings of transfusion reaction.
r Recheck identifying information of blood and
patient compatibility.
r Recognize evidence of hypotension/shock, severe
respiratory distress, sepsis, fever, and urticaria;
intervene appropriately.
